A <term>Consul</term> was a magistrate of the commercial courts; an <term>Aedile</term> (originally a Roman office) was an official responsible for the maintenance of public buildings or guild property; and a <term>Prefect</term> served as a chief administrator or overseer.</note>

### AND TECK, <term>COUNT OF MONTBÉLIARD</term><note>original: "Comiti Montis Belgarum." Montbéliard was a sovereign county in eastern France held by the Dukes of Württemberg.</note>, LORD IN SACHSENHEIM, ETC.
## TO HIS MOST
->MERCIFUL LORD,<-
-><term>SENDS GREETINGS</term><note>original: "S. D." abbreviating "Salutem Dicit," a standard formal greeting in Latin correspondence.</note><-

<image-desc>Circular library stamp on the right side of the page featuring a tree and the text "BIBLIOTHÈQUE DE PARIS".</image-desc>

FOR some years now, *Most Illustrious Prince, Most Merciful Lord*, such diligence has been applied by scholars in most disciplines and fine arts that *individual treatises and books on specific subjects, produced by various authors and published separately at different times, have been gathered into one body and volume and presented to the students of each art and discipline. This endeavor seems to have been undertaken primarily for this purpose: so that those writings which lay scattered and widely dispersed in each science—and which could not be sought out and read without trouble and expense—might be reduced into a single volume in this manner, [containing] the entire resources of the whole art, or at least the principal collection, as if in a most beautiful certain* <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "quodam" (meaning "certain" or "a sort of") indicates the start of the next page.</note>

# EPISTLE
<meta>catchword: love</meta>

theater, to be viewed and observed with pleasure by students; from which, as if from a well-cultivated and skillfully arranged garden <note>original: "ex horto quodam bene culto & artificiosè disposito"</note>, they might pluck every kind of healing herb, as well as various flowers and fruits, not only for their own utility but also for their delight. I decided that this same goal and purpose should be set before me in the present matter of chemical affairs. 

And since very many excellent men, gifted with the highest genius and adorned with singular wisdom, have written most excellently and almost divinely in various places concerning this art, both in our own time and in previous ages: I have taken care that their works—as many as could be tracked down with great expense and labor, sought out from every direction—be organized and arranged into a single body, a sort of <term>THEATER</term> <note>original: "THEATRUM." In the Renaissance, a "theater" was a common title for a book that aimed to provide a comprehensive, visual, or systematic overview of a specific field of knowledge.</note>. 

I am led by the best of hopes that through this work of mine, I might perform a service that is neither unpleasant nor unwelcome to students of <term>chemical philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophiæ Chemicæ." At this time, "chemical philosophy" referred to the theoretical and practical study of alchemy, including the transformation of metals and the preparation of medicines.</note>. By this means, having compared various authors with one another, they might more easily gather insights from one to the next, and thus more conveniently reach the goal of their pursuit. 

To your <term>Highness</term> <note>original: "Celsitudini." A formal title for a high-ranking noble.</note>, however, most illustrious Prince and most merciful Lord, I have humbly wished to inscribe and dedicate this *CHEMICAL THEATER*: since it does not escape me with what clearly merciful and laudable favor and

# DEDICATION.

*...love with which Your Highness <note>original: "V. Cels." abbreviated for "Vestra Celsitudo," meaning Your Highness.</note> embraces and fosters the chemical arts: then because it is not only customary in other sciences, but indeed in this, our Chemical art, it is absolutely necessary to seek patrons and supporters for published works; by whose protection and authority those works may safely go forth and be present in the public light. For which reason, with all the humility of mind I can muster, I offer and dedicate this very* THEATER *of Chemistry to Your Highness: and at the same time I humbly ask that Your Highness might most graciously deign to receive it with a serene and kind countenance, and to defend and protect it with your most illustrious protection. I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, with all my heart, that He may preserve and protect Your Highness, along with your most illustrious spouse and the entire renowned House of Württemberg, flourishing for a long time, safe and <unclear>surviving</unclear> <note>The text is slightly obscured by a stain here; "superstitem" suggests a wish for long life or outliving any current dangers.</note>. At <term>Strasbourg</term> <note>original: "Argentinae," the Latin name for Strasbourg, where the publisher Zetzner was based.</note>. On the Ides of September <note>September 13th.</note> in the year 1602.*

### To Your Highness.

->Most Devoted<-

### LAZARUS ZETZNER.

# ON THE TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY OF THE CHEMICAL ART.

## CHAPTER ONE.

->The Prophet ESDRAS, Book 4, chapter 8.<- <note>This refers to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra in some traditions).</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring ornate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

I WILL speak a parable before you, *Esdras*: *Just as you might ask the earth, and it will tell you: that it yields much earth from which pottery is made, but only a little dust from which gold comes.*

->SOLOMON, Ecclesiasticus chapter 38.<-

<margin>See Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note> p. 136.</margin>
*The Most High created medicine from the earth, and a wise man will not despise it.*

->DAVID, Psalm 12.<-

*The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver tested by fire, proven in the earth, purified seven times.*

->Others translate it thus:<-

*The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver tested by fire, proven three times, purified seven times.*

->Or:<-

*The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver tested by fire in an earthen vessel, purified seven times.*

->Or:<-

*The words of God are pure words, silver burnt to earth or powder in an <term>aludel</term> <note>A pear-shaped earthenware vessel used by alchemists for sublimation.</note>, cast back seven times.*

For this word <term>Aludel</term> is Arabic, which is "sublimatorium" to the Latins <note>original: "sublimatorium Latinis est"</note>; a term used frequently by that Arab, <term>Geber Abenhaen</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy.</note> (the foremost philosopher among the Arabic chemists), as well as by <term>Avicenna</term>, <term>Rhazes</term>, <term>Hali</term>, <term>Morienus</term>, and many other Latin authors. An Aludel, or "Sublimatorium," is the vessel in which <term>chemical sublimation</term> occurs. This is the raising of a dry substance by fire so that it adheres to its vessel. A "dry substance," I say—meaning the lower elements or matter. "By fire"—specifically one that is gentle, steady, moist, containing, drying, <term>digesting</term> <note>In alchemy, "digesting" refers to a process of slow, even heating similar to natural incubation.</note>, and close to the operations of nature. "Raising"—that is, conversion, or refinement, and perfection. "Adherence to its vessel"—meaning a vessel of the same nature, salty, and possessing the power to turn things into stone.

<margin>Geber, book 2, chapter 43.</margin>
<margin>Hermes Trismegistus, *Sift the matters*</margin>

# Of Truth and Antiquity

<margin>refined seven times in his sieve.
John Dastin, Book 3.
Moisten with the spirit seven times.</margin>...purifying. For by that <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collecting the purified solid that reforms upon cooling.</note>, repeated seven times or even more, silver (which is by its nature more impure and imperfect than gold) can be rendered much more perfect than any natural or common gold. Do not think that this perfection and purity comes to it by melting alone. For even if you examine it with the greatest diligence in the fire again and again, you will not render it more perfect or purer than natural gold unless you rightly employ that Chemical sublimation, repeated seven times or more. For this reason, that comparison is most true by which the prophet David compared the true and pure words of God to silver purified and prepared by the Chemical art, rather than to natural or common gold. For although that gold is considered the most pure and perfect among all metals, it nonetheless contains some dross within itself, however small and foreign. Otherwise, the prophet would have compared the pure words of God to gold rather than silver. <note>The author is referring to Psalm 12:6: "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times." # OF THE CHEMICAL ART.
<margin>A 5</margin>

### The Same Author <note>original: "Idem" — referring to the previous page's focus on authorities like Avicenna or similar medieval masters.</note>

<margin>Avicenna. Quicksilver and sulfur are the matter of all things.</margin>
*Metals can be transmuted from one into another, since they are natural things, and the matter of which they are made is the same.* <note>The "sulfur-mercury theory" was the standard medieval belief that all metals were composed of these two principles in varying degrees of purity.</note>

### The Same in another place.

*Dearest son, do not be repelled by the name of the "stone." For no one has ever been able, nor will they be able in the future, to dye gold except with gold. O dearest children of the divine art, turn away from every error of blindness, and notice that the truth consists only in three things, from which the true <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Elixir" or Philosopher's Stone was the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> of the philosophers is composed: namely, from the lunar stone, in which the sulfur is white; from the solar stone, in which the sulfur is red; and the stone of Mercury, which embraces both, namely the white and the red.* <note>The "lunar stone" refers to Silver, and the "solar stone" to Gold.</note>

### William of Paris <note>Guilielmus Parisiensis, likely referring to the 13th-century theologian William of Auvergne.</note>

*The intention of the philosophers is to make a spirit out of a body, namely pure philosophical quicksilver. However, since it is necessary to compose the stone from two substances, the <term>volatile</term> and the <term>fixed</term>, it is necessary first to produce their quicksilver from the union of these two, before the Elixir is made complete.*

### John Duns Scotus, the "Subtle Doctor."

*Some say that it is good to change the matter from one vessel into another from time to time, but this is not true. Rather, it is sufficient for the stone to be placed once in its vessel well-sealed, and not to leave it from there until the entire <term>magistery</term> <note>The "magistery" refers to the entire chemical process or "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is completed. Anything more than this comes from evil; just as in the generation of a human being, or of any plant, the seed is never placed in the womb more than once.*

### VINCENT the Monk, in Book 5 of *Natural History*. <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a famous medieval encyclopedist.</note>

*Noah held this Medicine of the Philosophers, and at five hundred years of age, he fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.* <note>Alchemists often claimed that the long lives of Biblical patriarchs were due to their possession of the Elixir of Life.</note>

Furthermore, Arnald of Villanova, in a certain treatise speaking of <term>putrefaction</term> <note>A stage in the alchemical process where the matter turns black and "dies" before being reborn.</note> and the change of the stone's matter into various colors, cites that passage of the Prophet Joel, where he says: *The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood.* And the Englishman John Dastin says in Book 3: *The sun was darkened at its rising, and the moon declined from its light.*

### RAYMOND Lull, in the book *The Codicil*, chapter 53.

*However, we perform our secret dissolution—understood moderately within nine days—by grace freely given through the immortal man. For there is no passage from the first state to the third except through that which is the middle between this one and that. For this is a secret to be revealed to no mortal man.*

### CHRYSOGONUS Polydorus, or Osiander, as some would have it.

*The Jews [hold] that the Prince of Tyre, in the book of Ezekiel, practiced Alchemy.*

# ON TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY.
<meta>catchword: -tion</meta>

*...they say he was an adept, and therefore the prophet reproached him because, through his confidence in that art, he seemed to himself to be a God. For the Prophet (as they say) relates that the gold and silver which he held in his treasures had not been dug from the earth, nor demanded from subjects, nor snatched from enemies, but he had made it for himself, relying specifically on this art: and therefore he was wiser than Daniel, and had searched through all the secrets of nature, when he said to them in the person of God: I multiplied silver for them, and they themselves made gold for their idol.* <note>original: "Multiplicavi eis argentum & ipſi fecerunt idolo ſuo aurum." This is a reference to Hosea 2:8, interpreted here to mean that humans have the physical capacity to "make" silver and gold, even if they use it for the wrong purposes.</note>

For Oldradus and Johannes Andreas prove that this chemical art, commonly called Alchemy, is true and not prohibited, and that it is not improper for one metal to be transmuted into another. For (as they say) we see that sometimes a living thing is produced from a dead thing, as we see from worms, from which silk is produced, and many others: and glass is produced from grass. How much more so from metals, in which there is a greater agreement and similarity. For (as they teach, and as is held in the book *On the Properties of Things* in the chapter on Alchemy) all metals proceed from the same principle, namely from <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term>. <note>The "sulfur-mercury theory" was the standard medieval scientific explanation for the composition of all metals.</note> Therefore, since art imitates nature (<term>Digest</term> on adoption, Law: *If adoption*), these Alchemists do not seem to sin. <note>original: "ff. de adopt. L. Si adoptio." This is a citation of Roman Law. The "ff." stands for the Pandects or Digest of Justinian. The legal argument is that if nature can change things, and art imitates nature, then the artist has a legal right to perform the same transformation.</note> For since they are, as it were, from the same principle, the transition into similar things is easier for those sharing a common essence. For, as Saint Augustine says in his book *The City of God*, there are certain hidden <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "seminariæ rationes." This is the view of Oldradus and Johannes Andreas. Gratian cites this passage of Augustine in Cause 26, part 2, question 5, chapter *No wonder*. Furthermore, Augustine says in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*: "Indeed, of all things which are born corporally and visibly, certain hidden seeds lie hidden in these corporeal elements of this world." And Cardinal Gasparo Contarini, in Book 3 of *On the Elements*, says: "Nevertheless, in the generation of metals—"

### OF THE CHEMICAL ART.

[produc]tion, no one doubts that all things are made from quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*, literally "living silver."</note> and sulfur. For we see a worm naturally, and through natural craftsmanship, be changed into a fly, which differs from it in species; and a strangled calf into bees, grain into weeds, and a strangled dog into worms, through the putrefaction of boiling. <note>The author refers to "spontaneous generation," a widely held pre-modern belief that living creatures like bees or maggots could arise directly from decaying organic matter.</note> But we do not do this; nature does it, which we merely serve. Similarly, we do not change metals, but nature does: for it we prepare the material according to craftsmanship; since nature acts by itself, not us—we are truly its administrators. These are the words of Geber (also called Abenhaen or Ebenhaen). <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy; however, many Latin texts under this name were written by 13th-century European scholars using his authority.</note> St. Augustine also says in *On the Trinity*, book 3: "Just as we do not call parents the creators of crops, even though that creative power of God operates within them through the external movements applied by the parents." This is his point. For art imitates nature, and in certain things corrects and overcomes it, just as a weak nature is helped by the industry of physicians. This from Dastinus, book 1. <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386) was a prominent English alchemist who famously wrote letters to Pope John XXII defending the scientific validity of alchemy.</note> For art often assists nature whenever it is hindered. Geber, book 1, chapter 9 says: "Craftsmanship completes the defect of nature in many things." There are also those who assert that the hair of women can be turned into serpents. We also see stones and frogs fall from the sky, and stones created in the kidneys and bladders of men.

Avicenna, in his book *On the Soul*, first discourse, chapter 1, says: "A man can make a living thing out of barley. For if you take horse manure, which is nothing else than barley, and place it in a suitable warm spot, from it proceed creatures which they call Abumes <note>Likely a reference to a type of beetle or insect thought to be generated from dung.</note>: just as flies arise from the rot of the air, and lice from the rot of human humors." This from Avicenna.

For thus if by some hidden, concealed, and wonderful arrangement of nature, and a cleverness unknown to men, the <term>seminal virtues</term> <note>seminal virtues (*virtutes seminariæ*): A philosophical concept describing the "blueprints" or hidden powers within matter that direct its growth into a specific form.</note> burst forth into species appropriate to their modes and ends determined by nature, as St. Augustine says.

Because, as Aristotle says: "Anything does not come from anything, but a determined thing comes from a determined thing." <note>This principle of "like produces like" was used by alchemists to argue that they must start with the "seed" of gold to produce gold.</note>

And nothing suits a thing (says John Dastinus in book 1) except what is closest to it by its own nature.

The same Dastinus says: "Principles are created by nature, and through art, composites are made from them: so also our Stone is perfected by art, because it is naturally suited by nature to be perfected; yet nature does not have the motion to become a complete Elixir unless it is perfected by operation and art."

Furthermore, as Theophrastus writes in his *History of Plants*, book 2, chapter 6: "Natural mutations are seen in the genus of animals, either by reason of time, or for the change of locations, or by generation. For from a moth comes a grub, then from that a butterfly is born. And it is noted that this happens in many others." Likewise, water-mint...

# ON TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY

[...pennyroyal] as the same author says, unless it is restrained by cultivation, it seems to be changed into mint. These are his words. <note>The text likely refers to the common medieval belief, following Pliny, that *pulegium* (pennyroyal) could transform into *mentha* (mint).</note>

*Albertus in book 3 of Minerals, chapter 2: "The primary matter of metals is a subtle, oily moisture, which is incorporated into a subtle earthy substance that has been strongly mixed together, such that the greatest part of each is not only with the greatest part of the other, but also within the greatest part of the other."* <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval thinkers on natural science and minerals.</note>

Aristotle in book 3 of *Meteorology*, chapter 15, says that metals are made from a watery breath and a dry exhalation, which are quicksilver <note>original: *ar. vi.*, abbreviation for *argentum vivum*</note> and sulfur. All metals, however, to return to the matter at hand, are made from one and the same proximate matter—namely from quicksilver and sulfur—as everyone asserts. They differ, however, in form—that is, in purity and "cooking" <note>original: *coctione*, referring to the internal heat or "ripening" process of nature</note> or digestion. The stripping away of accidental properties, or the destruction of their essential forms and the introduction of others, is possible; and among those things that share a common nature <note>original: *habentibus symbolum*, a term used in Aristotelian physics for elements that share common qualities</note>, the transition from one to another is easy. Therefore, the transformation of metals exists. For just as there is a circular generation of elements, so it is with metals, from one into the other; this is what Hermes Trismegistus and other philosophers assert. *And the elements in turn are generated and corrupted among themselves; they therefore possess the same common primary matter. They differ, however, in form and species. Albertus on Minerals, book 3, chapter 6: "Among those things sharing a common nature in their matter, virtues, and natural powers, mutual transmutation is easy."* The same author, book 3, chapter 6.

Nor should it disturb you what Titelmannus <note>Frans Titelmans (1502–1537), a scholar whose "Compendium" was a standard textbook of natural philosophy</note> writes in his *Compendium of Natural Philosophy*, book 1, chapter 24, concerning celestial matter: that on account of the perfection and power of the most potent form in giving shape <note>original: *in informando*</note>, which was given to it from the beginning, it cannot pass from form to form, because a natural agent is lacking that could either impress another form upon it or take away its own. For he does not conclude from this that the same thing happens to lower natural things. For he says in chapter 25 that lower things do not have a similar situation, since "privation" <note>the lack of a certain form or quality that a substance is naturally capable of receiving</note> is not a true cause effective in itself of the transmutation from form to form, but only an occasion and a "cause without which not" <note>original: *causa sine qua non*—an indispensable condition</note>. For unless there were a privation of absent forms within matter, and unless it were suited to possess those which it does not have, it would never be transmuted from form to form. He says, moreover, that the true and efficient cause of this transmutation is a natural agent which, by dominating, impresses onto the matter impressions contrary to the existing form and suitable for the form it wishes to introduce; thus, by its active virtue, it causes the matter to pass from one form into another.

Let them, I ask, come to their senses—those who dare to overturn nature herself, the most skillful parent of all things, and all philosophy; and who [dare to overturn] this natural Chemistry, the better, admirable, and hidden part of philosophy, so exceptionally necessary for the human race, [denying it?] of its mother...

### OF THE CHEMICAL ART.

...emulatress of nature, which concerns itself with the natures of things, their causes, and the hidden virtues—especially of the mineral kingdom—they mock in their ignorance. This art is what the great Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the father of alchemy.</note> calls "true without falsehood, certain, and most true." It is an art approved by Plato, Eustathius, Suidas, Solinus, Strabo, Pliny, and many others; and which Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a celebrated 8th-century polymath and alchemist.</note> asserts is a "gift of God, the most high, blessed, sublime, and glorious." 

By its wonderful craftsmanship is composed that **Royal Powder**, or fusible salt; the oil, or non-burning sulfur of nature; the **Earth of the Philosophers**; the **Elixir**; **potable gold** <note>Drinkable gold, believed to be a universal life-extender.</note> (also called the gold of the philosophers); the **Water of Life**; and the **Tincture**. This is the **Precious Stone**—whether called Lydian, Indian, or Philosophical—the <term>Medicine</term> <note>In alchemical terms, the "Medicine" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, which "cures" base metals into gold and restores human health.</note> which performs marvelous actions across the three kingdoms of nature: animal, vegetable, and mineral, as will be explained to you more fully in the third chapter. For this reason, the ancient philosophers said that this Stone was itself animal, vegetable, and mineral. 

<margin>
*Albertus Magnus, "On Minerals," Book 3, Chapter 9. Regarding those who whiten through white things and yellow through yellow things, etc. Against the sophists and impostors.*
</margin>

Hence Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says in the *Rosary*: *“Alchemy is one hidden part of natural philosophy, necessary above all other parts. From it, a single art is constituted, to which there is no equal. For by it, imperfect precious stones are made perfect; the sick human body is restored to health; and imperfect metals are transmuted into gold and silver by a certain single, universal medicinal body, into which all the specific details of medicine are reduced and infused.”*

<margin>
*Geber, Book 1, Chapter 7.*
</margin>

May God, the best and greatest, grant that you do not fall perniciously into the hands and snares of those **impostors**. These men waste their efforts miserably on useless or perhaps forbidden things: sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophisticated" means "adulterated" or "fake."</note> white or red tinctures, "augmentations," "multiplications," and the "extractions of gold" (as they falsely call them). They knowingly and maliciously deceive the common people everywhere, promising them much—even mountains of gold. Through various and vain sophisticated labors, they consume their own wealth and the wealth of others. They spend their lives in false, dangerous, harmful, and deceptive practical studies and a thousand frauds. Some of these men chase after the bottle, others after fortunes, others luxury, others honors, and others the most shameful lusts. 

Because of them, that true, natural, rare, hidden, and divine Chemical Art—indeed, a science so supernatural—sometimes has a bad reputation among many, so much so that it is regarded and believed to be a mere illusion and total deception. You should hold these scoundrels, sycophants, impostors, and sophists as nothing; despise them, and keep them far from your mind. They are truly unworthy of the title "Chemical Philosopher." 

Instead, you should embrace and study sincere and proven chemical books and natural philosophy itself for a long time, deeply and with care—not for the sake of profit or glory. Look up to that sublime Chemistry, sent down from heaven by the **Father of Lights**; consecrate yourself to it, favor it, and pray for success. For that art is kept within the Divine power; it is bestowed upon or withheld from whomsoever He wills, He who is glorious, sublime, and filled with all justice and goodness. To Him, thanks must always be given and praises sung for His ineffable goodness...

For those called the Hesperides were the daughters of Hesperus, the brother of Atlas; they possessed gardens precious for their gold-bearing groves, where a watchful dragon acted as a tireless guardian, vigilantly observing the golden apples. Hercules killed this dragon and brought the golden fruit back to Eurystheus. This is according to Hesiod in the *Theogony*, Ovid in the 10th book of *Metamorphoses*, and Theocritus in *The Comast*. *Alchemy <note>original: "Χημεία"; translated here as the manufacture of gold.</note> of gold, etc. That is, Alchemy is the making of gold and silver. At that time, he also sought out and burned the books written by the ancients concerning the Alchemy of gold and silver, so that wealth from that art would no longer be available to the Egyptians, and they would not, relying on an abundance of money, rebel against the Romans in the future.* So says the author. ...cut them off and threw them into the sea; from the mixture of that blood with the foam of the sea, Venus was procreated. Consider also the story of the same god <note>Saturn, often associated by alchemists with lead or the "prime matter" that must be transformed.</note>, who is said to have devoured his sons as soon as they were born. Or of Aesculapius, who revived those who were already almost dead. Or of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, who transformed himself into a shower of gold. Think of the battle between Hercules and Antaeus; of the eyes of Argus being turned into the tail of a peacock; of Orpheus; of Pyrrha and Deucalion; or of the Androgynes, also known as Hermaphrodites <note>In alchemy, the Hermaphrodite symbolizes the union of opposites, like sulfur and mercury.</note>. 

Recall the Gorgon, who turned all who looked upon her into stone; and Midas, who, with the consent of Bacchus, turned whatever he touched into gold. Consider Jove turned into an eagle, flying up to heaven with Ganymede; Daedalus and Icarus; and the thick cloud with which Jupiter surrounded Io. Reflect on the Phoenix, which is always reborn; the Salamander <note>A legendary lizard believed to live in fire, symbolizing the "fixed" substance that resists heat.</note>; and the dragon that kills men with its heavy, poisonous breath. 

Then there is Demogorgon, of whom Boccaccio writes <note>Giovanni Boccaccio, the Italian author, wrote "Genealogia Deorum Gentilium," a massive reference work on mythology.</note> as the great-grandfather of all the pagan gods. He is described as being surrounded on every side by darkness, clouds, and gloom, dwelling in the very bowels of the earth. When he is born, he is clothed in a green cloak and sprinkled with moisture; he is not born of any parent, but is eternal and the parent of all things. 

Consider Vulcan, who, because he was ugly and deformed when newly born, was cast down onto the island of Lemnos. Or the medicine of Helen, which induced the forgetting of grief, anger, and evils in all who drank it. Eustathius, Suidas, and other most serious authors interpret these and similar fictions and enigmas of the ancient poets and philosophers as being properly referred to the Chemical art.

Even within various structures, such as the Labyrinth; in paintings and small images, such as the <margin>*The Sileni of Alcibiades.* <note>A reference to Plato's "Symposium," where Socrates is compared to Silenus statues—ugly on the outside but containing golden images of gods within. It serves as a metaphor for hidden wisdom.</note></margin> Sileni; and in characters or monsters like the Sphinx—with a maiden's face, bird's wings, and lion's feet—or the Chimera, which had the image and nature of a lion in its front part, a dragon in its middle, and a goat in its rear. These, along with various depicted and transmuted animals, were carved into the doors of temples and the walls of palaces. 

Of this same kind of fiction is the enigma of Nicolas Flamel <note>A 14th-century French scrivener who became legendary as an alchemist who supposedly discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, in which are depicted two <margin>In the Year of Our Lord 1393.</margin> serpents or dragons—one winged, the other not—and a winged lion, and so forth. These can still be seen today in the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ Parisiorum"</note>. Such things were understood only by the most learned men, who possessed knowledge of this chemical secret—this treasure so rare, so hidden, and so heavenly. 

In this way, Pythagoras and Plato obscured their philosophy with their use of numbers. Pythagoras asserted that God, our souls, and everything that exists in the world consist of numbers, and that the entire universe is born from their concord and harmony. Even Aristotle testifies in a certain letter to Alexander the Great that some of the books he published were written as if they had *not* been published <note>Referring to the idea that Aristotle's works had a hidden "esoteric" meaning for his students and a "exoteric" meaning for the public.</note>. You see, therefore, that the Chemical art is not a new art, nor an uncertain one, as the ignorant common people think.

## THE MATTER AND COMPOSITION OF THE MEDICINE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS AND

### Chapter II.

<margin>A very small part of the dregs is sufficient.</margin>
<margin>Secret fire.</margin>
<margin>Baths of the philosophers.</margin>
<margin>Mary’s Bath.</margin>
For that [medicine] is made from the pure substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>, acting as the female seed, or the matter and mercury; and from a moderate and small amount of the pure sulfur of gold or silver, which is connatural and homogeneous, acting as the male, or the form and sulfur. This is achieved by an artificial fire—gentle, even, moist, airy, steamy, and exhalable—which is close to nature. This fire subtly and continually moves, directs, and excites the process without overcoming the formative mineral power; rather, it assists the proportional and natural fire. These components are joined in an excellent mixture, once the heterogeneous dregs have first been removed gently and with great skill. They are brought by frequent sublimation <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid to purify it.</note>, or by grinding and roasting, to a state of solution and a fusible, mixable fixation <note>A "fixed" substance in alchemy is one that can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating.</note> that is invincible by fire and capable of perfecting—or transmuting—with every degree of excellence. Meanwhile, as I write more to you at my leisure concerning Chemical Harmony, the natural principles of metallic things and the Art, and the works of both nature and art, let these words suffice, and may you receive them well.

## DIVINE POWER, ACTION, AND OPERATION OF THE POWDER
->or Medicine of the Philosophers and Potable Gold<-

### Chapter III.

Whether you call it the Chemical Powder, the Philosopher's Stone, the fusible salt, the sulfur, the Elixir, the Medicine, or Potable Gold, it certainly possesses a wonderful power over the three kinds of things: animal, vegetable, and mineral. For this reason, the ancient philosophers said it was itself animal, vegetable, and mineral. <margin>Why it is called animal, vegetable, and mineral.</margin> Some call it "animal" because it possesses a soul and a spirit, or because water is its soul and life, which vivifies and nourishes the body or earth. They call it "vegetable" because it flourishes, is nourished, and grows by addition, increasing or multiplying either in its power or its quantity. <margin>A double multiplication.</margin> It is called "mineral" because it is extracted from minerals.

Regarding the animal kingdom: it restores every animal—whether man or beast—that is sick, either internally or externally, to health in a very short time. This is because it [restores] the primary qualities, or the elements themselves, which...

## OF THE CHEMICAL ART.
<page-num>23</page-num>
B 4
<meta>catchword: ...to be able,</meta>

...which deviate from natural symmetry, and it brings back to their own nature the weakened actions and the offending humors <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) had to be balanced for health.</note>—the causes of imbalances and corruption—whether occurring internally from within or falling upon one from without. For it is almost incorruptible, tempered through the elements themselves when purified, and separated from the dregs of the four elements, which are the primary cause of corruption. Therefore, it creates a tempered and healthy body, like the spirit of life, by whose power and help nature digests the indigestible and leads out everything undigested; it cuts away all superfluous and offending qualities, vivifies the spirit, hardens the soft, softens the hard, thins the thick, thickens the thin, fattens the lean, thins the fat, cools the hot, heats the cold, dries the moist, moistens the dry, and strengthens and confirms the natural heat or the substantive moisture.

And it is (as many write) like a universal medicinal body, to which all the particular properties and powers of medicines are reduced and infused. This is because it is like a certain "fifth nature" <note>Also known as the Quintessence, the "Fifth Essence" was believed to be a celestial substance superior to the four earthly elements.</note>, introduced by the ancient philosophers, or a most thin and pure essence and soul, resisting putrefaction or corruption for a very long time, and being only with great difficulty and labor corruptible. It consists in equality and homogeneity, freed from all mortal concretion—a celestial and simple substance of the elements, as if tempered from the elements themselves, purified and separated from the coarser matter and the heterogeneous superfluity of the four elements by that Chemical sublimation <note>Sublimation in alchemy is the process of heating a substance into a vapor and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it.</note>. Hence Eusebius in his book *Against the Philosophers*, chapter 44: "Socrates and Plato consider ideas separated from matter to be substances." Aristotle, on the contrary, in Book 1 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 2. For the Elixir or that powder of the philosophers, or potable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile." A liquid form of gold believed to have miraculous healing powers.</note>, is made from the homogeneous, purest, and most subtle substance of metal, which is mixable with any humor.

<margin>The Elixir is made into a substance from moderate and purest quicksilver <note>original: "ar. vi." for "argentum vivum," the metal mercury.</note>.</margin>
But what could you find under heaven more homogeneous and more similar, of a thinner substance, of a more tempered nature, and less subject to corruption or putrefaction, than the pure substance of metals, or quicksilver <note>original: "ar. vi."</note> itself? For the elements, as Aristotle pleases, are purest in their own center. Therefore, once the heterogeneous parts—which have come upon it by accident—are removed, there will remain a most pure and homogeneous thing, like its seed, spirit, and soul. There is no reason, then, for you to wonder or, being ignorant, dare to deny that hidden power of the Elixir, known or believed by so few—unless you also wish to wonder at or deny Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> and what is evident from experience, when he introduces the so-called "septic" faculties, possessing a caustic heat, yet burning without pain because of the thinness of the substance.

<margin>In the book *On Simple [Medicines]* 9, chapter on Lye <note>original: "Conia."</note>. Because of their greatest subtlety, they act most greatly and most quickly, and harm the least.</margin>
Do you still wonder, and do you cease to deny, when you see quicksilver—as the substance of metal—almost passable through fire, air, water, and earth without injury? And on account of the homogeneity of its substance, united and mixed through its smallest parts, it resists corruption for a very long time, and can almost never be overthrown by any injuries,

It argues that this substance is derived from purified mercury (quicksilver) and possesses unique, subtle properties recognized by ancient authorities like Aristotle, Plato, and Galen.</summary>

### ON TRUTH AND ANTIQUITY
<page-num>24</page-num>
<meta>catchword: There</meta>

...to be able [to do this], which certainly happens to no other thing of its kind, whether animal or vegetable? Arnald <note>original: "Arnaldus"; likely Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> in his book *On the Secrets of Nature*, chapter 1, says: *Mercury alone is incombustible and airy, which is a sign of perfection.* Furthermore, what would you say of gold? No matter how much it is heated, it does not diminish. Indeed, even according to Aristotle's testimony at the end of the third book of *Meteorology*, all metallic things are usually consumed by fire because they contain a "dry exhalation." But gold, alone among them all, is never consumed. As Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Roman "Natural History."</note> testifies, the more often it is burned, the more perfect it becomes, because of the equal joining and purity of the <term>mercury and sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, "mercury" and "sulfur" were not just the elements we know today, but philosophical principles representing stability and reactivity.</note> in its creation. Scotus <note>Likely Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232), a mathematician and scholar known for his works on alchemy.</note> also says in his *Alchemy*: *Just as all metals are called "imperfect" if you wish to compare them to gold, and all living things are imperfect if you compare them to the nature of angels and incorporeal substances separated from matter: so gold itself is more imperfect and impure than our Medicine—which is our Stone—even though it is of the nature of gold. This is because the Medicine is more refined and purified from its dregs, and abounds in a uniform subtlety. For simpler things are more perfect than complex ones, and they act more strongly and piercingly due to their subtlety, just as a sharp point stings more than a blunt one.* These are his words. To Aristotle, the elements are at their purest when in their own center. I do not doubt, therefore, that you will admit that gold itself—when reduced to its ultimate purity and extreme refinement and simplicity—is much more perfect and incorruptible than natural gold. When converted into a <term>potable substance</term> <note>Also called "Aurum Potabile" or drinkable gold, believed to be a sovereign remedy that could grant long life.</note>, it preserves the bodies of living creatures from decay and imbalance for a very long time. Hence Scotus says: *Fire takes away the existence of all matter, except for the Sun—that is, gold—so that other metallic bodies cannot be preserved in their being, except in the solar state.* Yet I would not want to assert that this medicine is entirely immortal, because it is made from a natural thing; but because it is composed of matter more incorruptible than all others, and has been reduced to subtlety and the greatest simplicity by the separation of the dregs of the corruptible elements, it will remain undecayed for a long time if you preserve it properly. When given to sick creatures, it will keep them in health for a long time. This is why doctors command us to use food that is less prone to decay.

<margin>Why the ancient philosophers practiced Chemistry.</margin>
Many of the ancient philosophers, inspired by the divine spirit, consecrated themselves to the knowledge, study, and pursuit of this supreme medicine, which is so necessary for the human race. They did so for this primary reason and goal: not so that they might use that <term>Chemical art</term> <note>original: "arte illa Chemica"; here referring to alchemy.</note> to change imperfect metals into perfect ones and thus grow rich, but so that they might cure sick men and preserve their lives to be as long-lasting as possible (to the glory of God) and keep them unharmed until the end-point predetermined by God. For it is more desirable and holier to cure a sick man and keep him in health longer than to grow rich with wealth—for in the abundance and unquenchable greed for such things, the soul might finally perish. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus 30 <note>A book of the Biblical Apocrypha, also known as the Wisdom of Sirach.</note>: *There is no wealth above the wealth of the body's health.* <note>original: "Non est census super censum salutis corporis"</note>

In this way, a person will be preserved safe and whole from disease until the end of life predetermined by God—provided that by using that medicine wisely, they do not otherwise harm the powers of their nature and the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific physical and mental temperament of an individual.</note> of the body beyond measure. <margin>It is appointed for men once to die, Hebrews 9. From this we gather that all things were made and created for the sake of man. This is not only a restorer and reformer of imperfect metals, but also of sick and infirm living beings. For there is a sufficient philosophical argument that the action of active agents works more strongly upon prepared subjects than upon those not prepared. Since this supreme medicine is nothing other than natural heat multiplied in the substance of <term>fixed Mercury</term> <note>Mercury that has been processed to remain stable and solid under high heat.</note>, and the power of heat is to gather things that are alike and separate things that are different: of necessity, this medicine, by its life-giving heat, will separate different elements in the bodies of animals, preserving the spirits and humors in a man more quickly than in the nature of metals. This is because a man, by his own natural heat, separates out different wastes, which metals are least able to separate by their own natural heat, as we understand by the persuasion of experiments.* So says that author. <margin>The miraculous power and operation of the Stone, or Chemical medicine, upon the vegetable genus.</margin> It performs these actions upon the vegetable genus: For the generations of trees and plants, as Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> writes in his *History of Plants*, book 2, chapter 1, are brought about either spontaneously, or by seed, root, tearing away, branch, sprout, the trunk itself, or even from wood cut into small pieces; and diseases often befall them, either common or specific, by which they perish. That medicine truly heals these. And because, as Lullius writes in the *Practice of the Testament*, chapter 27, nature by its own instinct greatly desires and seeks to be in the depths of an elemental body—in which it works by strengthening its natural heat and seed-bearing power—this medicine is able to permeate all bodies, which is why it is called <margin>Hyle</margin> **Hyle** <note>original: "Hyle"; a term derived from the Greek word for "matter," referring here to the fundamental, primordial substance of all things.</note>.

It withstands exposure to the vapors of sharp substances, the mixing of burning sulfur, extinction, calcination, and the repetition of reduction, and it easily accepts mercury. Furthermore, <margin>Its power upon precious stones.</margin> it cures and perfects the "sicknesses" or imperfections of precious stones—whether a lack of transparency, color, hardness, or weight—and restores them to their natural, or rather a more perfect, virtue. As Albertus <note>Albert the Great (Albertus Magnus), a prolific 13th-century scholar.</note> writes in *The Book of Minerals*, book 1, chapter 1, it transmutes one into another by that "antidote" of medicine which the Alchemists call the **Elixir**. By it, their sicknesses are cured, their hidden qualities are made manifest, or their manifest qualities are concealed. ### A LITTLE BOOK,
### WHICH IS TITLED THE TESTAMENT OF ARNALDUS
### OF VILLANOVA.

The Philosopher’s Stone, springing from the earth, is perfected or exalted in the fire; satisfied by a drink of the clearest water, it swells visibly on all sides for at least twelve hours. Then, placed in a drying chamber <note>original: "stupha"</note> and purified by the vapor of dry and moderately warm air, it acquires the solidity of its parts from the external heat, and being refined from superfluous moisture, it becomes fit for grinding. When these things are accomplished, a "virgin milk" <note>An alchemical term for the pure, white mercurial solvent or starting liquid.</note> is pressed out from its purer parts; this is immediately placed in the "Philosophers' Egg" <note>The oval-shaped glass vessel used to contain the alchemical work.</note> and does not cease to be cherished by a brooding heat <note>original: "pullifica concoctione," literally "chick-producing cooking," a metaphor for hatching the Stone like an egg.</note> until, stripped of its variety of colors, it rejoices with its companion in a snowy white color. From then on, without fear of danger, it endures the pains of an increasing fire, until, dyed with a purple color, it comes forth from the tomb with royal power. <note>This paragraph uses the metaphor of death and resurrection to describe the transition from the white stage (albedo) to the final red/purple stage (rubedo) of the Stone.</note>

### EVIDENT AND MANIFEST
# PROOF OF THE CHEMICAL ART.

### Taken from the *Antiquities* of Petrus Apianus. <note>Petrus Apianus (1495–1552) was a German humanist, mathematician, and astronomer. His 'Inscriptiones Sacrosanctae Vetustatis' (1534) was a famous collection of ancient inscriptions.</note>

In Padua, some years ago, a wonderful evidence of the alchemical art was discovered. A clay urn was found, marked with these verses:

DO NOT TOUCH THIS SACRED GIFT TO PLUTO, O THIEVES: <note>original: "Plutoni sacrum munus ne attingite fures." Pluto, as god of the underworld, was often associated with the hidden riches and metals found within the earth.</note>
THAT WHICH LIES HIDDEN IN THIS URN IS UNKNOWN TO YOU.
FOR THE GREAT OLIBIUS HAS ENCLOSED THE ELEMENTS, ARRANGED WITH HEAVY LABOR, <note>Maximus Olibius is a legendary figure; according to Renaissance lore, his tomb was found in 1500 containing a lamp that had burned for 1,500 years using a secret alchemical oil.</note>
BENEATH THIS MODEST VESSEL.
MAY PLENTY BE PRESENT AS A GUARDIAN FOR IT WITH HER FRUITFUL HORN, <note>A reference to the Cornucopia, symbolizing the infinite abundance provided by the "Philosopher's Stone."</note>
LEST THE VALUE OF SUCH A GREAT LIQUID SHOULD PERISH.

*Inside this urn another smaller one was found; when it was opened, two flasks were discovered, skillfully fashioned. One, of the purest gold, was full of a certain liquor, by which it is thought an ever-burning lamp had been preserved for many centuries. These verses were inscribed on the small urn:*

BEGONE FROM HERE, MOST WICKED THIEVES,
WHAT DO YOU WANT WITH YOUR SPYING EYES?
BEGONE FROM HERE WITH YOUR MERCURY, WEARING HIS TRAVELER’S HAT AND CARRYING HIS STAFF: <note>original: "cum Mercurio petasato caduceatoque." This refers to the god Mercury, patron of thieves, but also mocks "sophist" alchemists who worked only with common quicksilver (mercury) rather than the true "mercury of the philosophers."</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the archaeological "proofs" of alchemy into a philosophical and ethical defense of the art. The author, Fanianus, uses a rhetorical letter to justify the alchemist's work by comparing the "healing" of metals to the medical healing of the human body.</meta>

# GIOVANNI CHRYSIPPUS
### FANIANUS TO HIS FRIEND,
### JOHANNES PHILOPONUS, GREETINGS.

It is strange that while a physician heals a living creature <note>original: "animal"</note> wounded by so many great injuries and harassed by so many diseases, restoring it to its former health, a philosopher <note>The author uses 'philosopher' here specifically in the sense of a 'natural philosopher' or alchemist.</note> is supposedly unable to purge a metal of its inherent blemish—a task that seems less laborious and much easier. For who is there, if he examines the ailments of inanimate things just as he does those of living beings, who would not clearly see that the "casing of the soul" <note>original: "theca illam animæ," a poetic reference to the human body.</note> is exposed to medicines far more dangerously than a substance which shares nothing in common with the living except for its state of "sickness" <note>In alchemical theory, base metals were considered "sick" or "imperfect" versions of gold; the alchemist's task was to "cure" them.</note>? And yet, that same physician dares to lay hands upon the uncertain health of the sick and the wounded; but the philosopher does not dare the same with metal, as if danger to the former were not forbidden, while danger to the latter were strictly prohibited—as though someone could harm a man with more impunity than he could a piece of metal. 

If someone argues that from "damaged" metal, counterfeit money might be struck, why shouldn't he also conclude that from a "damaged" man many homicides might result? For if someone were to kill a man with impunity, would he not then fear to kill even more? Surely it is a greater crime to kill than to deceive. Is he not more harmful who, when he promised to heal the sick, kills them instead, than he who gives a bad coin in place of a good one? In the latter case, the matter concerns possessions or a small portion of them; in the former, it concerns the loss of life itself. Which, truly, is more precious? "But," you will say, "here the royal majesty is offended." <note>Counterfeiting was often considered a crime of "Lèse-majesté" (treason) because only the sovereign had the right to mint coins.</note> Is not divine majesty offended there? It is also more in the interest of royal majesty that a coin be removed from the treasury than a soldier from the army. Is it not, moreover, a greater thing to save a man than to increase the public treasury? 

Truly, we are able to deceive one another even where the law permits; from this, each person becomes more cautious in guarding his own property, and ultimately in guarding the cause of the Republic. We are indignant today if someone happens to use the resources given to men in common by nature—resources which, in the end, were made private property not through any social bond, but through discord; not through peace, but through war. Yet if someone kills another, we look the other way and think he should be spared. Thus, we neglect the commandment of God, which is that no one should love himself more than he loves another. How characteristic this love is of friends! And for those friends, as **Pythagoras** used to think, all things are held in common. Why then do we complain today if a friend takes some small portion of our private wealth? And for that reason, **Socrates** rightly used to curse the man who first separated "utility" from "nature" <note>original: "utilitatem à natura sejunxisset." This refers to the idea that what is morally right according to nature should never be separated from what is considered "useful" or "profitable."</note>; for he complained that this was the source of all destruction.

<summary>Fanianus argues for the moral legitimacy of alchemy, suggesting that "healing" base metals is a lesser risk than medical practice and that the fear of counterfeiting does not justify banning the alchemical art.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy vs medicine, ethics of transmutation, counterfeiting, natural law, Pythagoras, Socrates, Giovanni Crisippo Faniano</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Fanianus's introductory letter to Johannes Philoponus. It moves from the ethical defense of alchemy (comparing it to medicine) to an argument regarding the intellectual rigor required for the art, lamenting that it has fallen into the hands of the unlearned while being ignored by true scholars.</meta>

It is indeed both an evil to destroy metal and make it worse, and to kill a man—both are evils, and certainly one is to be avoided more than the other. But he who heals does not kill, and he who restores does not destroy. The physician’s hand is applied to the sick, not to the healthy and well; likewise, the hand of the philosopher <note>In this context, "philosopher" refers specifically to the alchemist or natural philosopher.</note> is applied to base and imperfect metal, not to the precious and perfect. Therefore, both should be entrusted to good and skilled men, not to the wicked, nor to the unlearned. If this is done, we may have hope for the health of man and for the value of metal.

For this purpose, this art—which we call by the ancient and hated name of Alchemy <term>Halchemisticen</term> <note>original: "Halchemisticen." The author notes that the term was already "exoso" (hated or detested) by 1559, likely due to the prevalence of fraudulent practitioners.</note>—has been established since the times of heroes for the great benefit of the Commonwealth <term>Reipub.</term> <note>original: "Reipub." (Res publica), referring to the state or the public good.</note>, provided it can be truly understood. For you know what the great philosophers, the poets, and even the historians report about it. Almost no one considers these miracles of nature to be vain, false, or invented to deceive. This is even more true because the precepts of this art are daily handled by anyone, and are adapted for use most of all by those who possess little talent or diligence.

And so it has happened, by some unknown fate—unless perhaps because the art seems too hidden or incredible—that it has been neglected and set aside by many professors of fine literature. Consequently, those who have contributed less to letters condemn it, or even despise it; what could be more unjust in human affairs? I would have you believe me—as I think you already do—that unless one is well-schooled in the disciplines of the great arts, he can achieve little profit in this art. For it is gathered from natural, mathematical, and even supernatural precepts. 

Since these matters are well-known and understood by you, they will grant you a wider entrance to it—if you believe this art is worth embracing. For beyond the innumerable effects of nature, it also ensures that he who masters it can increase his knowledge through great wealth and the removal of defects <note>original: "vitiisq;"—referring to the "vices" or impurities of metals that the alchemist "cures."</note>. But if you read our works with your sharpest wit, keen judgment, extensive knowledge, and most capacious memory, I do not doubt you will easily attain it. I would have you consider that this book was written and dedicated to you for that very reason, as I had previously promised in my letters.

Paris <term>Lutetia</term> <note>original: "Lutetia," the Roman name for Paris.</note>, October 19 <note>The "14th day before the Kalends of November" in the Roman calendar is October 19th.</note>, 1559.

# JOHANNES CHRYSIPPUS FANIANUS
## On the Art of Metallic Metamorphosis to Philoponus. <note>Philoponus translates to "lover of labor" or "lover of work," a common pseudonym or address for a dedicated student of the arts.</note>

<margin>The metallic art is manifold.</margin>
Among those things brought forward concerning metals, nothing is more wonderful than the art of metallic metamorphosis <note>Transmutation, or the changing of one metal into another.</note>, to which two others are added, making three arts of this kind that we chiefly use. The first is the art of mining (for in vain would divine nature have produced gold, silver, bronze, and iron, unless she had also taught how their veins might be reached). The second is the art of smelting the metals themselves, or the drossy ores, and from there crafting whatever is needed; this is called both the "craftsman's art" and "Chemistry" <margin>The Chemical art.</margin> from the word *chemeia* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς χημείας". Fanianus links the term to the Greek word for pouring or infusion.</note>. For what would it benefit us to have found the material unless we possessed the skill for its preparation? The third is the art of metamorphosis, of which we have set out to speak in this book; it is called Alchemy, from *Alchemia*. <margin>Alchemy.</margin> For the Greeks call salt *hala* <note>original: "ἅλα"</note> and fusion *chemeian* <note>original: "χημείαν"</note>; and this art is specifically concerned with a certain "fusible salt." <note>This reflects a Renaissance theory that the "Philosopher's Stone" was a type of specialized salt that could melt like wax or metal.</note> Thus, with every utility God has given to men, some art is joined through which that utility may be realized. The first two are mechanical and "surgical" <note>From the Greek *cheirourgia*, meaning "hand-work" or manual labor, rather than modern medical surgery.</note>; this third one is a part of that Philosophy which deals with the nature and causes of things. For it teaches the natures and causes both of metals and of all other things joined to them by some bond of nature. It is divided into two parts. <margin>Division of the art.</margin> The first is of discovery, and is called "Theory." The second is of arrangement, which is called "Practice." Therefore, we shall first investigate discovery, in which we will examine the nature of metals—not all of them, but only those that more closely approach the work of metallic metamorphosis itself; afterward, we shall speak of the second part. Some metals are mined for wealth, others for luxury, and others for the rashness of war. For <margin>The purpose of many metals.</margin> gold (with which bronze is often found) and silver (with which tin and lead are produced) are sought for riches; iron is sought for the sake of war and slaughter; and gems and pigments for the sake of pleasure. The Greeks call them "metals" <margin>Where "metals" comes from.</margin> either from *metallaō* <note>original: "μεταλλάω"</note>, which means to "search thoroughly" <margin>Definition.</margin> (for we are accustomed to search for metals within the veins of the earth), or from the phrase "being found after other things" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ μετὰ τὰ ἄλλα εὑρεῖσθαι"</note>, because they are found one after another. Thus says Pliny: because wherever one vein is found, another is found not far away—which he believes is the case in almost every material the Greeks call "metals." Gold is congealed from red sulfur—splendid, unconquerable by fire, most subtle, and most purified—and quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note>, through an excellent mixture, becoming pure and reddish. But one gold is better than another. That which is more "boiled" <note>Decoctum: fully processed or refined by heat.</note> and "digested" <note>Digestum: a term referring to the slow, steady heat that matures minerals in the earth.</note> is better, showing a glittering... <margin>The selection of gold.</margin>

### On the Art

<margin>The malleability of gold.</margin> No other metal can be expanded more widely or divided into more parts. Silver is ringing, sweet-sounding, and very bright. 

<margin>The generation of silver.</margin> It is formed from a white and very thin, but slightly oily sulfur—not sufficiently "cooked"—and a subtle and purified quicksilver <note>Quicksilver is the traditional name for Mercury.</note> that have not been perfectly mixed together. For in the generation of silver, more sulfur concurs than quicksilver. This is easy to detect because when it is mixed with 

<margin>The source of the color of gold and silver.</margin> gold, it takes on its color. Since the color of gold and silver arises from sulfur—acting like a "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that gives "matter" its specific identity and qualities.</note> upon the quicksilver, which is the "matter" itself—and since the power of color is greater in the former than in the latter, it follows that there is also more sulfur in it. Hence, we deny that there is an equal mixture of sulfur and quicksilver in silver. 

<margin>Nature’s error in silver, proven by experience.</margin> This is most clearly shown by experience itself: for if silver is burned in a fire for a long time, it eventually fails and turns into a snow-white powder, and whatever excess quicksilver is found there flies away. Therefore, while silver matches gold in the equality of both substances, 

<margin>The difference between gold and silver.</margin> it does not match it in their mixture. Because the sulfur of silver is not sufficiently digested <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturing or refining a substance through steady heat.</note>, it still possesses something oily; since this is contrary to quicksilver, it hinders the proper mixing, and as the quicksilver flies away, the sulfur is burned and perishes. This is also why silver is diminished by fire and eventually disappears. By the same reasoning, we are forced to admit that in pure gold there is an equal 

<margin>Nature’s integrity in gold.</margin> balance of sulfur and quicksilver. For no matter how much it is heated, it is not diminished at all; indeed, as Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), a Roman author who wrote "Natural History."</note> testifies, the more it burns, the more perfect it becomes. This happens because of the equal meeting and purity of sulfur and quicksilver in its generation. For equality—which, as Pythagoras <note>Ancient Greek philosopher who emphasized the role of numbers and harmony in the universe.</note> believes, is both the parent and the nourisher of friendship—is the cause of its invincible composition, as it is in all other things. I said "pure gold," however, because it is usually 

<margin>Silver naturally within gold.</margin> dug out of its mines containing some silver. If it had more quicksilver, the excess would fly away in the fire, and the mass 

<margin>Quicksilver is fleeting without sulfur. A digression.</margin> of gold itself would be diminished. All quicksilver without sulfur is extremely fleeting <note>Volatile; easily evaporated.</note>; it is held back by sulfur only when the proportion of equality is preserved. Otherwise, if the sulfur of the gold held back more than its own mass of quicksilver, the gold would hold onto whatever it touched and glued to itself because of the intensity of its sulfur, and it would change it into its own 

<margin>Antiphorae. <note>Counter-arguments or rhetorical responses.</note></margin> nature. Nor would there be need for so many circular paths to that most celebrated "Stone of the Philosophers" <note>The legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> as its authors have described. I would not, however, deny that there are, or have been, some who—using a small piece of gold, sometimes in the form of a powder and sometimes a more liquid material (though both are nothing other than the spirit of gold itself and a certain fiery vapor, which 

<margin>The wonderful power of the spirit of gold.</margin> Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change and for identifying fire as the fundamental element of the soul.</note> said was the soul)—have converted silver, bronze, tin, lead, iron, and quicksilver into gold. Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous Renaissance polymath, occultist, and alchemist.</note> writes in his books on the occult that he saw this and knew how to do it...

It concludes by referencing the Philosopher's Stone and the possibility of transmutation as witnessed by figures like Cornelius Agrippa.</summary>

### METALLIC METAMORPHOSIS

C 2

Philosophy has left it written in its books, and Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was an influential Italian scholar and priest who revived Neoplatonism and translated many hermetic and alchemical texts.</note> reports that it happens: truly, that small fragment is not so much the form or matter of gold alone, but rather a part of its purer and more vigorous essence which was enclosed in its very center, composed of both and drawn out by artifice. For the elements themselves, according to Aristotle, are purest at their center along with all other natural things. This part is the very "seed" of gold, its spirit and soul, by which they say it lives; and if it is properly drawn out, it will eventually become more vigorous, gradually advancing into greater powers through fire. 

For fire, as a certain author says, is its fodder and nourishment. For this reason, it is named the "Salamander" <note>In alchemical lore, the salamander was a creature that lived in and thrived on fire, symbolizing the ability of the "spirit" to withstand intense heat.</note> by some, and I have called it a "fiery vapor." For this same reason, it is called a *pyraustum* <note>original: "pyraustum". A legendary insect believed to live in fire; here used to describe the fire-loving nature of the gold-spirit.</note>, as well as that which nourishes the green herb; and the "Phoenix," because it is a unique spirit of such astounding nature, and because it acquires the principal colors, black and white. It is also compared to the herb Moly, which Homer says has a black root but a milk-white flower. Thus he says in Odyssey 10:

<margin>
*Various names for the spirit of gold.*
</margin>

> The root was black, but the flower was like milk; the gods call it Moly, and it is difficult for mortal men to dig up. <note>original Greek: "Ῥίζῃ μὲν μέλας ἔσκε, γάλακτι δὲ εἴκελον ἄνθος· Μῶλυ δέ μιν καλέουσι θεοί, χαλεπὸν δέ τ’ ὀρύσσειν Ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι."</note>

To those skilled in this art, what else can this seem to designate but that spirit, or whatever other material belongs to that philosophical stone? For its extraction from its own earth, in which it has already struck deep roots, is extremely difficult. The ancients attributed to that stone—of equally arduous extraction—the power to drive out every kind of sorrow and sickness, so that it might truly be called by the name "Moly" <note>The Moly herb protected Odysseus from Circe's magic; alchemists saw it as a symbol for the protective and transformative power of the Stone.</note>, and the power of converting other changeable metals, such as tin, copper, lead, iron, and quicksilver, into gold or silver—powers which we have taught that this spirit claims for itself. Hence, we may rightly call it Moly and the "salvation of metals." 

<margin>
*Comparison of the spirit of gold with the philosophical stone.*
</margin>

<margin>
*The salvation of metals.*
</margin>

For the utility of many things lies hidden not only above the earth, as Cicero says, but in its innermost darkness. These things, having arisen for the use of humans, are found by humans alone, and the "salvation" of metals is enclosed within these very things; it must be completely uprooted and extracted, not merely trimmed or cut away. But the greater and more divine their excellence, the more diligence they require. 

It will be fitting, first of all, to have taken *alupos* <note>original: "ἄλυπον". A Greek term meaning "painless" or "free from sorrow."</note>, even that medicine of Helen, which induced forgetfulness of grief, anger, and evil in all who drank it. Afterward, the structure of the gold must be dissolved, so that the natural spirit which is enclosed within may emerge—hidden beneath the falling monument—dazzling the sight in many ways. For nature has surrounded that "tabernacle" like a flint stone; until it has been released and sought its kindred ether, it gives off no flames, nor will it have the habit of any life whatsoever. But when it has departed from those fragile passages through which it was scattered, and is from all filth pur- <note>The catchword "purga-" indicates the next page begins with "purgatus" (purged or cleansed).</note>

It argues that this hidden spirit is the key to medicinal healing and the transmutation of base metals.</summary>

### ON THE ART

<margin>The various forms of the spirit of gold.</margin>
Once purified, it raises itself into infinite forms: at one moment it produces a plant, at another a stone, or some unusual animal; sometimes it appears as a sea, or a pearl, or a gemstone, or a metal. Emerging with a sweet brilliance from the flames when commanded, it immediately shifts into many myriads of colors. It lives always as an effector of wonders and a magician, never tiring of this labor, but growing daily in vigor and strength. Since we often struggle to define what this is, or how it can be liberated from that dark prison <note>The "dark prison" refers to the raw, unrefined state of matter or the physical body of the metal before alchemical purification.</note>, we shall explain it in order. For now, almost the entire contest of this art—which is most flourishing with great honor and profit—has been directed toward this end. As relates by Suidas <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia. It contains a famous entry claiming the Emperor Diocletian ordered alchemical books burned to prevent the Egyptians from becoming too wealthy to rebel.</note>, this art was once the long-time savior of the Egyptians against the fierce and formidable attacks of Diocletian, during a time when they could not sustain the labor of any more honorable or fruitful enterprise.

<margin>The power of this art shown by example.</margin>
<margin>What the spirit of gold is.</margin>
There are, therefore, those who distribute gold, and in turn make no end of separating the Elements from it, until a certain most pure nature—subject to no natural disturbances—remains. This they call the **fifth element** <note>Also known as the "Quintessence," a substance distinct from Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, believed to be celestial and incorruptible.</note>, or the temperament of the bodily substance. It is, in fact, like a certain "fifth nature" introduced by Aristotle, which is loose, free, and segregated from every mortal thickening; it lacks earth and moisture, and is neither airy nor fiery. Instead, being separated from these common and known natures, it is considered a more celestial substance. 

<margin>The method of extracting the spirit of gold.</margin>
For this purpose, they use a "bath" <note>In alchemy, a *balneum* or bath (like a double boiler) was used to apply gentle, indirect heat.</note> in which, by the relaxed heat of the fire placed beneath, the dross of the gold is, as it were, absorbed, and all things pass into an inward cleanliness. Its hard and almost adamantine <note>original: "adamantæa" — like a diamond; indestructible.</note> mass is crushed, undergoing an internal liquefaction and a "death" without loss. 

<margin>The excellence of gold.</margin>
Let no one think that such an intact metal can be diminished in any way by any fire. Pliny writes in his books on natural history <note>Pliny the Elder's *Naturalis Historia*, Book 33, discusses the unique properties of gold.</note> that gold is preferred above all other things for this very reason: that nothing of it is lost to fire. It endures safely through conflagrations and funeral pyres, and the more often it is parched, the more the quality of the material improves. For although its mass may decrease in size and weight, its strength remains, and it will never lack for anything. Indeed, not only does it not deteriorate—which is itself a miracle—but it shines more and more. It departs from its current state so that it may take on a new character for itself: it sheds its weight and exchanges it for lightness. In short—to conclude the matter in few words—there occurs a total reversal of its hardness and all its other qualities. But it also receives back the powers it held before, now ennobled by this transition, much more vigorous than its original ones, and shining with an inexhaustible splendor. 

<margin>Pindar’s opinion on gold.</margin>
