# THE METAMORPHOSIS OF METALS
### C 3

It can achieve something almost like what Plutarch writes of Lynceus: that he could penetrate even rocks and trees with the sharpness of his eyes. For there is sought for it, through the increased sharpness of its own wit, such a force of penetration that for all metals there is what is called the <term>turning of the shell</term> <note>original: ὀστράκων περιστροφή. This Greek proverb refers to a sudden and total reversal of a situation or a change in perspective, like flipping a game-piece.</note>. Yet there are some who seek silver-foam <note>Litharge or lead oxide</note>, or quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, or silver itself, or an egg, hair, or human blood, or urine, or wine, vinegar, or the herb called, as they say, Moonwort. And these people indeed terrify us by recounting various and horrific names, when all these things are but one family; and so, from one thing, as the proverb says, they make many. 

<margin>Various opinions of differing Philosophers.</margin>

But let us return to silver. Concerning the matter of the [Philosopher's] Stone—since there is no small contention among the greatest authors of this art—we must dispute more copiously in another place. 

<margin>The sulfur of silver.</margin>

Silver, therefore, as we taught above, possesses a sulfur that is only slightly oily; hence it melts in fire. I said "only slightly," for almost every metal has some amount of digested sulfur at its center; therefore, almost everything is also gold-bearing. 

<margin>Gold naturally within silver.</margin>

The testing of this matter is usually done with <term>Chrysulca</term> <note>literally "gold-drawer," likely referring to nitric acid or aqua regia used to separate gold from silver</note>. 

<margin>The effects of Chrysulca.</margin>

For this attacks the silver and draws it away from the gold, which settles like "star-struck blood" <note>original: *siderati cruoris*. Likely referring to a dark red precipitate or residue remaining after the silver is dissolved</note>, emerging incorrupt. The cause of silver's sweeter ringing sound is the subtlety of the quicksilver and the glue of the sulfur. 

<margin>The cause of silver's ringing sound.</margin>

That it consists of sticky sulfur, anyone can learn from experience by placing common sulfur—which is entirely glue—beneath mercury; for between these two, within a month, he will see the purest silver congeal, as we also have seen, using a time and place suited for this. 

<margin>The Author's wonderful experiment with mercury and common sulfur.</margin>
<margin>The Author's experiment.</margin>

Gold and silver are more beautiful the softer they are. 

<margin>The choice of gold and silver.</margin>

Tin is found to be compacted from thin and subtle sulfur and very fatty, dense quicksilver, poorly mixed; for this reason it is also "shrieking" <note>This refers to the "tin cry," a distinct crackling sound made when a bar of tin is bent, caused by the internal crystal structure shifting.</note>. It is born with silver and smelted from mixed veins. 

<margin>The generation of tin.</margin>

There are two types of lead: black and white <note>In antiquity and the Middle Ages, *plumbum album* (white lead) referred to tin, while *plumbum nigrum* (black lead) was true lead.</note>; the white is most precious. 

<margin>The types of lead.</margin>

The origin of the black is twofold: either it comes from its own vein, or it is born with silver and tin. Both consist of oily, bituminous sulfur and quicksilver of the same quality. 

<margin>What lead consists of.</margin>

This is easy to judge when, upon a glowing wick, it vanishes into virulent smoke, leaving no dross behind. We have learned by experiment itself to turn the purified lead into gold and silver. 

<margin>A wondrous metamorphosis of lead discovered by the Author himself.</margin>

It is first pounded and softened with a certain liquid in a cup, either a pot or a small shard, and from there it is cast into a glass vial so that it may be sprinkled in its own soap <note>original: *smegmati*. Likely a cleaning or fluxing agent used to strip impurities.</note>; thus, stripped of its shavings, it emerges bright. It is then given to the wick, and if any impurity remains, it is consumed by the fires, with silver and gold remaining. But quicksilver must be added to some extent according to the proportion of the material. Galen grants growth to this metal alone: because, as Pliny is the authority, if left alone in the earth it "revives" more fertilely <note>A common ancient belief that lead mines "regrew" their ore over time if closed for a period.</note>. 

<margin>Growth attributed to lead alone.</margin>

Copper and iron are of almost the same composition: except that iron has less quicksilver and more sulfur, which is oilier, and therefore it is very hard

<margin>All water is viscous, by example.</margin>
as most agree, a very viscous water, and therefore more dry than moist. For the surrounding heat and the very dryness of the earth drive out the diluting moisture of the water, while the glue is retained. How else can the structure remain—which, if the glue were removed, would again be powder—or a brick, or the wet form of mud? # ON THE ART <note>original: "De Arte"</note>

<margin>Everything written concerning this art is written in riddles.</margin>...spread a mist <note>original: "caliginem," completing the word from the previous page</note>. And there is almost no one, so far as I know, who has clearly narrated the precepts of that alchemical discipline until now: everyone has deliberately hidden everything with riddles and a kind of strange speech. Nor is this without reason: for it did not seem right not to wrap such great mysteries in certain coverings of riddles and portents of words, so that by this means the profane crowd might be perpetually driven away from them—just as from the Eleusinian mysteries <note>secret religious rites of ancient Greece known for their strict secrecy</note>—becoming too disheartened to dare to approach. For what is more absurd or intolerable than for a crowd of unformed and mad commoners, relying on such impregnable defenses and already raising their horns high enough, to walk away even more insolently? 

Thus Pythagoras and Plato obscured their philosophy with their numbers; and Aristotle testifies in a certain letter to Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> that he published some books in such a way as if they had not been published. So too Llull <note>Raymond Llull, a 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note> writes that his "wine" must be treated so harshly and strangely until it fails into ash or something lighter, or vanishes entirely. He asserts that a substance so treated vomits out that "fifth nature" <term>fifth nature: also known as the quintessence, the purest and most potent form of a substance</term> of his. Moreover, he uses that for his "Stone"; and then the Stone for reforming and ennobling metals. 

I ask you, please, what does or did wine ever have in common with metals, or what do you think it will have? He seems to deviate from nature no less than one who thinks a man is born from a donkey, a lion from a man, or some other even more alien thing. Furthermore, how many horrific monsters does he fashion everywhere from the characters of letters for himself and his students? He orders ridiculous things: that often 'b' is to be taken, 't' is to be left, and 'a' is to be changed into 'r', or if you prefer, 'r' into 'a', and a thousand other things (for it pleases me for a moment to play the role of Momus <note>the Greek god of mockery and criticism</note> and pursue Llull with sharper accusation). And so, impudently deluding the mind of the reader, he thrusts upon them mutual exchanges of letters in place of a description of the Philosopher’s Stone? 

But you will say these letters designate individual things which are needed to perfect that stone. They surely designate things that touch neither heaven nor earth. For what is the "menstrual solvent" <term>menstrual: in alchemy, this refers to a universal solvent, named for its cyclical power of dissolution and generation</term>? What are "rectified moonworts" <note>original: "lunaria rectificata," likely referring to purified mercury or silver-based ingredients</note>, "saltpeters," "quintessence," and innumerable things of that kind, even greatly different from each other, in relation to a single and unique Stone? For although that Stone—or whatever else not entirely unlike a stone it is—turns itself into many and various forms and produces things that seem most remote from its nature, yet since they do not differ at all, the matter is nevertheless one thing from the beginning: nor does it admit anything foreign to itself, otherwise everything would be in vain. And therefore, Llull is rightly accused of manifest lying by many; unless perhaps by depressing that liquid of wine down to the "fifth substance," the material of the Stone is most conveniently drawn out, or rather this is the work which a certain Execedistes <note>an unidentified person, perhaps a pseudonym for a specific alchemist</note> once placed before my eyes, showing great furnaces and the same adorned with various glass. The vessels were individual, having sediments in their seats,

...fragments, and within, a sacred gift dedicated to a different purpose. Why should I hide such a divine thing any longer? For inside there was a certain mass, rotated in a circle, presenting an image of the very world itself. <margin>Various forms.</margin>

It seemed to be remarkably fertile in wine, oil, milk, and every kind of precious stone and metal. <margin>Fire.</margin>

All these things were moved by their own fire, but one that was imperceptible and ethereal <note>original: "aethereo," referring to the pure, heavenly fifth element</note>. One thing especially seized me with incredible admiration: that it was confidently asserted that this one thing could produce so many, so diverse, and such complete things in their own kind, even with a small and weak support; once this support was made gradually stronger, all things would eventually return and coalesce into one.

<margin>Philosophical quicksilver.</margin>

<margin>What "menstruum" means to Llull.</margin>

For why should I again defend him from objections? It pleased me to challenge him only so that the matter itself might shine more clearly through dispute. Just as poets sometimes use "the Moon" to mean "a month" and "the Sun" for "a day"—because the sun completes its course according to the movement of the sky every day, but the moon only every month—so, on the contrary, Llull takes "month" to mean "the Moon" and calls it "menstrual" for that reason.

# ON ART

...to add a moderate heat, which it possesses, and he added a drier nature, together with color, a rounded shape, and an innate vital force, just like the world. Nor are there those lacking who go further and speak in wondrous ways, as is their habit, and call the very heart of the bird—which occupies the marrow and indeed the center of the yolk—the "fifth nature" <note>original: "quintam naturam," referring to the quintessence or the celestial element beyond the four earthly ones</note>. What of the fact that many more admirable things are testified to be made in the egg? For instance, they mention serpents and a form similar to a human—which they claim is effective with marvelous virtues—and which they call the true mandrake.

<margin>The true mandrake is even more so.</margin>

Then there is that "bird's milk" <note>original Greek: "ὀρνίθων γάλα" (ornithon gala)</note>, which is so rare to find that it has passed into a proverb, most suitable for the wealthy and those for whom any luxury is supplied. On this, Desiderius Erasmus wrote more, citing Aristophanes, Pliny, Eustathius, and Athenaeus. And does not Cicero report that Chrysippus wrote of a man who dreamed of an egg and thus stumbled upon a treasure? The dream-interpreter to whom he had related the dream judged that the yolk represented gold and the rest silver. And others, using the same cloak of truth, wrote that a certain stone called pyrite is the stone of the philosophers <term>stone of the philosophers: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term>. They argue this because it is entirely sulfur and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>, as we said before, of which two things alone that stone consists. Furthermore, they say it is bought at a very cheap price, found everywhere in Germany, and trodden underfoot by travelers.

<margin>An egg as a treasure to a dreamer.</margin>
<margin>Why pyrite is for some the stone of the philosophers.</margin>

What if someone objects to the impurity of that sulfur or the uncleanness of the quicksilver? They have an answer ready at hand: that both are cleansed and purified by one and the same cleansing agent <note>original: "smegmate," a term for a purifying detergent or soap</note>, which is suitable for such a great work among other things. Books are also circulated everywhere, as we said, by uncertain authors, full of questions more puzzling than the logical traps of the "Ceranites" or "Crocodilites" <note>ancient types of sophistical arguments or riddles intended to confuse</note>, intended to overwhelm the reader's mind with "Cimmerian darkness" <note>proverbial for total, lightless obscurity</note>, as the saying goes.

<margin>Proper to the work.</margin>
<margin>Books to be avoided.</margin>

But let the discourse return to where it wandered. We reviewed a little earlier the opinions of those who are rumored to have made no small progress in this discipline, though they hold varied views concerning both the matter of the stone and the work itself. It follows that we should examine each in order. For there is no small amount of deception or recognizable concealment in each. 

<margin>Against those who hold that gold is the matter of the philosophers' stone.</margin>

For those who affirm that gold is the matter of the stone seem to laugh at the wretched condition of those laboring in this pursuit. Since the beginning of the work is the corruption <note>in alchemy, "corruption" refers to the necessary decomposition or breakdown of a substance before it can be reborn</note> of the required matter brought about by fire alone—a kind of dissipation and tearing apart, or a division into the four elements—how can it be that gold is the matter of that stone? For gold is so far from being destroyed or corrupted by fire (no matter how increased or intense) that it instead becomes far more solid and vigorous. 

<margin>The beginning of the work.</margin>

Furthermore, those who have written on this subject among the ancients noted that in this corrupted matter there is a certain intolerable stench, like that of corpses. What odor, I ask you, does gold emit? Moreover, they say the same matter is soft; but what softness is there in gold? But you will say these names are present by the benefit of some other thing within the gold. Now the authority of those who ascribe only one thing to this work—a thing that is cheap and accessible—stands in opposition...

### THE METAMORPHOSIS OF METALS

<margin>Why the stone is called animal.</margin>
...they shout about the matter of the way, existing in every human being, and even being converted into that person. But nothing is scarcer or dearer than gold. Truly, that same gold is not found in any human except perhaps what has been implanted or introduced from the outside; nor can it be digested in a human—as iron is said to be in an ostrich <note>A common medieval belief held that ostriches could digest iron objects like horseshoes or nails.</note>—so that it is turned into chyle <term>chyle: a milky fluid of fat and lymph that forms in the small intestine during digestion</term> and finally into the human blood or flesh. Furthermore, how inanimate is it? For everything moved by an external pulse is inanimate. Yet they claim this Stone is "animal" <note>original: "animalis," which in this context means "animate" or "living," as well as "pertaining to the animal kingdom."</note>, either because it comes from an animal, or because it possesses a soul, or rather for the sake of both; none of which applies to gold. Therefore gold, as many falsely claim, is not the matter of this Stone; nor is silver. 

<margin>Silver is not the matter of the stone, nor are the remaining metals.</margin>
For how could it be, since it is consumed by fire? Yet the matter of the Stone, even according to the assertion of Arnaldus himself <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist who emphasized the importance of mercury.</note>, is a thing that is most eternal and impervious to fire. Therefore, neither are the remaining ductile metals suitable, for this reason alone: that they cannot endure the fire, whether they are joined with gold—a metal which, as we have said, loses nothing to fire—or whether they are exposed to the fire individually. Let us come to quicksilver.

<margin>Mercury is the matter of the stone for some.</margin>
For sulfur, which is easily consumed by fire, must be passed over here in silence. There are indeed those who claim that quicksilver—or as they call it, Mercury—is the matter of the Stone. Hence the saying: "Mercury is the Stone which the philosophers honor." 

<margin>The powers of Mercury.</margin>
It seems, moreover, to have more power for this metamorphosis. For it penetrates most deeply and stains with great speed. Its "flight" <note>referring to its volatility and the ease with which it evaporates when heated.</note>, however, is a drawback for it. 

<margin>By what names gold and silver have been endowed.</margin>
Accordingly, they teach that the Sun and the Moon—that is, gold and silver—should be mixed with it so that it does not flee the fire; this agrees with their fiction that the Stone has the Sun as its father and the Moon as its mother <note>A central tenet of the *Emerald Tablet*, an ancient foundational text of alchemy.</note>, namely gold and silver, as I interpret it. For they have not given these things any other names. But while we run through these things, I fear that they do not understand "common mercury" <note>original: "Mercurio vulgi," the liquid metal quicksilver used by smiths, as opposed to the "Philosophical Mercury" of the alchemists.</note>, which neither gold nor silver frees from flight. Otherwise, they would be lying when they say the Stone is one thing with the Sun as father and the Moon as mother, and that it cures human diseases. For common mercury and the Sun are two things that differ from one another by a wide margin. 

<margin>The principles of ductile metals.</margin>
Furthermore, if we too may speculate, Mercury itself is the father of the Sun and Moon rather than the son. For it was naturally suited in its own metal to generate the Sun and Moon, and any other metal along with a suitable sulfur, seeing as it is the natural principle <note>In the "Sulfur-Mercury theory," all metals were thought to be composed of these two substances in varying degrees of purity.</note> with it for the metals of gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron. To this, in what way can it be adapted for driving away diseases, since it is a deadly poison? Although Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> nevertheless has his doubts. 

<margin>Quicksilver is a poison, except according to Galen.</margin>
Hence, it contributes nothing to this work, because it is entirely common silver and sulfur. We have said "common." For there is another quicksilver, the very matter of the Stone itself—not from hair, or blood, or urine, or eggs: 

<margin>What the matter of the philosophers' stone is and from where.</margin>
for what do those things have to do with the Stone or with metal, since they recognize neither fire nor metals, nor a soul, even though they come from animals? Rather, it comes from "vile" gold and silver, at once foul-smelling and sweet...

# ON THE ART

...sweet-smelling, green, animate, found everywhere, but known by very few; rising in the middle of the sea, translucent, fleeting, and volatile until it has been united with its own sulfur and becomes a whole stone. It is then called **fireproof** <note>original: "apyros," meaning a substance that resists the action of fire.</note>, commonly known as a **carbuncle** <note>In alchemy, a "carbuncle" usually refers to a red, glowing stone like a ruby, symbolizing the finished Stone.</note>. <margin>An enigmatic description of the matter of the stone.</margin>
<margin>What fusible salt and philosophical mercury are, and where they come from.</margin>
Afterward, they also pour out this kind of **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: also known as mercury; in alchemy, it represents the principle of volatility and fluidity</term>, to which **fusible salt** from the same root is born nearby. Both—lest we seem to have retracted our previous statements—are the spirit and life of that common gold, even if they originate elsewhere. For they originate from the purest gold which has no dross, and from its own silver. But both, as has been said, are for a brief moment in the hands of the unrefined common people; yet this is neither the gold nor the silver of the blacksmith. For it cannot be such when it is recently dug from the mine, surrounded by earth and stone.

<margin>From pure gold and its silver.</margin>
<margin>What the matter of the stone itself is, which no one has revealed until now.</margin>
I add this: that gold and silver do not seem to be plainly in that matter, nor present in actual fact—as Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a major authority in medieval alchemy.</note> writes—but only in potential and power. And so as not to keep anyone waiting any longer, I will say in one word what that matter is. I will say it, and bring into view what no one has noticed in unfolding the volumes of this discipline, nor has anyone committed to writing: **It is nothing other than fusible salt.** This is even displayed in the name of the work itself, **Alchemy**, which is to say, the **fusion of salt** <note>The author is proposing a creative etymology, linking "Alchemy" to the Greek "als" (salt) and "cheuo" (to pour/melt).</note>. And so that anyone may easily persuade themselves of this, every nature, every name, and all qualities which they attribute to the "Stone," we can apply to salt itself.

<margin>The quality, names, and nature of the stone.</margin>
First, let us look at what they say: that the stone is **animal, vegetable, and metallic**. Furthermore, they say it is cheap, sold at a low price, found always and everywhere, born in the Mediterranean Sea, existing in any human being, receding into and giving birth to anyone, easily melting and hardening, and most friendly to both the divine and human body. Do these things not fit **salt**? Salt itself is both animal, animate, and metallic. Is salt not drawn out of animals? And is there not in it a certain swift and wonderful power of penetrating, purging, and preserving from rot? If it pleased Thales of Miletus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher often cited as the first to investigate the basic substance of the world.</note> to call that "Herculean stone"—that is, the **magnet**—a living thing because it seemed to attract and compel iron, why should we not also call salt "animate," since it wonderfully penetrates, purges, binds, dissipates, represses, and thins? Who would deny it has a "vegetable" soul, since it alters, increases, and gives birth? Salt is altered, growing into **anthracite** while putting forth certain branches like a plant, and it gives birth to the **philosophical mercury** itself. What of the fact that it is believed to have a certain genuine power of procreation, proven by this argument: that it awakens and sharpens seminal vigor? There are even some who say that women become pregnant from the mere licking of it...

<margin>The magnet is a living stone.</margin>
<margin>The effects of salt.</margin>
<margin>Animate salt.</margin>
<margin>The miraculous power of salt.</margin>

<margin>Salt is divine to Homer.</margin>

<margin>What imperfect metals lack.</margin>
imperfect metals especially lack? Add to this that those very authors from heroic times, 
<margin>What Alchemy is.</margin>

<margin>The Stone from stinking things.</margin>

Added to this is that some have written that the Stone is found among vile

From these things, the matter of the philosophers' stone and its origin become clear. It remains for us to teach in what manner those things which are its origin are turned into it—that is, into salt—and the salt into the stone, what sort of thing it is, and why it is so called. For it is not truly a stone, but only has a certain likeness to a stone. And once these things are untangled, that which we promised at the beginning regarding both the theory and practice of this art will be complete. 
<margin>The remote matter of the stone is turned into salt by fire alone.</margin>

# ON THE ART

> *And though near to the solid state, yet we restrain them with fire.*

> *Matter of iron, though extremely hard, is yet subverted by fire:*

> *Lie undiscovered, and subject to a similar fate;*
> *Nor is there a place for genius: your eyes being judge, they will conquer.*

But since fire in this art is manifold, we must see which one we especially ought to use. And indeed, a great controversy has arisen and remains among those skilled in the art concerning this matter. For some recommend dung—and not even that of which Columella <note>Columella was a 1st-century Roman writer whose work "De Re Rustica" is a primary source on ancient agriculture, including the uses of different types of manure.</note> distinguishes three types, but specifically horse dung: others recommend grape skins and pits, others the heat of ashes, others of bran, others a lit wick, others burning coals, and especially those of juniper because, as they say, they burn for a whole year unharmed by the fire <note>It was a common medieval belief that juniper coals could retain heat or stay "alive" for an exceptionally long time.</note>: others claim that the lukewarm vapor of water, which they call a bath <note>term: "balneum" — a water bath or "Bain-Marie," used for gentle, indirect heating.</note>, is a fire peculiar to this work.

<margin>
*Multiple types of fire.*
*Fire for the Stone.*
</margin>
Bernard, Count of Trevisan <note>A famous 15th-century alchemist often cited for his dedication to the "Great Work" over many decades.</note>, proposes a certain enclosed ethereal fire similar to human heat, which many others support. To me, however, of all these, that one seems to be chosen among the rest which the necessity of the work itself requires. For sometimes we shall use horse dung, sometimes also a lit wick, warm cloths, and glowing coals. 

<margin>
*The threefold degree of heat for the Stone.*
</margin>
Nor is it without reason that they establish a threefold degree of heat: one moderate, which is applied at the start of the work: another a little stronger, which we use for the lime <note>term: "calx" — the fine powder or "ash" produced after a substance has been roasted or calcined.</note> once the elements have coalesced into one: the last, unbearable [intense], by whose help we may achieve the desired end. For the whole power lies in the fire. By this fire we distinguish and tear apart that raw and undigested mass into those four elements; furthermore, we compose and drive those same elements into one: by this we turn it into lime and perfect what was begun. 

<margin>
*What kind of fire at the beginning and at the end of the work.*
</margin>
And unless the fire is gentle and mild at the beginning, it will glue together and constrict rather than dissolve: on the other hand, unless it gains strength when the matter requires turning into lime, it will frustrate the labor of the craftsman. As was the method of beginning, so should be the manner of finishing. Just as in all things it must be seen to what extent they go, and although each has its own measure, yet "excess offends more than deficiency," as Cicero says: so also in this business a certain governance must be applied, and the heat should be relaxed rather than intensified. 

<margin>
*A remote description of the matter of the Stone.*
</margin>
For those things which we said make one are from the number of those things which Aristotle wrote somewhere move with contrary motion. If anyone pays attention to his words, he will undoubtedly distinguish from which things that fusible and philosophical salt <note>A "fusible salt" is one that melts like a metal rather than dissolving in water; it is a key stage in creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> ought to be extracted. Moreover, those things are of such a kind that although they spring from the same fountain, yet by fire one is poured out while the other is compressed. For when the body liquefies and flows, the spirit freezes: and this action happens at the same time. Who [would] not [be moved] by such a great thing...

### METALLIC METAMORPHOSIS

...has he attained? Indeed, I pursue these matters not as most others do, addressing only the learned and those skilled in these things; rather, I write for my own crowd—that is, for the more unrefined and unskilled—since a teacher is superfluous to the learned. But since there is no place in this art that does not require deep investigation—for it is introduced by many in a way that is <unclear>helpless</unclear> <note>original: "ἀμηχανῶς"—meaning without a clear method or resource</note>—and since it is one of those three "unspeakable beasts" of this work (which are: the knowledge of the matter, the discovery of the vessel, and the method of the fire), nothing is more manifest at this time. I have spoken.

Regarding the **Vessel**: An abundance of vessels is of no use here; a single glass container suffices, shaped like a small leather bottle or an oblong egg <note>often called the "Philosophical Egg" in alchemical literature</note>, so that the separated and distinct elements may rotate in a circle and, by mutual collision, obtain the Stone—a thing remarkable and incomparable in its powers of altering, increasing, and generating. 

<margin>
The unspeakable beasts of this work.
The vessel of the stone.
The various operations of the stone.
</margin>

For since this one vessel is abundantly capable of all the operations performed on the Stone—that is, <term>sublimations</term>, <term>solutions</term>, <term>distillations</term>, <term>coagulations</term>, <term>cerations</term> <note>original: "cereficationum"—the process of softening a substance to a wax-like or "waxy" consistency</note>, and as they say, <term>calcinations</term> and <term>fixations</term>—why should we require many? In this vessel, at the beginning when the matter dissolves, a black substance is seen; afterwards it becomes multicolored, then white and bright, and finally red.

<margin>
The colors of the matter of the stone.
The method of sealing the vessel.
</margin>

However, it must be most tightly sealed, lest the enclosed internal air or "spirit" fly away, enticed by the free air outside; this is a misfortune that could hardly be repaired. The method of sealing is familiar to glassmakers themselves. Next follows what purposes it serves, once the Stone has grown from the proper matter in a suitable vessel with convenient fire and has been brought to its perfection.

In **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyro"—literally "water-silver" or quicksilver</note> it contributes greatly to the preparation of wealth, and in potions and pills <note>original: "catapotiis"</note> it contributes much to health. According to the teaching of Lully <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher and reputed alchemist</note> and others, the logic of this stage is extremely difficult and requires the greatest effort to execute. One part belongs to Medicine, the other to this Art, and to our "mixed bag," as they say.

<margin>
The fruits of the stone.
What the stone is and why it is so called.
</margin>

It is mixed into purified mercury first in such a proportion that the quantity of mercury is ten times greater, then a hundredfold, then a thousandfold, then ten thousandfold, and finally infinitely. This is the immense multiplication of the fermenting Stone—namely of gold and silver. It ends in a white and bright <term>calx</term> <note>a powder produced by roasting or "cooking" a substance; the alchemical "lime"</note> for silver, and a red one for gold. Thus, it is even called a "Stone." For a *calx* is nothing other than a "cooked stone." It is a powder so subtle that it cannot withstand even the slightest breeze. It is truly marvelous how penetrable it is. But experience itself will teach you these things better.

<margin>
The time for perfecting the stone.
</margin>

I shall therefore cease if I add one word: the time in which the Stone is brought to completion, whether in whiteness and brightness or in redness, is not fixed. This is the work of both the craftsman and of nature. Everyone sees how slow and how little-ripened nature's progress is. Sometimes it is completed in nine, twelve, or eighteen months, but very rarely; sometimes, as is usual, it lingers for about three years.

ON THE LAW
<meta>catchword: if it</meta>

### Concerning the
# LAW OF THE ALCHEMICAL ART,
->*That is,*<-
->The judgments and responses of various authors, and especially of<-
->legal scholars, regarding the daily question:<-
->**Whether Alchemy is a legitimate art.**<-

->From the Sibyl.<-

> I have nine letters and four syllables; consider me.
> The first three [syllables] have two letters each,
> And the rest have the remaining [letters]. And five are consonants,
> And of the whole number, there are twice eight hundreds,
> And three tens with seven. Do you know who I am?
> You shall not be uninitiated into my wisdom.
<note>original Greek: Ἐννέα γράμματ’ ἔχω... This is a famous riddle from the Sibylline Oracles, often interpreted by alchemists to refer to "arsenic" (ἀρσενικόν), which they viewed as a primary substance of the Work.</note>

->*Interpretation from Cardano’s book "On the Variety of Things."*<-
->BOOK X. CHAPTER 52.<-

When I happened upon these discussions, the illustrious Aimery de Ranconnet, <note>Ranconnet (1498–1559) was a prominent French jurist and scholar.</note> presiding judge at Paris, demonstrated that this art was approved by the Sibylline poem. Indeed, he did so with such precision that, whereas the responses of such oracles are usually ambiguous, in this case, the words of the riddle seemed clearer than the light of the sun. Therefore, I shall subjoin those things which that learned man expressed with such marvelous skill, just as I received them from him while I was in Paris. Now, those words are "I have nine letters," etc., as above. He says, therefore, that it is a name consisting of nine letters, which contains four syllables, of which the first three contain only two letters, and the remaining [syllables] contain the rest, namely three. In this name *arsenikon* <note>original Greek: ἀρσενικόν—meaning arsenic, but also "masculine" or "potent."</note>, all things seem to fit beautifully: for it consists of four syllables, *ar, se, ni, kon*: of which the first three contain two letters each, and the fourth and last contains three; so that there are nine elements in total. And these things are entirely clear through experience, which is plainly revealed in Greek. 

He then adds that five of these letters are consonants <note>original: "mutae"—literally 'mutes,' a term for consonants in ancient grammar</note>, so that we may understand there are only four vowels, *a, e, i, o*: the remaining five he called "mutes," that is, non-vowels, which are *r, s, n, k, n* <note>original Greek: ρ, σ, ν, κ, ν</note>. Then he adds that the number signified by these consonant letters is "twice eight hundreds and three tens with seven" <note>original Greek: ἑκατοντάδες δὶς ὀκτὼ καὶ τρεῖς δεκάδες</note>. That is, it is contained by twice a hundred and eight times, and by three times three decades: which is nine times and eight times ten, which is one hundred and seventy, so that the whole number is 370. <note>The author's arithmetic is complex here. In Greek gematria, the consonants of ARSENIKON (ρ=100, σ=200, ν=50, κ=20) sum to 370 if one 'n' is excluded or counted differently.</note> This number is signified by the five consonant letters,

# ALCHEMY,
## D
<meta>The "D" indicates the signature mark for the printer to organize the folded sheets of the book.</meta>

if you only count the letter that is repeated—that is, the $\nu$ <note>The Greek letter nu (n), which appears twice in "Arsenikon" (ἀρσενικόν).</note>—a single time. For when the letters $\epsilon, \sigma, \nu, \kappa$ <note>epsilon, sigma, nu, kappa</note> are taken together, they produce the same amount; among the Greeks, $\epsilon$ <note>epsilon</note> signifies 100, $\sigma$ <note>sigma</note> signifies 200, $\nu$ <note>nu</note> signifies 50, and $\kappa$ <note>kappa</note> signifies 20. When collected, they make 370. <note>original: "apud Græcos ε, significat C. σ, CC. ν, L. κ, XX." Note that Cardano is using a non-standard or specific cipher here, as epsilon is usually 5 in Greek isopsephy.</note> From this, he adds "with three [hundred] and seven," where $\tau$ <note>tau</note> signifies 300, and "seven" refers to the decades, for it relates to the previous numbers. <note>original Greek: "σὺν τ' ἑπτὰ" (syn t' hepta). The "tau" represents 300, and the "seven" refers back to the "seven decades" mentioned in the riddle.</note> Only the proper logic of the speech seems to conflict in three ways: "twice hundred-folds" <note>original Greek: δὶς ἑκατοντάδες</note>, and "seven ten-folds" <note>original Greek: ἑπτὰ δεκάδες</note>, and "with" <note>original Greek: σὺν</note> instead of "plus." Moreover, he casts away the second $\nu$ <note>nu</note>. Since the Sibyl does not explicitly say this, he reads $\tau$ <note>tau</note> in place of $\chi$ <note>chi</note> or $\gamma$ <note>gamma</note>. For the manuscript has "with seven" <note>original Greek: σὺν χεπτὰ</note>, which means "with seven added." He said: this could easily be true, as there is little difference in form between $\chi$ and $\tau$. Finally, she concludes that whoever knows this will not be a stranger to her wisdom. In this, it might seem marvelous that the prophetess departs so far from her purpose. But these, and far greater things, are the privileges of prophets, especially the inspired and the divinely frenzied. Added to this is the fact that the matter itself agrees with the words and the exposition of the name, as we have taught elsewhere: for by arsenic, copper is transformed into the likeness of silver, and gold is contained within orpiment. <note>Arsenic was used to "whiten" copper, making a silver-like alloy; orpiment (arsenic trisulfide) is a bright yellow mineral traditionally associated with gold.</note> If not this, the Sibyl might be able to indicate something else of great use. However it may be, the interpretation or the discovery is entirely admirable—at the very least, it is not unworthy of my books *On Subtlety* if they were not already finished. Thus, in arsenic there is the foundation of a certain present utility and the beginning of the work, just as in chalcanthum <note>Copper sulfate or blue vitriol.</note> there is the beginning of the transformation of iron into copper: for the color is changed immediately.

->*From Thomas Aquinas in his commentary on Aristotle's "Meteorologica," book 3, near the end.*<-

The immediate matter of metals is sulfur and quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, as the Alchemists say: so that in the stony places of the earth, sulfur and quicksilver are generated through a mineral power; then, from these, different metals are generated according to their different mixtures. Whence also these Alchemists, through the true art of Alchemy—which is nevertheless difficult because of the hidden operations of the celestial power called "mineral"—which, because they are hidden, can be imitated by us through the aforementioned principles, or through things derived from them, sometimes achieve the true generation of metals.

->*From the same author in "Summa Theologiae" II-II, question 77, article 2.*<-

If, however, gold were made through Alchemy, it would not be illicit to sell it as true gold, because nothing prohibits art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects: as Augustine says in book 3 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, regarding those things which are done by the art of demons. <note>Aquinas argues that if the alchemist manages to create real gold using the same natural processes as the earth, the product is authentic, not a counterfeit.</note>

->*From the same author in II-II, question 96, article 2.*<-

But if natural things are applied simply to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural power, it is not superstitious or illicit to use those things or their effects.

->*From Suidas, on the word "Chemia."*<-

Chemia is the making of gold and silver: whose books Diocletian <note>This refers to the Suda, a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia. The entry notes that the Roman Emperor Diocletian ordered alchemical books to be burned in Egypt around 297 AD to prevent the locals from gaining the wealth needed to revolt.</note>

# Concerning the Law.
<meta>catchword: IPRIS- (Likely a fragment of IURIS, referring to the "Laws" section continued on the next page)</meta>

...he gathered and burned them, because the Egyptians had plotted a revolution against him, and he treated them harshly and as enemies. At the same time, he sought out and burned books about the chemistry of gold and silver written by the ancients, so that the Egyptians would no longer acquire wealth through that art, nor, relying on an abundance of money, rebel against the Romans again. <note>This refers to the Roman Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD), who suppressed an Egyptian revolt and allegedly ordered the destruction of alchemical texts to weaken the province's economy.</note>

->*From the same source, under the entry "Deras."*<- <note>Original Greek: δέρας, meaning "fleece" or "skin." This citation is from the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note>

The Golden Fleece, which Jason obtained when he crossed the Black Sea with the Argonauts to Colchis, along with Medea, the daughter of King Aeëtes. This, however, was not what the poets say, but was actually a book written on skins <note>parchment</note> containing the method for making gold through chemistry. It is likely, therefore, that people at that time called it the "Golden Fleece" because of the profit and benefit that could be gained from that book.

->*From Pliny, Book 34, Chapter 4.*<-

There is also one method of making gold from orpiment <term>orpiment: from the Latin *auripigmentum* (gold pigment); a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once thought to contain the "seed" of gold</term>. This hope enticed the Emperor Gaius <note>the Emperor Caligula</note>, who was most greedy for gold. He therefore ordered a great weight of it to be smelted, and he did indeed produce excellent gold, but of such small weight that he suffered a loss—having attempted it out of greed—even though 14 pounds of orpiment were traded [for a small sum]. No one has attempted it since.

->*From Cardano, "On Subtlety," Book 6.*<-

Nevertheless, that metals can be transformed has seemed possible to many, due to the experiment with copper already mentioned above. They even seem to change color and weight because of fire, which makes it likely that their substance can also be changed. It was also believed that certain people had done this, as happened a few years ago before the most illustrious Prince of Venice <note>the Doge</note> and the wise men of the city, performed by a certain pharmacist from Treviso <note>original: "Tarvifino pharmacopola"</note>, of which event traces still remain. And since certain species of herbs can be changed into one another, it should not seem strange that metals can be transformed. But the matter is not quite so, for either none or not all can be changed into one another. For iron and copper, since both are similar in weight and thinness, and neither resists fire, can be transformed from one to the other if their color and hardness are changed—either truly or at least without a visible difference. None of the other metals can be changed into gold or silver. The only doubt is whether silver can be changed into gold. I believe this can be done: for in order for silver to become gold, it lacks density (which is why it must be made heavier) and color. But these can be added to the metal; if silver is made denser, its fatness <note>original: "pinguedo"; in alchemy, this refers to the oily, combustible quality of a substance</note> will be removed, it will resist fire better, and, as I said, it will gain weight.

->*And a little later.*<-

This is what that pharmacist from Treviso seems to have achieved, who, in the presence of the Prince and the wise men of the Venetian Republic, changed quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; long considered the "mother" of all metals in alchemical theory</term> into gold.

## OF JURISTS AND THE HIGHEST
### *responses and counsels in Both Laws, regarding the question*
<note>original: "in V. I. D." refers to "Utriusque Iuris Doctor," a Doctor of both Civil and Canon Law.</note>

->Whether Alchemy be a legitimate art?<-

->*From Oldradus, counsel 74, regarding sorcery, number 1.*<-

Whether an Alchemist sins, or whether it is a forbidden art. And it seems that it is so, and that the art of Alchemy is forbidden. For the text says <note>Referring to the *Canon Episcopi*, a famous legal text from the 10th century incorporated into Canon Law (26. q. 1. c. epis.)</note> that whoever believes any creature can be made, or changed for the better, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself, is an infidel and worse than a pagan. Furthermore, these Alchemists are "always learning, and never reaching the truth of knowledge" <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 3:7</note> [25. q. 5], and no wonder. Thus they give occasion for many deceptions. Nor is it a science that leads to piety, as is usually said regarding astrology [27. dist. si quis. & no. Inn. Ex de Sorti. c. qui.]. For it cannot be done without the "boiling of gold," which seems forbidden by law [Code of Justinian, On the public pursuit of gold, book 10, law 1]. 

On the contrary, it seems that those who produce gold or silver from tin or lead or another base metal—provided they do not do this through magic or another art hated by the laws [Code of Justinian, On treasures, book 10, law 1]—are not to be blamed, but rather praised. These are metallurgists, who through their own labor provide benefits for themselves and the Republic [Code of Justinian, On metals, book 11, law 1]. The laws favor them because of the public utility that seems to result from their office. For they can, even against the owner's will, enter another’s land to search for metal [Code of Justinian, On metals, law 2]. And note there that they do not say one species is changed into another (as is charged against them), because that is not possible. But they say that from one species of metal (namely tin), another species of metal (namely gold) can be produced. 

Nor is this inconsistent. For we also see that sometimes a living thing is produced from a dead thing: as we see in the worms from which silk is produced, and many others. And glass is produced from a herb. How much more so from metals, in which there is a greater agreement and likeness? For (as they themselves teach, and as is found in the book *On the Properties of Things* <note>Referring to the popular medieval encyclopedia by Bartholomaeus Anglicus</note> in the chapter on Alchemy) all metals proceed from the same principle: namely, from sulphur and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>. 

But by the power of the elements, some have a greater influence in one place than in another: in one mine tin is made, in another silver, in another gold, and so on for others. Since, therefore, art imitates nature [Digest, On adoption, law "si adoptio"], these Alchemists do not seem to sin if, through this power which is in herbs, or stones, or elements, they wish to make silver from tin. For since they are from almost the same principle and are similar, the transition is easier for things sharing a "symbol" <note>original: "symbolum," here referring to the Aristotelian concept of shared primary qualities (like heat or moisture) that allow one element to transform into another</note> [Institutes, In what ways obligations are dissolved, section 1]. For there are many virtues implanted in herbs...

<summary>This page presents a legal debate on whether alchemy is a sinful or forbidden practice, weighing the "heretical" claim of changing species against the "utilitarian" view of alchemy as a form of metallurgy. It concludes by arguing that because all metals share the same components (sulphur and mercury), alchemical transformation is a legitimate imitation of nature.</summary>

with herbs and stones <note>Citing the *Decretum Gratiani*, 16. q. fi. c. fi.</note>. For there are (as Saint Augustine says) certain hidden "seminal reasons" <note>original: "seminariæ rationes." This is a philosophical concept from St. Augustine suggesting that God placed the potential for all things within the elements at creation, which then emerge under the right conditions.</note> within corporeal things throughout all the elements. When the right temporal and causal opportunity is given, these burst forth into their destined forms, according to their own modes and limits [26. q. 5]. Nor is it surprising, as noted near the end. Therefore, if they attribute this power to God, they do not seem to sin. Furthermore, I see that there is no great penalty for one who gives, or pledges, brass in place of gold, even if done knowingly <note>Citing the *Digest* (Roman Law), on the action of pledges and on the crime of "stellionatus" or fraud.</note>.

->*From Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous expert in Canon Law.</note> on the chapter "Ex tuarum" regarding sorcery.*<-

But following the aforementioned points, another question can be asked, which Oldradus poses in counsel 69: whether Alchemy is forbidden and whether those practicing it sin. And it would seem so, because one species is converted or transmuted into another, as when lead is made into silver, or brass into gold, etc. But besides God, no one can transmute one species into another [as per 26. q. 5, in the section "Whoever therefore"]. Oldradus, however, concludes the opposite: that indeed one species is not changed into another different one, since all metals proceed from the same source, namely from sulfur and mercury <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or quicksilver.</note>. But where there is a better influence of the stars, a more precious metal is produced there. Hence, through the influence of the stars, and with herbs and stones (in which many virtues reside), one species of metal can naturally be converted into another more precious species; this is a point to be noted.

->*From Johannes Andreas <note>A celebrated 14th-century canonist.</note> in the additions to the "Speculator," under the title on the crime of forgery.*<-

Concerning Alchemists, it is often doubted whether they fall under the penalty for forgery. Some apply the words of Paul to them from 2 Timothy 4 <note>Likely referring to 2 Timothy 4:4, "turning away from the truth to myths."</note> at the beginning [see 26. q. 5]. And it is no wonder, for according to Paul's sentiment, they similarly provide cause for many deceptions. Nor is it a "science of piety" [37. dist. "si quis"]. It is also said that this art, where it strives for gold, cannot be done without the "boiling of gold," which is prohibited by law <note>Citing the Code of Justinian, Book 11.</note>. On the contrary, he who out of the mastery of art—without magic or other arts prohibited by the laws—makes a precious metal out of a base one, is to be commended. For in this he increases the wealth of the state <note>original: "rempub." or republic/commonwealth.</note> [Code, On metals, book 11, law 1]. And these metallurgists are privileged [contrary to the previously cited laws on treasures and the acquisition of property], so that they may enter another's land even against the owner's will. Nor do they change one species into another different one, but rather they make one species of metal better, such as making silver or gold out of tin or brass. This is not surprising, as we see silk produced from worms and glass from a plant, as is held in the *Book on the Properties of Things* <note>Referring to the popular medieval encyclopedia *De proprietatibus rerum* by Bartholomeus Anglicus.</note> where it discusses the Alchemist. For all metals proceed from sulfur and mercury. But from the power of the elements, there is a greater influence in one place than in another, from which it happens that in one place or mine, it becomes tin, in another silver, and in another gold. Since, therefore, art imitates nature <note>A fundamental legal and philosophical maxim: "ars imitatur naturam."</note> [Digest, on adoptions], Alchemists do not seem to sin, if through the power of herbs and stones...

<summary>This page presents a legal defense of alchemy, arguing that it is a natural art rather than a sin or forgery. Jurists like Oldradus argue that because all metals share a common origin in sulfur and mercury, refining them is a natural improvement rather than an impossible change of species.</summary>

...of a stone, or of other elements, they improve a metal into a more precious metal, since both are of the same species and principle. This is made consistent with the *Institutes* <note>Citing the *Institutes* of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law</note> [on how obligations are dissolved]: "it is consistent that what was introduced by words be removed by words." Augustine says in the book *The City of God* that there are in corporeal things, throughout all the elements, certain hidden seminal reasons <note>original: "seminariæ rationes." A concept where God implanted the potential for all life and forms into matter at creation.</note>, which, when a temporal and causal opportunity is granted, burst forth into their due species according to their own modes and limits. This is found literally in the section [of Canon Law] 26. q. 5, "nor is it a wonder," before the middle of the chapter. Likewise, we see that the penalty is not great for one who even knowingly gives brass for gold, for he is held by the crime of swindling <term>stellionatus: a Roman legal term for fraud or "shifty" dealings where a crime doesn't have a specific name</term>, the penalty for which is extraordinary <note>Referring to the *Digest* (ff), the primary source of Roman civil law.</note>. Furthermore, in our own days, we had Master Arnaldus de Villanova <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician, alchemist, and religious reformer</note> at the Roman Court, a supreme Physician and Theologian (about whom I wrote a counsel regarding the observation of fasts), who was also a great Alchemist; he allowed the rods of gold that he made to be submitted to every test.

->*From Andreas de Isernia <note>A famous Italian jurist (c. 1280–1353) who specialized in feudal law.</note>, in the Title on Feuds: "What are Regalia."*<-

What about Alchemy and Alchemists? Say that if they make sophisticated <note>original: "sophisticatum," meaning counterfeit, adulterated, or "imitation" gold</note> gold, they ought not to sell it for pure gold, because that is a falsehood. Nor is one freed from the charge of imitation by paying it out <note>Citing the *Digest* on the action of pledges</note>. Adulterated gold is not gold <note>Citing the *Digest* on legacies</note>. If, however, he should make true gold, he must not strike the prince's coinage from it without the prince's order; [otherwise] this gold would belong to the maker. For it is not illegal to sell true gold for true gold. For nothing forbids art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects, just as Saint Augustine says in *On the Trinity* regarding those things done by the art of demons. Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] says this in the *Summa Theologica* [2a 2ae, question 79], concerning things done regarding voluntary exchange. Add this regarding alchemy: whether it is permitted to practice Alchemy, say according to Oldradus in his counsels: that it is, provided it is not done through the magic arts, or through another art hated by the laws. See the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous dictionary of cases of conscience by Angelus Carletus de Clavasio (1491).</note> under the word "Alchemy." Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, the most influential jurist of the Middle Ages.</note> abhors it.

->*From Baldus of Perugia <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a leading jurist and student of Bartolus.</note>, in the same Title on Feuds, number 5.*<-

Likewise regarding coinage: that is, the authority for making public coins. Andreas de Isernia asks here about those who practice Alchemy: and he says that if "so much is spent for so much" and "such for such" <note>This refers to the principle of fair exchange or the intrinsic value being equal to the asking price.</note>, without any falsification of form or matter, the Alchemist is not punished: because it is an art invented by a perspicacious genius, and as if by a philosopher. Lord Oldradus also gave counsel on this in his writings, and Johannes Andreae <note>A celebrated expert in Canon Law (c. 1270–1348).</note> speaks of it in his additions to the *Speculum* in the section on the crime of forgery.

->*From Lord Fabianus de Monte S. Severino <note>A 16th-century legal scholar.</note> in the Treatise on Buying and Selling, question 5, number 8.*<-

But here it is asked incidentally, whether an Alchemist, or one practicing Alchemy, is punished for forgery. You should say no, because it is an art invented by a perspicacious genius, where "so much is spent for so much," and "such for such."

...without any falsification of form or matter, according to Andreas de Isernia and Oldradus in their legal counsels <note>Oldradus da Ponte (died 1335) was a highly influential civil and canon lawyer whose opinions were cited for centuries</note>, as Baldus reports in the chapter *Which things are regalian rights* <note>original: "quæ sint regal." Referring to the "regalia," or the rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign</note>. Johannes Andreae holds the same in his additions to the *Speculum* <note>The *Speculum Iudiciale*, a standard medieval textbook on legal procedure</note> under the title "on the crime of forgery." This was further confirmed by the Abbot of Sicily <note>Also known as Panormitanus, a leading expert in Canon Law</note> in the second chapter "on sorcery," where he cites Oldradus’s 69th counsel: that although one species cannot be changed into another except by God (as stated in the Decree, 26th question, 5th chapter, "The Bishops"), nevertheless, in this case, one species is not being transmuted into another. This is because all metals proceed from the same source and origin—namely, from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivo: "living silver" or mercury</term>. Rather, where there is a better influence of the stars, a more precious metal is produced there. Therefore, through the influence of the stars and with herbs and precious stones which possess great virtues, one species of metal can, according to him, be transmuted into another more precious species. 

But take heed, because Saint Thomas Aquinas says in the *Summa Theologica* <note>original: "secunda secundæ q. 77," referring to the section on justice and cheating in trade</note> that this is true only when the true art is known and "true gold" is made, for nothing prohibits the use of natural art. Otherwise, he says it is not safe if alchemical gold is given as true gold, since many properties exist in true gold that are not in the alchemical kind, such as the power of gladdening the heart and driving away many sicknesses.

->*From Albericus de Rosate in his Dictionary, under the word "Alchemy."*<-

As to whether alchemy is lawful, see below under the heading "Alchemy," and see below under "buying," section 5, the verse beginning "from this it is clear." Is alchemy a condemned art, and does the alchemist sin? It seems so: because if anyone believes any creature can be made, or improved by being transferred into another species except by the Creator Himself, he is an infidel and worse than a pagan (referring to the Decree, 26th question, 3rd chapter, "The Bishops" near the end). Likewise, alchemists learn many things but never arrive at the truth of the science (chapter 7, "not a wonder," near the middle), for they provide the cause for many deceptions. Nor is it a science that leads to impiety, as is usually said of Astrology (distinction 37, chapter "If anyone," and the notes by Innocent on the chapter "on sorcery"). Indeed, alchemy cannot be done without the "boiling" <note>original: "decoctione," a process of heating or refining</note> of gold, which seems prohibited by law (The Code of Justinian, *On the public pursuit of gold*, book 10, law 1). 

On the contrary, one who produces gold or silver from tin, lead, or another base metal—provided he does not do this through the magic arts or any other art hateful to the laws—is not to be blamed (as stated in the first law of the 10th book of the Code, *On Treasures*). For such men are metal-workers <term>metallarii: miners or smiths</term> who, by their own labor, obtain benefits for themselves and the State. The laws favor them because of the "public utility" that seems to result from their office. For they may enter a field to search for metal even against the owner's will (Law 2, "Certain persons"), and it is noted there that this would not otherwise be permitted (as in the Digest, *On the acquisition of ownership of things*). Nor do they say that one species is changed into another, as is charged against them—for that is not possible—but they say that from one species of metal, another species can be transferred, such as gold or silver. Nor is this inconsistent; for we see sometimes from a living thing a dead one is produced, as in [the case of] worms pro- <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "pro-"</note>

...just as there are creatures producing silk, and as glass is produced from a plant <note>referring to the use of wood ash or soda-rich plants like kali in glassmaking</note>, this is much more possible in metals, in which there is a greater affinity. For they say and note in the book *On the Properties of Things* <note>original: "de proprietate rerum." This refers to the famous medieval encyclopedia by Bartholomeus Anglicus</note> regarding Alchemy, that all metals proceed from the same principle—namely, from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivo: "living silver" or mercury</term>—but by the power of the elements, they have a greater influence in one place than in another; thus, in one mine tin is formed, in another silver, and in another gold, and so on for the others. Since, therefore, art imitates nature (as seen in the Digest "On Adoptions," the law *adoptio*), alchemists do not seem to sin if, through the power of herbs, stones, or elements, they make silver from tin. For since they arise as if from the same principle and are similar, the transition is easier among things that share a common symbol <note>original: "habentibus symbolum." A concept from Aristotelian physics where elements with shared qualities can transform into one another more easily</note>. See the Institutes, "In what ways obligations are dissolved," § 7. Indeed, there are many powers implanted in herbs and stones (16, final question, final chapter). For, as Augustine says, there are certain hidden "seminal reasons" <term>seminariæ rationes: latent potentials or "seeds" within matter</term> in all corporeal things throughout all the elements, which, when a temporal and causal opportunity is given, burst forth into their due species according to their own modes and limits (and the 26th question, 3, near the end, and the 16th question, final, near the end). Therefore, if they attribute this power to God, they do not seem to sin. Nor is it a great penalty if you have pledged brass for gold, even knowingly (as in the Digest "On the action of a pledge," law 1, and "On the crime of stellionate," law 2 <note>Stellionate is an old legal term for fraud or "shifty" dealing</note>).

->*The same Albert [Bruno] in his Dictionary, under the word "purchase."*<-

On whether a sale is rendered illicit and invalid because of a defect in the thing sold, or because of its hidden quality. Thomas [Aquinas] says in the *Summa Theologica* (2.2, question 77, article 2) that regarding a thing which is sold, a threefold defect can be considered. One is according to the **species** of the thing, such as if brass <note>original: "aurichalcum," orichalcum or a gold-colored alloy</note> is sold for silver, or wine mixed with water is sold as pure. Another defect is according to the **quantity** of weight or measure, such as if someone knowingly uses a defective weight or an unjust measure. The third defect is on the part of the **quality**, for instance, if a sick animal is sold as if it were healthy. In these three cases, if the seller knowingly offends, he commits a fraud and the sale is illicit, and he is bound to make restitution. If, however, he did so ignorantly, he does not sin; nevertheless, when it comes to his notice, he is bound to compensate the buyer for the loss. And from this it is clear that it is illicit to sell alchemical gold or silver for the "true" kind, because it is not pure like true gold, nor does it possess entirely the same properties—such as the power of gladdening <note>original: "lætificandi." Gold was traditionally believed to have the medicinal property of cheering the heart and soul</note>, nor is it effective against certain illnesses like true gold. If, however, *true* gold were made through Alchemy, it would not be illicit to sell it as true, because nothing prohibits art from using certain natural causes to produce true and natural effects, as Augustine says in the book *On the Trinity*, regarding those things which are done by the art of demons.

*From Alberto Bruno in the treatise on the increase and decrease of money, in the 1st presupposition, numbers 13 and 14.*

# OF LAW #
<meta>catchword: because [quia]</meta>

...[Regarding coins], three things are principally considered: namely, the material, the form, and the estimation or value, according to Law 1, joined with the final law, along with the notes there, in the Code "On the Value of Money," book 11 <note>refers to the *Codex Justinianus*, book 11, title 'De veteris numismatis potestate'</note>. And it is noted by Baldus in the chapter *Quanto*, "On Oaths." For first, the material must be upright <note>original: "proba," meaning pure or standard</note> according to the said Law 1, and Law 1, paragraph 1 of the Digest "On the Contract of Purchase," and the said chapter *Quanto*. Hence, it would not be permitted to mint money from Alchemy, which is to be understood as sophistical <term>sophistica: deceptive or counterfeit</term> alchemy, not regarding that which is found to be true gold or silver. This is possible according to the notes by Johannes Andreae in the additions to the *Speculum* <note>a famous legal work by William Durand</note> in the Rubric "On the Crime of Forgery," who reports (without naming the author) the words of Oldradus <note>Oldradus da Ponte, a famous 14th-century jurist</note>, whose words are usually found in Counsel 74, beginning "Whether an Alchemist." This is treated more broadly by Johannes Andreae in chapter 2, "On Fortunetelling," and by Baldus and Andreas de Isernia in chapter 1, in the title "What are Regalities," in the *Usage of Fiefs*. And according to St. Thomas, *Secunda Secundae*, question 92, from which they conclude that Alchemy is a true and permitted science. Regarding this, see something by Alberto de Rosate in his *Dictionary* under the word "Alchemy." And Johannes Andreae says, as above, that in his time there was a Master Arnaldus de Villanova <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, a supreme Physician and Theologian, and a great Alchemist, who through that art made golden rods <note>original: "virgulas aureas"</note>, which he allowed to be submitted to every test. And he wrote one book on that science which impoverished a thousand men, either because it is not true, or because it is not understood. And since I had a certain colleague in the law who was sweating much in that art <note>i.e., working very hard at it</note>, I wished to see one marvelous experiment for the purpose of knowing more. For we had with us an old Alchemist, though he was very poor. And in my presence, that colleague of mine caused one ounce of most precious silver to be reduced to the likeness of gold, in weight, in melting, and in malleability—saving the color, because it was not saffron-yellow, but changed to the likeness of a leaden color. And that colleague of mine had a way of giving it a saffron color. And that material suffered and sustained <note>original: "patiebatur & sustinebat," meaning it withstood or passed</note> some experiments, but not the final test <term>extremum experimentum: likely the process of cupellation or a strong acid test used by goldsmiths</term>. And when mixed with an equal amount of precious gold, it seemed to be gold of twenty characters <term>characterum: carats</term>, or more or less, according to how well that material was prepared. And a certain great Prelate, as well as many old Alchemists, were amazed by that experiment. And one old Alchemist, thinking himself rich, thought he could reduce that material to the true species of gold; and he could not. He thought the art itself was illusory, especially since so many men in forty or fifty years had not seen such a notable experiment, which was nonetheless sophistical, so that I did not wish to see another experiment. Nor would it be permitted, without consulting the prince, to mix copper material into gold or silver when minting, according to the law "Whoever [clashes] coins," Digest "On Forgery," and as noted in Law 2 of the Code "On those who forge money."

# OF ALCHEMY #

...because it is an art invented by human ingenuity, as if by a Philosopher. Thus say Andrea di Isernia <note>a prominent 14th-century Neapolitan jurist</note> and Baldus in the first chapter of "What are Regalities," and Baldus reports that Oldradus <note>Oldradus da Ponte, an influential legal consultant to the Papal court</note> advised as much in his own legal counsels.

->*Johannes de Platea on Law 1, in the Code "On the Price of Silver," which discusses the bringing in of treasure, book 10.*<-

I ask incidentally: mention was made above regarding those who seek and extract natural gold; but what of those who seek artificial gold? Do Alchemists pursue such gold lawfully, and can it be used for payment, or do they instead commit the crime of forgery? Johannes Andreae, in his additions to the *Speculum* under the title "On Forgery," commends those Alchemists who, through the mastery of their art and without using magic or other prohibited means <note>original: "sine re magica vel alia lege prohibita"</note> (referencing the single law of the Code "On Treasure"), create something precious from base metal. They do not change one species into another entirely different one, but rather they improve one species of metal—such as making silver or gold from tin or copper. For all metals originate from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the traditional name for mercury</term>, but through the power of the Elements, tin is formed in one location, gold in another, and silver in another, and so on for each. Therefore, since art imitates nature (as noted in the Law "Adoption" in the Digest "On Adoptions"), Alchemists do not sin if, by the power of herbs, stones, or other Elements, they refine a base metal into a more precious one, since both were of the same species and origin. For there exist in physical things, throughout all the elements, certain hidden "seminal reasons" <term>rationes seminales: latent natural principles or "seeds" that allow for the development of specific forms</term> which, when the right timing and causal opportunity are granted, burst forth into their proper species in their own ways and limits; so says the law in *26. q. 5. nec mirum* <note>a reference to Gratian's Decretum, suggesting that natural wonders are not necessarily miracles or magic</note>. Regarding this type of Alchemist, see Andrea di Isernia and Baldus in the title "What are Regalities," column 10. However, because such an operation is subject to many deceptions—as the said chapter "nor is it a wonder" warns—and because it is not a science of piety (referencing Distinction 37, "If anyone learns Grammar"), I advise that one should abstain from its practice. Nevertheless, Master Arnaldus de Villanova <note>a famous 13th-century physician, alchemist, and religious reformer</note>, a supreme Physician and Theologian as well as a great Alchemist, used to produce gold rods at the Roman court which he allowed to be submitted to every possible test. Indeed, if this work is performed so that the results are turned toward a pious cause, it is perfected by the permission of Almighty God (as in the cited texts "nor is it a wonder," "nor therefore anyone," and "let us read").

->*There follows a contrary argument by Angelus in his Summa under the word "Alchemy."*<-

Is it permissible to practice Alchemy? I respond: Oldradus holds in his counsels that it is, provided they do not act through magic or other means hateful to the law, as stated in the single law of the Code "On Treasure." For such men are metal-workers who, by their own labor, provide for themselves and for the benefit of the Commonwealth (Code "On Metals," Law 1). The laws favor them because of the public utility that seems to result from their profession. Indeed, they are permitted to enter a field, even against the owner's will, to search for metal (Law 3 and the law "Certain persons," with the notes there in the Code "On Metals"), a thing which is otherwise not allowed.

# ON THE LAW #

of the single law <note>original: "d. l. un." referring to the Code "On Treasure"</note> and the Digest "On acquiring ownership of things," law 3. The reason is that (as is said in the book *On the Property of Things* <note>a famous medieval encyclopedia by Bartholomaeus Anglicus</note> under the entry for Alchemy) all metals proceed from the same principle: namely, from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivo: mercury</term>. However, due to the power of the elements which have a greater influence in one place than in another, tin is produced in one mine and silver in another. Therefore, since art imitates nature (as per the Digest "On Adoption," the law on adoption), it is not a sin if, through the power existing in elements or herbs, alchemists wish to make silver out of tin. For since they exist in the same principle, the transition is easier for those things sharing a common symbol <note>original: "habentibus symbolum," a term from Aristotelian physics regarding shared qualities between elements</note>. See the Institutes "By what means obligations are released," section 1. Since many powers are implanted in herbs and stones (26, question 5, near the middle), this is not surprising.

But notwithstanding these arguments, I believe that alchemy is illicit for many reasons. First, because no one is found who possesses the true art of this kind, even though it is claimed of many. But experience proves this false. Furthermore, we see that those practicing it commonly consume much of their wealth, and one must judge by what commonly happens. Hence it is said of them in the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3: *always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth.* They perform many experiments, and yet perfection is never reached; they consume their time and their lives. Nor does that which they produce have the truth of gold or silver, but only the appearance. Therefore, alchemists are simply to be condemned. 

This is evidently proven because no one wishes to practice it in public, which shows they act wrongly, because they "hate the light" <note>An allusion to the Gospel of John 3:20: "For everyone who does evil hates the light."</note>. And if they ever do produce something real, it is either done at a loss once expenses are calculated, or by some deception—such as secretly inserting real gold—or by some diabolical fallacy. In order to keep them intent on such work, the devil sometimes makes real gold for them by secretly adding real gold. Since, therefore, such an exercise is against the public utility (as is clear from the waste of resources) and because they commonly use these materials to make counterfeit money <term>monetam falsam: forged or debased coinage</term>, those who practice it are simply to be condemned.

Is alchemy a sin and a rejected art? Albericus <note>Albericus de Rosate</note> argues this in his *Dictionary of Civil Law* under the entry "Alchemy." Baldus in chapter 1, "What are Regalities," and Thomas Aquinas in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 77, article 2, finally seem to hold that they do not appear to sin if they attribute their work to God. This is because they do not change one species into another (as is charged against them), because that is impossible. Rather, they say that from one species of metal (namely, tin) another species of metal (namely, gold or silver) can be produced. This is not inconsistent with reason.
