For all metals proceed from the same principle: namely, from sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum vivo: mercury</term>. But through the power of the elements, they have a greater influence in one place than in another; thus, in one mine tin is formed, in another silver, and in another gold. Therefore, the practice is lawful, provided it is not done through the magic art or any other art hateful to the laws <note>original: "l. 1. C. de thesaur. lib. 10," referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 10, Title 18, on Treasure</note>. For such people are to be praised. 

Add, however, the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous 15th-century manual for confessors by Angelus Carletus</note> under the entry "Alchemy," which holds that this art is illicit for many reasons. First, because no one is found who possesses the true art of this kind; though much is claimed by many, experience proves it false. Furthermore, we see that those practicing it commonly consume much of their wealth, and one must judge by what commonly happens. Hence it is said of them in the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3: <note>original: "2 Tim 3:7"</note> *Always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth.* They perform many experiments and never reach perfection; they consume both time and life. Nor does that which they produce have the true nature of gold or silver, but only the appearance. 

Therefore, alchemists are simply to be condemned. This is evidently proven because no one wishes to practice it in public, which suggests they are acting wrongly; for they "hate the light." And if they ever do produce something true, it is either done at a loss once expenses are calculated, or through some deception—such as substituting true gold—or by some diabolical fallacy. To keep them paying attention to such things, [the devil] sometimes produces true gold for them by secretly adding it. Since such an exercise is against the public utility—as is clear from the waste of resources and because they commonly use it to make counterfeit money—those practicing it are simply to be condemned.

But I hold the common opinion: that this art is licit. The reasons given in the *Summa Angelica* do not prove the art itself is illicit just because no one possesses the true art; that is a failure of the practitioner, not a defect of the art itself. Nor do the other reasons hold up, as is self-evident. Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus hold the same view. As to whether profit from alchemy is licit, or if selling its products is unjust, Thomas says (in the place cited above) that if true gold is made through alchemy, it is not illicit to sell it as true. For nothing prohibits using art and certain natural principles to produce natural effects. However, if it does not have the true species of gold, the sale is unjust, as it is then sophisticated <term>sophisticatum: adulterated or counterfeit</term> gold.

# ON THE LAW #

<page-num>60</page-num>

<header>Of the Law</header>

...they have approved [this art]. Only one person contradicts it: Angelus, in his *Summa Angelica* <note>A 15th-century alphabetical manual for confessors by Angelus Carletus de Clavasio</note>. But aside from the fact that the authority of a single Doctor <note>A learned authority or teacher of the church</note> against the common opinion is of no weight, as everyone knows, there was certainly one great canon lawyer, Jerome of Zayetin <note>Hieronymus de Zanitinis, a prominent 15th-century Italian jurist</note>, who in his chapter on "accusations" responded most precisely to each and every one of Angelus's arguments. This is the diamond-hard foundation built from the authority of great and famous Doctors and Jurists—not to mention the authority of Thomas Aquinas, who in two or three places most clearly approved of Alchemy. Pliny also writes in book 34, chapter 4, that there were Alchemists in the times of the Emperor Gaius <note>Gaius Caesar, better known as Caligula</note>. Nor is it relevant what he says—that their craft was not profitable. First, because in the question of whether Alchemy is a lawful art, one does not ask whether it is lucrative or fruitful, but only whether it is prohibited by divine or human law. Second, because it is possible that those craftsmen of whom he speaks were not sufficiently skilled, while others might be more skilled; as we commonly say, there is a wide difference between craftsmen <note>original: "l. inter artif. ff. de solut." — a reference to the Digest of Roman Law, specifically regarding the varied skill levels of artisans</note>. Furthermore, the things Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> relates about Alchemy and the artificial making of gold are marvelous: that the Egyptians were able to sustain a long war against the tyrant Diocletian, relying on their art—that is, their craftsmanship.

But let us see certain other arguments. For Aristotle writes in the *Metaphysics*, books 2 and 4, that art imitates nature in certain things, and that many natural things can be produced and perfected by art. He names *colcothar* <term>colcothar: iron oxide residue from vitriol</term> and *calchantum* <term>chalcanthum: copperas or blue vitriol</term> as examples, saying that those two inks <note>or pigments</note> are not only born in minerals but can also be made by art. Let a third example be set forth concerning salt. For (as Pliny says in book 31) salt is either made or produced [naturally]. In Poland there is mineral salt; in France it is artificial, and the property, nature, and efficacy of the latter is the same as the former. The fourth is electrum, which Pliny (book 33, chapter 4) and many others write is not only natural but also artificial. Legal texts speak of this artificial and manufactured electrum in the laws regarding legacies and the acquisition of property. The fifth is quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term>, which the aforementioned Pliny (book 33, chapter 1) says is in one form native and in another artificial; and he calls the latter *Hydrargyrum* <note>original: "Hydrargyrum," from the Greek for "water-silver"</note> to distinguish it from the other. Guillaume Philandrier <note>A 16th-century French scholar</note>, in his commentaries on Vitruvius, counts four types of it: two native and two artificial. In the same place, he shows that steel, sandarach <note>a red arsenic mineral</note>, verdigris, copperas, and cinnabar are sometimes produced naturally and sometimes made by human art. Since these things are so, we can conclude without absurdity: just as art can imitate nature in so many other things, it is not unreasonable to say that it can imitate nature in the working of gold and silver. Certainly Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath</note> writes in the 16th book of *On Subtlety*, and many say this is known to them, that copper can be made from iron by applying copperas <note>original: "chalchanto"</note>; and Cardano in the same...

<meta>This page continues the legal and historical defense of alchemy, moving from the opinions of canon lawyers to the testimony of historical figures and the scrutiny of both Divine and Civil law. # OF ALCHEMY #

<page-num>61</page-num>

<header>OF ALCHEMY.</header>

...in the same book he testifies that a certain pharmacist from Treviso converted quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> into gold in the presence of the most illustrious Prince of the Venetians and the wise senators. It is true that Julius Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar and physician</note> denies that he believes this, but he relies on a weak argument: namely, that if the Venetians had seen this—since they are of such great greed (as he himself writes) that they would even make a treaty with the Turk, the enemy of the Christian name—they would never have let that pharmacist go. Instead, they would have forced him with tortures to reveal his art, and perhaps would have hanged him from the gallows. But it is likely that the pharmacist, by public safe-conduct and perhaps even a hostage or other security, had protected and provided for himself. It is certainly not honorable to suspect everyone of everything. 

It is well-established that there were countless grave men in past centuries, and there are now, who practiced this art and declared it to be profitable for them. Among these were Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and polymath</note>, the Count of Treviso, Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, author of the alchemical poem "Chrysopoeia"</note>, Avicenna <note>The influential Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina</note>, Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry"</note>, Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, the Majorcan mystic and philosopher</note>, Bonus of Ferrara, Morienus, and Tolod., and especially Arnaldus de Villanova, a most excellent physician. We see also in our own times Jean Fernel <note>Johannes Fernelius (1497–1558), a French physician who famously served the French court</note>, considered a prince in the medical art, who in his book *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "de abdit. rer. caus."</note> held the same art perfectly and was practiced in it, although toward the end he jokingly eludes the unwary reader with three verses from Augurellus. However, the authority of that one man, Fernel, outweighs the authority of many other contradicting physicians (as some say).

But primarily and before everything in the question of whether any art is lawful, one must consider whether it is prohibited by any divine or human law. For lawful or unlawful things are distinguished thus in the *Digest* <note>The author cites the "Digest," a major part of the Roman Law code compiled by Emperor Justinian</note>: *Law 1, on concubines; the Law "When the Senate," on doubtful matters; Law 1 and throughout the entire title on colleges and corporate bodies.* 

As for Divine law, I certainly find no text where Alchemy and the making of gold are prohibited, even though the divine legislator Moses prosecutes countless vices and crimes in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Nor do I think he prohibited distillations and the use of alembics <note>Alembic: an early chemical apparatus used for distillation</note>, or the making of gold and silver, any more than he prohibited the casting of jewelry, rings, and other such ornaments with which Solomon and other Kings were adorned. It is unknown to no one how great the use of gold plates and foil was among the people of God, especially in the Temple of Jerusalem. 

As for Civil law, certainly not a single letter in the *Digests*, the *Code*, the *Institutes*, or the *Novels* <note>These comprise the "Corpus Juris Civilis," the foundation of Western civil law</note> could be shown that pertains to the prohibition of Alchemy; rather, the art of Smelters <note>original: "Fusorum ars"</note> is approved, praised, and decorated with rewards in *Law 1 of the Code on the excuse of craftsmen.* Thus, Vessel-makers and Smelters are frequently named, as if practicing a (without controversy) legitimate art, in the law *In the presence of Labeo*... in the laws regarding obligations and actions, and in the laws regarding the legacy of gold and silver. And regarding Miners <note>original: "Metallariis"</note>, that they practice a legitimate art—

# OF THE LAW #

<page-num>62</page-num>

<header>Of the Law</header>

<meta>catchword: C. nor</meta>

It cannot be doubted from the title of the Code on Miners <note>original: "tit. Cod. de Metallarijs lib. xj." Referring to the Codex Justinianus, Book 11</note>. Regarding canon law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority (the Church)</note>, two texts are usually opposed: but it is easy to respond to both. The first is in the chapter *Spondent* <note>A famous decree by Pope John XXII issued around 1317</note> from the *Extravagantes* <note>A collection of papal decrees not included in the major organized bodies of Canon Law</note> concerning the crime of forgery. **There, Pope John XXII condemns alchemists, yet he does not sentence them to death, but only to perpetual infamy.** But that text was not written infinitely and generally about all alchemists. Rather, it specifically and properly concerns only those who (to use the words of the text) fashion gold or silver through a sophistical <term>sophistical|In a legal context, this means "fraudulent" or "deceptive"—creating something that looks like gold but lacks its substance</term> transmutation. Therefore, that text does not pertain to those who fashion gold that is not rejected or adulterated, but is upright and true. 

Just as Giovanni Andrea <note>A celebrated 14th-century Italian canon lawyer</note> testifies in his additions to the *Speculum*, Arnald of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> in his time used to make rods of gold which he submitted to every test. Therefore, all the Doctors, both civil lawyers and canon lawyers, did not care for that decree <note>original: "extravagantem"</note> of the Pope, as we said above. Indeed, Giovanni Augurello, the Great Poet, freely dedicated and presented his little work on alchemy <note>The poem "Chrysopoeia," published in 1515</note> to Pope Leo X, to whom it is well known that the gift was most pleasing. This response to that text should therefore suffice; not to mention that many today do not accept the authority of that legislator, who was the Pope; and they say that if his authority is approved in one chapter, it would also have to be approved in the next chapter, where he established certain things according to his own whim concerning the Franciscans and other monks, and the law "he who is not compelled" <note>original: "l. qui non cogitur ff. de judic."</note> would have to be approved. 

The other text that is opposed is in Chapter *Episcopi*, Question 26, Case 5, which is said to be taken from the Council of Ancyra <note>The OCR reads "Auquirensi," a corruption of "Ancyrano," referring to a 4th-century church council</note>, and it is written thus: "Whoever believes that any creature can be made, or transformed for better or worse into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things, is an infidel." First, the citation of the "Council of Ancyra" <note>original: "Auquirensi"</note> is ridiculous because it never existed or could have existed. It should be corrected to AQUILEIA. But even more ridiculous is the citation of that text where they condemn those who believe a transformation into another species occurs. 

Certainly, this pertains to our question no more than what the Emperor writes: that it is possible for all things to be converted into money <note>original: "l. 2. C. de constit. pecun."</note>. For that text does not speak of species of metals or similar things, but of the species of persons: that is, of sorcerous women, who said that at night they were transformed into various species of animals and wandered through the woods and groves with Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, frequently associated in medieval church law with the "Wild Hunt" and early concepts of witchcraft</note>. Therefore, in the section "If indeed Satan" <note>original: "§. fiquidem fatanas"</note>, the text says: "he transforms himself into the species of different persons." Therefore, it is ridiculous to twist a text that speaks of the diabolical transformation of persons toward the transformation of metals, which can be done through the industry and skill of certain craftsmen without any diabolical or magical artifice, as Thomas Aquinas <note>The influential 13th-century theologian who argued that alchemical gold was real if it possessed the true qualities of gold</note> shows in the aforementioned places. Indeed, there is a text under the same question in...

<summary>This page defends alchemy against two major Canon Law objections, arguing that Pope John XXII only banned fraudulent gold-making and that prohibitions against "transformation" refer to witchcraft and demonic illusions, not the physical craft of metallurgy.</summary>

# OF ALCHEMY #

<page-num>63</page-num>

<header>OF ALCHEMY.</header>

<meta>catchword: C. nor</meta>

<margin>C. nor is it a wonder,</margin> where it is written thus: There are within bodily things, throughout all the elements, certain hidden seminal principles <note>original: "seminariæ rationes." A philosophical concept, rooted in St. Augustine, suggesting that God placed "seeds" of all potential future things within the initial creation</note>, which, when a temporal or causal opportunity is given, burst forth into their proper species. I will also add this: that our laws approve of medicine made from poisons, or from poisonous things, as if those things which are poisonous by nature can, through art and skill, be corrected and changed into health-giving substances, as the text implies regarding the Mithridatic remedy <note>Mithridatum was a famous complex "universal antidote" used in antiquity and the Middle Ages</note> in the law *quod saepe*, section *venena* <note>original: "l. quod sæpe, §. venena. ff. de contr. empt." A reference to the Digest (Pandects) of Roman Law regarding the sale of poisonous substances for medicinal use</note>.

There remains that argument: that many alchemists produce counterfeit money; many have also been sorcerers, impious, atheists, and necromancers. It is also said that Ramon Llull <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath often associated with alchemy</note> and Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine</note> were defiled by magical arts. The piety and honesty of these disputants is to be praised; yet they must be asked to consider that the vices of the practitioners are by no means to be imputed to the art itself. For the art is one thing, the artisan another. The use of an art is one thing, its abuse another <note>original: "l. quicunque & l. seq. ff. ad leg. Corn. de fals." Referring to the Cornelian Law on forgeries</note>, where the art of minting is approved; yet those who have tinted or fashioned gold or silver coins are condemned. Thus, in the first law of the Digest on extraordinary trials, professors of the medical art are praised, among whom, however, there are said to be impostors who use incantations, imprecations, and exorcisms. Likewise, "Mathematics" is simply condemned in the Code concerning sorcerers <note>original: "l. 2. C. de malefic." In late Roman law, "mathematicians" often referred specifically to astrologers and fortune-tellers</note>, even though not all mathematicians should be condemned, but only the impostors. Thus, poisoners are punished by death <note>original: "l. capitalium. §. venenarij ff de pœn."</note>, even though the poisons themselves are not condemned, as was just said regarding the law *quod saepe*. Indeed, if arts were to be condemned because of the abuse of their practitioners, which art would be approved today? Would it be Jurisprudence [Law], in which there are so many pettifoggers <term>pettifogger|A legal practitioner of low status who uses unethical or "shyster" methods</term>? Or Medicine, in which there are so many poisoners <note>original: "benefici," likely a typo for "venefici" (poisoners/quacks)</note>? Or Theology, in which there are so many sophists? Therefore, judgment and selection should be applied: let the chaff be separated from the grain on the threshing floor; the bad fish from the good in the net; the counterfeit coins from the upright ones in the Republic. Let the harshest punishments, investigations, and inquiries be established against those who sophisticate gold or silver, and against forgers and corrupters of money, as opposed to skilled artisans. But (as the Legal Consultant says) "the penalty for a crime committed by another should be removed from those who are touched by no fault" <note>original: "l. ult. D. de bon. damnat." A principle that one should not be punished for the sins of others in the same field</note>.

->F I N I S.<-

<summary>This page concludes a legal defense of alchemy by arguing that the existence of frauds, sorcerers, and counterfeiters does not invalidate the science itself, comparing it to corruption found in law, medicine, and theology. It emphasizes the legal principle that an art should be judged by its proper use rather than its abuse by "impostors."</summary>

### TO THE MOST EXCELLENT MAN
# PETER SEVERINUS, DANE
### PHYSICIAN TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF DENMARK.
### *Thomas Moffet, Englishman*
-> sends greetings. <note>original: "εὖ πράττειν" (eu prattein), a Greek greeting meaning "to fare well" or "to do well."</note> <-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, surrounded by foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

Ever since I turned my mind to the love of chemistry <note>original: "Philochemiæ."</note>, most distinguished Severinus: I have greatly desired that its excellence might become known to every student of medicine. Indeed, I have drawn such health and sweetness from it that I would hardly consider it the part of a man, let alone a philosopher, not to wish it shared with others. However, when I perceived that your most ingenious "Idea" <note>A reference to Severinus's influential 1571 book, *Idea Medicinae Philosophicae* (The Idea of Philosophical Medicine), which defended Paracelsian principles.</note>—a work worthy of immortality <note>original: "cedro digniffimam," literally "worthy of cedar oil," used in antiquity to preserve precious scrolls from decay.</note>—was not received with sufficiently high honor by the common crowd of physicians, and that you had lost both your oil <note>A play on the Latin proverb *oleum et operam perdere* (to lose both oil and labor), meaning to waste one's efforts fruitlessly.</note> (with which you intended to soften stones) and nearly all your labor: I feared indeed that they would act much more unfairly toward this little book of mine, since they were in no way moved by the charm <note>original: "θέλγητρῳ" (thelgetrō).</note> of such elegant and divine speech as yours.

Perhaps it happened because, believing the "Antichemists" to be dry and sober men, you thought they should be bathed not with salt <note>In classical rhetoric, "salt" represents wit, sharp criticism, or stinging truth.</note> but with oil, and should be led to the perception of truth by soft speech, as if by some Theban plectrum <note>A reference to the myth of Amphion of Thebes, whose music was so beautiful it moved even the stones to form the city walls; Moffet suggests Severinus tried to move "stony" doctors with gentle persuasion.</note>. I, however, am of a different mind, and I am entirely of this opinion: that they are no longer to be bathed with oil, but rather rubbed hard with salt, and must be awakened either by the branding iron of the satirists or the stings of the logicians. For many of them have begun to hold Chemistry in such hatred that they shudder at the mere mention of its name, and (such is the foolish intemperance of their minds) they are immediately forced to vomit. Others, indeed, vehemently praise Chemical remedies: but as often as <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Roman god of fire, here representing the alchemical furnace or the process of heat-driven transformation.</note> has committed a fault through their own negligence,

### DEDICATION

...sent, they so often attack the art anew, or malign its teacher. Nor is the number of those at all small who grant the chemist full honor only so long as he practices outside the province of metals and minerals. For they believe that one must abstain from these minerals with greater religious dread than from a horned viper <note>original: "ceraste."</note> or a common serpent; but by what shadow of reason they do this, I cannot sufficiently grasp. For if they loathe the poison of minerals, why do they employ the viper? For no animal is found more leprous, nor any mineral so noxious. 

Add furthermore that God has instilled such an <term>antipathy <note>original Greek: "ἀντιπάθειαν" (antipatheian). In Renaissance medicine, this refers to a natural, occult repulsion between two things.</note></term> between humans and serpents—such as you will never see between man and minerals—so great, indeed, that at the mere sight of them, as if seeing a public enemy of the human race, we tremble all over. Then, since mineral salt is found not only in every vegetable by which we are nourished or changed, but also in every animal: surely it is necessary either to provide nothing at all to the sick, or to approach the use of minerals, however reluctantly. 

Besides, since we know this order of the sublunary liturgy <note>The "liturgy" or service of the world below the moon, referring to the natural cycle of life and sustenance.</note> was prescribed by God—so that minerals might supply nourishment to vegetables, these to beasts, and beasts to men—how great (good God!) is the stupidity, what ignorance bewitches us, that we do not acknowledge the greatest similarity between humans and minerals? 

More correctly, in my opinion, spoke he who called man a <term>Microcosm <note>From the Greek "mikros kosmos," meaning "little world." This is the central Renaissance idea that the human body contains all the elements and principles of the entire universe.</note></term>: for in his nature is placed something of God, of Angels, of beasts, of plants, of the devil, and finally of the whole universe; and certainly not without merit. For in truth, as much virtue as dwells in us, so much of God is within; as much wickedness, so much of the devil; as much reason, so much of the Angels; as much movement and voluntary sense, so much of the beast; as much growth, so much of the plant; as much of salt, sulfur, and mercury, so much of the minerals. For he was made...

### EPISTOLA

...is man, who like all other composite things is made from the mineral of the earth: and all things, after the body has been broken down <note>original: "analysin." In this context, it refers to the chemical or natural decomposition of the body into its constituent parts.</note>, will return sooner or later to their own dust. But why do I bring these "owls to you," who spend your life in "Athens"? <note>This is a classical idiom (noctuas Athenas) meaning to bring something to a place that already has plenty of it; Moffet is saying it is unnecessary to explain these truths to someone as wise as Severinus.</note> Or why should I speak to those haters of wisdom <note>original: "Misosophos."</note> who, like parrots, ignore the teacher who instructs them, and will never escape from their own labyrinths—full of monsters as they are—even with the help of Ariadne’s thread? Nevertheless, it pleased me to attempt something to call them back, if not in the hope of making progress, then at least out of a desire to take the risk: for truly **the Achaeans came to Troy by trying.** <note>original Greek: "ἐς Τροίλω πειρώμενοι ἦλθον Ἀχαιοί." An ancient proverb suggesting that great deeds require persistence and trial.</note> **O best of children, through trial all things are accomplished.** <note>original Greek: "Καλλίστα παίδων, πείρᾳ θὴν πάντα τελεῖται." A quote from the poet Theocritus.</note> 

There are many reasons why I should dedicate these first fruits <note>original: "præludia," literally "preludes" or "practice exercises" of an army.</note> of our army to you. First, there is your extraordinary kindness toward my countrymen, which you revealed two years ago in your homeland to our most illustrious ambassador, Peregrine Bertie <note>Peregrine Bertie, 13th Baron Willoughby de Eresby (1555–1601), a prominent English diplomat and soldier.</note>—son of the most noble Duke of Suffolk—and to me especially; you opened your heart to us not by the bushel or the peck, but by the full granary. 

Next, because to dedicate a work on medical well-being <note>original Greek: "εὐεξίαν" (euexian), referring to a state of vigorous health.</note> to men unskilled in medicine (as most nobles and senators are) seems as pointless as offering a farmer a speech in praise of Monarchy, or offering a soldier a treatise on the science of agriculture. But above all, I was moved by the contemplation of your singular learning and your proven expertise in this cause, O excellent Severinus. Refreshed by the mere shadow of your reputation, I easily persuade myself that I shall truly and solidly triumph over all those who revile chemical remedies. 

You would have received this *Defense* <note>original: "Apologiam."</note> last year, had I not been waiting day by day for your own "golden response" against the opponent of Paracelsus <note>original: "Antiparacelsistam." This likely refers to Thomas Erastus, a major critic of Paracelsian medicine.</note>. But since I know that—whether due to the ingratitude of the age, the sweetness of silence, or being called away by royal business—you have not yet sent the auxiliary forces of chemistry, I considered it my duty to seize upon the arrogant chemical-haters <note>original: "Misochemicos."</note> in the meantime. I intend to strike down their haughtiness <note>original Greek: "ὑψηλοκαρδίαν" (hypsēlokardian).</note> with this first skirmish, as if with the [sling] <note>The catchword "fundula" suggests the next page begins with a reference to a small sling, continuing the David and Goliath imagery.</note> of a single little shepherd.

# TO THE STUDENTS OF PURE OR CHEMICAL MEDICINE
### Thomas Moffet, Physician, sends greetings.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

I find that saying of the Comic poet <note>Likely referring to the Roman playwright Terence or Plautus, who were frequently cited for their moral maxims.</note> to be quite wise, my dearest brothers: *That a wise man is driven to take action by these three things: Necessity, Law, and Custom.* Had it been otherwise, I would have refrained not only from this kind of writing, but from the publication of any of my books at all. For I see such a widespread ease for anyone to send their works to the press, that even the most shameless **Venus** <note>Used here as a metaphor for lustful or indecent literature.</note> and any foolish opinion whatsoever has obtained its own printing. However, since it is necessary to encourage you through writings—you whom I cannot reach with a living voice—pardon shall be granted (if I am not mistaken) to necessity; and it will be attributed to me not as a passion for writing, but as a spirit for teaching the truth. 

Furthermore, we are warned by the brevity of nature and life that trees must be planted, whether early or late, which may benefit a future age; and that man was created for a life of citizenship, and thus also for the distribution of those things he has received from God, the Best and Greatest, to others. 

Moreover, I might seem to feel too little honor toward Zwinger, Aragosius, Severinus, and my other most excellent teachers (whom Hippocrates commands us **to hold equal to our parents** <note>original Greek: "ἴσα γενέτῃσιν ἡγήσασθαι." This is a famous line from the Hippocratic Oath, emphasizing the debt of gratitude a student owes his teacher.</note>), if I did not dare to freely defend their chemical remedies (in which they especially delight) against any enemy, when they are sprinkled with various accusations by impudent men. I must keep their innocence, their immunity, and their rights intact and protected <note>original: "sartum tectum," a legal phrase meaning "in good repair" or "undamaged."</note> by every means and muscle. 

Nor would I do these things for their sake alone (since to rely on the authority of men in a scientific <note>original: "Physica," referring to the study of the natural world.</note> dispute seems plainly **absurd** <note>original Greek: "ἄτοπον."</note>), unless I also saw in the reality of the matter that physicians who lack chemical remedies are like smiths who use a dull axe, or perhaps one broken in the middle, for their cutting. Finally, since I see it is customary for the most distinguished men to enter into every argument which might remove from them not only the crime but even the accusation—

...separate the group; and may assert their innocence both in speech and in writing before the people. For now, driven by I know not what sting of pride, they are unable to keep any measure in their insults, and they triumph at every table over the books of that **Anti-Paracelsian**, as if they were the spoils of **Metellus**. <note>Quintus Caecilius Metellus was a Roman general famous for his triumphs; Moffet suggests his opponents are arrogantly celebrating a victory they haven't truly earned.</note> Yet if the poor wretches perceived how little strength his battle-line holds, and if they examined his arguments in the scales of truth, justice, and equality: surely they would flee from his banner with no less speed than **Mars**, that swiftest of the Gods, fled from the embrace and adulterous bed of **Venus** after he had exposed himself to the mockery of gods and men. <note>A reference to the Homeric myth where the god Vulcan caught Mars and Venus in a golden net while they were together, exposing them to the ridicule of the other Olympian gods.</note>

For in the first part, what else does he show us but the great impiety of **Theophrastus**? <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> Which surely theologians would have handled more accurately and more justly. For let doctors care for what belongs to doctors; *let smiths handle the tools of the smith*; <note>A Latin proverb meaning people should stick to their own area of expertise.</note> since he is also a man, he ought to have been more fairly disposed toward a fellow man—or at least not to have cast aside his humanity so far as to take delight in "slaughtering the dead" and raging against the deceased. What if Paracelsus, regarding the creation of the world and divine administration, felt something contrary to the Holy Scriptures? Did he differ in that from pagan writers? Or why do we not bear his fictions with the same mercy that we grant to those who hate church discipline (among whom this Anti-Paracelsian reveals himself to be not the least) or as we forgive the impiety of **Galen**? <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the classical authority on medicine whose theories the Paracelsians were challenging.</note> 

But since it is abundantly clear that he has overstepped the rules of <term>kata pantos</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ παντὸς; an Aristotelian logic term meaning "true of all cases."</note>, <term>kath' auto</term> <note>original Greek: καθ' αὑτὸ; meaning "essential" or "by its own nature."</note>, and <term>katholou proton</term> <note>original Greek: καθόλου πρῶτον; meaning "universally first." These three terms refer to Aristotle's requirements for a scientific demonstration.</note>, and even the very law of humanity: I do not wish to stir this mud any further, lest I stir up a most unpleasant odor for you (whom I have always intended to please), and hinder myself as I hasten toward greater matters. I know that the **Anti-chemists**, even if attacked by no one, will collapse under their own weight along with that god of the idolaters, and have already wasted away from a long-lasting heat of spontaneous fury. However, since they will know that I [wrote] this [little book] not so much with a mind for tormenting them or in expectation of a triumph, but for the sake of their own health...

Amen, yes, and amen.

# ON THE RIGHT AND EXCELLENCE OF CHEMICAL MEDICINES.

### An Apologetic Dialogue.

#### Philerastus the Chemist. <note>Philerastus is a fictional character whose name implies he is a "Lover of Erastus," the primary critic of chemical medicine.</note>

I have revealed to my teacher my plan for deceiving the Chemist; he praises, commends, and proclaims it, even promoting this work with his prayers, and he has equipped me with various kinds of weapons and a multitude of tricks. Yet, to be honest, I would rather fight with the Aetolian boar, with a bear, a lion, or a hydra <note>original: *excetra*; a multi-headed serpent or monster</note>, than with Chemists: who overwhelm anyone speaking to them with the foulest smell of sulfur or with mercurial fumes. I also hear that a certain Chemist dwells not far from here, who intends to pickle us Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the traditional authority on ancient medicine who relied on herbal humors rather than chemical minerals.</note> like herrings in salt, and then hang us up in the smoke to dry. By Pollux! Unless the sign deceives me, he lives here in the neighborhood—but look, here is the man coming out. Hear, heaven and earth, while I devise Daedalian <note>Referring to Daedalus, the mythological craftsman; meaning clever or labyrinthine deceits.</note> deceits and learn all of this man's skill through a new pretense. 

<term>Ch.</term> <note>The Chemist</note> Phew! I think either a wild cat or a weasel has passed this way, it smells so foul. 

<term>Ph.</term> <note>Philerastus</note> Should I go to him? Should I stop, should I stop? No, my mind is firm; I will seek him out, wherever on earth he has gone. 

<term>Ch.</term> Greetings, stranger. 

<term>Ph.</term> And greetings to you, neighbor. 

<term>Ch.</term> Whom do you seek so anxiously, guest? If I can be of any help in finding him, just command me.

**PHILERASTUS:** By Pollux <note>original: *Pol*, a common Roman oath</note>, I accept your kindness, and when I return home, I will gladly proclaim it. I am looking for a Chemist; the more effort you give to help me find him, the more closely I shall always love you. At the first opportunity, I will return the favor.

**CHEMIST:** Although hardly anyone is worthy of such a grand name, nevertheless, I will not deny that I am called so by the common people.

**PHILERASTUS:** Oh, how happy I, Philerastus, am! I see the very goods I have longed for right here in the harbor. What God, or what kind of God, has provided such an opportunity to anyone? My master, my patron, my most desired father, greetings!

**CHEMIST:** You are talking nonsense, Philerastus; for I do not remember me ever being your master, or you being my servant. But tell me, where have you set sail from? Where is your homeland?

**PHILERASTUS:** I set sail from Galenic Athens <note>The "Galenic Athens" refers to traditional medical universities that followed the ancient Greek physician Galen; Philerastus is signaling his departure from old-fashioned medical schools.</note>; my homeland is Germany.

**CHEMIST:** Why then did you come here, stranger? Why do you greet me as if to mock me? Why did you bid farewell to Galenic Athens to put in at this port?

**PHILERASTUS:** Because where I see nothing but the corruption of morals, a poverty of knowledge, and the emptying of purses, that is no desirable dwelling place, even if I were offered a scepter there.

**CHEMIST:** Careful with your words, I pray. I hardly think the men of such works are "Athenians"; but if they were such, you are right to flee, and you do well, stranger, to strictly abstain from their company.

**PHILERASTUS:** Indeed, the entire race of Athenians and Galenists are, in my opinion, among men like Monkshood, Wolfsbane, and Chameleon-plants <note>original: *Napelli, Aconita, Chamæleontes*. These are poisonous or deceptive plants; Philerastus suggests the traditional doctors look impressive but are intellectually or morally toxic.</note>; they feed the eyes and minds with the elegance of their color or brilliance, but they are of no good use.

**CHEMIST:** Be silent, I beg you. If the Galenists transgress the precepts of Ethics, I would wish for the Theologians to catch them and the Politicians to punish them. It is your duty, since you are a physician, to argue against their errors in medicine. For that law of justice, "according to its own nature" <note>original Greek: *καθ' αὑτὸ* (kath' hauto). This is an Aristotelian logical term meaning something belongs to a subject by its very definition.</note>, sufficiently proves how little it suits a practitioner of Logic to run off into someone else's province. But tell me in good faith, stranger: Have you deserted the Galenists forever, or have you come to taste my speeches and steal away my secrets?

**PHILERASTUS:** I? Come to steal your secrets? I could not possibly do it; and even if I were most capable of it, piety would forbid it.

**CHEMIST:** Yet many of your kind come here and greet me flatteringly; they address me courteously and ask how I am sustained. They look up at my work and my art as if they were touched by divine praise. But when they return to their schools, they reveal their true resentment, and they rage freely—or rather, quite vulgarly—against the supporters of chemistry. There are others just like them: they love Chemistry as much as they think it serves their profit; but when it requires expense, then they reject it as a useless science.

**PHILERASTUS:** But I embrace and love it so uniquely, as is only fair to love it; there is nothing left to me of such value that I would not be led to give it for the sake of learning Chemistry. For Chemistry is the source of solid philosophy, the key to wisdom, the soul and marrow of natural sciences, the root and goal of medicine, at which wise men have aimed their sights. Do you wish for me to praise it more?

# On Chemical Medicine

...hunger is what allows one to reach the kernel. **CH.** Enter then. But before you proceed, step into this dressing room <note>original Latin: *apodyterium*, the room in a Roman bath where one undressed</note>, and there strip off your credulity, and afterward your sloth. **PH.** I agree with what you command regarding sloth, and I feel it is necessary. But as for credulity, if anyone strips it away entirely, this discipline will leave no deeper a mark on them than wheat sown in the sea. For according to that Aristotelian maxim, **the learner must believe** <note>original Greek: δεῖ μὲν τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν</note>, so that you may have a student who is honorable, modest, benevolent, attentive, teachable, and like clay to be molded in any direction. **CH.** On the contrary, intelligence befits a student; credulity does not. For if you subject yourself to credulity, O Athenian, you will mock the immortality of the soul, the omnipotence of God, the creation of the world, and the entire doctrine of the Christians, following the example of Galen <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated medicine for 1,500 years; the Chemist here accuses him of being a pagan materialist</note>. Nothing was so wickedly defended by him that it would not be confirmed, in turn, by your own vote of approval. Therefore, do not place any more faith in me—let alone anyone else—than in what we say that is either manifest to the senses, or consistent with reason, or in harmony with the Divine Scriptures. **PH.** You advise me well. **CH.** Now descend into the bath, and wash away opinion, deceit, pride, and the rest of the obstacles to the sciences. **PH.** Consider it done; see, I return to you now with "washed ears" and a purified soul. Is there anything else you wish? **CH.** Only that you lay aside your mystic cap and silk toga and put on a chemical cloak, perhaps of a coarser texture, but far more suitable for our operations; now, in place of a book, take these toothed forceps <note>tongs used for handling hot vessels</note>; they shall be your teacher. You are now excellently equipped; this is how a physicist <note>In this context, a "physicist" is someone who studies *physica* or the natural world, rather than just a modern doctor</note> ought to be adorned. Follow me now. **PH.** By my faith! What do I see here? What kind of furnaces, and how many? I pray you, what is the name of this place? **CH.** **The Workhouse** <note>original Greek: Πονητήριον, implying a place of hard labor or toil</note>. **PH.** A harsh and bitter word. **CH.** Perhaps to you, whom Galen has rendered lazy as you sat until now in a heated room <note>original Latin: *hypocausto*, a room heated from below, typical of a scholar's study</note>. But those who prefer labor and sweat (for which it is written the Gods sell all things) to any most desirable leisure are differently minded. **PH.** But surely such a choice selection of glass, vessels, and all these furnaces is not acquired at a low price; Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, here representing the heat of the furnace</note>, the leaven, the clay, and the solvents to be drawn out also absorb much money. **CH.** As if you have forgotten that saying from the Comic poet: "It is necessary to spend if you seek a profit." Nor yet will the expenses be so great that they will not be surpassed a thousand times over by the gain. For in exchange for money, you will buy incomparable knowledge, the demonstrator of all Physics; no merchant has ever enjoyed so happy an exchange, and no moneylender so fruitful an interest. Do not, therefore, stick in that mud of avarice, but rather imitate Montanus, Fernelius, Arnald of Villanova, Fracastoro, Cardano, Gessner, Zwinger, Aragosius, Brickmann, Plater, and the "golden chick of Denmark," Severinus <note>This is a list of famous 16th-century physicians and polymaths who embraced chemical or observational methods late in their careers</note>; who, after making such long detours into Greece, Arabia, and every province of ancient medicine, were not ashamed to be **late learners** <note>original Greek: ὀψιμαθεῖς</note> of this art, and of their own...

### Apologetic Dialogue

...and for old age to build a laboratory of this kind, like a most honorable monument.

**PH.** You name memorable men, the only true ornaments of this age; and relying on their authority, I thirst most greedily for **Chemistry** <term>Chemia: The early modern study of matter, encompassing both what we now call chemistry and alchemy, often focused on preparing potent medicines</term>. For I am accustomed, when about to attempt something, first to debate with myself whether it is right to do it; then, whether other good men have done it before me. Indeed, our choice is confirmed when we perceive that the most famous and prudent men, who themselves lived always in honor, want the same things and do the same as we. But here I am stuck: whether it would be more right to follow in the footsteps of so few men, or to follow the opinions of the ancients, who in this wrestling-ground of preparations seem either to be no experts at all, or total strangers. Spare me, I beg, if I now run back to the stations of the **Galenists** <term>Galenici: Followers of Galen, the 2nd-century physician; they focused on balancing "humors" rather than chemical extractions</term>: I do so not so much out of love for them or hope of victory, but for the sake of knowing the truth, and so that I may seem to have laid aside all credulity for you.

**CH.** I praise your intention, and in turn I answer you: to imitate the ancient physicians in all or most things is just as if you were to seek a model from a rough, unfinished work. For medicine around the time of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of Medicine"</note> was like a recently conceived fetus, in which only confused outlines and rough sketches of limbs were seen. **Galen** later made this more distinct with his method, and posterity—both Arabs and Greeks—made it richer with a various supply of medicines scraped together from street-healers and barbers. Yet none of them progressed so far—oh, what "famous" Architects of medicine!—that they either understood or passed down the method for distilling rose water. Indeed, in no part of Medicine did they not leave behind the most shameful error, which later, wiser offspring wiped away like a fertile sponge.

**PH.** You speak the truth, and in my judgment it can be felt by the senses themselves. For just as old men feel one way and boys another—the latter correctly, the former according to the reasoning of their age—so too it deserves no wonder at all that we, in this "greying age" of the world, find certain things unknown to our fathers, or apply the **hand of Apelles** <note>original Latin: *Apellis manum*; a reference to the famous Greek painter, meaning to put the finishing, perfecting touch on a work</note> to their inventions. This is especially true since they themselves looked at Medicine only through a cloud, and—to use your word—as something not yet formed into an embryo. Therefore, just as **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> missed the truth in Galen, and Galen missed diligence in Hippocrates, and Hippocrates missed method in the ancients: so too, to desire nothing more than what is found in individual writers is the mark of a slave bound to a surly master, not of a learned explorer of science. Now, however (leaving aside the faults of the ancients), I ask you to explain the names and uses of the **furnaces**.

**CH.** Those are called: **Neptune**, the **Sea**, the **Bain-Marie** <note>original Latin: *Maria*; a water bath used for gentle heating</note>, and the **Temperate Zone**. This one is the **Horse's Belly** <note>original Latin: *Venter equi*; a method of providing gentle, consistent heat by burying a vessel in warm, fermenting horse dung</note>; that is called the **Hens' Nest**. Over there **Egypt** is placed; on the right **Persia**, **Mauritania**, **Etna**, the **Serpent**, the **Furnace of Sloth** <note>original Latin: *Accediæ furnus*, likely referring to an "Athanor," a self-feeding furnace that required little attention from the chemist</note>, and the **Ostrich's Belly**.

**PH.** Alas! What you say seems to seek ashes <note>original Latin: *cinerem quærere*, a pun on laboratory ash and worthlessness</note>; away with that ambiguity, by which you seem not to want to teach me...

# On Medical Chemistry

...[not only] the novice, but Chemists seem even to drive away the advanced. 

**CH.** Indeed, they do this on purpose, and with great right. For beyond the fact that no law forbids the coining of new names <note>original: ὀνοματοποιεῖν (onomatopoiein)</note> in new arts, it is sanctioned by the voice of Hippocrates and of fairness itself: that sacred things must be handed down obscurely to profane men, "until they have been initiated into the rites of knowledge" <note>original: πρὶν ἢ τεleiωθῶσιν ὀργίοισιν ἐπιστήμης</note>. Add further that Nature hunts for her majesty in secret silence, and offers us the kernel of a chestnut only hidden by its husk and rough covering. Although in truth, I affirm that no name has been given to things by Chemists which a person imbued with a perfect knowledge of **Polygraphy** <term>Polygraphia: The study of multiple ways of writing or secret codes, common in Renaissance occultism</term>, Etymology, Notation, Analogy, and Physical interpretation <note>original: anagoges</note> would not understand at the very first reading. So far is it from the truth that they should deservedly desire an explanation of terms, or justly blame them for obscurity. 

**PH.** I do not disagree, yet in my mind, to use only that speech in teaching the sciences which only some **Kabbalist** <term>Cabalista: A student of Jewish mysticism; here used generally for someone who seeks hidden, mystical meanings in texts</term> could reach—like a Delian diver <note>A classical proverb referring to someone who can dive deep into difficult or "deep" philosophy without drowning</note>—seems to be nothing other than inviting men to a most sumptuous feast and then, just as they are about to sit down, driving them away with masks and phantom ghosts. But my eyes hasten to see the preparations of those medicines which your books profess to be superior to all others. 

**CH.** Be present then, and enter into this **Zodiac** <term>Zodiacus: Historically the circle of constellations; here the Chemist uses it as a metaphor for the laboratory as a microcosm of the universe</term>. 

**PH.** I remember seeing a cleaner place; but for what reason do you call it a Zodiac? 

**CH.** Because here the signatures of animals are kept—not those imaginary ones of the Astrologers, but true and vital ones. For I maintain that a double life exists in animals: one which works in themselves, and another which works in us. When the first fades away, the second takes command: and from the death of the creature, it provides either a medicine for the alteration of the body, or food for its nourishment. 

**PH.** But since you do not wish me to be credulous, I deny that life exists in dead animals; for by the same reasoning, one might prove with no trouble that life exists in stones, metals, and stars, as well as in beasts that have breathed out their souls. I, however, recognize only a triple life: the rational, the sensitive, and the vegetative. This is what not only **Aristotle** but every nation of physicians before **Paracelsus** <term>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a radical Swiss physician who championed the use of chemicals in medicine</term> was born has defended. 

**CH.** And yet in this you are shamefully hallucinating, my "Athenian" <note>A rhetorical jab at Philerastus's devotion to classical Greek philosophy</note>. For your **Galen** asserts in plain words that life is either nothing but forces, or the action of forces. If, therefore, force is present in dead animals, metals, stars, and stones, why should we not say that life is also present? Is this opinion to be tolerated in Galen, yet condemned in Paracelsus? Did not **Hippocrates** also note throughout his books on diet that the preservation of life happens through nourishment, and its declaration through operations? Just as a man is said to live as long as he can produce the actions predestined for a man; so also as long as a **Magnet** attracts iron, amber attracts straw, and **Rhubarb** <note>Rhubarb was a prized medicinal root used as a purgative to "attract" and expel bile</note> attracts bile, it ought to be judged a sober and dry opinion to attribute life to them, not the [opinion] of a drunken man—

<summary>The Chemist defends the use of obscure terminology as a way to protect sacred knowledge and introduces the vitalist theory that life—defined as a functional force—exists even in minerals and "dead" medicinal substances.</summary>

# Defense of the Dialogue

...human imagination.

**PH.** You establish, then, Chemist, that life is nothing other than an energy implanted "from within" <note>original: ἐκ δόθεν (ek dothen)</note> <gloss>from within</gloss> in all things; that is, a disposition of man toward human actions, of stars toward astral ones, of Angels toward Angelic, of beasts toward bestial, of plants toward botanical, of minerals toward mineral, of metals toward metallic, of foods toward nutritional, and of medicines toward medicinal operations.

**CH.** You conclude correctly. And truly, since death is nothing other than a perpetual cessation from preordained actions: why should we admit that animals die completely before they are stripped of every action for whose sake they were predestined?

**PH.** So animals that possess a soul live for themselves; but when deprived of this soul, they live afterward within us and produce "magnetic" <note>In this context, "magnetic" refers to "sympathetic" medicine—the idea that properties are transferred through a natural, hidden attraction between substances.</note> actions—is this not what you mean?

**CH.** Exactly. and for that reason, I speak of the "life" of a bull’s spleen not only as that which attracts, digests, and expels within the bull's body, but also that which, within us, clears obstructions of the spleen and stimulates the menses. So too the "life" of a beaver's testicles (as far as we are concerned) is said to be that which cures "suffocation of the womb" <note>A common historical diagnosis for various female ailments, often involving respiratory or emotional distress</note> and aids a slow-coming fetus. Thus even the salts and oils of the human skull, the elk, vipers, toads, and crayfish have obtained a vital faculty against epilepsy, the "nightmare" <note>original: incubum; likely referring to sleep paralysis</note>, leprosy, plague, quartan fever <note>A form of malaria that recurs every four days</note>, and so on. Nor is the logic different for other things; only he who does not feel the heat of fire or see the roundness of the heavens fails to see the life inherent in them.

**PH.** I understand, but where are you leading me now?

**CH.** Into "botanical physics" <note>The study of the natural properties and hidden powers of plants</note>, filled with the sulfur, salt, and mercury <note>Known as the "Three Primes" (Tria Prima) in Paracelsian chemistry, these were believed to be the fundamental components of all matter: soul, body, and spirit.</note> of all vegetation.

**PH.** But since you have done me the favor of allowing me to "speak freely" <note>original: παῤῥησιάζειν (parrhesiazien)</note> <gloss>to speak freely</gloss> with you, please do not let it be bothersome to hear those things which our colleagues usually object against these botanical extractions.

**CH.** On the contrary, unless it is a burden for you to speak, it is a pleasure for me to listen.

**PH.** They argue that they have practiced medicine for many years with great success using the "crude" <note>Meaning unprocessed or non-chemically refined herbs</note> preparations of plants; and that in purging, altering, and dispersing the humors (which are the chief works of the medical art), these have exercised their powers no less than these new-fangled preparations. Furthermore, they cry out that it is to be feared lest bodies be suddenly changed by those more subtle extractions, and that in the meantime a great loss of "native heat" and "primordial moisture" <note>These were the "calidum innatum" and "humidum radicale," the two essential fluids believed by traditional Galenic doctors to sustain life and vitality.</note> might occur. However, they do not condemn Chemistry at all; but they claim they do not see why it should be extolled above the other preparations of the apothecaries.

**CH.** Indeed, I greatly praise the fact that they do not condemn Chemistry, and I likewise disapprove of those who use only chemical medicines for every disease. For when one must war against mice or ants, the strength of a Pygmy <term>Pygmy: In classical mythology, a member of a race of tiny people; here used to represent a small or standard force</term> will suffice; yet he who would contend with a lion or the Aetolian boar <note>A reference to the massive, monstrous Calydonian boar of Greek myth</note> has need of the hand of Hector or the strength of Giants. That is, in my opinion, chemical medicines are needed—or, so that you may perceive their excellence more clearly, as if placed before your very eyes, tell me what kind of [success] the followers of Galen <term>Galenici: Doctors who followed the traditional teachings of the 2nd-century physician Galen, relying primarily on herbal mixtures and the balance of humors.</term> have in...

<summary>The Chemist explains the concept of vital energy (life) persisting in animal and plant parts even after death, which can be extracted through chemistry to treat specific human ailments. Philerastus presents the traditional Galenic counter-argument that crude herbs are sufficient and chemical extractions might be dangerously potent.</summary>

## On Chemical Medicine

...of any liquid. **PH.** In cases of wasting disease <note>Latin: *atrophia* - a condition where the body fails to absorb nutrients and withers away</note>, do they not command a diet? **PH.** Truly, they prescribe easily digestible <note>Latin/Greek: *euchymos* — producing good "humors" or fluids in the body</note> boiled foods; they order their juice to be squeezed out, the fat separated, the dregs cast aside, the nutritional divided from the non-nutritional, and finally each part separated that might hinder easy digestion. Likewise, in place of bread, they recommend starch <note>Latin: *amylum*</note> soaked in milk; and they believe that wine should be chosen which is most purified from all foam, tartar, and dregs. **CH.** Correct; but why do they not provide bread, wine, and meats prepared in the common way? **PH.** Because if devoured in that way, they would generate more excrement than nourishment; they would not restore nature, but in reality would overwhelm it. **CH.** Indeed, I marvel that you are so sharp-eyed regarding restorative foods <note>Latin: *Analeptica* — strengthening or recovery-aiding medicines and foods</note>, yet so stubbornly opposed to the chemical preparation of medicines. For if the extraction of the best juices of food is necessary to restore the body, how much more fitting is it to clarify and purge all medicines meant to alter the body? Add also that the parts of some remedies are poisonous, others destructive, many useless, and none—except perhaps by accident—health-giving in their raw state. **PH.** What do I hear? Are not the powers of medicines so mixed by nature in their entirety that they cannot be drawn out separately by any human invention?

<margin>3. On the Faculties of Simple Medicines, Book 3 <note>A reference to the works of Galen, the authority of ancient medicine</note></margin>
**CH.** By no means, by Hercules! For you have heard in the school of your Galen that Aloe, when thoroughly washed, is stripped of its purgative faculty; the same also happens to copper scales or burnt copper. The Moderns <note>The "Neoterici" — contemporary physicians and chemists of the author's era</note> also teach you that only that part of Rhubarb <note>Latin: *Rhabarbarum*</note> purges which the wine absorbs through soaking; indeed, in a whole pound of the entire substance, barely six ounces of Rhubarb are found that can move the bowels even a little bit. The rest, like a <term>fruitless burden of the earth</term> <note>original Greek: ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης (etosion achthos aroures) — a Homeric phrase for something useless or heavy</note>, ought to be committed to the sewer rather than administered to men. **PH.** Truly you speak plausibly, Chemist. For just as different kinds of liquids are found within us—some of which are medicinal, like biles; others nutritional, like blood; others on the contrary excremental, like urine—why shouldn't it be the same in all kinds of medicines that physicians use for the alteration of the body? I approve, therefore, of this "artistic anatomy" of theirs, and I strongly desire to learn it quickly. **CH.** Indeed, I wish you to attend to this as well: Nature has given us nothing pure, but has mixed all things with many impurities, so that she might instill in us from infancy the need for this knowledge as if by a spur of necessity. Observe the method of bread-making: first, how the wheat is separated from the chaff by long threshing and a kind of "Chemical" selection; then the bran is divided from the fine flour by a coarser sieve, and later by a finer one. We cook the sifted flour, we chew what is cooked, we bake it again in a triple furnace <note>A metaphor for the digestive stages or the "heat" of the stomach</note>: and yet it is not so purified by us but that the "internal Chemist" <note>The author refers to the *Archeus*, a concept popularized by Paracelsus describing an internal force that acts like a chemist to separate nutrients from waste</note> implanted in each limb finds some excrement to be eliminated by the summoned expulsive power. No less can be said of honey, milk, and any liquid...

<summary>The Chemist argues that just as we refine food (like wheat into bread) to make it digestible, we must chemically refine medicines to separate their healing "essence" from poisonous or useless waste. He uses the examples of Rhubarb and Aloe to show that only certain parts of a substance possess medicinal power.</summary>

### Apologetic Dialogue
#### Page 79

...this history can be referred back to anything most familiar to human nature. For if substances are presented while infected by that monthly waste <note>Latin: *menstruo*—referring here to the body's natural cycle of shedding impurities</note> in which they were born, they will leave behind various dregs. If these remain too long in the body without being expelled, they will produce measles, smallpox, leprosy, and the most poisonous diseases. How much more is it necessary, then, to separate the pure from the impure, the dead from the living, and the destructive from the familiar and useful in medicines like Hellebore, Colocynth, Spurge Olive, Turpeth, Leafy Spurge, Rhubarb, Senna, and Agaric—in short, in all purgatives? In these, there are not "many" <note>Greek: *polla*</note> good things, as in the drugs of Egypt, but <term>a few good things mixed with many baneful ones</term> <note>Greek: *paura men esthla memigmena, polla de lygra*—a reference to Homer’s Odyssey, describing drugs that can be either healing or deadly</note>. 

Indeed, not even the aromatics most familiar to the human heart are purified so perfectly by the hand of nature that they do not offer us further occasion for purification, imposing on us a certain necessity for labor. For a pound of cinnamon yields only half an ounce of oil; a pound and a half of cloves yields only a quarter; an ounce of nutmeg yields half a dram; a quarter-pound of aloeswood yields one dram. Yet in that oil (or "sulphur"), all that aromatic power hides, as if in a certain radical and spiritual moisture. 

The same logic holds for the extraction of anise, cumin, wild carrot, fennel, roses, saffron, and so on. All the medicinal faculty is channeled into those smallest remaining parts, so that it might rightly be said of them, as it is of ants: "Nature is at its greatest in its smallest parts." 

If, therefore, the secret <term>arcanum</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the "inner essence" or "virtue" of a substance that effects a cure</note>—whether it be a purgative, a sweat-inducer, or something to provoke urine or vomiting—resides in the **sulphur** alone, what business have we with the **mercury** or the **salt**? If it is in the salt or the mercury, why is the sulphur given? When eighty idle, non-purging grains are found in one hundred and twenty grains of Rhubarb, why do the Galenic doctors <note>Followers of Galen, the traditional school of medicine that used whole-plant decoctions rather than chemical extractions</note> not remove them when they are about to purge the sick? Why do they mix them in? Does it seem right, when the nut is to be eaten, to serve the shells as food? 

Since ten ounces of poison are found in a pound of saffron (as the Chemists first discovered), then surely, unless your "Athenians" <note>A common nickname for the university-trained traditional doctors, implying they are more interested in philosophy and debate than practical results</note> could play with human skin with impunity, they would have long ago removed those poisons by separating the foreign matter through a tincture. 

Therefore, Guest, acknowledge now the excellence of **Chemistry**. By its benefit, you shall learn a "living anatomy," which elucidates the salts of simples <note>Medicinal herbs</note>, their Mercuries, their Sulphurs, and indeed their <term>influences, signatures, powers, stars, lives, and resurrections</term>. 

**PH.** Indeed, the brilliance, elegance, and refinement of your Chemists have so drawn me over to your side that there is great doubt whether I shall ever be enticed back to the school of Galen. However, you have not answered this: that the success of common remedies has been excellent, and their use has been healthy for many men. 

**CH.** Why not? Nevertheless, just as a knife cuts wood one way and an axe another, so we immediately remove those infirmities with almost no trouble, while...

# On Chemical Medicines
## Page 80

...at eradicating diseases, the Galenic physicians would not suffice for even a single month. I lie about nothing, my guest, and I feign nothing; I shall prove that the matter stands thus both by the voice of practice and by the weight of arguments. Is it not necessary in any medical operation to act **pleasantly, quickly, and safely** <note>original Greek: *hēsychōs, tacheōs, asphalōs*</note>?

**Ph.** It is necessary indeed, for both our senses suggest it and Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE), whom both traditionalists and chemists claimed as an authority</note> commands it. But why is it not possible to attain these three goals with common medicines?

**Ch.** Because fate does not will it. For if someone’s body needed to be purged, with what instrument would you say it should be done, O Athenian? <note>The Chemist addresses Philerastus as an "Athenian," likely a respectful but ironic nod to his classical, academic education.</note>

**Ph.** Perhaps with Rhubarb, Aloe, Senna, Mechoacan, Agaric, Polypody, Mistletoe of the Oak, Epithyme, Cassia pulp, or Manna.

**Ch.** These medicines are safe, I confess, but they are not sufficiently **pleasant**, either because of their excessive bitterness, their cloying sweetness, or at the very least, the massive quantity required.

**Ph.** I shall flee, then, to stronger things: Scammony, Turpeth, Spurge Olive, Leafy Spurge, and Elaterium <note>A potent purgative derived from the squirting cucumber</note>, which offer neither an unpleasant taste nor require a large dose.

**Ch.** But if these are administered alone, you will not purge **safely**; and if they are seasoned with many spices, as the modern doctors are accustomed to do, the purging will be no more pleasant than if you had administered three drams of Rhubarb or three ounces of manna. Thus, if you use mild <term>cathartics</term> <note>purgatives or laxatives</note> administered in the usual quantities, you sacrifice speed; if you use stronger ones, you sacrifice safety; and if you use either with "Galenic safety," the sheer bulk or the abundance of foul taste and smell destroys the pleasantness.

**Ph.** But in the <term>apothecary shop</term> <note>Latin: *officina*</note> we have various purging compositions mixed with such skill that they are considered second to none for evacuating the body quickly, safely, and pleasantly.

**Ch.** Ah, do not mention your shop any longer! If I were to examine it—putting aside our dispute and acting, as the Greeks say, **without passion** <note>original Greek: *aneu pathōn*—meaning objectively and without prejudice</note>—I would easily prove that no ancient purging composition is endowed with those virtues that Hippocrates desired. For if you bring up the *Hiera* of Galen <note>Hiera Picra, or "Sacred Bitter," a famous ancient remedy made of aloes and spices</note>—the "invention of the Gods," if it please the Gods!—what could be more offensive to the stomach, the nostrils, and the palate? What more unpleasant thing could be devised for all the limbs? 

Furthermore, those electuaries <note>medicinal pastes made with honey or syrup</note> like *Hamech*, *Diaphenica catholica*, and the rest: I frankly and truly confess that to many patients (back when I, unskilled in Chemistry, was forced to use them) they were so hateful that the patients even began to hate me. If they happened to see me by chance, they were moved to vomit! Though these substances are unpleasant enough on their own, they are administered by the men of your discipline in such vast quantities that they seem not to be healing men, but choking horses! O, the unhappy condition of princes, who offer up their bodies as lodgings—or rather, as tombs—for such impurities! 

And what shall I say of your pills, which are as large as the **bullets of skirmishers**? <note>Latin: *globulo ferentariorum*—referring to the lead balls thrown by light-armed Roman soldiers</note> You are accustomed to prescribe them in the number of seven, to honor seven-hilled Rome, or in the number of nine, for the Muses; you never prescribe them in even numbers, because **God delights in an odd number** <note>A quote from Virgil's *Eclogues* (8.75): *Numero Deus impare gaudet*</note>. You have your "Leaden" pills, "Golden" pills, "Useless" pills, "Useful" pills, pills of "Darkness," and pills of "Light"—without which I wish to be, and without which...

# Apologetic Dialogue
## Page 81

...to whom I do not wish to be called: and so, with beautiful names, you cover the most unpleasant medicines, just as one hides a viper with foliage. I say nothing of syrups—long and short, masterful, common, one or another—I know not whether they are more the deliriums of learned men or the games of women. I pass over likewise those aromatic confections, which are nothing if not childish: for if you infuse a little distilled oil of cinnamon, anise, cumin, pearls, amber, musk, or roses into boiled sugar, I shall be your slave unless you prescribe a medicine that is more pleasing and more effective under the name of *diacinamomo*, *dianiso*, *diacumino*, *diamargaritæ*, *diambræ*, *diamoscho*, or *diarosato aromatico* <note>These are traditional medicinal powders or electuaries based on the prefix "dia-" (meaning "made of"), such as "made of cinnamon," "made of anise," etc.</note>.

**Ph.** Truly, you do not merely examine our apothecary shop; you exhaust it. Yet, in truth, my mind has also shrunk back from those confections, seeing that they were full of either ingratitude or danger. For when I wish to purge bile, I am accustomed to write in this manner:

*Recipe: 2 drachms of choice rhubarb; 1 scruple each of Indian spikenard and cinnamon; let them be infused in endive water overnight; to the strained liquid add 1 ounce of syrup of roses; of chicory with rhubarb, 1 ounce.*

Or thus:

*Recipe: 2 ounces of choice manna; 2 scruples of rhubarb infused in endive juice; 5 drachms of diacatholicon <note>A "universal" traditional laxative paste</note>; 2 drachms of Persian Tryphera <note>An ancient electuary, often used for digestive issues</note>; with chicory water in which 1 drachm of agaric had previously been infused: let a potion be made.*

If, however, the form of a pill be more convenient, I write thus from the *Medical Syntax of Colmar* <note>Likely a reference to a local pharmacopoeia or textbook from Colmar</note>:

*Recipe: 4 scruples of the species Hiera <note>Hiera Picra, a very old, bitter purgative powder</note>; half a drachm of choice rhubarb; half a scruple each of stag’s horn, ivory shavings, and cinnamon; with as much syrup of eupatorium as is sufficient: let nine pills be made.*

**Ch.** Ah, away with these rambling deliriums! Write instead:

*Take: 1 scruple and 12 grains of Tincture of Rhubarb; 3 drops each of distilled oil of spike <note>Lavender oil</note> and oil of agarwood <note>xyloaloës</note>.*

If indeed phlegm is to be evacuated, prescribe:

*Half a drachm of Tincture of Turpeth <note>A root used as a strong purgative</note>; 6 drops of anise oil; 2 drops of clove oil. Mix.*

Or thus:

*Take: 16 grains of Tincture of Bulgarian Spurge; 2 drops each of anise and cinnamon oil.*

Whenever you would purge black bile <note>Melancholy</note>:

*Take: half a drachm of Tincture of Oriental Senna; 5 grains of Tincture of Black Hellebore; 2 drops each of anise and fennel oil; 1 drop each of parsley and cinnamon oil. Mix.*

And thus, with a tiny amount of medicine, you will accomplish more than if you had prepared those most tedious recipes. Such is also the condition of our aromatics, diuretics, diaphoretics <note>sweat-inducing</note>, anodynes <note>pain-relievers</note>, and emetics <note>vomit-inducing</note>: which you will find explained more fully and applied diligently to every suffering in our *Chemical Antidatary*, soon to be printed (unless I am deterred by the ingratitude of men).

**Ph.** Truly, these remedies of yours are superior to those of the Servitor <note>The "Servitor" was a title for Mesue the Younger, a major medieval medical authority</note>, Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, author of the first official pharmacopoeia in Germany</note>, Wecker <note>Johann Jacob Wecker, a 16th-century physician</note>, and even the formulas of the Augsburgers <note>The Pharmacopoeia Augustana</note> and all the druggists, by the allure of their taste and flavor, the smallness of the dose, and the speed of their operation; even we most stubborn Athe— <note>The sentence cuts off as the physician likely begins to call himself an "Athenian" (academic traditionalist) or perhaps "Atheist" in the chemical sense</note>
