### On Chemical Medicine
#### Page 82

...Athenians <note>The text begins mid-word with "-nienses," likely "Athenienses," referring to the common academic or philosophical debates often associated with Athens.</note>, we are forced to admit. Now, the hinge of the entire question turns on this: can they be administered just as safely? For a rumor has reached our ears—and not an interrupted one <note>original Greek: "ἀδιάκοπος" (adiakopos), meaning continuous or incessant</note>—that chemical remedies are by far the most dangerous of all, and that they have carried off various patients because of their excessive violence in action; indeed, they cause such a loss of innate heat <note>A traditional medical concept (calidus innatus) referring to the vital heat that sustains life</note> that all the restorative broths in the world cannot repair it.

**CH.** I know, guest, that chemical remedies are traduced not only among the Athenians but in every country; but how entirely without merit this is done, let justice see to it. I shall easily prove my point by citing the testimonies of princes, counts, and other heroes, as well as citizens and theologians. For these remedies have begun to be in use and highly valued not only in the courts of the Emperor and the King of Denmark: but they are so uniquely sought after by our courtiers and the more sensible part of humanity that they constantly grieve that they cannot always use them. However, just as the sharpest and best razor, when used by a foolish surgeon, inflicts a lethal rather than a healing wound: so also all the safest and best chemical remedies have a bad reputation because of the lack of skill of those using them, and **the errors of the craftsman are considered (against all sense of justice) to be the errors of the art.** <note>original Greek: "καὶ τ’ τεχνίτε σφάλματα... νομίζεται εἶναι τῆς τέχνης"</note> On the other hand, if a chemist has attained enough knowledge to understand the *What*, *How Much*, *to Whom*, and *When* a medicine ought to be administered: I would not refuse to be handed over to any trial, provided he does not pluck out his eye <note>An idiom for ignoring common sense or established rules</note> by following the prescriptions of the apothecary shops, but practices medicine much more securely and with the highest praise. But now, the hour warns us to proceed into the Theater of Minerals; come then, follow me.

**PH.** I am unwilling, I say, for what do these things have to do with a doctor?

**CH.** When skillfully applied, they make a man blessed, and to use the common opinion, almost equal to a god. <note>original Greek: "ἰσόθεον" (isotheon)</note>

**PH.** You would have said "equal to a demon" <note>original Greek: "ἰσοδαίμονα" (isodaimona); here Philerastus plays on the word to suggest a more sinister or malevolent power</note> more correctly; for however much I may value your extractions from animals and vegetables, I will always have a religious scruple against approving the use of minerals. When applied externally, I acknowledge that divine powers are sometimes exerted; but when administered internally, they take on the nature of poison, and unless the judgment of both the ancients and the moderns deceives me, they are more malignant than an asp.

**CH.** Beware of saying so: lest perhaps you inflict such a wound upon both the ancient and modern sects that

What of the Arabs, who successfully and to their great credit administered both harmful and harmless minerals internally? May I never encounter an enemy so bold as to claim, after reading their works, that I am misusing their support. Mattioli indeed <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist</note> (to bring in the judgment of the Moderns as well) affirms that the use of metallic remedies is necessary in diseases with deep-seated roots. Julius Alexandrinus also says in eloquent words that Antimony is the greatest secret <note>The text uses "arcanum," a term often used by Paracelsus to describe a powerful, "hidden" curative mystery</note> in fighting the plague. Johann Crato, after infinite battles with the Chemists, used to call native cinnabar <note>original: "minium nativum," likely referring to mercury sulfide</note> the "magnet of epilepsy," and he was the first to show it to me. That pious Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), the Swiss polymath</note>, of most blessed memory, ascribes such powers to oil of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid</note> that he thinks a man hardly worthy of the title of physician if he wishes to do without it.

<margin>Epistle 22 to Oeonus.</margin>
<margin>Book on the French Disease.</margin>
<margin>Book on simple purges.</margin>
William Rondelet highly recommends the "Barbarossa pills"—which are full of quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>—in various ways against that cosmopolitan plague <note>A common historical euphemism for syphilis, also called the "Great Pox"</note>. Gabriele Falloppio, as well as Hector Nonnius—men of great experience and learning—praise "Saffron of Mars" <note>Iron oxide, often used as a tonic</note> to the highest degree for the cure of jaundice and for clearing obstructions of the spleen. Felix Platter prefers antimony <note>original: "stibium Antimoniatum"</note>, when administered with the right preparation, mixture, and dosage, over white hellebore; and he used it most successfully while I was his guest. Joachim Camerarius prefers crystalline Borax (the preparation of which he received from the Landgrave of Hesse) for skillfully inducing vomiting over all other medicines, and rightly so. I could also mention the *Masterwort* of Zwinger, or the works of Thilaeus, Orionius, the *Oxylaeum* of Aragosius, the *Pactolus* of Hagecius, the *Turtle*, *Eagle*, and *Dragon* of Severinus <note>These colorful names—Turtle, Eagle, Dragon—refer to specific chemical preparations or alchemical "monsters" used as medicines</note>, and the golden preparations of other metals and minerals. These men believe a pious and cautious physician should no more abstain from their use than from the administration of wine. Thus, whether you wish to stand by the judgment of the ancients or the vote of the moderns, you must grant that mineral and metallic remedies not only deserve their place among physicians, but ought to be preferred over all other medicines in many internal conditions.

**PH.** I grant it, and at the same time I see the unbearable impudence of those who pretend, without any blush, that the use of metals displeased the ancients and moderns. However (if you will allow it), setting aside the authority of men, turn your attention to the points of reason with which the Anti-chemists seem to have shattered your thesis.

**CH.** Let us hear them at last.

**PH.** They say the best minerals, however they are prepared, possess no similarity to the human body. Indeed, many of them—namely quicksilver, antimony, arsenic, salts, flower of copper <note>Verdigris or copper oxide</note>, chalcitis <note>A copper-bearing mineral</note>, vitriol, and alum—diminish the very substance of metals by their remarkable corrosive power. It is far-fetched to think they would not penetrate right to the marrow of the human body, which is soft, membranous, and fragile.

# ON CHEMICAL MEDICINE
## Apologetic Dialogue
### Page 84

...would be. If, therefore, they [minerals] can neither restore us because of the difference in their substance, nor alter our condition without the danger of erosion or corruption: who, I ask, will not condemn their use, and who will not mock you, the authors of such remedies?

<term>Ph.</term> Indeed, Athenian <note>A common nickname in these dialogues for university-trained Galenic physicians, implying they are more interested in academic theory than practical cures</note>, both of their opinions regarding harmful and harmless minerals are too harsh to even mimic the truth in the slightest. For long experience has proved that gold does much for the strengthening of the heart, silver for the brain, iron for the spleen, and copper for the liver; whether they are quenched in an appropriate liquid while glowing hot, or administered after being reduced to their saffron-colored powder <note>original: "crocum," a term for a fine metallic oxide powder</note> and their own essence. Furthermore, vitrified Lead <note>original: "Saturnus vitrificatus"—Saturn is the alchemical name for lead</note> (not otherwise than if it were a kind of bile) moves the bowels; sulfur nourishes the lungs, and the liquid of crystals purges the kidneys like the best kind of serum. But let it be: suppose minerals have obtained no similarity with the human body. Shall we reject their use for that reason? Why then do we not exclude, by the same logic, colocynth <note>the bitter apple, a harsh purgative</note>, hellebore, vipers, and other such destructive medicines that are entirely antipathetic to us?

<term>Ph.</term> Because there is not such a great difference between them and us. For these [plants and animals] were once endowed, together with man, with a vegetative soul <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "anima vegetativa" is the level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition, found in all living things</note>; minerals, however, are not.

<term>Ch.</term> Beautifully put—as if you did not also give plants and animals to men only after they have lost that vegetative soul.

<term>Ph.</term> But when I said that minerals or metallic medicines have no kinship with the human body, I wanted this to be understood: they do not contribute to the restoration of the spirits. For I have seen gold, corals, pearls, emeralds, carnelians, hyacinths, and other little stones of a precious kind—when crushed and cooked—benefit those with consumption <note>original: "phthisicis," referring to tuberculosis or similar wasting diseases</note> no more than if they had swallowed glass or flint. Therefore, the "Athenians" shout that these things were invented by the Arabs and by fanatics for the emptying of the patient’s purse, not the restoration of the body. And I do not see how their shouting can be proven false. For the parts of all metals, stones, and minerals are so thick that they cannot pass into our body, which is very rare <note>thin or porous</note> and endowed with the subtlest spirits.

<term>Ch.</term> Nay, your friends err more truly than the "Athenians" shout. For certain minerals pass through not only the human body, but gold, tin, and lead, like a flash of lightning. Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum," mercury</note> proves by its own example that I say nothing far from the truth; for its cold spirits strike a man far off with paralysis, while its hot spirits affect the distiller with a remarkable burning in the head. Since quicksilver is present in all metallic things, they will indeed produce spirits—when exalted in this way—that are not only analogous to our own in their subtlety, but much more penetrating. And to speak of stones, who will deny that those invisible spirits of the magnet <note>the loadstone</note> are subtler than our own, by which it [attracts] iron...

Mineral salt also is endowed with such subtlety that the weight of a few grains permeates a great mass of flour. Minerals, therefore, have their own "spirits" that surpass ours in subtlety; they are so far from being unsuitable for restoring the body that their very fineness allows them to work where others cannot. 

**Ph.** [Philerastus] Let it be: you may use precious stones, gems, gold, silver, iron, sulfur likewise, and other non-harmful minerals as far as I am concerned, whether you think they contribute to the body's nutrition or its transformation. But far be it for vitriol, chalcitis <note>a copper-bearing mineral</note>, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, arsenic, antimony, and other such leprous, impure, and corrosive minerals to be ingested into the human body, and used to the perpetual infamy of your name and the art itself. 

**Ch.** [The Chemist] Why so, my guest? 

**Ph.** For when oil of vitriol—so often praised even by Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a famous Swiss physician and naturalist</note>—eats through a pewter plate, who will not justly fear a similar danger in our membranous stomach? Or is it not likely that antimony will strip the very intestines bare, since when melted with gold it leaves not a speck of filth behind? <note>Antimony was used in metallurgy to purify gold, "consuming" the base metals</note> Since Mercury also makes all metals brittle, why should we not rightly fear that, if placed within us, it might grind the flesh, cartilages, and even the very bones—the columns of the whole body—into powder, as if with a millstone? As for arsenic, we know it to be of such unbridled malice that no one was found to ingest it into the body before the bold Paracelsus <note>The Swiss physician (1493–1541) who famously championed the use of toxic minerals in chemically altered doses</note>. 

**Ch.** You hurl sharp weapons indeed, but they can easily be blunted by an "awakened philosopher." For if oil of vitriol is to be banished from the human body because it eats through pewter, what will become of distilled wine <note>alcohol</note>, the spirit of vinegar and honey, or even salt and the juice of lemons and citrons? For any junior physician <note>original: "semestris Medicus," literally a "six-month doctor"</note> recognizes that each of these consumes pewter. 

**Ph.** But not in such a short span of time as that vitriolated spirit does. 

**Ch.** On the contrary, in even less time, if the method of administering it is compared. For I would not wish you to think any Chemist is endowed with such a stupid wit that he would dare to offer oil of vitriol mixed with no other liquids; but rather, he adds as many drops of vitriolated oil to a pound of rose water or another liquid as are sufficient to provide a pleasant acidity. If you immerse as much pewter in that mixture as you would in vinegar, I invite any punishment if the pewter is not found much more corroded by the vinegar. Truly, if this oil of vitriol or even of sulfur does not deserve to be used because of its "erosion," where will we put the Spanish flies <note>cantharides</note>? He used exactly the same arguments against the use of oil of vitriol as you have; but how he did so without any blushing or conscience is clear from this: only three days after the dispute, he used the very same oil on the same patient. The next day, he purged the patient with a most unpleasant medicine, but with the worst success, as he himself and all the friends realized the following morning with the greatest sense of grief. Truly, I feel that the life of such a pious and excellent patient was worthy to be ransomed by the heads of a thousand idolaters <note>A sharp religious insult directed at the rival Catholic physician</note>; for he was faithful to his most illustrious Lord and lived a life before others unstained by any serious blemish. A sixth man holds it suspended; a seventh drives it headlong <note>a reference to distillation</note>; an eighth buries it in verdigris; a ninth encloses it in tin; and a tenth "kills" it in this way: *“Take as much quicksilver as you wish. Chemists, however, deprive Mercury of its soul by fiery fixation alone <note>the process of making a substance resistant to fire so it does not evaporate</note>, and thus they neither waste their labor nor ever torture the patient. **Ph.** But our Galenic Doctors (for so they delight to be called) contend that the more harmful minerals are exposed to the violence of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire, here used to mean the alchemical furnace</note>, the sharper they become and the more pernicious a power they obtain. Certainly wine pressed from grapes is raw; but when cooked by the fire of the sun, it is made sweet and <term>pleasant to drink</term> <note>original Greek: *καὶ ἡδύποτον* (kai hedypoton)</note>. # ON CHEMICAL MEDICINES
## Page 88

...when burned, they cast off the poison implanted in them, and are rendered healthy by the fire. Furthermore, experience teaches that many medicines, as long as they retain their old nature, are extremely sharp and hostile to our bodies; but once the violence of the fire has tamed them, they become suitable for healing. I see you gather from these words: that arsenic, mercury, antimony, and any other eroding and highly poisonous metallic and mineral substances obtain a healthy power by the benefit of fire, and if they are reduced into their own salt—just like vipers <note>It was a common medical belief that the venomous viper, when processed into salts or "flesh," became a potent cure for poisons and skin diseases.</note>—they cast off all malignancy, putrefaction, poison, corrosion, and bitterness.

**Ch.** You conclude correctly: and so that you may believe the same, you may choose any poison from the entire larder of Nature, and I will not refuse to drink it after its fixation <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat, often through repeated burning or chemical bonding.</note> has been performed in the fire.

**Ph.** Do you then condemn antimony, vitriol, arsenic, mercury, and other medicines of that kind which are not yet fixed?

**Ch.** Most clearly—unless by chance they are mixed with those things which either soothe their bitterness or restrain their malignancy like a bridle; for in this way, that facility for causing harm will be removed, and the medicinal faculty, having found a suitable vehicle, will be exalted.

**Ph.** I readily agree. But two scruples still trouble me, which I wish to be quickly plucked out. First, I do not understand: by what means do medicines burned all the way to fixation retain their medicinal power? Second, I fear that from long ignition, much empyreuma <note>A term for the acrid, burnt smell or toxic charring that occurs when organic substances are overheated.</note> is acquired, which anyone who philosophizes correctly will admit is most disagreeable and very harmful to us.

**Ch.** I will pluck out both scruples using the "living voice" of both your Galen and our experience. For who, in theriacal salts <note>Salts derived from Theriac, a famous ancient "universal" medicine made of dozens of ingredients including herbs, honey, and minerals.</note> receiving so many kinds of flowers and spices, ever smelled empyreuma or noticed a failure in their operation? The only thing missing is that they do not act with such great danger: which, in my opinion at least, is more desirable to lack than to enjoy. Therefore, understand that the nature of fire—not just any fire, but chemical fire—is such that it always retains the secret <term>arcanum<gloss>The hidden, essential healing principle of a substance.</gloss></term> lurking now in the salt, now in the sulfur, now in the mercury, and never permits it to fly away. As for empyreuma, Pyrotechny <note>original: *Pyrotechnia* — literally "fire-art," the early modern term for chemistry and alchemy.</note> shows us this: the longer medicines remain in the fire, the less "burnt" quality they have in them; because, of course, the foreign sulfur <note>Chemists believed that "impure" or "foreign" sulfur was the cause of combustion and toxicity in minerals.</note> has vanished through long combustion.

**Ph.** You have defeated me, Chemist: and you have defeated me so thoroughly that I, who sought to "fish out" your skill with certain sneaky little questions, intending to return to the Galenic institutions, now will not refuse to serve a perpetual servitude there. I will take the place of an ash-blower <note>original: *ciniflonis* — a humble term for someone who works the bellows or handles ashes in a laboratory.</note>, a clay-worker, or a watchman; in short, I will admit no condition that would not be an aid to learning this most excellent science.

**Ch.** You do well, Athenian; for according to that saying of the comic poet: *There is a God who sees us and moderates all things;* things will turn out well for the well-deserving, and the same will be true for the ill-deserving. # FIVE MEDICINAL LETTERS
## WRITTEN BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

-> TO HIS BROTHER PHILALETHES. <-
-> *Greetings from the Chemist.* <-

You write that a certain Galenist <note>A follower of Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium. Galenists often opposed the new "chemical" medicines of the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> has come to you, equipped with a great number of insults and lies, like spears fitted with throwing-straps. Although he demands not that a shield be brought out, but a whip <note>implying the opponent wants to punish rather than debate fairly</note>; nevertheless, I have decided to spend as much time responding to him as this patient I am currently attending allows me leisure. "It is necessary," you say, "for Chemists to withdraw entirely from the authorities of the fathers." If they do this in some matters, I judge it an honorable disgrace; but if in all things (as he maliciously pretends), I consider it most unjust. For I strongly approve of that saying of Hippocrates, and I praise the opinion of all physicians: <note>original: ἥνπερ ἐκ περιπτώσιος ποιῆται τὴν ἀρχὴν, καὶ τὴν καταφορὴν ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων μεθοδεύῃ</note> *“that which takes its beginning from experience and directs its course based on observable phenomena.”* Indeed, a discourse that flows from demonstration and practical work is elegant; conversely, that which comes from imagination alone is inelegant and fruitless. It is no different for the Chemists, Philalethes, who leave Galen behind in various places with the same freedom with which he himself once abandoned the opinion of his ancestors concerning a single element. But let us hear the rest of the insults with which he intended to set fire to my *Chemical Basilica* <note>The "Basilica Chymica" (Royal Chemistry), the author's primary textbook on iatrochemistry.</note> as if with a fire of evils. He says that Chemists are ignorant of all more refined learning: that they have not read the Greek authors, have barely greeted the Arabs <note>Medieval Arabic physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes were central to the medical curriculum.</note> from the threshold, and have been taught only by Paracelsus—a drunkard, a magician, an impostor, a quack <term>agyrta</term>, a wandering charlatan, a craftsman of obscurities, and someone hated by heaven and earth. In short, he spewed out a great flood of such words—I know not whether from his mind or from a more filthy mouth. But lest he should think that we are only spirited in the chemical wrestling-ground...

# ON CHEMICAL MEDICINES
<header>On Chemical Medicines</header>

...fears, and is only a fighter at home, in the manner of a rooster: I, the least of all Chemists, challenge that Thraso <note>original: "Thrafonem"; a reference to the braggart soldier character in Roman comedy</note> in his own arena, and I am in no way afraid to clash with him alone on the Greek or Arabic plain <note>This refers to the classical Galenic (Greek) and Medieval (Arabic) medical traditions.</note>. For the books of Hermes Trismegistus, Isaac <note>likely Isaac Hollandus</note>, Bacon, Norton, Ripley, Voschius, and nearly infinite others, written many years before Paracelsus was born, have greatly instructed us and led us out of this nearly inextricable labyrinth. Regarding the vices of Paracelsus, I offer this by way of response:

<margin>Hippocrates, *Book on Ancient Medicine*</margin>
It is rare to see a man without fault; but I most love him who fails the least. Indeed, it must be a meddlesome Galenist, and one no less wicked, who, carrying the eye of a serpent <note>An idiom for being hyper-critical or looking for trouble.</note> in the chest of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus.</note>, fails to see his own crimes in the meantime. Yet, even if he were scandalous and most contaminated by every name of vice: I have said more often that it is the duty and sign of a Chemist not to imitate just anyone or anything, but to seize those things which are good and transfer them into the use of life. For just as Venus, offering and clinging to herself, arouses a lustful grandson, but does not burn a chaste and modest youth: so too the vices of Paracelsus or any other author perhaps delight a wicked mind, but they do not move a chemical or purified <note>original: "depuratam"; implying a mind refined by the alchemical process</note> mind. Natural Cabala <note>A tradition of uncovering the hidden secrets of nature through spiritual and mathematical insight.</note>, <term>Pyrotechnia</term> <note>The art of chemical transformation using fire.</note>, the exaltation of medicines, the contemplation of physics, cheerfulness, wonderful invention, and the singular genius of Paracelsus—these are the things that delight, capture, allure, and attract Chemists. As for non-natural Magic, drunkenness, slander, and contempt for method—all those things are indeed rebuked by Chemists, not only in those Greek and Ethnic authors, but also in Paracelsus himself. Truly, so that I may reveal his own gods to that slanderer, whoever he may be, I affirm that there is no vice in Paracelsus that could not be attributed either to Hippocrates or especially to his own Galen. *Paracelsus was obscure*: I admit it, and the cause demands it. But Hippocrates was also most obscure, and was understood by Galen neither in his words nor his sentiments. *He ignored method*: Hippocrates also did not know it, or at least despised it, while he thrust upon us medicine that was raw, indigestible, unrefined, and full of confusion of things and tautologies. Perhaps he did so with the plan that all opportunity for labor might not be snatched away from his posterity, whose laziness he foresaw. He adds further: *that Paracelsus sometimes sets down contrary principles; and that Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note> does not differ from himself as much as Paracelsus differs from Paracelsus.* Indeed, unless pardon is given for this <term>mnemonic</term> <note>original: μνημονικῷ; referring to an error of memory.</note> error, we shall again lead forth Hippocrates, who disagrees with himself infinitely. I call to witness Cardano, Rorarius, and even Erastus himself, who noticed his various contradictions. *But Paracelsus was also a mage, an impostor, and had commerce with demons. He indulged in drunkenness so much that for whole days and nights*...

That Galenist is entirely alienated from justice; he possesses nothing sound, nothing modest. For what does it matter to me whether a writer is read in Greek or English? Italian or French? Is it right for us to be so delighted by foreign light that we hold our native suns in contempt? What prevents us, *if intelligence is present* <note>original Greek: "ἐὰν νῦς παρῇ"</note>, from Switzerland, England, or any other land surpassing the Greeks in medical knowledge, just as they once excelled in the mechanical arts? Are the Greeks the only physicians? Is there no change in things, no turning of the tide? Indeed, there is much. For Italy, France, Germany, Spain, Denmark, and our whole divided... <note>The sentence ends mid-thought at the bottom of the page.</note>

### BY THOMAS MUFFET:
<header>THOMAS MUFFET:</header>

...Britain, set apart from the rest of the world, where the mistresses and protectors of all arts flourish. Here the sciences sit enthroned, here Medicine dwells, here is the shrine of Hygieia and Panacea <note>Hygieia and Panacea were the Greek goddesses of health and universal remedy, daughters of the god of medicine, Asclepius</note>; here Hippocrates, though an exile from his own people, is welcomed, and the works of Galen are polished by the writings of those very men whom he himself called bears, lions, boars, and utter barbarians. Therefore, regarding that multilingual skill which was found lacking in Paracelsus: just as I do not find fault with it, I also would not want it to be so highly praised by that Galenic slanderer, as if it were essential to the nature of a good physician. For a physician is made not so much by <term>polyglottia</term> <note>original: "πολυγλωττία"; the knowledge of many languages</note> as by <term>polypraxia</term> <note>original: "πολυπραξία"; much practice or the performance of many deeds</note>. A physician is hired by the sick for his effective work, not for his speeches. Furthermore, since many of the Greeks knew no language besides their own native tongue, a difficult but necessary choice is forced upon the Galenist: either he must condemn the pillars <note>original: "Atlantes"; referring to Atlas, who held up the heavens</note> of his own medical family, or he must frankly admit that a man instructed only in his mother tongue can be a leader in medicine.

Besides, that very Hippocrates whom he pretends to love contends that these seven things suffice for perfect medicine: *Nature, instruction, a place suited for study, training from childhood, devotion, industry, and time.* This is correct; for they proceed with Nature as their guide, and if she resists, all efforts become void. For Nature is like a field; instructions take the place of seeds; training from a tender age corresponds to the farmer who sows at the right time; a place suited for study corresponds to the air providing nourishment to things growing from the earth; devotion is the cultivation; industry is the servant of cultivation; and finally, time strengthens all these things in a physician so that he may be perfectly nourished. Hippocrates says that when these seven things meet in a student of medicine, he can become a physician who walks through cities <term>not in word only</term> <note>original: "μὴ λόγῳ μόνον"</note> <term>but also in deed</term> <note>original: "ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔργῳ"</note>. However, he does not require that <term>fluency in many languages</term> <note>original: "πολυγλωττολογίαν"</note>, which perhaps adorns a physician but does not make one. It is more useful for the elegance of his person than for establishing the essence of a physician. And indeed, what other benefit does that skill bring, unless it be that we appear learned in words when the facts are lacking (which is a sign of foolish ambition), or that we might understand Arabic or Greek authors (which is indeed instructive).

For when all these have been read through, what else do we carry away, I ask you, than various bundles of errors, obscurities, sophistries, lies, contradictions, and the obstacles of deceptive experiments—all for a single ear of truth? This shall be the praise of the multilingual, this their ornament—so it was necessary to describe them. If they have any use in medicine, it is surely this: that they know how to translate books from one language to another. This will not only fail to increase their skill in medicine but will even greatly diminish it, while they are forced to devote their labor to words, neglecting reality and practice.

But let us proceed further: *Paracelsus was ignorant of Logic, Physics, Astrology, and Geometry.* And what shall I say of those followers of Galen, none of whom has defined his own art in a way that satisfies others or himself? For this one contends it is an art; that one a science; a third...

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
<header>CHEMICAL LETTERS</header>

...both and neither, but in a certain way: the fourth definition is determined by the end goal; the fifth by the work performed; the sixth by the outcome; the seventh says *Medicine is the art of caring for health*, but then it adds, *in the human body*. As if indeed the nature and name of medicine applied more to this than to the care of plants, or even to <term>veterinary medicine</term> <note>original: "κτηνιatρικῇ" (ktēniatrikē)</note>. As for the Physics of the Pagans, since it is of no use even to Christians, I strongly desire it to remain unknown not only to Paracelsus but also to myself. Add to this that no <term>axiom</term> <note>original: "ἀξίωμα"; a self-evident truth</note> placed within it is so stable that it cannot be shattered instantly by a single argument, just as a potter's little jars are broken by the strike of a pebble. 

Our astrologers too, about to predict (if the gods allow) on what day, what hour, and what moment a sick man will die or recover, go out and stumble against a stone they didn't see, returning home looking ridiculous with broken legs. Such great ignorance is also found among the geometers, that they claim to hold the exact circumference of the earth and sea, yet they know the distance from London to the little town of Iselin <note>likely a reference to a nearby village or a contemporary geographical error</note> no better than the most ignorant person. 

Indeed, as that Galenist does not blush to call Paracelsus "the hatred of heaven and earth," he seems to have deliberately overstepped the bounds of modesty. For Paracelsus was most dear to heaven because of his supreme skill in astronomy, and dear to the earth because of his living anatomy of mixtures. From these mixtures, he drew out not that common little soul, but another "working" essence, gifted with various tinctures, stars, influences, and powers. 

I had to write these things in favor of Chemistry against that Galenic slanderer; I do not doubt that he would now pay much gold to ensure a Chemist knows nothing, though nothing is of such value that it could make him repent of his insults, since he is abusive by both fate and choice. I add and command this alone by way of a <term>colophon</term> <note>a finishing stroke or concluding note</note>: if he does not stop snarling at the doors any longer, let him be driven from the house as quickly as possible—or at least sent to that place where iron is usually worn away by iron <note>a metaphor for a place of hard labor or harsh conflict</note>. Farewell, and adorn this "Sparta" <note>a classical idiom meaning "fulfill the duty of the position you have been given"</note> which you have obtained with your virtue, just as you have done until now. Given at London, January 29, 1583.

->*TO THE GERMAN TRUTH-LOVER*<-
->*Greetings from the Chemist*<-

You have written again and again that you do not wish that Galenist to be driven from the house. Yet he finds nothing to reproach in you except this: that you seem to trust in the senses alone for the thorough learning of medicine. Truly, if he knew how much weight the testimony of the senses carries regarding physical things, he would become "quieter than a fish" and would not be ashamed to feel and act as you do. For had it been without the senses, reason would never have conceived any movement of nature; by their ministry, reason was led as if by the hand from singular things to a knowledge of a more universal nature, and it established various laws of both things and sciences. 

Hence, reasoning is not undeservedly called by Hippocrates "a certain synthetic memory of those things received through the senses." For the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "διάνοια" (dianoia); discursive thought or reasoning</note>, seeking its beginning from singular instances, finally arrives at the truth...

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
### THOMAS MUFFET:
<header>THOMAS MUFFET:</header>

...leads [the physician to his goal]; however, as often as it proceeds not from evident observation but from a probable fabrication of reason, it leads a man into a path (not to depart from the word of Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was an ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>) that is clearly impassable. Indeed, in the management of physical things, Christ himself—the fountain of all reason—clearly teaches that the greatest faith must be placed in the senses. <margin>John 20:27; Luke 24:39</margin> For when that Thomas, called the Twin, doubted somewhat concerning the resurrection of Christ, He said: *“Reach your finger here, and see my hands; and reach your hand here, and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.”* <note>original Greek: "Φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν σου ὧδε, καὶ ἴδε τὰς χεῖράς μου. καὶ φέρε τὴν χεῖρά σου, καὶ βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν μου καὶ μὴ ἄπιστος γίνου, ἀλλὰ πιστός"</note> And again: *“Touch me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me having.”* <note>original Greek: "ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε. ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει, καθὼς ἐμὲ θεωρεῖτε ἔχοντα"</note> Would that philosophers, following the example of such a true teacher, had established their physics according to the rule of the senses, rather than the dream of their own imagination.

If you were to ask these philosophers now by what means sensible bodies are made from non-sensible elements, or how acids are made from tasteless things, they do not answer: *“Come, touch, see; apply your eye and finger.”* Instead, they say: *“Believe, contemplate, imagine.”* And they have ruined that Aristotelian maxim: *“The learner must believe.”* <note>original Greek: "δεῖ μὲν τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν"</note> Truly an ungenerous saying, and most unworthy of such a patron of philosophy. For nothing more disastrous could happen to a novice physician than to build the foundation of his art upon credulity, thought, opinion, uncertainty, sand, marsh, or quicksand.

Indeed, how much better it would be to imitate those men who, when about to build, look upon various houses—well-made, polished, convenient, and built with precision—so that, having sought an example from every best thing, they may build a similar dwelling for themselves at their own expense. For this reason, they make a selection for the foundation from one place, the walls from another, and elsewhere the private rooms, the entry halls, the facade, and the roof-tiles. If they are even able to invent and add something of their own, that is counted as a gain and will be to their greatest honor. For why should it not be the case that, just as masters of architecture have added many noble things unknown to our fathers, so too it should be in medicine? Medicine is so much a rival to architecture that they use the same method of "curing" or "restoring."

Do not, therefore, believe even the most ancient physician, much less Apollo <note>The Greek god of healing and father of Asclepius.</note> himself, beyond what he has given as a true **demonstration**, <note>original Greek: "ἀπόδειξιν" (apodeixin)</note> sanctioned by the reckoning of the senses and the voice of long observation. Indeed, that great Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the dominant medical authority for over a millennium.</note>—the god of the Galenists—affirms in clear words against the Sophists that all physical <term>axioms</term> <note>Self-evident truths or principles.</note> took their origin from the senses and through the senses, and if we depart from them, no demonstration will remain. 

But [an opponent] objects: *“It is not safe to follow the judgment of the senses, because they are so frequently and easily deceived. For if the organ is impaired, the medium infected, the object placed too near or too far, or the manner of receiving it is unfit, not only the ears, but the tongue, nostrils, skin, and even the very watchmen of the eyes are deceived. Indeed, among a thousand men enjoying health (as far as one can judge), few perceive things perfectly, or in the same way as others: for what is sour to this man, is harsh to another; what seems sharp to one, appears bitter to two others, etc.”*

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
### THOMAS MUFFET:
<header>CHEMICAL LETTERS</header>
<meta>catchword: much [multam]</meta>

...is believed, and so forth. Come now: let us grant for the sake of argument the principle that the Galenist <note>A follower of Galen (129–c. 216 AD), whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> seeks: yet he could never persuade anyone that the senses were so completely dull that, while maintaining a sound mind, one would deny the whiteness of snow or the heat of fire. Or if he were to do that, would you not think him a man worthy of being treated with the tortures of the insane and beaten with rods on every side? 

But he objects again, that *it is shameful to entrust judgment to the senses while excluding reason*: a thing which never entered our minds, even in a dream. But just as a judge in the forum, not rushing his own sentence, inclines toward one side or the other based solely on the report of eyewitnesses: so too in medical controversies, we wish reason to act as the judge, but only according to the prescription of the senses, which serve reason in the place of messengers and as intermediaries. 

And therefore we establish that the material cause of the human body is "earth," enriched by that triple substance of **salt**, **mercury**, and **sulfur** <note>These are the *Tria Prima* (Three Principles) of Paracelsian alchemy, believed to be the fundamental building blocks of all matter.</note>—not because Paracelsus, Isaac, or Geber <note>Paracelsus, Isaac Hollandus, and Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) were foundational figures in the alchemical and chemical tradition.</note> say so, but because we see, touch, and taste those three principles, and through the teaching of the senses, we recognize them to be true. Since Galen did not admit this teaching, hear into what shameful errors he unwittingly fell. For when it had long been debated among the ancients whether the differences in flavors arose from the elements or from some specific matter, Galen used to say that all of this must be attributed to the mixing of the elements. 

<margin>Book 2, *On the Powers of Simple Medicines*</margin> Where then does Galen get acidity? Naturally, from a very weak heat that changes the medicine or food without overcoming it. Just as can be seen in unripe apples and in the belches of half-digested food. But what can be perceived as more acidic than "radical vinegar" <note>Concentrated acetic acid.</note>, or the oil of vitriol and sulfur? Both of these consist of such extreme heat <margin>Book 7, *On the Powers of Simple Medicines*</margin> that they have begun to be called "fiery medicines." 

Now let us come to sweetness, which, according to Galen's opinion, is produced by a very temperate heat: whether it be innate (as in honey) or acquired, like everything made sweet by fire. Nevertheless, the "liquor of white lead" <note>Lead acetate, also known as "sugar of lead," which is famously sweet but highly toxic.</note> and "butter of vitriol" (both extremely sweet substances) sufficiently prove that sweetness can be obtained through the most violent fire. Finally, that remarkable bitterness of opium clearly demonstrates that this flavor is not born from excessive heat alone; a point which I do not know whether Galen proved more than he simply invented. 

Also, having despised the judgment of the senses, Galen turned the pulses into poets, playing as **Spondees**, **Pyrrhics**, and **Tribrachs**, in the **Dorian**, **Ionian**, or **Sybaritic** styles <note>Galen used the names of poetic meters (feet) and musical modes to describe the varying rhythms of a patient’s pulse.</note>. At times he even ascribes Lydian music to them, mixing Pyrrhics with Spondees, Iambs with Trochees, and Anapests with Dactyls; finally, he divides their various alternations into other names, perhaps, but much more obscure ones. 

From this you may see that we should approve not whatever Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, or Paracelsus writes, but that to which the senses, the eyes, and experience bear witness: from which all physical knowledge (if there is any at all) is drawn as if from the spring itself. Apply therefore...

# THE LETTERS OF THOMAS MUFFET
<header>THOMAS MUFFET</header>
<meta>catchword: much [multam]</meta>

...much rue, celandine, fennel, eyebright, and many remedies for sharpening the sight <note>original: *oxydertica remedia*. These herbs were traditionally used to treat eye ailments and "clear" the vision.</note>, lest the eyes of men, as if infected by the filth of bleariness, see nothing, or little, or wrongly through the weight of authority. Do not, I say, permit the authority of anyone to bind you, but having tasted the opinions of individuals, correct those that are false, or confirm those that are true. Thus at last you will attain medical Theory and Practice—not of the kind they dreamed of, but which you yourself, having seen with your own eyes <note>original Greek: *autotheasamenos* (αὐτοθεασάμενος), meaning an eyewitness or one who sees for themselves</note>, know to be good. Finally, prove yourself a Chemist; see each thing for yourself, and retain what is yours: accurately separate the homogeneous (I say) from the heterogeneous. 

For what has a physician to do with the causes of the soul? Let the Theologians dispute that. Let cooks examine the causes of flavors; painters, colors; perfumers, odors; and Musicians, the causes of sounds. For you, it shall be enough to have known what profits and what harms your subject <note>The "subject" here refers to the human body or the patient.</note>. For you will never truly see these secondary qualities affecting the external senses, either in the mixture of the primary ones or in any other figment of the philosophers. 

Rather (if you long to see this), perform a living anatomy of vegetables, animals, and metals; and where the tincture, flavor, or odor dwells—where the poison, where the Theriac <term>Theriac: a famous ancient "universal antidote" and panacea made of many ingredients; here used metaphorically for the healing essence of a drug</term> of medicines lies hidden—behold it not with the eyes of others, but with your own. This is indeed a province worthy in which all physicians might grow old, and one full of practical exercise. And so I have made it clear that the physician's opinion ought to be in harmony with the judgment of the senses, and I do not doubt that even the Galenist <note>A follower of the traditional medical system of Galen.</note> would say the same as I. Farewell. Given at London, February 8, 1583 <note>original: 6th Ides of February 1583</note>.

->TO PHILALETHES THE CHEMIST, GREETINGS.<-
<note>"Philalethes" is a Greek-derived pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth," a common name for correspondents in alchemical and philosophical letters.</note>

You ask of me, Philalethes, what a novice physician should do in this variety of authors and sects: whom should he follow most? Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, Paracelsus—this one, that one, all of them, or none? Believe me, it is a burning question and full of difficulty. Yet if the matter stood by my vote, I would agree with all physicians as much as they agree with the truth: and I would leave them just as much as they leave it. Otherwise, it would seem like the tyranny of Phalaris <note>A notoriously cruel Greek tyrant.</note>, not a decree of justice, if those whom Nature brought forth free should be enslaved to the judgment of a single philosopher, as if they were captives recently bought at an auction <note>original: *ab hasta emptos*, literally "bought from the spear," referring to the Roman custom of placing a spear at public auctions of war booty and slaves.</note>. 

For since, according to that saying of Hippocrates, "Medicine is long" <note>Referring to the famous aphorism: "Life is short, Art is long."</note>—whether compared with the age of the Physician, the course of time, the difficulty of judgment, or the uncertainty of experiment—how should I let myself be persuaded that the finishing touch was so applied to medicine by one, or indeed by all Physicians, that nothing can or should be added or taken away? Yet I see most people, who are excessive admirers of ancestral doctrine, fleeing to the authority of the Fathers like some Maenian column <note>The *Columna Maenia* was a place in the Roman Forum where debtors were tried; Muffet suggests traditionalists hide behind old names to avoid intellectual debts.</note>, and adopting that weapon of the Pythagoreans: "He himself said it" <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς ἔφα* (autos epha). This refers to the "Ipse dixit," where an assertion is accepted solely on the teacher's authority.</note>. When this collapses, they seek help from the papists, and immediately summon those reinforcements of asses: *One must believe the fathers, the councils, and the successions.*

# CHEMICAL LETTERS
### G

*The families of the Asclepiads <note>The Asclepiads were a guild of physicians in ancient Greece who claimed descent from Asclepius, the god of medicine.</note>, the Arabs, the customs and rites of the Academies, etc.* Yet the example of Paracelsus <note>original: *Helvetium*, referring to the "Swiss" physician Paracelsus.</note> proves that he alone knew better things and discovered more medicines than all of them. Indeed, I see that the very porch of medicine—local anatomy—is of such great magnitude that five hundred Olympiads <note>An Olympiad is a four-year period; Muffet implies two thousand years of study.</note> of physicians have not sufficiently encompassed it. For who does not see that fiction of Aristotle’s, that some nerves take their origin from the heart? Who does not mock the error of Plato, who established a double passage in the lungs: one to carry drink and food into the stomach, the other as a messenger for air? Hippocrates also and Galen (of whom the former stripped medicine bare, the latter expanded it) were caught in various and most false paradoxes by Vesalius, the sun of anatomists. 

Yet Columbus <note>Matteo Realdo Columbus (1516–1559), an Italian anatomist.</note> corrects Vesalius; Fallopius corrects Columbus; and my most dear teacher Felix Plater corrects both of them. After so many centuries, Plater has noted new and most beautiful things regarding the position, use, and formation of the parts. And thus Alpha emends Beta, Beta emends Gamma; nor indeed will the Omega <note>The final or last.</note> anatomist be so diligent that he will not be corrected either by the pen of another, or at least by himself. Is it now likely, Philalethes, that nothing should be added to or taken away from medicine, in whose harbor so many reefs of errors are found, upon which blind youth strikes at the very first voyage? 

But let us set sail deeper and look for a moment at physiology, the sum of which is this: *the human body comes from humors, humors from elements, and elements from principles.* If you truly ask from which humor man is made, they respond: from bile, from both types of phlegm <note>Galenic medicine distinguished between different types of pituita (mucus/phlegm), such as salty or sweet.</note>, and from blood, coming together into a certain common humor called "seed." But if you should inquire further, whether the human body is prior by nature to the seed, or the seed to the body? Good God, what yawning stupidity you would see here, what timidity! For if they assert the first, the effect must be prior to the cause, which is absurd; but if they deny it, then man was made from something other than human seed, and they would destroy their own "eternity of the world" <note>The Aristotelian belief that the world and species have no beginning or end, which was a point of contention with Christian theology.</note>, which they had made the foundation of their entire religion. 

Nor is it different in the doctrine of the elements: for some want the element to be one, others multiple, others infinite, innumerable, or immobile; these say there are two, those three, some four, others affirm there are eight. Yet they all agree with one voice in this: that no element, as it truly is, can be perceived by us, and that it is destitute of all flavor and color. If you then ask: how can a mixture of flavorless elements produce so many types of flavors and colors, they run to that shield of Galen: <margin>Book 2 of *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, chapters 2 and 3.</margin> *Where the sense grows dull, there one must go to reason as the more divine part of man. For sense is common to the beasts as well as man; but that clearer eye of reason perceives those things which escape the overly dull edge of the senses.*

-> ### LETTERS ON CHEMISTRY ### <-

And so, by the response of a versatile philosopher—by which it is easy for an impudent man to prove anything or indeed to dilute anything—they imagine that a necessary and noble question has been satisfied. <margin>2nd Book on the Use of the Pulse</margin> But if Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the dominant medical authority for over a millennium, whose work was often treated as infallible.</note> mocks the school of Moses and Christ because some of its principles are held without logical demonstration (and this in physical matters, as he himself asserts), how much more rightly should Galenic physiology be received with laughter and hisses? For even in physical matters, his work testifies not to the demonstration of the senses, but to the dreams of the imagination. <margin>Book on whether the habits of the mind follow the temperament of the body.</margin> Indeed, to make a more equal analogy <note>original: *$\alpha\nu\alpha\lambda o\gamma\iota\alpha$*</note>, if Galen thinks Hippocrates should not be believed as a witness, but only when he provides a demonstration, why should we not listen to Galen with the same liberty when he demonstrates, yet reject him in turn when he raves?

But you ask: *Is trust to be placed in those ancient writers, or rather in the moderns?* Truly, in these more recent ones. Because in this aging era of the world, we have acquired not only the gifts of languages, but also a distinguished method. By its benefit, we read the writings of the ancients not in a confused mess, stuffed together in a hurried work just as they were born, but elegantly arranged, distinguished by their proper places, chapters, and parts, and illustrated in various ways. In this way, we seem like a raven sitting at the very top of a tower; though compared to the ravens on the ground he looks like a mere sparrow, nevertheless, because of his loftier position, he sees further than they do and judges objects more accurately. 

For even if nothing is said by the moderns that was not said before, you will nonetheless find many things that are said more correctly, plainly, elegantly, clearly, at greater length, or more subtly. For example: Chemistry was treated by that "thrice-greatest" Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius ter maximus*, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational chemical and alchemical texts were attributed.</note>, born around the time of Moses, but he spoke so obscurely that neither his contemporaries nor later Latin speakers could grasp his meaning. After him followed Zoroaster, Solomon, and then the family of the Arabs; yet among them, before Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), a prolific polymath and often called the "Father of Chemistry."</note>, no one that we know of defined Chemistry, divided it into parts, or enriched it with its own instruments, actions, materials, and effects. To this foundation, however, Paracelsus and other distinguished chemists added both clarity of speech and an orderly arrangement of facts. They can truly say this of themselves: *He dictated us, and we him.* <note>Muffet suggests a reciprocal relationship where moderns give voice to the unspoken truths of the ancients while the ancients provide the foundation for modern thought.</note>

Indeed, although Galen grants the highest honor to Hippocrates as the founder and father of medicine <margin>1st Book on the Use of the Parts</margin>, he nonetheless frequently argues that Hippocrates' speech is inexact, improper, obscure, ill-formed, indistinct, and at times lacking or, conversely, superfluous. And when Galen finds a lack of diligence in him, he rebukes his confused and disorderly tradition. <margin>2nd Book on the Regimen in Acute Diseases</margin> Sometimes he even silently accuses him of ineptitude, forgetfulness, error, and falsehood; and regarding the medicines to be given to those suffering from pleurisy, Galen disagrees with him entirely.

I will tell you a most delightful thing, my dear William, about a certain "Galenic idolater"—a man who worships antiquity. Since this man condemned anything that was not ancient or written by Galen or Hippocrates themselves, I presented him with a little book by Hippocrates *On Elegance* in a German trans- <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "German translation" or "to a certain German" is likely intended.</note>

### TO PHILALETHES THE CHEMIST, S.P.D. <note>S.P.D. stands for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a standard greeting meaning "Sends his fondest greetings."</note>

You have often asked me, Philalethes, since I allow myself to be bound to no author, whether I follow my own path, and whether I grant more to my own judgment than to the decrees of all the classic authors? I do not wish this. But I would be led by the light of nature, not by that blind omen of nature by which we lean into the abyss, and having abandoned truth, we join ourselves to error as a companion. What, then, do you understand by the "light of nature"? Do we drink in art by nature, or do we obtain knowledge by descent from our ancestors? I do not maintain this either. For when newly born, we seem like "erased tablets," <note>A reference to the *tabula rasa* or blank slate; the idea that the mind is born without innate knowledge.</note> upon which the actual exercise of the sciences is not inscribed; rather, a certain small potential grows by the kindness of fate, the "midwifery" of teachers, and the passage of time. 

What then is the light of nature? In the judgment of our first nature—that of our original integrity—it is like a certain flash of lightning; not innate, but implanted in us by God, by which we discern the false from the true with a more divine eye of the mind. For I think there are two kinds of physicians: some are "God-taught" <note>original: "Theodidactos"</note>, such as the Apostles were; others, however, are illuminated through the mediation of that lightning flash, such as the ancient Chemists <term>Chemistæ: in this context, "Chemists" refers to alchemical physicians who sought the hidden properties of matter.</term> were. And just as lightning flashes now from this region of the sky, and now from that, so also the light of nature takes its origin from various places. Sometimes it comes immediately from God, as in Adam, who, while he was "whole of life and pure of crime," <note>Another quote from Horace (Odes 1.22.1), used here to describe Adam's state before the Fall.</note> not only knew but also named all things. 

But after the First-Formed man <note>The "Protoplast," a theological term for Adam as the first created being.</note> moved into his own wit and turned away from that state of piety, it was all over for that first light of nature; and in its place, fantasy, error, and opinion infected both him and all his posterity by a certain secret contagion of the seed. From this it has happened that the greatest part of those things we know is the smallest part of those things of which we are ignorant; indeed, it has brought it about that nothing is truly known, if you define science as the perfect knowledge of a thing. Yet those come closest to this perfection who, though lacking that whitening and brighter lightning of nature, enjoy its substitute—denser and thicker, to be sure, but nonetheless pointing out the way to truth for us, and in a way indicating it. # THOMAS MUFFET

...acknowledging that famous Adam, who perfectly knew by divine inspiration the essence, nature, and underlying substance <term>hypostasis — the essential personhood or fundamental reality of a thing</term> of his own body and indeed of every body, as well as their efficient, formal, instrumental, and final causes. We, however, also seem to know the same, but as if through a mist, and "in part," as the Apostle says <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly... but then shall I know even as also I am known."</note>—that is, through analogies, similarities, collections, and the comparison of the macrocosm <term>the "great world" or universe</term> with the microcosm <term>the "little world" of the human being</term>. 

Hence we say that the body of man consists only of sulfur, mercury, and salt <note>These are the "Tria Prima" or three primary principles of Paracelsian chemistry, representing soul, spirit, and body.</note>: not because we know it as perfectly as Adam did, but because the dissolution of all kinds of bodies, whether by nature or by art, shows this to be the case. But how are we persuaded that this axiom <note>original: "ἀξίωμα" (axioma)</note> is true: that bodies are composed first of those things into which they are finally dissolved? Indeed, numbers and syllables make this plain; for just as they were composed, once they are broken down, you see them contain individually as many units as they represented when they were combined. 

And so, an analogy having been made from bodies to their properties, from nature to art, and from one art to another, those three principles are truly drawn out—principles that will never be destroyed by the effort of any Galenist <note>Followers of Galen, the ancient Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated medicine before the rise of chemical medicine.</note>. For there is one and the same law for both nature and art. All things are similar, however dissimilar they may seem, and all are in harmony, though they may appear discordant. 

Wherefore not without merit did Hippocrates show the management and operation of all nature within us, by making a comparison with the effects of the arts and sciences. 

<margin>See Hippocrates, Book 1 On Diet, section 8.</margin>

For in truth, the vital spirit is the substance of the blacksmiths; the generative faculty is the shaping power of the weaver; the temperament is that of the potter; the ripening <term>concoctio — the internal "cooking" or digestion of the body</term> is that of the goldsmith; hearing is the substance of Music; flavor is that of Cookery; and our internal regulation is so much a rival to architecture that whether you look at the action or the end, you see hardly any difference. 

Indeed, Hippocrates proves that nature has given men a versatile mind from this: that they feel some things, speak others, and do others, and the same people repeatedly teach contrary disciplines about the same things. He notes that certain deceptive arts are found—such as wrestling, trading, drinking, and gaming—which we all admire when someone performs them skillfully, and we think it a matter of virtue; yet we do not understand the cause, which arises from the very likeness of nature. 

If the Galenists understood this harmony of nature and art well enough, they would never deny that millers, bakers, cooks, internal chemists <term>archaei — the vital forces that act as internal "alchemists" to direct bodily functions</term>, distillers, porters, carriers, caterers, musicians, clever servants <note>Muffet uses names like Parmeno and Geta, stereotypical "clever slave" characters from Roman comedy, to personify bodily functions.</note>, master-craftsmen, sculptors, goldsmiths, fullers, weavers, messengers, smiths, and architects can be found in the human body. Much less would they mock the authors of such words with more than cynical bitterness.

<meta>This page continues Thomas Muffet’s defense of chemical medicine. Having previously established that humans can understand the body through analogy with the macrocosm, Muffet now moves to criticize the Galenic school (the traditional medical establishment) for ignoring the literal "earthy" composition of man in favor of abstract theories.</meta>

->EPISTOLÆ CHEM.<-

...nothing can be more aptly compared with these parts, if you consider their duty and use, as he clearly observed. Do you wish for me to reveal to you some of the errors of the Galenists <note>Followers of Galen, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated medicine for over a thousand years.</note>, into which they have fallen to the perpetual infamy of their name because they despised the light of nature? Hear one, and it is a noble and notable one. When God said that man was made from the soil, what else did He intend, Philalethes <note>A name meaning "lover of truth," likely addressing the recipient of the letter.</note>, than that one studious in recognizing human matter should weigh the substance of the soil, distinguish it, dissect it, and examine it; suggesting that the principles of the human body are surely to be found there, and nowhere else? The Galenists, lacking this light, ascended to the regions of fire and air, and descended into the waters; and thus, with the earth mixed among them, they fabricated man not according to God's prescription, but by the pleasing invention of their own fantasy. Moreover, although they see in the earth neither blood, nor phlegm, nor yellow or black bile <note>The four humors of Galenic medicine.</note>: yet they affirm that man, both by law and by nature, is nothing else but these.

Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, on the contrary, and other distinguished Chemists, having drawn such light from God, realized that the material principles of man are hidden in the earth from whence he came: with continuous and unremitting labor they dissected its veins, opened its guts, broke its bones, melted its marrow, and left no stone unturned, so that they might diligently examine the bodies contained therein. At last, by the benefit of Pyrotechny <term>Pyrotechnia — the "art of fire," a synonym for chemistry or the laboratory refinement of substances</term> and Alchemy, and through their long and more than Herculean labors, they discovered nothing simple in the earth except the *vaporous, the inflammable, and the fixed*: and nothing mixed that was not composed of these same simple things. 

Wherefore they establish that the principle of man is also twofold: one part volatile, the other truly fixed. The volatile is in turn twofold: the first is vaporous, which is called Mercury; the second is inflammable, which has received the name of Sulfur. Mercury is the vaporous principle of the body: in itself boundless, moist, liquid, the vehicle of the natural balsam: incorporating Sulfur with salt, just as water incorporates lime with sand. Sulfur is the inflammable principle of the body—fatty, light, uniform—the fuel of the vital balsam. Salt, however, is the fixed principle of the body, providing weight, solidity, and maximum strength, yielding to neither iron nor fire by itself. 

There are two types of differences among these principles: some are domestic, when compared to themselves, and others are exoteric, when compared with others. The principle in man is called "domestic" which is born to keep the body in its integrity; but that which corrupts the body itself is called "foreign." This [domestic principle] is either born from the parents and produces perpetual health, or [the foreign principle] is contracted from a nurse and external diet, inducing a long-lasting dyscrasia <term>dyscrasia — a medical term for an "ill-mixture" or imbalance of the body's fundamental components</term> of the body. In order that we might more rightly examine the particular nature of both the foreign and domestic principle, it is worthwhile to investigate all sulfurs, salts, and all mercuries...

Now, all sulphur in the macrocosm <note>The "greater world" or the universe at large.</note> (which is the light of the microcosm <note>The "lesser world," referring to the human being.</note>) belongs either to perfectly animated things or to imperfectly animated things. Perfectly animated things include animals and vegetables; imperfectly animated things include minerals. Furthermore, the sulphur of animals and vegetables is found to be either native or artificial. Native sulphur is that which nature itself casts out and sends forth to be handled by the senses: such as the exuding fats of all animals, the wax of bees, the resins of trees, the "tears" <note>Sap or resin droplets.</note> of the larch, turpentine, fir, styrax, pitch-pine, and mastic; as well as the gums of cherries, lac <note>A resinous secretion from insects.</note>, laserwort <note>original: "laserpitij"; an ancient medicinal plant, possibly silphium.</note>, panax <note>All-heal.</note>, cedar, frankincense, myrrh, and so on. 

Artificial sulphurs, however, are the oils, "burning spirits" <note>Alcohols or volatile distillates.</note>, resins, tears, and combustible gums extracted from both sources—that is, from both animals and vegetables. Mineral sulphurs are also drawn out by the benefit of both art and nature. By nature, they appear as the spontaneous "efflorescences" <note>Crystalline or powdery crusts forming on a surface.</note> found underground, such as amber, bitumen, oils, fats, sulphurs, and all oily substances. Various artificial sulphurs are also extracted from pyrite, jet, fossil coal, bitumen, "earth of the sun" <note>original: "terra solis"; likely referring to a preparation of gold or a specific mineral thought to be solar in nature.</note>, and finally from every metallic substance in which that combustible sulphur is found.

And so much for the types of sulphur; however, no more varieties are found in the macrocosm—whether made by art or nature—than are found within the bodies of the whole human race. For just as animal differs from animal, tree from tree, and mineral from mineral, it is likewise clearly established that men do not share the same face, nor color, nor symmetry, nor the same texture, because their sulphur is not identical in all things. 

For those whom the Galenists <note>Followers of the traditional humor-based medicine of Galen.</note> call "melancholic," they abound in a pitch-like, naphtha-like, black, dense, and impure sulphur. Those of a "bilious" <note>Choleric or irritable.</note> temperament, however, abound in a sulphur that is waxy, saffron-colored, amber-like, fir-like, yellow, transparent, and subtle. The "sanguine" <note>Cheerful or ruddy-complexioned.</note> types possess an amaranthine, clove-colored, red, clear, and scarlet sulphur of a moderate temperament. Finally, the "phlegmatic" are also endowed with sulphur, but it is like cherry-gum, arabic gum, or mastic; it is gummy, white, compact, lumpy, sticky, thick, and catches fire only with great difficulty. 

Furthermore, just as in the macrocosm some sulphurs are benign and suitable for nutrition, while others are only medicinal; so it is in the human body, which nourishes its sulphurous parts with sweet sulphur, but sends "foreign" sulphur to the gallbladder, using it in place of a stimulating drug to purge the bowels. 

To this we add that, just as in the macrocosm some sulphurs are found to be very hot, such as petroleum, while others are Narcotic, such as the sulphurs of henbane, opium, and vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid or its sulfate salts.</note>; so too is "petroleum" found in the body as the author of fevers—both universal and particular, internal and external. Conversely, the sulphur of vitriol and opium is seen in "suffocation of the womb" <note>Hysteria.</note>, fainting <note>original: "lipothymia".</note>, "the dead evil" <note>original: "malo mortuo"; a necrotic skin disease or form of leprosy.</note>, leprosy, and other diseases. # LETTERS ON CHEMISTRY

### THOMAS MUFFET

### G 4

...subtle, some intermediate (as fossil coal, melted sulphur, and exalted amber among minerals; naval pitch, resin, and turpentine among vegetables; tallow, grease, and fat among animals; and those multiple grades of spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol or distillates.</note> among artificial substances, demonstrate more than enough); so also are diverse sulphurs found in humans, the thickness of which produces long fevers, while their subtlety produces shorter ones. And just as fossil coal maintains not only a longer-lasting but also a more violent flame than a lamp—because the latter enjoys a subtler nourishment while the former a denser one—by the same reasoning, the same argument can be told concerning fevers: of which the sulphur is sometimes spirituous, as in the Ephemera <note>A fever lasting only one day.</note>; sometimes somewhat thick, as in synochal fevers <note>A continuous, non-intermittent fever.</note>; often very thick, as in tertian fevers <note>A fever that recurs every third day, historically associated with malaria.</note>; and sometimes thickest, pitchy, and very similar to fossil coal, as in quartan fevers <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day.</note>. From here emerge those varieties, lengths, shortnesses, transplantations, mixtures, and true rules of paroxysms, fevers, and crises. If Hippocrates had seen this, he would have asserted not only that most fevers arise from some sulphurous matter, but universally all of them; and he would have attributed no burning either to those spirits of the air, or even to phlegmatic ones. For who has ever discovered air, or water, or even earth, devoid of all sulphur, to be set on fire? But if this was never <unclear>seen</unclear> in the macrocosm <note>The "greater world" or the universe.</note>, by what means would you find it in the microcosm <note>The "lesser world" or the human body.</note>? 

Truly, let yourself be persuaded by the burning dart, lightning, the candle, comets, the "leaping goat" <note>original: "capra saltante"; an ancient term for a type of streaking atmospheric light or meteor.</note>, the spark, falling stars, the *ignis fatuus* <note>original: "igne fatuo"; a "will-o'-the-wisp" or swamp gas fire.</note>, Helena, Gemini <note>original: "Helena, Gemino"; names for types of St. Elmo's fire or twin atmospheric lights seen by sailors.</note>, or other meteors burning like fire, that the air can sometimes catch flame; you would show yourself too credulous by not attending to the fact that their flame takes its origin not from the air, but from a certain fatty exhalation. According to its thickness, subtlety, abundance, or scarcity, all those fiery specks in the air turn out brighter, clearer, darker, more opaque, shorter, or longer-lasting. To this, since it is not the nature of heat to be ignited, but to ignite whatever can be burned: why do we define a fever as "ignited heat," and often from phlegmatic or earthy matter, when neither, if destitute of every kind of sulphur, could be ignited even a little bit? Indeed, all watery things (of which kind we make phlegm) as well as truly earthy particles, are born to extinguish fire—so far are they from nourishing it when poured over it. Therefore, sulphur alone is the nourishment and seat of all sublunary fire; all other things grow hot only from the mixture or (so to speak) the proximity of this. And so much for sulphur. 

But just as some parts of the body are called sulphurous <term>pre-eminently</term> <note>original Greek: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν" (kat' exochēn); used here to mean "par excellence" or "in the highest degree."</note>—namely tallow, the omentum <note>A fold of fatty tissue in the abdomen.</note>, fat, grease, glands, marrow, bile, and whatever oily thing is seen here and there—so also some are called Mercurial in the same way, such as water and what is commonly called phlegm, and their receptacles...
