...common; likewise, some parts are saline <note>Salt-based</note> in nature, such as the bones, the heavier internal organs, ligaments, cartilages, the tougher membranes, serum, kidneys, nails, hair, etc. When these parts are broken down through the chemist's art, more **Salt** is found in them than **Mercury** or **Sulphur**. 

However, if you wish to learn about the action and truly marvelous revolution of **Mercury** within the human body, you must first look at it in the mirror of the "Greater World" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe at large.</note>: there, for every type of water and incombustible liquid that exists, a corresponding Mercury is found. Nor is the situation any different within us (Philalethes), for some people abound in mineral Mercury, others in vegetable, and others in animal. 

Among the mineral types, one Mercury is distinguished as that of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note>, another of the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, a third of **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, a fourth of **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, a fifth of **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, a sixth of **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, and a seventh of **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>. 

Among the vegetable types, one person might possess the Mercury of lemon balm, thistle, sage, or betony; while another possesses that of satyrion, celandine, valerian, or brassatella <note>Historically identified as adder's-tongue or a similar herb.</note>. 

Furthermore, among the animal types, the Mercury of the lion, tiger, puppy, cow, horse, bear, or elephant is imparted now here, now there; if not in its very essence, it is at least marked with those same powers. 

Finally, the **Mercury** of humans is either natural or foreign. The **natural** is sweet, mild, and neither hot nor cold beyond the second degree, nor does it exceed its proper quantity. The **foreign** Mercury, however, like quicksilver, is dominated by an imbalance <note>original: "dyscrasia"</note> of either extreme heat or extreme cold; it is designed to putrefy, erode, weaken, and unnerve, and even to undermine the very bones which are the stabilizers of the entire human fabric. 

From this source, therefore, arise apoplexies, paralyses, bouts of foolishness, rheumatisms, dropsies, leucophlegmasia <note>A condition involving pale, cold swelling of the skin.</note>, edemas, excessive salivation <note>original: "ptyelismi"</note>, and "floods" of the stomach, brain, heart, bladder, spinal cord, and other parts. These do not arise from "pituita" or "phlegm," which are nothing more than fictitious names <note>Muffet is rejecting the traditional Galenic four humors in favor of Paracelsian chemistry.</note>. 

Having explained these things regarding the volatile principle of the body <note>Mercury</note>, I now come to the anatomy of **Salt**, or that fixed principle. Salt is also either domestic or foreign. The **domestic** is pleasant, mild, and preserves the body from rotting; it is the bond of unity and, as it were, the proper seasoning of health. The **foreign** Salt, however, has acquired a sharp acrimony, acidity, burning, bitterness, erosion, piercing, stimulation, and perforation—either through a defect in the "seeds of fate" <note>Perhaps referring to hereditary disposition.</note> or through one’s own intemperance. It is the author of all internal and external ulcers, boils, abscesses, and openings in the skin. 

There are said to be various species of Salt within a human being. Some take their origin from minerals: 
* arsenical 
* ferruginous <note>Iron-like</note> 
* venereal <note>Copper-like</note> 
* vitriolated 
* aluminous <note>Alum-like</note> 
* gem-like 
* ammoniacal 
* crystalline 

Others are taken from plants: those like nettle, smartweed, pepper, opium, tartar, arum, or ginger. Others still are derived from animals: those like the viper, wild beast, wolf, dog, lizard <note>original: "stellionares"</note>, Spanish fly <note>original: "cantharidei"</note>, scorpion, or tarantula—and not without good reason. For just as a person is affected differently by the bite of a tarantula than by a lizard or a viper, so also...

# CHEMICAL EPISTLES
**G 5**

Indeed, a certain **Salt** excites laughter, titillation, and a most pleasant itching; another, however, brings on immense bodily pain, restlessness, insanity, and hydrophobia <note>original: *hydrophobiam*; a morbid fear of water, often associated with rabies</note>, so that you would think the man was not pricked by an internal stimulus, but wounded from without by a rabid dog. 

Just as the *Dipsas* <note>A legendary desert serpent whose bite caused unquenchable thirst</note> induces an immense thirst with its bite; the *Haemorrhois* a flow of blood; the *Amphisbaena* inflammation; the *Basilisk* mortification <note>Death of the tissues</note>; the *Asp* a deep slumber; the *Drynius* cardiac distress <note>original: *καρδιωγμὸν* (kardiōgmon); a Greek term for heartburn or oppressive pain at the heart</note>; the *Stellio* <note>A spotted lizard</note> a livid bruising; the *Salamander* a freezing cold; the *Solifuga* <note>A venomous spider or insect</note> the plague; the bean-spider blisters; and the *Scolopendra* <note>A venomous centipede</note> induces putrefaction: so also does the salt of dropsy, of menstruation, of pleurisy, of eating-ulcers <note>original: *phagedænicus*</note>, of mercury, of carbuncles, of boils, of narcotics, of the pestilence, of herpes, and of gangrene. These salts produce those very same symptoms wherever they have established a home or center for themselves within us after their <term>separation</term> <note>In Paracelsian chemistry, diseases are caused when the three principles (Salt, Sulphur, Mercury) separate from their balanced state.</note> has occurred. 

For as long as this salt remains immersed in the <term>mercurial liquors</term> <note>The volatile, fluid components of the body</note> that continually flow here and there through the veins and wider vessels, it cannot ulcerate the body—both because of its constant motion (preventing a fixed center) and because it is mixed with a liquid contrary to itself. 

Wine shows us this same truth: when it is fresh must, it resembles a divine nectar in its remarkable sweetness and delight, and it wonderfully charms the tongue and palate of those prone to drink. Yet, once the parts and spirits have been separated, it casts off a most salty and sharp <term>Tartar</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate; in alchemy, the solid "salt" that settles in wine casks</note>, as well as a most sour and plainly corrosive vinegar. Since, therefore, the number of fluids flowing in the body is infinite, it is no wonder if such diverse forms and operations of salts also appear, giving birth to various species, shapes, and figures of ulcers, as well as various symptoms. 

And so you see clearly that the **Light of Nature** is nothing other than the analogy of that **Great World** <note>The Macrocosm or Universe</note> with the **Microcosmic body** <note>The human being as a "little world"</note>. You see also that the art of nature and the nature of art agree, and that the same power is the worker of both—even though to the Galenic mind (for Hippocrates felt otherwise) these things seem not only different, but even opposite. 

Farewell, and love me as you usually do, my dearest Philalethes. 

Dated at London, June 17, 1583 <note>original: *15. Kal. Quintilis*; the 15th day before the Kalends of July</note>.

# THOMAS MUFFET
**G 5**

<margin>Pliny, Book 29, Chapter 1.</margin> ...whenever he brought forth his tablets. Hippocrates of Cos, that famous man, shortly before the Peloponnesian War, realizing that medicine lacked established rules, traveled extensively. He did not only gather information from the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; his temples functioned as early hospitals where "cures" were recorded on tablets</note>, but also transcribed case histories and cures of diseases from the accounts of all the philosophers and physicians he met. Thus, through multifaceted experience and diligent observation, he was the first to give birth to Medicine. The most reliable witnesses of his travels are those *Epidemics*—or rather, his "Travel Observations"—in which he made such progress that no <term>Galenist</term> <note>A follower of the 2nd-century physician Galen, whose theories dominated medical schools for centuries</note> has yet been found who could equal, let alone surpass, the skill of Hippocrates. 

As for the Arabs, only someone completely ignorant of their lives and writings could fail to know that they visited various regions and crossed over to islands for the sake of knowledge. Indeed, to show you that you have written nothing of substance, I declare that there is no physician, whether here or elsewhere, flourishing with true praise and learning, who has not also left his homeland for a time to bring back various discoveries from other nations to enrich Medicine. 

But you say: *Those for whom everything grows at home have no need to import food from elsewhere, and can live content with their own farming.* Yet, for those whose land is sterile and where agriculture yields little, they must engage in trade and keep away internal hunger by fetching nourishment from abroad. 

You write that your Academies and cities are so rich in the number and excellence of their physicians that foreigners seek them out as a model of knowledge. Although I, as a Londoner <note>original: *Ludipolentis*; a neo-Latin term for a resident of London</note>, would wish for this above all things, the reality of the matter proves it false. For in which of our Academies is a local <term>Anatomy</term> <note>The dissection of a human body for study</note> performed more than once every ten years? (If I were to speak of "living anatomy" in this way—which nonetheless seems the greatest part of Medicine—you would hardly understand me, my dear Endymion <note>A figure from myth known for eternal sleep; Muffet implies his opponent is dreaming or out of touch with reality</note>). 

Who demonstrates Physiology by the evidence of the senses rather than by mere opinion? Who leads the student to the sickbed and shows him, with a true and sincere mind, the affected area, the type of ailment, its cause, the sequence of causes, the outcome of the disease, its movement, its connections, and its degree—following the model of Hippocrates and the physicians of Padua <note>The University of Padua was the premier center for medical education and clinical observation during the Renaissance</note>? 

Furthermore, what hope is there for a future physician when those primary and royal professors read in no particular order, but seize now this little book, now that one, and spend an entire year explaining—or rather entangling—ten <term>Aphorisms</term> <note>Short, pithy medical principles, specifically those written by Hippocrates</note>? Is this how one teaches an art, reads methodically, instructs a student, or masters Medicine? The duties of a Medical Lecturer should rather be these: to hand down the entire art to the disciples, beginning from both types of anatomy, and to devote every effort to their fastest and truest education. But this title does not fit your leaders. Their speeches, works, and virtues cannot carry such a weight. As I live, I pity them, and I grieve for the fate of our Academies with tears that continually fall.

### CHEMICAL LETTERS

...whenever I see among them several medical students, brought out onto the plain like certain most noble horses; yet if you see them running in the <term>diaulos</term> <note>original: *diaulo*; a double-lap footrace in ancient Greece, used here as a metaphor for the rigors of practical medical application</note>, they are found to be either fearful, or prone to bucking, or out of breath, or weak-kneed, or stumbling. And this is not so much their own fault as the vice of their Predecessors, from whom they received infinite flaws of doctrine and impediments to science in place of the one true interpretation. 

How much better it would be for a medical beginner, cultured in those languages and the humanities, to betake himself in the very bloom of his youth to **Paduan Athens** <note>Padua was the leading center for medical and anatomical study in the Renaissance</note>, where in a single summer he might learn thoroughly the shapes and synonyms of almost all herbs, and in the course of one winter, the anatomy of corpses. In the following year, let him carefully weigh **Galenic physiology** <note>The study of how the body functions according to Galen's theories of the four humors</note>, read accurately from its very elements to the perfection of the body and the full explanation of all actions; and let him learn all those signs which are called either pathological, or aetiological, or even prognostic. 

And so, with two years successfully completed, let him afterwards join himself as a constant companion to the lecturers and diligently observe their practice (which he will very easily obtain); and thus, warned by the errors of others or educated by their prudence, he will produce for himself the richest fruit. From a good Physician <note>original: *Physico*; meaning a natural philosopher or student of nature</note> he will emerge the best Doctor, and as it says in **Homer**, *superior to all others* <gloss>original: πάντων ὑπείροχος ἄλλων</gloss>. 

As for **Chemistry**, which is the marrow or rather the soul of all Pharmacy: although it is cultivated by some most skilled men in your region so that they might be a source of wonder to the sluggish <term>Galenists</term> <note>Followers of traditional Greek medicine who often resisted new chemical remedies</note> wasting away in idleness—yet the knowledge of all those combined with the expertise of foreigners in this area will seem as much smaller as the Sun is greater than the Moon, or as springs and basins of water are more abundant than the rivulets flowing from them. 

*But (you say) however much you praise **Padua, Basel, Paris, Bologna, Montpellier**, and other famous overseas Academies; nevertheless, we often discover this one thing: those who travel there for a long time return home empty-handed, bringing back nothing but a futile and sometimes lying history of things and men; others indeed learned that Italian lewdness, German drunkenness, Swiss boorishness, or French hypocrisy, which they never afterward set aside upon returning to their homeland. And these are the primary "ornaments" of travelers, which you cannot enjoy without the mark of a bad man, nor be without if you wish to maintain a good reputation.* 

To which I respond, there is a great variety among travelers, and not all set out with one mind, nor do they return with the same benefit. Therefore, I desire judgment in travel, and indeed that of **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus, known for his wisdom and resistance to temptation during his long travels</note>; lest, when physicians ought to be philosophizing with the Muses alone, they be turned by some **Cup of Circe** into swine and *unmanly men* <note>original: ἄνδρας ἀνήνορας; a Homeric phrase for men who have lost their strength or virtue</note>, to use the poet’s word. But if the beginner abstains from her house and the songs of the Sirens, and does not easily submit himself to idleness de- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "de-" for "derelinquet" or similar, continuing the thought that the student will not abandon his studies.</note>

...[he will not be] deceived, and will have performed only those things which belong to the art—not as it is described by you—but he will return more learned than **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, and will keep his homeland sound and protected from infinite diseases as if from the most dangerous traitors of the body. Do not wish any longer to imitate those fireside philosophers who spend their lives in a bedroom, where no one is rained upon nor scorched by the sun, and who prefer the authors of their own library to the theater of nature itself and the living voice. 

Arise, I say, collect yourself; God helps industry. And with this "fire-starter" <note>original: *igniario*; a metaphor for Muffet's provocative words</note> given by me, burn more and more daily with a zeal for travel; or if you are not moved by my stimulus, let at least the authority of **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **Avicenna** move you. Since they were the princes of all Medicine, they nevertheless drew their knowledge from various regions and from foreign springs. They were truly ashamed to be more desirous of leisure than of knowledge, and they believed that erudition was to be purchased not only with labor, but also with spirit. 

Therefore you are now safe nowhere, Endymion. A cliff looms in front, and an enemy from behind; if you blame travel, you condemn Galen, you wound Hippocrates, and you kill **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian physician and philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age</note>. If you approve of it, you then disapprove of yourself, and you run back to my side, which you deserted all too rashly. 

However, since it is better to run back than to run badly—and the path to good habits is never too late—even in this old age of yours, sell your estates, board a ship, visit foreign lands, build furnaces, learn **Chemistry** <note>original: *Chemiam*; at this time, chemistry and alchemy were often used interchangeably to describe the study of matter and its medicinal applications</note>, and cultivate a new Medicine that does not waver in opinion, but is confirmed by the senses. Unless you do this, it will be rightly said of you and those like you what **Martial** <note>A Roman poet known for his witty epigrams</note> once wrote concerning lazy sailors:

> *You idle, boys, and you know nothing,*
> *Sluggish as old age and sticky resin:*
> *And even now, wandering through calm waves,*
> *You play at leisure in a safe ship.*
> *I do not think you are sailors; but "Argonauts."*
> <note>original: *argonautas*; Muffet is making a pun here. While the Argonauts were heroes of myth, the Greek word *argos* means "lazy" or "idle." He is calling them "idle-sailors."</note>

->Listen: and at last wake up, Endymion.<-
->Given at London, March 29, 1584.<-

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE OF MIDDELBURG’S BOOK ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY.

->In which is taught what a student of true Chemistry, aspiring to perfection, ought to know and what they ought to avoid.<-

### Preface.

<margin>Alchemy is a part of natural philosophy.</margin>
No one, unless they wish to do an injustice, will call into doubt that the part of natural philosophy which treats the principles, causes, properties, passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to how a substance is acted upon or its reactions to external forces</note>, and transmutations of metals is the most noble. I have added "transmutations" so that I do not seem to speak only of that common part of Physics <note>Hoghelande uses "Physics" in the broad Aristotelian sense of the study of nature</note> which determines the matter and form of metals, their place of generation, ductility, color, taste, smell, and similar things; but rather of that part especially which teaches how to convert one metal into another.

<margin>It is taught that the transmutation of metals is possible.</margin>
That this is possible requires no further proof, since experience provides the evidence, eyewitnesses in almost every part of the world confirm it, and the most serious authors assert it.

<margin>Experience: Georgius Agricola, Book 9 of *On the Nature of Fossils* <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555) was a German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy."</note>.</margin>
For iron, by means of waters bubbling up spontaneously from the earth and even by a simple artifice, changes into copper <note>original: *æs*; likely referring to copper or bronze</note>, and quicksilver <note>mercury</note> cooked with sulfur is changed into silver—though without profit, unless a greater skill of the craftsman is added.

<margin>By witnesses.</margin>
There remain people in France, England, Germany, Bohemia, and the Low Countries who, with their own hands—having cast a very small quantity of a certain powder (which they had received prepared by others) into quicksilver heated by fire—reported that silver or gold was produced from it, capable of passing every test.

<margin>By authority. Book 6 of *On Subtlety*; Book 1 of *On Occult Philosophy*, chapter 14; in the additions to the *Speculum* <note>Likely referring to the *Speculum Maius* by Vincent of Beauvais</note>; the rubric on the crime of forgery <note>original: *de crimine falsi*; a legal reference regarding the authenticity of metals</note>.</margin>
Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician</note> narrates that in the presence of the Prince and the most distinguished Senate of the city of Venice, quicksilver was converted into gold by a pharmacist from Treviso. Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a renowned German polymath and occult writer</note> says that by the "spirit of gold"—or rather by its form or its purer part—imperfect metals and quicksilver can be turned into gold, and that he himself has seen and known this.

<margin>All metals are of the same essence, but differ accidentally <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accidental" difference is one that does not change the core essence of a thing, such as color or shape</note>.</margin>
He testifies

# PREFACE.

<margin>That the transmutation of metals is possible is proved by similar examples.</margin>
Andreas the Jurist <note>Latin: *Andreas I. C.*, likely referring to a *Iuris Consultus* or legal consultant</note> testifies that in his own time, Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> was present at the Roman court and produced certain golden rods, which he allowed to be subjected to every possible test. But why is it a wonder if anyone believes that metals can be transformed among themselves? They share the same matter and essence, and are distinguished only by "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or degree of "cooking" that do not change the fundamental nature of a substance.</note>—namely, the location of their generation and whether they have been "cooked" more or less—when we see the same thing happen in trees, crops, and plants? It is certain that earth, wood, twigs, shells, and even the skins and bones of animals are converted into rocks and stones by the power of natural waters flowing spontaneously and by their "petrifying virtue" <note>original: *lapidificandi virtute*; the inherent power to turn objects into stone</note>. 

<margin>Transition is easier between similar things than between dissimilar ones.</margin>
<margin>Book 1 of *On Minerals*, chapter 7.</margin>
<margin>A wonderful metamorphosis.</margin>
Yet what could be more different than stone and wood, or animal hides and bones, since they differ entirely in their category and substance? Regarding the earth, the fact is too well known to need proof. I will only mention certain accounts most worthy of report from Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential philosopher-scientist</note>, who relates that in his time, a large tree branch was found in the Danish sea near the city of Lübeck; on it was a nest with young birds, and all of them—the birds, the nest, and the branch—had been turned into stone. 

<margin>Georgius Agricola seems to suggest this spring is in Iceland, near Mount Hecla. See Book 2 of *On the nature of those things which flow spontaneously from the earth*, where more of these examples are found.</margin>
<margin>And Book 7 of *On the nature of fossils*.</margin>
He also relates that when Emperor Frederick heard there was a spring in which everything submerged was turned to stone, he sent a sealed glove there for the sake of discovering the truth. When half of it had been submerged in the spring for several days along with part of the seal, the half immersed in the water was turned to stone, while the remaining part was not changed at all. 

<margin>Unblemished witnesses are to be believed.</margin>
But perhaps some will admit the transmutation of metals, being convinced by the testimony and consensus of very famous men, yet they will deny that this can be done for profit or with "infinite increase" <note>This refers to "multiplication," the alchemical process of increasing the quantity or potency of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. I believe they should be answered in this way: if in legal judgments—where a person’s wealth, life, or reputation is at stake—we must believe two or three witnesses according to both divine and civil law, then it is much more equitable for this to apply in the Chemical Art. This art is proven true by reasons, analogies, examples, and witnesses—not just three or four, but almost countless ones. For we have the writings of the most learned and upright men, such as Saint Thomas Aquinas <note>While primarily a theologian, several alchemical treatises were historically (though perhaps spuriously) attributed to Aquinas</note>.

<summary>Hoghelande argues for the possibility of alchemy by drawing analogies to petrifaction in nature and cites the testimonies of historical figures like Albertus Magnus and Emperor Frederick. He concludes that the vast number of scholarly witnesses to alchemy should provide more legal and intellectual certainty than the small number of witnesses required in a court of law.</summary>

# PREFACE.

<margin>In the place cited above.</margin>
The testimonies of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts were attributed</note>, Ramon Lull, John of Rupescissa, Marsilio Ficino, and Arnald of Villanova—whom the legal consultant Giovanni Andrea calls a "Theologian, a supreme Physician and Alchemist"—as well as Rhazes, Avicenna, and many others, are all beyond reproach. They testify to a most true art, one that rivals its mother, nature. Why should we judge that credit must be withheld from such distinguished men, and believe instead certain <term>pretenders</term> <note>original: *sciolis*; refers to "smatterers" or those with superficial, prideful knowledge</note> who, with perverse judgment, scoff that the art is vain and counterfeit? These critics claim it was handed down enigmatically and obscurely for no other reason than to keep the minds of idle men occupied. Far be it from us to think that those ancient philosophers of venerable authority would have deliberately wished to entrust some falsehood to memory; they always devoted their greatest effort to seeking the truth, and they sought fame for posterity not from trifles and empty things, but from difficult and sublime matters, resting on a true and stable foundation.

<margin>That a Philosopher does not knowingly lie.</margin>
To this is also added the consensus of diverse nations: for records concerning the <term>metamorphosis of metals</term> <note>The transformation of one metal into another, such as lead into gold</note>—not only by the Latins, but also the Greeks, Egyptians, Arabs, Chaldeans, Gauls, Germans, Spaniards, and English—are handled daily by the hands of curious men. These authors all cry out, as if with one voice (though in dissonant tongues), that the art is most true. They preach that nothing more magnificent or sublime has been granted to man in this world by God Most High, second only to the Divine Law in which lies the salvation of the soul; and therefore it must be investigated with the highest zeal and sought with wakeful labor.

<margin>That Alchemy is true is proven by the consensus of nations.</margin>
<margin>Nothing is more sublime than Alchemy, except for the Holy Scriptures.</margin>
<margin>Why the art is contradicted. Abuse, the error of workers, or ignorance do not invalidate the art. Book *On the Soul*.</margin>
Perhaps those who deny the art are mistaken in this: that while infinite numbers of people devote themselves to chemistry, they see no one who boasts of having attained the knowledge. But to the wise, and those who scrutinize the causes of events, nothing happens that is worthy of wonder. For how few work in the proper matter? Scarcely one in thousands. What wonder is it, then, if they are frustrated in the proper end? Wherefore Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose name was often attached to alchemical treatises in the West</note> said, not without wit: *He who takes what he ought, and mixes, and works as he ought, from there proceeds that which ought to proceed.* And most people in—

<margin>Why someone very rarely attains the art. That greed and poverty are great obstacles.</margin>

<margin>Secrets are not to be made public. Proverbs 10.</margin>
...they are quite learned and unrefined <note>original: *ἄμουσοι* (amousoi); a Greek term meaning "without the Muses," used here to describe people who lack the cultural or spiritual depth to grasp complex ideas</note>, for they do not even understand common Latin speech—how much less the metaphors and analogies of the wise? Others, though they may be learned and of a sharp mind, nevertheless do not possess the books, either because they do not wish to spend the money to pay their price out of greed, or they cannot out of poverty, or because they are unable to find copies in the places where they dwell and shrink from the prospect of travel. Those, however, who have attained both the books and the Art through the grace of God, remember the saying of Solomon: *The wise man hides his knowledge, but the mouth of the fool is near to destruction* <note>Proverbs 10:14</note>; for indeed, reasons are not lacking as to why those who know do not reveal themselves. But if we must deny things that we have happened to see very rarely or never at all, then the credibility of all history, both sacred and secular, will be diminished. For who would believe in the sulfurous and fiery rain from heaven during the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, or the strength of Samson, and many other things whose similar examples are never recounted except among fables?

<margin>Book 13, at the end.</margin>
<margin>Things whose causes are unknown or which happen rarely should not be accused of falsehood.</margin>
Who, while running through the *Annals* of Publius Cornelius Tacitus, would not burst into laughter when he reads that a fire at the Colony of the Juhones <note>Referring to an event in Tacitus’s *Annals* 13.57 involving the Ubii tribe near Cologne</note> was extinguished not with water, but with clubs and clothes stripped from the body? Does he not seem to be telling a fable? And yet, we believe it could have happened then, and we know for certain it happens even more often today in the territory of Liège <note>original: *Leodiensi agro*; a region in modern Belgium famous for early coal mining</note>, where miners dig out <term>bituminous coals</term> <note>original: *carbones bituminosos*; mineral coal, which was a curiosity to those used to wood charcoal</note> from under the earth, which are black and like stones, for use in the hearths of blacksmiths. Who would not believe that pure lies were being told by Georgius Agricola <note>A famous German "father of mineralogy"</note> when he says that on Mount Hekla in Iceland, there is a fire that consumes water but does not burn <term>flax</term> <note>original: *stupa*; the coarse part of flax or hemp</note>? But investigators of natural causes know that the <term>bitumen</term> <note>A naturally occurring flammable petroleum substance</note> from which that fire is stirred up is extinguished by dry things and nourished by water. Truly, in vain have philosophers written so much about the miracles of nature, and in vain have physicians written about very rare diseases (or those occurring only in certain places) and their cures, if the slander of anyone who has seen or known none of these things should find a place. Indeed, such people are not absurdly compared by Master Pietro Bono of Ferrara <note>A 14th-century alchemist</note> to children who, from the beginning of their birth—

<margin>Those who deny rare events are similar to [children].</margin>

<margin>...ignorance, or things difficult for them to grasp.</margin>

Why do they not believe *St. Thomas* [Aquinas] <note>The influential 13th-century theologian who argued that alchemical gold could be real if produced by natural processes</note> when he says that nothing prevents the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note> from using natural causes to produce natural and true effects? For what reason do they not follow the opinion of *Marsilio Ficino* <note>An Italian priest and philosopher (1433–1499) who led the revival of Hermetic philosophy</note>, who asserts that all living things, both plants and animals, multiply by a certain spirit of their own? He claims that this spirit is confined within metals by a thicker matter, but if it should ever be properly separated and preserved in its own natural seat, it could, beyond any doubt, generate something similar to itself. 

He who does not yield to the consensus of such great men and so many nations will not admit himself defeated by reason, or even by experience itself; instead, he will attribute the effect of **transmutation** to the Devil and the trifles of worthless magicians rather than to God and the power of Nature. I once asked a noble and not unlearned man, when in familiar conversation he laughed at the **Chemical Art** as vain, whether he would believe it possible if someone were to provide a demonstration of the Art before his very eyes? He denied it. 

But what can you do with such backwards men, who only admire common things and admit nothing except what tastes best to their own palate? To them, the majesty of Nature is a joke; exploring the properties of things or discovering the hidden operations of metals are received with laughter as if they were mere delusions. But by whom is the Art most strongly opposed? Truly by those who have never caught even a scent of it, or have never read chemical books except in a hurry—clearly in the same way that **dogs lap water from the Nile and run** <note>original: *canes e Nilo*. A classical proverb referring to those who approach a subject superficially or hastily to avoid being "caught" by the difficulty of the material</note>. <margin>...when they ignore it.</margin>...ignore? What is more reckless than for an unskilled person to pass judgment on a matter they do not understand? As the **Comic poet** <note>original: "Comicus"; referring to the Roman playwright Terence</note> long ago cried out, and not in vain:

> Nothing is more unjust than an ignorant man,
> Who thinks nothing is right except what he himself has done.

To these is added another class of men: namely, those who wish to achieve the greatest riches suddenly with only one or two gold coins. When they have once been deceived by some fraud, they condemn the **Art** <note>Alchemy</note> rather than the imposter. In this, they imitate the nature of a dog; for, lacking judgment, they rage at the stone with which they were struck, while ignoring the person who threw it. <margin>Many attribute more to their own intellect than is fair.</margin>

Truly, if anyone looks deeply into the cause of slander in others, they cannot sufficiently marvel at the arrogance and tyranny of many. These people judge the Art to be vain—thinking that nothing but mere fictions are handed down by **chemical authors** <note>Alchemists</note>—solely because they themselves are not capable of understanding such great mysteries. These secrets are revealed only to a very few, and at times appointed by God. Yet, in other matters, these critics are confident they can penetrate the most obscure things with the sharpness of their own minds. It is as if God had given them everything, and there were nothing else in the nature of things that could be hidden from them, or as if nothing can be known except what they themselves recognize. <margin>Glory sought from the contempt of others is foolish and empty.</margin>

There are also those led by the desire for some vain, minor glory, who insult the Art and tear it apart with open insults, so that they might seem to others to be a little wiser and not to share in the "madness" of the masses. They foolishly and far too stubbornly claim that those searching for the **secrets of Nature** labor under a kind of disease, hoping that their own opinions cannot be proven wrong by experience. 

But they are very much deceived in their own opinion. Many among the common people everywhere know that those who have witnessed the works of nature and art are the ones to be believed, while those who hold this science in low esteem are rejected as unworthy. <margin>No wise person has denied the Art.</margin> For since they despise the powers of Nature and Art, they are deservedly excluded from the fruits of those works. The exact opposite of what they hoped for happens to them: while they wish to be seen as wise and learned, they are called foolish and ignorant by the masters of this science because they laugh at the Art. As <margin>Book on the Soul, chapter 2.</margin> **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose writings were foundational to medieval alchemy and medicine</note> himself affirms, no one who was wise ever denied the **mastery of the stone** <term>magisterium lapidis; the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone</term>. # PREFACE.

...should remain silent, and not condemn what they themselves are ignorant of. Let them reflect with that same **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to both medicine and alchemy</note>: *if this art exists, how it exists; and if it does not exist, how it does not exist.* <note>original: "hæc ars si sit, quomodo sit; & si non sit, quomodo non sit"</note> Or let them await the time when God—perhaps to restrain the tyranny of the Turks, or for some other reason—might one day stir someone up who will openly prove that the art is most true, even though God is powerful enough to defeat and overthrow the enemies of His name without it. But if they are unwilling to be silent, let them act in the philosophical manner of disputation, without insults, and first try to tear down the arguments of **Petrus Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Pietro Bono, an influential 14th-century alchemist who wrote the 'Precious New Pearl'</note> and others.

<margin>In the *Precious New Pearl*.</margin>
<margin>The Art can neither be sufficiently proven by logic, nor destroyed by arguments.</margin>
Although this art cannot be sufficiently proven by logic, neither can it be undermined by debate. Therefore, **Ramon Lull** <note>Raymundus Lullius (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note>—who otherwise provided the most exquisite explanation for everything done in the art—did not care to assert its truth with words or arguments, but only said: *That which is seen by ocular experiment needs no proof.* <note>original: "Id quod experimento oculari videtur, probatione non indigere"</note>

<margin>In the *Testament*.</margin>
And **Blessed Thomas Aquinas** <note>The famous theologian; several alchemical treatises were attributed to him in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, though modern scholars often consider them pseudo-epigraphical</note> said to his companion Brother Reginald: *Do not care,* he said, *about the words of modern and ancient philosophers discussing this science, since Alchemy has established its seat in the capacity of the intellect and in experimental demonstration.*

<margin>The truth of Alchemy consists in the capacity of the intellect and experience.</margin>
<margin>It is not expedient to know that the art is entirely true and certain, and why.</margin>
<margin>Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
Indeed, it is not even beneficial to know that this art is true and entirely certain, so that the saying of **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD)</note> regarding the doubts of the Soul might most appropriately apply here: *it is worthwhile to consider whether all doubts about the soul should be resolved, or whether instead we should place our profit in the doubts themselves.* No one, therefore, should wonder if Saint Thomas, Lull, and others outstanding in learning and genius neglected to defend the art with words, since the doubt of men has yielded profit rather than harm for them and for all posterity. For by that reasoning, God provides for the safety of those who work legitimately; and He teaches them to reap no small benefit from their enemies. Nor should it be thought that they lacked words or reasons, but perhaps they could not speak without publicizing the **secrets of Nature** <note>original: "Natura arcana"</note>. <meta>This page follows the preface's opening arguments where the author, Theobald de Hoghelande, defends alchemy against its detractors. He moves from dismissing the arguments of the ignorant to defining the actual nature and purpose of the "Philosophers' Stone."</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>Those disputing unknown things cannot reach correct conclusions.</margin>
For almost all the arguments brought against the Art proceed from nowhere else than ignorance of those things which are done in the Art. Thus, many speak of substantial forms, of the proportion of mixtures, and of the vessel of Nature and Art, and by disputing unknown matters, they reach unknown conclusions. Therefore, leaving those aside, I proceed to the goal of my proposition.

<margin>What the Philosophers' Stone is.</margin>
The intention of the philosophers of this Art is to produce a certain mineral virtue from the purest seed of gold and silver artificially—yet with the benefit and help of Nature—in the form of a most subtle white or red powder. This powder can be multiplied infinitely and has the power <margin>Virtues of the Stone.</margin> to penetrate quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; also known as mercury</note> and other base and impure metals in an instant, cleansing them of all impurities, and leading them to a more perfect state, namely that of gold and silver. Furthermore, it has the power of restoring the infirm human body and bringing it back to a true balance <term>temperamentum: the healthy proportion of the four bodily humors</term>, or preserving a healthy body in health until the end appointed by God. <margin>The Philosophers' Stone, the Elixir, and the Medicine are the same.</margin> This powder, endowed with such great virtue, is called the *Elixir* by the Arabs, and the *Medicine* and their *Stone* by the Latin philosophers. 

However, I would wish to warn the younger students that the name "*Stone*" is widely applied and used in different ways. <margin>The name of the 'Stone' is widely applied. Chapter 10 of the *Rosarium*, part 1. In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin> For sometimes the raw material of the Art, which Nature has provided us, is called the *Stone*. Hence **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> in his work *To Lilio*: *Although our stone naturally contains the tincture within itself, because it was perfectly created in the body of the earth, yet it does not have motion by itself to become the perfect Elixir unless it is moved by Art and operation.* <note>original: "Quamvis lapis noster tincturam in se naturaliter contineat... nisi moveatur arte & operatione."</note> Likewise **Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval Latin manuscripts</note>: *From the stone proceeds quicksilver, for the water is extracted from it, which is called quicksilver.*

The principles constituting the Elixir are also called "stones," which are three in <margin>The three principles of the Stone.</margin> number: namely quicksilver, Sulfur, and Tincture; or, Body, Spirit, and Soul; or, Earth, Water, and Fire—and a fourth resulting from the first two, which is Air. For the Sages of this Art have bestowed these names upon them. Regarding quicksilver <margin>In the printed treatise.</margin> that saying of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath</note> must be understood: *The third stage of the work is the reduction of the stone into natural earth.* Explaining this...

Whence Lull <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> writes: *The generation of both the stone and the Medicine is achieved and completed by reason of the similarity and subtlety of the parts to one another.* Finally, to settle the matter in a single word: at whatever stage of the Work the matter is—whether the parts of the matter are joined or separated—it is called the "Stone" or "stones." Indeed, the name "stone" is even transferred to other things entirely outside of the philosophical work. I have chosen to gather these points here because they will be the foundations of what is to be said; without knowing them, one could hardly understand what follows, especially since I myself must frequently use the word "stone" without making constant distinctions.

...is more probable. Therefore, regarding this Philosophers’ Stone or Elixir, or spiritual powder—[not because it is invisible and impalpable by its nature, but because, like a spirit, it most quickly pervades and penetrates both metallic and human bodies by its spiritual power]—since men of every kind and of every condition, whether noble or common, learned or unlearned, rich or poor, set it before themselves as a goal and hurry toward it with panting breath, nor are they deterred by labors or expenses, however great, from pursuing with all their strength that which they have desired with burning vows, thinking that they will only then achieve the highest happiness in this life if they are not frustrated in their expectation: I have judged that I would do a worthwhile thing if, because of the sought-after difficulty of the matter, I attempted to call back the greater part of those laboring from their purpose.

<margin>What moved the author to write this book.</margin>

Indeed, a mad opinion has invaded the minds of many: that the stone of the philosophers is altogether easy to make, prepared with light work, and happens by some fortune or chance, provided that the will to seek it is not lacking. For it is, they say, a Gift of God, and He bestows it upon whom He wills; and thus He can confer the benefit of the art upon me, and someone like me, just as much as on others more learned. Whence, what I am ashamed to report, even peasants and unlearned women now chatter about the secrets of the philosophers, and attempt experiments, and dare to promise themselves that fortune which not even the most learned and watchful men can hope for, except by the mercy of God alone.

<margin>Many falsely persuade themselves that the Elixir is easy to prepare.</margin>

This most detestable error takes its origin partly from the writings of certain philosophers, and partly also from the mere fables of idle men. For in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "turba Philosophorum"; a famous 12th-century Latin alchemical text depicting a debate among ancient philosophers</note> it is called *the work of women, and the play of children* <note>original: "opus mulierum, & ludus puerorum"; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the "secret" is known, the labor is as simple as household chores or play</note>. And Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note>, citing Democritus, says: *our work is light, and needs little help*. The author of the Treatise which begins: *All wisdom is from God* <note>original: "Omnis sapientia à Deo"</note>, attributed to Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and bishop, famously associated with alchemy in medieval lore</note>, says: *I intend to write of the true, light, and infallible art*. And there is the common verse:

<margin>The cause of the error.</margin>
<margin>The Book to Eutychia.</margin>

# PREFACE.

...is trodden upon by all today. There is one who might seem to have written his little book on the *metamorphosis of metals* <note>The author likely refers to the "Metamorphosis Metallorum," a famous alchemical treatise often attributed to Eirenaeus Philalethes.</note> out of a certain zeal of charity, were it not clear to the more skilled that he handed down the science too sparingly. <margin>A story.</margin>
When I was still a young man in Paris, I remember hearing that a certain gardener had thrown fire into a pile of useless and wild-growing weeds to reduce them to ash and prepare lye <note>Lye (lixivium) was traditionally made by soaking plant ashes in water; it was essential for making soap and cleaning.</note>. But, as it happened, a lead pipe for channeling water had been forgotten or unnoticed in that place due to its age. By the power of the fire, the lead melted and was converted into gold—not by chance, but by the undeniable power of a certain herb mixed among the others. Later, after removing the ashes, he found the gold, sold it, and received a great price. Truly, if those who tell such idle tales had tasted the secrets of nature even in part, or had used their judgment, they would not have so easily believed the lies and impostures of such deceitful men.

<margin>Like is generated from its like.</margin>
They would surely have considered that a human is generated from a human, a lion from a lion, and a plant from a plant, and that one should not seek in nature what is not within it. For how could a plant tint <note>original: "tinget"; in alchemy, the "tincture" is the power to change the color and quality of a metal.</note> or fix <note>original: "figet"; "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to the heat of fire.</note> a metal, and defend it from burning, when the plant itself contains neither tincture nor fixation and is consumed by fire?

<margin>The error of the practitioners.</margin>
Yet there were not lacking, nor are there lacking today, those who seek the highest secret of the Philosophers in animals as well as in vegetables. They experiment with whatever they come across—whether found in loose papers, misunderstood books, or works composed through the fraud and greed of imposters—hoping that they will find by chance what the Philosophers believe must be sought with the highest labor and continuous study, and obtained from God through prayers.

<margin>A dangerous experiment. The two-fold reason why the stone is sometimes called a "Salamander."</margin>
Thus, not without immense danger, some assert that live salamanders must be thrown into a most carefully sealed pot and burned, hoping they will bring back gold from it—when instead they ought to fear death <note>This likely refers to the danger of explosions or toxic fumes, such as mercury vapors, released during such misguided experiments.</note>. They believe this happened successfully for others based on hearsay alone, or perhaps because the Philosophers sometimes called their Stone (which is perfected by fire) by the name "Salamander," due to the similarity...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument against the notion that alchemy is an easy or accidental craft. Having previously discussed the "Metamorphosis of Metals" and the legend of the gardener's gold, the text now addresses why some philosophers describe the Great Work as "children's play."</meta>

# PREFACE.

...likeness <note>original: "tudine"; likely completing "similitudine" (similarity).</note> drawn from the Salamander, which the ancients believed lived in fire and was nourished by it; or, perhaps because its body is marked with various colored spots, like the Stone which changes from color to color and sometimes even demonstrates many colors at once. 

But to respond in part to the sayings of the philosophers cited above, I say that in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <margin>Response to the cited sayings of the philosophers.</margin> <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> it is not simply said that the art is "women’s work and children's play," but that it becomes so only after the completion of the cleaning of the stone and its whitening <note>original: "dealbationem"; the alchemical stage of Albedo, or whitening, which follows the blackness of Putrefaction.</note>, because from then on it is brought to its end by cooking alone. For so Socrates <note>In alchemical literature, "Socrates" is often a persona used to voice specific doctrines rather than the historical Greek philosopher.</note> says in that same book: *I have already shown you the arrangement of the white lead; once this is known, nothing follows but women’s work and children's play.* 

But how much difficulty there is in separating, purifying, and joining the elements of the stone is testified by the books of the philosophers and the frustrated labors of those who have tried it. Whence the author of the *Lily* <note>Likely referring to the "Lilium intelligentiae" or a similar treatise; "The Lily" was a common title for alchemical and medical works.</note>, who most faithfully interprets many sayings of the *Assembly*, writes in this manner: *Once the Stone and its operation are known, it is nothing else than the mockery of women and the play of children.* And certainly, we concede that the stone is easy to prepare for those who are knowledgeable and experienced, but not so for the inexperienced. 

As for Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous alchemist who supposedly spent a fortune and sixty years searching for the Stone before succeeding.</note> asserting that the art is so easy, we can presume that he was thinking of the later part of the work, just as Socrates did in the *Assembly*—especially since in his whole treatise he makes no mention at all, or only very sparingly, of the first part, which is the most difficult of all; instead, his parable encompasses only the end of the "cooking" <note>original: "decoctionis"; the long process of heating the alchemical matter in a sealed vessel.</note>. Or, we might say it seemed easy to him because after so many poorly placed expenses and forty years of labor, he finally attained the knowledge in the space of two years through the reading of books and by the help of divine grace—knowledge which he had previously attempted in vain for the span of so many years. We can also gather that the practice was not so easy for him from the fact that he writes that he knew the art for two years before he seriously set his hand to the work. 

It may be called "light" or easy by others <margin>Why it is called easy by others.</margin> in comparison to other operational arts which require many various instruments, physical exercise, and a great deal of labor; whereas this art requires only one single matter, one vessel, and one furnace with a suitable fire.

<meta>This page continues the author's refutation of those who believe alchemy is easy. Having addressed the "children's play" metaphor on the previous page, the author now explains that while the art is "once-and-done" in terms of its reward, the path to discovery is intentionally obscured and difficult, requiring self-examination and specific character traits in the practitioner.</meta>

# PREFACE.

<margin>The philosophers said many things to deceive the unwise.</margin> ...furthermore, while other arts are practiced for almost an entire lifetime, this one, once perfectly discovered and practiced, requires no repetition, since the practitioner has been enriched and has attained his desire. Who would even dare to deny that the philosophers put forward such things—as they did many others—to deceive the unwise? But I would wish that those who consider this art so trivial would recall that well-worn adage: *beautiful things are difficult* <note>original: "difficilia esse quæ pulcra." A Greek proverb (Chalepa ta kala) often cited by Plato and later Renaissance humanists to emphasize that worthwhile goals require great effort.</note>. Likewise, that saying of 

<margin>The preparation of the Stone is difficult.</margin> **Roger Bacon** <note>original: "Rogerij Bachonis." Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher who emphasized the study of nature through empiricism and was posthumously associated with alchemical secrets.</note>: *In those things in which God has placed great virtue, He has also placed great difficulty.* If only they remembered that it is called the "Stone of the Philosophers" <note>The Philosopher's Stone (Lapis Philosophorum), the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the elixir of life.</note>, and not the stone of the rustic or the ignorant—a name which, by itself, should rightly deter anyone who is not completely foolish. Instead, let them consult **Pietro Bono of Ferrara** <note>A 14th-century physician and alchemist, author of the influential "Precious New Pearl" (Margarita Pretiosa Novella).</note>, 

<margin>In the *New Pearl*.</margin> and he will answer that the search for this art, its truth, and its practical experience appears stronger, more difficult, more hidden, and of a longer duration than the search for all other things. Since this is most true, 

<margin>It is fitting for everyone to know themselves.</margin> let each person examine himself and prove himself a sharp judge of his own vices and virtues before he attempts to enter the inner shrines of this science. Let him carefully weigh whether he finds in himself those qualities which the Philosophers require in their disciples—which are indeed many, and greater than common opinion suggests. I shall endeavor to the best of my ability to set these out before the eyes of all, as if on a display board. But to propose some order for the things to be said, 

<margin>The order of the discourse.</margin> I shall divide this book into four parts. In the first, I will recount the impediments that occur regarding the person of the craftsman, and certain outcomes. In the second, I will show how difficult it is to extract the truth from the writings of the Philosophers. In the third, I will reveal what difficulties arise concerning the practice <term>praxis; the actual laboratory work or "doing" of alchemy as opposed to theory</term>, inserting everywhere (as far as my memory allows) the authorities of the Sages in this art, so that no one may think I am saying anything out of a desire to increase the difficulty more than is fair, or to serve my own purpose rather than the benefit of the readers. In the fourth part, I will demonstrate by certain reasons and examples why this art should be avoided by everyone—or, if I fail to persuade them of that, how it might at least be practiced with the smallest possible expense.

PART ONE

# ON THE OBSTACLES THAT HOLD BACK THE CRAFTSMAN from reaching the knowledge and goal of this precious science.

<margin>In the *Timaeus*.</margin>
In all matters, whether the greatest or the smallest, **Plato** <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC), the Greek philosopher, whose dialogue *Timaeus* discusses the creation of the world and was highly influential in alchemical thought.</note> commands that divine help must be implored. Since this science—according to the testimony of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the legendary Persian alchemist known as the father of chemistry.</note>, **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail, c. 900–960), an influential Arab alchemist whose works were translated into Latin.</note>, and other philosophers—is nothing but a perfect divine inspiration and a secret of the glorious God, who grants it or withdraws it from whom He wills, it is fitting, above all, that he who desires to be initiated into this art should ask the Triune and One God with a suppliant mind to deign to illuminate his intellect and bestow wisdom upon him. For there is no wisdom except from God, who does not deny it to those who seek and ask with a sincere heart and good intention. 

<margin>Science must be sought from God.</margin>
<margin>What kind of craftsman Alchemy requires.</margin>
<margin>In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin>
But because the Lord does not listen to sinners, it is necessary—if he wishes to be heard—that he love, revere, and fear God, from whom he expects every good thing. For the *fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom*, as the **Royal Prophet** <note>King David, traditionally credited with the authorship of the Psalms.</note> says. Wherefore **Alphidius** <note>An Arab alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> most rightly says: *Son, I preach to you the fear of the Lord, as well as love with unfeigned obedience.* 

<margin>One who fears God.</margin>
<margin>Treatise 2.</margin>
And **Senior** states: *You who are studious in the fear of God shall see the secret and the visible power of this stone; and, instructed by the spirit of the Most High, you shall find it, so that you may know that all wisdom is from God.* And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition and alchemy.</note> adds: *Son, I advise you above all things to fear God, in whom the effort of your undertaking rests.*

<margin>Shrinking from sins.</margin>
<margin>Book of Wisdom, chapter 1.</margin>
Furthermore, let him have a contrite spirit and one that shrinks from sins; because, as the **Wise Man** says, *Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins.* <note>A quote from the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note> 

<margin>In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin>
<margin>To brother Reginald.</margin>
<margin>The Summa of Perfection, chapter 86.</margin>
Hence **Alphidius** says: *You cannot have this science until you purify your mind for God, and until God knows that you have a contrite spirit.* And **St. Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). Though a theologian, several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed to him in the Middle Ages.</note> says: *By having peace with your God, always set an ordained goal for your work.* And **Geber**: *Sons of iniquity and malevolent wickedness, flee from this science, for it is your enemy and adversary, and it will place you in the misery of poverty.*

<margin>One who is humble.</margin>
<margin>Treatise 2.</margin>
<margin>In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin>
Let him be humble, and let him not seek this science to surpass others or to boast of possessions and riches. For thus says **Hermes**: *It is necessary for the student of this science to drive away the vice of arrogance from himself, and to be pious and upright.* And **Alphidius**: *If you are humble, its knowledge and wisdom will be perfected; but if not, its arrangement will be entirely hidden from you.* And the **Author of the Dialogue between Nature and the Son of Philosophy**: *The arrogant and the ambitious are found unworthy and rejected, not only by God, but by the science itself and every gift of God.*

->But<-

<summary>This page establishes that alchemy is a divine gift rather than a mere physical craft, requiring the practitioner to be pious, humble, and free from sin to succeed. It draws on a wide array of authorities, from Plato and the Bible to legendary alchemists like Geber and Hermes, to emphasize that spiritual readiness is the prerequisite for alchemical knowledge.</summary>

--- Page 129 ---
<meta>The previous page established that alchemy is a divine gift requiring the fear of God and a pure conscience. This page addresses the counter-argument: if Christian piety is required, why were the great masters of the art—such as Geber, Rhazes, and Avicenna—Muslims rather than Christians?</meta>

->Theobald de Hoghelande<-
<meta>catchword: Learned</meta>

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But someone might call the aforementioned things into doubt and argue in this way: You require that a person devoted to this art be a Christian and pious; for otherwise, he will not know or worship the three persons in the Godhead and the one God in the Trinity, nor will he be able to love and fear Him. Furthermore, you desire a contrite soul, a conscience pure from sins, and humility—virtues that are specifically required in Christians. However, it is well known that **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), often called the "father of chemistry."</note>, **Rhazes** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and physician whose alchemical works were foundational in Europe.</note>, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 970–1037), the famous Persian philosopher and physician.</note>, and other Arabs who wrote about this art were Saracens and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometiſtas"</note> and did not have knowledge of the true God. Yet, their books testify that they were the most skilled in this science, which we even admit flowed down to the Latins <note>Medieval European scholars who read and wrote in Latin.</note> chiefly from them. Therefore, neither piety nor the fear of God seems to have anything to do with the matter, provided that talent, books, and wealth are not lacking.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
I respond that piety, however misplaced <note>original: "præpoſteram," meaning inverted or out of order from the author's Christian perspective.</note>, was not lacking in them; they flourished with the greatest virtues and recoiled from crimes, as is sufficiently evident from the books of **Geber** and the passage cited above. For we know that even the Turks today have more devotion and approach their temples and sacred places with greater reverence, and show more brotherly charity to the needy and wretched, than by far the greatest part of Christians. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at if God—who examines the intentions of men no less than their works themselves—rewarded them with the most splendid victories, this most precious science of all, and finally other benefits and temporal gifts, even though they were ignorant of the true worship of God. All these things, however, are small in respect to the eternal happiness which the professors of the Christian faith expect, while those others are rejected. Furthermore, it is better to have a false god whom one fears and worships—and by whose fear the wicked wills and evil deeds of men are restrained—than to have no god at all, as many **Sophists** <note>In alchemy, "Sophists" refers to fraudulent practitioners who used logical tricks or chemical deceptions rather than true natural philosophy.</note> do. For those are not worthy of the name of Alchemists who seek this science solely with the intent to satisfy their own greeds, and not for the glory of God, the comfort of their neighbor, or the relief of poverty.

<margin>The Prudent [Man]. The tricks of the Philosophers in hiding the science.</margin>
But I return to the purpose. Besides what has already been said, let the craftsman be prudent and possess a naturally subtle and profound talent. Let him excel in excellent judgment, so that he knows how to distinguish the true from the false, and the power of nature from works that go against nature. This is necessary because philosophers, in order to deceive the unwary, often introduce certain reasons for their sayings which seem true in appearance and likeness, yet are false.

<margin>Chapter 13. *On the Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 12. *The Sum of Perfection*. *The Book of Secrets*, chapter 2.</margin>
Hence **Geber** says: *We attract only the prudent to the art.* The same author says: *We shall hand down the art in such a speech that it will not happen to be hidden from the prudent; however, to the mediocre, it will be most profound, and it will exclude the foolish irrecoverably.* And **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel or another Arabic author known as Haly in Latin sources.</note>: *I have not made this book for the ignorant and the unknowing, but I have composed it for the prudent and those possessing Wisdom.* **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: *Let foresight, reason, and steady expectation be applied by the craftsman.*

<summary>The author defends the necessity of piety in alchemy by arguing that even the famous Muslim alchemists were virtuous and God-fearing in their own way, unlike modern "sophists." He also emphasizes that alchemy requires a "prudent" mind capable of seeing through the intentional riddles and "tricks" used by philosophical authors.</summary>
<keywords>Geber, Rhazes, Avicenna, Christian vs. Muslim piety, virtue, prudence, alchemical secrecy, Haly, Morienes, Sophists, ethics in science</keywords>

->Book on the Difficulties of Alchemy<-
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

<margin>Learned.</margin>
The practitioner must be learned, so that where natural talent does not reach, this defect may be remedied through education. Hence the universal path: "We hide this matter with a strong concealment <note>original: "absconditione forti"</note>, so that it cannot be grasped by the unlearned."

<margin>Skilled in the Latin language.</margin>
Above all, he should be skilled in the Latin language, for how else could he understand those works which are for the most part written and published in Latin? Nor should anyone think that alchemical books are translated into other languages with the same ease or accuracy as books of other sciences.

<margin>Philosopher.</margin>
He should be well-versed in natural philosophy and other sciences. Hence **Arnaldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: "Whoever wishes to reach this science and is not a philosopher is a fool, because this science deals only with the secrets of the philosophers." And **Morienes** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: "Whoever pursues this science must know the other sciences, and especially **Logic** <term>Dialectics: The formal art of reasoning and logical argument, considered essential for deciphering alchemical allegories.</term>, since the Philosophers of this art have spoken only under veils and figures." And **Alphidius** <note>An early alchemical author, likely of Arabic origin, whose works circulated in medieval Europe.</note>: "I have composed this book for no one but a philosopher."

<margin>In the "Key of Philosophy": Knowing the principles of Nature. "The Sum of Perfection" at the beginning. In "The Secrets of Alchemy."</margin>
Furthermore, the craftsman should not be ignorant of the principles of Nature and art, because he who ignores the beginning will not find the end. Hence **Geber**: "He who is ignorant of natural principles within himself is very far from our art, for he lacks the true root upon which to found his intention." And **St. Thomas** <note>Works on alchemy were often attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) in the Middle Ages.</note>: "I urge that no one presume to begin the work unless he is very skilled and experienced in natural principles."

<margin>Industrious and hardworking.</margin>
**Avicenna**: "Know the roots of minerals, so that from them you may perform your work." Moreover, he should be industrious and hardworking, so that what he has attained through natural talent and learning, he knows how to support through his own industry and labor—and if he happens to err, how to correct it. **Haly** <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid or Haly Abenragel, figures central to the Arabic alchemical tradition.</note>: "This mastery is not given to you for your boldness, strength, and cleverness alone, without any labor; for men labor, and God grants them fortune."

<margin>"The Sum of Perfection," chapter 26.</margin>
**Geber**: "And indeed, you must exercise yourself with the greatest urgency of labor and with the duration of immense meditation; for with these you will find it, and without them, you will not."

<margin>Constant.</margin>
The Philosophers also require a craftsman of constant will, who does not attempt now this, now that; for the art does not consist in a multitude of things, but rather that he persists in a work once begun until its completion, and does not leave the work imperfect. Hence **Rosinus** <note>An Arabicized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist.</note> citing **Rhazes**: "In this business, if the difficulty of doing and tedious exhaustion makes the worker negligent, it deprives him of the expected joy, suffocates hope, and destroys efficacy." And the author of the *Ladder of the Philosophers*: "When you are in the work, let there be diligence with patience and suitable expectation, otherwise the end is loss and sadness."

<margin>Not prone to anger. Patient.</margin>
He should not be headstrong in anger, lest he cast the books aside if he does not understand them at first glance, or if his beginnings succeed less happily, he should not scatter and disrupt the vessels, furnaces, and other things necessary for the work in a fit of rage. But on the contrary, let him be patient and long-suffering, awaiting the action of nature—which is very slow—with a calm mind.

<margin>"The Rosary," chapter 3, part 2.</margin>
Hence **Arnaldus**: "Be long-suffering, and do not seek to finish hastily or quickly..."

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>

<margin>In the *Secret of Secrets* to Alexander.</margin>

And **Aristotle** <note>Referring to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a popular medieval book of advice supposedly written by Aristotle for Alexander the Great.</note>: "May divine providence help you to hide your purpose." <margin>Not wasteful.</margin>
He should not be prodigal, nor should he vainly distribute his money in the presumed hope of future things; lest if by chance he does not find the art, he be left in misery, or lest by chance when he has already approached the end of this mastery through his investigation, his funds are consumed, and he is forced to abandon the true end because of poverty.

<margin>Not greedy. Cautious in discerning the illusions of the devil.</margin>
Nor should he be greedy, for he will profit nothing in his studies and labors if he fears to incur expenses and becomes a slave to money. He should be cautious in discerning and guarding against the illusions of the devil, who often mixes himself into alchemical operations so that he may keep the workers occupied with vain and useless things, having set aside the works of nature, just as I will narrate below what happened to me and a certain friend of mine.

<margin>Wealthy.</margin>
He should be sufficiently wealthy, for it is not enough to be ingenious, learned, industrious, and not ignorant of the works of nature, if under the pressure of poverty he is forced to postpone this science to pursue other less noble things to sustain a needy life; he should be secure in food and clothing.
