### On the Difficulties of Alchemy

<margin>The material of the Stone is cheap.</margin>
And another says: The expenses of our art do not exceed the price of two gold coins at the first purchase; however, since it necessarily happens that the operator often errs (for the right path is not discerned except through error, as Baccen says in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, framed as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>. And Alphidius <note>An influential Arab alchemical authority often cited in medieval Latin works.</note> says: "He who does not err does not arrive, and he who does not destroy does not amend, and he who is not saddened is not gladdened"), a poor man cannot afford to begin again or repeat the work as often as is necessary.

<margin>Arriving at the art through many errors.</margin>
For so says the author of the book *On the Perfect Mastery*: Since no one can be certain of the experience of this matter, I advise you that once the action has begun, you should not cease from it. If you have not operated correctly the first time, repeat it a second, a third, and even more if necessary, until you perfectly grasp what you seek. Neither the labor of your hands nor the expense of materials should move you from this task, because with persistence you will prevail, and you will receive a reward for the labor of your hands and profit for the cost of the materials. And the author of *The Universal Way* says: it is necessary for the artisan to arrive at perfection through many labors and errors, for this most excellent work is scarcely led to its end without hindrance.

<margin>The artisan should have a large supply of books.</margin>
Let him have a great supply of books: for no one should persuade himself that a single book can be found which truly describes the whole art in a continuous series of discourse, as many foolishly believe.

<margin>A foolish opinion.</margin>
For that would be to detract from the majesty of nature, and such an attempt would be deservedly condemned by all as a betrayal of the celestial seal; he should be forbidden water and fire <note>A traditional Roman formula for exile or excommunication.</note>, and his writings should be abolished by fire as a plague to the world and contrary to public peace. Therefore, it is not in vain that many books were composed by one and the same author on a single subject, so that, evidently, what he delivered incompletely in one, he might complete in another.

<margin>The philosophers handed down knowledge dispersedly and in parts.</margin>
For so says **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational authority of medieval alchemy.</note>: "We have not proposed to show everything in one volume, since one book opens and explains another." The same says in another place: "Let the wise artisan study our volumes, gathering our dispersed opinion which we have proposed in various places, lest it be made public to the wicked or the ignorant." Moved by that reasoning, **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> wrote over sixty volumes on this art; others wrote six, eight, or fewer.

<margin>Authors divided the work at will.</margin>
Or if any author composed only one book, he encompassed only one part of the work, which some philosophers have distinguished into three, many into four, and some even into five and six "regimens" <note>The various stages or "rules" of the chemical process, such as calcination, dissolution, etc.</note>; many also into two, and they have confused these among themselves so that it is not known what is first, middle, or last. Or if he included several parts of the work at once, he did so briefly, interposing many falsehoods among a very few truths.

<margin>Final Chapter.</margin>
Just as **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, when he had composed a large enough volume on this art under the name of the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers."</note>, nevertheless concludes at the end thus: "I have given you above the methods of the elixir in a complete discourse, not in riddles, but in a plain series of speech, addressing your discernment clearly, since rightly to God nothing..."

<meta>catchword: nothing</meta>

<summary>The text argues that while alchemical materials are cheap, the high cost of the work stems from the inevitability of repeated failure and the need for a vast library of books. It explains that alchemical authors intentionally scattered their knowledge across multiple volumes to prevent the secrets of the "Great Work" from being discovered by the unworthy.</summary>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...nothing in this art is contained better or more perfectly than these aforementioned things, though they are shortened by brevity; yet for those who understand, they are extensive enough. The same author says elsewhere: The wise have announced the work in brief words, although they have added many other words so that it might not be understood except by the wise. 

<margin>
*In the book which is called the Flower of Flowers. Chapter 31. The Testament.* <note>The "Flos Florum" and "Testamentum" are famous alchemical treatises traditionally attributed to Arnald of Villanova or Ramon Lull.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
*The Rosary, chapter 1.* <note>The "Rosarium Philosophorum" (The Rosary of the Philosophers) is a major 16th-century alchemical text.</note>
</margin>

Therefore, the practitioner has need of many books and diverse authors to open, as Lullius <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> says, the various understandings found among many peoples; for that which could never be grasped through the teaching of one might be understood through the teaching of another—perhaps because it was given in a figure <note>original: *figura*; a symbolic representation or metaphor common in alchemical writing.</note>, and so on. And Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: *Book opens book, and speech opens speech.* <note>original: *Liber librum aperit & sermo sermonem.* A famous alchemical maxim suggesting that one author’s obscurities are explained by another’s clarity.</note>

<margin>
*Chemical books are rare and difficult to find.*
</margin>

And indeed, by this impediment alone, many learned men are greatly delayed from achieving their desires. For books written about this art are difficult to find, and they are obtained from their owners with even greater difficulty. For those who possess them guard them like Sibylline oracles <note>A reference to the rare and prophetic books of Ancient Rome, kept under strict guard.</note>; nothing could be more absurd or untimely than this, for they do not easily share them with others, whether by prayer or for a price, unless that price is quite large. 

Those that are printed, however—for which we are largely indebted to the Doctor of Medicine Guglielmo Gratarolo and the Basel printer Pietro Perna <note>Gratarolo and Perna were central figures in the 16th-century printing of alchemical compendia, such as the *Verae alchemiae*.</note> (to whose heirs, in my opinion, it would be only fair to show gratitude if anyone should master the art)—are very few compared to those which still lie hidden. 

<margin>
*Caution in buying chemical books. An example.*
</margin>

On the contrary, it often happens that beginners <term>tyrones</term> <note>Latin for "recruits" or "novices."</note> in this art buy false and adulterated books, void of all reason and doctrine, in place of true and good ones, since those that boast of a "practical" method usually please beginners more. 

I knew two otherwise distinguished and prudent men who were wise in other matters. One of them had bought at a high price a manuscript "practice" by Philippus de Rovillasto of Piedmont <note>A lesser-known alchemical author.</note> (not knowing it had actually been printed), while the other had a French booklet by a certain Joannes Salinarius (or Jean de Saulmur) concerning the preparation of salt. Each of them believed the true doctrine and practice of the art was contained in his little book. They wished for nothing more than for some practitioner to be given to them whose labor they might use to dig such a treasure out of the books, since they themselves were occupied with other business and did not know how, or were unable, to apply their own hands to the work. 

Although they were warned by me in a friendly manner that no truth was contained in those books, and that they should therefore spare their money and make no further expense, I heard later that they—entangled by a false hope of profit—did not obey my advice, but exposed themselves to be deluded and deceived by others. 

<margin>
*The practitioner must be studious.*
</margin>

However, it is not enough to have many books acquired at great cost, unless there is a reader who is diligent, assiduous, and enduring. For one does not need a space of some months, but of years, to understand the authors' parables, riddles, ambiguities, tropes, figures, and transpositions. Therefore, Agadimon says most rightly in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient philosophers.</note>: "He who thinks he can quickly gather fruit from our books is mistaken; for it would have been better not even to look at them than to have touched them rashly." For books...

# ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I

...our predecessors do a great injustice to those who read our writings only once, twice, or thrice; such readers, being deprived of understanding and all diligent study, also—what is worst of all—lose their wealth, labor, and time. However, he who **bends his back** to read our books, and devotedly makes time for them, applying both memory and mind, and is not distracted by vain thoughts, but prays to God as Solomon did for wisdom rather than for riches, shall reign in the kingdom <note>original: *in regno regnabit*; likely a reference to the "kingdom" of alchemical mastery or the "Regnum Dei."</note> without fail until he dies. And the Author of the *Perfect Master* <note>original: *Auctor perfecti magistri*; likely referring to a specific medieval alchemical treatise.</note> says: I ask you, son, to search the books of the philosophers with unceasing reading; for he who is lazy in reading books will not be able to be prompt in preparing things. This is because a hand cannot easily become accustomed to <term>practice|The physical manipulation of materials and laboratory work</term> if the mind refuses to sweat in <term>theory|The intellectual understanding of alchemical principles and philosophy</term>. For he will approach the operation more securely in whose mind many images and various types of operations arise.

<margin>
*The Correction [of Fools], chapter 2.* <note>original: *Correct. c. 2.*; likely referring to the *Correctio Fatuorum*, an alchemical text attributed to Richard the Englishman.</note>
</margin>

And Richard the Englishman <note>Richardus Anglicus (12th-13th century), a name associated with several early medical and alchemical texts.</note> says: Study removes ignorance and leads the human intellect back to true science and the knowledge of every thing. Therefore, all who love the benefit of this art are bound to persist in studies and to draw the truth from books, not from fictional tales and faulty works; since this art is not truly found except after the completion of study and the understanding of the philosophers' sayings. All the wise men of this art everywhere affirm exactly the same thing, though I shall refrain from citing all their authorities. Yet even after several years of study, however successful, a long period of experience is still required, for the foundation of the art is <term>experiment|The practical testing and experiential learning in the lab.</term> 

<margin>
That the craftsman must experiment.
*On the Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 2.
Ibid., final chapter. <note>original: *De investig. perf.*; referring to the "Summa Perfectionis" or "De investigatione perfectionis" traditionally attributed to Geber.</note>
</margin>

Hence Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the most famous figure in early Islamic alchemy.</note> says: it is necessary to reach the goal by working, searching, and experimenting. Again: let the craftsman exercise himself until, by studying and experimenting with persistent labor, he arrives at knowledge. And the *Lily* <note>original: *Lilium*; likely the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a common title for alchemical works.</note> says: Alas for you, sons of doctrine! Any of you who undertakes labors does not hope to have fruits except after a time, and he who sows seeds does not hope to reap except after the harvests; how then do you wish to have this offering after reading a book only once, or after testing the first <term>regimen|A specific stage or method of treatment in the alchemical process.</term>? Do not be weary, therefore, of proceeding to the second and third part of the regimen, until the **King is crowned with a red crown** <note>This is a famous alchemical metaphor for the *Rubedo* or "Reddening" stage, signaling the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

<margin>
In how much time the Stone can be completed.
Chapter 42 of the *Testament*.
</margin>

I would not, however, wish anyone to be deceived by the authority of Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist.</note>, who completed the work in nine and a half months, since he (as I said above) understands only the latter part of the work. I warn that even less credit should be given to others who assert that the work is perfected in an even shorter space of time. Let them rather hear Lullius <note>Ramon Lull.</note> saying: The course of nature completed lasts for a space of two years; hence the stone takes one year, and the <term>elixir|A substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or prolonging life.</term> another year for every new artist who has never done it before. But for every good and experienced artist who is subtle, one year and three months suffices. 

<margin>
Of the Stone, the elixir, and the medicine.
</margin>

To ensure that this passage of Lullius is better understood, I will not begrudge, for the sake of the younger students, explaining what he calls the stone, what the elixir, and the medicine...

->THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE<-

<margin>
That these names are used in various ways.
</margin>

...of medicine, <note>original: *dicinæ*; this is the conclusion of the word *medicinæ* from the previous page.</note> examples occur everywhere of Lull and other authors using these names indiscriminately for a work perfected in every way. For Lull says this of the stone and the elixir: "This stone converts every diminished and imperfect body into infinite Gold and Silver, according to how the elixir has been refined and prepared." Of the elixir alone, Roger Bacon says: "The red elixir turns things yellow <note>original: *citrinat*; to turn the color of a citron or lemon, a stage in the alchemical process.</note> infinitely." Of the medicine, Arnaldus says: "If the metal which you must convert through medicine is not of sufficient color, let more of the medicine be added." I could cite infinite authorities of the philosophers on this matter if there were a need. 

Nevertheless, I will demonstrate with cited examples that the names "Stone," "Elixir," and "Medicine" sometimes signify an imperfect work. But since I have spoken abundantly above concerning the naming of the "Stone"—showing that the mastery is called a "stone" in every degree of the work—I shall make mention only of the "Elixir" and the "Medicine," and first indeed of the elixir. 

Arnaldus in *The Rosary*: "Be careful in the commissioning of the elixir, and work there wisely." The same author says: "The lime <note>original: *Calx*; the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been calcined or burned.</note> which is placed into the elixir must be sublimated so that it is entirely simple and uniform." Concerning the medicine, the same Arnaldus says: "We calcine the medicine so that it may be dissolved more quickly, and we dissolve it so that it may be better cleansed and melted." 

But in the previously cited place, when Lull says the stone is of one year and the elixir of another, by the name of the "Stone" he understands the earlier part of the work, in which the matter of the stone is dissolved, divided, cleansed, and joined together once more, and finally raised up from the bodily dregs into the <term>quintessence|The "fifth essence" or purest state of matter, beyond the four physical elements</term>. 

By the word "Elixir," however, he refers to the later part, which encompasses the fixing and the <term>tincture|The power of the alchemical agent to "stain" or transform the color and nature of a base metal</term> of that which has been cleansed—not only in this place, but elsewhere throughout his works. For thus he says in the *Codicil*: "To weaken the work is nothing else than to attribute the due and natural form to the sulfur or the stone, and afterward to the elixir and the medicine." 

<margin>
In the *Practice of the Testament*, chapter 2.
In the *Mirror of Alchemy*, chapter 2.
*The Rosary*, part 1, chapter 23.
</margin>

<margin>
In the preface.
</margin>

<margin>
Chapter 24, part 2.
Chapter 21.
*The Rosary*, chapter 23.
</margin>

The same author says in the *Testament*: "Our mastery is divided into two parts: namely, in creating the stone, and in composing the medicine." By some other authors, on the contrary, the "Elixir" is called the first part of the work and the "Stone" the later part, as it is for the Author of the *Universal Way*: "The elixir is the first and principal foundation, and the root of the precious stone, which is afterward converted through the second operation into the stone itself, or the medicine." 

Bernard and Richard the Englishman and certain others also distinguish the work into three parts: namely, into the **Rebis**, the **Elixir**, and the **Tincture** (or medicine). 

<margin>
In the *Practice*, chapter 22.
</margin>

<margin>
Chapter 5.
</margin>

<margin>
In the commentary on the *Table of Hermes*. <note>original: *Herm.*</note>
</margin>

Thus the **Rebis** is the first part, named from "the double thing" <note>original: *re bina*; a reference to the dual nature of the starting material, often mercury and sulfur.</note>—namely, the dissolving and the thing to be dissolved. The **Elixir** is indeed the second part, in which the soul is extracted from the dissolved body by long boiling (for they thought that "elixir" took its name from "boiling" <note>original: *ab elixando*; a medieval folk etymology connecting the Arabic *al-iksir* with the Latin *elixare*, to boil.</note>, or they wished it to seem so because of the similarity of the words. Whence Saint Thomas says: "It is necessary at the beginning of our operation that the things to be converted into the elixir be first boiled before one proceeds to the composition of the stone"). The **Tincture** is indeed the third part, which Lull also calls the "Medicine"...

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>On the Difficulties of Alchemy, Book 1</header>
<sig>I 2</sig>

...cates, <note>original: *cat*; likely the conclusion of a verb such as *medicat* (to heal or medicate) from the previous page.</note> but he preferred to name the first two stages, when contracted into one, the **Stone**. For some, the work is even divided into four parts, as they distinguish between the **tincture** <note>A substance capable of infusing color and quality into a base metal.</note> and the **medicine**, so that the tincture precedes the medicine, just as the author of *The Counsel of the Marriage of the Sun and Moon* <note>original: *consilij conjugij massæ Solis & Lunæ*; a famous alchemical text. The Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver.</note> divides it into **Ir, Xir, Ixir, and elixir**. <note>These terms represent progressive stages of refinement in the Arabic alchemical tradition.</note> For this reason, chemical authors must be read with extreme attention and consideration, since they very often confuse these terms and many others. This was well known to the author of the *Universal Way*, who said: "The Philosophers in their books called the elixir 'the stone,' and the stone 'the elixir,' making no distinction of names between the two, so that they might blind the foolish."

<margin>
Chapter 5.
</margin>

But to return to the discourse from which I digressed: the craftsman attempting these experiments must be healthy and of firm strength, so that he may be sufficient for the labor. This labor is not small, as witnessed by **Lord Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas; several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed to him in this period.</note> who affirms that he suffered such great labor, stench, and bodily detriment that he would in no way wish to attempt the work again, unless driven by pressing necessity. 

<margin>
That the craftsman devoted to experience ought to be healthy.
</margin>

The craftsman must not be blind, nor mutilated in his hands. For if he is deprived of sight, he will be unable to arrange and mix the material as required, nor can he observe the colors appearing in the work; consequently, he cannot rule the fire, since the governance of the fire depends upon the appearance of the colors. As the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a key 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: "the colors will teach you how you ought to administer the fire." If he lacks hands, he will no longer be helped by those limbs which serve as the ministers of nature and through which this art is perfected. 

<margin>
What things the craftsman requires.
</margin>

I have stated above that the craftsman must be sufficiently wealthy; namely, so that he can buy the necessary books of this art and, setting aside other business, pore over them. Furthermore, he must be able to undertake the practical test of his learning. He can test nothing, however, unless he has a suitable house, or at least three or four rooms. He must also incur expenses for vessels, furnaces, and a fire that continues night and day—which must be fed now with coals, now with oil, or other material, as necessity demands. 

<margin>
Alchemy is an enemy to the poor. **Geber**, *Sum of Perfection*, ch. 7, and **Albertus Magnus**.
</margin>

In addition, a servant or a companion must be sought who—while the craftsman is sleeping, occupied, or sick—may supply the continuous and perpetually persevering fire, and not allow the "seed" <note>The developing alchemical matter.</note> which has already been nourished for a long time to die out or grow cold. If all these things are gathered together, the craftsman will see that he has need of no small sum of money. Therefore, it is not without reason that the philosophers call this art an "enemy to the poor," because it requires the expenses of many years. Finally, the craftsman must take every precaution lest he be reduced to poverty and become a laughingstock to others, should he happen to err in the work or should the time be prolonged, as happens in most cases. 

Since it is now clear from what has been said what kind of craftsman is required, and since it is extremely difficult to find anyone upon whom God has bestowed such great gifts of mind, body, and fortune, the entire art is rightly judged difficult and dangerous; any person who is not imprudent will avoid it as something most ruinous.

# Theobald de Hoghelande
<page-num>132</page-num>

But perhaps someone will rise up and say: Since you require the fear of the Lord, integrity, a subtle and deep mind, education, industry, patience, constancy, leisure, books, wealth, and not a few other things from others, and you yourself admit in this very treatise to being a student of Alchemy, do you claim for yourself those things which you so greatly require in others? I respond that I lack many things, and I confess freely: if I, as a young man, could have conceived and ruminated upon all the obstacles and difficulties that now stand before my eyes, or if I had been so fortunate as to have a faithful advisor who, by setting forth all the hindrances of this art, had called me back from the beginning—just as I hope to do with this little book—I would never have entered this arena <note>original: *palæstram*; literally a wrestling school, used here as a metaphor for a place of difficult struggle or study.</note>. I have more than once grieved, when the memory of lost time comes to mind, that I ever looked at chemical books even through a window <note>original: *per tranſennam*; a metaphorical expression meaning to look at something briefly or indirectly.</note>.

But the same happened to me as happened to many others: when I was a young man, naturally inclined toward investigating the secrets of nature and moderately endowed with the goods of fortune, a little French book by **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous alchemist who supposedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Philosopher's Stone.</note> happened to be presented to me in Paris by chance.

<margin>
Magnificent book titles deceive many.
</margin>

I first marveled at the magnificent title of the work, then, moved by curiosity, I inspected, read, and re-read it. In it, I noticed little ambiguity and little obscurity; on the contrary, the author voluntarily exhorted the study of that science to which no other could be compared, describing its virtues. Since he promised not only immense riches but also memory and health to those who seriously sought it, and added that it was so easy as to be scarcely believable, I confess I was overcome; I surrendered.

Therefore, with the greatest zeal, I immediately obtained as many books of this art, printed or manuscript, as I could find, and for several months I diligently studied them. But since, among the other authors, he most frequently cited the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba philoſoph:*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between ancient Greek philosophers.</note>, which he often calls "blessed," and I had two little books inscribed with the name *Assembly of the Philosophers*—one in the French tongue, the other in Latin, which was later printed in Basel by the efforts of **Petrus Perna** <note>A significant 16th-century printer in Basel known for publishing Hermetic and alchemical texts.</note>—I finally put aside the others and devoted my labor primarily to the French *Assembly*, not knowing it had been collected by that same Bernard. First, I began to marvel at the agreement of both books; then, when he introduced **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher, here used as a legendary authority in alchemical tradition.</note> speaking about the matter of the stone in this manner:

->“Our work requires in the beginning nothing but two natures of one essence, of which one is cheap, the other dear; one hard, the other watery; one red, the other white; one fixed, the other volatile; one bodily, the other spiritual; one cold and moist, the other hot and dry.”<-

As I read further, I found Bernard concluding his little book on the transmutation of metals with this sentiment:

->“Our work is made from two mineral substances of one root, or essence, taking all things raw, drawn from the mine, clean and purified, joined by a suitable fire, as the matter requires, cooked continuously until the two become one.”<-

I drew an example from the seeds of the male and female: as long as they are kept apart in their own places, they cannot be called or be the matter of a living creature, but only then, if they have been joined in the womb, is the potentiality brought into actual being.

<meta>This page continues the autobiographical account of Theobald de Hoghelande's early alchemical failures. # THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...of seeing and hearing foreign things, I undertook a journey and set out for Italy. Where, although I was permitted to enjoy the familiarity and conversation of many who practiced chemistry <note>original: "Chemica"; referring to the early modern art of alchemy and chemical medicine</note>, I nevertheless thought they should all be carefully avoided; for I judged that I could learn nothing from anyone, but that others, on the contrary, could learn a great deal from me. When I had traveled through almost all of Italy, as far and wide as it extends, I returned to my homeland after two years, where new obstacles delayed me for some time, preventing me from applying myself to the practice. 

<margin>
*The author’s fruitless experiments.*
</margin>

Finally, however, I began. And first indeed—since I thought the purification of materials was required—I ordered an ounce of gold, thoroughly purified by antimony <note>Antimony was commonly used in the Renaissance to "purge" gold of impurities, as the gold would sink while other metals formed a slag on top</note>, to be drawn out into leaves. As for quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, at first I tried to sublimate it from common salt; soon, seeing that I was making no progress, I tried with salt and vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid salts or copper/iron sulfates</note>, and then attempted to "revivify" the sublimate <note>To turn the powdered mercury sublimate back into liquid liquid metal</note>. 

But when the Mercury was not made any cleaner even in this way, I finally thought that it could not be better purified or sublimated than by gold, with which it is known to have the greatest affinity. 

<margin>
*The Sum of Perfection, chapter 41.*
</margin>

As Geber <note>An 8th-century Arabic alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan), though the works cited here are likely by a 13th-century European "Pseudo-Geber"</note> says: "The matter must be chosen with which the spirits to be sublimated most agree, and into which they may be more deeply mixed; for that matter to which they are more closely united is more powerful in retaining dregs than that to which they are not." To this was added the testimony of Bernard himself, to whom I deferred greatly. 

<margin>
*In the Epistle to Thomas of Bologna.*
</margin>

For he says that there are certain sublimations of Mercury from its own proper bodies, which are joined and mixed with it by amalgamating through their innermost parts; having been elevated and joined with these many times, the Mercury loses its superfluities and its nature is not destroyed; afterward, it is suitable for the philosophical work and is powerful in dissolving metallic species. I interpreted its "proper bodies" to be gold and silver, because among the metals they abound most in quicksilver. I also thought that Lull meant this when he said: 

<margin>
*In the Testament and Codicil.*
</margin>

"No humidity is more properly and promptly converted into the substance of sulfur than that in which the qualities of its own sulfur have been sufficiently introduced through natural ingenuity, which is done by artifice." 

Therefore, when I had several times sublimated quicksilver from gold powder obtained from filings—and yet found it neither brighter nor more beautiful, but rather more filthy—then for the first time I began to doubt somewhat, and my confidence turned to anxiety. Finally, taking heart again, since the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> commanded that no material should be taken unless it was "crude, pleasant, and sincere"; and likewise Bernard said: 

<margin>
*In the Parable.*
</margin>

"the work is made from two crude mercurial substances drawn from the mine," I began to reflect: If crude matter is to be taken, there is no need to waste time and tire the mind with sublimations that will be of no use at all. Therefore, I gradually placed gold drawn into the thinnest leaves into quicksilver that had been pressed through leather and linen <note>A method for filtering liquid mercury</note>, with the Trevisan <note>Bernard of Trevisan</note> prescribing the proportion, and remembering a common verse.

Frustrated by his lack of success, he decides to pivot toward using "crude" materials based on his interpretation of alchemical authorities.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Hoghelande has just completed his travels through Italy and returned home. ### On the Difficulties of Alchemy, Book I

*Mercury destroys all gold leaf,*
*He dissolves it, softens it, and draws the soul from the body.*
<note>original: "Mercurius Solem foliatum deftruit omnem..."</note>

I believed, moreover, that it was most effective if everything were mixed cold rather than heated; for I thought nothing could be more foolish than to scorch the material with a fierce fire at the beginning of the work. The Sages teach that the matter must be governed by the slowest fire, and fostered in the manner of the nourishment of eggs <note>a common alchemical metaphor comparing the Great Work to the gentle, steady heat required for a chick to develop inside an egg</note>. These same Sages say one must beware lest its "flowers" be burned at the start. I believed that the artists of this age stumble most in this regard, as they—to save on costs or because they do not trust others—amalgamate gold in the common manner of goldsmiths. Once all the materials were joined in an oblong glass vessel, hermetically sealed and placed upon the athanor <term>athanor: a "philosopher's furnace" designed to maintain a consistent, gentle heat over a long period of time</term>, I began to supply a slow fire in many ways I had previously attempted. What shall I report? Everything proceeded according to my wishes. First, I marveled at the extraordinary attractive power of the Mercury, and I recalled that saying of Pythagoras in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts</note>. 

<margin>A mockery presented to the author by a demon.</margin>

The Philosophers tell in many ways how their "companion" follows them without fire, just as a magnet follows iron. Then, during the boiling, colors gradually began to emerge and appear on the surface of the Mercury, so that I seemed to clearly see the two materials allowed to act upon one another. On the third day, I saw the greater part of the surface occupied by three colors—green especially, red, and ashen-gray—not confused together, but distinct in their boundaries, not unlike the colors of a rainbow. Whenever I recall that day, Virgil’s verse comes to mind:

*As I saw, how I perished, how a wicked error carried me away.*
<note>original: "Ut vidi, ut perij, ut me malus abftulit error" from Virgil's Eclogues</note>

And this was not without cause, since that error—or rather, that mockery presented to my eyes—was later the cause of much labor and expense. If I exulted with joy at that time, no one should doubt it, considering the sight; for I hoped that through these middle colors I would gradually reach the "Blackness" <note>the *nigredo* stage, signifying the death or "putrefaction" of the old matter</note>, and by boiling further, I would obtain the "Whiteness" and finally the "Redness" <note>the final stages of the Great Work, *albedo* and *rubedo*</note>. But that joy was not long-lasting for me. For a few days later, the fire having been extinguished by a chance accident during the night and the vessel having cooled, it happened that I saw no further alteration. And then that passage from Augurellus occurred to me: <margin>Book 3 of the *Chrysopeia* <note>A famous alchemical poem by Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524)</note>.</margin>

->*As soon as the fire shall cease,*<-

THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

Likewise, I began to weigh more carefully the things that had happened to me, and to fear the illusions of the devil, who desires to keep men—who are otherwise of good will—detained among frivolous things and lies. He does this so that, having left the straighter path, they might waste their time uselessly and no longer care to investigate the truth, and finally, having been plunged into the abyss of despair, they might occupy themselves with a **Sophistical work** <note>original: "opus Sophisticum"; in alchemy, this refers to "false" or deceptive chemistry that mimics the appearance of gold without true transformation</note>. And so, when I had returned to my books, which I had not seen for many years, and with my judgment increased somewhat by the outcomes of so many experiments, I began to join my reading with whatever practice I could. At last, by the favoring grace of God, I began to recognize the **sulfur of the philosophers** <note>original: "sulphur philosophorum"; not common brimstone, but a theoretical active principle of growth and color within metals</note>, and to understand their writings better from day to day. 

I saw that I had sought in vain through such long and difficult journeys that which I had already possessed at home for a long time. For when the Philosophers use the name "gold," they do not mean crude and common gold, but their own. Indeed, common gold is a "dead body," and it performs nothing except what is administered to it by the industry of man; moreover, nothing enters the "Work" unless it has been **digested** and has sought the "heaven of the air" <note>This refers to the process of sublimation or distillation, where a substance is vaporized and refined</note>. On this matter, Lullius <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy</note> says: *Some wish to dissolve gold and silver with Mercury, which is a useless thing, unless their bodies are made **spiritual** through refinement, just as Mercury is, and afterward to join them and keep them over a graded fire.* Likewise, Arnald <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says: *No body remaining in its own nature coagulates Mercury, nor does Mercury itself heal bodies, because in the testing it recedes from them; for coarse things are less suited to simple things, and simple things to coarse ones.*

I have judged that these things—even if I have treated them perhaps more diffusely than the labor of brevity I promised in this work might seem to require—have not been done absurdly, nor without benefit to many. For those taught by the example of another will hereafter be more cautious, since I have found that not only I and my friend, but also others, have been mocked by such **diabolical tricks**. Although they spent their effort on useless things and handled experiments that were even contrary to nature, they sometimes had "happy beginnings" which, once accidentally interrupted, could never be restored or brought back to the same state. Therefore, I advise that everyone avoid an art so subject to the illusions of the demon; or at least, let no one trust too much in the first progress they propose for themselves, unless clear reason appears and the work succeeds happily when repeated. Indeed, one should count such accidental success among the primary difficulties of the art.

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

If anything should delay [the progress], perhaps it is not permanent, or it can be compensated for in some way or manner. But here there is nothing of the sort; one certain gate or door must lie open if one desires to enter a house walled and closed on all sides. Unless this gate is open, one promises oneself access or progress to the inner chambers in vain. Thus, all <margin>*Alchemy is not learned except through books or the voice of a teacher. Books are difficult to understand.*</margin> the effort of chemists is mocked if they hope to perceive any fruit from this art without the writings of the philosophers being well-examined and understood—unless they are born under such a happy star that they attain knowledge of it through the voice of a living person or through divine revelation. Whoever attempts the **Stone** <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and curing all diseases.</note> otherwise, and trusts that he will find it by chance, I judge him to be insane and deserving of being sent to Anticyra <note>A city in ancient Greece famous for its hellebore, a plant used in antiquity as a treatment for madness.</note>.

But how arduous and laborious it is to understand the books of the philosophers written on this subject, who could declare more aptly than the Wise themselves? Having experienced the difficulty of the art, they transmitted it to posterity according to the accepted custom of the ancients. Let us hear what they say. Rosinus <note>Often identified with Zosimos of Panopolis, an early Graeco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: The philosophers wished <margin>*To Eutychia.*</margin> to reveal nothing of this art openly to their successors, so that those things which they placed figuratively in their books cannot be known unless they are shown by God or by a teacher. Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note> says: We have written this art, having discovered it, <margin>*The Sum of Perfection, last chapter.*</margin> only for ourselves and not for others; it is, however, most true and entirely certain. The *Lilium* <note>Referring to the "Lilium Intelligentiae" (The Lily of Intelligence), a popular alchemical text.</note> says: We have not composed our books except for ourselves and our sons; he who comes to understand them is one of us; but he who does not understand is contrary to us. 

Morienes <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the art to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> speaks to the same effect: There are books composed about this art under a figure <note>A "figure" or "allegory" used to hide the literal meaning from the uninitiated.</note>, the greater part of which seems very obscure and cannot be understood except by their own composers. Hortulanus says that only he who knows the operation of the Stone understands the words of the philosophers. For he says: "O dearest reader, if you know the operation of the Stone, I have told you the truth; but if <margin>*In the exposition of the Table of Hermes.*</margin> you do not know it, I have told you nothing." <note>original: "O lector charissime, si scis operationem lapidis, tibi dixi veritatem, si vero tu nescis eam, nihil tibi dixi."</note> 

But if one asks why they wrote at all, let him hear the author of the *Universal Way* and Geber: "By these things <margin>*Last chapter, The Sum of Perfection.*</margin> which we shall say, we shall entice you, son of doctrine, to investigate the art and to find it truly." But let us inquire into the modes of hiding, and let us investigate the cause of the difficult understanding of chemical books. This will become more evident if we weigh the reason why other sciences are easier; for opposites placed beside one another shine more clearly. Every other art and science proceeds <margin>*Various ways of hiding the art.*</margin> rhetorically and in a certain order in its writings through chapters, principles, and terms, with definitions and explanations of names and instruments, by which one arrives at the knowledge and notice of its conclusions and its work; it teaches and explains in whatever ways it can. But this art, in a plainly contrary way, delivers its work without any notice of the principles of the art, terms, or instruments, mixing false things with true and true with false, now too diminished, now over-abundantly, and without order—and more often in a preposterous <note>meaning "inverted" or "back-to-front"</note> order—and it strives to deliver everything obscurely and to hide it as much as possible. Rosinus <note>Often identified as Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist.</note> says: Know that the Philosophers never set down a true word without mixing many false things with it, and they called this whole secret by fictitious names. And the Author of *The Marriage of the Sun and Moon*: The Philosophers have often placed the end before the beginning in their treatises, inserting the beginning at the end. Whence they sometimes suppressed the first work and spoke of the second, and sometimes they treated the first work while omitting the second; sometimes they spoke with the roots of science, and sometimes without numbers. For this reason, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says in the *Book of Roots*, which is the second of the seven, that the wisdom of the author is greater than his book; for he can take away the beginning or the end, with the root or without the root, as the first inventor. Thus he says. It is therefore no wonder if those studying and working in this science err greatly, because no one dares to assert that the intention of the philosophers was certainly and determinedly this or that, unless they already possess it in practice or are close to it.

<margin>Twelve reasons why the philosophers wrote obscurely.</margin>

Hence Geber says: 
<margin>*The Sum of Perfection*, chapter 7.</margin>
Our art is preserved in divine power; it is bestowed upon whom He wills and withdrawn [from others]. And Morienes <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist.</note> says:

<margin>The philosopher’s duty is to teach.</margin>

And in another place: "Let God be a witness over us; do not forbid those of our brothers who are worthy, and do not reveal these things to the unworthy."

<margin>It is not the way of philosophers to deceive others.</margin>
It is therefore not to be wondered at if they wrote their books on this art obscurely, or veiled in many circuitous phrases, since it is established that this was done by them with great reason and not by chance—nor, as many think, because they were too gullible and deceived themselves, seeking to deceive others in turn. Such behavior does not befit a man of integrity and a philosopher, who strives to transmit a memory of himself to posterity that is uncontaminated by any stain of dishonor.

<margin>The ancient philosophers took care that science should not spread to the common people.</margin>
Indeed, this mode of writing should not seem new or be disapproved of, unless we also condemn the custom of all the ancients in their manner of philosophizing. For Aristotle, in a certain letter to Alexander <note>Referring to the legendary correspondence between Aristotle and Alexander the Great, popular in medieval occult literature.</note>, says that some of his works were published in such a way that they would seem as if they were not published at all. And Plato, in a letter to Dionysius, says: "Take care that these things never fall into the ears of men who are inexperienced in discipline and learning." There is also a letter from Lysis to Hipparchus <note>Lysis and Hipparchus were Pythagoreans; the letter discusses the secrecy of the sect.</note>, from which I will translate a few points here: "To remember the divine precepts of that man (meaning Pythagoras) is a pious duty," he says, "nor is it right to make the good things of philosophy common to those who have not even been able to dream of the purification of the soul. It is not lawful to hand over to everyone those things which we have obtained with so much labor, just as it is not permitted to profane men to reveal the secrets of the Eleusinian goddesses <note>The "Eleusinian Mysteries," secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note>; for those who do such things will be held as equally unjust and impious." And he continues below.

<margin>At the beginning of the book *On the Responses of the Philosophers*.</margin>
Many have reported to us that they philosophize publicly, which Pythagoras forbade. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> also forbids his writings to be communicated to everyone. "Beware," he says, "lest for the sake of profit or vain glory you hand these things over to wicked and unworthy men; for no small danger hangs over both you who publish it and me who trusted you. These things are to be communicated only to those who have led their lives toward the salvation of the soul; for even the Gods themselves handed down these things to men not openly, but enigmatically."

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
It is also right to remember the words of our Savior <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6.</note>, that pearls are not to be cast before swine, and that which is holy is not to be given to dogs. But I shall return to where I digressed. Since philosophers deliberately—sometimes by inverting the order, sometimes by mixing the false with the true, sometimes by adding or subtracting...

<summary>Theobald de Hoghelande defends the intentional obscurity of alchemical and philosophical texts, arguing that secrecy is a traditional duty intended to protect sacred knowledge from the unworthy and the "profane." He cites various authorities, including Plato, Aristotle, Pythagoras, and the Gospel of Matthew, to show that true wisdom must be veiled in metaphors.</summary>
<keywords>Theobald de Hoghelande, secrecy in alchemy, Alphidius, Senior Zadith, Pythagoras, Porphyry, metaphors, pearls before swine, Eleusinian mysteries, philosophical tradition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the deliberate obscurity of alchemical writers. The previous page concluded by noting that philosophers did not hide their secrets by chance, but with a specific reason: to protect the art from the unworthy.</meta>

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK...

<margin>Enigmas increase the obscurity of the art.</margin>
...they sought after obscurity, increasing it through enigmas, tropes <note>In this context, tropes are figures of speech or metaphors.</note>, allegories, and comparisons to such an extent that one needs the thread of Theseus <note>A reference to the Greek myth where Ariadne gives Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth.</note> to be led out of the inescapable windings of this labyrinth. Regarding enigmas, let this example from Aristotle the Chemist <note>original: "Aristotelis chemici"; likely a reference to one of many medieval alchemical texts falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Aristotle.</note> suffice: "Make a round circle from the male and female, and from it extract a square, and from the square a triangle, and from the triangle make a round circle, and you shall have the mastery <note>The "mastery" refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process or the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note>."

<margin>Testament, Chapter 5. Tropes.</margin>
Likewise, that saying of Lull <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century polymath; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.</note>: "A thing whose head is red, eyes black, and feet white, is the mastery." A thousand other such examples occur everywhere. One may observe a trope in this saying of Senior <note>Ibn Umail, a 10th-century alchemist known in the West as Senior Zadith.</note>: "Take things from their mines, and exalt them to the peaks of their mountains, and lead them back to their roots."

<margin>Allegories.</margin>
Allegories are found everywhere among authors, such as the vision of Aristaeus, the story by Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a legendary 15th-century alchemist.</note> of the king and the fountain, the hunt of the lion by Senior, Merlin’s tale of the King preparing himself for war against his enemies, and the story by Antonius de Viva petra <note>Antonio di Girolamo da Filicaja, an Italian alchemist.</note> of the virgin desiring to rule—as well as the fictions of many others. It would be a long task to bring all these together here, and it would cause boredom for the readers rather than any use.

<margin>Similarities.</margin>
Reason suggests that I should dwell a little longer on similarities and comparisons, since so many errors and so many frauds take their origin from a poor understanding of them, leading to a loss of great expense and—what is most important—of so much precious time.

<margin>Philosophers compare the stone to all elemental things.</margin>
Therefore, so that they might exclude the unworthy from the art, while clearly handing it down to the learned and the prudent, the philosophers compared their Stone to all elemental things, whether they be corporeal or incorporeal, visible or invisible, celestial or terrestrial. Hence Mireris <note>An alchemical authority often cited in the "Turba Philosophorum," an early Latin alchemical assembly text.</note> says: "If you call it spiritual, you do something probable; if corporeal, you speak the truth; if celestial, you do not lie; if earthly, you report what is true." In it are also the figures of the heavens, the earth, summer, autumn, winter, and spring, as well as masculinity and femininity. Likewise Alphidius <note>An Arab alchemical author often quoted in medieval texts.</note> says: "Know, my son, that in the books of the wise are the four elements, and the figure of every vegetable, of every animal, and of every stone; in which there is also a similarity to the sea, mountains, rivers, heavens, and lands, and of all crops, bodies, spirits, substances, and colors." If anyone expects from me the reasons for everything the philosophers said, he is mistaken; for this is not the purpose of my work nor my labor, as it would require a separate volume. It is also extremely difficult to always grasp the mind of every sage, since they frequently understand not only the manifest forms and external properties of things (which are subject to the senses), but also the internal and hidden ones, until they are revealed by the art.

<margin>Everything manifest is the opposite of its hidden part.</margin>
For they say that everything external is the opposite of its internal part; thus, what is cold and moist in its manifest state is hot and dry in its hidden state. The same must be judged regarding the colors of things, as can be seen in lead, which is livid and black on the outside, but red on the inside.

<summary>This page explains how alchemists used enigmas, allegories, and complex metaphors to hide their secrets from the unworthy. It emphasizes that the Philosopher's Stone can be compared to almost anything in nature because it contains both manifest and hidden properties that are often opposites.</summary>
<keywords>enigmas, allegories, metaphors, Philosopher's Stone, Aristotle the Chemist, Lull, Senior Zadith, internal vs external properties, alchemical symbolism</keywords>

...is red, which is evident from its calcination <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its chemical or physical state, often resulting in a powder.</note>, when it passes into minium <note>original: "minium"; a red pigment, typically red lead or cinnabar.</note>. The same is also seen in vitriol <note>A term for various sulfate minerals, such as iron or copper sulfate.</note>, which is clearly blue, or green, or declining toward greenness, but through roasting is transformed into red colchotar <note>original: "colchotar"; the red iron oxide residue remaining after the distillation of vitriol.</note>. Thus, its depth and inner nature, previously hidden, is revealed to the sight; and conversely, that which was previously manifest is hidden. 

Since the philosophers have borrowed names from the forms and properties of things—both manifest and hidden—and similarly from colors, and often from the state and condition of the work or from the place where the stone is generated (indeed, from all elemental things), it is no wonder if they vary greatly and call the same

<margin>The wise always speak the truth, however they may name the stone.</margin>

thing by different names. For they do not care about words, says the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 13th-century alchemical florilegium.</note>, but about the nature and properties of the things described; and by the name of one thing they often mean another, for things are not subject to words, but rather words to things. And thus they have always spoken the truth regarding the power of their intention, though not always regarding the literal power of the speech. 

Hence Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umail.</note> says: "The wise have used various tropes <note>Figures of speech or metaphors.</note> in their comparisons, and they differ in names, but the understanding toward which they beckon is the same." And Alphidius <note>An alchemical author often cited in medieval texts.</note> says: "The wise have multiplied parables, names, and actions in this work—using the hearts of brute animals, gall, the juices of herbs, and everything that is in the earth and upon the earth—so that they might take the art away from the foolish and demonstrate it to the intelligent. Know that you do not need those names, but only one name, which is **water**, and one action, which is **to cook**." 

And Mireris <note>Likely a reference to an alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Morienus.</note> says: "Every wise man has called it by his own name, yet every name is true and direct." For they say this art is in the likeness of the heaven and the stars, and they have spoken truly; for in it are the **seven planets** <note>In alchemy, the seven planets correspond to the seven metals: Sun/Gold, Moon/Silver, Venus/Copper, etc.</note>. They assert that that part of this thing which is raised upward is similar to the heavens; that which descends downward, they call **earth**; that which is hot, they refer to **fire**; that which is airy, to **wind**; that which is moist, they call by the names of **seas** and **waters** and the animals of the sea. That which is of a green color, they refer to **vegetables** and **trees**; that which is joined and dry, to **stones**; but that which is separated, they refer to **sand** and say it is **ash**. That which is mobile, they refer to **winged creatures**; that which is flowable and meltable, they compare to **oil**—and for this reason its names are multiplied. 

And Anastratus says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "The envious <note>In alchemical literature, "the envious" refers to masters who deliberately hid their secrets to prevent the unworthy from succeeding.</note> have likened this secret to trees, metals, winged creatures, and reptiles, and varied the names as much as they could." Although these sayings of the wise ought to suffice, nevertheless, for the greater utility of the readers, I shall not be loath to bring forward certain examples. Starting with **man**, we shall proceed to animals, vegetables, metals, intermediate minerals, colors, the distinction of moist and dry, and similar things. 

<margin>The Stone is likened to man, and why.</margin>

First, therefore, the Stone is compared to **man**, because it is reached only by human reason and science, and because it is perfected only by man, or because of the **soul of the stone**...

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK K
->#### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE####<-

...which they compared to the human soul. Whence the author of *The Marriage of the Sun and Moon* from the *Greater Assembly* <note>original: "Turba majori"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note>, if I am not mistaken, says: "Take a man and strike him upon a stone, drawing him out until he dies, and becomes a spiritual body; afterwards, restore his soul to him." It is truly a wonder that the ignorant and unlearned, who focus only on the sound of the words and not the hidden meaning, do not apply the same logic to similar things when they read such passages. For who would be so insane as to think, according to the literal letter, that a man must be seized, beaten, and killed so that the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> might be produced from him, and finally that the soul, once removed, should be poured back into him? 

In the same way, those who insist on the literal words of the philosophers possess no greater judgment when they believe that the <term>Elixir</term> can be composed from animals, vegetables, intermediate minerals <note>original: "medijs mineralibus"; substances like salts, alums, and vitriols that were categorized between "metals" and "stones."</note>, and common stones. Havel, in the works of Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist known for his symbolic imagery.</note>, deservedly mocks them. "These people," he says, "said that the father of gold and silver is an animal of the land and sea, or a man, or a part of a man, such as hair, blood, menstrual fluid, or the placenta; and some said it is found in trees, plants, and herbs; and some in stones, arsenics, and other minerals; and they have been alienated from the truth of the science." 

But let us proceed further. Sometimes the Stone is called a "helmeted and tall man," <margin>The Stone is sometimes called a Helmeted Man, King, or Queen.</margin> specifically when its moisture is collected through distillation by means of a cucurbit and an <term>alembic</term> <note>A two-part distilling apparatus; the "helmet" refers to the alembic's cap (the capitellum) which covers the boiling vessel (the cucurbit).</note>. In this way, the compound of the Stone is also called "King" and "Queen." Hence we read in the *Assembly*: "Venerate the king and his wife, for you do not know when you will need those things which improve the king and his wife." 

<margin>Man & woman, male & female.</margin> Thus they are called "Man" and "Woman," or "Male" and "Female," on account of their union—that is, their action and passion. Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, an early Egyptian-Greek alchemist.</note> says the Art of Goldsmithing consists of male and female. They are likewise called "Father," "Mother," and "Son," <margin>Father, mother, and son.</margin> regarding the generators and the generated result. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "Its father is the Sun, its mother is the Moon." And the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical florilegium.</note> states: "She, like a pious mother, cherishes her son." 

Sometimes they speak only of the woman, leaving out the name of the male, as does Theophilus in the *Assembly*: "The woman, fleeing her kin, becomes domestic to them through herself, though by force"; here, "woman" stands for the moisture of the stone, because it is unstable, inconstant, and flees from the fire. Sometimes they speak only of the man. There is no need to provide examples for every instance, as they occur everywhere among the authors. Let it suffice to have warned that all these things are said in different respects: sometimes they speak of the principles of the stone—namely earth, water, and fire, or body, spirit, and soul—individually and separately, and sometimes of all of them joined together. 

<margin>Old man. Youth.</margin> They have even called the Stone "Old Man" and "Youth." Hence Rhasis <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian polymath and alchemist.</note> says: "Our Stone is first an old man, and finally a youth," because whiteness is at the beginning of the work, and redness is at the end. And in the *Assembly*: "Take a tree, and place upon it a man of great age," and so on. 

<margin>Nursing child.</margin> When the "earth" of the work gradually drinks up its own "water," it is called a "nursing child" <note>original: "puer lactans"; a common metaphor for the stage where the dry matter absorbs the liquid distillate.</note>. Hence Eminganus in the *Assembly* says: "Behold the nursing child, and do not hinder him, for in him dwells the secret." They are called by the same names: brother and sister, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, father-in-law, son-in-law, brothers of the same womb, companions, the red servant, the virgin, the girl, the clothed man...

<summary>This page explains that alchemical terms like "man," "king," and "nursing child" are metaphors for chemical substances and processes rather than literal instructions. It warns readers not to mistake these allegories for recipes involving human or organic matter.</summary>

<margin>The Stone is compared to animals.</margin>...clothed in most beautiful garments, a King crowned with a red diadem, and so forth. In the same way, they likened the Stone to animals because of the blood by which they live, for the soul of every animal is in its blood. For they compared their <term>Tincture</term> <note>The "Tincture" is the active, transformative power of the Stone that "colors" or transmutes base metals into gold.</note> to blood because of its redness, and because it gives heat and life to the body just as blood does for an animal, which, if deprived of it, is also deprived of life. The author of *The Lily* says: "If animals are governed by a slow fire, the composite becomes sweet." And Acsubufon in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; a foundational alchemical text.</note> says: "Take the animal called the *kenkel* <note>A symbolic name for a substance, likely derived from a corruption of an Arabic animal name.</note>, and the moisture which it ejected." But they did not only use the general name of "animal"; they also descended to specific species. Thus, they called it a Lion, a griffin, a camel, a horse, a dog, or a calf, for the reason mentioned above, or because of some property which these animals have in common with the Stone. Whence, in the *Allegories of the Wise*, Hermes says: <margin>Albertus, *The Secrets of Alchemy*</margin> "If you consume a third part of your camels, and two-thirds remain, you have already reached your goal." This comparison seems to be drawn from the length of a camel's neck, which is like a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation.</note> through which the spirit ascends, of which Haly speaks in his *Secrets*: "Take a male Corascene <note>Likely referring to Khorasan, a region in Persia; used here as a symbolic chemical reagent.</note> dog and a little bitch of Armenia, <margin>The Stone is compared to birds and all winged things. To Fish.</margin>and join them together, and they will give birth to a dog the color of the sky." They even gave the names of birds, insects, and all winged things to the Stone, because it is raised upward and, as it were, flies—though also for other reasons. Thus they called it a rooster, a hen, a crow, or an eagle. Alphidius says: "Let no water be of such a kind, except that which is made from the beetles of our water." Likewise, they compared it to fish, whence Mundus says in the *Assembly*: "Take a part of the fish's gall, and a part of the calf's urine, etc." And in the *Riddles of the Wise*: "There is in our sea a small round fish, lacking bones and <margin>To parts of animals. To the Humors.</margin>legs, etc." They also compared it to the parts of animals: the heart, liver, stomach, head, brain, eyes, belly, breasts, nerves, and veins. Also to their <term>humors</term> <note>The four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament.</note>: bile, blood, phlegm, and melancholy (black bile). Whence Morienes says: "Take the phlegmatic and the choleric, and grind the blood with them." They also used everything originating from animals, such as hair, the afterbirth, nails, and even menstruation, seed, and milk. This is because, just as animals are generated from the seeds of the male and female, and grow and increase by the addition of the menses, and are nourished by milk (which is nothing other than menses or blood "twice-cooked"), <margin>In the book titled *The Flower of Flowers*. To excrement.</margin>so too is the Stone. Hence, Arnaldus de Villa Nova says: "It is nourished by its own milk, that is, by the sperm from which it came from the beginning." They even compared it to the excrement of animals—dung, urine, and sweat—because of the "dregs" of the Stone and the separation of the pure from the impure, or because of its foul odor, or the evaporation of its superfluous moisture, which is called "infant's urine" by Lull <note>Ramon Lull, a famous philosopher and alchemist.</note>. I could assign many other reasons for these names here from the *Stellics* of Plato and his commentator Hebnabes Hamech <note>Ibn Umayl (Senior Zadith).</note>, but I do not wish to be tedious. They also compared the Stone to an egg, because just as in an egg there is <margin>To an egg.</margin>white and red (namely the white and the yolk) and a shell which takes the place of the earth, so...

[ter]ra <note>Completing the word "terrae" from the previous page: "...earth, so too in the stone."</note>, so too in the stone. Whence **Mireris** says: "Do you not see that by the heat of the hen's nutrition, a flying cock is made from an egg? Similarly, by the heat of this putrefaction, a flying cock is made from our egg." And **Hermes**: "The disposition sought by philosophers is one, in our one egg." They also called the stone a **poison**, and compared it to a **basilisk**, a **dragon**, a **viper**, a **salamander**, a **serpent**, **lizards**, and other **reptiles**, and a **toad**. Whence in the *Riddles of the Wise* <note>original: "ænig. Sap." or "Aenigmata Sapientum"</note> we read: "Take a viper and deprive it of its head and tail, for in those places its poison lies hidden." And **Hermes**: "Then it becomes a <margin>Treatise 2.</margin> dragon eating its own wings, and killing itself." And the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical text.</note>: "An eagle flying <margin>Poison and reptiles.</margin> into the sky and a toad walking upon the earth is the **mastery**." <note>The "mastery" or *magisterium* refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> The reason for this can be given: just as the basilisk, the viper, and similar venomous creatures kill living things by their breath, touch, or bite, and poisons corrupt human nature, so too the **sulfur** of the philosophers kills the "**living Mercury**" <note>Quicksilver or the philosophical principle of fluidity</note> by its vapor and touch, and changes its nature.

On the other hand, the stone is also called a **theriac**, <margin>Theriac and medicine.</margin> an **antidote**, a **medicine**, or a **medicament**. <note>A "theriac" was a famous universal antidote or "wonder drug" in medieval medicine.</note> For just as poison is kept away from the heart by theriac and medicines, or its force is blunted and sick bodies are restored to health, so through the **Elixir**, the poison is taken away from **Mercury**. And while it transforms into gold, a healthy temperament is granted to it, and other "leprous" and impure bodies of metals are cleansed and transmuted into gold or silver. Therefore, the author of *The Perfect Mastery*—whether that was **Rhasis** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian physician and alchemist.</note> or someone else—says: "The Elixir is a composition made of clear species, an antidote, medicine, and purgative for all bodies needing to be purged, cured, and converted into true **Lunific** and **Solific** matter." <note>Terms meaning "moon-making" (silver) and "sun-making" (gold).</note>

They also likened the stone to trees, shrubs, plants, herbs, roots, flowers, and all **vegetables**. <margin>Vegetables.</margin> Whence **Balgus** in the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, an early alchemical dialogue.</note> says: "Certain fruits come forth from a most perfect tree in early spring and bloom at the beginning of their emergence." And **Hermes**, in *To the Men of Wisdom*: "The <margin>Treatise 1.</margin> juice is extracted in 150 days." Also in the *Riddles of the Wise*: "It is a root which is ground with its stalk and juice," etc. Thus we read everywhere of white and red **roses**, of **Moonwort** (*Lunaria*), **Mercury-herb** (*mercurialis*), **sea purslane**, **celandine** (*chelidonia*), and **woad** (*geldo*), and many others. And this is indeed because of the green color which is characteristic of plants. Wherefore **Mireris** says: "No vegetable nor any fruit appears in its sprouting without a green color being present there; similarly, the sprouting of this thing is green," although in some cases the philosophers seem to have followed either the naming or the "heat of dryness."

But <margin>Images and figures appearing in the work.</margin> since I have dealt with reptiles and plants, it is possible that, beyond the reasons already mentioned, certain names were given to the stone because of the wonderful variety of figures that appear in the work itself, as several colors emerge at once. Just as we sometimes imagine strange forms of animals, reptiles, or trees in the clouds or in fire, as I found in a certain fragment of a book attributed to **Moses**, in this manner: "When the body has been dissolved, there will appear..."

...will appear: sometimes two branches, sometimes three, sometimes more; sometimes the shapes of reptiles; sometimes as if a man were sitting upon a chair with a head and all other limbs, and so forth.

<margin>Gums and resins.</margin>
They also compared the stone to **gums**, **resins**, and other liquids flowing from trees, shrubs, or plants. Whence **Mundus** <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says in the *Turba*: "Our gum is stronger than gold." And **Mary** <note>Maria Prophetissa, a foundational female figure in alchemical legend.</note>: "Join gum with gum in a true marriage." Likewise, they compared it to parts of trees and plants, such as leaves, roots, bark, and dry wood.

<margin>Metals.</margin>
They also compared it to **metals**, both imperfect and perfect; partly because all metals exist in the stone in power and potential, and partly for various other reasons. For in the beginning of the **decoction** <note>The prolonged heating or "cooking" of the alchemical matter.</note>, while the stone is black and very raw, it is called **lead**; but when it sheds its blackness a little and begins to whiten, it is called **tin**:

<margin>Lead. Tin.</margin>
likewise, when the **calcined** <note>Reduced to a powder through dry heat.</note> body is deprived of its moisture so that it cannot flow as it used to, they called it **iron**, because iron only flows with great difficulty.

<margin>Iron.</margin>
Whence **Anastratus** says in the *Turba*: "Take iron and make thin plates from it, and sprinkle them with poison."

<margin>Copper.</margin>
Similarly, they called the stone **copper** and **latten** <note>original: "ære & latonem". Latten was a copper alloy similar to brass.</note>. Whence in the *Turba*: "No true **tincture** <note>The transmuting agent.</note> is made except from our copper," for the same reason as with iron, or because of a color similar to copper. **Mireris** says: "The copper of the philosophers is not copper, but they called it copper because of the color."

<margin>Silver.</margin>
They also compared the stone to **silver** when it is already perfectly whitened and needs nothing but the **Lunar ferment** <note>In alchemy, silver is associated with the Moon (Luna); the "ferment" was a substance added to "ripen" the work into a specific metal.</note>.

<margin>Gold. Quicksilver. Coins.</margin>
To **gold**, however, when it is perfectly red. To **quicksilver** when the stone is already dissolved and turned into quicksilver. They even called their stone **coins**, **money**, and a **treasury**. **Astratus** in the *Turba* says: "Take a part of the philosophers' copper and mix it with coins." To understand the aforementioned, the saying of **Rosinus** <note>The Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist.</note> is helpful: "When the philosophers say 'our copper,' 'our money,' 'our gold,' or 'our magnesia,' they wished to speak of a copper related to themselves; similarly regarding gold, lead, magnesia, and money related to them."

<margin>Intermediate minerals.</margin>
They likewise likened the stone to the **intermediate minerals**: **orpiment** <note>A yellow arsenic sulfide.</note>, **arsenic**, **sulfur**, **marcasites**, **magnesia**, and **tutia** <note>Zinc oxide.</note>: either because of their astringency; or their weight; or the sparks of gold and silver with which they shimmer (since the same happens in the philosophical work), according to that saying of **Morienus**: "The stinking earth quickly receives golden sparks"; or by reason of their oiliness, or the sulfur they contain within; or for many other causes, which are many. A few will serve as examples.

<margin>In the Key of Wisdom.</margin>
**Parmenides** in the *Turba*: "Take quicksilver and coagulate it in the body of magnesia, or in sulfur that is not consumed by fire." **Senior** <note>Ibn Umail, an Arabic alchemist whose works were translated into Latin.</note>: "Unless there were a power of congealing Mercury in orpiment, the **mastery** <note>The *magisterium*, or the completed alchemical process.</note> would never be completed."

<margin>To brother Rainald, chapter 2. Salts.</margin>
And **Saint Thomas** <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical work attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>: "Take our **antimony**, or the black earth with eyes, etc." Likewise they compared it to all **salts**, **alums**, and **vitriols** <note>original: "atramentis," meaning black metallic sulfates used in making ink and in chemical reactions.</note>. And to salts indeed, because they open, cut, thin, corrode, moisten, dissolve, and...

He clarifies that these are allegorical names based on the material's appearance or chemical behavior during different stages of the alchemical process.</summary>
