-># On the Difficulties of Alchemy<-

...they **calcine** <note>To reduce a substance to a powder by heating it, usually to remove moisture or volatile components.</note> metals and make them flow. And because some of them are **volatile** <note>Easily evaporated at normal temperatures.</note>, they compared those to the **spirit**, but the fixed ones to the **body**.

<margin>Alums and Vitriols.</margin>
**Alums** and **vitriols** <note>original: "atramenta." In alchemical texts, this refers to metallic sulfates like green vitriol (ferrous sulfate).</note> are astringent and abound in raw moisture; however, when calcined, they are drier and more "fiery," assuming a red color like a stone. This stone first suffers from excessive moisture when dissolved, which perishes through long **coction** <note>The process of "cooking" or heating the substance over a long period.</note>, and is finally turned into redness.

<margin>Strong Waters.</margin>
The philosophers also compare their **spirit** to **corrosive waters** <note>original: "Aquis corrosivis" or "Aqua fortis." Usually refers to nitric acid or a mixture of acids used to dissolve metals.</note> because just as waters composed of salts, vitriols, and alum corrode and dissolve metals—dividing and separating them from one another—so too the spirit or "water of the philosophers" dissolves its own body and separates the **tincture** <note>The transformative essence or color-giving property of the alchemical stone.</note> from it. Hence the author of the *Rosarius Minor* <note>The "Lesser Rose Garden," a shorter version of a famous alchemical collection of sayings.</note> describes the praises and works of **strong water**. He says: "It dissolves the solid and makes it liquid, cleanses the unclean, corrodes the superfluous, penetrates all things, softens the hard, and is the key to the whole art," etc. **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> also frequently uses "strong waters." But since something must also be said about the **mineral mediums**—namely salts, vitriols, and alums—in the third part of this book, I shall move on to **colors**, from which the Philosophers have borrowed infinite names.

<margin>Colors.</margin>
I showed above that the stone was named after the **green** of all vegetation. But since, besides that color and other intermediate ones, the philosophers enumerate three principal ones—namely **black**, **white**, and **red**—they have named the stone most especially after these. Because of its **blackness**, they took names from all things called black. Thus it is called **antimony**, **pitch**, **coal**, the **raven**, the **raven's head**, **lead**, **burnt copper**, and **burnt ivory**. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic founder of alchemy.</note> says: "The raven's head is the origin of the art," that is, the blackness. And **Socrates** in the *Turba* <note>Socrates appears as a character in the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), a famous early Latin alchemical text.</note>: "Without lead, no true tincture is made that has power," that is, without blackness. Because of its **whiteness**, they took denominations from all white things; hence the whitened stone is called **talc**, **marble**, **silver**, **ivory**, **flower of salt**, **bones**, **crystal**, **crystalline lights**, **pearls**, **lime**, **eggshells**, **calcined moon** <note>Refers to calcined silver.</note>, **snow**, **hail**, **potash** <note>original: "cineres clavellati."</note>, **white earth**, **candid stone**, and **starry, splendid white powder**. Likewise, it is named after all things red, reddening, or made red through the art. Therefore, the red stone is called **saffron** <note>original: "crocus." Often refers to a fine reddish-orange metallic powder.</note>, **cinnabar**, **minium**, **red hematite stone**, **burnt human blood**, **egg yolks**, **calcined alum**, **coral**, and **gold**. I have not provided examples because they occur everywhere in infinite numbers. Similarly, because we need two natures or qualities in the work—namely the **moist** and the **dry**—they called their "Water" by the name of every moist thing: **vinegar**, **urine**, **sweat**, **milk**, **syrup**, **broth**, and countless others. **Bacon** <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the English friar and scientist often credited with alchemical secrets.</note> says in the *Turba*: "Return its sweat to it." And **Borates** <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> in the same place: "Govern the stone with the syrup of pomegranates."

<margin>Every moisture.</margin>
<margin>Of the sea and [of the sea].</margin>
...also of the seas and rivers; hence **Mireris** named "three seas" for the three **quicksilvers** <note>original: "argenta viva." Mercury.</note> or three waters which the philosophers need in their work,

-># The Names of the Matter<-

philosophers, namely the Sea of Egypt, of the South, and of the Indians. And Aristhenes in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," a famous 12th-century Latin translation of earlier Arabic alchemical texts depicting a debate between Greek sages.</note> says: "Take the **body**, and place it in the water of our sea."

<margin>In the Book of Figures and Images.</margin>
Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail.</note> says: "The Sages have named their stone 'the sea' because their clouds and rains ascend out of it." For this reason, Lucas says in the *Assembly*: "Take the cloud and cook it with its body until it becomes tin." They have also used the names of **bile** and **galls**. Hence Rosinus <note>A common alchemical corruption of the name Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> says: "The galls of which the philosophers have spoken are nothing other than the **water of sulfur**." This is perhaps because of the yellow color of bile, or because they are bitter, hot, sharp, and pungent.

<margin>Oil.</margin>
By the names of **oil**, **butter**, **fat**, and **ointment**, they wish their **tincture** <note>The transformative essence or concentrated spirit capable of changing the color and nature of a metal.</note> to be understood. This is because just as all fatty things cling more tenaciously and are not easily washed out of cloth, clothes, or other things they have fallen upon, so too the tincture of the philosophers cannot be removed once it has entered its own body. Hence that saying of Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>: "Water washes and cleanses, but oil tints and colors." Hermes says: "Sulfur is the ointment of our earth." Senior says: "Fatness and fats are names for the **divine water**."

<margin>On everything dry.</margin>
In the same way, they understand their **earth** by the names of everything dry, such as **stone**, **sand**, **lime**, **ash**, and so on. Hence Attamanus says in the *Assembly*: "Take the ancient sea-stones." And Dardaris says in the same place: "Take the white moisture, and soak the sand with it."

They also use the names of all things that are drying, constricting, coagulating, gathering, or attracting. For this reason, the matter is compared to the **magnet** and **iron**, and to **semen** and the **womb**. Hence Pythagoras says in the *Assembly*: "Know that this thing, which the philosophers have described in so many ways, seeks out its partner without fire, just as a magnet seeks iron." Nor is it without reason that it is compared to semen and the womb.

Conversely, the **water** is called by the names of all things that dissolve, moisten, soften, loosen, rarefy, purge, wash, and cleanse. Hence the saying: "Our water is the **soap of the wise**, washing away all impurities." It is likewise called a **knife**, a **carver**, a **spatula**, or a **sword**, because it divides the pure from the impure and separates the **soul** from the **body**.

From earthly things, the philosophers ascended to celestial ones, and they compare their materials to the **heavens**. Hence Hermes says: "Heaven is the male to the female, and earth is the female to the male."

<margin>Heaven. Earth. Planets.</margin>
They also compare it to the **Planets**, as in the *Allegory of the Wise*: "Our work is made from the seven Planets: first from **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, second from **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, third from **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, fourth from the **Sun** <note>Gold</note>, fifth from **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, sixth from **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, and seventh from the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>." They also speak of the **conjunctions** of their planets, their oppositions, and the eclipses of the luminaries, and of the **tail and head of the dragon** <note>Astronomical points where the moon's path crosses the sun's; in alchemy, these represent stages of a chemical reaction or the union of opposites.</note>,

<margin>Chapter 24.</margin>
just as Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> does in his *Testament*. And Anastratus says in the *Assembly*: "The Moon is joined to the light of the Sun." And another says: "Mercury meets the rays of the Sun." Similarly, they have compared their materials when they are dissolved to **smoke**, **wind**, **air**, and **vapor**.

<margin>Wind. Vapor.</margin>
Hermes says: "The wind carried it in its belly." And Morienes <note>A legendary hermit and teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "If the smoke were not white, the **ethereal gold** <note>original: "aurum ethees." Refers to gold in its spiritualized or perfected state.</note> would not be completed." And Pythagoras says in the *Assembly*: "The science of this art is nothing but vapor and water."

Hoghelande explains that these terms are not literal but describe the chemical properties of attraction, cleansing, and volatility.</summary>

-># Book of the Difficulties of Alchemy<-

->K 4<-

Indeed, they have even moved on to things that do not exist, mentioning **virgin's milk** and **bird's milk**. <note>In alchemy, "virgin's milk" (lac virginis) usually refers to a white, mercurial liquid or a specific solvent used to "wash" the matter.</note> Hermes says: "Hidden things shall appear, and the virgin's milk shall be whitened." <margin>Names vary according to the diversity of the work.</margin> We also read in the works of the same author, and in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*, about **bird's milk**. Thus far we have spoken of the names of the stone itself or of the things that compose it; however, a no less significant variety of names arises from the diversity of the work and the "regimen" (the method of treatment) of that same stone. Rosinus <note>A Latinized name for the 4th-century alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> shall be my witness, <margin>Book of the Interpretations of Divinations.</margin> of whom I shall provide a single example: "Know," he says, "that crushing and whitening are necessary; thus, in whatever ways things are whitened, crushed, thinned, divided, or separated—or by whatever operations these things are done, or through which substances—the Stone receives its names from those methods, operations, and substances." Because some things are purified through **distillation** (as water is through an alembic), some through **sublimation** (as spirits are), some through **solution** (as salts are), some through **washing** (as cloths are), some through **burning** (as lime is), some through **division** (as metals are separated from one another through the *cineritium* <term>cineritium: the process of cupellation, where metals are refined by heating them in a cup made of bone-ash</term>), and some through **straining** (as through a cloth or filter): when it is said, "sublime it," or any of these other terms, understand that you must then "whiten" it, and so on.

<margin>The work of the stone is compared to the four seasons of the year.</margin> They even compare the work to the **four seasons** of the year. For they compare the **solution** <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> of the stone to **winter**, because winter is cold, moist, and rainy. They compare **coagulation** <note>The thickening or hardening of the liquid matter.</note> to **spring**, which is warm and moist, producing flowers and making all vegetation sprout. They compare **reddening** <note>Rubefactio: the stage where the matter turns a deep red, signaling high potency.</note> to **summer**, which is hot and dry; and **fixing** <note>Fixio: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> to **autumn**, when the fruits are gathered. But to put an end to these comparisons, I conclude briefly: everything that can be said or discussed concerning the elements and their qualities—concerning their confusion in the **primary matter** <term>materia prima: the formless, original substance from which all things were created</term> and their distinction, their properties and sufferings; concerning the creation of the world, its beginning and its end; concerning corruption and generation; concerning matter and form, act and potential; concerning virtues and vices, peace and war, the victor and the vanquished, the pursuer and the fugitive, love and hate; concerning the strong and the weak, the healthy and the sick; concerning things that burn and things that prevent burning; concerning unity and multitude, conception and birth, life, death, and resurrection; concerning paradise, its height and glory, and concerning hell and the abyss—all these and many more can be said of this venerable stone.

<margin>Nothing in the world can be compared to the stone.</margin> Hence Senior <note>Senior Zadith, or Ibn Umail, a 10th-century authority.</note> says: "This stone is different from all other stones in its natures and its perfection, in its intake of nourishment and its growth during its preparations; none of our usual operations can be compared to it, because it is from the seed of the world <note>original: "de semine mundi"; some versions read "mundo" (from the world).</note> and possesses much blessing." And if it were, as some think, made of common stones, earths, or vegetables, it would not be called **Wisdom**, since neither death nor life is in those things, nor marriage, nor conception, nor the generation of offspring, nor nourishment; for our preparations (which we know from our 'animals' and our 'stones' which we have seen and worked upon) do not come from the vanities and preparations of those common things. This, therefore, is that stone...

<meta>catchword: wondrous (mirabili)</meta>

<summary>Hoghelande explains that the Philosopher's Stone is named after the chemical processes it undergoes (like distillation or cupellation) and the "seasons" of its development. He concludes that the Stone is a universal microcosm, representing everything from biological life cycles to the theological concepts of Heaven and Hell.</summary>

->### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE<-

...miraculous, to which no other thing in the whole world can be compared, and against which the imprudent strike themselves. These are the bonds, more than those of Vulcan, <note>In mythology, Vulcan caught Mars and Venus in unbreakable, invisible metallic nets. Here, it refers to the "trap" of literal language.</note> in which those who follow the mere sound of words are held entangled, rather than seeking the hidden understanding veiled beneath them. Whence the same **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"—referring to Zadith Senior, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umail.</note> says: "The hearts and eyes are blinded, and the ears are made deaf to these similes and judgments among all men: they read and do not understand; they study and do not perceive; they are ignorant of the truth and yet they cast it away. For whoever wanders from the truth shall be plunged into vanity." And in another place: "Men do not understand the words of the wise, nor do they perceive what is intended; hence they falsify the truth-tellers and justify the liars with their own opinions. They ought to lay the blame upon themselves, not upon the wise." For their error arises from ignorance of the authors' intention when they hear diverse words that are unknown to their understanding, since they possess a hidden meaning. Indeed, they understand them only according to the literal letter and designation, and thus they are deceived, since the meaning is buried in concealment.

<margin>In the Book of Figures and Images.</margin>
<margin>From whence the error of the practitioners proceeds.</margin>

<margin>Equivocal terms.</margin>
Having explained the similes of the **Stone** and the obscurity arising from them, let us pass on to **equivocal terms**—those words that have multiple meanings. These alone, even if no other cause of obscurity existed, would be enough to turn a mind that is not sufficiently steadfast away from its purpose. This method of concealment is the opposite of the previous one: for there, one single thing is called by many and infinite names; but here, many different things are grouped under a single name. This way of teaching is surely much more obscure than the other and holds more difficulty. A great and unusual variety of names might easily cause even a cautious man to stumble or suspect a trap; but in discerning equivocal terms, no one can bring enough wit or prudence unless they are very well-versed in the writings of the philosophers. I shall bring forward two examples, and I will go no further than the "matter" of the Stone, which everyone generally asserts consists of **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term> and **sulphur**. I shall choose these specifically so that beginners <note>original: "tyrones"—novices or apprentices in the art.</note> may become accustomed to understanding the books of the philosophers, since these are the principles of the art and the entire work, and its foundations. Let us weigh, therefore, in how many ways these are spoken of by the philosophers. But first concerning **Sulphur**, which is more famously used for that "buttery" and common combustible substance than needs an example. For it is also taken to mean the **philosophical earth**. Whence **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says: "It is a property of our quicksilver that it is congealed by the vapor of its own sulphur." The same author says: "Our sulphur is a subtle earth or a dry water, in the belly of which the fire of nature is powerfully multiplied." It is also taken to mean **quicksilver**, the other part of the Stone. **Morienes** <note>A legendary hermit and alchemist, teacher of the Prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "When **Laton** <note>A term for an impure metal (often likened to brass) that must be cleansed to become gold.</note> is burned with sulphur, and moisture is frequently poured over it, then all its obscurity and blackness are taken away from it." This means when the philosophical earth is irrigated by its own water or quicksilver. And **Rosinus** <note>Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> says: "Nothing acts upon the **Sun** <note>The alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> except our sulphur, which blackens and consumes the Sun."

<margin>1.</margin>
<margin>2. In the Codicil. In the Practice of the Testament, chapter 22.</margin>
<margin>3.</margin>

Whence Plato <note>Alchemical texts often attributed quotes to ancient philosophers like Plato and Aristotle that do not appear in their known works.</note> says: "All gold is sulfur." Having demonstrated how many ways "sulfur" is spoken of by the philosophers, it remains to be shown that the name of "quicksilver" is used in almost as many ways. First, indeed, for the "common kind" sold everywhere and known to all; then for "the other part" constituting the matter of the Stone—namely the "humidity of the Stone" or the "water of the philosophers." In other sciences, this would be considered shameful and worthy of reproach, and it could call their truth into doubt; in this art, however, the philosophers do not consider it a fault. Indeed, they deliberately contradict not only others but even themselves, clearly so that they may exercise the reader and test his judgment to see whether he errs in the choice of natural things—accepting those things which are against nature rather than those friendly to nature—or vice versa. first they should be <term>calcined</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note>, and afterward they should be dissolved, since once they have been calcined they are dissolved more easily, because the heat of the fire, penetrating the parts of the body, allows the water to enter after it, and thus it is more receptive to <term>solution</term>. In the same chapter, as if yawning and waking from sleep, he says it is expedient for bodies to be dissolved through water alone without calcination. Should we think that such a great teacher, and one so brilliantly versed in other sciences, had a lapse in memory? Far from it; rather, he did it intentionally and with diligent effort, not only in this place, but in many others besides, just as Lullius and the rest do, whose examples—no different from these—occur everywhere. It is not necessary to collect them here, since I must move on to another art of veiling the doctrine.

That art consists in their use of unusual and unknown names, or, if the names are known, they are twisted to an entirely different meaning, so that they seem to speak in a peculiar dialect by which they understand one another. Thus, besides the metals which they have designated with the names of the planets—namely, that gold is called the Sun, silver the Moon, copper Venus, iron Mars, tin Jupiter, lead Saturn, and quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note> is called Mercury—they introduced infinite other names. <margin>Unusual names.</margin> These include Laton, Azoth, the soul, the Lion, the Dragon, foliated earth, Cambar, marteck, kahul, adkibrick, boritis, zandarich, muchal, Corfuphle, ferment, <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent.</note>, coagulum, poison, and countless similar terms.

They have especially entangled everything with the names for "gold" and "silver," so that the meaning of such words can hardly be extracted even by many years of study. Thus Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "The ferment of gold is gold." Hermes says: "Sow your gold in foliated earth." Rosinus says: "Unless you place gold in gold, you have nothing, because the great is not in the small." Likewise in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," an influential early Latin alchemical text.</note>: "The Sun does not tint unless it is tinted." And Lullius says: "This science chooses gold for the father and silver for the mother, because our medicine is drawn out from these two bodies prepared in the same sulfur and arsenic."

The difficulty arising from unknown or non-common words is increased in no small measure by unknown <term>characters</term> <note>Special symbols used as shorthand for substances or processes.</note>. <margin>Characters.</margin> For besides the symbols for the planets, which are known to almost everyone, they have granted peculiar symbols to sulfur, salts, inks, alums, and middle minerals—indeed, even to the elements themselves, and to calcination, sublimation, and the other operations of the art. Many have also used the transposition of letters, or hidden numbers and signs, in the writing of their books.

But nothing hinders students as much as the lack of skill of those who transcribe books. <margin>Transcription.</margin> These people omit words they do not understand and which they deem absurd; or, what is worse, wishing to "correct" them, they pervert the entire sense and the author's meaning. They even frequently transfer the glosses <note>Explanatory notes written in the margins of a manuscript.</note> of unskilled men into the main text. Those who translate books published in a foreign language into another are not free from a similar vice. <margin>Translation.</margin> This can be seen in several places in the later Latin edition of Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist.</note>, and in Morienes, who was converted from the Arabic into the Latin tongue by Robert... <note>Robert of Chester, the 12th-century scholar credited with the first translation of an alchemical work into Latin.</note>

<margin>Variety of styles</margin>
...by Robert of Castre <note>Robert of Chester (Robertus Castrensis), a 12th-century translator who brought Arabic alchemical works into Latin.</note> differs so much from the other translation that in many places it seems to be by a completely different author. The style of the authors of this science is likewise manifold and varied, which brings no small hindrance to readers. For some establish their discourses physically—or naturally—following the progress of nature; others follow the method of teaching used by medical doctors; some explain things arithmetically; and some even follow the rules of astronomy and geometry.

<margin>Physical style</margin>
Naturally and philosophically, they speak of corruption and generation, of action and passion, of the elements and their qualities, of matter and form, of the faculties and powers of the soul, of the four seasons of the year, of vapors and rains, of the rainbow <note>original: "Iride"</note> and its cause, of man and woman, of conception and birth, of the fetus, and many other such things.

<margin>Medical</margin>
Those who follow the style of medical doctors, however, discuss the healthy and the sick, the changing of "complexions" <note>The balance of humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) or qualities (heat, moisture) that determine health.</note>—namely, from cold and moist into hot and dry, and vice-versa—of rawness and digestion, of the inspection of urine, and of the "crisis" of the birth and origin of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>. They compare this to the crises of acute diseases and putrid fevers, so that once the first movement is seen, one can testify to the end result.

<margin>Arithmetical</margin>
Arithmeticians have also obscured this science with their distinctions of numbers, both in part and in the whole. They have hidden the terms and the goal of the entire work within divisions of numbers, as they have also done with weights, since they add and subtract from the sum of the "root" at will, sometimes building up the whole from parts so that the unlearned cannot grasp it. An example of this is that passage from Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist often cited in Latin as "Senior Zadith."</note>: "Understand the principle of number, the first and the second, and you say two; and those are three in number; then you say three, which are six in number; then you say four, and they become ten manifest numbers, but four hidden ones." There is also that saying of Eximenus in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a famous early Latin alchemical text.</note>: "I command you to coagulate <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note> so that two become three, and four one, and two one."

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
The author of the *Three Words* also says that one must extract two from three, since three are not extracted from two; rather, by three are understood two and seven. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says in the *Seven Treatises*: "It is water which divides itself into four others; namely, one to two, and three to one, of which the third part is for color, but two-thirds for moisture, which are the weights of the wise for water."

<margin>Astronomical</margin>
The philosophers speak astronomically of the zodiac and the signs of the zodiac, of the poles and their exaltation and fall, of conjunctions and oppositions, of the eclipses of the luminaries, of the infusion of solar light into the Moon and the stars, and of the "turncoat" nature of Mercury, who is good and fortunate with good planets, but evil and unfortunate with bad ones, and of the operations of the planets upon these lower things, and similar matters.

<margin>Geometrical</margin>
They speak geometrically of boundaries and angles, of the square, the triangle, and the circle—likewise how the square and the triangle ought to be made round, and vice-versa. Hence that saying from the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a key alchemical text.</note>: "Convert the quadrangle into a circle, and you shall have the <term>Magisterium</term> <note>The "Mastery" or completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>." Likewise, concerning the furnace...

<margin>Book of the Secrets of Alchemy, in the preface.</margin> Haly says that the construction [of the work] requires the necessary rules of Geometry. He says: "Whoever possesses this book should read something of Geometry, learn its measurements, and correctly assemble the construction of the furnaces, and not exceed the proper measure."

<margin>Impossibility</margin> To these things, finally, add that the philosophers seem to command impossible things. Because of this, every treatise on the art could appear not only difficult, but entirely deceptive and fraudulent. For they order that the elements be distilled, washed, and cleansed, and finally—which seems ridiculous—<margin>Book of Secrets, chapter 9.</margin> be joined together by a certain weight. Haly says: "You must take the stone and separate its natures, that is, the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire." Arnald says: <margin>The Rosary, part 2, chapter 8.</margin> "When you have the elements divided, wash them—namely, by distilling the water and air, but by strongly <term>calcining</term> <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to burn off impurities or reduce it to a dry powder.</note> the fire and the earth." 

If, however, someone thinks the elements are named here metaphorically—as, for example, in the distillation of wax or honey, where the <term>phlegm</term> <note>The watery, tasteless byproduct that appears first in the distillation process.</note> that comes out first is called "water," the yellow oil that follows in the second place obtains the name of "air," the red oil in the third place is "fire," and the dregs remaining at the bottom are allotted the name "earth"—he is undoubtedly mistaken. For Arnald says in the previously cited passage that the "fire" must be calcined, which cannot take place with red and easily flammable oil. Furthermore, the philosophers do not care for elements that can be perceived by the touch, as is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts.</note>. Regarding the weight <margin>The Rosary, part 2, chapter 24.</margin> of the elements, the same Arnald says: "Take care in the compounding of the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The transmuting agent or "medicine" of the metals.</note>, and work there wisely, so that you know how much you ought to add of water, of air, of earth, and of fire; otherwise, if you do differently, the work will be of no value." 

But what mathematician was ever found so subtle that he could grasp the invisible elements—I mean air and fire—and those things that cannot be felt, by measure or weight? Especially since Eximenus says in the *Turba*: "Two of the elements are seen, and their power and work are known; but the other two are neither touched nor seen." It seems no less absurd that they say the elements must be converted, since that seems to be the work of God and nature alone. Hence the Alchemical Aristotle says: "Convert the elements, and you will find what you seek." And truly, <margin>The doctrine of elements is most obscure.</margin> by this tradition of the elements, the philosophers have so obscured the art that many people—being troubled by this difficulty and not grasping their meaning—shrink away from the study of the books. Or they believe all these things are mere fictions invented for the concealment of the art, especially since the philosophers say that the whole work is finished with one thing and one single process. 

I will not deny that I was once among their number, though undeservedly; yet now, with Raymond Lull, I confess that the whole art depends upon the division and cleansing of the elements. For thus he says: <margin>The whole mastery depends on the elements.</margin> "The whole <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium" — the complete alchemical process or the "great work."</note> consists in dividing the elements from the metals, and purifying them, and dividing the sulfur of nature from the metals. For the whole labor is in this, and the entire fatigue of the mastery is in the division of the elements and the sulfur." And Arnald says: "If you do not divide the elements of the stone, it cannot..."

He cites authorities like Haly, Arnaldus de Villanova, and Raymond Lull to show that successfully separating and purifying these elements is the true secret of the work.</summary>

->PART THREE<-

# IN WHICH THE DIFFICULTY OF PRACTICE IS TREATED.

So far I have spoken about the obstacles that arise from the artist's own limitations or from the difficult understanding of books; it follows that I should begin a discourse on the third part of this treatise, which will deal with <term>praxis</term> <note>Praxis refers to the practical, hands-on application of alchemical theory in the laboratory.</note>. Although this might seem to depend entirely on the understanding of books—since once the books are understood, the matter, the management of the work, and the rest that follows can be known—nevertheless, it is one thing to investigate the theory of the art and quite another to attempt it and apply one's hand to the work. <margin>Many things are discovered by experience which are thought to be false or impossible.</margin> Many things are discovered through experience itself which could not be comprehended through theory alone. Furthermore, many things which appear easy at first glance are found to be very difficult when one approaches the practice; and conversely, I thought it better to treat this subject individually. I indeed can certainly affirm to anyone that I would never have understood the philosophers when they reasoned about the division of the elements unless, by working and experimenting, I had discovered the <term>sulphur of nature</term> <note>In alchemy, "sulphur" is not just the yellow chemical element, but a philosophical principle representing the active, masculine, and "soul" aspect of matter.</note> and of art. Nor, however, should anyone think because of this that I profess total knowledge of this science, since experience has often mocked me as I tried, and I still desire the knowledge of many things, which I do not even dare to hope for—both because of a lack of books (of which I nevertheless have more than a hundred copies) and because of many obstacles by which I do not deny I am held back.

<margin>The matter of the stone is called by the names of all things. Book to Eutychia.</margin> But as I prepare to approach this third treatise, the first thing I encounter is the <term>matter</term>, which is the basis and foundation of the entire philosophical work. If this foundation is laid rashly, nothing solid can be built upon it. Although the Philosophers say this matter is one thing, they have named it with more than a thousand legions of names, as Rosinus <note>Rosinus is a medieval Latin name commonly associated with Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist.</note> says: namely, by the name of every thing that is found on earth, in the sea, or in the air. They have likened it to all things; they have called it a "Hermaphroditic monster" (being both male and female), heaven and earth, both corporeal and spiritual, chaos, a <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "microcosm" or "little world" implies that the alchemical matter contains within itself the entire structure of the universe.</note>, a confused mass containing within itself all colors and all metals in potentiality, and a thing than which nothing in the world is more wonderful.

<summary>Hoghelande transitions from the theoretical confusion of alchemical texts to the practical difficulties of the laboratory (praxis). He emphasizes that hands-on experience is necessary to understand concepts like the "division of elements" and introduces the "materia prima" (the starting material), which philosophers intentionally obscured with thousands of metaphorical names.</summary>

THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...more miraculous, since it impregnates itself, conceives itself, and gives birth to itself. <note>This refers to the alchemical concept of the Stone as a "hermaphrodite" or "Rebis," containing both active and passive principles within itself.</note> This they [the philosophers] conceal most greatly, nor do they call it by its proper name.

<margin>The matter of the stone is greatly hidden. In the *Keys of the Philosophers*.</margin>
Hence the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note> states: "We have named the Stone through a description of its roots, for we cannot name it otherwise." And Alphidius says: "This stone proceeds from a most glorious, sublime place of the greatest terror, which has brought death to many wise men; it is similar to anything else, and its name cannot be spoken." And another author writes: "He who names the stone is ignorant of its power, for he who knows its power does not name it." Indeed, some assert that it does not even have a proper name. For so says Alphidius: "If the stone has a proper name, they [the philosophers] do not dare to make it common for the reasons handed down by them." Hence Rosinus <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Graeco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: "I feared not a little lest God should remove His grace from me because I explained this supreme wisdom to you, since all philosophers would rather die than call it by its proper names." And an unnamed author states: "No one can reveal the name of the stone under the condemnation of his own soul, because he could not give an account before God."

<margin>The stone has no proper name. The name of the stone must not be made common. In the *Treatise on the Philosopher’s Stone*.</margin>
Another says: "The state of the whole world would perish if our stone were named in books; or if they sometimes call it by its proper name, they do so secretly, and often add something fictional to its name." Hence Agmon in the *Turba* <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> says: "Where it is useless, it is named magnificently and significantly; where it is useful, it is most hidden." Some of the philosophers asserted that this stone is found in every thing, in every place, and at all times. Hence many, having been deceived, have sought it in vegetables and animals, or in things drawing their birth and origin from them—from which they judged elements could be separated—but in vain, since individual things do not produce anything except what is like themselves.

<margin>The error of those assuming the art is found in vegetables and animals.</margin>
Mocking these people, Senior <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly influential in the West.</note> says: "If it were said to such men, 'A sheep gave birth to a man,' or 'birds give birth to fish,' or 'a palm tree bore pomegranates,' they would surely respond: 'You have told a fable; things do not generate except what is like themselves, and each tree bears only its own fruit.'" And yet these men, more foolish than the fools, prepare that which has no tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is the power of the Stone to transform or "dye" base metals into gold.</note> in itself from every thing that tends toward nothingness; they believe they are doing well, but they acquire nothing except labor, because they are blinded from the truth by impossibility. Indeed, the most natural and perfect work is for each thing to generate its own kind, as a plant produces a plant or a goat produces a goat, as the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle.</note> says. Since, however, these materials [vegetables and animals] are foreign to the nature of metals, it is impossible for generation to occur in metals from them, because metals are not generated except from their own proper seeds.

<margin>Aristotle's *On the Soul*, Book 2. Metals are generated from their own seeds. In the *Instauratio Florum*.</margin>
Therefore, Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> advises, not without reason, to inquire what the <term>sperm of metals</term> <note>The "sperm" or seed of metals was theorized to be a specific form of Mercury or Sulfur that acted as the "starting material" for metallic growth.</note> might be; for that which is not in a thing cannot be found in it. Now, metals are not in animals and vegetables, nor in blood, hair, menstrual blood, and the like, although philosophers have sometimes used such names metaphorically, as was declared above. Certainly, for the generation of a human or an animal, there is no mixing of any thing except the see[d]—

<summary>Hoghelande discusses the intentional secrecy surrounding the name of the Philosopher’s Stone and critiques "fools" who attempt to create it from organic materials like plants or animal blood. He argues that alchemy must follow the laws of nature, where like only generates like, meaning the Stone must be derived from "metallic seeds" rather than biological ones.</summary>

# On the Difficulties of Alchemy, Book 1

...[seed] of the male and female in a natural vessel, namely the womb, where it is converted from one thing to another through a natural preparation, until a human and animal are formed therefrom, without the entry of any other thing except the blood of the menses, which is similar to it. <margin>Nature must be imitated by like things.</margin> And in vegetables, the proper seed of each tree or plant is committed to the earth without the addition of any other thing, where, nourished by the food of its own nature and called forth by the heat of the sun, it germinates and increases. So also the mastery <note>The *magisterium*, or the Great Work—the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> of the philosophers does not need the mixing of anything foreign, but from its own metallic seed sent into the "philosophical earth" prepared by art, it produces a stone capable of being multiplied unto infinity, if it is nourished by its own proper menstruum <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent or life-giving fluid, named by analogy to the uterine environment.</note> and connatural moisture, and is excited from potentiality into action by the heat of the Sun of the philosophers.

<margin>The error of those who suppose the art lies in salts, alums, and vitriols.</margin> Others have believed the philosopher's stone to be found in salts, alums, vitriols <note>original: *atramentis*, literally "inks" but referring here to vitriols or metallic sulfates.</note>, and boraxes <note>original: *bauracibus*, referring to various alkaline salts.</note>, or that through them more perfect metals can be brought to such a state that they may "tinge" <note>To transform or color other substances, a primary goal of the Stone.</note> unto infinity. They are led to this because they see that through the "cementing" <note>A dry refining process using salts to purify metals.</note> of these, the metals are purged of impurities, and a more vigorous and splendid color is joined to them. They also know that from these, certain waters are drawn forth by the power of fire, which they call "strong," "gradual," and "royal" <note>The early names for acids like nitric acid (*aqua fortis*) and *aqua regia* (royal water), which can dissolve gold.</note>, by which they think gold and silver are dissolved or promoted to a higher degree of color. 

But the philosophers do not care for a solution of this kind, since it is rather a corrosion and a certain shattering of the whole into the smallest parts, which can simply return again into silver and gold by melting. And if any color comes to the perfected metals, it vanishes with repeated meltings and long attraction, because these substances do not alter the metal intrinsically, but only superficially. They do not penetrate the metal because they are immiscible with them, nor do they offer metallic fusion, nor do they have in themselves the other differences of properties which the philosophers require in their stone. Therefore, they are rightly rejected by those who are not entirely foolish and dull.

<margin>The second cause of error.</margin> However, some are perhaps deceived because the Sages sometimes use the name "dry water," which these seekers think fits no things better than salts, alums, and vitriols, which when dissolved easily pass into water, and by a little heat return again to their former solid shape. But the philosophers understand nothing else by "dry water" than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*, or mercury.</note>, for the reason that it does not wet what it touches, even though it is liquid and fluid like water. Let them believe Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father" of Islamic alchemy.</note>, who says thus in his *Book of Furnaces*: 

<margin>Chapter 19. Third [cause].</margin> "Endeavor to resolve the Sun <note>Gold.</note> and Moon <note>Silver.</note> into their own dry water, which the common people call Mercury." They are also deceived in that the philosophers speak everywhere of salt. As for instance the author of the *Soliloquy*: "He who works without salt is like one who shoots with a bow without a string." And in the *Book of Salt and Alum*: "If God had not created salt, the Elixir would not be perfected, and alchemical study would be in vain." And in the *Allegories of the Sages*: "He who works or acts without salt does not resuscitate the bodies of the dead." Likewise another says: "Salts are the roots of your work."

<summary>This page argues that the true alchemical process is biological and internal, requiring the "metallic seed" rather than common corrosive chemicals like salts and acids. Hoghelande clarifies that alchemical terms like "dry water" and "salt" are metaphors for philosophical Mercury and the foundation of the work, not literal household ingredients.</summary>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...of the work. Let those people know that the philosophers do not speak of common salt, but of that mineral salt which they require in their work, a term drawn from the likeness of calcined things <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>. Since salt can be extracted from all such things, they rightly say that the salt is also extracted from the lime <note>original: *calce*, referring to the powdery residue left after heating a metal.</note> of their metal; yet by this they <margin>Alang. [referring to an authority].</margin> signify nothing other than their "earth." According to that saying of an unnamed Author: "That which remains below in the gourd-shaped flask <note>original: *cucurbita*, a vessel used in distillation.</note> is our salt, that is, our earth." And in the *Allegories of the Wise*: "Note that these bodies are alums and salts, which flow from our bodies." And the Author of the *Ladder of the Philosophers* says: "The work of the Second Water is to exalt the earth into a 'miraculous salt' by its own attractive power alone."

Some have sought the matter of the Stone in "middle minerals" <note>Substances that share properties of both metals and earths.</note>, such as tutia <note>Zinc oxide residue from furnaces.</note>, <margin>The error of those who suppose the art lies in middle minerals and marcasites.</margin> magnesia, and marcasites <note>Iron pyrites or other metallic ores.</note>, and especially in antimony. For since the philosophers say that metals and their Stone consist of sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*, literally "living silver."</note>, and these can be drawn out of antimony by a simple craft, they believe nothing prevents the matter of the Stone from being sought there. But while the philosophers require sulfur and quicksilver, they do not want just any kind; they want them to be pure, clean, lacking all defilement, homogeneous, and non-combustible <note>original: *non adustibilia*, meaning they do not burn away in the fire.</note>, but rather enduring over the fire and capable of melting. However, the quicksilver and sulfur of antimony are, in their roots, impure and unclean, and can be purified by no craft. Furthermore, they are heterogeneous and easily flee from the fire, or else they do not flow; thus, the nature of antimony and the remaining marcasites will be held suspect by all those of sound mind.

<margin>In stones and gems.</margin> Certain people investigate the principles of the art in stones, gems, and crystal. But if those things which approach more closely to the nature of metals cannot provide the matter for the Elixir, then surely neither can gems, crystal, or other stones. For if that which seems more likely to be the thing is not it, then surely neither is that which is less likely. Therefore, since these cannot cause alterations in the bodies of metals—because they do not "enter" them, and nothing alters what it does not enter—nor do they provide a metallic fusion, but only a glass-making fusion <note>original: *vitrificatoriam*; they turn to glass rather than blending with metal.</note> or none at all, they shall be rejected as entirely foreign to the art. Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical authority often cited in Latin translations.</note> commands this very thing: "Beware, my son," he says, "and separate yourself from dead bodies and stones, for there is no path in them, because their life is not increased, but rather tends toward nothingness; such are salts, orpiment <note>original: *auripigmenta*, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, arsenic, magnesia, marcasite, tutia, <margin>In sulfur.</margin> and things similar to these."

Others presuppose the matter of the stone to be in common sulfur. For since philosophers require homogeneity, fixation, and "tincture" <note>The power to change the color and quality of a metal.</note> in the matter of the Elixir, and sulfur contains all these within itself, it is rightly judged as the matter of the stone or a part of it. As Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous alchemical authority.</note> says: "Sulfur has a homogeneous and very strong <margin>*The Sum of Perfection*.</margin> composition, and is of a uniform substance." In the same place: "It gives complete weight to each of the metals, and it purifies and brightens them from foulness." And a little later: "By God Most High, it illuminates every body, since it is light and tincture." Likewise, Pythagoras—

<summary>Theobald refutes the use of common salts, "middle minerals" like antimony, and gemstones in alchemy, arguing they lack the purity and "metallic" nature required for the Philosopher's Stone. He begins to discuss the merits and arguments for using sulfur as the primary matter, citing authorities like Geber.</summary>

### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK II
### Sig: L 2

...as stated in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba* [Philosophorum], a famous early alchemical text</note>: "The overflowing water of sulfur is from sulfur alone." And Acsubofon <note>A speaker in the *Turba* dialogue</note> says in the same place: "Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs." I respond that Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist</note>, most learnedly and sharply—as is his habit when describing the truth—hides it in wonderful wrappings of words, no differently than one who would hide a grain of wheat under a great pile of chaff. Therefore, he is not speaking of common and combustible sulfur, but of the "sulfur of the philosophers." For this reason, he adds in that same passage that it must not be used without mastery <term>Magistery: the specialized chemical process or "art" of the master alchemist</term>, because without it, sulfur achieves none of these things, but rather corrupts and turns the work black.

<margin>The Sum of Perfection, chapter 85.</margin>
And elsewhere, where he speaks of the nature of sulfur and arsenic, he says that sulfur has within it two causes of corruption: an inflammable substance and an earthy dross. Through the first, its nature cannot withstand the fire, since it always burns and is burned, and it produces blackness in every work. Through the second, it has neither "fusion" <note>the ability to melt</note> nor "ingression" <term>Ingression: the ability of a substance to penetrate and transform a metal</term>, because if it were to be fixed <note>made resistant to heat</note>, it would prevent melting; and it is never fixed unless it is first calcined <note>heated to a powder</note>, but when it is calcined, it can in no way be melted in the craft, because it is reduced to an earthy substance.

<margin>The Rosary of the Philosophers, part 1, chapter 3.</margin>
Geber says these things regarding common sulfur, as do Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note> and all others. How much this differs from the sulfur of the philosophers, anyone even moderately versed in chemical books can easily see. Common sulfur is clearly foreign to quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*, literally "living silver"</note>; but the philosophers' sulfur is sought from the innermost depths of the quicksilver of perfected bodies <note>Refers to the essence extracted from gold or silver</note>. It is nothing other than a simple, non-burning fire—living, giving life to other dead bodies, maturing them, and supplying nature’s defects. This is because it possesses an abundance of maturity, being perfect in its own nature and further purified by the craft. Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemist known as Zadith ben Hamuel</note> said: "The Sages satisfied men when they said our sulfur is not the sulfur of the common people, because common sulfur is consumed by fire, but the white sulfur of the wise burns with a burning of whiteness and improvement."

<margin>The difference between common sulfur and the sulfur of the philosophers.</margin>

<margin>Regarding common quicksilver.</margin>
Since, therefore, the matter of the Stone cannot be drawn from all the substances mentioned above, it seems to follow that quicksilver must provide it to us, as the Mercurial nature alone corresponds to all the known characteristics of the matter of the Philosopher’s Stone. For quicksilver alone is incombustible and "homogeneous"—meaning it either remains in the fire with its whole substance or retreats from the fire with its whole substance. It prevents burning, enables melting, and perfects metallic bodies. Those bodies are less easily burned and possess greater perfection when they participate more in its nature; those with less are of lesser value. Avicenna <note>Famous Persian polymath and physician</note> also affirms: "It alone receives into itself what is of its own nature and rejects what is foreign; and since it is metallic, it contains within itself everything we need for our mastery." But lest these things be understood as referring to common quicksilver, its "flight" <note>evaporation or volatility</note> stands in the way, for it cannot be halted unless by the power of sulfur joined to it or by a metallic vapor. The Philosophers also say that their Mercury is not the Mercury of the common people. Furthermore, since especially...

<summary>Hoghelande distinguishes between common sulfur and quicksilver and the "philosophical" versions required for alchemy, arguing that the true "Stone" is derived from the internal essence of perfected metals rather than crude minerals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the raw materials for the "Great Work." While the previous page distinguished between common sulfur and the sulfur of the philosophers, this page addresses whether "imperfect bodies" (common metals) can be used as the base for the Elixir.</meta>

->### THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE<-

...even if the philosophers command that a body be dissolved or calcined <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its properties, often reducing it to a powder</term>, neither process can apply to common quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>, since it is entirely airy and spiritual. Therefore, the substance of the Elixir must be sought in "bodies" <note>In alchemical terminology, "bodies" refers to solid metals</note>: but these are either perfect or imperfect. Since these [imperfect bodies] cannot give a perfection which they do not possess—as they consist of impure sulfur and quicksilver that are under- or over-cooked <margin>On imperfect bodies.</margin>—and are quickly consumed by fire and other burning agents, they cannot provide us with the Elixir. For the Elixir must be of a more subtle substance and more fluid melting <note>original: *liquidioris fusionis*</note> than those common bodies, and of a greater "fixion" <term>Fixion (or fixation): the state of being resistant to fire and not evaporating or changing</term> than they are in their own nature. 

It is also impossible, as Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says, to fix the unfixed, or to clean the unclean, because that which was not in a thing beforehand cannot be found within it, nor can anyone <margin>Rosary of the Philosophers, part 1, chapter 10.</margin> give what he does not have. Furthermore, for those [imperfect metals] to become the Elixir itself, it would first be necessary to convert them into the likeness of the two perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver</note>, which would be a pointless effort, since we already have the two perfect bodies made by nature. 

Nor does it hinder us <margin>Objection.</margin> that the philosophers more often mention an imperfect or unclean body. For instance, Morienes <note>A legendary hermit and alchemist</note> says: "Unless you have cleansed the unclean body, rendered it whitened, and sent the soul into it, you have directed nothing of this mastery." Likewise, Astanus in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical dialogue</note>: "The imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment." And Geber in the *Book of Furnaces*, chapter 9: "We extract the paste to be fermented in the usual manner from imperfect bodies." <margin>Book of Furnaces, chapter 9.</margin> And from this we hand down to you a general rule: that the white paste is extracted from Jupiter <note>tin</note> and Saturn <note>lead</note>, while the red paste is from Venus <note>copper</note>, Saturn, and Mars <note>iron</note>. 

This passage of Geber has greatly troubled even the most learned men, leading them to think that the body or matter of the Stone should be sought from imperfect metals, while the form should come from common gold and silver. However, both the matter and its form must be taken from one thing alone; for it is established that the matter of the Stone is unique in both species and number, even though it is later spread into many streams, as Morienes testifies. "This mastery," he says, "proceeds first from one root, which is afterwards expanded into many things, and again returns to one." And the *Lily* <note>original: *Lilium*, an alchemical text often attributed to Bernard of Trevisan</note> says: "Soul, body, and spirit are together, and it is one thing, having all things within itself to which nothing foreign is introduced." Haly <note>Likely Khalid ibn Yazid, an early patron of alchemy</note> says: "The stone is one, upon which you should not mix any other <margin>Book Two, chapter 9.</margin> thing; the wise work with it, and from it comes that with which healing is done; nothing else is mixed with it, neither in part nor in its whole." 

Therefore, when the Philosophers mention an imperfect or unclean body, they mean nothing other than their own "earth," for which Arnaldus will be my ample witness. "Mercury," he says, "is joined <margin>In the *Flower of Flowers*</margin> with the earth, that is, with the imperfect body, which is called the Mother Earth because earth is the mother of the elements." He does not mean that the matter to be fermented should be taken from common bodies—lead, tin, bronze, or iron—but from his own composite turned into earth, which...

<summary>Theobald de Hoghelande argues that the "imperfect bodies" mentioned in alchemical literature are not common base metals like lead or iron, but a specific "philosophical earth" derived from a single unique source. He contends that perfection cannot be produced from naturally impure substances, dismissing the use of common metals in the creation of the Elixir.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the "imperfect bodies" (common metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron) serve as a starting point for the alchemical process, but only because they contain the potential for perfection within them, much like a seed contains a plant. It transitions into discussing why "perfect bodies" (gold and silver) are ultimately necessary for the final Elixir.</meta>

->### ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY<-

It is still imperfect in respect to the ultimate perfection to which the philosophers strive to lead it, both by reason of the "tincture" <term>Tincture: the color-giving and transforming power of the Elixir</term> which was taken away from it and later restored through the Art. Nor does it argue to the contrary that Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in Arabic and European alchemy</note> expressly says that the **white paste** must be extracted from Jupiter <note>Tin</note> and Saturn <note>Lead</note>, while the **red paste** is indeed extracted from Venus <note>Copper</note>, Saturn, and Mars <note>Iron</note>. For I have shown above that all metals, both perfect and imperfect, are contained in the "philosophers' composite" <note>the starting material for the Stone</note> by virtue, power, and a certain likeness, as is also clear from the allegory of Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note>. Therefore, since the **white Elixir** does not go beyond the limits of whiteness and the "fixion" of the Moon <note>Silver</note>, its "paste" or "body" is said to be extracted from white metals that are only slightly "cooked" <note>alchemical "cooking" or decoction refers to the application of heat to mature a substance</note>, namely Saturn and Jupiter; these must then be fermented with the Moon, for the philosophers affirm that whiteness in the work is a sign of "rawness" <note>original: *cruditatis*</note>. Hence, the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note> says: "until whiteness, we do not use a strong fire, because the white is raw and half-cooked." However, a raw metal cannot be perfect. Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova</note> says: "The white work is the work of winter, but the red is the work of summer." The red paste, moreover, is said to be extracted from Venus, Saturn, and Mars, because these metals possess within themselves a redness—either manifest or hidden—to which the composite is led by a greater heat of cooking. However, it is still imperfect, because it has not yet reached the end in which it is completed, nor has it attained the form by which it is perfected, which is the **solar ferment** <note>Gold, used as a "yeast" to finalize the transformation</note>. Nor should it seem strange to anyone if Geber commands that his red paste also be extracted from Saturn, since minium <note>red lead</note>, which is made from its ash, demonstrates that Saturn has a hidden redness within itself. And Zeno says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers"</note>: "This red lead is of our work." But these things are said for those who claim Geber’s authority is false; I suspect he wrote such things more out of a zeal for hiding the truth than for any other reason, as he was accustomed to mixing many falsehoods with a few truths. If anyone thinks the word "extracting" does not admit such an interpretation, let him know that this usage is very common among the teachers of this art. Regor <note>Possibly a corruption of a name like Roger Bacon or a specific authority</note> says: "The sign of the goodness of the first cooking is the extraction of its redness and its conversion into blackness"—not because he wants the redness taken out, but only that it be putrefied and cooked until it becomes black. And in the *Turba*: "In the belly of the appearing blackness is a hidden whiteness; hence it is necessary to extract that whiteness from its blackness." Rosinus <note>Often identified with the Greco-Egyptian alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis</note> says: "When the wise men say, 'Take the spittle of the Moon and the gum and melt them together,' even when they melt, they did not command them to become red, but only that the flowers be extracted from their bellies."

<margin>In perfect metals.</margin>
Therefore, since the matter of the Stone is sought in vain from imperfect metals, it remains that it must be drawn from **perfect metals** <note>Gold and silver</note>. However, if these should communicate their perfection to others, they themselves will remain imperfect, because they cannot "tinge" <note>dye or transform</note> except as far as they can extend themselves. But if we wish to perfect them more than they are in their own nature, it is necessary to [seek] them in their root...

...could be done; however, before I proceed further, I will interject a few small points which will be not only pleasant to know, but also extremely useful to all seekers of the truth. First, however, it occurs to me that the philosophers have said their Stone is "every thing." They did this, as the *Rosarius* <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers," a foundational 16th-century alchemical florilegium</note> says, because it possesses within itself everything it requires and everything necessary for its own perfection. The philosophers testify to this truth everywhere, and especially Senior <note>Senior Zadith ben Hamuel, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose work was translated into Latin</note>. He says: "The Stone of the Wise is perfected in itself and from itself: the root, the branches, the leaves, the flowers, and the fruits." For it is like a tree whose branches, leaves, and fruits come from it, through it, and to it; it is the whole, and the whole is from it. He also says: "The Stone of the Wise, which they have named 'every thing,' has within itself the whole that it needs from the body, from the sun, from the waters, from the spirits, from the souls, and from the tinctures." It is also called by every possible name, as the *Rosarius* says, for the sake of hiding it, and because of the dignity of its nature, and because of its various "regimens" <term>Regimen: the specific stages of heating and governance in the alchemical process</term>, and the marvelous variety of colors appearing during the work, and the participation of all the elements existing within it. Pythagoras says in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among Greek philosophers</note>: "They have called it by many names because of the excellence of its nature." And the *Lilium* <note>likely the *Lilium Alchimiae* or "Lily of Alchemy"</note> states: "Sometimes, in the operation of the Stone, all the colors that exist today in the world or can be imagined appear; thus, according to the different colors appearing in the work, its names are diversified by various philosophers." There is also another reason: because this Stone is perfected from all four elements, it is called by the name of any elemental thing. There is also a third reason: so that the foolish might not recognize it.

<margin>Five reasons why it is called by every name.</margin>

<margin>Comparison of the nature of the Stone with the nature of man.</margin>

Furthermore, the philosophers call their Stone animal, vegetable, and mineral. This is not because it can be made indifferently from animals, vegetables, or minerals, as many people believe, wasting their money and labor on such things in vain. Rather, it is called "animal" because of the soul, which properly belongs to man, the most noble of animals (if indeed it is right to count man among the animals); although a soul is attributed by these philosophers to minerals as well as vegetables, it is not in the same sense. Bonellus says in the *Turba*: "Our copper, like a man, has a body and a soul." It is also called animal because of the "blood," which properly belongs to animals, and without which they die. Hence the *Lilium* says: "The spirit converts the body into a tinctured spirit, just as blood is; for that which has spirit also has blood." And Dardaris says in the *Turba*: "In the whole regimen, one must use nothing but permanent water <term>Permanent Water: a symbolic term for the universal solvent or 'mercury of the philosophers' that does not wet the hands</term>, for its power is spiritual blood." Morienes says: "That which best joins bodies together is blood, for it vivifies and unites them, and makes one body out of them all." Aristotle says: "Blood is the soul, and the soul is life, and life is our stone." This is not because there is truly a spirit, soul, or blood in it such as there is in a man, but by a certain non-inelegant likeness. For just as a man is said to be dead by the separation of the soul from the body, and his corpse remains like a statue...

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s explanation of how the alchemical "Stone" mirrors the biological and spiritual processes of life, death, and resurrection. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the Stone’s self-sufficiency.</meta>

Theobald de Hoghelande

...is more like [a corpse] than a man: so too in the Stone, once its better and radical essence has been separated—which gives form and "tincture" <term>Tincture: the transformative essence or "color" that allows the Stone to transmute metals</term> to the Stone, and which is the "soul" of the philosophers—there will remain a certain formless matter. As far as metallic form is concerned, this matter has no proper name because it is no longer within the care of nature, as Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "Every body, when it lacks a soul, will be dark and obscure." And just as we believe that in the resurrection the soul will be restored to the body, and that bodies thereafter will be eternal and incorruptible: so in this art, after the body has been de-animated and purged by fire and water through the proper "regimen" <term>Regimen: the controlled sequence of heating and chemical stages</term>, its soul—that is, the tincture, extracted not from elsewhere but from its own body—is returned to it. Only then does it take on a metallic color and form, but one far more illustrious than it had before. I shall prove that what I have said is true by the common consensus of the wise, producing their own opinions.

Hermes says in the *Allegory of Wisdom*: "The spirit extracted from the stone is white, but the soul is red; when these are returned to it, it lives and rejoices, because it is adorned with its original beauty and light. It is then most joyful when it has risen again, because it dies no longer." Zion says in the *Turba* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "The tincture of the Stone is the life of those things into which it enters, and it is the loss and death of those from which it is extracted." Bonellus says in the same work: "That nature from which moisture has been taken away, when it is left through the nights, appears like something dead; and then that nature needs fire, until the body and its spirit are turned into earth, and then it becomes dust like a dead man in his tomb. Once these things are completed, God will restore its spirit and soul, and with all weakness removed, that thing is strengthened, and after its corruption it is improved, just as a man after the resurrection becomes stronger and younger than he had been in this world." Rosinus says: "When the spirit and soul are extracted from the body, the body remains dead; return its soul to it, and then it lives; and know that the resurrected dead shall be eternal."

<margin>To the Bishop of Sarzana.</margin>

->On the Difficulties of Alchemy<-

...because of the respiration of air. Hence Bonellus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical dialogue</note>: "The breathing of humans is from the air, which for them is life itself after God; similarly, copper is inspired by moisture, by which it takes up life and is multiplied and increased like all other things." And this much indeed concerns the **animal stone** <term>Animal stone: an alchemical substance described as having the properties of a living, breathing creature</term>.

<margin>Why it is called the vegetable stone.</margin>
Indeed, they called it **vegetable** by its similarity to the vegetative soul, which is nonetheless common to all animals. This is described as a certain power in living things that converts nourishment into the substance of the being nourished, so that it may preserve its existence, bring it to its proper size, and allow it to generate another like itself in its own species. Therefore, since these three powers—namely the **nutritive**, the **augmentative**, and the **generative**—are found in the Stone (though not in exactly the same way as in plants), they called it "vegetable" for no absurd reason.

<margin>Four nourishing faculties in the stone.</margin>
Furthermore, just as the power of nourishing requires four other subservient faculties to perform its duty—namely the **Attractive**, the **Retentive**, the **Digestive**, and the **Expulsive**—the same are considered within the alchemical Work. Through the **Attractive**, the substance of the Stone draws from Mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*</note> that which it needs for the craft and which is familiar to its nature; it does this through an elemental virtue that desires to fill a vacuum. Through the **Retentive**, it holds the substance for "coction" <term>Coction: the alchemical process of "cooking" or maturing a substance through steady heat</term> by reason of the vacuum's longing. Through the **Digestive**, it transforms what is retained into the likeness of its own substance, just as it changes quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> into the substance of coagulating sulfur. Through the **Expulsive**, nature casts out what does not suit it; for as someone says in the *Assembly*, water does not add more weight to a body than the metallic humidity it contains, because the humidity of the water passes away while the metallic humidity remains.

Lest anyone think these are my own inventions, let them see the *Codicil* of Raymond Lully <note>A 13th-century polymath and mystic to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> and his *Testament*, chapter 32. Moreover, that the Stone grows and can generate its like—though it is not necessary to prove this, since it is the very goal and purpose of the entire chemical study—I will nonetheless propose some sayings of the philosophers on this matter. First, Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, who speaks thus in his book on the chemical art: "It is decreed among those most skilled in philosophy that the Stone can 'tincture' <term>Tincture: to transform or dye a base metal into gold or silver</term> innumerable parts. Every spirit is capable of being multiplied, but no body; and since our Stone has been made most volatile, and so to speak spiritual, and entirely fiery, and has been frequently repeated through manifold solutions and coagulations, why would you not believe the Stone can tincture innumerable parts? This is clear if you would sniff out the reason of nature and its wonderful gifts with keen judgment <note>original: *emunctis naribus*, literally "with wiped nostrils," an idiom for discernment</note>. For the more you dissolve the 'Sun' <term>Sun: in alchemy, this refers to gold or the perfected male principle</term> and coagulate it again, the more you will be able to tincture. Likewise, the more wives a man takes, the more offspring he will have." The author of the *Treasury of Philosophers* also says: "The water of the wise is like a grain of wheat: for it is nourished and putrefies, and is corrupted, then it germinates, rises again, and multiplies itself."

<margin>The Rising Dawn.</margin> <note>original: *Aurora consurgens*, a famous medieval alchemical text often attributed to Thomas Aquinas</note>
And another: "The philosophers wish to nourish their metallic grain until it grows and brings forth fruit of its own kind." Also the author of the *Dialogue between Nature and the Son of Philosophy*: "The Stone, or the medicine, which..."

He cites major authorities like Lully and Ficino to prove the Stone's ability to multiply its transformative power through repeated chemical cycles.</summary>
