<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s explanation of how the alchemical "Stone" mimics the functions of living organisms. He specifically transitions from the internal mechanisms of nourishment (begun on the previous page) to why the Stone is categorized by the three kingdoms of nature: mineral, vegetable, and animal.</meta>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...that which you seek sprouts and is multiplied, just like a grain of wheat falling into good earth, which, when it has died, brings forth much fruit: therefore, when it is corrupted <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breakdown of a substance's form so a new, higher form can emerge.</note>, you will be able to produce many other grains from it.

<margin>Why it is called the mineral stone.</margin>
The stone is called **mineral** because its matter, or the things from which it is composed and constituted, are mineral and metallic; they cannot come from anywhere else if metals are to be truly transmuted.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
If anyone alleges that, by the same reasoning, the stone could be called "vegetable" or "animal" because its origin might be from plants or animals;

<margin>Solution.</margin>
I respond that there is no underlying reason for this—on the contrary, it is plainly repugnant to nature—for metals to be found in animals or vegetables, since their principles are plainly different and can in no way be mixed together so as to persist in the fire. For the Philosophers, it is enough that there is some similarity (even if not fitting in all respects) to attribute a name to their stone. Nor should anyone flatter himself simply because the fluidity of **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> is halted by the juices of certain herbs, or because a color different from the natural one is sometimes induced in that coagulated mercury and in imperfect metals by things originating from animals or vegetables. Such things act only externally and do not penetrate deeply, nor do they induce a metallic form unless it be a corrupt one; they can never give the true form of gold and silver. But the Sages themselves will be my witnesses that the reasons I have brought forward—as to why the stone is called animal, vegetable, and mineral—are the true ones. 

For **Rosinus** <note>original: *Rosinus*, an Arabic alchemical author known in the West as Zosimos</note> says: "Take this **animal stone**, that is, one having a soul within itself, namely a mercurial soul, sensing the presence and influence of its **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: here referring to the primitive, "raw" material of the stone</term>, its magnet, and its **calamine** <note>zinc ore</note>, and reaching its peak through local motion, by following and fleeing." The author of the *New Light* <note>original: *Novum Lumen*, likely referring to the works of Sendivogius</note> also says: "It shows certain virtues of the soul; it moves and is moved, it acts and suffers <note>original: *agit & patitur*; in medieval philosophy, 'to suffer' means to be acted upon by an external force</note>." Rosinus continues: "It is called **vegetable**, that is, communicating its power implanted by nature to its own kind, multiplying the virtue of its influence just as a root does to a trunk or to herbs."

<margin>Chapter 11.</margin>
It is called **mineral** because it is extracted from a mine. The author of the *Universal Way* says: "The philosophers named it the vegetable stone because it is vegetated <note>empowered with life-force</note> and grows. Animal, because it has a body, soul, and spirit, like animals."

<margin>The Book on the Nature of the Sun and Moon.</margin>
It is called **mineral**, because the things from which it is composed are mineral in their nature. **Michael Scot** <note>A 13th-century mathematician and scholar</note> says: "The stone is called mineral because it is made from minerals alone; vegetable because it is nourished and increased, which are the powers of vegetation; animal because it is refreshed by scent and corrupted by stench"—though this last part must not be understood according to the literal sound of the words.

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
The author of the *New Light* says: "This is the stone which is found on the summit of mountains and is deservedly called mineral. It is also said to be animal because it has a soul, and it is also called vegetable because it is vegetated."

<margin>The Philosophers must be believed.</margin>
Therefore, learned men and followers of alchemy need not seek other reasons; let them believe the Sages and their Masters, if only they desire to be their disciples.

He warns against using plant or animal extracts, which only produce superficial changes rather than true metallic transmutation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s argument regarding the composition of the Philosophers' Stone. # BOOK ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

...they desire. Nor should they fear that an **Elixir** <note>In alchemy, an elixir is a substance capable of transmuting metals or healing the body; Hoghelande argues here that mineral-based ones are safer and more effective than those derived from plants.</note> composed from minerals is less conducive to health than that which they seek in vegetables and minerals, since all philosophers and physicians alike have always commended the excellent endowments and virtues of gold.

<margin>The Elixir is nothing but spiritual gold.</margin>
Moreover, the **Elixir**, or the **Philosophers' Stone** of which we speak, is nothing but gold, yet it is a thousand times more perfect than common gold. If gold were not its basis, the study of alchemy would be in vain, since the principle of gold-making must necessarily proceed from gold, just as the principle of fire-making proceeds from fire; for it could not transmute imperfect metals into gold unless it were gold itself; for <note>original: "simile enim à suo simili generatur"</note> *like is generated by its like*. I do not deny that certain elixirs can be made from honey, wine, and similar things taken from both animals and vegetables for the preservation and sometimes even the healing of human bodies; but these have nothing to do with our **Elixir** of which we treat, to which they can in no way be compared. Indeed, in the context of metallic metamorphosis <note>The transformation of one metal into another.</note>, they are to be renounced and rejected as useless. If the Philosophers sometimes say that their stone receives help from other things, and they name foreign things alien to the nature of metal, they usually do so with a certain addition—namely, that some things are more "closely related" than others. And this is one of the most common <term>sophistries</term> <note>Deceptive arguments used by alchemical authors to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note> of the wise in this art. For this reason, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> wished for the apprentice of philosophy to be a person of profound reason.

Furthermore, some believe the stone is called "mineral, animal, and vegetable" by the philosophers because it does not only lead human and metallic bodies to health and a true temperament <note>The balanced state of the four humors or qualities.</note>, exercising its force and power upon them, but also acts upon vegetables. As **Lull** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a major figure to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says, it rectifies all plants in the springtime through its great heat. For if a quantity the size of a millet seed were dissolved in water and placed around the trunk of a vine, or in the heart of a tree, flowers and leaves would be produced by artifice and would bear fruit in the month of May. Although this reasoning is not inappropriate, the authority of the philosophers will always have greater weight with me, especially since something more of energy and hidden doctrine may be detected in it than can be perceived by just anyone.

Now let us examine why they said their stone is found in every thing and in every place. I have shown above, from various sayings of the wise, that the **Philosophers' Stone** consists of **Mercury** and **Sulfur**, or <term>Water and Earth</term> <note>In this context, these are the two primary elemental principles of all matter, not common water and dirt.</note>, which elements are most conspicuous in the stone; indeed, I have demonstrated that both are called the "stone." Since, therefore, there is no corporeal thing that does not consist of water and earth, and no place is void of the moist or the dry, they rightly affirm that their stone is findable everywhere. **Hermes** says: "Our Art stands in need of two natures: namely, the Moist and the Dry." And in the *Allegories of the Wise*: "The two stones of the Wise are found on the banks, and on the peaks of mountains, and in the bellies of rivers, and in the walls of royal houses; they are even found cast out in dung."

<margin>Treatise.</margin>
<margin>Practical Testament, penultimate chapter.</margin>
<margin>Why the stone is said to be found in every thing and everywhere.</margin>

He explains that the Stone is called "vegetable" or "universal" not because it is made of plants, but because its power can accelerate plant growth and its constituent elements (Water and Earth) are present in all things.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s explanation of the material of the Stone. Having established that the work is based on gold, he now addresses the common alchemical riddle of why the Stone is said to be "found everywhere" and in "vile things."</meta>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...to seek <note>original: "quærere"</note> by which words it is certain that nothing else is understood than water and earth, or the moist and the dry. But because the spirit or water predominates in the work—since with it, from it, and through it the entire **magistery** <note>The "magistery" refers to the entire process of the Great Work or the mastery of alchemical transformation.</note> is accomplished—the teachers of this science have said that this is found everywhere. Hence **Hermes** says: "The secret of any thing and life is in one water, and this water is capable of receiving nourishment, in humans and in others, and in water is the greatest secret: for water is that which becomes grain in wheat, oil in the olive, and in certain trees various gums and fruits; and the principle of human generation is water." **Hamuel**, in the *Senior* <note>Referring to the "Senior Zadith," a common authority in medieval alchemy.</note>, says: "There is no thing in the world more known than the Stone; everyone and every man needs it, and it is with him; he cannot even be without it." The philosopher intends, through all that he says, water; for water is found in every place, in valleys, in mountains, and with both the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak. And **Alphidius** says: When he says, "Our Stone <margin>*In the Clavis Philosophica*</margin> is from a vile thing, lacking price in the eyes of men, despised, which men trample underfoot in the streets and from which they move away," what else should he understand but water? The author of the *Confession of the Marriage of the Mass of the Sun and Moon* <note>Referring to the union of Gold (Sun) and Silver (Moon).</note> says: "The Stone is called vile because it is of no price in the eyes of the ignorant, yet it is most dear, because nature does not work without it—namely, without the moist—for the **Philosophers' Stone** is aqueous and moist, and moisture is most vile." And **Rupescissa**: "The nature or matter of the Stone <margin>*The Book of Light*</margin> is a thing of vile price found everywhere, because it is a **viscous water** <note>original: "aqua viscosa"</note>." Others have looked not at water alone, but at all the elements, which <margin>*To Thomas of Bologna*</margin> are in all things. Hence **Count Bernard**: "When the Philosophers say that the Stone is made from every thing, they understand it to be made from the four elements, from which every generable and corruptible thing is made." And the *Rosarius*: "It is found everywhere because of the participation of the elements." **Rosinus**: "As man is composed of four elements, so also is the Stone; therefore the Stone is in man." Some wish for the **radical moisture** <note>The <term>radical moisture</term> (humor radicalis) was believed to be the essential, life-sustaining fluid found in all living beings that acts as the fuel for natural heat.</note> to be understood by such sayings, or the heat innate to all things: for any thing in the world, that is, every elemented body, has in itself a radical or formal heat by cause of which it persists, and there is no thing so cold that it is not cherished under the heat included in itself as if in a root. Some prefer to interpret these things figuratively, among whom is **Marsilio Ficino**, but more, as I believe, from a desire to show off his wit or to veil the truth than because they actually feel so; as when it is said the Stone is everywhere, it is understood to be in all the glass, in all things, that is, in all metals, which are their things, <margin>*In the Emerald Tablet*</margin> according to that saying of **Hermes**: "All things are born from one thing"; where **St. Thomas** and **Hortulanus** interpret "things" as "metals"; "In all time," namely of its work; "In every man" of his own **complexion** <note>The physical and mental constitution of a person, determined by the balance of their humors.</note>. **Lullius** in a certain place wished nature to be considered, so that namely the Stone might be found in every thing in which it is made by nature, for it is foolish...

<summary>Hoghelande explores the alchemical paradox that the Philosophers' Stone is "found everywhere" and is "vile," explaining it as a reference to the universal presence of water, the four elements, or radical moisture.</summary>
<keywords>water, elements, radical moisture, vile thing, Hermes, Hamuel, Alphidius, Rupescissa, Bernard Trevisanus, Marsilio Ficino, Emerald Tablet, magistery</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s investigation into the universal nature of the alchemical "Stone" and transitions into the second great hurdle of alchemy: the "regimen" or the specific method of preparation. # BOOK ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

<margin>On the intention.</margin>
...to seek <note>original: "quærere"</note> something that is not in the thing. And another says: The **Philosophers' Stone** <term>The legendary substance sought by alchemists, capable of perfecting base metals and the human body.</term> is in all things in which it is nourished. And **Senior** <note>Refers to the author Senior Zadith, often identified with the 10th-century alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail.</note> says: They have said this
<margin>Alchemy, ch. 3.</margin>
stone is in every thing, and this is from the clever riddles <note>original: "sophismatibus"</note> of the wise. However, it is certain that it occurs in every thing that possesses a capacity for preparation. **Lull** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> also says elsewhere that the stone is found in every place
<margin>Testament, ch. 37.</margin>
by reason of its properties. Though these things are true, nevertheless the intention of the philosophers is focused on nothing other than the elements, and especially water, as I have said.

<margin>Knowledge of the regime is necessary, but most difficult.</margin>
Having enumerated the difficulties arising regarding the knowledge of the true matter, which is the key to the entire art, let us proceed to its preparation, and consider whether the Wise are any clearer on this subject. For it profits nothing to know what the Stone consists of, unless its preparation is likewise known, which **Senior**
<margin>Book of Figures and Images.</margin>
called the most difficult of all things. And **Baccen** in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts.</note> says its regime is greater than can be comprehended by reason. **Mandinus** says in the same place: Ignorance
<margin>In the Key of Wisdom.</margin>
of the regime has caused many to go astray. **Senior** says: Many know our stone, but they do not know its power; yet if they knew the power, what would it be worth unless they knew the operation? However, they cannot know
<margin>Testament, ch. 29.</margin>
the operation except through the gift of God, or through the instruction of a Master who might teach it. And **Lull** says: Nothing in this science is secret, except the manner of the work and working. We shall find that Lull spoke the truth if we more diligently examine the individual methods of preparation and the variety of authors. For
<margin>The variety of authors breeds difficulty.</margin>
some have described the regime of the stone so succinctly that they seem to have handed down mere enigmas. Thus speak **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note> and the Author of the *Perfect Magistery*: The perfect preparation of bodies and spirits is through the removal of the superfluous and the addition of what is absent. **Morienes**: The work is nothing else than the extraction of water from the earth, and the returning <note>original: "remissio"</note> of that same water upon it. **Lull** describes different modes of operation throughout his works, for in one place he says: Two operations are
<margin>Testament, ch. 33.</margin>
necessary for you: corruption, which occurs under the preservation of its form, and generation. Elsewhere he says: Thinning <note>original: "rarefactio"</note> and thickening <note>original: "condensatio"</note> is the original path
<margin>Testament, ch. 26.</margin>
in the transformation of the elements, through their various degrees. The same author: From the coarse make the simple, from the heavy make the light, soften the
<margin>Ibid. ch. 24.</margin>
rough, make the hard soft, the bitter sweet, and you shall have the magistery. The *Rosary*: Kill the living, and bring the dead back to life. Another: Dissolve, coagulate, and color. And **Emiganus** in the *Turba*: The definition of the art is
<margin>The Golden Work.</margin>
the liquefaction of the body, the separation of the soul from the body, and the joining of the soul to the purified body. **Haly**: The greater art is accomplished through four magisteries: Dissolving, coagulating, whitening, and reddening. **Philotis** in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba"</note> says: The whole magistery is that the higher becomes the lower, and the
<margin>Alchemy, ch. 1.</margin>
lower the higher. A certain other author commands one to divide, cleanse, and gather together. Some have described the regimes of the stone more diffusely, but not more clearly. For **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova, a renowned 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> and **Lull** and certain others assign four modes
<margin>Efferarius the Monk.</margin>
of operation: Dissolving, washing, congealing, and fixing.

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

The author of the *Counsel on the Marriage of the Sun and Moon* <note>original: "Consil. conjug. Solis & Lunae"</note> wishes the material to be calcined, dissolved, coagulated, then calcined again, and waxed <term>Inceration: the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency by adding liquid.</term>. The author of the *Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "perfecti magist."</note> says it should be calcined, dissolved, distilled, and coagulated with a gentle fire. **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Italian humanist and philosopher (1433–1499) who integrated alchemy into his Neoplatonic world view.</note> first composes, putrefies the compound, dissolves what has been putrefied, divides the dissolved, cleanses the divided, unites the cleansed, and thus completes the work. The author of the *Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scalae P."</note> and **Ripley the Englishman** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a highly influential English alchemist and author of the *Twelve Gates*.</note> hand down twelve modes of operation: **Calcination**, **solution**, **separation**, **conjunction**, **putrefaction**, **congelation**, **cibation** <term>Cibation: "feeding" the material with liquid to maintain its required moisture.</term>, **sublimation**, **fermentation**, **exaltation**, **multiplication**, and <margin>The Sum of Perfection, ch. 38.</margin> **projection**. **Geber** and **Arnaldus** in the *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "flore fl."</note> name eight: sublimation, descension, distillation, calcination, solution, coagulation, fixation, and creation. **Haly** <note>Likely referring to the 11th-century Arabic author Haly Abenragel.</note> says: All operations <margin>Book of the Secrets of Alchemy, ch. 13.</margin> of this art are contained within six things, which are: to put to flight <note>meaning to volatilize</note>, to pour, to wax, to whiten, to dissolve, and to coagulate. **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemical source.</note> teaches seven arrangements, namely: sublimation, calcination, solution, <margin>In the Key of Wisdom.</margin> ablution <note>washing or purification</note>, ceration <note>waxing</note>, coagulation, and fixation. **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the preeminent Persian philosopher-physician.</note> names just as many, but not in the same order: sublimation, solution, putrefaction, ablution, coagulation, calcination, and fixation. Others name still other processes, all of which there is no need to collect in this place. Since, therefore, the authors vary so greatly, and it is necessary that <margin>The diversity confuses the minds of readers.</margin> the minds of readers be distracted by such a multitude of works, who can trust that they will ever see light in such thick darkness? Does not such diversity necessarily give birth to difficulty, when one calls **solution** the first step of the work, another calls it **calcination**, and a third says **sublimation**, and so on for the rest? For if the first order varies, the remaining steps must necessarily vary as well. But if they were at least in agreement regarding these same "regimens" <term>Regimen: a specific stage or systematic method of treatment in the alchemical transformation.</term>, but they are not even that, since individuals define them as they please. For **calcination** is said to be the pulverization of a thing through fire by the removal of its humidity which consolidates the parts; yet some teach how to calcine their bodies not with fire, but with water <margin>In the *Apertorium*.</margin>, among whom is **Lull**. For thus he says: The calcination of the earth is not done by fire, as the **Sophists** <note>In this context, deceptive or false alchemists who take instructions literally.</note> believe, but through its own proper spirit. It has already been said above that by the name "spirit" in this art, nothing other than water is indicated. But what could be more different, while one commands the body to be deprived of humidity, and the other orders water to be added? The same must be judged regarding **solution**, which is defined as the reduction of a dry thing into water; this cannot happen except through the union of the solvent and the thing being dissolved, so that, for instance, the body becomes spirit and the spirit becomes body. Nevertheless, <margin>The Rosary, part 1, ch. 1.</margin> **Arnaldus**, asserting the contrary, says that to "dissolve" is to divide bodies, which is nothing other than to separate the parts of a compound and to make two or more out of one. By the same reasoning, **sublimation**—which is defined by **Geber** and others as the elevation of a dry thing with adherence <margin>Book of the Flower of Flowers.</margin> to its vessel, and by **Avicenna** as the elevation of the most subtle parts from the fixed parts—others affirm to be nothing but the refinement of the coarse <note>The OCR reads "glossae," likely a typo for "grossae" (coarse/thick material).</note> matter—

<summary>Hoghelande catalogs the conflicting alchemical procedures prescribed by famous authorities like Geber, Ripley, and Avicenna. He highlights how even fundamental terms like "calcination" and "solution" are defined in completely opposite ways, leading to immense confusion for practitioners.</summary>

<page-num>175</page-num>
<header>On the Difficulties of Alchemy, Book [1]</header>

...and that the whole work of the philosophers is completed by a single sublimation. For so says **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note>: Our water sublimes bodies not by common sublimation <note>original: "sublimatione vulgari"</note>, as the dreamers understand it—believing that to "sublime" is to ascend higher or to be raised by fire—but for the philosophers, to sublime is to refine, to cleanse, and to purify. They disagree most greatly in the remaining modes of operation in the same way; if I wished to examine them more diligently, I would become too long-winded. I will add only this: since it is clear from the above that many "regimens" of the work are described, some practitioners, having rejected such variety entirely, desire only a single decoction <term>Decoction: A process of heating a substance in a fluid, similar to boiling down a broth, often meant to represent the slow "cooking" of metals in the earth.</term>, after the likeness of nature in the places of mines, or like a fetus in the womb. As the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note> says: "Although the philosophers often say, 'put it in its vessel and close it firmly,' it is nevertheless enough to put it in and close it once, until the whole mastery is fulfilled; anything more than this is from evil."

<margin>The *Testament*, chapter 14.</margin>
**Lull** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), or more likely a later author writing under his name.</note>, however, requires three gradual transformations, or rather "digestions," after the likeness of those which happen in the human body: the first of which is in the stomach, the second in the liver, and the third in the veins and limbs. Such a great diversity of authors cannot fail to pour the greatest darkness over the eyes of those working and studying.

<margin>The knowledge of weights is most difficult and especially necessary.</margin>
But let us move on to the weights, and first let us hear from the masters themselves how much it matters to know them; for however well the material has been prepared and well mixed, unless the quantities of the things are just and according to reason, the craftsman labors in vain. The author of the *Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "perfecti magist."</note> says: "Beware lest you approach the compounding before you find the complete weights of the things to be compounded."

<margin>The *Rosary*, part 2, chapter 24.</margin>
The author of the *Dialogue of Nature and the Son of Philosophy* says: "Due proportion is the key to all secrets." **Arnaldus** says: "All things exist under a defined limit and certain disposition. Therefore, for every weight a weight is needed, and for every measure a measure." **Haly**: "If the quantity of weights is unsuitable in the compound, with the parts of its nature transcending through increase or decrease, the specific property of the compound is destroyed with it, and its effect becomes empty and void." **Chambar** in the *Assembly* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic sources.</note> says: "If you compose without weight, delay occurs, and it will be thought an evil thing." **Rhazes** <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925), an influential Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says: "He who is ignorant of weights should not labor in our books, for the philosophers have set down nothing of their affairs, nor hidden anything else but this." Those who are experienced in the books of the philosophers will find that **Rhazes** spoke the truth; for they depart into such diverse paths that it is shameful to report—and even if it were not shameful, I would not be able to do so. Yet if they named only a single weight for the solvent and the solute, we could certainly reach it by some guess; if not at the first attempt, then at least after several turns, by placing so many various parts in glass vessels until, by the favor of divine grace, we attained it. This is especially true since it seems to matter very little whether a little more water is added or not; for one must think that if a little more water is added, the body is dissolved faster but coagulates slower, but if less is added, it is dissolved slower, but coagulates faster, so [that...]

<meta>Catchword: ut (that)</meta>

<summary>Hoghelande discusses the internal contradictions of alchemical authorities regarding whether the "Work" requires one simple process or many complex stages, before identifying the secret of weights (proportions) as the most difficult and intentionally hidden aspect of the art.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande's critique of alchemical literature, moving from the confusion over the number of "regimens" or stages to the wild inconsistencies in "weights" (proportions of ingredients) and the absolute necessity of the correct vessel.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>
<header>THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE</header>

...so that all things fall back into one; nor do the philosophers seem to exceed the twelfth part in this regard. 
<margin>Variety of the Wise regarding weights. *Book of Furnaces*, chapter 19.</margin>
For **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Islamic and Western alchemy.</note> and **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1433–1499) who also wrote on medicine and alchemy.</note> take twelve parts of water; **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist who allegedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Stone.</note> takes ten; **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arab alchemist whose works were highly influential in the West.</note> takes nine, according to the number of the nine eagles. Hence some say: "Between nine and twelve, you cannot go wrong." But the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> asserts that three parts of water and one of the "body" <note>The "body" usually refers to the solid metal or base material being transformed.</note> should be taken. Others say more or less: some command the water to be poured over so that it rises three fingers above the material.
<margin>*On the Chemical Art*, chapter 19.</margin>
But even if someone has attained that first "weight" <term>Weight: In alchemy, this refers to the specific proportions or ratios of ingredients (earth, water, etc.) rather than just physical mass.</term> which is sought in the dissolution of the body, I do not see what is to be expected of the remaining weights, which are required in the composition of the purified elements and the addition of the tincture <term>Tincture: A potent substance or "elixir" capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver by "staining" them with its properties.</term>; for in these, a much greater variety is seen. For the authors do not stop at twelve parts of water or earth, but ascend to fifty and more. For **Arnaldus** says 
<margin>*The Rosary*, part 2, chapter 15.</margin>
to pour in water by turns while grinding, until the earth itself has drunk a fiftieth part of its own water. Others take less water and more earth; others, on the contrary, assert that more water and less earth should be taken, so that one is unable to extricate oneself from so many and such great meanderings—especially if one considers the operations of Nature, whose secrets in the combination of sulfur and quicksilver (mercury) cannot be 
<margin>Philosophers confound the weights of the first, second, and third regimen.</margin>
investigated or known by us through any inquiry. To this is added another difficulty: that when the philosophers prescribe weights, they do not distinguish whether they want them taken in the first, second, third, or fourth work. Instead, confounding everything, speaking now of the solution of the body, now of the conjunction of the elements, and sometimes indeed of both at once, they mix up the proper proportions of the parts. But if they only said that water and earth (which can be touched and seen) were to be weighed, it would be one thing; but since they want even air and fire to be balanced, I cannot help but judge the proportion of weights to be most difficult, and I must lament the failed labors and errors of so many craftsmen.

<margin>How necessary the knowledge of the vessel is.</margin>
It is next that we treat the vessel in which the "mastery" <note>original: "magisterium," the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is made. Knowledge of this is most necessary, as it is like the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> in animals, in which they are generated and receive both growth and nourishment; for neither the matter, nor its preparation, nor knowledge of weights will help the craftsman unless he has a suitable vessel in which to perfect the operations of art and nature. For "place" is the principle of generation, and the place generates that which is placed within it. Nor does it matter, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath credited with many alchemical works.</note> says, whether something is done in artificial vessels or in natural ones; for in both, elemental and celestial virtues operate, provided the artificial ones are shaped after the manner 
<margin>In the preface to the *Secrets of Alchemy*.</margin>
of the natural ones. Whence **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer/alchemist.</note> says: "Unless the matter of the mastery finds a vessel suitable for itself, the whole work is destroyed, and its practitioners do not find what they seek; nor does the thing itself come forth into the effect of generation, because when it has not found the cause or root of its generation, even the heat itself happens upon the destruction of the operation." And **Morienes** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught the secrets of alchemy to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "If the ancient wise men, and those who came after them, had not provided their explanations concerning the quality..."

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s discussion of the practical difficulties in alchemy. Having previously discussed the confusion over proportions and weights, he now addresses the intense controversy regarding the "Philosophical Vessel"—the container in which the Great Work is performed.</meta>

<page-num>177</page-num>
<header>ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY, BOOK I</header>
<sig>M</sig>

...if they had not discovered the [utility] of the vessel in which the mastery <term>Mastery: original "magisterium," referring to the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosophers' Stone.</term> is prepared, no one would ever have reached its perfection. However, since the authorities claim this vessel is unique and "singular," the discovery of it poses no small hindrance to seekers. It does not even seem likely that such diverse regimens of the art—namely sublimation, calcination, distillation, solution, inceration <note>The process of softening a substance until it has a waxy consistency.</note>, and the like—could be carried out in a single vessel. Either, therefore, there cannot be just one vessel, or all these preparations of the matter must be rightly judged as nothing but mere fictions and verbal riddles—unless, perhaps, one understands the "vessel" to be the "Water of the Philosophers," which is sometimes taken to mean the container itself. 

Hence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundations of alchemy are attributed.</note> says: "The vessel of the philosophers is <margin>The Water of the Philosophers is their vessel. *Book of the Flower of Flowers*.</margin> their water." And **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: "The Stone, as the philosophers say, is made in one vessel, and they speak the truth; for our entire mastery is made with our water, and from it: for the water itself dissolves the bodies, calcinates them, reduces them to earth, whitens, and cleanses them." Likewise, another author says: "In our water, all modes of operations are performed—namely sublimation, distillation, solution, calcination, and fixation—and they are done in said water as if in an artificial vessel." Likewise, **Sulphur** is named the "vessel of nature" by **Lull** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> in a certain place. 

Yet, although they say all operations can be done with "water," that water itself must necessarily be contained in some physical vessel, regarding which the wise disagree greatly. For different vessels are prescribed by different authors: one prescribes glass with a long and narrow neck and a round belly; <margin>Diversity of the Wise in describing the vessel of the work.</margin> another a cucurbit <note>The lower, gourd-shaped part of a still.</note> with an alembic <note>The cap or "head" of a still used for distilling.</note>; a third, a vessel with two pipes; some a vessel-on-vessel; others prescribe an aludel <note>A series of pear-shaped pots used as condensers in the process of sublimation.</note> or a "sublimatory," and infinite other types. Many require not just one vessel for the whole work, but different ones for each individual stage, so that such a great diversity is an index of the maximum difficulty. 

To this must be added the various forms of vessels named for their similarity to either the material or the operation itself. Thus **Haly** <note>Likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince associated with alchemy.</note> calls the vessel an "egg." He says: "Take the egg, and strike it with a fiery sword," for the egg is its enclosure. Some also call it a "sieve-maker’s tool" or a "sieve," because in it the parts are divided and cleansed, and in it the mastery is perfected. **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arab alchemist.</note> says: "Sift it with a sieve and a thread," that is, with a cucurbit and an alembic. And **Mireris**: "It must be sifted seven times with its own sieve." Some have named their vessel "marble," because in it the matter of the philosophers is ground. 

It is also called a "sepulcher" <note>A tomb or burial place.</note>. Hence in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba" (Turba Philosophorum).</note>: "Let a tomb be dug for that dragon, and let the woman be buried there with him." All of this is done for the purpose of concealment, and it is not likely that the philosophers have described it anywhere in open words, as witnessed by **Maria** <note>Maria the Jewess, an early alchemical philosopher (c. 1st–3rd century AD) credited with inventing several types of chemical apparatus.</note>, who speaks in this manner: "The philosophers teach everything except the Vessel of Hermes, because that is divine, and hidden from the nations by the wisdom of the Lord: and those who are ignorant of it do not know the regimen of truth, on account of their ignorance of the Vessel of Hermes." **Senior**, the author of the *Lily*, says that the vision of it is to be sought more than the written description of it. Nor does the difficulty arise only from the <margin>Difficulty in the size of the vessel.</margin> shape of the vessel, but also from its quantity—namely, so that it is neither too large nor too small.

<margin>On the sealing.</margin> [The vessel should not be larger] than is right. For if it is too large, the vapors of the stone or the subtle spirits will be too greatly dispersed and will not return to their body. But if it is too small, the revolution of the elements of the stone cannot be completed, and its "seed" will be suffocated. For just as the revolution of the elements occurs through the movement of the firmament—by which subtle bodies strive to ascend higher, while that which is heavy remains below—so too do the philosophers assert it happens in the work of skilled chemists. Likewise, no small difficulty lies in the sealing of the vessel: for within it are the most subtle spirits which, if they are not detained, will cause the <term>mastery: original "magisterium," the successful completion of the Great Work</term> to perish. Hence the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says: "Keep the vessel and its fastening secure, so that it may be powerful in preserving the spirits." Certainly, if there were only a single, continuous, and linear decoction <note>A process of boiling or heating.</note> in the work, a long vessel would seem sufficient, whose neck could be narrowed and sealed with a glowing hot iron. But since they command us to sublimate, distill, and calcinate, I find no reason how the airy vapors can be contained in the vessel—no matter how the clay or glues are prepared—unless the vessel must be broken after each operation. Yet the wise sufficiently imply this is not necessary when they say the entire mastery is perfected in a single vessel.

<margin>Knowledge of fire is necessary. *Secrets of Alchemy*, chapter 8.</margin> Let us proceed further to the fire, without the knowledge of which every operation of the craftsmen is invalid; for the success or failure of this matter arises from the suitability of the fire, as **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer and alchemist.</note> says. And **Plato** says: Fire adds benefit to the perfect and harm—or corruption—to the corrupt. Hence, when its quantity is good and suitable, it will bring perfection; but when it increases beyond measure in things, it will ruin both the perfect and the corrupt. And **Alphidius** <note>An early, possibly mythical, Arabic alchemical authority.</note> says: The agent in this whole world is one, namely heat; for without heat, there is no motion or action, since heat is the root of the disposition itself. **Morienes** <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: The greatest efficacy of this work is weighed in its fire, for with it the minerals are prepared and the souls are retained in their bodies; fire is also its entire nature and its perfect trial. And: if you know how to give the fire, water and fire are sufficient for you. **Maria** <note>Mary the Jewess, an early alchemical figure credited with inventing the water bath (*balneum Mariae*).</note> says: The whole governance lies in the temperance of the fire.

<margin>How difficult it is.</margin> I have recounted the necessity of knowing the fire; let us now hear how difficult it is to find a <term>regulation of fire: the controlled application of heat, "regimen ignis"</term> that is agreeable to nature, and let us weigh what **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name for the 10th-century alchemist Ibn Umail.</note> says. He says: Men who work in this science are deceived more in the regulation of the fire than in any other thing, because they have not known the temperance of the fire. For many know the substance, but they are ignorant of the fire's regulation, in which lies the entire perfection. **Hermes** says: The science of fires is a miraculous gift. But perhaps someone will ask why the regulation of fire is unknown, since art imitates nature as much as it can; and in minerals we see a nearly linear path—namely, a slow and equal heat—because it cooks the metals in the deep recesses of the earth and leads them to perfection. Therefore, once the matter, its disposition, and the vessel are known, if all things are governed by a slow fire, the philosopho-

<meta>This page continues Hoghelande’s discussion on the requirements for the alchemical "stone." ### Book on the Difficulties of Alchemy

...[philo]sophers, then it would be necessary for the stone to be procreated from it. Indeed, one might correctly reason this way if nature had handed over the seed of the stone in a pure and perfect form, complete in all its parts, just as she does with a grain of wheat or the seed of another vegetable. Such a seed, when committed to the earth, warmed by the heat of the sun, and moistened by the dew of heaven, rises up without human help into a form similar to that from which it took its origin. But it is not granted to nature by God—as <term>Lullius: Ramon Lull, a 13th-century polymath and attributed alchemical authority</term> says—that <margin>Testament, chapter 88.</margin> she can generate the philosophers' stone without the skill and operation of human hands. 

For this reason, the philosophers command that the stone be freed from its bodily bulk and then cleansed of its superfluities. To achieve this, they describe various "regimes" or methods of management, all of which cannot be accomplished with a fire that is too slow. Consequently, some authorities hand down four principal degrees of fire, ignoring the intermediate stages between them. And although the <term>Elixir: the medicinal or transformative substance sought by alchemists</term> could be perfected by a single fire that is equal in all respects, it would be extremely difficult to judge how that fire should be composed and how such heat might be stirred up, since authors vary greatly on this point. 

Some assert that their matter should be kept in the heat of a <term>bath: "balneum," usually a water bath or "Bain-Marie"</term>, or in ashes or sand. The author of the *Lily* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a text often attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova.</note> says that a flaming fire should be applied which reverberates above the vessel. He says that once the "Dragon" is placed and buried in the vessel, a fire of five dried logs should be kindled in the pit of the furnace, which must be continuous and neither diminished nor increased. <margin>The variety of fires.</margin> Alphidius requires the heat of dung. For he says: "To cook with fire is to hide the matter in moist horse manure, which is the 'fire of the wise.'" Others seek that heat in grape-skins, sawdust, straw, or juniper coals. Morienes <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary early alchemist.</note> praises pigeon dung and olive leaves. Many think the philosophical fire should be nourished with oil, tallow, butter, or "burning water" <note>original: *aqua ardens*, referring to distilled alcohol or spirits.</note>. They compare this to the heat of a healthy man, or a hen sitting on eggs, or the heat of the Sun when it is in the sign of Aries <note>The start of Spring.</note>. 

Furthermore, Count Bernard describes a certain "ethereal" heat—vaporous, digesting, continuous, not violent, subtle, surrounded, airy, enclosed, non-burning, altering, penetrating, and living. Johannes Pontanus, whose letter is prefixed to the practical works of Philippe de Rouvignasco, describes an altogether marvelous fire—one that can hardly be understood by anyone—in this manner: It is mineral, it is equal, it is continuous, it does not vaporize unless it is stirred up too much; it partakes of sulfur, it is taken from somewhere other than the matter itself; it destroys all things, it dissolves and congeals, and likewise it calcinates; it is artificial to find, and is a shortcut without any expense (or at least very little). This fire provides a moderate ignition which performs all the necessary sublimations, and it cannot be grasped except through deep and profound thought alone. 

I would think that he means the "Water of the Philosophers," which is frequently called "fire" by the wise. For so say Menardus and Dardaris in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: <margin>Philosophical water is called fire.</margin> "Quick-silver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*, or mercury.</note> is a fire that burns bodies and mortifies them more [than any other]."

<summary>Hoghelande argues that the Philosophers' Stone requires human artifice rather than just nature. He surveys the bewildering variety of "fires" (heat sources) recommended by different alchemical authorities, ranging from horse dung to "ethereal" mineral fire.</summary>

...than fire. And another says: "The fire I will show you is water." <note>original: "Ignis quem tibi ostendam est aqua." A common alchemical paradox suggesting that the "fire" which transforms the matter is actually a corrosive liquid or a "mercurial water."</note> But it seems to stand in the way that he says it is taken from somewhere other than from the matter. In this way, even the "earth" of the Philosophers is sometimes called fire. Whence the author of the *Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scalæ philos." referring to the *Scala Philosophorum*, an anonymous alchemical text.</note> says: "Know that our water is oil, and our earth is dry fire." Therefore, since we are ignorant of which of so many kinds of fires we ought chiefly to choose, the entire inquiry into it will deservedly be full of difficulties; these the philosophers increase not a little 

<margin>Four kinds of fires according to the philosophers.</margin> 
while they often speak of four kinds of fires: namely, the Elemental, the natural, the unnatural, and that which is against nature. The craftsman should have a complete knowledge of all of these before he takes up the work. Concerning fire, I find this riddle: "The shore of the sea, human blood not fully burnt, and the red juice of the grape is our fire."

<margin>The difficulty in knowing the furnace. *Book of Furnaces*.</margin> 
Moreover, it is manifest that the secret of the furnace is contained under the heading of fire, since fire cannot be produced except in a suitable furnace. That various types of furnaces are reviewed everywhere by the philosophers can easily be gathered from <term>Geber: the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential authority in medieval alchemy</term>, who alone—to omit other authors—enumerates seven: namely, those for <term>calcination: reducing a solid to powder by heat</term>, sublimation, distillation, descent <note>original: "descensorium," a furnace for a type of distillation where the vapors are forced downward.</note>, dissolution, and fixation. Yet, they nevertheless seek only one single furnace, which they call the "secret furnace" when they wish to indicate it, while its proper name is hidden. The craftsman happens to err similarly from the increase or decrease of this furnace.

<margin>On the proportion of furnaces.</margin> 
For a large furnace gives a large fire, but a small one gives a small fire, just as also depends on its thickness or thinness; for a thick furnace gives a condensed and strong fire, while a thin one gives a weak one. Likewise, spacious air-holes give a clear and large fire, while narrow ones give a weak one. For this reason, the craftsman must primarily labor so that he may find the equal proportion of the fire he seeks.

<margin>The time of the birth of the stone.</margin> 
It remains for me to say something about the rise and birth of the stone, and about its limits. For every natural action has its own motion and a determined time in which it is perfected and finished within a greater or lesser space of time, as <term>The Philosopher: almost always refers to Aristotle</term> says. Necessarily, the philosophers' stone will also have its own certain and 

<margin>When it is said to be born.</margin> 
determined time within which it may arise and be completed. Moreover, the Philosophers want it to be born after the most accurate cleansing of its elements and purification from all pollutions in a certain <term>albedo: the "whitening" stage of the alchemical Great Work</term>, which shines with an admirable brightness, surpassing all the whitenesses of the world. It flees and vanishes from the fire unless the craftsman knows how to impose an end to the <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid</term>, and in that very hour joins the soul to it. This follows the example of the fetus in the womb, which from the beginning of conception is continuously perfected until the time of birth; at the time of birth, it is perfect in itself, and if it does not come out then, it is suffocated and dies, because it then requires the help of the expulsive power. And once it is born, it then needs to be perfected for the last time, because it lacks the movement of walking, knowledge, and speech. In the same way, this stone arises perfect through itself...

but it lacks the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura," the power to dye or transform metals</note>, and a stable <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio stans," the state where a substance remains solid and does not evaporate in the fire</note>, and the matrimonial union <note>the chemical bonding of the "male" and "female" principles</note>. Therefore, it requires the help of a craftsman to extract it immediately and complete it before it flies away from the fire, or before it grows old and becomes sickly. <margin>In the *Key of the Philosophers*.</margin> Hence Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> says: "The root of this science is in the hour of its composition." And Alphidius says: "Every creature can be increased until it is perfected; however, when it has reached the end of its perfection, it tends toward the loss of diminution, or descends. All things in the world direct their journey along a path of this kind." We see something similar happen in those things subject to our own will—namely, in the baking of bread and the making of honey and sugar. When these have reached the full extent of their cooking, they are perfected and must be removed from the fire; if they are cooked further, they are burnt and destroyed.

It is necessary, therefore, for the craftsman to be attentive and vigilant, so that he does not exceed the limit in the work, and to follow the advice of the author of the *Lily* <note>Referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous alchemical text</note>, who says: "Hold to this work with Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> so that it is repeated continually until the change becomes visible to your sight, such that the vision of the work itself teaches you."

<margin>The variety of terms regarding the "end" of the work.</margin> However, the philosophers have never indicated this "limit" except mystically and quite obscurely. They have varied it deliberately so that it cannot truly be grasped or known by anyone except through the grace and kindness of God—for if that limit remains unknown, a knowledge of all the aforementioned things is of no help. For some define this limit as one year, according to that saying of Plato: <margin>In the *Quarters* or *Stellar Books*.</margin> "The fewer days of preparation are the circuit of the greater light <note>The sun</note>." Others say nine months, some one hundred and fifty days, or one hundred and twenty, even one hundred; some say eighty or seventy, or even forty. There are even those who define this limit as nine or seven days, or even three, and in infinite other ways. Yet there is but one limit and one day—indeed, one hour and one moment, as some will have it—in which the perfection or the annihilation of the entire work occurs. <margin>To Eutychia.</margin> Moses <note>In alchemy, Moses was often cited as a master of the chemical arts</note> says: "This work happens as suddenly as clouds coming from the sky," and as Hermes says, "even in the blink of an eye." And Rosinus <note>The Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis</note> says similarly: "This work happens in a single moment, and its efficacy lies in the purification of the stone from its foul oils <note>original: "unguento fis suis," likely a corruption of "unguine foetidis suis," referring to the combustible sulfurous impurities</note> and other things that hinder its power." Hinting at the difficulty and danger of knowing this limit, Mireris addresses Mimenfidus thus: "If you work philosophically and do not exceed the limit in the work itself, you shall be twice blessed. If you see this suddenly, admiration, terror, and trembling will come upon you; therefore, work cautiously." And Plato says: "Beware lest you reach a harmful limit in the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the stage of decay and blackness, or *nigredo*</note>; for if the work contracts a delay in its dissolution, it will perhaps increase in its corruption; therefore, beware of this." And someone in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: "Even if everything has been performed by you with reason, if you are ignorant of the <term>whitening</term> <note>original: "dealbatio," the *albedo* stage where the matter turns white and pure</note>, you lose your hoped-for joy." <margin>*Book of the Secrets of Alchemy*, chapter 7.</margin> And another in the same place: "If the composite..."

even those who imagine the work of the stone to be so light and easy that anyone, even a lucky peasant or unlearned man, could gain knowledge of it or hope for some fruit from it—though it is already clear enough to those gifted with intellect that it must be prepared not by chance or accident, but by study and labor day and night, aided by the grace of God. Therefore, our stone is ours and not the peasants', and belongs entirely to our philosophy, just as a son belongs to the father who begot him." Thus far Lullius.

### THE FOURTH AND FINAL PART OF THIS BOOK,
->*which teaches that the Chemical art should be avoided by everyone, and concludes.*<-

I believe I have spoken more than enough above regarding the three types of obstacles that make this science so extremely difficult. Even though these are very great, if anyone is not moved or called back from his purpose, but instead continues, trusting in his own wit and judgment, and hopes that through his industry all obstacles can be removed or overcome and his goal reached, let him become more cautious by the example of others. Let him look as if from a watchtower at the fruitless studies of the most learned men who have published books on this art. <margin>Many learned men have not attained knowledge of the art.</margin> Let him examine the small works of Giovanni Bracesco <note>Giovanni Bracesco (c. 1481–1555), an Italian alchemist known for his dialogues on Geber and Lull</note> and the criticisms against them by Tauladanus <note>Robertus Tauladanus, a critic of Bracesco's interpretations</note>; let him see the book on the Chemical art by Lorenzo Ventura <note>Lorenzo Ventura (16th century), an Italian physician and alchemist</note>, who boasts that he brought two hundred and fifty volumes of this science into the library of the most illustrious Count Palatine, and has fifty more besides these; and he will see the shameful and monstrous errors of those men. Meanwhile, I will remain silent about those who, in our age, have undertaken to explain and clarify the *Rosarium* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note> of Arnaldus de Villa Nova and the little chemical books of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and founder of iatrochemistry</note>—men who do not blush to admit they are paraphrasts and interpreters of things they do not understand. But just as the madness of these men earns laughter, so the frustrated labors of others deserve pity—those who, though they shone with doctrine and erudition and spared neither labor nor expense in searching out the secrets of metals, nevertheless had the truth hidden from them, doubtless by the will of Almighty God, who searches the hearts and minds of men. This is truly a great example for all who follow this art without due consideration. <margin>An example to be taken from others.</margin> For if the practice of this art, or rather its very matter, was hidden from such learned and distinguished men who did not lack the books of various authors, what hope is there for me or those like me, who possess less wit and erudition? We do not even have books—which is the most important thing in this—except for a very few compared to those which Ventura says he had at hand.

...are in their hands? Finally, what is to be expected for those who have not even "greeted the Muses from the threshold" <note>original: "musas ne à limine quidem salutarunt"; a Latin idiom meaning they have not even begun a basic education</note>, who understand neither the roots of minerals nor the manner of their generation? They have never cared to investigate the hidden secrets of nature, but, led only by greed or ambition, or similar corrupt desires, they hurry to these feasts with unwashed 

<margin>The unlearned are to be entirely excluded from the art.</margin>

hands, like cattle to their fodder. Truly, I judge this art to be as easy for them as if they were trying to pull the stars down from the sky with their own hands. Hence, it is no wonder if, relying on such bad beginnings, they meet an even worse end; for, having "boiled away" <note>A pun on alchemical "decoction," implying they have spent all their money on failed experiments</note> their wealth, they are forced to spend their old age in sorrow and poverty. They experience the "metamorphosis" they expected to see in the metals within their own lives instead; of them it could be wittily said: "What they had—namely, riches—they lost; what they did not lose they have—namely, poverty and misery." Furthermore, since the knowledge of this art falls to very few, and that 

<margin>Because of the uncertain end and outcome, everyone should avoid the art.</margin>

only by the benefit and mercy of God—whose will is unexplored by us, and whose judgments we should rather fear than presume anything for ourselves—and since the time we spend in this world is so short and precious that it cannot be recovered by any amount of wealth, a man consults his own interests poorly when he prefers uncertain and doubtful outcomes over certain and secure ones. Rather, let him pursue Theology, Jurisprudence, Medicine, Architecture, or similar fields, in which even moderate minds can make such progress that they can help others with advice, labor, or resources, and prepare for themselves a name, fame, riches, and honors, or at least provide for their family. For no one is barred from the State or from performing any duties whatsoever, even if he has not reached the very highest peak of his faculty or science, which happens only very rarely. Not all Theologians are equal in doctrine or experience to **St. Augustine** and **Thomas Aquinas**, nor are all Jurists equal to **Papinian** <note>Aemilius Papinianus, a celebrated Roman jurist</note> or **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a highly influential medieval jurist</note>, nor all Physicians to **Hippocrates** or **Galen**, nor all Architects to **Proclus** or **Archimedes**. Nevertheless, even today, many men of varying degrees of erudition are held in high esteem within those same faculties, and they have no reason to repent of their 

<margin>A comparison.</margin>

time as if it were ill-spent. But in the Chemical art, the plain opposite occurs. I am accustomed to comparing this art to a certain very high mountain: on its northern side, it is precipitous and broken; on its southern side, it slopes gently. This mountain divides two regions. One, the northern side, is very rarely touched by light, but is mostly covered by dark clouds and dense gloom, blasted by violent winds, horrific with woods, and rough with thorns and briars. It has no path, but the ground is entirely hindered by mud, or snow and ice, and it produces nothing for the comfort or necessity of man. The other side, the southern one, is illuminated by the sun all day long, fanned by the sweetest breezes, marked by hills bearing vines and trees fertile with every kind of fruit; it is watered by sweetly flowing springs and streams, and by meadows green from afar with a thousand...

He uses a vivid geographical allegory of a mountain to contrast the misery of failed alchemy with the fruitfulness of established sciences.</summary>

# On the Difficulties of Alchemy
### Book 5

...adorned with distinct kinds of flowers, beautiful houses, and shaded bowers; in short, whatever could be desired for living well and blessedly in this world may be found there in great abundance, but it is a place to which no entry is granted except by way of a mountain.

<margin>The obstacles of the Alchemists.</margin>
Whoever sets out to pursue the Alchemical arts <note>original: "Chemica"; here referring to the "Divine Art" of alchemy</note> enters a region exposed to the north wind imprudently and without counsel, and plunges himself into the greatest difficulties. He might wish to enjoy the delights of that other southern region, but he finds no beaten path; the mud swallows his footsteps, the snow and ice deceive him with their slipperiness, thorns and briars prick him, and finally, a steep and rocky mountain prevents him from ascending to the summit.

<margin>A way to knowledge is prepared by labor and study.</margin>
What should he do? He would weary the heavens with prayers and sighs in vain, unless—seizing an axe—he cuts down the trees and thickets with great force and labor, breaks through the rocks with iron and fire, and opens a path for himself among them. Or, if God and the stars favor him, someone might let down a ladder or a rope from the very top of the mountain's peak, by which he may be pulled upward to gaze upon the garden of pleasure from above, and finally gather the fruits with full hands, quench his hunger and thirst, and, after enduring the hardest labors, enjoy the long-desired rest.

<margin>It very rarely happens that someone attains the art through another's teaching.</margin>
But how many are there whose stars are so kind, or who ascend the mountain by another's effort? For who would dare to reach out a hand to another, unless to a man conspicuous for his faith, constancy, generosity toward the poor, and holiness of life—one whom he has long tested through many trials and found to be not arrogant, not ambitious, but humble and mild, and seeking not his own glory, but the glory of God?

<margin>The craftsman must either quickly turn back or persist constantly in the work.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, that whoever has entered that region without due consideration should either turn back, or, if he wishes to proceed further, he must not fear solitude. He must steady his steps against the wind, ward off the cold with double clothing and furs and other warmth, fit boots to his legs because of the mud, support his gait on the ice with a iron-tipped staff, and finally prepare steps for himself on the mountain, ascending to its very summit by his own effort <note>original: "suoque Marte"; literally "by his own Mars," a Roman idiom meaning by one's own strength or prowess</note>.

<margin>All obstacles must first be removed.</margin>
Unless he does this, he will be deprived of all the fruit of his labors. It is to be feared that he might finally fall from the mountain's cliffs and be crippled or lose his limbs, or be swallowed by a muddy abyss, or be trapped by deep snow and ice, or be torn by thorns, or end his life miserably through hunger, cold, and thirst. In other faculties and sciences, no one labors or exercises his talent in vain; even if he does not reach the highest rank, he at least earns some degree of status among his peers.

<margin>All alchemical study is useless unless the full art is attained.</margin>
However, he who treats of Alchemy, unless he truly masters the metamorphosis <note>the transformation of base metals into noble ones</note> of imperfect metals into gold and silver—which is the goal of the art and the conclusion of the entire study—has spent his life in vain and will suffer the repentance of time lost through lack of counsel. Who then, unless he be imprudent, would pursue such doubtful things? I speak not of princes and nobles, for whom it matters little if they spend a few hundred gold pieces annually on a most honorable, beautiful, and pleasant thing (provided all is done with reason and counsel), but of men of my own condition; who, I say, would pursue such uncertainties, from which nothing results but the loss of ti— <note>catchword "tempo-" refers to the Latin "temporis jactura" or loss of time</note>

<summary>Hoghelande uses the allegory of a treacherous mountain journey to warn that alchemy requires extreme labor, moral purity, and divine favor, noting that unlike other sciences, alchemy offers no "partial success"—it is total mastery or total failure.</summary>
<keywords>allegory, mountain, obstacles, metamorphosis, gold and silver, labor, perseverance, moral requirements, waste of time</keywords>

# THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE
### Book 5 (Continued)

...should he expect a waste of time and labor, poverty, and want, rather than those things from which certain rewards, honor, riches, favor among his peers, and admiration are expected? What is more foolish than to search for things which, after you have acquired them with the greatest labor and extraordinary expense, you do not even dare to make public? How miserable do you think your life will be when, in the midst of great fortune, you still long for fortune, and feel shackles thrown upon you so that you cannot do what you wish? Thus, you might rightly say with the poet Horace:

<margin>The wretched life of those for whom success results in loss.</margin>

> *To what end is fortune mine, if I am not permitted to use it?* <note>original Latin: "Quo mihi fortunam, si non conceditur uti?"; from Horace, Epistles 1.5.12. The author suggests that even if an alchemist succeeds, the need for secrecy prevents him from enjoying his wealth.</note>

<margin>Each person should be a friend to himself rather than to anyone else.</margin>
But you might say you will be able to do good for others; that is indeed a splendid and magnificent goal, but even this cannot be done except in secret. Furthermore, in order to be a friend to others, you will be an enemy to yourself; to promote others, you will lower yourself and commit yourself to a double-edged fortune, your mind always suspended between hope and fear. To give to others, you will first consume your own goods, lose the flower of your youth, and cast yourself into the deepest pit of despair. 

Meanwhile, no gratitude at all is to be expected from ungrateful relatives, kinsmen, and friends, who will believe you give not out of love but out of abundance, and with a very stingy hand when you could have given most generously—if, that is, you had actually attained your wish. But if you fail, no one will return even a farthing <note>original Latin: "teruntium"; a Roman coin of negligible value</note> to you, even if you have spent everything you own. Rather, you will be laughed at, and you will waste away exposed to the mockery of all.

<margin>To the ungrateful, nothing is ever enough.</margin>

<margin>Hope in things that very rarely happen is deceptive.</margin>

And since not even one in ten thousand of those who practice Chemistry <note>original: "Chemica"; referring here to the "Divine Art" of alchemy</note> achieves the goal he set for himself, should it not be feared that you will waste your effort with the ten thousand, rather than obtain the sought-after thing with that single one? 

<margin>Why the study of Alchemy is to be avoided.</margin>

Therefore, I would wish all and every person to be kindly asked and warned to avoid Alchemy like a plague or some kind of cancer; for it creeps in once you have admitted it and feeds upon the inner parts of a man, gnaws at the soul, and allows no rest because of the hope of vast wealth. This hope—no differently than the fear of evil—makes human life not only difficult and laborious but hastens old age and death. 

<margin>Alchemy makes a man restless.</margin>

"Hope that is deferred," says the wise man, "afflicts the soul"; if that is true in other matters, it is certainly most true in this art. <note>original: "Spes quæ differtur... affligit animam"; a reference to Proverbs 13:12</note> 

<margin>Proverbs 13. It creates diseases and other inconveniences of mind and body.</margin>

Who could now enumerate the diseases which the fumes, the stenches, the exhalations of raw and sublimated mercury <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note>, and the inhalation of other poisonous things, the long nights without sleep, and the daily labors bring to the bodies of Alchemists? Who could report the burns from "strong waters" <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; nitric acid</note> or glowing metals, or the weariness of the soul as they see their hopes fall into nothingness, contrary to what they presumed? 

Who could briefly touch upon the countless expenses? For these, glass vessels must be sought here, iron pots there; in another place, basins or clay resistant to strong fire are needed. Mercury, the marcasites <note>Iron pyrites or similar metallic minerals</note> of gold and silver and of other metals, and similar materials must be fetched from the very veins of the earth across vast distances. 

<margin>It costs a great deal.</margin>

Furthermore, worthless fellows, spendthrifts, and sycophants are summoned even from other provinces and from across the Alps to deceive. I omit the infamy which for the most part accompanies these gold-seekers <note>original: "auripetas"</note>, and the doubtful judgments of men regarding them, while...

<margin>It makes one hateful and infamous.</margin>

<summary>Theobald de Hoghelande warns against the pursuit of alchemy, arguing that it leads to financial ruin, social isolation, and physical illness from toxic fumes. He emphasizes that even success brings the misery of forced secrecy and the ingratitude of relatives.</summary>

# ON THE DIFFICULTIES OF ALCHEMY

Everyone speaks of these seekers according to their own perception: one person suspects an impostor, another a forger or a <term>debaser of currency</term> <note>One who illegally alters the metal content of coins.</note>. Those who judge less harshly claim the seeker is merely a spendthrift, ill-advised in his own affairs, and rushing willingly toward poverty; many even pity him, as if his well-being were already a lost cause. 

<margin>The difference between true and false alchemy.</margin>
But although these aforementioned things are as far from the followers of true Alchemy as heaven is from the earth, they cannot apply to the true philosopher who skillfully investigates the secrets of nature. Such a man does not require many or expensive things, nor does he need to seek from afar what is found for sale everywhere. Nor is he in danger from vapors or fumes. Yet, before he reaches the point where he understands the writings of the philosophers, knows the matter of the art and its management, and other necessities, it happens that he must attempt many things and spend much. He may not be entirely safe from exhalations, nor can he escape the judgments of the common people. 

Furthermore, I will remain silent for now regarding certain otherwise honest and learned men who, upon hearing the name of an "Alchemist," shudder and tremble as if they had seen a cruel wild beast; they judge him an impostor before they even know him. 

<margin>It is not without God’s judgment that the art is held in low esteem.</margin>
Thus, this art, the most worthy of all, is judged vile and wicked—and not without the judgment of Almighty God. Although this may seem difficult and unjust to those just beginning, in the course of time, when they begin to understand and taste the obscure sayings of the philosophers, and some of them (though very few) reach the goal, they then rejoice in their hearts. This is not so much because of the hope or abundance of gold and silver, but because the art is judged impossible and vain by others. They secretly laugh at the foolishness and wickedness of those who previously mocked them. Even if some suspicion arises, they can securely despise the talkativeness of men because of the divine grace bestowed upon them, appealing to the behavior of the majority. 

<margin>The vain judgments of men.</margin>
"What?" the critics would say, "If this man were overflowing with such great riches, would he not do this or that? He would support a numerous household, he would buy land, he would build, he would walk about pompously dressed and accompanied by a retinue of servants, and he would undertake some great project!" Truly, they would be right—if everyone were of the same mind. But both in the past and in our own age, there are those who have learned to bear riches moderately and not to exalt themselves because of them. They loathe arrogance, pomp, and the other vanities of the world, and have learned to embrace a secure and constant restraint and a humility that is never shaken by the waves of the sea. 

Let those who meditate on such different paths know that this art is given by God only to the <term>poor in spirit</term> <note>original Latin: "pauperibus spiritu"; a reference to the Beatitudes in the Gospel of Matthew, suggesting that humility is a prerequisite for alchemical success.</note>. 

<margin>To whom the Art properly belongs.</margin>
For so says <term>Alphidius</term> <note>An author frequently cited in medieval alchemical texts, such as the "Rosarium Philosophorum"; his true historical identity remains uncertain.</note>: "God has granted this art to the rational sons of Adam, and specifically to the poor." Let them hear the <term>Blessed Thomas</term> <note>The text refers here to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). In the late Middle Ages, several alchemical works were attributed to him, though modern scholars doubt he wrote them.</note> saying: "This art either finds a man holy or makes him holy." This is not through the art itself, but because it is impossible that a man should not prostrate himself humbly before the face of God and give Him immortal thanks, for He gives such treasure and wisdom to so very few.

<summary>Hoghelande discusses the public's negative perception of alchemists as frauds or fools, contrasting this with the "true" alchemist who seeks wisdom and spiritual humility. He emphasizes that the success of the Great Work is a divine gift reserved for the "poor in spirit" rather than the greedy or the vain.</summary>
