THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE

...attained it solely through the mercy of God. It is therefore no wonder if the philosopher keeps himself within the limits of reason, and meditates so much on things that pertain to the glory of GOD and charity toward his neighbors while neglecting his own interests. And why, after all, should he spread to the common people things that would soon be harmful to him?

<margin>One must not make public things that can harm their author.</margin>
Commonly known are the events that happened just a few years ago to <term>Bragadino</term> <note>original: "Bragadino." Marco Bragadino (c. 1545–1591) was a famous Venetian alchemist who claimed to produce gold but was eventually executed for fraud.</note>, who, when he had professed the art of changing base metals into gold in Venice and was called "the Great Alchemist" by the people by way of excellence, was approached by Lord <term>Piccolomini</term> <note>original: "Toparcha Picolomineus." Likely referring to an outlawed member of the influential Italian Piccolomini family.</note>, who had been outlawed by certain princes of Italy. He asked for a loan of thirty thousand gold coins and, moreover, imprudently desired to be taught the art so that he might prepare as much for himself hereafter as he wished. Bragadino, lifeless with fear since he neither had as much as the other requested, and much less understood the art, nevertheless dared to deny nothing because of the other's cruelty and rashness; he promised both. But as he delayed and shifted his ground, making now this and now that excuse, the other pressed more sharply and threatened death unless he fulfilled the promise—for he did not wish to be laughed at by anyone or held in low esteem. Therefore, Bragadino was forced to protect himself with a crowd of attendants against the ferocity of the one laying snares for him. This would have helped him little had not Piccolomini himself—unmindful of his own safety while handing a noose to the other—fallen into the traps and been captured. Bragadino escaped then, reserved for a worse fate of his own. 

<margin>The history of Bragadino.</margin>
<margin>One should learn from the danger of others rather than one's own.</margin>

Yet it could perhaps happen that the same art might one day fall into the hands of the unworthy, whom God—not as a fierce avenger but as a just judge—might punish harshly as an example to others, for He uses both the good and the bad for the glory of His name. I heard from a certain nobleman of our age that a certain Italian monk, relying on this art, renounced his religion and his order and came to Germany so that he might live more freely, having detested the cowl and the harshness of monasteries. But while he conducted himself incautiously, two men wormed their way into his closest friendship, by whom he was later murdered in a certain forest while traveling, in a most terrible crime. One of them showed the powder found with the monk to various princes and magnates as his own, and deceived men with a thousand impostures under the false name of knowledge. Who, therefore, would not take heed from the example of these two and hide his secret? For if revealed, it brings either death or, at the very least, perpetual fear and voluntary exile far from one's homeland and family. 

For a long time, many controversies were debated among the ancient philosophers about what the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum," the ultimate goal or supreme virtue of human life.</note> might be, while one man praises virtue, another glory, pleasure, the absence of pain, health, strength, security of the soul, and similar things to the heavens. Certainly, it is not to be doubted that the greatest part of them, if they had any knowledge of the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis philosophici." The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the Elixir of Life.</note>, would have preferred it to all the aforementioned things and other things in the world, since with it, immense riches and everything that can be obtained with gold and money can be had...

<margin>The disputation of the ancients concerning the highest good.</margin>

<meta>catchword: beri,</meta>

### Book on the Difficulties of Alchemy ###

<margin>The wonderful properties of the Elixir.</margin>
...be liberated, diseases driven away, and health can be preserved. For if experts and each person in their own art are to be believed, since authors unanimously hand down that this <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: "elixir." The supreme goal of alchemy, also known as the Philosopher's Stone, believed to transmute base metals and serve as a universal medicine.</note> reduces the human body to its true <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperamentum." In medieval medicine, this refers to the perfect balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which resulted in perfect health.</note> (I mean in those prepared for it), and provides a sublime memory, perpetual cheerfulness (unless external violence occurs), wisdom, and boldness, why should we not believe that a body so disposed can flourish with various virtues and almost all the goods, so to speak, of body and soul? But who would judge that to be the <term>highest good</term> <note>original: "summum bonum."</note>, the attainment of which is so uncertain, and which, after you have attained it, you do not even dare to make public, unless you wish to be sought by snares on all sides and exposed to a thousand dangers, or to live in perpetual fear and terror?

<margin>No one can be happy in perpetual fear.</margin>
Those who in ancient times achieved something exceptional rejoiced to be seen and known, and to enjoy their fame while they lived; this science alone rejoices in shadows and seeks hiding places, nor does it dare to show its head until after death. And even then, it only emerges through some little book written and left with friends, by which the authors wish their fortune to be witnessed by posterity, and especially by students of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chemiæ." In this period, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were often used interchangeably.</note> whom the highest God deems worthy of that gift. While glory is the greatest spur to those aspiring to difficult things in other human actions and sciences, in this art it brings an obstacle instead, dulls the vigor of the mind, and could call anyone away from a journey successfully begun. And indeed, no honest man who measures his happiness by heaven and the love of God ought to seek the greatest riches, since it is most difficult to restrain the mind in great fortune, and to abstain from injuring others, or from doing those things which merit reproach and blame in this world, and eternal punishment in the age to come.

Since therefore this science, however excellent, is so uncertain because of the obstacles and difficulties described above, that hardly anyone dares to hope for it except very unadvisedly and rashly—since countless people miserably waste their resources and time, expose themselves to the mockery of men, bring diseases and poverty upon themselves of their own accord, and accelerate old age—finally, since the art once attained carries so many dangers with it, I again advise everyone, especially the young and men of moderate fortune, that each should take care for his reputation and safety. One should neither tread nor enter this path, or if he has entered, he should withdraw his foot quickly, lest he become wise too late like many others, and pay the penalty for his folly with a late and useless repentance.

<margin>The disadvantages of Alchemy.</margin>
But so that he who chooses in no way to acquiesce to my advice, but prefers rather to try his fortune, may also derive some utility from this little book, I will give some healthy precepts.

<margin>Precepts most useful to all Chemists.</margin>
First, let him examine himself and consider whether he possesses the conditions required in a <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "artifex." This refers to the alchemist as a skilled craftsman or "artist" of nature.</note>, and above all, let him look to his family estate and finances, lest if he remains empty of his purpose, he should later suffer from poverty or be forced to abandon the work begun.

<margin>1.</margin>
Let him accumulate for himself the books of diverse authors, because otherwise...

-> THEOBALD DE HOGHELANDE <-

<meta>catchword: of the Elix-</meta>

...because their understanding is impossible, let him not cast aside a book read once, twice, or thrice, even if he does not understand it, but let him reread it ten, twenty, and fifty times and even more: then let him see in what the authors most agree, for there truth lies hidden, but let him primarily look to the possibility of nature. Whence the Philosopher [says], let your intention <margin>Senior in the *Key of Wisdom*, book 3, chapter 4. <note>original: "Senior in clavi Sap." Refers to Zadith Senior, a famous 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were foundational in Latin translation.</note></margin> be according to nature. Furthermore, let him know the roots of minerals, so that he may perform his work from them; otherwise he will labor in vain. Let him not use the work of others, for no one devotes effort to others with the same spirit as they do for themselves. Furthermore, this art is no different from some kingdom: it is <margin>The Art is impatient of partnership.</margin> impatient of partnership, unless minds are joined by faith, innocence, and especially by the love of God. Therefore, <term>Geber</term> <note>original: "Geber." The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic and Western alchemy. His works defined the "Mercury-Sulfur" theory of metals.</note> does not without reason place the "mutilation of limbs" among the obstacles to the art. But to whom do limbs seem more mutilated than to those who seek the art through the work of others, and profess themselves unworthy of the investigation of natural things?

Therefore, he who has no leisure, being distracted by other business so that he cannot find time for the reading of books or the practice of the art, should rather abstain from it, because there is nothing he can expect according to his wishes. Or if he abounds in riches and does not fear expenses, let him seek for himself some upright and learned man, skilled in several of the most common languages, and moderately practiced in common <term>distillations</term> <note>original: "destillationibus." The process of purifying a liquid by heating and cooling.</note>, <term>sublimations</term> <note>original: "sublimationibus." Heating a solid to turn it into vapor and then back to solid, used to purify substances like sulfur or mercury.</note>, and <term>calcinations</term> <note>original: "calcinationibus." Heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or reduction to powder.</note>—not because these are absolutely necessary in this art, but so that he may know how to distinguish philosophical works from common ones. Let him establish an annual salary for him and supply the books and instruments necessary for the art, but with the mindset that he does not take the loss of his money badly, even if for several years the craftsman does not even know where best to begin. For one should not think that the hand should be set to the work after reading just any book, perhaps false and composed by some impostor, but after a space of several years when he considers himself to have thoroughly understood the authors. For thus we read in the <term>Allegories of the Sages</term> <note>original: "Allegorijs Sapientum." A popular medieval collection of alchemical maxims.</note>: Do not begin the work before you know it, because if you do not know the work, you will err, and your work will perish in vain. Once he has received [a method], let him not change it unless for a great cause, <margin>5.</margin> even if he seems a bit slow to one who is in a hurry. 

Let him keep the wandering and unlearned who profess themselves to be alchemists far from his light, for they will teach no one what they themselves do not know. If anything can be learned from them, it consists entirely in various furnaces and fires and their degrees, which can be known from them by giving a small gift; or if they seem worth keeping for that reason, let the vessel always be kept sealed and covered on the outside: if the matter is to be looked at, or <margin>6.</margin> removed, or something is to be mixed, let them be sent away from the house. Let each person beware of books and papers which contain various "recipes" (as they call them) and promise <term>whitenings</term> <note>original: "albificationes." The *albedo* stage, believed to produce silver.</note> or <term>reddenings</term> <note>original: "rubificationes." The *rubedo* stage, the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone to produce gold.</note>, <margin>7.</margin> the multiplication of gold and silver, or the extraction of gold from copper and silver. Nor let him easily believe those who promise abbreviations of the work, or of the Elix-

# On the Difficulties of Alchemy
<meta>catchword: of the Elix-</meta>

...ir's perfect augmentation, for it is necessary that nature have its complete time in which to perfect its action; if anyone disturbs its motion, he will accumulate not profit but loss and inconvenience for himself. Furthermore, no one can grant increase to the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Elixir" or Philosopher's Stone was the goal of the work, believed to transform base metals into gold and heal the body.</note>, or intensify its virtue, who does not know the art entirely and has not previously brought the work to completion through the path of experience. <margin>8.</margin> Let him flee all common <term>sublimations</term>, <term>calcinations</term>, and solutions, for nothing of utility is to be expected from them, since the regimen of the philosophers is far different from common methods. <margin>9.</margin> Let him avoid all things that cost a great deal. If he believes the art is situated in gold and silver, let him take a small quantity of them—namely one <term>drachma</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams.</note> or at most two—and if the principles prove successful, he can later repeat the work with a greater weight. <margin>10.</margin> Let him despise all <term>cementations</term> <note>original: "cementationes." A process of purifying gold using heat and salts.</note>, and oils, and "graduated waters" <note>Waters applied in increasing degrees of strength or heat.</note> by which some boast they can effect certain wonders, since there is little profit in them, and more loss and danger. For let us grant that some gold or silver might be extracted from imperfect metals in that way; certainly it will be meager, and will hardly respond to the expenses and labors, nor will it admit any further augmentation. Let him condemn all vegetables and animals, or things that have their origin from them, as well as intermediate minerals; let him take nothing except the metallic nature, stick to that, and spend his effort on it, otherwise he will lament his labor, expenses, and time. <margin>Summa Perfectionis, Chapter 7. <note>original: "Sum. perf. Cap. 7." A reference to the "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," the most famous alchemical work of the Middle Ages, attributed to Geber.</note></margin> Nevertheless, let him not promise himself a prosperous outcome even if he has worked in the proper matter, since—as witnessed by Geber and other philosophers—this entire art depends on God, who grants to whom He wills and also takes away, He who is sublime and glorious and filled with all justice and goodness: for if God knew a faithful mind was in him, as the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilium." Refers to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a common alchemical text.</note> says, He would certainly reveal the truth to him. <margin>Conclusion.</margin> Therefore, if anyone should be frustrated in his desires, let him not curse God, nor place the blame for his ignorance on the philosophers, or rebuke them, but blame himself, for presuming more of himself than was right, and for not obeying the one who urged him to abstain from the art.

# SUMMARY OF THIS WORK.

**The First Part** *contains three treatises.*

*The first of which teaches the three principles of <term>Physics</term> <note>original: "Physices." In this context, it refers to Natural Philosophy—the study of how the physical world operates.</note>, which indicate the Theory of Chemistry.*

*The second [teaches] the three principles of chemical practice.*

*The third contains manual practice and its application to the work.*

**The Second Part** *teaches the seven philosophical steps, through which the minds of students may be able to reach the summit and the goal of truth and its virtues in this art.*

# TO THE READER
### PREFACE.

You have here, most excellent reader, the Theory and Practice of the whole **Chemical art**, <note>original: "artis Chemisticæ." In this period, "chemistry" and "alchemy" were used interchangeably to describe the art of separating and purifying natural substances.</note> which (unless you wish it so) you cannot remain ignorant of after reading this little compendium. Read and reread it many times, with the attention of a calm mind, passing over nothing hastily or without consideration. If you gather together the opinions of our mind which are scattered here, nothing of those things which are beautiful in this art will ever be able to remain hidden from you. You will find here, beneath a **hard shell**, <note>original: "duro cortice." A common metaphor in alchemical literature meaning that the truth is hidden under difficult or symbolic language.</note> the fluid of true medicine, by which you may be able (with the help of God) to relieve yourself, as well as your friends and the poor, from the ailments of the body. Let it not repent you of your labor in exercising the **practice** <note>original: "practicam." This refers to the actual laboratory work—the "hands-on" aspect of chemistry.</note> which we have described for you; for by building, we ourselves have become builders in this art, not by reading alone. If it should happen by chance that you do not achieve your desire on the first or second attempt, do not lose heart, but repeat the matter a third and fourth time. It happened to me often while I was wandering in error that I eventually became master of that which my soul sought. Nothing prevents a man from reaching this art more than faintheartedness and impatience. I would only warn you of this one thing: that you do not exceed the limits of medicine for the human body in the beginning; for if you seek the **metamorphosis of common metals**, <note>A reference to the transmutation of base metals into gold. Dorn advises the reader to focus on healing before attempting "high" alchemy.</note> you will weep over your error. Farewell, and look with favor upon our labors.

->What Chemical Philosophy is.<-

### CHAPTER 1.

Chemical Philosophy teaches us to investigate the hidden forms of things according to the truth of the matter, and not by mere appearance. The true disciples of this philosophy enter by two paths: **Opinion** and **Experiment**. <note>original: "Opinionem, & experimentum." Dorn uses "Opinion" to mean theoretical reasoning or hypotheses, and "Experimentum" to mean physical experience or trial.</note> For those who happen to rely on only one of these, it is necessary that they themselves, as well as others, be deceived by their teaching or their work. However, whoever has examined both and judged one by the other, they shall not be frustrated in their labor, nor shall others to whom they bring help or counsel. **Opinion** indeed presupposes doubtful things, which nevertheless appear true through philosophical reasoning; these things, finally, experience...

<margin>What nature is.</margin>
### CHAPTER II.

Among the Chemists, nature is said to be the exercise of the Heaven with the Elements in the generation of all things that exist. This artifice is perfected by a twofold instrument, namely, by disposition and by influence. Nature, by corrupting the matter, disposes it toward a power receptive of form and of celestial influences: which finally, at its determined time, breaks forth into action and specific form. This is the meaning of that saying of the philosophers: **Form acts according to the disposition of the matter.** <note>A fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics and alchemy: the "form" (the essence or identity of a thing) can only manifest if the "matter" is properly prepared to receive it.</note>

<margin>What form may be.</margin>
### CHAPTER III.

Form is the action and potentiality of the ethereal region <note>The "ethereal region" refers to the heavens or the celestial realm, which was believed to impose identity upon the lower elemental world.</note> into the elemental. Through the mutual transmutation of the elements, nature fits the matter, enclosing the form within it like a seed in a womb: pregnant by this virtue, like a mother it produces the offspring into specific action. This is what the philosophers mean when they say: **Form is led out from the potentiality of matter.** For matter itself is able to bring forth what is generated in it by form. It must be concluded, therefore, that form is the agent acting upon the matter, which undergoes its action; between these two, a magnetic nature offers itself as the mediator, acting like a craftsman. Indeed, from the universal form of the whole, nature never ceases to excite specific forms daily, nor is it any more idle than the motion of the heavens.

<margin>What Matter may be.</margin>
### CHAPTER IV.

To us, Matter is the entire elemental region, which although it is divided into four parts (which we call elements)—fire, air, water, and earth—nevertheless there are two principal ones, namely fire and water. This is because air seems to be nothing other than water resolved through heat and persisting since the creation of the world, while earth is water condensed, or rather dried out, by heat and dryness. Fire strives by its own nature, as much as it can, to convert water into itself; so that it may perform this more easily, it seeks two means, according to both qualities of each: <note>The text here begins to explain how the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) interact through shared qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>

<summary>Dorn defines the "Chemical Art" as the interaction between celestial influences and elemental matter, establishing a philosophical framework where nature acts as a craftsman to bring specific forms out of raw matter. He identifies fire and water as the primary elements, viewing air and earth as modified states of water.</summary>

[qualities]: first, so that by its heat it might consume coldness, and by that heat and its own dryness it might consume the watery moisture. We see clouds suspended by the heat of fire, holding a middle path between water and fire; for if the heat of the fire—which is weaker near the surface than in the heart of its own sphere—is overcome by the coldness of the water, this middle state is converted into one of the extremes as the victor. And so fire (as nature disposes) is frustrated in its own effort: while it strives to consume one thing, it generates another from it, which in turn returns to that from which it was generated. This **circulation of transmutation** is the primary cause of generation. 

We see fire performing a similar action in bodies composed by nature. Take wood, for example: when it is brought to the fire, its <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustibility, oiliness, and the "soul" of a substance.</note> does not burn until all the watery moisture has been converted into air; however, once this is consumed, the fire passes equally into the air, and finally into itself, while the more solid parts of the wood fall away as ash or earth. Therefore, it should not be said that the elements of such wood have been destroyed, but rather separated from their composite state, each returning to its own proper sphere. 

A doubtful question was raised among the philosophers on this matter: does fire consume more than it generates? It seems sound to say that the operations of **ethereal fire** <note>original: "ignis ætherei"; the celestial or divine heat that permeates the universe and gives life.</note> and **elementary fire** <note>original: "ignis elementaris"; the physical, destructive flame found on earth.</note> are equal. For if more were consumed by elementary fire than was generated by ethereal fire, a <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuum in rerum natura"; the idea of "empty space" was considered impossible in the Aristotelian physics of the time, as "nature abhors a vacuum."</note> could be identified in the nature of things, which would be utterly absurd. If, however, the ethereal fire generated more than the elementary fire consumed, the excess could not be contained within its already determined place; thus, the "womb of nature" would necessarily burst. 

It will be answered more briefly, however, that nothing is consumed by fire, but through the mode of transmutation, what departs from one element is added to another. Thus, wise nature daily and solicitously procures new forms to be awakened from the elements—transmuted in this way with one another and with **form**—so that what has been deformed through **corruption** <note>The breakdown or decay of a substance into its components.</note> may be reformed through **generation**. The operation of nature is circular, just like the celestial motion of the stars. 

Many overly curious <term>physiologists</term> <note>original: "physiologi"; here meaning natural philosophers or scientists who study the physical world.</note> who are not yet experienced in these matters are also accustomed to thrust this argument upon us, by which they attack the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; literally the "fifth essence," a pure, incorruptible substance that Chemists believed resided within all things, distinct from the four physical elements.</note> of the chemists. Truly, they shall not defeat it unless they bring forward something stronger. They say: "Natural bodies consist of four elements; where shall the fifth element be?" 

We answer that all natural bodies consist of the four elements together with **Form**, which is also "something," and indeed the purest part of any composite. Nor do they consist of these alone, because a true union cannot occur except through some **bond** <note>original: "vinculum"</note>; otherwise, there would only be a juxtaposition or a collision. For the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>The four basic qualities of Aristotelian physics: Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</note> cannot come together into one because of their mutual opposition. Therefore, it was necessary for those qualities to be composed into elements that possess two qualities each, so that they might be joined more easily. By this bond, nature composes all bodies. The philosophers are accustomed to [tell] us...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transformation of elements, moving from the movement of fire and generation to the classification of elements and the process of "corruption"—the chemical breakdown of matter.</meta>

<header>OF THE CHEMICAL ART</header>

...to hand down this truth in a riddle, saying: "Make peace between enemies, and you will possess the entire <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the successful completion of a chemical or alchemical process.</note>, that is, the chemical mastery." To conclude regarding the elements, we say they are threefold: Simple, Composite, and Decomposite. Simple elements are those that are neither corrupted nor subject to composition; it is not *from* these, but *through* these that all other lower elements exercise their powers, which they also receive from them. Composite elements are those which are joined together and suffer corruption. Decomposite elements are those which already come together in composition through corruption. Whoever knows how to convert these into those—the impure into the pure, the composite into the simple—will be the greatest chemist and a skilled worker of wonders.

### *Concerning Corruption.*

### Chapter V.

Chemical corruption is nothing other than the resolution of a whole composed by nature into its constituent parts. Indeed, every composite, if it is resolved, must necessarily be dissolved into that from which it was first composed. Therefore, natural bodies are resolved into the elements and into the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam"; the fifth essence or purest part of a substance, which sits above the four physical elements.</note> of which they consist. We should not think this contradicts the opinion of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), a revolutionary physician who proposed that all matter is made of three principles rather than four elements.</note>, who says: "Every natural body can be resolved by art into only three things: namely, Salt, Sulfur, and Liquor," because air is always found mixed with the liquor or sulfur. Thus, it is not within the reach of the art to enclose pure air, entirely secret from the other elements, in any vessel. Although nature leaves nothing empty, but fills it with composite air from the beginning of creation, yet that air is not separated from the elements by art, but remains mixed. 

It is daily evident to chemists that nothing can be elicited from bodies by the art of separation except water, oil, and earth. And although the oil may be clearer at the start of <term>distillation</term> <note>original: "stillationis"; the process of heating a substance to separate its components.</note> than at the end, it cannot be said to be different in nature, but only by accident: that is, at the end it is more scorched than at the beginning. It remains for us to say that our chemical corruption differs from natural corruption in this: it separates individuals from their species to their genus. No artisan, once the specific form of things is destroyed, can introduce that same form back into that matter. Nature, however, from elements separated in any way from any bodies, can daily rouse forms similar to the previous ones, and diverse ones, and with the greatest effort strives to expand genera into species for the preservation of individuals. But because the corruption of one is the generation of another (as the <term>Academics</term> <note>original: "Academici"; referring to traditional university scholars and Aristotelian philosophers.</note> say), we shall rightly speak of generation.

<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

### On Generation.
### Chapter VI.

**Generation** is said to be the hiding of what is manifest, and then the manifestation of what was hidden. For all bodies are enclosed within three dimensions, namely: manifest <term>Height</term> <note>original: "Altitudine"</note>, hidden <term>Depth</term> <note>original: "Profunditate"</note>, and <term>Breadth</term> <note>original: "Latitudine"</note> which lies in between these. The Philosophers hand this down to us secretly in these words: <note>The author is likely referring to Alchemical "Philosophers" or Hermetic traditions.</note> "There is no passage from one extreme to another, except through the middle." That is to say: from the manifest form of any body, the hidden form cannot become known to us except through the <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "corruptionem"; here meaning the dissolution or breakdown of a substance's outer appearance or state.</note> of what is manifest. In this way, the property of the hidden is revealed. This shall be demonstrated geometrically, so that it may be better understood physically.

When one face, or rather the surface of some solid geometric body designated by the letter **A**, is turned toward us in such a position that the remaining planes are not entirely visible, we can measure the length of that surface which is manifest or facing us. Let us suppose it to be 5 feet. Such also is the height of the other surfaces opposite one another, **b**, **c**, and **f**, whose planes are not known to us except through the breadth of 4 or the depth of 6; when these are multiplied together, they make 24. These, in turn, multiplied by the manifest height of 5, reveal 120 cubic feet, which were previously hidden from us.

In a not dissimilar way, Chemists are accustomed to investigating the latent forms of natural bodies through a "middle" way—namely, the turning of manifest forms into hidden ones. This conversion occurs through the <term>corruption</term> of the specific form and the <term>generation</term> <note>The creation or "coming into being" of a new substance following the destruction of the old.</note> of a more general form—namely, the conversion of <term>decomposite</term> <note>See page 198: elements that have already undergone a prior stage of composition and breakdown.</note> elements into composite ones, and of the impure into the pure.

->*On the excellence of the Ternary.*<-

### Chapter VII.

By the sacred <term>Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternario"; the number three, often seen in alchemy as representing the union of body, soul, and spirit.</note>, the entire world was constructed through unity, in order, number, and measure. For <term>Unity</term> <note>original: "Unitas"; the number one.</note> is not a number, but a covenant of harmony. The <term>Binary</term> <note>original: "Binarius"; the number two.</note>, however, being the first number and the source and origin of discord, was severed from unity through the assumption of matter; it cannot be joined back into one again except by a bond that is utterly indissoluble: which is only one. 

Certainly, he labors in vain who strives to couple equals with equals, for only by an unequal [number] do equals come together into one. "God delights in an odd number." <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet"; a famous quote from the Roman poet Virgil's Eclogues, often cited by alchemists to explain why the "third" element is necessary for chemical or spiritual union.</note> Therefore, the Unary <note>Unity or the number one</note> overcomes and animates the binary (that is, one and one) into a ternary through the simplicity of unity, by a bond that is indeed unbreakable: for the one cannot be divided into any parts. 

Indeed, one and one cannot be joined into two [permanently], since the "two" which ought to bind them are in themselves dissolvable into one and another. Therefore, let the binary be rejected, and the ternary will be reducible to the simplicity of unity: as <term>Johannes Trithemius</term> <note>A famous 15th-century German abbot, cryptographer, and occultist.</note> says in his letter to Germanus Gnaus, and elsewhere: "This ascent, my Germanus, is not human, but familiar only to those..."

->*On the elementary world.*<-
### CHAPTER VIII.

The elementary world is seen to consist primarily of three parts: Minerals, Vegetables, and Animals. Beyond these, there is nothing in this world (that falls under the senses) that we are able to find. Therefore, making a beginning from the minerals, as the foundation of the other parts, I shall come to the remaining material bodies. The Earth is indeed the foundation and the vessel of all things, as much of the celestial influences as of solid bodies. All celestial motions occur around its center. All heavy things are carried toward its center, unless they are held back by the benefit of the earth’s solidity. And all light things flee from its center. As <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the authorship of the Hermetic Corpus, the foundational texts of alchemy.</note> says in that most secret of secrets (which they call the <term>Smaragdine Tablet</term> <note>Also known as the Emerald Tablet; a brief, cryptic text highly revered by alchemists as a summary of their art.</note>): *The Earth is its nurse* <note>original: "Terra nutrix"</note>, and a little further down, *It ascends from the earth into heaven, and again it descends into the earth: thus it receives the power of the superiors and the inferiors.* <note>original: "Ascendit à terra in cœlum, & iterum descendit in terram: sic recipit vim superiorum & inferiorum."</note> In the same place, we see that he has ascribed the powers of the inferiors primarily to the earth. For she is the producer of wonders from the seed of heaven and the <term>menses</term> <note>Refers to the "menstruum" or solvent/source material in alchemical generation.</note> of her sister. As the same Hermes says: *The Sun is the father of the one thing, the Moon truly the mother; the wind carried this thing in its belly* <note>original: "Rei unius pater est Sol, Luna vero mater, portavit ventus hanc rem in ventre suo"</note> (and again what was said before) *the earth is its nurse.*

->*On Minerals.*<-
### CHAPTER IX.

Minerals are those things which are found in the bowels of the earth, thickened into diverse forms and species by the mixing of this [earth] and water, according to their different proportions. Of these, there are three kinds: namely stones, metals, and <term>middle minerals</term> <note>original: "mediorum mineralium"; substances like salts, vitriols, or alum that sit between stones and metals in their properties.</note>. And although all these are generated from a proportional mixing of earth and water, they nonetheless consist of the four elements, just like vegetables and animals: for it was said above in chapter five, that every liquid and <term>sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur often represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance.</note> have hidden air within them. Stones are fashioned by nature from much earth and little water, according to a greater or lesser degree; therefore they are not meltable, but rather brittle in fire. That some come out more brilliant than others, and transparent, happens because of a greater purification of the earth and a clarification performed by nature: since we see even by art that very dry ashes pass into transparent glass, nor can art, by the most curious imitation, mimic the smallest work that was very easy for nature. Metals, indeed, are on the contrary fashioned from much water transmuted into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>, and a little earth converted by nature into sulphur: by which it happens that they are meltable rather than brittle. By long-lasting boiling the water is thickened—provided it does not evaporate—while on the other hand the earth becomes clear: for [the hidden things are made known] by the manifest...

# OF THE CHEMICAL ART
<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>OF THE CHEMICAL ART</header>

manifest things, and these to those, are always and in all things contrary. The <term>metallic principles</term> <note>The fundamental building blocks of metals in alchemical theory.</note> differ in a threefold state: they are either most remote, such as a mixture of earth with water; or remote, such as <term>vitriol</term> <note>A term for various sulfate minerals, often used as a starting material in alchemical processes.</note>; or they are immediate, such as <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury; original: "argentum vivum"</note> and <term>sulfur</term>. From these latter two—depending on the purity of both, or the impurity of one or the other, or of both—nature is said to generate noble or less noble, or even entirely base metal, by means of subterranean heat over scarcely a thousand years. Thus it happens that the longer minerals have been under the obedience of celestial influences, the more they are rightly thought to have acquired the most effective celestial virtues through a firmer and more valiant power, among those things which have the corporeal strength to restore and preserve; and a metal is more noble the less its metallic form has been oppressed by its matter. The general form of metals is equal in all of them, but because of the varying disposition of the matter (as was said above in the second chapter), it breaks forth into various specific forms. But if the universal form is joined to matter disposed in an equal proportion of parts, it must break forth into the most noble species of all, which is Gold: for the place already contains the equalized parts, and nature also knows how to apply proportioned heat as an instrument.

Therefore, Gold is not colder than its heat, nor hotter than its cold; likewise, it is not drier than its moisture, nor more moist than its dry part, but is everywhere tempered, united, and compacted by nature with such perfection that it is thought to yield to no artificial fire at all. Yet the philosophers say that by a natural fire, it can be resolved into its primary matter: and unless it is so resolved, it would be impossible for it to be digested in the human stomach. Because it is not said to be burned by the most vehement fire—which conquers other metals and consumes stones—but is instead rendered purer and more perfect, until it reaches the highest degree of its perfection; then the philosophers hand down that it rejoices in the fire like a <term>Salamander</term> <note>A mythical lizard-like creature believed by alchemists to live in and endure fire without being consumed.</note>. I think they do not mean monetary gold, but gold so purified by <term>antimony</term> <note>A metallic element used in the refining of gold to remove impurities.</note> that nothing of any other mixed metal remains in it.

Wherefore all seem to labor in vain who attempt to make <term>potable gold</term> <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary medicinal elixir made of dissolved gold, believed to grant longevity or cure all ills.</note> (as <term>Marsilio Ficino</term> <note>An influential Italian Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile Hermeticism and Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> says), unless they first resolve the gold into its primary matter—that is, into quicksilver and sulfur—which is the first, proximate, and immediate matter of all metals. Let this, therefore, be the conclusion regarding Gold: that because of its perfection and its likeness to the celestial Sun, it was granted the name "Earthly Sun" by the philosophers. These philosophers also named pure silver (which goldsmiths call "cupelled") the "Earthly Moon." Because it lacks the color, constancy, and weight [of gold], it lacks that compaction and restriction of pores by which metals acquire weight, such as quicksilver. Everything that is naturally "cooked" is made first black, second indeed white, and third red: which last color is excessive, and from perfection...

# BOOK THE FIRST
<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>BOOK THE FIRST.</header>

...application, superabounding. For every natural body to be perfect, it is required that it lacks in nothing, nor exceeds the limits of perfection; which perfection holds the middle path in all things. Now, the middle between black and white is pale, just as between white and the greater perfect red, it is **yellow** <note>original: "citrinum"; in alchemy, the *citrinitas* is a stage of transition between the white and red works.</note>. Hence it is that gold, holding the middle between white and red, has a yellow color, neither exceeding nor diminished. Yellow is nothing other than a determined proportion, the middle between the colors of red and white. 

From this it also follows that all those—as many as think that silver and the other diminished common metals can be transmuted into gold by means of gold—happen to be deceived, as are those who listen to them willingly. For gold has no more color than it needs to color its own <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury; original: "argentum vivum"</note>. Experience has taught learned men that a <term>medicine</term> <note>Often referred to as the Elixir or the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "healing" base metals into noble ones.</note> can be made from gold which can tinge pure silver, or another properly purified metal, into the perfect color of gold; however, no more gold is made by this art than the weight of gold from which such a medicine was drawn. 

Therefore, the advice of those who urge that one should seek in a place that which is not naturally contained within it seems foolish: such as seeking a superabundant color in gold, and a superfluous weight, which it might give to others. For even if it had these, it would not be gold, but something more colored than gold, and not a perfect metal. If, for the reasons already alleged, this perfection of transmutation is not in gold, it will not be in any other mineral [for what was not of perfection in the perfect thing should not be sought in the more imperfect], nor will it be in vegetables, and even less in animals, which by nature are more distant from gold and agree less in the generation of gold than gold itself. Nature also delights in a nature similar to itself, and is transmuted more easily into it than into a foreign one. 

But since in the transmutation of an imperfect body, the highest perfection or a "perfect medicine" is required, which cannot be elicited more closely than from the most perfect thing which is of its own nature (for the better and closer things are always to be chosen in all matters, for the sake of an easier transition): since also every perfection of bodies depends on the <term>temperament</term> <note>The balanced proportion of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of their parts in composition, nothing will be more temperate than gold, or closer to that matter. Wherefore, this perfection of transmutation must be sought from gold, or from nothing. 

Without doubt, the philosophers—men not greedy or thirsty for any mined or common gold—describe transmutations not of common or mined metals, but of their own, and **philosophical** ones. Consulting their own age and posterity, they have endeavored with the greatest labors to find, from the consideration of the temperament of natural gold, the temperament of artificial gold: which they extracted not only from one body, but from diverse ones, as much from vegetables as from minerals and animals. Thus, the gold of the philosophers is a certain...

## THE CHEMICAL ART
<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>THE CHEMICAL ART</header>

...a certain tempered medicine compiled by art, which, like a form separated from its body, has been reduced to such subtleness that it acts upon matter prepared by nature like a celestial form. Indeed, a universal form <note>In alchemical philosophy, the "form" is the essential quality or "soul" of a substance that gives it its specific properties.</note>, once it has taken on a specific shape and is separated from an individual body, retains an active power. It can then impress this power onto a foreign body by the virtue of unity, the strengths of which it has now assumed; at that point, it makes all things one with itself—even if this medicine was drawn from an "untempered" <note>An "untempered" body is one where the four elements or qualities are out of balance.</note> individual. For by art, any elements from any source can be reduced into a single tempered unity. 

Now we must speak of the remaining lower metals. The philosophers have dedicated these to the planets due to the similarity of their qualities: **Tin** to **Jupiter** (hot and moist); **Copper** or bronze to **Venus** (cold, though slightly hot and moist); **Lead** to **Saturn** (cold and dry); and **Iron** to **Mars** (hot and dry). Similarly, these four seem to correspond to the four complexions <note>The "four humors" or temperaments that were believed to govern human health and personality.</note>—not the humors in the physical body of the physicians, but the elemental body—owing to the aforementioned qualities. 

Therefore, whenever the **Choleric**, **Melancholic**, **Phlegmatic**, or **Sanguine** temperaments could be reduced to a balanced state through a most perfectly tempered medicine, the philosophers considered that Copper, Iron, Tin, or Lead had been transmuted into gold. Thus, the wise hidden under the names of common metals their physical and philosophical medicines. They prepared these medicines from common metals for the transmutation of their own "philosophical" metals, so that by using such ambiguous terms, so great a treasure of medicine might remain hidden from the ignorant masses. 

In the meantime, even learned physicians who made no small profession of philosophy were scarcely able to understand this, until **Aureolus Theophrastus Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, a Doctor of both medicines, a Swiss and noble man, revealed the whole matter. He did so with a genius more divine than human, through long travels, and by the company of learned men in all places. He published this knowledge in countless books for the grace of learned men and for the common utility, writing primarily in **German** <note>original: "Germanicè"</note> so that he might provide a wealth of knowledge even to those who were unskilled in the Latin tongue. Following the liberty of this teacher, I have wished perhaps to treat this matter more openly; for I desire that others might profit as much through me as I have through him.

Now it remains for me to speak of the "intermediate minerals" and their corresponding extremes, such as all the **marcasites** <note>In early chemistry, "marcasite" was a general term for various metallic sulfides or minerals that looked like ores.</note>. There is found a golden marcasite, a silver one, a tin one, and a lead one (this last I consider to be **antimony** <note>original: "antimonium vel Stibium"</note>). These I have seen; the others are as yet unknown to me, such as the copper and iron varieties. There are also **magnesia**, **tutia** <note>Zinc oxide, often found as a crust in smelting furnaces.</note>, **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide used as a pigment.</note>, **arsenic**, many salts, alums, sulfurs, and others of that kind, which contribute more to a "physical transmutation" than to that common metamorphosis, which, if not unknown to philosophers...

<page-num>205</page-num>
<header>Book One.</header>

...at least neglected. Therefore, they are called **middle minerals** <note>These are substances like antimony, bismuth, or various salts and vitriols that share properties with both metals and stones.</note> because they do not entirely resemble a metal, nor a stone in every respect, but they possess a great deal of affinity with both. Concerning the other of these extremes—namely, **stone**—it would be superfluous to treat it specifically here, since it has been handled abundantly enough by Pliny, Albertus Magnus, and other most approved authors. It is only fitting for my purpose to state the difference between a metal and a stone: a stone neither melts nor is it malleable <note>original: "malleo ductilis," meaning it cannot be hammered thin without breaking.</note> under a hammer; a metal, however, is workable under the hammer and liquefiable by fire. **Middle minerals**, however, do melt, but they cannot be drawn out; instead, they shatter into fragments, in which respect they resemble stone, though in their melting they resemble metal.

### *On Vegetables.*
### Chapter X.

**Vegetables** are defined as those things which take nourishment from the earth through a fixed root. These are of three types: **herbal**, which are vegetables that are not preserved in the earth beyond a year or a little more, but once the leaves and stalks have dried out, they are propagated by nature through the decay of the seed dropped into the earth. **Arboreal** vegetables are the largest, which rise up through solid roots into trunks and solid branches, and are preserved for many years. **Plant-like** <note>This likely refers to shrubs or perennial bushes.</note> vegetables are the middle ground between these, being larger than herbs but much smaller than trees, yet reflecting the form of both; they remain green and are preserved longer than herbs, yet they perish sooner than trees. 

But because these things are known to all philosophers, even the most mediocre, I thought they should be passed over briefly—noting only this: that just as they provide food for living beings, they likewise provide a <term>medicamentum</term> <note>A medicine or healing essence.</note> when they have been purified by art from their own corrupting matter. For the power of the "form" <note>The essential life-force or medicinal quality of the plant.</note> is hindered by the matter that restrains its action. It will be better to separate this essence outside the stomach than to do so within the stomach of a sick person, which is already too weak to perform such a separation. Truly, if they are meant to be food, they should be administered with the body <note>i.e., eaten as whole food.</note>; for the more general parts of the body—namely the natural <term>liquor</term>, <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>balsam</term> <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, these represent the vital fluids, the combustible principle of life, and the preservative essence that prevents decay.</note>—must each be nourished by its like. For excesses and deficiencies that cause imbalance must be reduced to equality by their contrary—that is, by a tempered substance. This must be most diligently considered by the physician, both in preparing vegetable medicines and those drawn from the parts of living beings.

### *On Animals.*
### Chapter XI.

**Animals** are bodies that, being naturally moved by themselves, take nourishment through the mouth. Alchemists, not without reason, consider a threefold motion in natural things: **Corrupting**, **Generating**, and **Animating**. Philosophers say that motion happens either *per se* <note>In itself / by its own nature.</note> or *per accidens* <note>By happenstance or secondary cause.</note>. That which happens *per se* is natural and causative, such as the motion of the **First Mover** <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere in the geocentric universe that moves all others.</note> and the Zodiac...

<meta>This page concludes the introductory discussion on the natural order—specifically the types of motion and the classification of living souls—before transitioning into Book Two, which focuses on the practical application of alchemy.</meta>

<page-num>206</page-num>
<header>OF THE ALCHEMICAL ART</header>
<meta>catchword: they can,</meta>

...be mediated, or caused, as is the case for the <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>These are Aristotelian terms: "generation" is the coming-into-being of a thing, while "corruption" is its decay or dissolution.</note> of things. Motion which occurs by chance or through local movement is either rectilinear (straight-line) or curvilinear (curved). Rectilinear motion is perpendicular, oblique, or transverse. Perpendicular motion is that carried either upward or downward. Curvilinear motion is either circular or bent. Circular motion is either revolving or rotating. A knowledge of these motions is not useless in this art; however, because these matters belong to the Philosopher and the Geometer—both of which an Alchemist <note>original: "Chemistam"</note> ought to be—let what has been said so far suffice. Animals have this in common with vegetables: both take in nourishment for their growth, though animals do so through a mouth and plants through a root; the latter are, in turn, lower than animals in their senses. There are three kinds of living creatures: reptiles on the earth, winged creatures in the air, and swimming creatures beneath the waters. In brute animals, there is a double motion of the soul: the vegetative and the sensitive. In the human soul, a triple motion is held, for to the previous two is added the motion of the <term>rational soul</term> <note>In period philosophy, the rational soul was the highest level of existence, granting humans the ability to reason, which was thought to be eternal.</note>, which is perpetual.

# BOOK TWO.
->*On Alchemical Practice.*<-
### CHAPTER I.

After the Alchemical art has been treated theoretically as much as is lawful, it remains now to prove by experiment—or by the senses—what the Alchemist can attain through imagination or intellect. The **practice** of Alchemists is a demonstration made tangible to the senses, manifesting from hidden things those latent forms of nature which the philosopher previously grasped through certain and known reasons of philosophy and the intellect. For I do not believe one should rely so heavily on the writings of authors alone that, if a superior experiment teaches something else, it should not be preferred over the opinions of those who often happen to assert and judge matters they have not deeply inspected, and which are inconsistent with themselves. The Alchemical craft turns chiefly upon three things: namely, the **place**, the **instrument**, and the **operation**. The "place" is twofold: specifically, the furnaces and the vessels containing the matter itself. The "instrument" is also double: the **destroying fire** and the **generating fire** <note>original: "ignis corrumpens, & ignis generans." Destroying fire breaks substances down (analysis), while generating fire encourages the growth or maturation of the "Philosophical child" or stone.</note>. Likewise, the "operation" is double: **solution** and **congelation** <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid and hardening a liquid back into a solid.</note>.

->*On the Alchemical Place.*<-
### CHAPTER II.

The furnace itself, or the vessel containing the matter, is considered by Alchemists to be the "proper place." Furnaces vary among different craftsmen, and vessels are formed in diverse ways according to anyone’s judgment. However, according to the three perpendicular motions—namely upward, downward, and sideways—we shall first set down a triple and unique furnace, never seen before this, in which three different operations can be performed,

->*On the Structure of the Triple Furnace.*<-

### CHAPTER III.

It will be worthwhile to demonstrate the structure of this remarkable furnace before arriving at the operations themselves. Let two walls be erected, built of bricks laid flat, distant from each other by the interval of a cubit <note>An ancient unit of measure, approximately 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note>, and of a height and width of a foot and a half: such as can be seen marked with the letter **B**. From one wall to the other, let four iron bars be extended transversely, upon which the bricks forming the first floor are supported, which is designated by the letter **R**. In the middle of the said floor, let a round hole be left open, four digits wide, through which the neck of an inverted earthenware <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation; the name comes from the Latin for "gourd."</note> without a bottom may protrude below, having a base pierced at the neck, etc., marked with the letter **E**, which can be closed with a pointed lid marked with the letter **F**.

Upon this base, three walls—or two opposite ones—are to be built with the bricks set either on their sides or flat, one cubit high, touching each other or meeting at right angles. Upon these walls, other iron bars are to be placed in a row, so that there is a finger's width of space between one and the next; these will serve as the grate for the middle furnace, as marked by the letter **V**. Now we have constructed a <term>descensory</term> furnace <note>A furnace designed for distillation by descent, where the distilled substance flows downward into a receiver rather than upward.</note>, and the vessel will also be called a descensory.

Upon this grate, it is necessary to erect three other walls similar to the previous ones, with this single change: after the walls have been half-built, a curved iron bar is to be inserted into the opposite walls to hold an earthenware cucurbit suspended above the grate, and a hole must be left in the middle wall through which the neck of the cucurbit may protrude, which appears marked with the character **Z**. After the cucurbit has been placed in the furnace, the side that had remained open for inserting the cucurbit can be closed, leaving one or two holes, or more, through which the coals can be stirred with an iron rod.

Upon these walls, four other iron bars are again to be placed, upon which bricks may form a base with a round opening in the middle through which coals can be fed; subsequently, that hole must be closed with a removable brick. This base is designated for us by the letter **X**, and the hole by the letter **I**. Again, upon that base, build a wall rising to the width of a single brick, leaving a small door marked with the letter **H**, through which coals may be cast into the said hole. Upon this wall, it is proper to construct another perforated base entirely similar to the first. Thus the <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" the heat from the roof back down onto the material being heated.</note> is completed, marked with the letter **A** and an arch. Finally, upon this base, [build] again four walls rising to the height of a cubit...

### CHAPTER IV.

Four bricks are to be erected sideways in a square so that they do not touch each other, leaving an interval of four digits <note>A "digit" or finger's breadth is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly 0.75 inches.</note>. but double in height—that is, two stones high—leaving a small door through which the coals can be stirred with an iron tool; this is marked with the letter **B**. The four corners of the lower chamber are to be closed, but those of the upper vaulting <note>original: "concamerationis"; referring to the internal arched structure of the furnace.</note> are to be left open, so that the heat may pass through these holes and enter the side furnaces. Above this furnace, we shall erect a small tower made of earth, or preferably copper, wider at the bottom than at the top, marked with the letter **C**. To the four sides of the said furnace, four other furnaces are to be fitted, designated **E**, **H**, **G**, and **F**. All the upper shells should be perforated with small holes (wide enough for a chickpea to pass through), as marked with the letters **A.B.** Each of the lower shells should have a small door cut into the side near the bottom, four digits wide and six or seven high. These four doors should correspond exactly to the four holes of the lower middle furnace, so that the aforementioned iron dampers can be inserted between them. They must move freely so they can be raised or lowered to open or close the passage as needed to regulate the fire. 

Now we have the complete furnace, which we are accustomed to call the <term>acedia</term> <note>From the Greek word for "sloth" or "lack of care." In alchemy, this refers to the "lazy" furnace (athanor) because it does not require constant tending.</note>, both because it is slow in its operation due to the gentle fire, and perhaps because it appeals to the lazy, for once the tower **C** has been filled with coals, the fire does not need to be tended for several hours—the duration of which you can measure by the height of the tower.

### CHAPTER V.

I consider **vessels** <note>original: "Vasa"</note> to be more than just chemical tools; rather, they hold the second place for matter and substance, right after the furnaces. This is not unlike how nature herself utilizes the globe of the earth and its caverns as vessels for the "cooking" <note>original: "decoctione"; referring to the natural heat of the earth maturing ores over time.</note> or generation of minerals. Similarly, in animals, the mother's matrix <note>original: "matrice"; the womb or site of biological development.</note> acts as a vessel, while the womb serves as the furnace. The vessels used by Chemists are made partly of glass, or the most compact potter's clay, and partly of copper or other purer metals. Their forms may be seen above, where we have illustrated the furnaces.

# BOOK TWO.

...[which] nature employs in the generation of things. **Internal fire** is proper to every substance and is naturally implanted within it, a fact which the Chemist must also take into account. Chemists use **violent fire** for calcination <note>roasting a substance to a powder</note>, for subliming drier substances, or for melting metals. They use **tempered fire**, adjusted by degrees, during distillation, whether ascending <note>vapor rising</note> or descending <note>vapor falling</note>. They use a **natural fire**—one similar to natural heat—while they putrefy, digest, congeal, or fix substances through circulation. These operations are defined in the following chapter.

->*On operation.*<-
### CHAPTER VII.

**Operation** is the name given to the application of hands and instruments for carrying out chemical work. The work of Chemistry is twofold: namely, **Solution** and **Congelation**. The solution of a body is its calcination. Congelation is the actual condensation of a spirit <note>a volatile or gaseous substance</note> into a vapor. Solution is usually performed in various ways at the discretion of the craftsman—either by itself, or together with its companion process, namely congelation. It is done "by itself" when a body is placed in an earthenware vessel and, through the unrestrained exhalation of its spirit, is crumbled into a very dry lime <note>original: "calcem"; the powdery residue left after heating</note>. This is also commonly done while the material lies in a ceramic pot, constantly stirred until it dries into a powder.

Indeed, solution and congelation occur at the same time when a body is placed in an earthenware or glass **cucurbit** <note>original: "cucurbita"; a gourd-shaped chemical vessel</note> and dried; the vapor is so retained by a glass **beaked helmet** <note>original: "galeam rostratam"; the top part of a still, commonly called an alembic head</note> that the spirit, having been released into the air and then congealed again into a watery body, is received in a glass vessel placed below. By this method, the earthy body is dissolved into lime, and the watery part into an airy spirit, which is again congealed into a watery body—all in a single operation which the common people call **distillation**, but the Philosopher <note>referring to the learned practitioner of the "Hermetic Philosophy" or alchemy</note> more properly calls **separation**.

Solution can also take place simultaneously with congelation through a closed **reverberatory vessel**, made of two earthenware vessels joined together with a strong clay sealant so that the matter cannot "breathe" <note>leak or escape</note>; when done in a reverberatory furnace, they usually call this **sublimation**. There is also another type of solution performed by itself which they call **putrefaction**; this is when a dry body is sprinkled again with plenty of its own water, enclosed in a double cucurbit, and placed in the *acedia* furnace <note>the "slothful" or slow-burning furnace described on previous pages</note>. But if the body is soaked in only a little water, or at least less of it, it will be congealed by the same technique: as the dry overcomes the moist, it is then called "congelation performed by itself."

In a **bain-marie** <note>original: "balneo Mariæ"; a water bath</note> or "sea-bath," a solution is made which can be called putrefaction; the vessel is either doubled and suspended over vapor, or submerged halfway in water, yet enclosed on all sides by vapor. The final type of solution performed by itself, and the most beautiful, occurs when a liquid—having been frequently rectified <note>purified</note> by distillation and rarefied—is hidden in a double glass vessel or a **pelican** <note>original: "pellicano"; a circulatory distillation vessel with arms that return the liquid to the main body</note>. With the uppermost part of the vessel protruding from the furnace, it is worked by a slow fire until no more vapor rises, but in

# BOOK THREE.
->*On the practice of chemical operation.*<-

### CHAPTER I.

In the preceding treatise, we defined the operations of the Chemists; in this one, however, we shall put them into practice, insofar as they are used in medical matters. For it is not our purpose to treat individually those things which have been written by others in the past; rather, we shall endeavor to propose certain general ways of operating to students, by which they may most easily grasp all the preparations of natural medicines. Therefore, by demonstrating the use of a triple furnace, we will teach how to distill and prepare for medical use the three parts of the world: namely, the vegetable, mineral, and animal. 

For the mineral part, we shall take **Roman vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum Romanum"; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note>, which we will prepare into an oil in the middle **reverberatory furnace** <note>a furnace where the heat is "reverberated" or reflected from the roof onto the material</note>. In the same heat, wine will be distilled into a **quintessence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the highly purified "fifth essence" or concentrated alcohol</note> in the uppermost furnace, and in the lowest furnace (the **descensory** <note>a furnace designed for distillation by descent, where the product flows downward</note>), the more solid parts of animals will be turned into oil and water. Whoever knows how to correctly imitate these three operations from the demonstration we provide, there is nothing that might come into his mind about which he should despair of being able to prepare by a **scientific** <note>original: "physica"; referring to natural philosophy and the study of nature's laws</note> rather than an **empirical** <note>original: "empirica"; referring to practice based on trial and error without theoretical understanding</note> method. 

I say this so that it may be seen by everyone what the difference is between scientific preparations and empirical ones. For it is fitting for a true man of science to prepare his own individual ingredients (called **Simples** <note>original: "Simplicia"; medicinal ingredients used on their own rather than in a compound</note> by pharmacists) without the mixture or addition of any other thing that might change the nature of the substance being prepared. Finally, he will be able to mix or blend such juices or powders—having first purified them on their own—into medicine if he wishes; but the simpler the medicine is, the more powerful it will be. 

Nor should it frighten us that some physicians once wrote that simple medicines kill, since they use that term ("simple") differently than the Chemists do. Physicians say that **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Reubarbarum"</note> is a simple, but Chemists assert it is a compound, which they demonstrate both by art and experiment, not by words alone. Indeed, when empirics try to imitate scientists without the knowledge of science, they do not... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

### *On the preparation of Vitriol into an oil.*
### CHAPTER II.

Take three or four weights of **Roman** or **Hungarian vitriol** <note>original: "Vitrioli Romani vel Hungarici"; these are sulfate minerals, typically copper sulfate (blue) or iron sulfate (green)</note>, which, placed in an earthen pot capable of withstanding a strong fire, should be burned with glowing coals until whatever moisture it contained evaporates. Or rather, you shall distill all the moisture to preserve the spirit, as will be said below. When you see a hard mass at the bottom of the vessel, throw burning coals in and around the pot: in this way, you will **calcine** <note>original: "calcinabis"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it</note> it into a very deep red mass. 

Finally, remove it from the fire, break the pot, and crush the mass into a powder. Place this into an earthen **cucurbit** <note>original: "cucurbitam"; a gourd-shaped glass or ceramic vessel used as the base of a still</note> with a long neck, made of the same clay used for goldsmiths' melting pots, leaving two-thirds of the vessel empty. However, place the pot, previously protected with **lute** <note>original: "luto"; a clay-based paste used to seal or protect vessels from high heat</note>, in a transverse position, as seen depicted in the middle **reverberatory furnace** <note>a furnace that reflects heat back onto the substance being heated</note> and marked with the letter **G**. To the protruding neck, fit a glass vessel designated by the letter **O** (which they call a **retort** <note>original: "retortam"</note>), placed in cold water and submerged with a lead ring so that the vacuum does not lift it out of the water. The joints must be secured with strong lute so they do not breathe <note>leak air or vapor</note>. 

Next, the fire must be lit under the cucurbit, and gradually increased through four degrees, each of which should last two hours, until it is completely buried in glowing coals. That violent fire must be continued until the retort, which was previously dark and filled with spirits, now gradually clears, so that what it contains can be seen inside. Once this is perceived, you must stop, and when the fire has gone out on its own, separate the receiving vessel. Whatever oil it contains should be removed, stored in a solid glass container, and kept closed for use with the best artificial wax. You will find the method for making this kind of wax in the book by **Philippus Ulstadius** <note>a 16th-century Nuremberg physician known for his works on distillation</note>, titled *The Heaven of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Coelum Philosophorum"</note>. 

It must be noted that the earthen cucurbits should not be damaged by the fire or develop even the smallest crack, otherwise the oil and the labor will be lost; therefore, care must be taken that they are made from the best clay. The **calcantum** <note>another name for vitriol or copperas</note> or vitriol must also be dried very well before it is distilled; otherwise, the oil will be diluted with much **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmate"; the watery, inactive portion of a distillate</note>. This, however, can be removed by distillation in a **bain-marie** <note>original: "balneo Mariae"; a water bath used for gentle heating</note>; in this way, the pure oil will remain at the bottom of the vessel,
