# SPECULATIVE [PHILOSOPHY] #

The passage toward salvation must be made by working philosophically. For what does it profit to have heard of the arts in the Universities, or to have read of them privately, unless they are brought from potentiality into action, any more than his "hail" <note>original: <term>χαῖρε</term> (chaire)—a standard Greek greeting</note> profits a parrot? Certainly nothing: because all knowledge that is not proven by experience is not an art, but a clinging ignorance. Now let us proceed to the voluntary separation, which is perfected by moral philosophy. Once the preparation of the body is complete, it will easily be separated from the remaining parts, when whatever the body has desired beyond philosophical necessity has been denied to it by the soul—at the urging of the mind or spirit. What "philosophical necessity" is shall be discussed later. From this separation results the **first union** <term>unio prima</term> <note>In alchemical thought, the first stage of reunification where the soul and spirit join after being purified from the 'dross' of the physical body</note>, namely that of the spirit with the soul, through the continued study of moral philosophy. These things had to be proposed to students first, so they might know by what reasoning I have mixed metaphysics with physics and morals here, and when moral matters are to be compared to metaphysical ones, and these to those and to physics: lest perhaps I seem to have blocked the entrance for readers to grasp the matter (as many usually do) while they are stuck in a labyrinth.

->*On philosophical study, and the first grade.*<-

### CHAPTER II.

The study of philosophers is the diligent inquiry of the true and the necessary. The **True** is that from which nothing can be absent, to which nothing can be absent, and much less can anything oppose it. The **Necessary** is all that which we cannot be without. Truth, therefore, is the highest virtue and an impregnable castle, inhabited by very few friends, but besieged by countless enemies; it is currently hated by almost the whole world, but it is an insuperable pledge to those who possess it. In this citadel is contained the true and undoubted **stone and treasure of the philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and granting enlightenment</note>, which, not gnawed by moths nor broken into by thieves, remains forever while all other things dissolve—placed for the ruin of many, for the salvation of others. 

This is the thing commonly considered most vile, greatly despised and hated, yet not hateful, but lovable and precious to philosophers above gems and pure gold <note>original: "aurum obrizon"—gold that has been refined and tested for purity</note>. She is the lover of all, an enemy to almost all, findable everywhere, yet found by very few—almost none—crying out to everyone through the streets: "Come to me, all you who seek, and I will lead you into the true path." This is that thing preached only by true philosophers, which conquers all things and is conquered by nothing, penetrating every hard and solid body and heart, making firm everything soft, and strengthening everything hard to resist. She meets us all, and we do not see her, shouting and saying in a loud voice: "I am the way of truth, pass through me: because there is no other passage to life," and we do not want to hear her. She emits a scent of sweetness, but we do not perceive it. She offers herself to us daily as a feast in sweetness, and we do not taste her. Gently, toward salvation...

# PHILOSOPHY. #

[sa]lvation draws us, and yet, resisting its pull, we are unwilling to perceive it. For we have become like stones, having eyes and not seeing, having ears and not hearing, having noses that do not smell, equipped with mouth and tongue but neither tasting nor speaking, doing nothing with hands and feet nor walking. O how wretched is such a race of men! They are no better than stones—indeed, they are far inferior to them, because it is not the stones, but these men, who must give an account of their actions! "Be transformed," it says, "be transformed from dead stones into living **philosophical stones** <term>lapides philosophicos</term>." <note>In alchemical philosophy, this represents the transition from a "base" spiritual state to an "ennobled" one, mirroring the transmutation of lead into gold.</note> I am the **medicine** <term>medicina</term>, correcting and transforming that which is no longer into that which it was before corruption, and even into something better—and that which is not into that which it ought to be.

Behold, I am before the doors of your **conscience** <term>conscientia</term>, knocking day and night, and will you not open to me? Yet I wait mildly, nor do I depart from you in anger, but I endure your injuries with patience, desiring to lead you by exhortation through that very patience. Come again, and come again more often, you who seek **wisdom** <term>sapientia</term>, and buy for free—not with gold or silver, and even less by your own labors—that which is offered to you of its own accord. A sounding voice, sweet and pleasing to the ears of those practicing philosophy! O inexhaustible fountain of riches for those thirsting for truth and justice! O solace for the imperfection of the desolate! Why do you anxious mortals seek further? Why do you wretches agitate your minds with infinite cares? What madness blinds you, I ask? Since everything that is outside you—which you seek when it is not with you—is actually within you, though not *from* you. 

It is usually the vice of the common crowd to despise what is their own and always crave what belongs to others. Here, we take "what is our own" as that which is appropriated for us, for we have nothing good from ourselves; but if we are able to have any good thing, we receive it as a gift from Him who alone is good. Conversely, whatever evil we have, we have appropriated to ourselves from an external evil through disobedience. Therefore, nothing is truly a man’s own from himself except the evil he possesses. Whatever good he has from the Good, he does not have from himself, but possesses as a contributed "own" thing from the Good, provided he receives it. The **life [that is] the light of men** <note>original: "vita lux hominum" — a reference to the prologue of the Gospel of John</note> shines in us (though obscurely) as if in darkness; it is not from us, yet it must be sought *in* us, and not *from* us, but from Him to whom it belongs. He planted it in us so that in His light—He who dwells in inaccessible light—we might see light; and in this we might excel His other creatures, having been made like Him for this reason: that He gave us a spark of His own light. Therefore, **truth** <term>veritas</term> is not to be sought in ourselves, but in the **image of God** <term>imago Dei</term> which is within us. 

Further, so that we may satisfy the definition of the True, we say that nothing can be added to the True; for what can be added to the One, I ask, if anything is even lacking, or what can strive against it? Since nothing truly exists besides that One. Who is ignorant that nothing is **perfect** <term>perfectum</term> except that One, which is neither diminished in any part nor admits anything superfluous, but is so abundant in power and virtue that from its abundance...

...to grant to those who are failing, and to always abound equally. For what can be such a thing, except that alone which gives to everything that is its being, and does not receive its being from another? But being itself is the whole of what can be, which nothing hinders, because besides it there is nothing. That which is nothing, truly is not, and conversely, that which truly is not, is nothing. Whatever is outside of the truth, truly is not: because truth is that one thing which is everything that truly exists. 

Falsehood, therefore—which is nothing except that which is contrary to true being, and ought not to exist, and exists only through the privation <term>privatio</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "privation" refers to the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note> of true essence—is nothing: because it truly is not. Whence true philosophers conclude that **sin** and **death** are nothing, because they do not proceed from true being, but from the privation of true essence. 

**Sin** <term>peccatum</term> therefore is the privation of good, which is the efficient cause of death: because **death** <term>mors</term> is the privation of life, which life is the end of the good. From the good of truth, a stimulus results, against which the stings of death shall not prevail, and against which it is hard for anyone, no matter how stubborn, to kick <note>A reference to the biblical idiom "to kick against the pricks" (Acts 9:5), meaning to struggle uselessly against fate or divine will.</note>. 

Whoever would wish to add anything to the truth would be forced to substitute falsehood for truth under some cloak; for truth, supported only by the garment of perfection, is not afraid. But if that first parent of ours <note>Referring to Adam.</note> had not stripped off this **garment of justice** <term>amictus justitiæ</term>, he would not have feared to be seen naked—as he was not seen before, nor was he truly so, but was fortified with every beauty. 

Adam, therefore, deprived of the perennial garment of truth, sought a false cloak from the leaves of trees, by which he confessed his error within himself and said before the Lord: *I am naked, Lord.* God, taking pity on him because he feared and confessed having lost the truth, decided to restore to him freely the wedding garment of perennial glory in place of the lost cloak of earthly happiness, through His own Son: who said and showed Himself to be the way of truth and the life for us, and by His death took away from us the perpetual death by which we all deserved to be punished. 

See then, brothers, how great is the effect of truth, that it is beneficial and peaceful toward its enemies, provided they recognize it. We have all sinned with Adam, but there are very few—and almost none—who openly confess their nakedness with him; rather, everyone desires not only to appear but to be more perfect, though he himself is the most imperfect of all, and most naked when cloaked in fine linen and purple. We have inherited this vice from the first appetite of our first parent: that our flesh, above all else, desires—whether by right or by wrong—to know, to possess, or to be honored, which is the most destructive pursuit of men in this age. 

Again, truth is subject to no power or worldly strength; therefore, nothing hinders it, for it is itself true **strength** <term>fortitudo</term>, surpassing the power of the whole world. Even if the body of one possessing the truth were cut into a thousand pieces, his soul suffers nothing: but rejoices in that **martyrdom** <term>martyrium</term>. This is the power of truth, which few have attained, but below you shall hear more widely of its excellence. Now we shall say...

# PHILOSOPHY #

...let us discuss further what properties truth possesses, namely **piety** <term>pietas</term> <note>In this context, piety refers not just to religious devotion, but to a dutiful respect for the natural order and the divine source of knowledge.</note> joined with **justice** <term>justitia</term> in an inseparable bond. For piety is a grace given by God, which teaches everyone to know themselves strictly. **Justice**, indeed, is said to be the rendering to each person what is their own; whoever possesses these virtues is the wealthiest of all. It must also be known in this place that piety produces peace and mercy, which will be discussed in their proper place.

It remains now for us to look at the other part of philosophical study, which is **necessity** <term>necessitas</term>. We cannot do without food and clothing; therefore, they are necessary for us. However, anyone (even one who possesses them) can do without delicacies in food and drink, as well as the luxury of clothing made of fine linen, scarlet, or purple; therefore, these things are not necessary. 

There are few who observe "philosophical necessity." As for "vulgar necessity," who—even the most unlearned person—does not endure it against their will, desiring to be without only that which they cannot attain? The common crowd judges all things superficially according to appearance; there are almost none who judge according to depth. From this it happens that **truth** is loathed when it comes into the light under a "torn bark" <note>The "torn bark" or "ragged shell" is a metaphor for truth appearing in a humble or unattractive physical form, such as a poor teacher or a plain book.</note>. Today, splendid clothing, bracelets, necklaces, and jewels have more power than truth and wisdom themselves. 

Is it any wonder, when the highest wisdom has been made foolishness to the world, while this [worldly] vanity is called wisdom? The Holy Scriptures bear witness to this. Christ, who is Truth itself and Wisdom, is removed by the "wise" of the world; He who is not of the world, yet nevertheless overcomes the world. **Barabbas** the thief, however, is chosen instead, because he was of the world and vicious. 

Why should we wonder, then, if the world shrinks from the professors of the true arts as if from poison, since it persecuted Truth itself? Even the Gentiles <note>The author uses "Gentiles" here to refer to non-Christian classical philosophers like Cicero or Terence.</note>, followers of the world, openly admit this when they say that "truth breeds hatred, while compliance breeds friends." <note>A famous Roman proverb from Terence's play *Andria*: "Obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit."</note> By this doctrine of theirs, they seem to wish to persuade men toward ambition rather than toward virtue and truth. 

I say these things because, in this "iron age," <note>The "Iron Age" is a classical concept (from Hesiod and Ovid) referring to the final, most degenerate era of humanity characterized by greed and conflict.</note> if anything is brought to light from the true and indubitable fountains of true philosophy for the benefit of the commonwealth, it is rejected if it is not in harmony with the doctrine of the Greeks and Gentiles. It is rejected by those who have swallowed the dregs of that study which that vain school of philosophers invented. 

Tell me, I ask, you men of judgment: how can it be that a Gentile, lacking the true light entirely, brings light to others? They possessed a human and worldly wisdom, which is reckoned as foolishness before God because it is not from God; and yet, every parent twists their child toward learning it throughout their middle years. Afterward, if it happens that such a "false philosopher" is compared to a true **Speculative Sage** <term>Sophus</term>, the former soon bursts into insults, despising every good and true thing that he did not hear from his own schoolmaster—as if there were no good or truth except that which proceeded from Gentiles who were ignorant of the truth. For the **Speculative Mind**, aided by the true light of truth, can—I see—attain in a single year or a single moment...

...than the persistent and relentless labor of a man’s whole life, seeking light without light from those who themselves lack all light. But let us see what the doctrine of the pagan <note>original: "gentilium"; referring here to the Classical Greek and Roman philosophers who lived before or outside of the Christian revelation.</note> philosophers might be. They place the **highest good** <term>summum bonum</term> in living well, which they divide into the honorable and the useful. They consider the ambition for honors and praise as the highest form of honor; finally, the acquisition and preservation of riches—whether acquired by right or wrong, by war or by toil—they call "useful." From these things, they expect nothing after death except to have left a memory and fame of themselves to posterity. Partly denying and partly ignorant of the **Resurrection**, they fashion a thousand trifles in poems—devoid of truth—to the perpetual destruction of others and themselves. 

Behold! This is why the professors of the true arts are so hated by those who carry a great reputation in various arts and faculties. Even if experience places the truth before their eyes, it is rejected as false unless it is confirmed by the inexperienced opinions of those who have never experienced the truth; and anyone who wishes to profess the truth is judged a fool with great clamor. If someone rightfully loathes these various authors, their disciples in the universities soon threaten to punish them or subject them to the greatest disgrace, which they call "riding the donkey" <note>original: "equitationem asini"; a medieval form of public humiliation where a person was forced to ride backward on a donkey through the streets.</note>. Meanwhile, they do not see that it is their own daily solace to ride like donkeys through the streets, while they try to disgrace others. Should the truth be kept silent because, as the pagans teach, it breeds hatred? By no means; rather, it befits a philosopher to face death rather than deny the truth. In all things, truth must be observed as the highest good among Christians; blessed are those to whom it is granted by heaven to persevere in it to the end, which (alas, how wretched!) happens to very few. Let us pray to God that He makes us partakers of this alone. It must be concluded, therefore, that truth alone is to be sought and carefully searched for in all things. Now, listen to how one must leap further to its summit.

### Recapitulation of the first stage and the second chapter.

Philosophers direct their study toward the investigation of truth through opinions consistent with reason, in matters that escape the senses. But the study of **Chemists** <term>Chemistarum</term> <note>In this context, "Chemist" refers to an alchemist or a natural philosopher who works with the physical properties of matter to find hidden truths.</note> is to free the imperceptible truth from its shackles within perceptible things, so that they may hunt for celestial virtues with a very subtle wit. Whoever wishes to learn the Chemical art must learn philosophy—not the Aristotelian kind, but that which teaches the truth. 

Some disciple of Aristotle might say: "Do you make Aristotle a liar?" Not I, but he makes himself one; for his entire doctrine consists in **ambiguity** <term>amphibologia</term> <note>The use of double meanings or vague language to avoid a direct statement; a common critique of Scholasticism by Renaissance thinkers.</note>, which is the best cloak for lies. Since he himself criticized Plato and the others for the sake of seeking fame, he could find no more convenient in—

### *On the second degree of philosophers, which is called Knowledge.*

### CHAPTER III.

**Knowledge** <term>Cognitio</term> is the certain and undoubted resolution of opinions conceived about the truth, achieved through experience. An **opinion of truth** is a doubtful presumption clinging to the mind. The **experience of truth** is a manifest demonstration. **Resolution**, indeed, is the laying down of doubt. We cannot become certain about any doubt otherwise than by experiencing it, and nowhere better than within ourselves. Therefore, let us verify what we said above about the truth, beginning with ourselves. We said above that piety consists in the knowledge of oneself. From this, it follows that I begin philosophical knowledge from [self-knowledge] itself. But no one can know himself unless he knows *what*—and not just *who*—he is, upon whom he depends, or to whom he belongs (for according to the law of truth, no one is his own master), and for what end he was made. Once these things are known, piety begins, which concerns two things: namely, the Creator, and the creature similar to oneself. It is impossible for a creature to know itself by itself, unless its Creator is known first. How can the effect be known before the cause? Does not every beginning precede its middle and end, or shall someone approach a matter from the end?

God is without beginning and end, existing through Himself, filled with all glory, which He did not wish to possess alone out of His own generosity, but wished to make us—whom He created in His image—participants in it; we are the first pattern and mystery of His generosity. How does it happen then, that we are ignorant of that wonderful secret of the truth? Listen, brother: just as we were created by the Most Precious from the most vile, so on account of the matter...

### SPECULATION

<meta>catchword: wines</meta>

...from which we were made, we are more prone to any vile thing than to that which made us most precious after being vile: indeed, we would have been superior to the angels, if we had remained in such a rank of dignity. Wonder, as many of you miserable mortals as are with me, that the highest **Craftsman** <term>artifex</term> <note>original: "artifex"; the author uses this term to describe God as the ultimate Alchemist or Architect of the universe.</note> of all things wished to handle with His own hands the most vile material from the mud of the earth, and from it to raise up a most precious creature. Let us not think this was done without cause, but rather so that we might recognize what we are, and restrain ourselves from the pride of arrogance. Those who do otherwise—there is none among us who does not hate the poor man whom God has chosen, even though he consists of the same mass from which we were all made. Hence it happens that God is no respecter of persons, but a lover of **poverty** and **humility**, and an enemy of lofty **pride** <term>superbia</term>.

No one can know the Creator better than a craftsman is known from his work. We see, therefore, who He is: the one who can raise up the most precious thing from the most vile; certainly, none can do this except Him who created both. In no way can a butler change wine into water <note>original: "vinum in aquam"; likely a rhetorical inversion of the Miracle at Cana to show that only the Creator has power over the essence of His creations.</note>, yet He can do it who created both wine and water. He did something even greater when He **transmuted** <note>original: "transmutavit"; a technical term in alchemy for changing one substance into another.</note> earth into a living soul, and what is greatest of all, He endowed it with the supreme gift of blessedness, namely, His own **image and likeness** <note>original: "imagine similitudineque suis"; a reference to Genesis 1:26.</note>. Through these it is given to all to be saved—those who receive this gift—but what shall be given for free to those unwilling to receive it? Certainly nothing; let them therefore have what is theirs, so that the place of justice may be preserved. What is proper to each is what he chose from the beginning: namely, damnation. The gift of eternal salvation is free for those who receive it with thanksgiving.

Since, therefore, we are both a vile and a dear price, let each of us see what he prefers; the matter is clearer in itself to those who understand than any explanation could make it. We know the vile thing that we are, and the most excellent One from whom we proceeded. It remains in this matter that we weigh why, or for what end, we were made. Almighty God created the first man, **Adam**, in His image and likeness, so that he might be for God Himself for glory in eternity, and be immortal, not anxious, in need of nothing, always rejoicing in God, and not subject to earthly passions. 

But because he did not recognize so great a gift, he made it vile. He knew, however, that he was made perfect and wise, but he did not remain in that knowledge. Let us consider, therefore, how much good comes from knowledge, and how much evil comes from the contempt for this gift and the word of God; for it rendered him a dying man instead of an immortal one. For he who dies eternally always lives in the agony of death, and never ceases to die; hence it is that such a state is called "perpetual death," just as the life in which we shall live for God in eternity is called "eternal life," and we shall never cease to live. When, therefore, our first parent made all of us rebels and enemies to God along with himself, Almighty God, moved by **mercy**, wished to enter into peace with us who are hardened—He who is the author of peace. Who will be so stony-hearted that when divine...

-># PHILOSOPHIA.<-

...of divine goodness <note>The text begins with the second half of the word "divinæ."</note>, who would revolve this mystery in his mind and not be reconciled with his enemy, even if he has received an injury from him? How does it happen, then, that among mortals, neither the one who offends nor the one who suffers the offense is willing to approach the other for the sake of **reconciliation** <term>reconciliatio</term>? Certainly for no other reason than that no one knows himself, and consequently, neither God his creator, nor his neighbor as an equivalent creature; thus it happens that he who is ignorant of peace does not embrace it. For **peace** <term>pax</term> is the root of **mercy** <term>misericordia</term>. For he who does not have peace will not practice mercy, nor will he even attain it until he possesses peace. There is no reason for us to confuse peace and mercy in this place; because peace is the cause of mercy, just as **piety** <term>pietas</term> <note>pietas: Here meaning a sense of duty and religious devotion.</note> itself is the cause of peace. Therefore, if we have peace with God through the knowledge of piety, we shall necessarily have it likewise with our neighbor, whether enemy or friend.

This is especially true when we consider that the supreme **Craftsman** <term>artifex</term> of all things, through the embrace of peace, showed His mercy to a little worm who was a slave to the devil. O miserable mortals, as many of us as expect mercy from God, before whom we do not acknowledge our own misery? From where, I ask, does Mercy come, if not from the confession of misery, brought about through **contrition** <term>contritio</term> of the heart for the sake of amendment? For if we are not ignorant of our own misery and that of our brothers, but weigh them with an equal balance, then even if we have become wealthier in the goods of this world, we will not consider ourselves more abundant in eternal riches than those who are utterly destitute of worldly wealth. Who among mortals truly considers this, and will not console a needy brother with the sharing of the goods entrusted to him alone in this world? Show me one who considers this, and I will soon show you one who recognizes such a divine secret.

In all these things, God did not yet wish to fully explain His love toward us. Truly, while His **justice** <term>justitia</term> accused us—a justice from which nothing can ever be diminished, any more than from His mercy—did He not wish to spare us rather than His own son, in whom "Peace and Justice have kissed each other"? <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10, a common motif in Christian philosophy to explain the harmony of God's attributes.</note> Why, therefore, do we not embrace one another as brothers made equal in Christ, when the supreme Craftsman of things embraces us, miserable little worms, and in His only-begotten Son makes us the most excellent creatures from the most vile things made by our own evil? As many as acknowledge God in the Son, and likewise the Son in the Father through the **Holy Spirit** <term>Spiritus Sanctus</term> [whom they do not resist], they also acknowledge their brother, and none others.

These are the true and indubitable foundations of true **philosophy** <term>philosophia</term>; but because they are not yet known by all, though heard by many, a doubt might still linger in the minds of some who are not well-resolved, as to whether the mental representation of these things can excite the love of truth within us. It will be worth their while to set aside this ambiguity by an experiment conducted by themselves and within themselves, in the manner that follows. Let each one diligently consider within himself those things which have been said above, and having tasted them...

# SPECULATIVA

...which he should more often ruminate upon with a sincere soul: thus, he will perceive a few sparks gradually shining more and more each day before his mental eyes, growing into such a great light that, in time, all things necessary to him will become known. He will no longer remain stuck in doubt regarding the truth; instead, by gradually becoming accustomed to the exercise of **piety** <term>pietas</term> and justice, through the ritual and path previously mentioned, he will feel a tranquility of mind. Attracted by this peace, he will finally understand that there is greater delight in the soul than in the body.

True knowledge does not begin until the Soul—presented with a comparison between eternal and fleeting things, between life and destruction—chooses to be joined with the mind. This attraction brings greater delight than that of the Body. From this knowledge, the **Mind** <term>mens</term> arises, and the voluntary separation from the body begins. The soul, looking on one hand at the filth and mortality of the body, and on the other at the perpetual excellence and happiness of the spirit, desires to be connected with the latter (as the divine state is so disposed). The body is utterly neglected so that the soul may seek only that which it sees God has intended for salvation and glory. The Body is then compelled to submit to the union of the two now joined.

This is that wonderful "transmutation of the philosophers" of body into spirit, and spirit into body, of which it is left said to us by the Sages: **make the fixed volatile, and make the volatile fixed** <note>original: "fac fixum volatile, & volatile fac fixum"</note>, so that you may have our **mastery** <term>magisterium</term> <note>magisterium: Often refers to the "Great Work" or the successful completion of an alchemical process.</note>. Understand this to mean: make from the stubborn body something manageable, which, through the excellence of the spirit agreeing with the soul, becomes a most constant body capable of withstanding all trials. For gold is proven by fire, which rejects everything that is not gold. O, most excellent **Gold of the Philosophers** <term>aurum philosophorum</term>, with which the sons of wisdom are enriched—not with that common metal which is so greedily desired!

Come forward, you who seek the treasure of the philosophers with such varied effort: recognize first what that **rejected stone** <note>A reference to the "stone the builders rejected" (Psalm 118:22), frequently used in alchemy to describe the common or overlooked material that holds the secret to the work.</note> is before you seek it. It is a wonder above every miracle that anyone should desire what is unknown to him. It certainly seems foolish for men to seek something whose truth they do not recognize while investigating, for no hope is left in such a search. I advise all seekers, therefore, to first learn the true existence of what they seek before they begin the search; thus, they will not happen to be frustrated in their labors. The wise man seeks what he loves, and he cannot love what he does not know—otherwise, he would be a fool. From knowledge, therefore, is born the love of the truth of all things, which alone flourishes in all true philosophers.

However, when these things are repeated more deeply than the literal words sound, they allow one to draw out all science and art in all things, both heavenly and worldly.

# PHILOSOPHIA.

<margin>Q 4</margin>
...the **children of wisdom** <term>sapientiæ filij</term> are born. You seekers of the hidden secrets of nature <term>secretorum indagatores</term> labor in vain when, having entered upon a different path, you attempt to uncover the virtues of earthly things through the earthly alone. Learn, therefore, to know heaven through heaven—not through the earth—but rather the virtues of the latter through the former. For no one ascends into the heaven that you seek, unless he who descended from heaven (which you do not seek) enlightens him <note>This is a paraphrasing of John 3:13, applied here to alchemical or philosophical enlightenment.</note>. You seek an **incorruptible medicine** <term>medicina incorruptibilis</term>, which might not only transmute bodies from corruption into a true balance, but also preserve those balanced bodies for a very long time: you will never be able to find such a thing anywhere else but in heaven. Heaven, by its own power, through invisible rays converging from all sides into the center of the earth, penetrates all elements and generates and nourishes all things composed of elements. No one can generate within himself, but only in one like himself, which also comes from himself. Even a child of mixed parentage retains the nature of both parents within itself, so that in that child, both parents can be found in potential and in act. Who will remain stuck any longer—unless he is a stone—in this **philosophical generation** <term>generatio philosophica</term>? If this knowledge is still not enough for you, dear reader, along with that which was given in **our Key** <term>Clave nostra</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific instructional text or a symbolic "key" to the author's system.</note>, there is no reason for me to deal with you at greater length. But lest a handle for complaining about me remain for you, I will say more. Learn to know from yourself whatever is in both heaven and earth, so that you may become wise in all things. Are you unaware that heaven and the elements were once one, and were separated from each other by divine craftsmanship so that they could generate both you and all things? If you know this, the rest cannot escape you, or else you lack all wit. Again, in every generation, such a **separation** <term>separatio</term> is necessary—the kind I said above must be made concerning yourself—before you apply the veil to the studies of true philosophy. You will never make the "one" you seek out of other things, unless that "one" you have heard of first comes to be from within yourself (and you shall hear more of this in what follows). For such is the will of God: that the pious follow the pious work they seek, and the perfect may complete the other thing upon which they have been intent. To men of evil will, nothing is given to reap except what they have sown; indeed, what is more, their good seed is often turned into weeds because of their malice. Act, therefore, so that you turn out to be such as you wish your work to be.

### CHAP. IV.

**Philosophical love** <term>Amor philosophicus</term> is said to be the union of secrets from the "one" back into the "one" through peace. Peace, indeed, is the concord through the union of parts in the whole. God especially loves union, because He is one, and whatever He ever created, He enclosed under union. From a "determined one," made through an "indefinite one," proceed all things that are finite; and again, each thing tends back toward its own "one" by natural instinct. If any things should deviate from this, they are judged by philosophers to be held under the secret **binary** <term>binario</term> <note>The number two, symbolizing duality, division, or fallen state.</note>, and must be reduced to union through the **ternary** <term>ternarium</term> <note>The number three, symbolizing the restoration of unity or the divine trinity.</note>. ### SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

<meta>catchword: comple-</meta>

God [created] heaven and earth: and all things that are in them, united together in a hidden way, yet revealed in their secrets. Under the name of "earth" are included the **Elements**, which are contained by heaven; they embrace one another with such a bond of love that one can hardly see its equal among other creatures. We see even the brute animals joining themselves in a completely divine order with a more sincere bond—those which consist of purer elements, such as the birds <note>original: "volatilia"</note>; others agree less so, due to the lesser purity of the matter from which they are fashioned, yet they are still joined, albeit more indiscriminately. 

Let us come to the most excellent creature, created from the vilest matter: namely man, whom God created from the **slime of the earth** <term>limo terræ</term>, a creature movable by itself, which He soon made one with a **rational spirit** <term>spiritu rationali</term>. Who does not perceive that man, when moved by [the spirit] alone, is more irregular than all other living beings? Yet it is true that, being made rational, there can be no work of God more excellent. 

From this man, while he was still in that most excellent state before the Fall, God separated woman—**bone from his bones, and flesh from his flesh**—so that they might be more firmly united than other living creatures. They are not said to be "united" unless they were first removed from a single whole, but rather merely "joined." Since man could not procreate within himself, it was necessary to procreate in another. For this reason, human generation is to be revered above all others, because it happens between two who were previously one, and are made one again through divine marriage; as the Scripture testifies: **And they shall be two in one flesh** <note>Genesis 2:24</note>, for whose sake each shall leave father and mother and shall cling to the other, his own part. 

It must not be thought otherwise than that the wife is one part of the husband, and he the other inseparable part of her body. When we see them behaving otherwise, we shall judge them not to be "united," but only "joined"—not by true love, but either for the sake of base gain or rather to extinguish an illicit appetite; and when that fire has cooled, everything cools at once. Such is not **philosophical love** <term>amor philosophicus</term> <note>In alchemy, "philosophical love" refers to the permanent, chemical bonding of substances that cannot be separated, mirroring the ideal spiritual union.</note>: for being kindled by an entirely inextinguishable fire, it is never put out; whatever spirits are united through the spirit remain in union, while those bodies which are merely joined through the body are easily dissolved. 

There is also a specific love of parents toward children, and children toward parents, which can in no way be compared to philosophical love. For a father would not wish to suffer the loss of even his smallest joint for his son, nor a son for his parent, much less a sister or brother for a sibling, or any friend for another. Who is there who would willingly undergo death for himself, much less for someone else? Where, then, is such love to be sought? Certainly nowhere else than from whence love itself proceeded. **For God so loved the world** <note>John 3:16</note> (understand this as "man") that He willed His own Son to be born as a man, who could die for men, and by his death pay the debt of justice by which we were bound to be punished. For the Son of God could not die, but having been made man, he died—a perfect man, the Son of Man—and as a just man, [satisfied] justice...

# PHILOSOPHIA.

...completed. O marvelous love of God toward men! Not from the empty philosophy of Aristotle, nor from the rest of the Wise of this world, do such happy waves flow—which (while that philosophy keeps us occupied with vain studies) we pass by, oh miserable companions: toward another philosophy our souls are called by that divine love.

*A Dialogue in which the Spirit strives to draw the Soul and the Body to itself. The speakers are Spirit, Soul, Body, and the Philosophy of Love, designated by these letters:*
->S. A. C. & Ph.<-

**S.** Come then, my soul and my body, flee now, follow your spirit; let us ascend this high mountain opposite us, from whose peak I will show you this fork in the road <note>original: "bivium," referring to the Pythagorean "Y" symbol representing the choice between virtue and vice</note> of which Pythagoras spoke through a cloud and without light. To us, eyes are opened, and the Sun of piety and justice shines before us; with it as our guide, we cannot turn aside from the path of truth. Turn your eyes first to the right, lest they see vanity before they have perceived wisdom. Do you see that shining and invincible castle? 

**A. & C.** We see it. 

**S.** In it dwells Philosophical Love, from whose fountain flow living waters; he who tastes them once will thirst for vanity no longer. From that place, so pleasant and sweet, one must proceed straight to a more pleasant one, in which Wisdom <note>Sophia</note> lingers: from whose fountain also gush waters far more blessed than the first; if enemies taste them, they must enter into peace. Most of those who arrive there tend to reach higher, but not all achieve what is desired. 

There is a place beyond those mentioned, which mortals can scarcely approach unless they are taken up to the rank of immortality by divine power. But before they are introduced, they are forced to strip off the world, the spoils of this fleeting life being left behind. Once they have arrived there, they no longer fear death; rather, daily they embrace it more sweetly than anything in the world was ever judged sweet or worthy of their embrace. 

Whoever proceeds beyond these three places vanishes from the eyes of men. But if it pleases you to see the second and third places, let us ascend higher. See, above the first crystalline citadel, you see another of silver, and beyond that a third of adamant <note>a legendary rock of impenetrable hardness, often associated with diamond</note>; the fourth, however, does not fall under the senses until one has come beyond the third. This is the golden place of perpetual happiness, free from anxiety and filled with every everlasting joy. 

Now let us turn our eyes to the left. See, you behold the world full of pleasures and riches, in which nothing can displease the fleeting eye; but let us see the end of this pilgrimage. You clearly see a dark valley filled with smoky mist at the edge of the horizon. 

**A. & C.** We see it indeed. 

**S.** When those who enter this wide path arrive there, their comforts are turned...

### SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

...into torments, of which there is no end: but if you would lend a more attentive ear, you could perceive from here their wailing, unless the noise of the joy of those who so anxiously head toward their own ruin prevents you. 

**A. & C.** We hear it indeed, but why is it that those people do not return here? 

**S.** Because they do not see this valley of misery until they have passed the last way of repentance <note>original: "pœnitentiæ," referring to the process of atonement or changing one's mind</note>, after which there is no return. 

**A. & C.** Are there then other ways through which they can turn away from that grave danger? 

**S.** Indeed, there are only two side paths, pressing to the right here toward us, as you see. For from this place in which smoke now rises, everyone who repents must make their passage through the first castle, so that they may see for themselves what you now see. 

**A. & C.** We wonder that they do not see the valley of misery sooner. 

**S.** It is no wonder, because the way is flat, easy, and pleasant, seducing people by its allure; moreover, on any flat ground, the horizon is short. But if they had climbed up here as we have, they would have perceived the end of both ways. 

**A. & C.** By what names are they called? 

**S.** The broad path is called the **Way of Error**; of the side paths, the first is called the **Way of Infirmity** <note>original: "infirmiratis," implying sickness or physical weakness as a catalyst for spiritual change</note>, the second the **Way of Poverty**, and this one in which we stand is called the **Way of Truth**. At the entrance of each is placed an Angel of the Lord, who is named the **Drawing of the Divine Spirit** <note>original: "tractus divini spiritus," referring to the theological concept of prevenient grace—the way God "pulls" or "attracts" a soul toward salvation</note>. Here at this first pass, He draws everyone; if wretched mortals resist this drawing, the reins are loosened for the stubborn, whom the Lord still waits for once they have entered the way of error, until—having for a time abused worldly delights through their own insolence—they fall into infirmities of the body, and not undeservedly, for that through which they had been drawn into error. Very few, to whom it happens to recognize their error, return to this place by the first way of repentance. The remaining greatest part, along with those who did not repent in the first place, proceed further in their stubbornness. Some who refused to be corrected through infirmity, and others who have not yet been corrected, are permitted to fall into poverty by their own cause; of these, very few enter the later way of repentance. Most, however, proceed blindly in error until they fall into the pit from which one may not rise. 

**A. & C.** We see few returning through the ways of repentance. 

**S.** The body hinders this. 

**C.** But I would rather die a hundred times than complete that broad way to its end. 

**S.** Because you have seen, you speak thus; but see that you are mindful of this in the future. 

**C.** Wherever you go, I will follow most promptly; but before we depart from here, tell me, I pray, how did it happen that we did not enter the broad way? 

**S.** Those to whom it is given from heaven to receive the first drawing of the Lord should credit it to God, not to themselves. 

**C.** Yet all are drawn. 

**S.** It is true, but all do not receive the drawing. 

**C.** What is the occasion for this? 

**S.** Because, standing at the fork in the road, they turn their eyes more toward the vanities on the left than toward this river of living water on the right, which flows with such admirable skill from the peak of the mountain where smoke now rises. 

**C.** What is the name of the mountain and the river? 

**S.** Each is called the First Drawing of the Lord. Are there others...

# PHILOSOPHY

[Are there any other] attractions besides these three that you have already explained? 

**S.** There are many intermediate ones between these, which are felt by everyone in their own **conscience** <term>conscientia</term>, but they are made little of by those who, as was said before, refuse to receive them. 

**C.** What is it about this river that you lead us to admire? 

**S.** Have you, or has anyone, ever seen such a great volume of water falling from such a high place without a terrifying roar? You do not know that hanging water—which surpasses all the forces of the world—is able to terrify even an intrepid man, or even **Mars** <note>The Roman god of war, used here as the symbol of ultimate bravery</note> himself (if such a person exists), through the stirring of sound and wind, as can be seen in many places. 

**C.** Certainly, I have been on certain hills where the water flowing down from a bridge at a distance could have knocked down passersby, however strong they were, who were terrified and shaken by the wind; unless, by a certain industriousness and reclaimed strength, the minds of the men had conquered and made a passage for themselves. 

**S.** The first attraction in this place is the admiration of the river, which is followed by a desire to taste the water and a very great love for seeing its source. This attracts the one who tastes it—just as a **magnet** <term>adamas</term> <note>original: "adamas," referring to a lodestone or magnet that draws iron</note> attracts iron—to this place, so that he may see what the distinctions of things are. 

**C.** I would never have considered this by myself, even if I had seen the opposite happen in lower places. 

**S.** Your eyes are made of flesh, which do not perceive those things that transcend the world. Those who see things superficially, or only from what is manifest, do not think there is anything else in the nature of things besides that which falls under the senses. It does not happen that any of these people approach this place, unless their **spirit** <term>spiritus</term> feels and receives the attraction of the Lord—from the wonderful consideration of the river and the mountain—as a special gift. 

**C.** This is the only thing I still desire to know from you before we depart from here: What is the meaning of such a difficult access to such pleasant places? Why is it so because of the roughness and narrowness of the path, and because of the perfectly straight course of this river, such that one could hardly outline anything straighter with a stretched string? 

**S.** I see, my **Body** <note>Referring to the character C (Corpus)</note>, that you willingly prolong your stay here so that you may feast your eyes longer on **worldly masks** <note>original: "mundanis larvis," referring to the deceptive illusions or phantoms of the physical world</note>. The fact that these eyes of yours often twist toward the left (even if you seek the right) gives me reason to suspect that you inquire about these things not so much out of a curious desire for knowledge, but because you see that after you depart from here, you will be deprived of the sight of the world. 

**C.** Let us put these things aside; at least answer me. 

**S.** Regarding the difficulty, so that you may be satisfied, understand first that no entrance lies open to glory by any way other than through the **cross** <note>original: "crucem." In this philosophical context, it signifies hardship, self-denial, or spiritual trial</note>, just as no access to any arduous thing is open except through the greatest labor. Otherwise, what is easily gained would be lightly esteemed, and what is gained with difficulty would be held in high regard. The lightness of the roughness—just as life comes from death—is the goal, no less than the vastness that comes from narrowness. Also, everything that leads into the path of truth must be a straight road, lacking in detours. Now you have what you wish for; there is no reason for us to linger any longer. Follow us. 

**C.** Let this be the last thing. 

**S.** You have now heard everything that is necessary; I will not delay. 

**G.** <note>Likely "Genius," a guiding spirit or companion</note> At least, **Soul** <note>Referring to the character A (Anima)</note>, stay with me for a little while. 

**A.** Neither you, nor the Spirit...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue at the gates of Philosophy. Having just established the definition of Philosophy as the "Love of Wisdom," the speaker (Philosophy) now provides a historical and allegorical overview of the human condition, moving from the Fall of Adam to the current Age of Grace, explaining how the path to wisdom was lost and subsequently reopened.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>
<header>SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY</header>
<meta>catchword: first</meta>

Although I do not doubt that, through the initial drawing of the Lord, you heard from His angel about the effectiveness of philosophical study and knowledge, you were then heavier with the mass of the body than you will be now, and were scarcely able to bear everything. It will be worth the effort, before you come to the fountain of love, to briefly repeat those things which seem necessary here. Before the fall of Adam, neither the "wide and left-hand way" nor the "valley of misery" existed; instead, the entrance to these most happy places lay open to everyone from every side. After man’s first disobedience, the Lord narrowed this once-vast way into a very narrow and difficult path (as you see), at the entrance of which He placed a Cherub angel <note>In Genesis, the Cherubim guard the way to the Tree of Life after the expulsion from Eden.</note> holding a two-edged sword in his hand to keep everyone from entering that happy homeland. Turning away from here because of the sin of their first parent, the sons of Adam constructed for themselves a wide path to the left—the very one you have avoided. 

Long afterward, God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "D.O.M." standing for Deo Optimo Maximo, a standard Latin honorific for the Deity.</note>, entered into the secrets of His mysteries. There, with mercy acting through love and justice through accusation, He decided to snatch the sword of His wrath from the angel's hands, substituting a golden three-pronged hook in its place and hanging the sword upon a tree. Thus, the wrath of God was changed into love while justice was preserved. Before this happened, that river <note>Likely referring to the River of Grace or the Waters of Life mentioned later.</note> was not as it is now, collected within itself; rather, before the fall, it was spread equally over the whole world like dew. But afterward, it returned to the source from which it had proceeded, until finally—when "peace and justice kissed each other" <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10, often used to describe the reconciliation of God and humanity through Christ.</note>—the water of grace descended more flowingly from on high, now washing the whole world. 

Those who turn toward the left-hand path partly see the sword hanging on the tree and, knowing its history, pass it by because they are too deeply rooted in the world. Some see its power but neglect to investigate it; others neither see it nor wish to have seen it. All these direct their pilgrimage straight toward the valley, unless some are pulled back toward Mount Sion by the "hooks of repentance" or penance. In our own century (which is the age of grace), the sword has been transformed into Christ our Savior, who ascended the tree of the cross for our sins. All these things denote the eras of the laws of nature, of divine law, and of grace. Now, hear what the state of the "way of errors" consists of.

->*The Structure of the World.*<-

**Ph.** God said to Adam after the fall: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread," and "in pain your wife shall bring forth." He cursed the earth because of man, and it was made sterile—the same earth which previously, with no cultivation but only heavenly abundance, produced the most bountiful fruit. But although it is now stirred by human labor, it seems to barely bring forth briars and thorns. From the time man stripped off the truth, necessity itself rendered him anxious about seeking food and clothing. Necessity is the "second mother" of studies and the first inventor of the primary arts, such as agriculture and the keeping of livestock. And so began...

It concludes by introducing the "Structure of the World" and the origins of human labor and necessity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Philosophy regarding the history of the human condition. Following the previous page’s discussion on the fall of Adam and the closing of the path to wisdom, the speaker now describes the progression of human civilization from basic necessity to industrial complexity, and finally to the corruption of war and greed.</meta>

<page-num>255</page-num>
### PHILOSOPHY.
<meta>catchword: after</meta>

The first and honest men sought only those things which they could not do without; however, the impure usurped not only those things, but everything else that was weaker than their own strength, through both fair means and foul <note>original: "per fas & nefas," a common Latin idiom meaning "through right and wrong."</note>. At first, nakedness taught man to cover his bare flesh with leaves; eventually, as is the custom, industry was gradually increased by necessity, leading him to cover himself with the skins of animals. Soon after, hunger taught him to dig, to sow, and to gather the harvest in its proper season; to take care of the flock, the herds, the cattle, and the pastures; and to provide for the feeding of the family, the instruction of morals and the laws of nature, and the preservation of peace. He learned to protect himself and his herds from the injury of the rains and the weather with huts and roofs. All of this was the initial anxiety of necessity. The first fathers of that age lived happy and content with these arts in times of peace.

After the earth was filled, it was no longer possible for everyone to have their own portion and for all to be farmers or shepherds; instead, it became necessary for those who had nothing to serve others in various ways. Curiosity produced various kinds of clothing and buildings; from this, tailors, shoemakers, and builders <term>fabri: a broad term for craftsmen, smiths, or masons</term>—who are identified by the needle and the hammer—took their origin. The wealth of these men, gained through labor, sought leisure for some, who acquired for themselves as much land as could supply them with food and clothing. Among the rest, there was growth: considering the scarcity of things in one place and the abundance in another, they practiced commerce. From this emerged carriers and the drivers of pack animals. Nor did the method of eating lack its own arts; for bakers, oven-keepers, butchers, cooks, and vintners were devised for the assistance of travelers.

All these things were administered in good faith from the beginning, until self-interest and brotherly hatred broke in. From that time, the temperaments of men were changed, and the hunger for possession grew just as much as wealth has increased to this very day, in which no one trusts anyone else, nor even themselves. For his own convenience, everyone changed huts into splendid houses, which eventually grew into villages, towns, forts, cities, and suburbs into great metropolises—yet they were not immune to hatred. Later, the injury of time gave birth to lazy men who wished to live not by their own labor, but by the labor of others, and simultaneously brought forth war, especially among neighbors. This, in turn, gave rise to ditches, walls, ramparts, and bulwarks for defense against injuries. Against the swarm of any and all vices—which leisure is known to feed—the execrable and diabolical kind of cannons and artillery <note>original: "bombardarum & tormentorum," referring to early gunpowder weapons and siege engines.</note> was brought up from the underworld. By these, the society of the whole human race would collapse, had it not been guarded by divine help. Indeed, this last of the new arts completed the fabric of the world <note>original: "mundi fabricam," meaning the complex structure of human civilization.</note>. 

And because of the variety of the things I have mentioned, those who love the world call it "beautiful." But you, listeners, judge what sort of beauty is found in those things which, the more they abound, the less they are peaceful and the more they are full of anxiety. As you have heard, all things concerning the world are fleeting, nor is there any man, poor or rich, who [can keep] a hair of them...

...carries away with them after death. See, therefore, in what things wretched mortals place their hope, and with how much care they acquire for themselves nothing—which ruins those who refuse to be content with their lot. Now, I pray you, hear the story of this pilgrimage through the transitory world.

->*The worldly pilgrimage, which we call the Way of Error.*<-

Once the twenty-first year of age is completed <note>original: "ter septeno," literally "three times seven," which was historically considered the age of full maturity</note>, the majority of people reach the crossroads of choice. Here, the course of everyone is slowed by the hook of the Angel of the Lord. However, many crawl under it, others leap over it, and—while very few are actually caught—the greatest part breaks out between the hook and the entrance of the road. All of them flee from salvation, as many as strive to evade this pull, and they enter the world without any bridle to restrain them. The largest part of these people, having wasted themselves on delicacies and worldly pleasures, are permitted by the Lord our God of mercy to fall into poverty. This is intended to draw them back to the earlier way of repentance <note>original: "resipiscentia," meaning a return to one's right mind or a change of heart</note>. But the human race is utterly useless; since it is now innate for man to resist God, he does not stop seeking means by which he might, through his own effort, escape the snares he set for himself. He does not seek help from Him upon whom alone every gift of mercy depends.

Because of this, it happened that they built for themselves a massive workshop on the left side of the road, in which every kind of labor is practiced. This house is governed by Industry, who receives everyone except for the lazy and the sluggish. On one side are the literary workshops of various studies, to which those who had neglected their education betake themselves. Most of these then move to the manual workshops located on the other side. In these, they test the things that were once committed to writing by wiser men, so that they are not led into false opinions by the "letter" alone, remaining inexperienced in practical matters as they were before. Others, who practiced trade to their own loss, and those who fell into poverty while applying themselves to the manual arts, dream day and night of new forms of things and unheard-of inventions. The merchants and mechanics display these everywhere to anyone for a price, so that they might repair their losses and then reach more opulent heights.

After they have achieved this wealth, they depart from Industry and head toward the second region of the world. They make their crossing via the Bridge of Infirmity. Before this bridge, the Lord’s second "pull" tries to lead the lost sheep back to the true fold. Of these, only a very few enter the way of repentance. The rest stubbornly cross the bridge, and they use the goods they have now acquired through Industry more freely than they did their previous possessions. But because a good God wishes to pull them back, He allows infirmities to rule over them. Then, seeking a remedy from themselves rather than from Him, they flock to a hospital <term>xenodochium: a Greek-derived term for a building providing care for travelers, the poor, or the sick</term>, also constructed on the left and very large, which is presided over by Medicine. There, a huge number of pharmacists, surgeons, and physicians are found, each performing his own duty. Once health has been recovered...

# PHILOSOPHY

...settled, they depart not having become richer as they were before, but diminished in their goods. The greatest part of them passes over the bridge of old age while resisting the Lord’s pull, with scarcely one or two entering the final path, which is called repentance. When one has arrived at the third region of the world <note>Likely referring to the final stage of life: old age</note>, one can see nothing except the bent backs of the elderly, the wrinkles of their faces, lameness, lamentations, and sighs. One hears a heap of other such wearinesses, and whatever fates await each person, until the final lodging of death is reached. What happens after that I am content not to know, leaving the judgment to God (to whom it belongs). Now that the structure of the world and the state of the pilgrimage are known, let us see what the outcome of the Way of Truth is, so that by making a proper comparison of opposites, you may know which way—of error or of truth—is the way of salvation.

->*The Way of Salvation.*<-

**Philosophy.** You heard before that the sword of the first angel’s pull was hung from a tree above the riverbank. In its place (now in this time of grace), Christ—the restorer of the human race, God and the Son of God—hangs before our eyes. He attracts those passing by through his manifest love, veiled by no figures, more effectively than a magnet attracts iron—unless perhaps the dregs of the world and "garlic" <note>original: *allium*. A biblical metaphor referring to the leeks and garlic of Egypt, symbolizing worldly attachments and physical desires that distract the soul</note> stand in the way. 

Whoever is drawn by the wonder of the river appearing from afar and the example of inexhaustible love offered close at hand betakes themselves here to us. As many as we are who serve as ministers of truth, we gladly take you up to be educated, as you will hear more fully hereafter. Before that happens, however, now that food and drink have been taken, let us give thanks to God, who gave all things that are necessary for everyone. We give you, God the Father, immortal thanks, because you have deigned to nourish us with your word and your creatures, and to lead us all the way to this place in the hope of a better life. Thy will be done, that what was begun through you alone may be perfected in us. Amen. 

Now let us go to the fountain of love, so that you may drink. Behold, quench your thirst: you shall no longer be called the Rational Spirit <term>Animus</term> or the Breath of Life <term>Spiritus</term>, nor the Soul <term>Anima</term>, nor two separate things thereafter, but you shall be called the one Mind <term>Mens</term> <note>Philosophy suggests that the fragmented parts of the human psyche are unified into a higher "Mind" through divine love</note>. Having been made stronger, you can then resist your enemy, the Body, with which you must struggle manfully until it is actually separated from you by the natural course of life. Afterward, you may hope to be joined to it again in that same place, more pure and refined through a divine mystery, to the glory of Him who created all things. 

How you must fight, you will hear from the following fourth step, namely Assembly <term>Frequentia</term>. I will accompany you as you approach the first milestone; meanwhile, I will briefly depict the progress of the entire Way of Truth before your eyes. Departing from Assembly and having been instructed, you will arrive at the camp of Wisdom <term>Sophia</term>, where you will be received and refreshed with food much more powerful than before. Up until now, you have tasted only milk...

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Philosophy on the "Way of Salvation," transitioning from her final advice to the "little ones" into a dramatic dialogue between the Body and the Mind. It maintains the theme that spiritual discipline leads to eternal joy.</meta>

# SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>258</page-num>

...for (until you are stronger and able to bear more robust things) you are still like little children. For Virtue will teach you how great the fruit of true love is, and how much delight the submission <note>original: *succubitus*. In this context, it refers to the body yielding or "lying under" the control of the spirit.</note> of the body brings to the mind—truly no less than the victory brings to a soldier fighting his enemies for the palm of victory. Further, you will pass to Power, the sixth step, from which you will learn not only to recognize the exercises of virtues, but also to perform them. Finally, this will lead you to the seventh and last step of philosophy: a miracle, in which the martyrdoms of the world become joys. Briefly, the end of this way is the very beginning of the joy of eternal and perpetual life. May the almighty and merciful Lord, who has led you this far, lead you further; may He be your companion for the rest of the journey. Go, and fare well, brothers.

->*A Dialogue in which the Mind and the Body are the speakers.*<-

**Body.** Oh! Who has become my companion now? Where are you, my soul? 
**Mind.** Look, I am here; what do you want from me? 
**Body.** I do not see you. 
**Mind.** Now you admit once again, as you did before, that you are blind. 
**Body.** Where then is the Spirit? 
**Mind.** Do you seek me even though I am present to you? 
**Body.** Good God, do both of you now speak with a single voice? 
**Mind.** Why is that a surprise? Have you forgotten what I said above: that you would have to deal with only one thing? You were complaining then that you had to deal with two. 
**Body.** What am I hearing? Have you cast a spell on my eyes? 
**Mind.** Far be it from me to use sorcery. Rather, having taken a drink together from the fountain of love, we have been brought back into one, so that you should no longer think you must battle with two, but with a single mind. 
**Body.** "Mind" <note>original: *Mens*</note> gives the start to many things: tables <note>original: *mensae*</note>, measures <note>original: *mensurae*</note>, and months <note>original: *mensibus*</note>. <note>The Body is making a play on words based on the Latin root *mens-*, showing its preoccupation with physical things like food, quantity, and time.</note>
**Mind.** If only you had learned to measure your table, and remembered that there will be an end to your months! 
**Body.** You say a strange thing; you know it is impossible for me to live without food. 
**Mind.** I know this and more: that man does not live by bread alone—are you ignorant of this? 
**Body.** Since you live by something else, why have I not yet seen you eating? 
**Mind.** Again, you bring your blindness into the open. 
**Body.** How so? 
**Mind.** I live by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord. 
**Body.** If only it were permitted for me to live like that! 
**Mind.** In the future it will be permitted for you too—though not before you die. 
**Body.** You mention something far too harsh. 
**Mind.** It is nothing but joyful. 
**Body.** You make death joyful? 
**Mind.** Indeed, for those who have known her. 
**Body.** Do you know her? 
**Mind.** I know her very well. 
**Body.** I beg you, describe her to me, for she shows herself to be feared by everyone. 
**Mind.** I will most willingly comply with you in this matter now; no one fears her except you. 
**Body.** You do not? 
**Mind.** Not in the least. 
**Body.** You are mad from too much wisdom, more than can be said. 
**Mind.** You are the one who is mad. 
**Body.** Yet I know that everyone abhors death. 
**Mind.** You only think so. <note>original: *Rere*. A play on the Latin verb *reor*, meaning 'to suppose' or 'to imagine'.</note>
**Body.** Speak so that you may be understood. 
**Mind.** I will speak to the point so that you understand: the mind of man is immortal; therefore it does not fear death, but rather manfully overcomes it. The body is entirely subject to death, which is why it dreads it above all else. 
**Body.** How do you know that the mind is not subject to death?

### PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>259</page-num>
<sig>R 2</sig>

**Mind.** It is known from this, namely: everything that has taken its origin from death is mortal; that which draws its beginning from life does not die, nor does that which exists as a middle point between life and death when it clings to life.

**Body.** You speak much too obscurely.

**Mind.** I speak nothing if not clearly.

**Body.** What is life?

**Mind.** It is the soul of the body.

**Body.** What then is death?

**Mind.** It is the deprivation of life.

**Body.** I have not come away any the wiser for this.

**Mind.** Listen; what you consider to be death is to me the beginning of eternal life, and nothing more pleasant can happen to us, provided it were not troublesome to you. But you detest it because you know that by death you are deprived of worldly delights; yet you are ignorant that between these and eternal joys there is less comparison and similarity than that between gall <note>original: *fel* (OCR: *sel*). A bitter substance often contrasted with the sweetness of honey.</note> and honey <note>original: *mel*</note>, which I know you have tasted at some time. Finally, so that you may better recognize this difference, you should consider what you already know: namely, that the continuation of all the worldly pleasures that can ever happen to you brings boredom—or rather, I should say, nausea—and what is far worse, it brings weakness and sometimes death. If you now desire food, after you have filled your belly with it several times, you will seek another; when you have been satisfied with that, you seek yet another, and you will never cease in this world to seek what you cannot find, for your desires have not been satisfied. What about drink? In the meantime, while it passes through the channel of the throat, it delights; but when it can no longer enter further, it causes great torment, yet the body cannot abstain from that which kills it: nevertheless, you fear the death that you bring upon yourself. Oh miserable and insatiable body, which does not know how to beware of that which harms it, and fears that which it is! You see, therefore, that the human Body, when it is out of harmony with its own mind, is unhappier than the beasts, since irrational creatures desire nothing beyond what is necessary for them. But rational beings carefully procure not at all what is needed, but rather what kills. Let us now come to those things which are sought outside the body for its use, such as riches of every kind, for which the bodies of men—not having followed the mind—are tortured daily in strange and diverse ways. What do they not strive for? What dangers do human hearts not undergo, by which they drag the soul to destruction and pull the miserable body away from the spirit? They do this for no other reason than to fashion an idol for themselves out of their own body, which, adorned with fine purple and scarlet linen, with necklaces and bracelets, they do not fear to worship silently above God. Who will deny that this is a greater idolatry of oneself than of another, or that death is the end of all these things? O ignorant body, you fear nothing except yourself: for death took its beginning from you through appetite, and you desire nothing but what is of yourself—namely corruption, which brings on the death you fear. See, therefore, how little you are consistent with yourself, and how you could resist others when you cannot even resist your own impulses. Come to your senses, I pray, while you can; cling to us, and do not wait until it is too late. We have now come to the gardens of the multitude <note>original: *frequentiae hortos*. Likely an allegorical location representing a place where many gather to learn or a state of abundance.</note>; there it will be permitted for you to hear more about this.

### *Recapitulation of the fourth Chapter, and of the third step.*

Know, brothers, that all things which have been said above, and will be said hereafter, can be understood concerning alchemical preparations. For in no other way than we have spoken of the separation of the parts of man through speculative Philosophy, is it to be understood concerning the separations of the remaining bodies performed by fire. And unless such a separation occurs, the Alchemists labor in vain seeking the universal medicine <term>medicina universalis|A legendary "panacea" or elixir sought by alchemists, believed to cure all ailments and even perfect "imperfect" metals into gold</term>, which can heal all diseases without distinction. All things which have been said concerning man in this book must be considered most diligently, for there is not a single little word in it that does not refer to the chemical art, and was not placed there for its explanation. Such is the philosophical love between the parts of inanimate things, and enmity, as there is in the parts of man. Truly in those, no more than in these, a true union cannot be made unless the corruption of the said parts is first taken away before the conjunction: wherefore it is your task to make peace between enemies, so that friends may come together into one. In all imperfect bodies, and those falling short of their final perfection, friendship and enmity are born together: if the latter [enmity] is removed by the wit or industry of man, it is necessary for the other part to return to its final perfection, which we have declared in the union of man. 

Separate therefore by fire the parts from each body; purify the impure ones, as those which are pure do not need cleansing. Mix pure things with pure, yet sublimate <term>sublimato|The process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collecting the condensed solid. In alchemy, this was used to "spiritualize" or purify matter</term> the heavier things with the lighter first; thus will happen what was said above: the fixed becomes volatile, and the corporeal becomes spiritual. Thus far we have touched upon the comparison of physical alchemy; wherefore we must pause here until we have followed those things which remain in metaphysical alchemy. 

The reader must nevertheless be warned here, so that he understands what has been said from a distinct comparison, or otherwise he must necessarily be confused; therefore it will not be troublesome to set down the difference of those things about which there could be doubt. Whenever hereafter I make mention of inanimate things, I wish to be understood as referring to vegetables and minerals, which although they have their own "vegetative soul" <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, the "vegetative soul" is the lowest level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition, found in plants.</note>, yet for the sake of distinction from sentient beings, it must be done thus. And so I have spoken above regarding inanimate bodies, lest anyone think I wish to contradict the alchemists, who attribute spirit, soul, and body in their own way to all natural bodies: which they can demonstrate to the eye whenever there is need, even to those who deny it. Likewise, I place "sentient beings" <note>original: *sensitiva*</note> for irrational animals, nor do I mean rational beings [humans], who although they have a sentient soul along with the rational one, I shall nevertheless take the more powerful one—namely the rational—as their primary meaning. Finally, regarding the aforesaid, it should not be ignored that rational separation is twofold: namely voluntary, which we spoke of above, and natural,
