->PHILOSOPHY.<-
<sig>R 3</sig>

...which does not pertain to chemists: the separation of sensible and inanimate things is also twofold, namely natural and artificial, the latter of which concerns chemistry. Voluntary separation occurs while the parts remain in the whole; natural and artificial separation do not. The instrument of voluntary separation is the spirit and the breath of life; of natural separation, it is death; and of artificial separation, it is fire. 

Nothing will stand in your way now, so that you may hereafter be able to equate rational alchemy with that separation and union which can occur in sensible, inanimate things. Truly, do not think that I have placed **Rational Alchemy** first in vain, because if these—the rational and the natural—are not understood, you will necessarily happen to be ignorant of the artificial. But lest I seem to have failed you in natural Alchemy, you shall now hear as much about it as may suffice for your understanding of the rest: I shall begin with separation. 

You know that man, having completed the term appointed for him by nature, is resolved into his parts (which we said above are **Spirit, Soul, and Body**), this being worked by the corruption of death. Through the extinction of the natural fire, as the *radical moisture* <term>humore radicali|radical moisture; in medieval medicine, the vital fluid believed to maintain life and body heat, acting as the fuel for the "natural fire" of the body</term> fails, the Spirit and Soul recede, leaving the body; which again is separated into its elemental parts through putrefaction occurring in the earth. Every element returns to its own: the earthy part the earth devours, the watery part the water, and so with the rest. Spirit and soul return to where they proceeded from: not that they are forever separated from the body, but so that they may be joined into one in a better composition by *divine artifice* <note>original: "artificio divino"</note>, after which union they shall be separated no more. This is the greatest virtue of inseparable union, and the compaction of parts into one. 

Again, unless the elements of rational bodies are nourished by elements, they cannot retain the spirit and soul. Food and drink cast into the stomach are "cooked" into digestion (for the separation of the parts of bodies cannot occur otherwise than through corruption or putrefaction) and by the artifice of nature, the pure is separated from the impure. Thus, by the better substance of the food and drink—earth, water, air, and Fire—the earth, water, air, and fire of the human body are nourished. Meanwhile, the more impure matter of the earth, water, air, and fire of food and drink is ejected through the bowels or other *emunctories* <term>emunctoria|organs or canals of the body, such as the kidneys or pores, that carry off waste</term>. Each part of this gross matter again seeks its own element (as we have said). 

Fire in man is a devouring element, consuming the other purer elements: therefore, nourishment is necessary, otherwise it consumes itself; and once consumed, no place is left for the soul nor the spirit. Such fire is the union or soul of fire and the other elements, without which no elements are composed, but are separated. In the elements there is a *philosophical love*: embrace this alone if you desire to be a physicist or natural philosopher; otherwise, you will turn out to be not a physicist, but rather a destroyer of nature.

### On Constancy, the fourth philosophical grade. Chapter V.
### In which Mind, Body, and Constancy converse.

**Mind:** I greet you most warmly, O Constancy. **Constancy:** I also bid you welcome, most pleasing visitors and guests; from where do you come, I ask? **Mind:** From this philosophy of love, we make our journey toward the camp of virtue. **Constancy:** I ask that you rightly make a stay with me for a little while, until the labors undertaken in your pilgrimage may be relieved, refreshed by some rest. **Mind:** We shall obey you most willingly in this matter. **Constancy:** Enter then these gardens of diligence, and freely enjoy those things which are in them as if they were your own. **Mind:** We give you immense thanks. **Constancy:** Not to me, but to God himself, to whom all things belong. Sit down, for those things with which I can receive you are prepared; let us pray to God:

> May you deign to nourish us, O Almighty Father, with your blessing. Amen.

Take care of yourself, O Body, while I meanwhile feed the Mind. Listen, Mind: Since **Constancy** <term>Frequentia|literally 'frequency' or 'crowding'; here used in the philosophical sense of 'constancy' or 'persistence' in one's duties</term> is the perseverance of one’s conception regarding the love of truth, there is no other entrance to the virtues except through diligence. In this place there is no rest; hence it happens that no place here seems built for the body, but rather the watchful tillers of the garden of virtues look for life under the open sky. Do you see this land? Unless it were continually cleared, instead of the sweet flowers and herbs which it produces, it would yield nothing but thistles and nettles. It will happen no differently with the Body which you lead around, if you become sluggish. This has been given to you as a colony <note>The author uses "colonia" to imply a territory that must be settled, governed, and cultivated</note>, just as these gardens are entrusted to me day and night. Whatever tares <note>original: "lolij"; referring to darnel or weeds that mimic wheat</note> grow over it must be removed by you. You will be able to overcome this no better than when you have removed excess <term>crapulam|intoxication or the physical distress caused by overindulgence in food or drink</term>; for it is that, surely, which induces sleepiness and sloth. You shall also remove idleness, so that the most powerful root of vices may perish. You shall grant nothing to the body beyond what is necessary; whatever is superabundant grows into a vice. You heard above what is necessary for the body; now hear what is healthful for both it and you. If you neglect to correct the Body, it will go badly for you because of it, and for the body itself: because the reason—which the body has cast aside—has now become yours, not its own. Consider that the knowledge of God has been entrusted to you (as indeed it is). Therefore, you shall not be excused on its account, since you are in the place of a pedagogue <note>A "pædagogus" was a tutor or guardian in the ancient world, often a slave responsible for a child's moral upbringing and safety</note> to it; nor shall it be excused on your account, because it first made itself a slave from being free. See, therefore, how I act with these gardens; I care for them in two ways, namely by uprooting and by irrigating. In the former, I pull up the useless overgrowing herbs by the roots, lest they suppress the good ones in their growth. You must do likewise with your body: first rejecting evil thoughts and enmity from yourself, you shall restrain the body from every evil work. It is not fitting for a teacher to teach one thing and do another; for if you give the body the opportunity for sinning, why, I ask, do you seize it? The Body contemplates nothing; it is the soul <note>original: "animus"</note> that exercises the silent operations of the imaginations, which the body finally strives to execute. Conce...

# PHILOSOPHY.
<sig>R 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: between</meta>

[Concep]tion belongs to the mind, while execution belongs to the body. If I were to pull out the darnel weed and meanwhile sow tares <note>original: "lolium... zizaniam"; both refer to weeds that mimic wheat, commonly used in Biblical parables to represent deceptive or harmful influences</note>, would I have corrected anything other than the very thing I myself committed? See to it, therefore, that you do not attribute more to the body than it is capable of. It is true that the body itself is more prone to executing crooked concepts, and delights in them more than in good ones; but cast away all evil thoughts from yourself and substitute good ones in their place. Then the body will be able to work nothing but good, or at least cease from all evil. This is one method of conquering the body; now hear the other.

If I were only to protect my gardens from useless things, I would certainly have accomplished little or nothing, since there is another far more necessary care to be applied to those things which have been planted: namely, irrigation. This is the other part of the nourishment for all plants, without which they cannot grow. In the same way, you shall water your Body with living water, which is the word of <term>GOD</term>; meditate upon this day and night, and upon nothing else besides this, so that the body is able neither to speak nor to do anything other than that very thing. 

You see now that bodies can be best compared to fields or gardens, which we read that Christ our Savior also did in the Gospel. The good seed (He says) which falls upon well-cultivated land brings forth good fruit; in no other way does the word of <term>GOD</term>, which falls upon a softened heart, nourish the body of him whose heart has been contrite and humbled. It is certain that, from the time of the first fall <note>The "Fall of Man" in Genesis</note>, the hearts of men have been hardened like stones; unless they are softened by the word of <term>GOD</term>, they remain hard forever. Pharaoh’s heart was hard from his mother’s womb (as all hearts are); but because it was not softened by the word of <term>GOD</term>, it remained hardened. We are all born rebellious and enemies to <term>GOD</term>, and we remain so until that enmity is uprooted by the Supreme Farmer <note>A metaphor for God as the "Husbandman" (John 15:1)</note>, to whom you, O Mind, must show yourself a servant. You have the seed, the field, and the water; nothing more is lacking but assiduous, uninterrupted labor. You must never cease to turn over in your mind those things which you have already heard and will soon hear; otherwise, through a lapse in effort, you will give a place to your enemy. 

These are the things which Lady Virtue commissioned me to say to you, by whom you will be taught more extensively. We give great thanks to God, who deigns to illuminate our hearts with His light and to make them softer by His word. Amen.

->Go happily, brothers, and seek Virtue.<-

### Recapitulation of the fifth chapter and the fourth grade.

It is impossible for any craftsman to become prompt and fit in his art unless he acquires a habit for himself through frequency and assiduousness of work. What benefit would it be to a baker to have seen another baker working often, or even very frequently, unless he, putting his own hand into the dough himself, repeated the act so many times that, having now become a practiced baker, he was able to teach another? This is what often happens to those desiring to learn the **Chemical Art** <note>original: "artem Chemicam," referring to Alchemy, which in this period was viewed as both a physical laboratory practice and a spiritual discipline</note>: some think they can attain it by reading alone, others by only a very few operations; which however...

Among all the arts that Nature has ever granted, this is held to be the most difficult and the least known: truly it is a Herculean labor, surpassing the Mind, Body, and the lifespan of men, unless it be granted to one among hundreds of thousands to conquer—that is, to reach the perfect goal of the art. I advise all investigators of this art to pray to God assiduously, to study, and to work; it cannot be but that they shall attain that which they have asked for in the name of Jesus from the Giver of Lights <note>original: "datore luminum"; a reference to James 1:17</note>. Many are accustomed to wish for what seems useful to them, but they obtain from God only what is truly useful. In brief, I say this to many: God helps diligent and frequent efforts, but despises the negligent: Let us love the good, so that we do not desire the evil.

**M.** Did you hear what Constancy <note>original: "Frequentia"; the personified character from the previous page</note> said? **B.** I did indeed. **M.** Did it please you? **B.** Not entirely. **M.** Why so? **B.** All things were said about me, but toward what end they tend, I do not know. **M.** For your benefit and happiness. **B.** May God grant it. **M.** Tell me, I pray, do you know that after this life there will be another? **B.** I know indeed. **M.** Do you also know that after the death of the body there is an eternal death? **B.** I am not ignorant of it. **M.** You must live in this world so that you may live for eternity. **B.** What else am I doing? **M.** Daily you die more. **B.** You are insane. **M.** Listen: he lives in this world who dies and lives for Christ. **B.** Who understands this? **M.** Have you not heard in the Gospel, that unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone? **B.** What is that to the point? **M.** You are that grain which fell into the earth, because you are nothing but earth. **B.** But I heard that Constancy referred the grain in the Gospel to the word of <term>GOD</term>. **M.** Now I hear that you have taken notice. **B.** Indeed. **M.** You are not a good theologian. **B.** May you be one for me. **M.** This word, "has died," has an active meaning if the grain of wheat is taken for the word of <term>GOD</term>—that is, it "has mortified" <note>The speaker is playing on the Latin grammar of John 12:24. ### *On Virtue, the fifth step of philosophy.*

### CHAPTER VI.

**M.** O Sacred one, command your gates to be opened to us. **V.** Who are you who wish to approach us? **M.** We are two young pupils of philosophy. **V.** What do you seek? **M.** To learn Virtue. **V.** You seek a just thing, which must in no way be denied to you. What teachers did you have before? **M.** Philosophical Love, and Constancy <note>original: "Frequentia"; used here in the sense of persistent application or spiritual gathering</note>. **V.** I am glad such ones gave you your beginnings. What moved you to undertake these studies? **M.** The desire to know the truth. **V.** The knowledge of truth is the root and mother of all things that God has instituted. But for what end do you wish to know it? **M.** So that we may be able to practice it. **V.** Toward whom? **M.** Toward God and neighbor. **V.** A good intention indeed, to which I pray God gives a happy outcome. What are your names? **M.** My name is Mind; this one's name is Body. **V.** From whom did you receive them? **M.** I was called "Mind" by philosophical love; he retains the name "Body" from the common crowd. **V.** How does the Mind agree with the Body? **M.** In nothing at all; instead, everything between us is in controversy. **V.** What do I hear? **M.** The Body is reluctant to leave the world. **V.** Everything that has once put on the world flees from salvation, and cannot be pulled back from it except with the greatest labor. Enter, brothers, and what I can provide for your sake, I pray you consider with a fair and good mind. Body, lie down on your belongings and take care of your belly. Mind shall be fed by me. O Heavenly Father who refreshes all, may you deign to nourish us in eternal life by your word of truth. Amen. Listen, Mind: the virtue of things is the truth of each individual thing; and truth is the efficacy known through experience; and efficacy is a celestial influence. Whatever is not from heaven ought not to be called virtue, but a false image of it. Once, philosophers who were ignorant of God depicted virtues for us, because they did not understand His son, in whom all the virtues of God were made. Even more recent thinkers are accustomed to divide virtues into Theological and Ethical, than which nothing can be more absurd among learned men: because every virtue is from God, therefore it is theological; that which is called ethical cannot be a virtue unless it is from God. The fortitude of the Romans against their enemies was actually persistence; their magnanimity was pride; their prudence was fraud and deceit; their abstinence was ambition for honor (and so with the rest)—these were vices rather than virtues, because they were prepared not for the glory of God, but for the glory of men and themselves. # SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

<meta>catchword: acqui-</meta>

...regarding virtue, which they divide into Faith, Hope, and Charity. From these three, and within them, the whole of truth consists; whatever is not found in them is false, whether in rational and sensible things or in those that are inanimate. For **Faith** is the certainty of those things which are heard and not seen. For this reason, it is said that faith comes from hearing <note>original: "fidem ex auditu esse"; a reference to Romans 10:17</note>, because what is seen is not faith, but certain knowledge demonstrated through the eyes. Sacred Scripture offers testimony of this: *“Because you have seen, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”* <note>original: "Credidisti quia vidisti. Beati qui non viderunt, & crediderunt"; John 20:29</note>

In natural things, there is a certain truth that is not seen by the external eyes but is perceived by the mind alone. Philosophers have gained experience of this, and they discovered its power to be so great that it performed miracles. Therefore, it is a wonder that men have performed miracles through faith, when even inanimate things can achieve the same through the power <term>virtute</term> <note>In this context, "virtus" refers to the inherent medicinal or magical power of a substance.</note> granted to them. 

The whole of the art consists in this: that a spirit <term>spiritus</term> of this kind be liberated from its shackles, just as it was said above that the mind must be made free from the body. Therefore, the body is a prison in which the virtues of the soul are hindered, and the spirits of natural things cannot exercise their powers. The efficacy of the spirit in such inanimate things—relative to the nature of the object—is of the same kind as the indubitable faith found in man. Therefore, true faith is the virtue of men, while for all other things, the truth of their efficacy is their faith. 

For example, an inexperienced physician <term>physicus</term> <note>Refers to a traditional doctor of the era who studied natural philosophy but often lacked practical laboratory experience.</note> of nature would not want to believe that the carcass of any venomous animal—even if completely dry and withered—when placed upon a wound infected with venom or a pestilential abscess <term>apostemati</term> <note>A swelling or internal pocket of infection, common in descriptions of the plague.</note>, would draw all the poison entirely into itself. Yet this is very well known to the chemists <note>original: "chemicis"; here referring to alchemists or iatrochemists who followed the teachings of Paracelsus.</note> who scrutinize nature’s powers, and they have discovered it through the magnetic force of nature. 

Since such men do not believe that nature can perform what it is capable of, being unworthy of its virtues, they do not deserve to attain even the smallest secret from the treasure chests <note>original: "scriniis"; literally "scroll-cases" or "cabinets," used here metaphorically for nature's hidden archives.</note> of nature itself. If they see an experiment performed by someone else, they do not inquire further as to the reason why such a thing happens; instead, content with the experiment alone, they merely use it. In this great ignorance, the unlearned part of the physicians remains stuck, saying, "It has this property," without curiously investigating from where it comes. 

But the chemical physician <term>chemista physicus</term> is not content with the experiment alone, nor with knowing that a property comes from heaven, but inquires from *which part* of heaven it comes. He performs an anatomy of the "great creature" <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe itself.</note>, making a comparison with that which can be observed in the microcosm <note>The human being, viewed as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>. This he strives to accomplish by four modes and instruments: namely, **Geometry**, **Hydromancy**, **Pyromancy**, and **Astronomy**. 

*   **Geometry** is the investigation of the earth in natural things.
*   **Hydromancy** is the investigation of the waters.
*   **Pyromancy** is the investigation of the fires.
*   **Astronomy** is the investigation of the celestial virtues.

These are the inquiries that the craftsman, moved by philosophical love, willingly undertakes. He is sustained by **Hope** (on which he also feeds) to arrive at that truth of the matter in which faith is already implanted within him. It is evident, therefore, that Hope is the stimulus of faith, or the certainty of future truth. Unless one knows for certain...

<summary>Virtue explains that Faith, Hope, and Charity are the foundations of both spiritual and natural truth, arguing that the "chemist" discovers the hidden "miracles" of nature—such as magnetic attraction—that traditional physicians ignore. She introduces four elemental sciences (Geometry, Hydromancy, Pyromancy, and Astronomy) as tools for investigating the Macrocosm.</summary>

### PHILOSOPHIA.

...[that] he will acquire what he pursues, his effort grows cold; but when he has confirmed a confident opinion, aided no doubt by persistence and talent, there is nothing he cannot achieve. But it must not be overlooked here that faith is proven through charity <term>charitatem</term> <note>Christian love or benevolence, seen here as the active expression of belief.</note>, just as a good or bad impulse can work for good or evil. Therefore, charity is faith perfected in action: who can judge true faith otherwise than as taught by Him who is Faith itself—that it is to be known by its works? Some who understood the matter said that charity must begin with oneself; this I believe should be understood as follows: a Christian must first acquire the habit of virtue through practice before he is able to exercise it toward others in action. 

Learn then, O Mind, to exercise charity toward your own body by restraining its vain appetites; in this way, it will be ready to join you in all things. I will see to it that it drinks with you from the fountain of virtue, and then, the two of you having become one, you may have peace in union <term>unione</term>. Approach this fountain, Body, so that you may drink with your Mind to satiety, and in the future, you may no longer thirst for vanities. O wonderful efficacy of the fountain, which makes one out of two and brings peace between enemies! The fountain of love can make a mind <term>mens</term> from spirit and soul, but here it makes one man from mind and body. We give thanks to you, Father, because you have deigned to make your sons sharers of your inexhaustible fountain of virtues. Amen. Go now, you who have been made a wise man, toward Power <note>Potentia, likely a personified stage or figure in the philosophical journey.</note>, from whom you will learn Constancy, and fare well.

->*Recapitulation of the sixth chapter and the fifth step.*<-

In every thing, there is its own power <term>virtus</term> and a heavenly influence <term>influentia cœlestis</term>, which nonetheless can by no means be seen by the external eyes, though its effects can. We see the attraction of iron by a Magnet <term>Magnete</term>, but we cannot see the magnetic force hidden within the stone itself, because it is a spirit <term>spiritus</term> and does not fall under the senses; so it is with other things. Wine has various powers within itself, which were recognized by philosophers through the experiment of the chemical art <term>ars chemica</term> <note>The early term for alchemy and chemistry.</note> during its separation: its Spirit warms and dries, yet the Body produces the complete opposite, for it moistens with cooling. One can see the experience of these in "burning water" <note>original: "aqua... ardentem"; a term for distilled alcohol or brandy.</note> and in vinegar. 

These faculties are entirely contrary because of the separation; before it, they were not so diverse, because they then shared more of the mixture through natural union. Who (unless out of his mind) will deny that such powers exist in all other natural bodies to a greater or lesser degree? He will not be a philosopher who denies that bread or grain has a spirit within it no less effective than the spirit of wine, although it is not as abundant in bread as in wine; nevertheless, it is equally effective for an equal quantity of its spirit. If such a thing can [be obtained] from bread and wine...

### SPECULATIVE PHILOSOPHY

...if spirits can be separated by art <term>artificialiter</term> <note>Referring to the alchemical process of extracting "spirits" or essential essences from matter through distillation.</note>, how much more does their natural separation occur within a human being? From these examples, philosophical transmutations <note>original: "transmutationes philofophicæ"; in this context, the term refers to alchemy, the art of transforming one substance into another.</note> can be understood. Do we not already know that the purer substance of both bread and wine is transformed into flesh and blood? And that from an invisible vegetable form, a visible animal form is made? It is not the "species" or essence of things that is changed by this, but rather their outward forms. Who can still doubt that philosophical transmutations can be performed through art within a human being—changes far better than those nature herself achieves through the transformation of bread and wine? For there are other bodies in the nature of things that possess a greater natural power and celestial influence; from these, no differently than from wine and bread, spirits can be separated and transformed into the substance of man, into flesh and blood. This can be achieved more excellently through art than through nature. But why should I repeat these things so often, which are clearer than light to philosophers? He who refuses to believe this should test it through the chemical art <term>artem chemicam</term> <note>Alchemy</note>; but if he is ignorant of it, let him learn before he experiments. For if he attempts to do such things through the common art of distillation, he will only waste his oil and his labor. No one should be forced to act for his own benefit, but only warned; if he chooses to despise the warning, he does so to his own ruin, not the ruin of the one who warned him.

->ON POWER, THE SIXTH DEGREE.<-
->CHAPTER VII.<-

->*A dialogue in which Power and Man are the speakers.*<-

<margin>M.</margin> Open, I pray, divine Power. <note>The speaker "V" stands for "Vir," the Latin word for Man or Hero.</note> P. Who wishes to be introduced here? M. A man. P. From where do you come? M. I have been sent by Virtue. P. For what purpose? M. To be confirmed in the virtues which I received from the Minister of Truth. P. Correct; but by what means do you believe this can be done? M. Through Power. P. Through whose power, then? M. The power of Truth. P. In whom do you believe Truth resides? M. I do not doubt that all truth is situated in the power of the Most High alone. P. Now you have shown yourself worthy of confirmation. Therefore, pay attention to the things I am about to explain to you. Power <term>Potentia</term> is the Constancy <term>Constantia</term> <note>In this moral framework, "Power" is defined as the steadfastness or "constancy" to maintain the virtues one has been given.</note> of the virtue received from the Lord. There is no reason for anyone to think he can have even the smallest spark of virtue from anywhere other than from God. If anyone seeks it from himself, or from any source other than the one mentioned, he will obtain vice instead of virtue, to his own destruction. This is how the Gentiles <note>Referring here to the ancient Greek and Roman pagans.</note> of old used to hunt for virtues through "heroic works" (as they called them), for no other reason than to leave a famous reputation to posterity, wretchedly placing their highest good <term>summum bonum</term> and happiness in that fame. But what followed for them, the outcome of such "memorable" deeds has clearly taught us. Their kingdom, because it was founded on sand and not upon rock, necessarily collapsed—and indeed, no greater trace of this ruin...

# PHILOSOPHIA.

...hardly a trace of them is left behind, except so that the folly of these men may be revealed to posterity. For if the Gentiles <note>A term often used in these texts to refer to pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers.</note> had built upon the rock of truth, their kingdom would have remained stable. One must not follow the footsteps of men, but of truth, in which all things are stable. You cannot be better strengthened, brother, than through virtue itself, which is nothing other than truth. If you strive with all your might to observe this truth in all your works and words, she herself will strengthen you more every day, until, having become powerful in battle like a lion, you are able to overcome all the forces of the world and fear neither death nor whatever violence diabolical tyranny can devise. Just as pure gold in the fire always shines more purely and gloriously for a very long time without any loss, so too do the professors of truth rejoice to be strengthened in every martyrdom—of which you shall hear more fully below. But this is worthy of note: just as skill and readiness are granted through the frequent practice of all arts and works, so too are they gained from the diligent observation of truth, in both deeds and words. The constancy of virtues is infused from heaven unto power <term>potentiam</term>, which finally, through uninterrupted observation, passes into a miracle <term>miraculum</term>. This is what you must now long for; travel by this path. Farewell.

->*Recapitulation of the seventh chapter and the sixth degree.*<-

Although virtues are extracted from natural bodies—even inanimate ones (as has been said)—unless they are further led to their extreme power by the chemical art <term>artem Chemicam</term> <note>Alchemy, specifically the process of refining and concentrating the essential properties of a substance.</note>, they will not be fit for any excellent work. But the more they are purified and made subtle through diligent chemical observation, the more they approach their primary celestial influence, and consequently, they penetrate and work more effectively. Thus, the work they achieve in Medicine for any infirmities whatsoever is truly to be regarded as a miracle.

### On the seventh miracle, and the final Philosophical degree.
### CAP. VIII.

A miracle is the effect of the constancy of Truth. In declaring this, we shall use only a single example, through which the miracle will be clearly revealed. A certain Philosopher <note>This likely refers to Anaxarchus of Abdera, a follower of Democritus, who was said to have defied the tyrant Nicocreon in this manner.</note> was taken by a tyrannical Emperor for his profession of truth and subjected to this martyrdom: that he should be pounded alive with a pestle in a hollowed-out iron stone. He said: "Pound away, tyrant, pound this little body <note>original: "corpusculum"</note> of mine; you shall never pound my mind." Because this made the Emperor feel poorly—as he did not want the philosopher to speak the truth any longer, which he could not bear to hear—he ordered the executioner to cut out the philosopher's tongue. But the philosopher bit it off with his own teeth and spat it into the Emperor's face before his body was pounded into a pulp. O, the admirable constancy of the man, which...

# SPECULATIVE [MATTERS]
<meta>catchword: which (quæ)</meta>

...not terrified by such great martyrdom, and undergoing death with the greatest joy, she overcame the tyranny of the world? <note>This likely refers to "Truth" or "Virtue," personified as a woman, which was discussed on the previous page as the only force capable of overcoming death.</note>

->*Recapitulation of the seventh degree, eighth chapter, and the conclusion of the entire previous work.*<-

Just as there are seven philosophical degrees through which an entrance to the heights is opened for the mind, there are also seven chemical operations through which the practitioner can reach that most excellent secret of medicine. Chemical <term>putrefactio</term> <note>Putrefaction: the process of breaking down or "rotting" a substance to its base state.</note> is compared to philosophical study; for just as philosophers are prepared for knowledge through study, so natural things are prepared for <term>solutio</term> <note>Solution: the dissolving of a solid into a liquid state.</note> through putrefaction. Philosophical knowledge is compared to this solution; for as bodies are dissolved through solution, so are the doubts of philosophers resolved through knowledge. In the same way that the frequent practice of studies follows from philosophical love, the first union occurs through the <term>congelatio</term> <note>Congelation: the process of thickening or solidifying a substance.</note> of the chemists through persistence and the repetition of operations. Just as the wits of philosophers are sharpened by frequent company, so the parts of bodies are refined by chemical <term>ablutio</term> <note>Ablution: the washing or purifying of a substance.</note>. In the same manner that philosophers are united through virtue, elements are joined at their smallest levels through <term>compositio</term> <note>Composition: the combining of different elements into a new whole.</note>. As philosophical virtues are confirmed through power, so spirits are fixed in their bodies through <term>fixio</term> <note>Fixation: making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand fire without evaporating.</note>, so that they no longer flee. Not differently than how philosophical works show their power through a miracle, the medicines of Chemistry reveal their perfection through <term>projectio</term> <note>Projection: the final stage of the Great Work, where the medicine is "cast" upon a base metal to transform it.</note>. You now have, most excellent reader, the entire intention of our work. If you do not profit from this in true metaphysical, natural, and chemical philosophy, you have no reason to complain of me, for I have most clearly declared to you whatever was obscured by others. Fare you well, and look with favor upon this little work, such as it is.

### PHILOSOPHICAL TINCTURES

I would now make an end, were it not that philosophical love for students held me back and reminded me to add our philosophical tinctures to the precepts of Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>. By these tinctures, cures—both external and internal—can be achieved through the renovation of the blood. These are the simplest and most powerful medicines drawn through the alchemical art. I have described the method of their preparation, along with their administration, from the *Great Surgery* <note>Original: "Chirurgia magna," one of Paracelsus's most famous medical texts.</note> of the said Paracelsus, so that those things which were said above concerning philosophical medicines may be more easily understood.

->*On the tincture of the Sun, that is, of Gold.*<-

When the tincture of the Sun <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) is the symbolic name for Gold.</note> is extracted, its body remains white, but the tincture itself is pure, and is separated from the impure—that is, from its own body.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for creating alchemical tinctures, following the theoretical stages mentioned on the previous page. It specifically details the extraction of the "Tincture of Gold" using salt water and spirit of wine.</meta>

<page-num>271</page-num>
# PHILOSOPHY

This separation is necessary. The <term>Tincture</term> <note>A concentrated liquid extract containing the medicinal or spiritual essence of a substance.</note> must be clarified or "exalted" in its degree—which is doubled five times to forty-eight <note>original: "bis 24." In Paracelsian alchemy, this likely refers to a specific scale of potency or a measurement of "degrees" of perfection.</note>. It does not progress any higher than this. At that point, it can be administered to anyone for the restoration of the blood to its original state, as will be explained in the section on administration.

->*The extraction is as follows.*<-

The "body" <note>The physical metal, in this case, gold.</note> must be "corrupted" <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down of a substance's outward form to release its inner essence.</note> from its metallic nature by hammering it through salt water. Then, the residue must be washed with fresh water. Afterward, the tincture is extracted using spirit of wine. Finally, it is "elevated" (distilled) away from the tincture, which then remains at the bottom.

->*The extraction of salt water.*<-

Salt water is made from salt that is naturally most pure and white, without the boiling or artificial preparation usually used to make salt. Let it be melted several times, then turned into powder and mixed with the juice of radish roots. Stir it well, then distill it after it has dissolved. Mix this with equal parts of "green blood" <note>original: "sanguineo viridi." This is a common alchemical metaphor for vitriol (iron or copper sulfate), prized for its reactive properties.</note>, and distill the whole mixture five times. In this liquid, a plate of <term>Sol</term> <note>The alchemical name for Gold, associated with the Sun.</note>—purified first by antimony—is dissolved into powder. Let it be washed carefully with pure distilled water until the saltiness is gone; for the salt allows itself to be washed away and does not mix deeply with the gold's substance but remains separate.

->*Spirit of wine is made in this way.*<-

Take one measure of the best, pure, unmixed wine (either red or white). Place it in a circulatory vessel that is very well <term>luted</term> <note>Sealed with "lute," a paste made of clay, lime, or resin to make the vessel airtight.</note> and blocked. Submerge the vessel in a <term>balneum maris</term> <note>A water bath or "Mary's bath," used for gentle, indirect heating.</note> to the depth of the wine and let it boil for ten natural days. Once cooled, let it be distilled in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used for distillation.</note> or a phial at a low temperature until the spirit rises. As soon as it shows its "sign," stop immediately; for what follows is <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>"Water of life," or brandy/strong alcohol, which the author considers distinct from the pure "spirit."</note>, not the true spirit. 

Pour this spirit of wine over the residue, which is like <term>Alcool</term> <note>In early chemistry, "alcohol" (from the Arabic al-kuhl) referred to an extremely fine, impalpable powder, rather than just a liquid.</note>, so that the liquid floats six fingers' width above it. Place the vessel, well-sealed, in a warm bath for one month. Then the Tincture of the Sun (gold) will rise into the spirit, and a white powder will remain at the bottom of the vessel; these two must be separated from each other. Melt the powder, and it will become a white metal. Allow the spirit to evaporate according to the rules of the art, and the "juice" will remain at the bottom like a liquid. You shall refine (graduate) this five times in a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note> large enough for the amount of liquid. Such refinement happens only through "elevation" (distillation), which makes the matter subtle, but it cannot be refined beyond the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The Quintessence: the purest, most medicinal part of a substance, stripped of its physical impurities.</note>—that is, 2. 4. 0. <note>These numbers likely refer to a specific weight or proportion used in the final stabilization of the medicine.</note> Otherwise, it will be "burned" by proceeding any further.

->*The method of administration.*<-

Mix one <term>drachm</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams.</note> of this with one ounce of Venetian <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous, complex herbal jam or electuary used as a universal antidote and panacea.</note>. Give one <term>scruple</term> <note>A small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams.</note> of this mixture on an empty stomach.

Afterward, let the patient be covered in bed so that they may sweat; let this continue for 10 or 12 days.

->*There is also in coral a most excellent tincture for purifying the blood.*<-

The "body" of the coral should be ground finely into a powder <note>original: "alcool." In early chemistry, "alcohol" referred to any fine, impalpable powder before it was applied to spirits.</note>, and its tincture should be extracted just as it is from gold, by means of spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol/ethanol.</note>. Let them rise together sixteen times <note>Refers to a process of repeated distillation or refluxing to increase potency.</note>, and afterward let them be separated through distillation. The rising must be done over an entirely open fire; then, in a <term>Mary’s bath</term> <note>original: "balneo Mariæ." A water bath used to provide gentle, even heat, named after the legendary alchemist Mary the Jewess.</note>, the liquid should be separated six times and poured back over the dregs. This oil should be administered with theriac water—specifically, one scruple of the oil should be drunk with one drachm of the same water.

Theriac water <note>A medicinal water based on Theriac, a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "panacea" used against poisons and diseases.</note> is made with five ounces of spirit of wine, two and a half ounces of theriac, one ounce and two drachms of Roman myrrh, and two drachms of oriental saffron. Let all be mixed and distilled together at once; let it be administered as has been stated.

->*The dosage for administration is:*<-

One ounce and two drachms of it should be mixed with ten ounces of chicory water or germander <note>A medicinal herb of the Teucrium genus.</note> water. Two drachms of this mixture should be given in the morning and evening. The patient should fast for five hours after taking the dose, and for the same amount of time after dinner. This should be continued for six or seven days. Distilled waters made from <term>fumitory</term> <note>original: "fumo terræ," literally "smoke of the earth." A plant used for skin and blood ailments.</note>, chicory, or similar plants should also be given.

->*Tincture of Balsam.*<-

Take half an ounce of balsam and twenty ounces of spirit of wine; place them together in a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized alchemical vessel with two "arms" that allow condensed vapors to flow back into the main body, facilitating constant circulation.</note> or a double vessel, and let them circulate in the Sun for a month. Once this is done, it allows itself to be distilled together with the spirit through an alembic. This distillation is better than using a retort in this instance, provided the mixture remains together in one composition. To this, you will add half an ounce of another balsam, and let the closed vessel be digested so that the balsam which was added can mix with the others, and that which comes out of its body may be perfected. For whatever is to be "graduated" <note>Refers to the alchemical process of increasing a substance's "grade" or intensity of its primary qualities.</note> must bring its substance together into one body. And when this has been made volatile as described above, add again half an ounce of another balsam, which you will "exalt" as before, adding and graduating up to two ounces. This is the most powerful preparation of Balsam, which renews and cures what other preparations cannot; for the sake of its own preservation, it has acquired this virtue from heaven above all other things.

->*The dosage is as follows:*<-

**T**ake the balsam prepared by itself <note>original: "per se præparato." Meaning a substance prepared without foreign additives.</note> in a weight equal to five grains of barley; administer it with old white wine twice a day until it is apparent that the blood has been purified.

->*Tincture of Antimony*<-

**I**t has been discovered in this world that nothing purifies gold better than antimony. For this reason, if it is prepared as a drink for a human being, it can perform the same service, and even better. There is no reason for the learned to marvel that our teacher <note>Likely referring to Paracelsus, the father of iatrochemistry.</note> makes this comparison. Let them first learn to recognize and compare the <term>Anatomy</term> <note>In this context, "Anatomy" refers to the structural and spiritual correspondence between things, rather than just dissection.</note> of the "great first creature" <note>The Macrocosm or the universe.</note> with the "last creature" <note>The Microcosm or Man.</note> before they pass judgment. Just as the sun holds primacy among the stars, and gold among the metals, so does man hold primacy among the living things. For the sake of this perfection, all these things converge metaphysically into one. Therefore, just as antimony thoroughly cleanses gold and consumes other metals, so may it—for the reasons we have stated—re-purify a man. It does this not by a mere emptying of the bowels <note>original: "exoneratione alvi." Common medicine of the time relied heavily on laxatives; alchemists sought "radical" or root-level cures instead.</note>, but through a fundamental purification, by which it spiritually eradicates every superfluity. This is a most excellent <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum." A "secret" or powerful mystery; in alchemy, a high-level medicine that acts on the life force.</note>, the construction of which is as follows: Take the best antimony reduced to a fine powder <note>original: "alcool."</note>, which you shall heat in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat onto the substance being heated without direct contact with the flame.</note> that is well-sealed for one month. From this, it will become volatile—first white, then yellow, and finally a light red or saffron color. You shall then extract its essence from the **Lili** <note>original: "lili." A Paracelsian term for the "lily," signifying the perfected, rejuvenated matter or the "flower" of the substance.</note> by means of **spirit of wine** <note>High-proof alcohol/ethanol.</note>, such that the liquid floats twenty fingers deep above it. Let it be mixed until it is well colored, keeping it well-sealed, as you know how to do. This is the highest preparation of the "Lily," which purifies a man fundamentally, both inside and out.

->*Its administration is as follows:*<-

**I**n a cask of fresh wine in September or October, always add half an ounce of this tincture for every twenty measures of wine. Let them both be allowed to digest and be purified together. Patients should drink this wine for three or four weeks, or longer, in preference to all other drinks, or even without any others.

->*Tincture of the Salt of the Philosophers*<-

**T**ake salt of gold, salt of antimony, and salt of lemon balm <note>original: "melissæ."</note>, half an ounce of each; eight ounces of pure, rocky common salt. Mix them together, and let it be eaten on a slice of bread on an empty stomach. Do not wonder that we here include salt of gold and salt of antimony, which are not common salts, but "philosophical" ones. Once you have learned those things which it is proper for you to know in this art, you will wonder no longer.

->*Another Philosophical Salt*<-

**T**ake salt of germander <note>original: "gamandreæ."</note>, salt of chicory <note>original: "cichoreæ."</note>, and salt of valerian, one ounce of each; half an ounce of salt of wormwood <note>original: "absinthij."</note>; one drachm of salt of **vitriol** <note>Sulfate minerals, often used to create acidic or metallic salts.</note>; and one pound of pure, rocky common salt. Mix them together, and let it be eaten as described above.

### *The <term>Arcanum</term> <note>original: "Arcanum." A deep secret or hidden mystery; in Paracelsian medicine, it refers to the potent, inner essence of a substance that has the power to heal or transmute.</note> through which those things set down above are elucidated.*

**H**eaven and earth, by means of man, generate man, who is their son, daughter, and offspring: from heaven he receives his intellect, and from the earth his body. Because he is of the earth, he exists within his body, and to the earth he shall return; yet that which is of heaven within him comes from the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the stars. Paracelsus believed the "astral body" of man was a direct reflection of the celestial heavens.</note>. Furthermore, he possesses one thing more by the gift of God, through which he is able to rule over the stars, provided he has learned this from God. Heaven and earth exist together, and so too do heaven and man; but just as man is from the earth, he must for that reason be understood according to the earth and from the earth. Yet, insofar as he is from heaven, he must also be judged according to heaven. Therefore man, heaven, and earth are one, as are air and water. If a man knows how to transmute things in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>The "greater world" or the universe at large.</note> (such as turning all things into salt), how much more should he know how to do this in the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "lesser world," referring to man as a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>—that is, within himself? Whatever he can do outside himself, he can do within, provided he recognizes that the greatest treasure exists in the man within the man, and not outside of him. From his inner self proceeds (albeit indirectly) that by which he works upon the outside world, which he sees with his eyes. Therefore, unless he is mentally blind, he will see—that is, understand—who and of what quality he is inwardly; by the light of nature, he shall know himself through outward things. 

It is certain that from the blood of man is generated <term>Natural Salt</term> <note>In the "Tria Prima" (Three Primes) of alchemy, Salt represents the principle of stability, physical substance, and preservation against decay.</note>, the balsam of his body, which contains within itself both corruption and the preservation from corruption. For in the nature of things, there is nothing that does not contain within itself as much evil as it does good. Likewise, from the bones and flesh is generated <term>Natural Sulphur</term> <note>The second of the Three Primes, representing the principle of combustibility, growth, and the "oily" heat of life.</note>, which is set ablaze on account of the drying out of the natural moisture, and sometimes consumes the whole body and itself. The cause of this fire is that man was, from the beginning, sulphur; this was transmuted into flesh and blood, which are the "middle matter" of man. The first nature (or matter) hates this middle state intensely and strives to lead it back to itself. When it has done so, the result is earth and ash—the remnant of the "first matter" of man and the subject of his "ultimate matter." 

Because man is generated in corruption, his own substance pursues it with hatred. Hence it happens that the natural sulphur of man recedes from the "middle creation" back toward the "first matter." As it approaches this state and assumes its nature, it passes into an elemental operation. This elemental fire is the cause of corruption, and it is ignited by the invisible sun, unknown to most: this is the <term>Sun of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "sol philosophorum." Not the physical sun in the sky, but a spiritual or metaphorical source of heat and enlightenment that drives alchemical change.</note>. Such are the virtues within man that, through the power of corruption, they are able to dry out the moisture; by this path, they reduce the salts of man into the nature of lime <note>original: "calcis." Refers to 'calx,' the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been burned (calcined).</note>, through which the body passes into a sulphurous state. Thus the body is reduced into <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "materiam primam." The formless, original substance from which all things are created and to which they return.</note>, toward which it has been made ready to receive the fire that corrupts man back to his original essence—just as we see in other creations, in the earth or the mountains. ->*Description of Potable Gold.*<-

Take one ounce of leaf gold, or gold in powder form; let this be dissolved into a juice; you shall add as much distilled vinegar as is sufficient; distill it afterwards, and separate [the components] from one another; do this until no taste of the additives remains. Then, let all be immersed together in five ounces of <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>original: "aquæ vitæ," literally "water of life," referring to concentrated medicinal alcohol.</note>, and let them be <term>digested</term> <note>heated gently to encourage chemical reaction</note> in a <term>pelican</term> <note>original: "pellicano." A specialized alchemical flask with two side-arms that cycle vapors back into the base, used for constant circulation.</note> for one month.

->*The description of that water of life is as follows.*<-

Take ten pounds of <term>burning wine</term> <note>original: "vini ardentis," a high-proof distilled alcohol.</note>; one handful each of roses, lemon balm, rosemary blossoms, wallflower, leaves of both hellebores, and marjoram; two ounces each of cinnamon, mace, nutmeg, cloves, grains of paradise, all types of peppers, and cubebs; six ounces each of the juice of celandine, mullein, and lemon balm; and five ounces of bean ashes. Mix them together and allow them to be digested in a pelican for 12 days; finally, separate it, and you shall reserve it for the use we have set down above.

### ->Conclusion of the philosophical key.<-

Having already provided the Key, I shall not be at all reluctant to hand over its use and its storehouses—specifically for the dissolution of these substances and the philosophical separation of their contents—to any diligent seekers of the secrets of nature. By this work, besides my other labors, and by a certain supernatural craftsmanship that elucidates the said Key, I wish to prove that I have lived more for others than for myself until now; the work itself teaches this, and all who have seen me will attest to it. 

It would be right, therefore, for me to rest for a while, until at last another of our profession might come along to lift the burden. Not that I am surrendering, but so that I might catch my breath to resume my strength against those who try (in vain) to defeat the truth of nature which Paracelsus <note>The author here positions himself as a defender of Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), whose radical medical theories challenged traditional Greek and Roman authorities.</note> professes. I see that I do not have much leisure, for that great Leader of his enemies is near. We must arise on both sides, for the weapons of war are sounding. 

However, with my stone and sling already prepared, I do not fear this giant, even if I seem like a pygmy to him <note>A reference to the biblical David and Goliath, representing the author's struggle against the "giant" establishment of traditional medicine.</note>. For Truth arms its own against deceitful, ambitious, and proud men—those who hide under a cloak of eloquence because they would never dare to come out into the light naked with simple speech, lest the vice hidden within their "decorated tomb" should appear <note>A reference to "whited sepulchers" from the Gospel of Matthew, meaning something beautiful on the outside but corrupt within.</note>. Therefore, I come to the encounter in the power of truth. Fare well as much as you are able.

# ON THE SUPERNATURAL
# CRAFTSMANSHIP.

It is proper for us to prove from the very beginning that our "supernatural craftsmanship" <note>original: "artificium supernaturalem"</note> is the legitimate offspring of nature, and that any other chemical arts are counterfeit. Modern Physicists and Metaphysicians stubbornly deny our <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quintam essentiam," the quintessence or aether; in ancient and medieval philosophy, this was the pure substance that made up the celestial bodies, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>. This provides us with the best argument against such men: that their own opinions for teaching are worthless. What will those men judge the heavens to be? Will they dare to deny us that there is a "fifth thing," separated by God from the four elements—as the pure is separated from the impure—or will they, by this very act, confess their ignorance? There is no doubt that they fail to understand this secret. If they were to admit to us that the heaven is indeed separated from the first four essences, it must therefore be a fifth essence. Unless, of course, they were to say that the heaven is also made of the four elements and four pure essences, so that there would be eight essences in total. By saying this, they would deny that a pure heaven exists at all, and they would claim it is just like the inferior elements here below. 

For in this context, "purity" refers more to a state of unity than to simple cleanliness. If the four elements were in the heaven mixed together just as they are here below, they would appear mixed there just as they do here—which is not the case at all. Instead, it appears to be a single, unique element, adorned with many celestial bodies—as many as are in the lower world—and these correspond to one another as effects correspond to their cause. 

This is the true "separation of elements" which it befits true Alchemists to imitate: namely, the separation of the purer substance from the impure elements, just as the superior is separated from the inferior. That common <note>original: "vulgaris"</note> separation, which is done by separating oils from waters and these from their earths, is a separation of qualities, not of elements. For instance, if an oil—which some call "air"—is separated from its earth and water, nothing else will have happened except that elements which are more viscous, fatty, or hot have been produced from their qualities through that separation. For every element is present in any one of these parts, regardless of how they are separated. It is more sensible, therefore, to name them in this way: namely, the "hot element" for the part to which <insert>it more...</insert> <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "magis" (more) indicates the thought continues on the next page.</note>

...heat adheres more to fire; moisture to water; coldness to air; and dryness—most of all—to the dryness of the earth. We shall make use of these terms below. But to return to the heavens: the ancient <term>Sages</term> <note>original: "Sapientes"; the author refers to the lineage of natural philosophers and alchemists such as Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> called that the incorruptible part of the universe, the "Superior World." They affirmed it was separated by God from the other lower part—the "Inferior World," which is prone to decay. They most aptly called this the universal <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "essentiam quintam," also known as the quintessence; the pure substance of the stars, distinct from the four earthly elements</note> and the natural form. The inferior world, however, they called the universal matter of nature, which is capable of receiving all its forms.

Before these two parts were separated from their "whole" (which is called <term>Chaos</term>), each contained the other in a confused state. Even after separation, each retains within itself a bond of the first union and love, daily desiring to be connected to the other. This very affection and desire is the cause of all <term>generation</term> <note>The process by which new life or substances are created</note>, and it is truly called "Nature." These are the principles of our Physics, which I have treated more extensively in my previous books.

Now, however, let us see what the principles of our supernatural craftsmanship are, lest those who so sharply and wrongly attack it say it lacks its own foundations. This art is properly nothing other than a craft consisting of natural principles, yet excelling nature through its artifice. Through some divine secret, it is necessary to use the same principles that nature herself uses, for we cannot build from anything else. But where Nature ends her <term>Physics</term> <note>The study of natural, physical bodies</note>, we begin our <term>Metaphysics</term>. We take those things which nature has left finished and perfected for us, and we "more than perfect" them through a certain supernatural craftsmanship. 

And because we cannot handle the entire great "heaven of nature" with our hands, nor enclose all the elements within our instruments, we are compelled—following the likeness and imitation of nature—to hunt for these things within natural substances. By our <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterio"; a technical term for the alchemist's skill or the "Great Work" itself</note> of separation, we separate our "heaven" from our impure elements so that we may fashion our own "Chaos." From this, we must begin this admirable work, which ought to excel the mastery of nature. Now, unless I am mistaken, in—

...more wonderful, you will understand why we say our metaphysics surpasses every work of nature. For the separation of the heavens from the elements, or the first division of **Chaos**, was not a natural craftsmanship, but purely divine. In this, however, we are truly said to *imitate nature*, because we work in this art by the method of corruption and generation, and we use the same principles as she herself does. We say more broadly that in any natural body composed of elements, the heavens and the elements are partially contained; otherwise, they cannot be generated. Therefore, while we separate these things, we are able to have form and matter similar to those from which **Chaos** existed before its own division. 

Why then does <term>Cerberus</term> <note>original: "Cerberus"; in classical mythology, the three-headed dog guarding the underworld. This is achieved through their intermediate nature, enclosed by us in our vessels along with them, by a supernatural mastery similar to the first division of Chaos—provided that God, without whom nothing is completed, grants it to someone, and if it has been correctly begun. 

This is the only way by which one may reach the **universal and metaphysical medicine** that cures all diseases without distinction, a cure about which modern <term>Physicians</term> <note>original: "Physici"; at this time, university-trained doctors who relied on ancient theories of "humors" rather than laboratory chemistry.</note> despair. Do they not see that all particulars are included in universals? Since, therefore, such a medicine is fashioned from the incorruptible heavens and from incorruptible elements (or those reduced to incorruptibility), and shaped not only after the likeness of the whole world but even after the **resurrection**, why will it not prevail against all corruptions of the human microcosm that relates itself to this medicine? 

If those <term>Zoili</term> <note>original: "Zoili"; plural of Zoilus, a Greek grammarian known for his spiteful criticism of Homer. It became a standard term for envious or pedantic detractors.</note> understood the mystery of the **resurrection**, perhaps they would not disagree with metaphysical truth. But because they follow the dreams of those who were ignorant of and denied the resurrection, they are least able to be capable of this secret, nor are they worthy of it. What is it to us? The more they try to resist the truth, the more nakedly they will uncover their own ignorance and the rudeness of their intellect, or the obscurity and blindness of their own mind.

...vituperate <note>The page ends on the catchword "vitupe-", likely leading to "vituperant" (they find fault), referring to those who give up on the study of alchemy too early.</note>

Let us turn to the students of the true arts and ask God to remove the mists from the eyes of others, so that they may be able to see those things which He wishes to be revealed to His own. With the foundations previously laid and the principles established in our unique **Chaos**, it will be worthwhile to teach the extraction of its parts from natural compounds to those who believe this metaphysical work was given by God to people of good will. We have said that these parts are indeed the heaven and the elements of all things. It is certain that these exist naturally in all things produced by nature; however, they are more abundant in some, less in others, and in some, they are even easier to extract than in others.

For this reason, it is the opinion of the philosophers that those things which are nearer and easier should be more readily embraced. Such substances include the best wine, <term>Tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartarum"; the potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine casks, used in alchemy as a source of "fixed" salts.</note>, fresh honey, <term>rosemary flower</term> <note>original: "Flos anthos"; specifically the flower of rosemary, highly valued in distillation.</note>, <term>red lily</term> <note>original: "Lilium rubeum"; likely the Lilium bulbiferum, used for its supposed solar properties.</note>, <term>greater celandine</term> <note>original: "Chelidonia"; a herb traditionally associated with the eyes and the "gold" of the sun.</note>, <term>mercury herb</term> <note>original: "Mercurialis"; the plant known as Mercury's herb, used in medicinal chemistry.</note>, and so on. From these, either by themselves or through other means, the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "essentia quinta"; the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance, distinct from the four physical elements.</note> can most easily be separated from its coarser elements, and these parts can distribute themselves into their predominant qualities—while the other elements still remain within each individual element.

It must also be noted that in this context, <term>philosophical wine</term> <note>original: "vinum philosophicum"; an alchemical term for any liquid—not just grape wine—that serves as a base for extracting essences.</note> can refer to any liquid from which its quintessence can be separated by artifice, as we will teach below regarding wheat, bread, grains, or juniper berries, and so on. Nor should you be ignorant—if you wish to be a practitioner in this art—that the form and matter from which the **metaphysical Chaos** exists are the quintessence, or the heaven (of which we have spoken) of all things, and the elements. Therefore, take care that you are not confused by the variety of names. For I cannot use any terms other than those which are necessary for this art. If, however, some things remain obscure or veiled in riddles by ancient writers, I will attempt to clarify them with easier explanations for others. I do not want you to think, however, that I am teaching you from my own self or from things I have dreamed up, but rather that I am describing to you in a clearer sense those things I have been able to learn from the most proven authors of this art—lest you despair along with the many who, whether because of the complexity or the obscurity of those writings, always turn away after a second reading and...

...they unjustly find fault, when they ought rather to criticize or sharpen their own dullness of mind and laziness. Nor do I desire, because I speak more clearly, for the way to be easier for those [unworthy] people, but for the truly dedicated students.

There is no reason, then, for you to wonder why I observe a different mode of writing in treating these matters than the ancients did. You may consider this done for your sake, so that you might understand better. Therefore, do not let the disciples of false arts hold you back from this study; they have not seen the light so far, nor can they bear it, nor do they wish others to see it. Let this be an example to you of their ignorance: you see none of them who would take up the pen against the ancient writers in this art to refute them with probable reasons and deductions from the art itself; instead, they merely afflict them with slanders and insults. Even when such a person (however learned he may be) is unable to prove these slanders, he compares upright men to "dark ones" and <term>ape-ists</term> <note>original: "simiistis"; a biting pun by the author. It is not enough to say, "This man is a rogue and a deceiver"; rather, he who dares to call others such things must bring forth the reason why he is so, or else he openly reveals himself to be such a person by that very act. For indeed, it is the Devil's way to call everyone else slanderers, because he wishes everyone were such; thus do his children also persecute the good. Yet some who appear to be **Chemists** have also wished to refute other **Chemists**, perhaps because they used different terms than the ancient true **Chemists** set down, or they attributed this art allegorically to the fabulous fictions of poets (by which figure of **Rhetoric** <note>original: "Rhetorices"; the formal study of persuasion. -># PREFACE.<-

Many people—either because they cannot master this art, or because they see others with a talent more fortunate than their own—attack either the art itself or those who have written more obscurely than their intellect can bear. They think they have gained praise for themselves by carping at others. But they do not write of what the truer **aim of the art** <note>original: "scopus artis"; the ultimate goal or target of alchemical perfection</note> consists, nor do they explain it more clearly or transparently. As for men of this sort, along with their biting "files" <note>original: "mordacibus limis"; a metaphor for abrasive, eroding criticism</note>, I hardly value them at a straw. 

If I can bring anything good to this art, or treat it in clearer words—while still maintaining due modesty—I will do so diligently, as befits a man out of **charity** <note>original: "charitate"; the Christian concept of brotherly love and duty to help others</note> toward any other. When they attack me, I shall see what and in what manner I shall respond. I am not willingly moved to act against others until I have been provoked by their words, deeds, or writings—as has happened before, falsely and wrongly, to the perpetrator's own harm and disgrace. These, then, are the things I set before pious and upright readers to be read first, and finally to be compared most exactly with the writings of the ancients; where they see them agree, let them grant them faith; otherwise, let them not. 

It would be impossible, however, for even an exceptional talent to learn the **solar art** <note>original: "solarem ipsam"; referring to the "Solar" work or the creation of gold/perfection</note> through reading alone. Therefore, he who wishes to fulfill his desire in this art must become a master by **working**. Writing can be compared to nothing better than a **key**: unless this is handed over, access to what is closed is not easy, and the key is useless unless it is inserted into the lock. In the same way, until you apply your hands to this work, you will not understand the **secrets** <note>original: "arcana"</note> which God has enclosed within the **nature of things** <note>original: "rerum natura"</note>, so that they might eventually be made known to men. 

We propose these things to you, then, so that you may receive the key by which you may learn, through sincere study, to unlock **physical** locks with **metaphysical mastery**. Meanwhile, whatever labors we have undertaken, we have brought them for your sake, honest Reader. Take them in good part, and farewell.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of alchemical philosophy, moving from a defense of his work to the specific theory of "metaphysical separation." It builds on the idea that the "fifth essence" or quintessence must be extracted from the four base elements of the physical world.</meta>

## CHAPTER I.
### *On metaphysical separation performed by itself.*

Previously, we said in the Preface that heaven is the **fifth element** <note>original: "quintum elementum"; also known as the quintessence, the celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements</note>, not because there are truly five elements, but only four. Their purer substance is supernaturally different from God, and it was drawn back into heaven into a state of union; the impurer part remained below, divided into four parts which constitute the lower and **elemental world** <note>original: "mundum inferiorem & elementarem"</note>, while the other part constitutes the ethereal world.

In no different a way, our **metaphysical quintessence** <note>original: "essentia quinta nostra metaphysica"</note> is drawn by supernatural mastery from the impurer elements of things through **separation** <note>original: "separationem"</note>. This separation is not of the kind many people imagine—those who stray from the truth, believing falsely that the four elements can be separated so that one is entirely free from the other. For if this were to happen, the **machine of the world** <note>original: "machina mundi"; the functional structure of the universe</note> would easily fall apart. But to prevent this, the Most High Creator of all things provided a way, and willed these four parts to be preserved under such a union that, although one can be distinguished from the others by its qualities, it nevertheless retains their essences within itself. 

He revealed this union to us more clearly in the heavens, where no distinction of parts is visible; yet he enclosed this unity under the bond of both superior and inferior nature: which are one and the same nature. Therefore, there are two types of separation: namely, one of the elements (as of the purer from the impurer), and another of the elemental qualities. This latter kind is **common** <note>original: "vulgaris"</note>, but the former is **metaphysical**. Nature, however, works through commixture alone, and this contains two operations: namely, **Alteration** and **animation**. We shall treat each of these more broadly in what follows. 

Now let us speak of the separation of the pure from the impure. This occurs in certain bodies **by itself** <note>original: "per se"</note>, as in wine, and in others through a **vehicle** <note>original: "per vehiculum"</note>, such as in grains and seeds. Although the **quintessence** <note>original: "essentia quinta"</note> lies hidden in all bodies produced by nature, it is found in none so abundantly as in wine, and it can be separated from nothing else so easily. For this reason, the philosophers preferred wine due to the ease of its separation—not because the quintessence is naturally better or more excellent in itself than that drawn from any other body. For that celestial virtue is universal and equal in all things; it is only different because of the diversity of the **subject** <note>original: "subjecti"; the physical matter in which the essence resides</note>, and only for as long as it remains within it. Once set free, it returns to its own unity. This is indeed one of the more hidden secrets of nature, through which the philosophers reached higher things. You shall, therefore, separate from any body its **spirit** with its **soul** <note>original: "spiritum ejus cum anima"</note>, as follows.
