## NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

...the mass to be understood, until the first division, namely of light from darkness.

->*And God also said: Let there be light, and light was made.*<-
<note>original: "Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat lux, & facta est lux." Genesis 1:3.</note>

With the <term>primordial matter and form: the basic "stuff" and "shape" of the universe before it was fully organized</term> of the world completed, God willed to create light. For light is the spirit in which the life of natural things was placed by the Lord their Creator. This light was indeed necessary to complete what was said regarding the earth and the abyss—namely, to provide illumination for the earth and to fill the formlessness and emptiness of the abyss. Therefore, light was the first ornament of the heavens and the elements; it was also the third and most powerful member of the <term>ideal world: the perfect blueprint of the universe as it exists in the mind of God</term>. For this reason, in the first instance, it is commended to us by the Supreme Creator and approved as "good" in these words:

->*And God saw the light, that it was good.*<-
<note>original: "Et vidit Deus lucem, quod eſſet bona." Genesis 1:4.</note>

One might hesitate at this point, wondering whether God did not also see that heaven and earth were good. Truly, anyone who looks upon these words with a pious mind understands that all things created by the only good God are, likewise, nothing but good. Furthermore, just because one thing might be "more good" than another, it does not diminish the dignity of the thing that is "less good." For the individual members of one and the same body are assigned their own specific roles and duties by the will of their Creator, so that one does not envy the other. We read the same thing concerning charity—that it is greater than hope and faith. Consequently, it does not follow that the other two are of lesser esteem. Indeed, it is read elsewhere that "by faith alone man is saved." Therefore, for God to "see the good" (as a certain righteous man said) is His way of confirming the good to us.

->*And he divided the light from the darkness.*<-
<note>original: "Et diviſit lucem à tenebris." Genesis 1:4.</note>

A similar doubt might occur: were the darknesses not approved by God, since the good light is divided from them? When something is divided from the "good," it usually seems to be "evil," as is seen in the separation of the sheep from the goats. However, in Genesis, this division should be understood in the same way we later read about the division of the waters from the waters, the higher from the lower, the heaven from the earth, and the man from the woman. In these cases, there remains a bond of union and a coupling through mutual desire; this arises from the fact that the divided parts were born from one and the same source, not from different ones.

->*And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night.*<-
<note>original: "Appellavitque lucem diem, & tenebras noctem." Genesis 1:5.</note>

It is known that the day arises from light, and that through the obstruction of light, night is introduced. Light is obstructed by the placement of an opaque or dense body in its way—such as the sphere of the earth, which creates the shadow of night. Therefore, to cover light with darkness is to close the day, just as to drive away the night with light is to introduce the day.

It interprets the division of light and darkness not as a moral separation of good and evil, but as a natural distinction between two parts of a unified whole.</summary>

# GENESIS
Y 4
<meta>catchword: Let (original: Fiat)</meta>

> *And there was evening and morning, one day.*
<note>original: "Et factum est vespere & mane dies unus." Genesis 1:5.</note>

The division of the parts that remain joined in union is here explained. Indeed, by "morning" we understand light and the <term>artificial day: the period of sunlight as opposed to the full 24-hour cycle</term>, and by "evening," we understand night and darkness; these two parts together constitute a single <term>natural day: the full 24-hour period including both light and dark</term>. This darkness should be understood as natural darkness, which God willed to be of service to us. It is entirely different from the "outer darkness" that exists outside or beyond the bounds of nature, into which we read the evil angel was cast down.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one day," it is the opinion of learned and pious men that we should consider this with the deepest reverence. They believe it refers to the completion of the <term>intelligible world: the perfect "blueprint" or conceptual version of the universe existing in the mind of God</term>. This "one day" is not numbered among the other five days in which they hold that this <term>sensual and visible world: the physical universe that can be perceived by the five senses</term> was materially established according to the pattern of that ideal world. Therefore, the physical world begins properly from the "second" day. 

In this system of thought, the first number—meaning the number two or duality—is representative of matter, just as unity (the number one) represents form, or rather, the "First Idea." Indeed, the Trinity is the offspring of unity, just as the number four is the offspring of duality. Thus, they argue that the world was created divinely as an ideal "one" under "one day," and not a "first" day. Only afterward was it created materially, following the order of its own idea, under the "first" number. It seems irreverent to try to confine "unity" (which represents the indivisible God) under the constraints of number and order. Although human reason teaches that numbers consist of units, we should not for that reason think that "Unity" itself is just another number in a series. For multiple units differ from the concept of Unity as much as the confusion of a crowd differs from simplicity. Because multiple units create a multitude, Unity cannot admit them into itself. 

For this reason, Moses said that under evening and morning "one day" was made, and not the "first" day, as many versions have it; it should not be doubted that this happened through the oversight of translators. Thus far we have spoken of the creation of the intelligible world, to which it is wrong to assign any location other than within the infinite Word of God, which occupies no physical space. Now, we shall speak of the visible world, built according to that model and image, which has its foundation and beginning in the great uncreated mystery.

# PHYSICS
344
<meta>catchword: of Physics (original: Physices)</meta>

->*Let there be a firmament.*<-
<note>original: "Fiat firmamentum." Genesis 1:6.</note>

The creation of the visible world is narrated by Moses as having been performed first on the second day, which can be called the first of the numbers not without merit. For the history of the material creation of the world takes its beginning from that day. Furthermore, Moses teaches that heaven was made through the creation of the firmament in the midst of the waters. This indeed corresponds most aptly to what was said above regarding the waters: namely, that the spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters. From this it is quite clearly established that all things first existed as waters, which the highest creator had taken up and prepared for himself as the first [matter] of his material creation. Here, "the midst" is not to be understood as an equal distance from the extremes, but rather as a separation, just as we say a conciliator or moderator between opposing parties is a "medium," lest the laws of friendship be thrown into confusion. Not otherwise here: so that the lower waters might not henceforth be mixed with the upper ones, the firmament was created by the Lord as a medium. Moses teaches this very thing, saying from the mouth of the Lord, *and let it divide the waters from the waters*; as if he had said, "let it divide the heaven from the elements."

->*And he divided the waters which are under the firmament.*<-
<note>original: "Et divisit aquas quæ sunt sub firmamento." Genesis 1:7.</note>

This division corresponds quite elegantly to the division that had been made between light and darkness: specifically by the principle through which the pure is understood to be divided from the impure. What, I ask, is purer than light? Is anything more impure than darkness among those things which were created? In the second place, heaven is far and wide purer than all the elements. Hence we see that the first division of those things contained under the unity of the waters was that of light from darkness, occurring on one day; and the second followed on the next day, namely the division of the heaven from the elements. 

From this, through physical contemplations, the first foundation of <term>Chemistry: in this context, the author refers to Alchemy, specifically the "Spagyric" art of separating and purifying substances</term> takes its origin. For the principal practice of that art is occupied with the division of the pure from the impure in any things produced by nature. From these things which have been said, therefore, it is clear that by "pure" we understand light and heaven; and by "impure," the earth and the elements, divided by the divine means of the firmament. 

Therefore, those thinkers seem to be "mistaken by the whole heaven" <note>an English translation of the Latin idiom "toto caelo errare," meaning to be completely and utterly wrong</note> who teach any other division of the elements than that of all of them together—remaining in their natural bond—from their pure heaven which was mixed with them by nature. Consequently, the <term>physico-chemists: scholars who combined natural philosophy with laboratory experimentation</term> (not those who run in vain without knowledge of true physics) have considered—and not rashly—that every body brought forth by nature is placed before one's eyes by this same nature, just as the dark waters are hidden within it. These they might divide by their own "fiery and artificial firmament" <note>likely referring to the alchemist's furnace or the heat of distillation</note> into upper pure parts and lower impure parts.

Furthermore, this division brings with it the division and difference which is now seen between the ancient physicists and Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note>. # PHYSICS

<sig>Y 5</sig>

He laid the foundations of Physics <note>original: "Physices"</note> primarily upon the upper part of Genesis. Those [traditional philosophers], however, float only upon the lower waters; from these, they establish the four so-called primary qualities as the pillars of their building within the four lower elements. Nevertheless, they are compelled to admit their own three primary physical principles: namely, form, matter, and privation <term>Privation: In Aristotelian philosophy, the absence or lack of a form that a subject should naturally possess</term>, even though they teach nothing less than what "true form" actually is. What they mean by "privation" other than a deprivation of natural light cannot be understood at all. In contrast, Paracelsus embraces this light of nature (of which those others seem deprived) with all his effort and strength, so that through it he may penetrate into the hidden mysteries and secrets of nature. If they have any regard for the nature of form, why do they not teach that it should be separated from its matter and liberated as if from a foul prison, so that it might be able to act freely? If they are ignorant of the method and the art, why, I ask, do they find fault with it? Furthermore, it seems foolish to both praise and despise that which is unknown. Indeed, it is the mark of a completely insane mind to be moved without cause or occasion. But our spirit calls us elsewhere.

We said before that the division of heaven from the elements gave the beginning to the Chemical Art <note>original: "arti Chemicæ," referring here to the practice of alchemy</note>. It remains for us now to clarify what the true professors of this art understood by their "heaven." It is nothing other than exactly what Paracelsus meant by his "sulphurous Mercury" <note>original: "Mercurium sulphureum"</note>. For after they have divided the upper waters from the bodies of their confused waters by means of their own artificial firmament, they set aside each part separately until they are used, as will be heard in the following sections. Let it suffice for now to have opened the fountain of our first principle—namely, Mercury—from which it flowed. Moreover, we shall look more deeply into the division of heaven from the elements. This was especially necessary for the successive generation and propagation of those things which God first created in the elements by the power and wisdom of His word. For nothing can generate within itself, but only in another which has been taken out of itself. Therefore, the primordial waters were necessarily divided, so that the final division of Adam from Eve might correspond to that first division, and vice versa.

->*And God called the firmament heaven.*<-
<note>original: "Vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum." Genesis 1:8.</note>

The firmament is to be considered as the whole natural heaven, extending from the position of the Moon (which is nearest to the elements) all the way to the extreme outer edge of the created natural universe, and not only for the height of the "fixed stars" (as they call them), as the infidels <note>the author uses "infidels" to refer to secular or pagan philosophers, likely including Aristotle and Ptolemy</note> teach.

We assert that the planets, which they also wish to call "wandering stars," are located in the firmament according to the opinion of Moses: to whom alone more faith should be attributed than to all the schools of the infidels. <note>original: "continuat"</note>...continues, while he offers himself having been caught up into the third heaven. Any pious and truly Christian person will judge this very event to have been supernatural from the fact that he must have seen, heard, and learned supernatural things there, rather than natural ones. Who, then, will doubt that the remaining two heavens, placed beneath the supernatural heaven, are natural? One is incorruptible, free from every quality, change, and vicissitude; the other, however, is corruptible and situated in the middle region, in which all changes, alterations of qualities, and meteorological generations <note>original: "meteoricæ generationes," referring to atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, or lightning</note> occur. For this latter one is most clearly called "heaven" by Moses on the sixth day, when he says, *that he might rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven*. The higher or lower positions of the planets do not constitute so many separate heavens, but they move freely in a single heaven with the rest of the stars, according to the order in which they were set in motion by the finger of their Creator from the beginning of their creation. They will preserve this same order and motion inviolable until the end of the age. They are not driven around as if fixed to some celestial body with nails or hammers—as the unfaithful <note>likely referring to secular or Aristotelian philosophers who believed in rigid celestial spheres</note> seem to imply well enough, albeit quite silently. These people do not see what is before their very feet, yet meanwhile, these Astronomers wish to recite to a hair's breadth <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail"</note> what happens in heaven. But why do they not openly confess it, when they teach instead that the fixed stars move perpetually at equal distances within the concavity of the firmament? The more wonderful—indeed, almost impossible—this seems to our human understanding, the more holily and firmly, and with greater veneration, we Christians must admire the craftsmanship of such a great Architect <note>original: "opificis"</note>. We do not wish, nor ought we, to call back these secrets of God to the scale of human intellect (as the unfaithful do), so that we might know by what logic all that was done by the Lord comes to pass. It should be enough for us to confess that all things are in His power, and that He Himself has done whatever He willed.

->*And it was made evening and morning, the second day.*<-

It will not be superfluous to repeat in passing on this second day what we said previously regarding the "one day" according to the opinion of some. For although this day is called "second" by Moses, it seems it should by no means be understood according to a numerical series and order, as we have heard. Rather, it is called "second" so that the perfect number of six <note>original: "senarius"</note> regarding the days of creation might be completed, which indicates to us the perfection of the world, just as the number seven <note>original: "septenarius"</note> indicates the bond of heaven with the elements; likewise, in supernatural things, it indicates the peace of the mind with the body, and eternal rest in their union.

# GENESIS
347

On this day, which is called the third, the second part of the visible world was created—namely, the element known as "the dry land," which was previously called earth. It is as if Moses had said: in the beginning of the world, God created its upper part, the heaven, and its lower part, the elemental earth. One might ask why Moses, from the beginning, made mention of the earth rather than the other elements like water, fire, and air? The reason is readily apparent: it was done because the earth is the lowest of all elements, and no other could better denote the lower part of the world. Furthermore, only the earth among the others is stable and fixed; from its center, as if from a spring or a foundation, the rest seem to sprout and rise upward through the agency of fire.

Who is so ignorant of true physics <note>original: "Physices," referring here to the study of natural laws and the physical world</note> that they do not know that fire—the lower element—has the first root of its origin in the center of the earth? From there, by its own tireless nature, it eventually rises upward toward the hollow of the firmament. As it penetrates and passes through the bodies of earth and water, it carries with it their purer and more subtle parts, turning them into air and lifting them into the middle region of the atmosphere. Once it arrives there, it can penetrate no higher, as the firmament blocks its path. Consequently, its heat, now weakened by too much expansion and overcome by the cold of the subtle earth, water, and the middle region, gives way. Together with the air and earth—having been turned into water through condensation by the fire—all these things become heavy and fall back down to the earth and water, returning to the place from which they had first come.

Physio-chemists <note>original: "Physiochemistæ," scholars who applied chemical principles to understand the natural world</note> call this "circular motion," and they imitate it in their own operations just as they do other natural processes. In this manner, the four elements, having been made volatile by the agency of fire, receive "seeds" <note>original: "femina," literally "seeds" or "feminine principles"</note> from the masculine nature of the higher stars. This occurs through influence and impression within the middle region—as demonstrated by meteorological generations <note>atmospheric phenomena like rain or dew</note>. Afterwards, by the falling motion described above, they carry these seeds into their four "matrices" <note>wombs or places of origin</note> so that they may conceive and produce their offspring, which have been ordered from the beginning of their fertilization by the Supreme Creator for the propagation of all things generated from them. Of this generation, there are four fathers and an equal number of mothers. However, of the other kind of generation, which occurs through influence alone, there is only one father and one mother—namely, the Sun and the Moon in a general sense; but in a specific sense, there are as many intermediaries of generation as there are remaining astral bodies.

Furthermore, I will by no means keep secret what the wise Chemists understand by their "elemental earth" in their art. It is, without a doubt, the very thing that Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist</note> wished to impress upon us through his "salt." For within it, the four elements have their seat and dwelling place, as if in their own home. This can indeed be demonstrated to the eye by an easy experiment, as will be shown more extensively below.

I will add, regarding the gathering of the waters, that this distinction happened solely through gathering, and not by division, as was the case with the separation of the waters from the waters <note>Refencing the separation of the "waters above" from the "waters below" on the second day of creation.</note>.

Furthermore, this former separation admits no further physical mixing of the divided parts, though it certainly allows for a spiritual one through influence, as we have said. The latter separation, however, allows for a physical mixing of its parts, yet not so completely that each part does not retain its own form and place to penetrate the earth and be mixed with it. However, it is impossible to reduce these to many parts; most wise Nature—the daughter of God—provides for this through the artistry of fire performing its office in the center of the earth. The ancient physicists <note>original: "Physici," meaning those who studied natural philosophy and the laws of the physical world</note> seem to have been ignorant of this; otherwise, they would not have hurled themselves into the flames of Etna, like that famous physicist and physician of his time, Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who, according to legend, threw himself into Mount Etna to prove he was an immortal god</note>. Nor would that historian of physics, Gaius Plinius <note>Pliny the Elder, who died during the eruption of Mt. Vesuvius</note>, once considered the secretary of nature, have allowed himself to be suffocated by its flames and smoke. Because both were unable to grasp this secret of nature with their intellect, nor investigate the causes of that burning, they were no less than despairing and wretchedly devoted themselves entirely as an unholy offering to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire; here used to mean the volcano's fire</note>. Thus, it is sometimes permissible to call such men "heathens" just as we call any other heathens.

->*And let the dry land appear, etc.*<-

The change of the name "earth" to "dry land" for the single element—namely, earth—indicates clearly enough that Moses wishes to explain in what sense he understands "earth" when he says: *God created the heaven and the earth; the earth was void and empty*. He does not use it only for the single element, but for all elements having a common center in the center of the earth and founded upon an uncreated center. Otherwise, he would have said as before, *And let the earth appear*. He reveals his mind more clearly by saying, *He called the dry land earth*. It is as if he were saying: I want you to understand "earth" through the term "dry land," which appeared from the gathering of the waters into one place from among the four elements.

->*The gatherings of the waters He called seas.*<-

Moses made no mention of the bubbling of springs, nor of the things that arise from them, such as rivers, but marked all the lower waters with the name of "seas" alone. From this, it is easy to conjecture that those other waters arise from these, and that they bubble up through the pores and passages of the earth, flowing back to their source. They leave their saltiness behind in the earth and are transformed into sweetness by their passage through it, with subterranean fire <note>A common early modern belief that the earth's internal heat acted like an alchemist's furnace, purifying water</note> effecting this very thing. Namely, a sweet vapor is raised up while the salt remains behind in its own proper place in the earth. This is clearly visible through chemical experiments <note>original: "Chemicis oculariter," literally "to the eye through chemistry"</note> in the distillations of seawater or any brine: the sweet distilled liquid is carried upward while the salt settles at the bottom. Therefore, springs and rivers are the matter...

...[spr]ings, lakes, and so on, flowing forth from one and the same place, globe, and sphere, united together in the gathering of the waters under the firmament. On the earth's surface, although seas, bays, lakes, and other such things appear to us to be divided or segregated, they nonetheless meet at one and the same center. Indeed, there are very few people who see that all these things—and even all others—come together, as is taught by these words: *into one place* <note>Genesis 1:9: "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place."</note>.

->*And God said: Let the earth bring forth, etc.*<-

These words must be referred back to what was said previously regarding the mental creation: *The earth was formless and empty* <note>Genesis 1:2. The author distinguishes between the "mental" plan of God and the physical manifestation of those plans.</note>. It is as if Moses were saying: The elements, or the lower part of the world (namely the waters under the firmament), were still formless, naked, and sterile, and without any power, until God gave them form by His word on the second day—both through the gathering of the waters and by the planting of fertility. The Most High clothed this nakedness with a green garment and filled its sterility with fruitfulness on the third day, progressing from vegetation (starting with the smaller herbs) to the largest trees; likewise, he moved from the infinite element, namely the earth, toward the waters and the air. The first ornament of the earth seems to be those things which, lacking senses, have a root fixed in the earth in place of a mouth, through which they receive nourishment, just as animals do through the mouth. For the earth is the nursing breast of nature for plants, and water provides them with milk. 

Inasmuch as they lack sex, they were given seed within themselves; and because they are deprived of free movement, they cannot come together like locomotive creatures. Therefore, those Physicists <term>Physicists: in this context, natural philosophers who studied the laws of the physical world</term> seem to be most delirious who attribute sex to plants through their labels of "male" and "female." For the similarity of two external forms in natural things—even if there is some slight difference—should not be judged as a distinction of sex, but should rather be referred to different species. Some, wishing to avoid this error, have fallen into a far greater one, assigning "greater" and "lesser" to plants under one and the same name. By this very act, they imprudently admit their ignorance of the names of natural things, as well as their powers and virtues; it would have been better to give names based on these qualities rather than on external forms. It seems foolish to assign a "male" that differs in species from its own matrix <note>original: "matrice," referring to the womb or the originating source.</note>. Furthermore, the earth is the matrix and mother of all plants, while their seed is the father. See, I ask you, how can the parents of these things agree in species? It is not so with animals and locomotive creatures, where each parent agrees in species with the other.

## DAY FOUR.

> *And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day from the night.* <note>original: "Dixit autem Deus: Fiant luminaria in firmamento cæli, & dividant diem & noctem." Genesis 1:14.</note>

What Moses had previously stated as a conceptual "idea"—*let there be light* <note>original: "fiat lux." Genesis 1:3.</note>—he now repeats as a physical reality. For "light" seems to be one thing, while a "luminary" <note>An object that gives off light, like the sun or a star.</note> is another. It is not unlike the relationship between the spirit and the body: although they are joined into one, the one is not the same as the other. In a similar way, light and a luminary relate to one another (to use a crude example) like the flame and the oil in a lamp, except that in a lamp these are consumed, whereas in the heavenly bodies they are more enduring. It is clear, indeed, that light was created before the luminaries. 

After the Most High God had adorned the earth with growing greenery, He wished to decorate the heavens with innumerable lights, as had been mentioned in the previous order of events. *The earth was formless and empty*; and shortly thereafter it is added, *And darkness was over the face of the deep.* <note>Genesis 1:2.</note> It should be noted that a wonderful mystery lies hidden in this sequence. For the Supreme Creator of all things wished to create vegetation before the sun and the rest of the luminaries, so that perhaps wicked men would not believe that those plants were created by the stars, or that they received their primary powers and virtues from them. He did this so they would not attribute to the creatures what belongs to the Creator alone. Nevertheless, the greater part of mankind fell into this very error, as can be seen among the unfaithful who worship the sun and stars, neglecting the true God, or at least remaining ignorant of Him. 

We Christians, however, acknowledge that all virtues—both natural and supernatural—are received from the unique power of God alone in all things. And although we confess (as is right) that all things were first created by God alone, and likewise animated and endowed with their own virtues, we see that He still chooses to use His own "means" <note>The author is discussing "secondary causes"—the idea that while God is the ultimate cause, He uses natural objects like the sun to perform specific functions.</note> for the propagation of those things which were to be generated in the elements after the creation. These means include the powers of the higher luminaries, which also proceed from Him, as we read:

*And let them be for signs and seasons.* <note>original: "Et sint in stationes & tempora." Genesis 1:14.</note> Are not the seasons, days, and years—following their cycles—the "secondary causes" for the production of things from the earth? Yet they still depend on the First Cause, namely God. This is clear from what follows: *That they may shine in the firmament of heaven and give light to the earth.* <note>Genesis 1:15.</note> Who, I ask, doubts that natural light is the life of natural things, and that supernatural light is spiritual life? For Christ asserts to us that He is the light and life of the world. Likewise, John says: *He was the true light* <note>original: "Erat lux vera." John 1:9.</note> (he says) *which enlightens every man coming into this world*, that is, He gives life. By analogy, for the earth to be illuminated by natural light is for it to be naturally quickened; just as to be illuminated by supernatural light is to be spiritually quickened. It is truly marvelous and worthy of the highest consideration that in the creation of the world, God willed opposites to come together into one: such as the bright heavens with the dark elements forming only one world, which also proceeded from a single beginning through a division into opposites. From this, furthermore, the venerable Trinity shining in unity can be clearly recognized by us in all natural things. Because that which must join two opposites into one must itself be a "third thing" that partakes of both. This is the very bond of nature, a mutual love situated in nature, like the longing of parts originating from a natural unity to return to it again. For God is the author of peace and reconciliation in all things. Where, I ask, would this be if there were no opposition? A few words are enough for one who understands, especially since this topic requires a sober and quiet treatment. Therefore, this mystery is not to be profaned, as it belongs to a higher place than mere Physics.

### PHYSICS

There is a certain <term>physiognomy</term> <note>Historically, this referred to the study of outward "signatures" or physical marks that reveal the inner nature or virtues of a thing, often influenced by the stars.</note> and an observation of the marks impressed or engraved upon lower things by higher ones through <term>influence</term> <note>In this context, "influence" (Latin: *influxus*) refers to the flowing down of celestial power into the physical world.</note>; it is through these marks that the forces and virtues of such things become known to us. This art is not taught in the schools of the unfaithful, nor does it spring from the vain opinions or dreams of men, but rather from the <term>light of nature</term> <note>The "light of nature" (Latin: *lux naturae*) refers to the innate wisdom and order found within the physical world, which scholars believed could be understood through observation and divine grace.</note> once it has been illuminated by the supernatural. Therefore, we must seek from the supernatural light in order to obtain the natural. Nevertheless, there are certain means granted by the Lord to men of good will, by which their minds are best prepared to perceive and understand these things, and are freed from every obstacle that might hold them back. Yet, truly, these things rarely or never happen to the lazy and the spiritually sluggish; and they are especially denied to those who, out of ignorance, hold such matters in contempt. Furthermore, the marks of lower things must be considered in two ways: either by external signs, or through the examination of internal qualities, which is taught by <term>Volcanic Anatomy</term> <note>A term from early chemistry and alchemy (referring to Vulcan, the god of fire) meaning the analysis of substances through the application of heat or fire to reveal their hidden components.</note>.

->*That they might shine in the firmament, and illuminate the earth.*<- <note>original: "Ut luceant in firmamento, & illuminent terram." Genesis 1:15.</note>

This passage was sufficiently declared in the preceding sections, where we compared light to life and illumination to the act of giving life; for this reason, it may be passed over.

->*God made two great lights, etc.*<- <note>original: "Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna, &c." Genesis 1:16.</note>

Regarding all the lights in general, it was previously said: *Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven*; <note>Genesis 1:14.</note> but now Moses begins a discourse specifically concerning the two principal ones: the sun and the moon. After God had placed the light in the firmament so that it might shine through the medium of the "greater light" and illuminate the elements by day—which are otherwise dark by their own nature—He did not wish for them to be deprived of light by night. Therefore, in His providence, He also created the "lesser light," which nevertheless receives its light from the greater one, so that the darkness of the earth’s shadows might be illuminated through the night. Thus, just as the sun introduces dryness to the elements during the day because of its heat, they are in turn irrigated by the moon at night with the dew of heaven. By the moon’s moistening and the sun’s nourishment, all things are propagated—by the power of God alone, yet through these aforementioned means.

->*And the stars.*<- <note>original: "Et stellas." Genesis 1:16.</note>

Because of the phrasing placed between the creation of the two lights and the stars—namely, *to rule over the day and the night*—a doubt could arise as to whether we should read "and *for* the stars" <note>This refers to a grammatical ambiguity in the Latin text between the accusative case (stars as the object created) and a potential dative reading (ruling over the stars).</note> rather than "and the stars." This would imply that the great lights also rule over the remaining smaller ones, and especially over the moon in respect to its duty and office. Whichever way it is read, it seems that there is little or no deviation from the true goal in the context of Physics; however, in the context of Theology, "and the stars" is the preferred reading.

# GENESIS

It is so. For the sun itself is known to be the king and lord of all the stars and the moon, for the reason that it provides light to all of them, and they cannot borrow it from any other source. Indeed, the sun is the fountain and the underlying subject of all natural light: it distributes this light to the moon—which is otherwise dark by its own nature—no less than to all the remaining stars, which, just like the moon, receive whatever light they possess from the sun. Nor does it seem to have been enough that the stars receive light from the sun directly; rather, God willed that they should also receive the universal or general <term>virtue</term> <note>In this period, "virtue" (Latin: *virtus*) refers to an inherent power or active celestial influence, rather than just moral goodness.</note> of the sun indirectly through the moon. This power they would then arrange according to their own nature and condition, eventually preparing it to produce their own specific forms within the elements. 

Who does not notice that every twenty-eight days the moon approaches the sun (in its own way) so that it may draw from it, as from a fountain, universal form and natural life? As the moon then moves away from the sun, making its passage through each of the heavenly houses, does it not carry this life down to all the other lesser lights? These stars, indeed (as was said before), prepare and arrange the general form they have received into a singular species unique to each. Then, through the <term>influence</term> <note>From the Latin *influxus*, meaning the "flowing in" of celestial energy into the physical world.</note> of their rays penetrating the heavens and the air, they push it forward into the elements. From where else, I ask, if not from here, can we all perceive such a great variety of species in nature itself across every individual thing? 

Yet, to know which naturally produced things correspond to their specific stars in the heavens—*this is the task, this is the toil* <note>original: "hoc opus, hic labor est." A famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, used here to emphasize the great difficulty of this study.</note> that must be applied regarding <term>spagyric astronomy</term> <note>A branch of knowledge that combined alchemy (the "spagyric art") with astrology to understand the chemical and medicinal properties of plants and minerals as governed by the planets.</note>. Let those endowed with a refined intellect judge what this means. No one can doubt that this wisest man and most powerful king, who was supernaturally enlightened by God even in natural matters, once wrote such wonderful works on <term>Physics</term> <note>In the early modern period, "Physics" referred to the general study of nature and the physical world, often called "Natural Philosophy."</note>. 

But through the injury of time and the wickedness of men—who are always and everywhere prone to evil and falsehood—the world has been deprived of this ray of natural virtue. They have caused the true light of natural wisdom to remain hidden until now, so that the truth is almost erased from human memory, not only in Physics but in all other arts whatsoever. May Almighty God grant that, having mercy on us at some time, He might command at least some sparks of that Solomonic Physics to be stirred up and sprout again in the world through His angels, through whom He also wished to reveal these secrets to Solomon from his infancy.

### THE FIFTH DAY

A difference appears from the very beginning of the creation of animals between their life and that of the plants. One should not, however, infer that plants do not live. Therefore, by these words—"above the earth and under the firmament"—a sufficiently clear mention of the creation of air and fire was made for those who understand; thus, flying creatures are also produced partly from fire (without which air cannot persist). Indeed, it is naturally impossible for air to be an element without the element of fire, just as the element of water can by no means be separated from the element of earth, unless it happens contrary to nature. ### A CLEAR AND VERY BRIEF EXPOSITION
### *of the Enigmatic and Truthful Discourse,*
### *left by Mercury Hermes Trismegistus.*

That Hermes Trismegistus, surnamed Mercury, was no commoner in his instruction regarding the doctrine of Genesis handed down by Moses; he left to posterity this spagyric Physics taken from that source. Truly, because it was enigmatic and compressed with extreme brevity, there have been various interpreters of it, each according to the different capacity of his own talent. It is known to everyone that all who have attempted this very difficult task have turned their focus toward the transmutation of metals, mostly in an allegorical sense. # PHYSICA

->**A full knowledge of the various kinds of Vulcanian anatomy is highly necessary.**<-

It is no wonder that those for whom the hidden mysteries of nature lie concealed are amazed that such a medicine can be found which is so universal that it can, without distinction, heal all diseases. This is because they are carried upward (as the saying goes) by only a single wing, and a very heavy one at that. Their minds can scarcely bear even the most obvious things, for they hold so fixedly to those ideas they were imbued with from youth that they will not admit better things, however slightly more hidden they may be. Therefore, such people should be left to their own wasting away when they prove stubborn. For the present, we let them go and speak instead to the students of truth.

Furthermore, every single thing possesses its own inherent virtue, yet it also contains its own poison <note>The author is likely referencing the Paracelsian concept that "the dose makes the poison" and that every natural substance contains both a healing "essence" and a toxic "dross."</note>, from which it can be purified by the **Chemistic art**. However, because of the degrees of "more or less," all things must be tested, and only those which are best are to be retained. In this way, the artist's labor is sometimes relieved of the intolerable burden that weighs upon the artificial extraction of the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" (Sol) represents Gold or the masculine principle, while the "Moon" (Luna) represents Silver or the feminine principle.</note> from all things.

If, therefore, you follow the opinion of father **Hermes**, and join the **Sun** to his **Moon**, and nourish their offspring in their own earth with a gentle fire, you will bring to perfection that medicine of which he speaks, saying: *all obscurity shall flee from you, and so forth.* <note>Original: "fugiet à te omnis obscuritas, &c." This is a famous line from the "Emerald Tablet" of Hermes Trismegistus, a foundational text of Western alchemy.</note>

But indeed, before you attempt this work, it is necessary that you return your very self to the simplicity of unity through the "Chemistic art" used in a moral sense. By this, you must first learn to drive away all obscurity of the mind from yourself; afterwards, illuminated from on high, you will perceive the light and the medicine that can dispel darkness and ignorance from both your body and your mind.

Therefore, you must learn with the greatest mental attention the moral philosophy that I propose to you in the following pages, and you must first diligently practice it within yourself in a moral way if you desire to become skilled in the things which father Hermes teaches in this place. You could not be taught in any easier or clearer words than those contained in this brief discourse—both here and in the exposition of the Hermetic art—in which he teaches that in this fleeting life, no art is more to be sought after than that which teaches the separation of natural bodies from their **binary** <term>Binary: In this context, the state of division, duality, or the conflict of opposites in unrefined matter.</term> and their reduction into union through the **ternary**. <term>Ternary: The number three, often representing the reconciliation of opposites into a stable third state, such as the alchemical union of Body, Soul, and Spirit.</term>

Truly, no better example could be given of the human **resurrection** than from this teaching. For the author suggests that the natural bodies of "senseless" things <note>The author uses "insensata" (senseless) to refer to minerals and chemicals that lack biological life but possess a "spirit" or essence that can be refined.</note>—divided and purified from their spirits—can be joined to them again for a resurrection, which is to say, a perfection. Just as human bodies are separated from their spirits or souls by death, so that later, by the will of God alone, they may rise again into eternal life through a conjunction better than the first. In no different a way, this art also teaches how to separate the spirits and souls of senseless things through **artificial corruption** (which is called **Chemistical death**), so as to reduce their ternary to a unity—that is, to a better life; although it is not an eternal one, it is nonetheless more excellent than that which they previously held from nature. For these "senseless" things live within themselves...

...themselves by a hidden motion, which, after they have reached a state of union, most clearly reveal this life through their operations upon foreign bodies. They are drawn away beyond and above nature through the speculative or meditative faculty alone, as well as through the discipline of the body—not merely by bridling its appetites, but by their total suppression <note>original: *castratione*. Finally, through the conjunction and alliance of the divine spirit with the soul—achieved by rejecting earthly things and embracing eternal and heavenly ones—these three are joined into one. In this way, through the likeness of Him who alone is one God in a trinity of persons, we are made closer and more conformed to Him for eternal life and His glory,

### ON THE SPAGYRIC METHOD OF DISPOSITION,
### *toward the true knowledge of the adopted philosophy, and the pure sight of the light of nature.*

->HERMES TRISMEGISTUS.<-

->With the expositions of Gerard Dorn.<-

It is true without falsehood, certain, and most true. That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to perform the miracles of the one thing.

And just as all things were from one, by the meditation of one: so all things were born from this one thing, by adaptation.

Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of every *completion* <note>original: "Thelesmi"; likely referring to the Greek *telesmos*, meaning perfection, completion, or the "will" of the world.</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it is turned into earth.

You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth into heaven, and again descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and lower things.

Thus you shall have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all darkness shall flee from you.

This is the strong strength of all strength. Because it will overcome every subtle thing, and penetrate every solid thing.

Thus the world was created.

From this shall come wonderful adaptations, the method of which is this.

Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus <note>Trismegistus means "Thrice-Greatest," traditionally referring to Hermes as the greatest philosopher, priest, and king.</note>, having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world.

What I have said concerning the operation of the sun is finished.

->### PHYSICS<-

...that which is devoid of truth. Although a better definition of both cannot truly be given, nevertheless, on account of its universality, it cannot be sufficiently understood by those who have barely been initiated into the sacred and hidden mysteries of nature. Therefore, it requires much elucidation, which we have concluded should be drawn from a division. Truth, therefore, can be understood in two ways. Taken in a physical way, it is not without falsehood. From this it is clear that the author does not mean this physical truth, but proposes to us a <term>spagyric: a term derived from the Greek words for "separating" and "combining," referring to the alchemical process of purifying substances by breaking them down and reuniting their essential parts</term> truth—that is, one purged of falsehood. 

For nature is truthful and, on the other hand, lying; it is both incorruptible and corrupt. It obtained truth in its creation through the Word of God, but falsehood from something added, to which, because it gave place, it is also forced to possess. Nor can nature by itself vindicate or separate its truth from its falsehood unless it is aided by the spagyric mastery. It is clear, then, that Physics concerns itself as much with the falsehood of nature as with its truth; but the spagyric art concerns itself only with the truth of natural things, purged of their falsehood. Therefore, the truth of any thing is properly called its incorrupt nature. 

One should not think, as many do, that <term>Hermes: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy, such as the Emerald Tablet, are attributed</term> spoke here only in a common way to his followers—as if he simply wanted to suggest to them that he was speaking the truth—but rather that under crude speech familiar to everyone, and even under every minor distinction, he has enclosed the greatest mystery of nature. This was done for this reason: so that those who are not his sons, "though seeing, they may not perceive, and though hearing, they may not understand." <note>A reference to the biblical language in Matthew 13:13 regarding parables.</note> For secrets cannot be hidden more safely than when they lie concealed beneath a manifest shell. 

We see God has willed to do this very thing everywhere in nature: namely, to cover what is precious beneath what is base, so that it might not be found by the unworthy. How much gold do cheap sand, mud, and despised stones veil from the eyes of those looking at things which the hand of the ignorant casts aside and the foot of the unlearned tramples? How secretly has He enriched regions that are sterile on the surface with unknown wealth, which He denied to fertile lands? Why do anxious mortals still complain? Since God has given all things to all people, saying: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and all things shall be added unto you." <note>Matthew 6:33.</note> 

Thus, the chief cause of each person's poverty and want is their own negligence. Although God willed that there be more poor than rich, so that the latter might exercise their charity toward the former, and the needy might follow Christ by taking up their cross; for He Himself willed to be the poorest of all on earth. From this it also happens that gold is not found in every stone or any kind of sand, and it is not granted by heaven to all to know those things which contain it, lest all likewise become rich. But let us return to where we started: to the truth of natural things, which father Hermes teaches must be sought through the spagyric art, and that the pearl must be separated from the base and the rejected. # TRISMEGISTUS

...[entirely] well known, but to very few, and it is certain to far fewer still. For example: it is known to most that some stones and some sand contain gold within them, but it is certain to no one except for him alone who has made a trial of that matter, and through the experience of the art has extracted it: he alone can say that it is certain. Indeed, the author intends in this place to prove the <term>spagyric: A term for alchemy, specifically the process of separating substances into their components and recombining them in a purified state</term> art to us by a certain authority excelling all others, which is experience—as if he were speaking: I myself have experienced that this spagyric art is true, certain, and most true. For I have learned the certainty of this art not through the authorities of men or writings, but by experiment alone. 

It must be noted, therefore, that what he had previously said in a physical way—that it is "true and without a lie"—he now repeats more deeply in a spagyric manner, as if he were saying: Within physical bodies there resides a certain hidden truth or incorruptible virtue, about which I have been made more certain through the spagyric craftsmanship; it will be a certain and most true medicine, if only it is freed from its shackles and from the foul prison in which it is held. 

From these things it appears clearer than light that natural philosophers are led only by an opinion of the truth, based on some indication of the external <term>physiognomy: Here meaning the outward appearance or "signature" of a natural object</term> of natural things, or by the false appearance of some effect, or by the authorities of writers; but spagyric physicians are disciples of experience alone, from which they also learn the certainty of truth. For there are two ways which philosophers happen to enter: opinion and experiment. Relying on only one of these, it is necessary that they deceive themselves and others with their teaching or work. However, whoever examines both and judges one by the other, these shall not be frustrated in their labor, nor shall others to whom they bring their work or counsel. Opinion indeed proposes doubtful things, though appearing true in philosophical colors, which must finally be verified by experience. 

*What is above (he says) is like that which is below, and vice versa.* Having first testified to the truth, he proceeds to its proof, drawn from a true physical <note>original: "Genesi"</note> Genesis. It is true, he says, that these lower elements are of one and the same substance as heaven itself, and they differ in no other way than by <term>accidents: In Aristotelian philosophy, non-essential qualities (like color, weight, or state) that can change without changing the underlying substance</term>, such as the corruptible and the incorruptible, the pure and the impure, the heavy and the light, the clear and the opaque, the active and the passive, male and female, etc.—all of which are accidents, not substances. 

Furthermore, heaven is incorruptible; hence it happens that of those things which are corruptible (the pure elements), none is raised higher than the concavity of the <term>firmament: The celestial sphere or the sky</term> in which the body of the moon travels. We say the cause of this matter is because the <note>original: "patiens"</note> passive receiver does not have absolute power over its <note>original: "agens"</note> active source, but rather the reverse; whereby it happens that heaven can be mixed with the elements through <term>influx: The alchemical and astrological belief that celestial powers "flow" down into earthly matter</term>, but these elements cannot be mixed with heaven. But although we call the elements "passive," this must be understood with respect to heaven, since they are able to act upon each other through the motion of corruption. # PHYSICS

<meta>catchword: ...rum mun-</meta>

[Fire] acts upon water, and water acts upon fire. However, these actions and passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> can produce nothing permanent within the elements by themselves without the aid of heaven. It appears that from water, through fire by a certain refinement, air is made and generated; yet this air is forced back into water, and fire—overcome by this water and air—is forced back into itself, and compelled to return to where it arose. We do not see the same happening with celestial actions upon the elements, because from those celestial influences, natural bodies are generated within the elements; these bodies, by their nature, do not return again to heaven or to the elements, except against nature, such as through death or the mastery <note>The "mastery" or *magisterium* refers to the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>. There are also other generations not unlike "meteorological" ones (even if they have not been thought of as such until now), occurring not in heaven, but in the elements of air and fire beneath the earth. These are helped, no differently than ethereal things, by celestial actions and impressions for the generation of minerals, stones, and metals. 

Furthermore, since a perfect generation cannot occur in heaven alone—no more than it can occur in a male—nor in the elements without heaven—no more than in a female without a male—each is instead one half of generation. Therefore, this difference was necessary, the division of two having been made from one, as will be told more fully later. Someone might perhaps say: "If heaven and the elements are different from each other, how is it that the author says they are the same?" He speaks of the identity of substance, not of accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or smell, whereas "substance" is the core reality of a thing.</note>, as he explains in what follows. For it is the nature of substances to generate, and not of accidents—though accidents nonetheless provide assistance and promote natural generation, they do nothing by themselves, no more than they can exist without substances. He concludes this likeness under the unity of substance, saying: *To perform the miracles of one thing.* 

Now he explains in a <term>spagyric: The alchemical practice of separating, purifying, and recombining substances, often for medicinal use.</term> way those things he had previously proposed in a physical way, in roughly this manner: It is necessary for the spagyric craftsman of wonders to have a most perfect knowledge of heaven and the elements, of their identity and harmony, before he can reach the unique goal of all Philosophy and the limit of universal medicine. By this knowledge, he may fabricate this most general medicine, performing the miracles of the universe through the "One thing," which alone can heal all diseases indifferently—both the "incurable" (as they call them) and any others whatsoever. 

It is certainly not surprising if there are very few physicians who can believe in this art, since it is worthy of the highest wonder even to those who have experienced it, such as Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> and others; what then will it be to the ignorant? But if anyone considers the "great works of God" <note>original: *magnalia Dei*</note>, included within nature by Him, though he may wonder for a while, yet with the greatest veneration he will judge it not impossible, if he be truly a Christian. Nevertheless, it is impossible for any mortal to understand this art unless he is first illuminated by the divine light; then also, in the making (as they say), he will see miracles bring themselves forth in it, which to the most learned—

# OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...of the world's wise men are hidden from the eyes and the mind. If someone does not immediately understand these things, they should consider either that they are not among the chosen, or that the hour of their election has not yet arrived. For it often happens that after many years, and having endured labors and studies even at great expense with patience, some are chosen—provided they have preceded this with many knockings, prayers, and diligent investigation. For the first Leader of <term>spagyrists</term> <note>original: "spagirorum Dux". Dorn often uses this title for Hermes Trismegistus or Paracelsus, the legendary founders of the "spagyric" or alchemical art of separating and recombining substances.</note> says: "Knock, and it shall be opened unto you; ask, and it shall be given; seek from the kingdom of God, and you shall find." Yet very few are found who do not grow weary of the labors and persevere until the very end. 

Consequently, it happens that the art sometimes undeservedly gains a bad reputation from such people; they cast upon the art the blame they should have more rightly attributed to themselves. Therefore, so that my modest work in this matter does not seem to fail anyone in its purpose, I will bring into the open a few small things that have been entrusted to me thus far regarding the understanding of this most excellent science, which teaches the unique and <term>universal medicine</term> <note>The "universal medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, believed to cure all ailments by restoring the body's harmony with the heavens.</note> of the ancient fathers. Hear, therefore, you who have ears to hear! 

It is necessary that a medicine of this kind be incorruptible, penetrative, and agile, just like heaven, so that it may act upon the elements and into every physical body no differently than heaven itself. Let us see, then, what the operation of heaven is within the elements. It is certain that they [the elements] do not live, except with a "short life," and are "dead" in terms of "long life" by themselves; they lost this long life along with man due to the curse following his sin. God did not curse the heaven because of man's transgression, and thus it retained its "long life." For this reason, the elements are "dead," because being destitute of a long and healthy life, they tend toward the death of the "short life"—namely, the curse of the earth—which remains with them only until the beginnings of its most hostile enemy, death (meaning diseases), pressing from all sides, reach the end of their course in all their products. 

They are, therefore, like a corpse separated from its soul, insofar as they lack that part of "long life." Unless heaven flows into their center from all sides, they cannot ascend upward from it by means of the central fire, nor can they conceive the spiritual seeds of heaven—even when their <term>matrices</term> <note>In alchemical biology, a "matrix" is a womb or place of generation where seeds of life take form.</note> are made spiritual in the middle region—so that they might descend into bodily matrices. For opposite extremes can in no way meet without a middle ground that participates in both sides. Thus, the long and healthy life of natural things is "heaven." Likewise, life is the repelling of death, and the beginning of death is the failing of life. 

Any physician, therefore, who knows how to join the incorruptible <term>spagyric heaven</term> <note>The "spagyric heaven" is the purified essence or "quintessence" extracted from matter, which possesses the life-giving properties of the celestial stars.</note> of long and healthy life to the internal and languishing "heaven" of a "short life" in sick bodies, will (by God's gift) restore that short life to health through the "miracle of the one." For both the languishing [internal] heaven and the incorruptible [spagyric] heaven joined to it are one and the same in substance; thus it happens that through substance...

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

<note>original: "TRISMEGISTI." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note>

...nature, no thing has being as what it is, but every thing is produced or born from it alone, out of that which has being from nothing, through the word of God alone and His power; and it does not have substance from the word: this itself is the first visible creature, namely, nature. The Author's <note>Referring to Hermes.</note> opinion seems to me distorted and mutilated by the omission of one word, namely **created**, through the negligence of translators rather than the printer; and I believe it should be restored in this way: *As all things were **created** from one, by the meditation [of the one], etc.* Hermes therefore hints with these words that this universal medicine must be made in imitation of the creation of the world, not merely composed, as is clearer below: **So (he says) the world was created.** This phrase also confirms my opinion that I have not wrongly or rashly restored what seemed mutilated. 

It should be gathered from these things that the <term>spagyric work</term> <note>Spagyrics (from the Greek 'to separate' and 'to join') is the alchemical process of breaking down a substance into its essential elements and then recombining them in a purified state.</note> for the universal medicine is both begun and completed in imitation of the creation of the world, and is therefore supernatural by likeness, although it is made from natural things. Furthermore, the author concludes physical generation from the supernatural creation of the world, a likeness having been made of natural unity to supernatural unity, and not of the unity of the spagyric artifice: for he has not yet reached the operation of that art. But he first briefly attempts to strengthen it with the firmest arguments against any detractors and ignorant people before approaching it, lest his sons be delayed by the trifles of the reprobate who also reprove it. For he adds: **So all things were born from this one thing.** 

He teaches that there was a single most general kind of created things, from which the remaining kinds, species, and individuals were born, and are propagated daily until the end of the world. There is no reason anyone should think "one thing" in this place ought to be referred to the Creator, but rather to one creature, namely primitive nature: which even the preposition, *this* <note>original: "hac", which is feminine, matching "nature" (natura) rather than the masculine "God" (Deus).</note>, seems to denote. For if the genitive "of the one" <note>original: "unius"</note> in that place—*by the meditation of the one*—referred to the agent "from the one" <note>original: "ab uno"</note> (which would be contrary to all rules of speech, for he would rather have said "they were from the one by the meditation of the same"), it is certain that he likewise ought to have said afterward: *so all things were born from this one* <note>original: "ab hoc uno", which would use the masculine form to refer back to God.</note>. 

These things were said by me only to warn the reader that one must be extremely cautious of the doubtful phrasing of the philosophers (which they call <term>amphibology</term> <note>From the Greek 'amphibolia,' meaning ambiguity. Alchemists often used intentionally vague language to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note>): not that I say Hermes wrote in this manner, but perhaps his interpreters, begrudging the author's naked meaning to all others but themselves, rendered it doubtful through their commentaries and interpretations. This will be easily perceived by whoever reads other commentaries and acutely weighs the matter itself: namely, that the interpretation of their "stone," as they call it, is far more difficult than the text and more obscure to the intellect. Furthermore, what the "one" and the "one thing" might be according to Hermes, must be interpreted from medical matters, and not from metal-working,

### PHYSICS

...not of the field, but human. <note>The previous page likely ended with a word like "bellaria," meaning "treats" or "delicacies," contrasting worldly trifles with human/divine nature.</note> God, therefore, is this one thing: He who alone existed before all ages, or a Being threefold in unity from eternity; and because He wished to create a "one," He made it similar to Himself insofar as it is one—that is, one nature, the first visible creature, and one world. For this world consists of spirit, soul, and body.

It is the opinion of many philosophers that the spirit of natural things is the medium <note>A middle-ground or bridge.</note> between the soul and the body. Others maintain that the soul is the medium between them, led by this reasoning: that the spirit is more subtle than the soul, and more fit as an extreme when compared to the very thick body, so that the soul is more subtle than the body but denser than the spirit itself. My own opinion, while leaving the judgment of the dispute still before the judge, <note>original: "adhuc sub judice." A legal metaphor meaning the matter is still undecided.</note> would suggest meanwhile that the spirit should not be separated from the soul any more than light from its lamp, or the lamp from its firmament. 

However, beneath the firmament, because the life of natural things is perceived by the senses through the motion of bodies rather than from the cause of motion itself—which is the <term>ethereal fire</term> <note>A celestial, subtle heat believed to animate the universe.</note>—they say by this argument that the spirit is more subtle than the soul, because the soul falls under the senses through motion, while the spirit does not. For the time being, therefore, I shall enjoy this latter opinion in this place, until a better one occurs. 

For if, according to Hermes, it is conceded that the "dense" and the "subtle" are the extremes, as the words sound: *You shall separate the earth from the fire*, <note>original: "Separabis terram ab igne." A famous line from the Emerald Tablet describing the separation of the subtle from the gross.</note> and then what was said before: *the wind carried it in its belly, that is, the air*, <note>original: "portavit illud ventus in ventre suo, id est, aer." Another quote from the Emerald Tablet.</note> it will necessarily follow that fire is the extreme and the spirit to Hermes, because it is far more subtle than the air in which it is carried. Indeed, the soul is more suited to the air than to the fire, if the effect of the motive life occurs in the air through a cause proper to the fire. 

In a similar way, every cause of motion is more subtle than its own motion and effect. For example: If a blacksmith must build a house, three things are chiefly necessary for him: **art** or **genius** for the spirit; **motion** or **operation** for the soul; and finally **matter** for the body. Someone might perhaps say that motion in this case is an <term>accident</term>, <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing.</note> which we concede in artificial things, but in natural things we deny it, because that motion is mixed substantially with both the substance of the spirit and the body. But in artificial motion, which no nature supports, once the craftsmanship has been led to its effect, all motion in it ceases. 

Concluding, therefore, we say that no motion can happen in any way without a mover and a moved. These three things are thus necessary for natural life: the **spirit** as the mover, the **soul** as the motion itself, and the **body** as the moved; these, joined together, make one natural thing. 

The summary adaptation of Hermes' likeness, for the approval of his mental concept, is this: In a way not unlike how God first created one world by meditation alone, He similarly created one world from which indeed all things were born by adaptation. By "meditation," he wishes to denote the simplicity of unity in the mental creation, and afterwards through "adaptation" to hint at the disposition or order under number, measure, and weight of matter...

### OF TRISMEGISTUS

...agreeable things. Since, therefore, the first member of order is number, and the first number is two, if the universal matter of the world is to be arranged in order, it was first (rightly so) to be divided into two, as is taught in Genesis: namely, into heaven and earth. This is especially true because the first number, two, is suited to <term>first matter</term> <note>The primordial, unformed substance from which all things were created.</note>. Hermes نفسه teaches this, saying: *That which is below is like that which is above.* <note>original: "Quod est inferius, est sicut id quod est superius." This is the most famous axiom of the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Western alchemy.</note> By these words it is clear that Hermes Trismegistus was instructed in Genesis by the Hebrews, even though he was an Egyptian, as Augustine testifies in his book *The City of God*, as well as Suidas, and others.

Accordingly, the founder of nature divided the single mass created in his name into two: into the upper heaven and the lower part, the earth. He did this so that what heaven could not do in itself, it might beget in its partner, the earth, just as Adam did in Eve; in this way, the last things might correspond most beautifully to the first, and the first to the last. This division was therefore very necessary, so that the generation which was once enclosed under a single newly-created thing might be led from potential into action. Beneath this spiritual and corporeal <term>binary</term> <note>The number two; the division into opposites like spirit and body.</note> lay hidden a third thing, which is the bond of the sacred marriage. This very thing is the medium that persists in all things to this day, participating in both of its extremes; without them it cannot exist at all, nor can they exist without this medium of theirs. Thus, they are "one out of three."

But someone might object, claiming it is the opinion of all philosophers who understand the art that no transition occurs except through a medium—specifically, from a prior perfect extreme to the perfecting of an imperfect one. Yet Hermes seems to teach here that the beginning of motion must be taken from the imperfect toward the perfect, in order to acquire the highest perfection. It follows also by the contrary: that whoever strives against the opinion of Hermes to proceed from the perfect to the imperfect will achieve an imperfect work, because Hermes placed the lower before the higher.

The answer is that it is foolish to think the author is teaching a "transition" in this passage, since he has not yet reached the practical treatment of the art. Nonetheless, such an order must be observed in the art from the very beginning. For it is certain that these lower elements are more imperfect than heaven, as is evident even from their simple elements, which, when brought into their own heaven, consist of a unity free from all composition. But because we are now occupied with lower things and cannot yet climb to higher ones—as our business is to handle these things with our hands—it will be necessary for us to ascend from these lower things, which are right at our doorstep, to their higher parts with which they are naturally mixed.

So that these matters may always become clearer from what follows, we must re-examine some of the points we have already set down. Just as among us no art can lack its craftsman, its material, or its tools, so the natural <term>magistery</term> <note>The *magisterium*, or the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> necessarily requires things that are suited to itself. Let us begin first with the genius or skill of the craftsman, which is the moving cause. Just as wood and—

These two fires differ from one another partly by their accidents—not by their substance—and they partly agree in their motion, though they differ there as well, one being circular and the other straight. Similarly, it should be noticed that just as the anvil is the lower instrument for smiths on earth, and the hammers are the upper active instruments, so for the natural craftsman, the more solid substance of the elements—such as stones and earth—take the place of the anvil and the nourishing matter; the stars, however, perform the office of the hammers.

Consequently, in conclusion, we say that the connection of the world is made and perfected by the doubles of body, soul, and spirit—both the upper and the lower—which differ only by accidental qualities, yet are similar in substance.
