# OF TRISMEGISTUS

Aa 3

...it may seem that there are fire, air, water, and earth, yet two are held to be the primary ones: fire and water. This is because air seems to be nothing other than water that has been dissolved by the power of the spirit of the Lord hovering over the waters during the creation of the world; whereas earth is water thickened and dried out through the gathering together of the lower waters.

Alternatively, they are divided in a different two-fold way: into the two manifest elements, earth and water, and the two hidden beneath them, air and fire. For air lies hidden under the water until it is revealed by the actions of fire, and fire lies hidden under the earth until it appears through human craftsmanship, or otherwise emerges naturally through certain vents, as seen at Mount Etna, Puteoli <note>A volcanic area near Naples known in antiquity for its sulfurous fumes and thermal activity.</note>, and other places. Fire strives by its own nature, whenever it can, to convert water into itself. To accomplish this more easily, it uses two means according to the two contrary qualities of each: first, using its heat to consume coldness; and second, using the dryness of its heat to consume moisture.

Indeed, we see clouds suspended by the heat of fire, holding a middle position between water and fire. If the heat of the fire—which is weaker at its extremities than in the heart of its sphere (where it is most intense)—is overcome by the coldness of the dissolved water, this middle substance is converted into whichever of the extremes is stronger. Thus nature, in its arrangement, thwarts the effort of the fire: while it strives to consume one thing, it generates another, which then returns to the state from which it was generated. This circulation is the most powerful cause of generation.

We see a similar process with visible fire acting upon bodies composed by nature. Take wood as an example placed in the fire: its sulfur <note>In alchemical thought, sulfur was the "principle of combustibility" present in all substances.</note> does not burn until all its watery moisture has been converted into air. Once that moisture is consumed, the fire returns to the air and then to itself, while the more solid parts of the wood fall away as ash or earth. Therefore, we should not say that the elements of such wood have been destroyed, but rather that each element, separated from its composite form, has returned to its own proper sphere.

Because of this, a doubtful question has arisen among philosophers: does fire consume more than it generates? It seems sound to say that the operations of ethereal fire and elemental fire are equal. For if more were consumed by the elemental fire than was generated by the ethereal, a vacuum <note>A reference to the Aristotelian belief that "nature abhors a vacuum"; a void was considered physically impossible.</note> could be identified in the nature of things, which is an absurdity. But if the ethereal fire generated more than the elemental consumed, the excess could no longer be contained in its determined place. In neither case would the womb of nature be forced to collapse or be compressed. 

The answer can be given briefly and more safely: nothing is consumed by fire, but rather, through the method of transmutation, whatever leaves one element joins another. Thus, wise nature daily and carefully provides for the raising of new forms from elements and forms transmuted in this way, so that what has been prepared through corruption <note>In natural philosophy, "corruption" is not a moral failing, but the necessary decay or breakdown of an old form to make way for the "generation" of a new one.</note> may be shaped through generation; and thus is the operation of nature...

# PHYSICS

...according to the celestial motions of actions and impressions. Many overly curious natural philosophers <note>Latin: *physiologi*; here referring to academic scientists of the time who studied nature primarily through Aristotelian theory rather than laboratory practice.</note>, as yet inexperienced in natural things, are accustomed to thrust this argument upon us to attack the chemists’ **quintessence** <note>The "fifth element" or pure essence sought in alchemy, believed to be the life-force of all things.</note>; however, they will not overcome it unless they bring forth something stronger. 

Bodies (they say) consist of four elements or essences; where then is the fifth element or fifth essence? We admit that bodies consist of four elements materially, yet we do not allow that they are composed of these alone, but also of **form**—which is certainly something real, and indeed the most powerful part of any composite, after the *bond of nature* <note>Latin: *vinculum naturae*</note> by which the elements are glued to their form. For the coarse and the subtle cannot, because of their mutual opposition, come together into one on their own. Therefore, it was necessary for them to be joined through the medium of life, so that they might be more easily united. 

Nature composes all things by this bond, which philosophers are accustomed to hand down to us in riddles. "Make peace," they say, "between enemies, and you shall have the entire mastery" <note>Latin: *magisterium*; the completion of the alchemical Great Work or the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. Concluding the matter of the elements, we say they are tripartite: **simple**, **composite**, and **decomposed**. 

*   **Simple elements** are those that are neither corrupted nor undergo any composition among themselves; it is not *from* them, but *through* them that all other lower elements exercise their powers, which they also receive from them. 
*   **Composites** are those that undergo corruption and are composed. 
*   **Decomposed elements** are those that have already come together in composition through corruption and generation. 

Whoever knows how to convert the latter into the former—the impure into the pure, the composite into the simple—will be a most great craftsman of wondrous works. 

Furthermore, coming to the matter of **form**, we define it (not as that which gives being or a name to a thing, as the unfaithful do) but as that which moves the ethereal region, both the upper and lower elemental regions, into action and the power of conceiving motion. Through the mutual transmutation of the elements into one another, nature prepares the matter, enclosing the **form** within it like a seed in a womb. Pregnant by its power, like a mother's womb, it brings forth the offspring from potentiality into a specific act. This is what the philosophers mean when they say: "Form is drawn out from the potentiality of matter." For matter itself is capable of giving birth, because form is generated within it. 

Therefore, the **form** enacts upon the matter that which it received from the **light of nature** <note>Latin: *lux naturae*; a Paracelsian term for the innate intelligence or divine spark within the physical world that guides growth and healing.</note>—namely motion and life—and offers itself as a mediating craftsman. Moreover, the light and life of nature is the spirit of universal action upon the elements through form. For from the universal form of nature, this spirit does not cease to daily renew those specific forms—originally created by God—which fail through corruption. A craftsmanship of this kind is perfected by a twofold instrument: *disposition* and *influx*. Nature, in its motion, by corrupting matter through an action stirred at the center, disposes it to be receptive to the power of form in the middle region and to celestial influxes, which thereafter, at their determined time, burst forth below into specific forms,

### TRISMEGISTUS

[...speci]fic [forms], according to the condition of the luminaries in the superior arrangement of concurrent forms, according to the saying of some: *Form acts according to the arrangement of matter.* <note>original: "Secundum materiæ dispositionem agit forma." This is a standard Aristotelian principle suggesting that the shape or "soul" of a thing is limited by the physical material it inhabits.</note> But they, having forgotten or not understood the arrangement of forms as well, rush past, passing over it in silence. It remains for us now to see what Hermes says about the genealogy of the **spagyric** <note>spagyric: a term often used by Paracelsus to describe alchemy, specifically the process of separating components and then recombining them in a purer form.</note> offspring. 

<margin>Its father (he says) is the sun, etc.</margin> <note>A famous line from the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus, describing the origin of the "Philosopher's Stone" or the "One Thing."</note> 

What the sun and moon are in the upper heaven is not for us to explain, since it is most well known even to the common people; however, there are few who understand their actions and virtues, and therefore an occasion is given here to describe them. For by a true knowledge of these things, the mind of the reader can reach higher things—namely, the spagyric arts. 

The celestial sun, then, is the great luminary of the day placed by God in the middle of the heaven. Why it occupies the middle place of the heaven is a matter clear in itself: namely, so that it may illuminate all the luminaries above and below itself, and fertilize the entire universe with its rays all the way to its center—upon which center its own eye, and the eyes of the other luminaries, are steadily fixed. Just as the fountain of life of the human body is the center of its heart—or rather, that secret which lies hidden within it, in which natural heat flourishes, heating, illuminating, and quickening the remaining limbs—in no different a way does the sun naturally quicken all the superior and inferior parts of the world with its heat and light, though it effects this through an intermediary. 

For this reason, it is called the "heart of the world" because of its heat, and the "eye" because of its light. Indeed, it surveys all things and penetrates even the most hidden recesses, down to the very center of the earth. In it, all natural celestial virtues are stored. In short, it is the most noble of all bodies in the created heaven and earth. By just reason, therefore, it is called the first father and parent of all things after God, since the seminal and formal virtue of every thing lies hidden within it. 

The first and most powerful masculine and universal seed of its nature is **sulfur** <note>In alchemical theory, Sulfur represents the active, solar, and combustible principle, rather than just the chemical element.</note>, the first part of all generations and the most powerful cause. Hence, it was put forward by Paracelsus: *the sun and man, through man, generate man* <note>original: "sol & homo per hominem generant hominem."</note>, because the natural life of all creatures takes its origin through the sun as an intermediary, and from its life comes all fleeting life. 

If the sun lives, therefore, it is necessary that it lives in something—namely, in its **radical moisture** <note>Latin: *humidum radicale*; the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all living things, acting as the fuel for natural heat.</note>, a most pure and simple air which tempers its heat with its moisture. It would be foolish to believe, as many do, that the sun is merely celestial fire. For life consists in the union of the spirit with the body through the medium of the soul, which is moved by this union to the act of natural life. Otherwise, it would be concluded, against the truth, that the sun does not live; for a natural union always occurs between two things, from whose harmony a third thing results as one or united. Nay, what is more, we say that the sun is the unique **element** <note>Here used in the sense of a fundamental "source" or "quintessence."</note> in which all simple elements are contained, just as in the heaven and the other celestial bodies, but in the sun, they are contained more perfectly.

...because of the life it pours into others, both above and below. The Sun, therefore, is the father and the masculine seed of all things naturally generated, and the Moon is the mother, as [explained] below. Finally, Hermes teaches that the Moon is the mother and wife of the Sun, she who carries the **spagyric** <term>spagyric: a term from alchemical philosophy meaning to "separate and recombine" components to reach a higher state of purity.</term> offspring, conceived by the Sun, in her matrix and womb—the wind carried it in her belly into the air, and the earth is its nurse, etc. <note>original: "vento gestat in aere, terramque nutricem" — This is a direct reference to the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Hermetic alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> And the first generation of things is first conceived in heaven, and thereafter perfected on the earth, as [noted] below. For the sun does not immediately imprint its vital influences on lower things, but through the moon, which conceives thirteen times <note>original: "ter atque decies" — literally "three and ten," referring to the thirteen lunar cycles in a solar year.</note> every year from her husband through their conjunctions, and giving birth, sends down the offspring, as will be heard later. 

Yet, just as she gives birth daily, she also daily conceives virtues from her husband; it is no different for any of the stars, although they are more fertile in their meeting due to their greater proximity. Conceptions and births of this kind happen not through physical contact, as they do on earth, but through influences and spiritual "aspects" <note>aspects: in astrology, the specific angular relationships between planets that were believed to dictate their influence on the world.</note> alone. For when she appears full to us, she actually conceives fewer virtues from the sun than when she is hidden and entirely joined to the sun, on account of the greater distance [between them at full moon]; but she conceives more in opposition than during lateral aspects. This is because the influences and rays of the sun are more powerful when they are straight than when they are oblique. 

We must not think, therefore—based on that common proverb—that the moon suffers a "defect" <note>original: "defectum pati" — a play on words; in Latin, a lunar eclipse or the waning moon was called a "defect," but the author argues that this is when she is actually most full of solar power.</note> when she is hidden, since at that time she is most imbued with solar virtues. Rather, because she is not visible to us then—partly because the solar radiance overcomes and obscures all natural light, and partly because only the middle part, which is opaque to us, is turned toward us—she seems deprived of light. Yet, she actually contains the most light then, and receives more from the sun than when she appears completely full in opposition.

We have decided that we should not pass over those things regarding these two great luminaries that are worthy of consideration by reason of their divine marriage through creation according to Genesis, and from the diligent and never-violated observation of their marriage according to the order divinely prescribed for them. Although these two are separate bodies, they are nevertheless of one and the same substance, just as heaven and earth came from a single abyss; just as here among us, man and woman were one human, then made into two, and afterwards joined again as "one flesh." However, the conception of the Sun's virtues by the Moon is not yet a perfected generation, but only the beginning of it, which must be perfected in lower things. The Moon is therefore the medium through which the superior seeds are placed into the "matrices" <note>matrices: used here to mean "wombs" or the formative environments of the lower elements.</note> of lower things, from which they later give birth to coarser "elementated" <note>elementated: things made of the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water), as opposed to pure celestial spirit.</note> things, whether mixed or decomposed.

Let us repeat these things a little more deeply in a **spagyric** manner. If the Sun and Moon therefore pour life into lower things, it follows that both are present in those things through life and potentiality; this power is indeed drawn out from any natural things through the **spagyric** art. For the life of the Sun and Moon is a union through Jupiter <note>In alchemical symbolism, Jupiter often represents a balanced or "temperate" state of matter.</note>, and it can deservedly be called a long and healthy life. If, however, the union of Mercury and Mars occurs through Saturn <note>Saturn, being cold and distant, was often associated with decay, lead, and "short life" or sickness in this symbolic system.</note>, a sick and short life will result. Therefore, when you have reduced any composite substance into its Mercury, Saturn, and Mars <note>In alchemy, these names refer both to planets and their corresponding metals/principles: Mercury (spirit/quicksilver), Saturn (lead/structure), and Mars (iron/force).</note>, and from these you have also extracted the Sun and Moon <note>The Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of Sulfur and Mercury.</note>, and joined them by the middle tempering of both "Jupiters," you will make one thing out of those three that is more excellent than it was before when it was composed by nature—though it will exist under a different form. By what industry this is achieved, nature herself teaches us through her daily operations, even before our very eyes, as the author teaches: <gloss>The wind (he says) carried it in its belly.</gloss> <note>original: "Portavit ventus in ventre suo." We touched upon this passage previously, which might be enough for sharp wits; however, so that I may be able to benefit everyone, I wish to treat this matter diligently, since it is most worthy of note and is of great use to those reading the more obscure writings of the **spagyrists** <term>spagyrists: alchemists who practice the "spagyric" art—a term coined by Paracelsus meaning to separate and then recombine materials to reach a higher state of purity.</term>. Indeed, all my study tends toward this goal: that I may, as much as I am able, promote the efforts of those people studious in this more abstruse philosophy. I know that while I try to instruct others and share my talent, I educate myself through the exercise of these labors—though grace and light depend on the powers above. 

The lower Sun and Moon are indeed raised upward from the center by the mastery of lower nature, until they reach the higher things in the middle region. While existing there, the virtues of the superior sun are infused into the superior moon—for by nature, like things rejoice in their likes. Like lower matrices <note>matrix: a womb or place of origin/shaping.</note>, they conceive superior seeds, for this is the duty and office of the wife. Now it appears most clearly to you what Hermes taught previously in these words from the beginning: *What is below is like that which is above, and what follows.* 

For the sun and moon in the higher heaven, and those in the lower, are similar in substance, though they differ in "accident" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essential nature of a thing, such as its lifespan.</note>—namely, through a long or short life. Therefore, under Mars (who practices the Vulcanian arts in his hearth-workshop, which is to say, the center of the earth), the lower universal sun lies hidden. By the impetus of its parent, this sun breaks out from the subterranean caverns through the wind. With such bellows Vulcan—or rather the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: in Paracelsian thought, the "inner chemist" or vital force that directs the growth and functions of an organism.</term>, to speak **Paracelsically** <term>Paracelsically: according to the theories of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who revolutionized medicine and alchemy.</term>—drives the purer and subtler parts of the elements from himself into the "heaven." This includes the lower sun (containing the purest substance of fire and earth) and the lower moon (the subtlest and purest substance of water, hidden under the form of air and carried in its womb). As the words sound: <gloss>The wind carried it in its belly.</gloss> 

By this process, the lower universal and feminine seed is carried through the air to be joined to the superior universal masculine seed, along with other specific seeds in the womb of the wind and the matrix of the air. It is certain that air consists of water and fire; likewise, heaven consists of fire and air. Under the name of "fire," the purest substance of the earth is understood to ascend together with fire; and under the name of "air," the purest substance of water is understood, according to the cycles of transmutation.

...one into another, by the already mentioned natural artifice. Therefore, the belly and womb of nature is a matrix fused from the purest substance of all the lower elements, converted into volatile air. Within this matrix, the universal seed of the sun is conceived through the mediation of the moon, and it is further specified by other luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refer to the planets and stars, which in Hermetic thought impress specific qualities onto matter.</note> for the various distinction of species. 

Therefore, after the author Hermes proposed three elements—two under the names of the sun and moon, and the third under the name of the wind—he now adds the earth under the comparison of a nurse and by its own name. He says the earth is the nurse of the fetus of nature that was previously conceived in the air. From her breasts, every fetus sucks that **mercurial milk** <note>original: "lac mercuriale." In alchemy, this refers to a refined, nourishing "water" or spirit that allows the metallic or philosophical embryo to grow.</note> for its nourishment and the sustenance of its life; this milk is the thicker substance of water remaining below near the earth. 

Thus, the volatile part of the elements (as has been heard), having been impregnated, soon returns to its fixed part, brings forth the fetus, and nourishes it from the fixed substance until it reaches perfection. **Spagyrists** <note>Alchemists who practice the "spagyric" art, which involves the separation and recombination of natural substances to create medicines.</note> of nature, having contemplated the cycles of such generations—neither sleepily, nor in passing, nor in vain—could not have learned their spagyric art better, but rather more solidly. 

Wherefore, so that they might generate a spagyric sun, they imitate nature: they dissolve the natural composite into its parts through their **Vulcanic Archeus** <term>Vulcanic Archeus: The "inner smith" or transformative power of fire (named for Vulcan, god of the forge) that governs chemical changes.</term>. They artificially drive the sun and moon from the center into the "womb of the wind" on high, and afterwards nourish them in their own earth. For just as everything generated takes nourishment from the earth, so too the spagyric fetus has its nourishment from the spagyric earth. This "earth" is understood in two ways: sometimes it refers to the lower part of the vessel (while the upper part is treated as the heaven). Sometimes **spagyric Jupiter** <note>In this context, Jupiter likely refers to a purified state of tin or a specific crystalline substance.</note>, which is fixed and purged of its "sweats" <note>Impurities or excess moisture released during heating.</note>, serves as our **foliated earth** <note>original: "terra foliata." A technical term for alchemical matter when it reaches a flaky, leaf-like appearance during the process of purification.</note>. In this earth, the volatile part—which was forced to descend back down after its ascent into heaven—is nourished and perfected. 

Concluding the theory of the spagyric art, the author says: *The father of all the **Thelesma** of the whole world is here.* <term>Thelesma: A term from the Emerald Tablet (likely from the Greek 'thelesmos,' meaning 'will' or 'attainment') referring to the ultimate power or goal of the alchemical work.</term> 

It is as if he were saying: "This secret that I propose to you is the father, origin, and source of all secrets and mysteries—the most chief and greatest among all other secrets of the whole world." For this reason, it must not be broadcast to everyone, and least of all to profane men; it is scarcely even for those initiated into the sacred mysteries, and even to them, only in very brief conversation. For what is more excellent, or more worthy of a philosopher, than to become a participant in a long life through the knowledge and use of the entirety of superior and inferior nature? By this, all the corruptions of a short life are routed and driven far away, along with the obstacles and impediments of the mind, by which it was formerly darkened and blinded. Is this not far superior to any fictions of poems, which are devised for idolatry rather than for the knowledge of the one God? Although these poems have been incorrectly interpreted allegorically by some, as if they embraced many famous mysteries, they are nothing less than the **mighty works** <note>original: "magnalia." The catchword "gnalia" at the bottom of the page indicates the completion of this word, referring to the "great things" or miracles of God.</note> of the one God alone.

...great wonders, which they have sung under the names of so many dreamt-up little gods and harlots. Although Ovid seems to have sensed something of the truth in his *Metamorphoses*, he nevertheless mixed in many more frivolous and impious things that contribute nothing at all to this matter. What, I ask, do the writings of the unfaithful profit for salvation? Surely nothing; indeed, they rather call men away from the study of truth while they are intent on such trifles. Yet they are valued more in this iron age than the writings of pious men who profess one God in all things. Would it not be better for the youth (with whom the most necessary beginning must be made if the world is to be reformed) to learn the works of God alone, rather than the dreams of men? Indeed, if **Physics** is taught rightly and as is proper from the sacred Genesis of the world, it leads to the knowledge of God through the great wonders of the Creator, and thereafter prepares the souls and minds of men for attained philosophy and heavenly wisdom.

Furthermore, if anyone has meditated deeply and loftily upon all that God, the Best and Greatest, did in the creation of the world for the sake and benefit of men, then at last he will understand the father of all secrets, and the most excellent mystery of the sacred **Thelesma** <note>original: "Thelesmi." A term from the Emerald Tablet—likely derived from the Greek *thelema* (will)—referring to the universal creative power or the "perfection" of the work.</note>, and the most secret **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: the alchemical art of separating, purifying, and recombining natural substances, often to create medicine.</term> work of a divine rather than human art, whose father—that is, the supreme secret—is found here in this brief and truthful text. 

Moreover, concluding his theory, the author teaches us to recognize the end of the spagyric work, so that we may know when to cease our labor. *Its power (he says) is whole, if it be turned into earth.* <note>A direct quote from the Emerald Tablet: "Vis eius integra est, si versa fuerit in terram."</note> Previously we heard that the more subtle parts of the lower elements are impregnated with heavenly virtues, and thereafter return into earth and water; and that such conceptions of virtues do not achieve their effect of generation before then. Now, in a similar way, the completion of the spagyric work is taught: that when that which the wind carried in its belly has been turned, or converted, into earth, the work will be completed. For by long and tireless **digestion** <note>original: "coctio" - literally 'cooking,' but in alchemy referring to the slow maturation of a substance through heat.</note>, liquids (even if they do not evaporate, but are retained) are thickened, and in the course of time are dried out into powder or earth. To the common people this would seem absurd, but only those who have made trial of this thing can believe it. 

But the time is long and tedious, and must be awaited with the greatest patience. The whole matter of this lengthiness consists primarily in the selection and preparation of the most suitable **matter** <note>In alchemy, "matter" refers to the starting material or "First Matter" used to begin the work.</note>. For some materials are remote, others more remote, and some most remote. Others are near, others nearer, and those especially near to perfection. Each of these is most necessary for the spagyric artist to know before he attempts the work; otherwise, he will lament his error. Having thus far instructed his students in the theory of this art, he next invites them to the **Practice**, as follows below.

## ON THE PRACTICE OF THE SPAGYRIC 
### WORK for preparing the medicine of 
### long life.

->*You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense, etc.*<- 
<note>original: "Separabis terram ab igne, subtile à spisso, &c." This is a famous instruction from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, the foundational text of Western alchemy.</note>

After Hermes demonstrated the **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: The alchemical art of "separating" substances into their core elements and "recombining" them in a purified, potent form. The term comes from the Greek words for "to tear apart" and "to bind together."</term> art theoretically, proving its validity by its resemblance to the creation of the world, he finally approaches the matter practically (as is consistent with reason) starting with separation. He is not unmindful of the "abyss" divided by the "firmament"—the division of the lower waters from the higher waters described in Genesis. *You shall separate (he says) the earth from the fire*, as a woman from a man, so that they might be able to generate. Indeed, in every generation, two things must first come together, as the active and the passive, the higher and the lower, which were previously mentioned both in sacred Genesis and in the spagyric art. Not only two things, but those which have been separated or divided from a single source. This kind of separation is properly called by the spagyric philosophers the "division of the elements," separating the purer parts from the more impure ones. The author teaches that the first operation is the preparation and cleansing of the components appropriate to this art.

Some think that the separation of the four elements is to be understood here, which I would not wish to deny to anyone, provided they speak of spagyric separation and not the common kind. Since under the name of "fire," two other elements are contained—namely, air and water. For no fire is devoid of air, nor air of water, since air is water "resolved" or broken down by fire, by which it is forced to ascend upward; but the earth partly ascends and partly remains fixed below. 

Some think that this phrase, *the subtle from the dense*, refers back to the former one—namely, *you shall separate the earth from the fire*. But I am of the opinion which seems to come closer to the author's meaning: that this is a specific and more philosophical purification than the former. Anyone who wishes may believe this, or not; they are by no means forced to. For everything that is "ethereal," or brought into a state of "subtlety" through ethereal powers, is called **subtle** by the spagyric philosophers. For as was said above, the ethereal and the elements are one in substance; once the "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the outward characteristics of a thing (like color or smell) that do not change its essential nature.</note> on both sides (by which alone they differ) are removed from them, they will easily return to being one. Therefore, the author's meaning is that by the separation of the subtle from the dense, the dense elemental matter can be made subtle and brought back spagyrically into ethereal subtlety. This spagyric separation is also called **solution** <note>original: "solutio." In alchemy, this refers to the "dissolving" or liquidizing of a solid substance, often seen as a spiritual or physical death before rebirth.</note>, and unless this precedes it, no spagyric composition can likewise be made. Therefore, this latter separation must be considered very carefully, lest it be confused with the former. From the order of the words in the sentences (even if there is no connecting conjunction), it is clear that my opinion conforms to the author's mind. Since he said first, *you shall separate the earth from the fire*, if he had explained this sentence through the one that follows (as some wish), he should have but al-

...but he also said the dense from the subtle, and not just the subtle from the dense. Because the earth is denser than the fire, which it even preceded in the earlier discourse—though in the later part the order of the substances is inverted. From this, it is clear enough that the phrasing is not identical except when comparing different operations. Nor can it be said that these words are merely adjectives, as if he had simply said "a dense thing." This is one of the most obvious ways that philosophers hide their meaning, from which you may learn their other methods of that kind. <note>The author is pointing out that alchemists purposefully vary their terminology or reverse the order of steps to confuse the uninitiated.</note>

Immediately after he indicated the material and the method of operation, he adds, in the most appropriate order, the **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: The art of separating and recombining natural substances to create potent medicines.</term> instrument and its tempering in very hidden words: *Gently* (he says) *with great skill*. <note>original: "Suaviter cum ingenio magno." This refers to the careful application of heat.</note> Those who are the sons of Hermes easily perceive what he means by these words, and no others do. For fire is the proper instrument of the spagyrists, just as it is for nature itself, and it is considered in many ways by these craftsmen. There is internal fire and external fire. The **internal fire** is specific to any substance and naturally implanted within it; the craftsman must take the best account of this. The **external fire**, however, is either violent or tempered through four grades, or it is similar to natural heat and very mild, just as nature requires for the generation of things. 

Chemists use violent fire either during **calcination** <term>Calcination: Heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state or drive off volatile parts, often reducing it to powder.</term>, for **sublimating** <term>Sublimation: The process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back to a solid, used to purify substances.</term> drier things, or for melting their metals. They use tempered fire, through its various grades, during distillation—whether ascending or descending. They use heat similar to nature's own when they **putrefy**, **digest**, **congeal**, or dissolve and **fix** <term>Fixing: A process that makes a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</term> substances through circulation. The teaching of father Hermes is that his sons should ultimately use that heat by which they can imitate nature in its operations, which is clear from the adverb "gently." The other part, "with great skill," denotes that this fire must be constructed with the utmost diligence and industry to match natural heat. There are various ways of constructing such a fire, left to each man according to the capacity of his own ingenuity, provided it is gentle, continuous, and uninterrupted. Some are accustomed to preparing such a continuous heat for themselves with great precision using various ingeniously crafted small furnaces; and some excite their fire with various materials. Our author does not mention all of these here because, striving for an enigmatic brevity, he considers it superfluous to list what is handed down everywhere in the writings of others.

Accordingly, he follows the rest in order: *It ascends* (he says) *from the earth into the heaven*. <note>original: "Ascendit à terra in cælum." This refers to the vapor rising during the alchemical process.</note> This most beautifully declares **circulatory distillation** <term>Circulatory Distillation: A process where a liquid is vaporized and then condensed back into the same vessel, circulating repeatedly to "perfect" the substance.</term>, and also that the spagyric vessel must be constructed in the likeness of the natural vessel. For we see that the entire heaven and the elements have the likeness of a spherical body, in the center of which thrives the heat of the lower fire, driving the more subtle matter of the elements upward into the air and raising it along with itself, as we have said before. Hermes wants us to have a vessel suitable for this in no different a manner...

...of its own imitation. However, since it would be impossible for us to construct any artificial vessel in which we could, like nature, artificially contain a fire lit in its center and suspended in the middle—and this for various reasons, especially because our artificial fire would be immediately extinguished in a closed vessel without free and open air—it was therefore necessary for our fire to be placed outside our vessel, and beneath the center of its round bottom, like the natural sun. The entire mastery of this fire consists primarily in this: that it be continuous and in the same light and vaporous state, like the fire in the center of the world, which daily and without intermission performs the natural mastery of the ascent from the earth into the heaven. This is done, according to the previous words, *With great skill* <note>original: "Cum magno ingenio." This refers back to the Emerald Tablet's instruction on the application of heat.</note>, which is to say, very similar to the natural fire (which is said to be the "skill" or "genius" of nature). 

The opinion of certain philosophers occurs here who reject the idea that metals are generated by subterranean fire—or at least only in part—affirming instead that generation occurs solely by celestial fire. In this, they fail to see how much they contradict not only Hermes but also the whole of nature. For the celestial sun does not enter materially into the composition of natural things, but only potentially through its influence and the impression of its form; whereas **elementary fire** <term>Elementary fire: The physical fire of the four elements, as opposed to spiritual or celestial heat.</term> is the most powerful part of the substance and matter of things being generated. To this fire, the "internal fire" must be compared—that is, the fire naturally implanted in the matter of Hermes.

The opinion of Father Hermes is this: With the fire acting from the outside upon the bottom of the vessel’s center, into the center of the matter, it drives the **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: The alchemical process of separating and then recombining the pure parts of a substance.</term> offspring toward the upper parts, as the words state: *It ascends from the earth to the heaven* <note>original: "Ascendit a terra in cælum."</note>. This means it moves from the lower part of the vessel (which is sometimes called the "earth") to the upper part, which is also sometimes called the "heaven" by the Philosophers. This passage can be understood in another way: the offspring of the Sun and Moon ascends—that is, its thick, earthy substance is converted or resolved into "heaven," meaning into a most subtle substance similar to the heavens. 

Next, after the author has demonstrated the spagyric **solution** <term>Solution: The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</term> to his sons and taught them by what instrument and artifice it is perfected, he immediately adds the **fixation** <term>Fixation: The process by which a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to fire.</term> in these words: *And it descends again to the earth* <note>original: "Iterumque descendit in terram."</note>. It is as if he were saying: After the dissolved substance of the spagyrists has stood for some time under the obedience of the internal celestial virtues through the artifice of ascent, it returns to its earth at its determined time of maturity. That is, that spirit which was previously made into a spirit from a body becomes bodily once again. This was long ago wrapped in a riddle by the philosophers: "Make the fixed volatile," they say, "and again the volatile fixed, and you will have the whole mastery." Nevertheless, there are many other chemical solutions and **congelations** <term>Congelation: The thickening or solidifying of a substance.</term> necessary in this mastery, which ought rather to be called "preparations." It is surely foolish to believe that this spagyric matter is not to be first chemically prepared and refined before it is taken up for the spagyric work. This very...

### OF TRISMEGISTUS.

All natural philosophers who follow the **spagyric art** <term>Spagyric: From the Greek words for "to separate" and "to bind," this refers to alchemical chemistry, specifically the purification of substances to extract their medicinal essence.</term> teach that preparations are necessary. These operations they have called purifications, subtilizations, solutions, and congelations. It is therefore necessary for the "body" to be dissolved into "spirit," and for the spirit to be reduced back into a body, if the craftsman is to truly imitate nature. For we see it happen naturally: water is resolved into a cloud, and the cloud is congealed again into water, so that what follows may occur: *And so it receives the force of things above and below* <note>original Latin: "Et sic recipit vim superiorum & inferiorum."</note>.

The author concludes his practical instruction with these words, which correspond appropriately to his first theoretical propositions: *That which is above is like that which is below, and vice versa.* By using the singular term "force" <note>original: "vim"</note>, and not doubling it, he indicates that the power of the superior nature is the same as that of the inferior nature, and vice versa. It is not a different power; otherwise, he would have said "forces" or doubled the singular noun. Rather, he wanted to teach—to confirm what he said earlier, namely, *To accomplish the miracles of one thing*—that the force and power in the union of things above with things below is at its greatest, reaching even to the "miracle" of spagyric philosophy.

Hence, having completed the practical part of this art, he teaches his followers and disciples the utility of this medicine and its use in two ways. The first is with these words: *Thus you will have the glory of the whole world.* For the glory of this world is seen to consist in wealth. Even true philosophers do not entirely despise riches, but only the abuse of them. Indeed, they consider a person in this world happy and glorious who, being wealthy, bestows his riches on the needy and the poor. Although the widow’s mite, taken from her own meager livelihood, was more acceptable to God than the huge, superfluous wealth of the opulent, nevertheless—so that the poor might be helped abundantly and not by a single coin alone—the **Lord God** <note>original: "D. O. M.," abbreviation for Deo Optimo Maximo, "To God, the Best and Greatest."</note> has sometimes bestowed wealth on certain people through this art and His gift. This was done so they would not think (as those do who inherit from parents) that wealth should be possessed for themselves alone.

However, because I have so far made very little profession in this specific area <note>The author is likely referring to the literal creation of gold or material wealth.</note>, I most willingly leave this topic to be explained more fully and copiously by others. I shall instead take up the second part, which concerns the medicine of the human body and the intellect. In pursuing this for the benefit of students and the common good of the Republic, I will explain what seems relevant to this matter according to the weakness of my own wit. 

Since God wishes the poor to be helped not only with gold or silver through brotherly charity, but also with remedies applied to remove their sicknesses—as Christ testifies in the Gospel through his rebuke: *I was sick (he says) and you did not visit me* <note>A reference to Matthew 25:43.</note>—Hermes therefore teaches this second, greatest utility of his spagyric medicine, which lies in the clarification of the body and mind, saying: *Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you.* Just as a twofold...

### PHYSICS

Since we know that there is infirmity of both body and mind, it follows that **spagyric medicine** <term>Spagyric: A term for alchemical medicine, involving the separation of a substance into its elements and then recombining them in a purified form.</term> must also be twofold in its effect, though not in its essence. For the author says, *all darkness will flee from you*; he does not say it will flee "from metals." By "darkness," nothing else is understood than the shadows of diseases and the sicknesses of both body and mind. Indeed, every sick body is "dark," not only in its outward color, but even its blood, urine, sweat, and all other things reflect this gloom. Conversely, a healthy body makes its splendor and serenity visible in every way.

The intent of the author, in short, is to teach those who have obtained this spagyric medicine that even the tiniest portion—perhaps the size of a **grain of mustard** <note>This is a common biblical metaphor (Matthew 17:20) used here to emphasize the extreme potency of the medicine, where a tiny amount produces a massive effect.</note>—no matter how it is taken, cures all diseases without distinction. This is due to the simplicity of the union achieved in the medicine, which is so effective that no variety or multitude of diseases can resist it.

Furthermore, there are various "darknesses" and infirmities of the mind, such as insanity, mania, rage, stupidity, and others of that kind, by which the soul is darkened and defiled; these are most perfectly cured by this one spagyric medicine. Not only does it restore health to the soul, but it truly sharpens the natural genius and the minds of men, so that all things become miraculously easy for them to understand and perceive. Nothing remains hidden from them, whether it belongs to the "superior" realms of the heavens or the "inferior" realms of the earth.

In summary, all bodies of natural things and of men, as well as their minds and souls, can be brought to the ultimate perfection of this world through this art—provided that God grants the discovery of the art described by Hermes. Nothing in the nature of things can be found stronger than this medicine, which is why the author says: *This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude.* <note>original Latin: "Hæc est totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis." This is a key line from the Emerald Tablet.</note> It is as if he were saying: This is the most powerful force and efficacy of all the powers and virtues of nature, almost as if it were above nature. Therefore, it could quite rightly be called a **metaphysical work** <note>Literally "beyond physical." The author suggests that while the medicine starts with natural ingredients, the final result transcends the normal laws of physics.</note> arising from natural things through spagyric mastery.

The author gives the reason for such great strength, saying: *Because it overcomes every subtle thing and shall penetrate every solid thing.* <note>original: "Quia vincit omnem rem subtilem, omnemque solidam penetrabit."</note> Almost every interpreter of Hermes until now has twisted the meaning of this passage to refer only to metals, in this manner: They say that it "overcomes" (that is, congeals) every subtle thing (such as **Mercury**, or common quicksilver) and "penetrates" every solid thing (meaning it will bring every hard, perfect or imperfect metal—such as **Gold**, **Silver**, **Lead**, **Tin**, **Iron**, and **Copper** <note>The author uses the planetary names for these metals: Sol (Sun/Gold), Luna (Moon/Silver), Saturnus (Saturn/Lead), Jupiter (Tin), Mars (Iron), and Venus (Copper).</note>—to its greatest spagyric and natural perfection).

However, because I have undertaken to treat and illustrate this matter specifically as a medical concern, and leaving everyone else to their own opinions, I shall pursue my duty according to my stated purpose and interpret it in this way: It "overcomes" (meaning it expels) every "subtle thing" (meaning the spiritual darkness occupying the mind), and it "penetrates" every "solid thing" (namely, every thick and hard bodily de-

...defect, even from the most solid parts, through spiritual penetration. Just as we previously related the "glory of the world" to riches, and "obscurity" to diseases, in this place we take "subtle" to mean the spirit and "solid" to mean the body. After the author of the **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: The alchemical process of separating a substance into its components and then recombining them in a purified, more potent state.</term> mastery has completed the practical instructions—having also listed the usefulness, application, and the excellence of its virtues—he did not want his disciples to be ignorant of the source from which this arduous work is derived. Therefore, he advises them with these words: *In this way the world was created* <note>original: "Sic mundus creatus est"</note>. It is as if he were saying that the spagyric craft must be learned thoroughly by studying the creation of the world. It is not that he wishes for something to be made out of nothing, as the world itself was made, but he teaches how to bring the highest perfection—which was created in things and placed there by heaven—from potentiality into actual reality. For this reason, "creation" here should be understood as the *order* of the world’s creation, so that the meaning of the words is this: the spagyric craft follows the same order, or one similar to that by which the world was created. For it must be admitted that this work is divine rather than human or natural, since man brings nothing of his own to this process except his service, and nature brings nothing except that in which it had already ceased to act.

What remains is for us to look at the sequence of **Genesis** <note>The first book of the Bible, which describes the seven days of creation.</note> in this context. We read there: *God created the heavens and the earth* <note>original: "Creavit Deus cælum & terram"</note>. Hermes says: you must bring the "heavens" and "earth"—which were created by God and placed together in a composite state—back from their potentiality into action, by dividing the "higher" from the "lower," so that one may generate a third thing from the two through their similarity. *He separated the waters under the firmament from the waters above the firmament* <note>original: "Separavit aquas sub firmamento ab aquis supra firmamentum"</note>, and so forth. To be brief: if you contemplate the whole of Genesis while calling upon divine light, you will find the spagyric art. Nor did it seem enough to Hermes until he progressed further to the miracles of this work, saying: *From this shall come wonderful adaptations, of which this is the manner* <note>original: "Hinc erunt adaptationes mirabiles, quarum modus est hic"</note>. This is as if he were saying: by observing this order, you will see wonderful successions of changes and compositions in our "elements" and "heavens," the manner of which is found here, namely in the imitation of the order of such a divine creation. Hermes seems to consider any philosopher crude and ignorant who might understand the creation of the world but remain ignorant of these "adaptations." Therefore, one must pray to God that He might deign to reveal the sequence of creation; once this is known, the spagyric craft can in no way remain hidden.

Furthermore, the author, filled with an insatiable desire to teach his sons and disciples completely, did not want the material from which this divine work is perfected to remain hidden from them. *Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Itaque vocatus sum Hermes Trismegistus"</note>, he says. It is as if he were saying: "I am called Hermes for this reason, because I am the interpreter of spagyric wisdom; and **Trismegistus** <note>Literally "Thrice-Great."</note> because the craft I announce to you lies hidden under a **ternary** <term>Ternary: A grouping of three. In this context, it refers to the alchemical Trinity of Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which the philosopher seeks to unite into one.</term> concluded into one." For God delights in an odd number, of which the ternary alone is the source and origin. The **unary** <term>Unary: The number one or the "Monad," representing unity and the source of all things.</term>, however, is not counted as a number, because the "one," divided into two, overcomes and animates the ternary through its simplicity with an indissoluble bond. # PHYSICA

...can by no means be joined, because they are soluble in one another by themselves. At this point, it would be highly necessary to explain the **Threefold** <note>original: "ternarium"</note> and the **Onefold** <note>original: "unarium"</note> more extensively, but because we are reserving that for the following sections for the validation of the art, we have decided to omit it for now; meanwhile, let us undertake to clarify the remaining clause concerning matter. *He says,* (he says) *“Having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world.”* <note>original: "Habens tres partes philosophiæ totius mundi." A famous line from the Emerald Tablet attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> It is as if he were saying that he had discovered the entire world consists of three main parts in every direction. Although the whole world seems to be divided into two visible parts, there lies hidden beneath these a third, inconspicuous part, dedicated to an equally invisible unity because of its simplicity. Yet each of these aforementioned parts—namely the **ethereal** and the **elementary**—is again subdivided into three parts: **body, soul, and spirit**, so that these are naturally situated in both heaven and earth.

Of the former division into the ethereal and elementary regions, made under a secret bond, the latter member—the elementary region—is assigned to the number two (the binary) for this reason: it is more material. Because of this, it was subdivided into the four elements. For two generate nothing but four from their first offspring. Spiritually, however, one may see any of these qualities divided into the four primary qualities <note>The four qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, and that under the binary, which will be discussed more broadly below. The philosophy of the entire world can also be called "threefold" by reason of coarser and decomposed matter. For there are three most general kingdoms by which everything that falls under the senses is categorized: namely, **minerals, vegetables, and animals**, the secrets of which were very well known to **Hermes** through experiment. As he testifies in the final conclusion of his **spagyric** <term>Spagyric: From the Greek 'spao' (to separate) and 'ageiro' (to combine). It refers to alchemical medicine produced by purifying and recombining natural substances.</term> philosophy, having completed all things, in these words: *What I have said concerning the operation of the sun is complete.* <note>original: "Completum est quod dixi de operatione solis."</note> It is as if he were speaking in this manner: "I have experienced what I speak of, and I have completed what I announce to you—namely, that the **operation of the sun**, which is the mastery of the universal spagyric medicine, is true, certain without falsehood, and most true, so that the last things correspond to the first." Not without cause, therefore, does he call this medicine the **artificial sun**; for just as the natural sun naturally infuses natural life into all things, in no other way does the spagyric sun refresh and recall this failing life, by driving away the diseases ready to expel it from its dwelling. This is that true medicine of the ancient fathers, and the root of long life; the **universal remedy** that heals all diseases indifferently, increases the vital spirits, and likewise delivers and preserves every body from corruption. As many as are ignorant of this art, though they be most learned in the academies, are accustomed to disapprove of it. What wonder, since they have never heard of such a thing in their schools? It does not follow from this that it should be condemned just because learned men are ignorant of it. Indeed, many things have come to light in our century which were unknown to most of the ancients, just as many things now lie hidden from us which were most familiar to the ancient fathers.

What does not pass into oblivion through the injury of time or the laziness of men? Furthermore, truth is suppressed by the ambition of those who, wishing well only for themselves, envy others even those secret writings they have stolen from elsewhere. Therefore, truth does not perish entirely; though it may lie buried for some for a time, it will emerge for others by the will of God, in whose heart all praiseworthy and good arts rest eternally alongside His wisdom. For God, the giver of all good things, distributes His gifts to whom He wills, and even takes them away from the ungrateful who abuse them.

There is no doubt that God revealed a certain medicine to the ancient fathers through His Holy Spirit <note>original: "spiritum sanctum suum"</note>, by which they might protect the corruption of their flesh—especially to those with whom He spoke and entered into a covenant. But after the vain desire of men to be wise by their own power led them to seek knowledge from themselves, and in things other than Him in whom alone is all salvation, their minds went blind. Led into a labyrinth, they sought now this herb, now another; tomorrow this root and then another; and the next day some mixture. Thus, experimenting daily without judgment, they never reached the target, nor did they possess any certainty in their teaching.

What also seems most absurd is that men are perhaps never content with what they have. Almighty God gave to each nation what He willed it to possess, for both food and medicine. Otherwise, if these things had to be sought from far-off lands, they would only be available to the rich, while the poor would have to die for want of them. On the contrary, God has far greater care for the poor than He ever had for the rich; sacred testimonies to this exist everywhere. But that slandering enemy <note>A reference to the Devil, often called the "calumniator."</note> teaches us to despise our own things and always desire the foreign, seeking that which is less "at hand" in order to make our appetites insatiable. We all have with us, wherever we live—indeed, within us, though not produced by us—everything that we seek outside ourselves from others, however it is described.

Let us see how the Gentiles and infidels, for their part, might argue against us Christians in this place. "Nature," they say, "desires a nature similar to itself, and rejoices in its own nature; for if it is joined to a foreign nature, the work of nature is destroyed." This is a marvelous saying to those who do not deeply consider what nature is; but to those who know her, nothing can be more true. 

But let us return to where the digression of this speech diverted us, and more fully prove the opinion of our mind, by which we assert that true Physics <note>original: "Physica," referring here to the study of the natural world and its divine laws.</note>—as well as true spagyric <term>Spagyric: A term for alchemical medicine involving the separation and recombination of plant or mineral constituents.</term> medicine—had its origin from Genesis <note>The first book of the Bible, used here to argue that alchemy mirrors the process of divine Creation.</note>, and not from any other source or in any other way than through divinely inspired contemplation. Let us see, therefore, how Johannes Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a famous German abbot, polymath, and occultist who influenced many later alchemists.</note>, the most excellent of the natural philosophers of our age, applauds Hermes in all things according to Genesis, as is clear from what follows.

## ON THE SPAGYRIC ART <note>original: "Spagirico Artificio"</note>
### The opinion of Trithemius.

->*The Unit (he says) is not a number, and from it all*<-
->*numbers arise.*<-

For before the universal water of the abyss—which is mentioned in Genesis—was divided, it was one. By this division alone, the unit produces the binary, the first of all numbers, not through its substance but through <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are properties that can change without changing the essence of the thing itself.</note>. *It is a number and is numbered, and it is not a number and is not numbered. It is not numbered because its nature is simple, yet it is numbered insofar as it is composed of accidents. To that extent, however, it cannot be numbered, because there is no number before it.* This is understood regarding that unity which Hermes explains in other words, using a likeness taken from Genesis. *That which is above*, he says, and what follows <note>A reference to the famous Hermetic maxim: "As above, so below."</note>. For the binary is denoted by Hermes through the "lower" and the "upper." *Let the binary be cast aside (says Trithemius), and the ternary shall be convertible to unity.* Hermes says the same thing in different words: *For performing the miracles of the one thing.* It is especially important to note here that unity is understood by both men in two ways. Indeed, Hermes counts unity, as we have said, through the "lower" and the "upper." But Trithemius does so through the constitution of the first number from the unit. Both measure unity by a vastly different reasoning afterward: One by the reduction of the upper and lower to the likeness placed in the miracle; the other by the rejection of the binary and the conversion of the ternary into the unit. Both certainly agree in a wondrous way on the same sentiment. Therefore, that natural unity itself is divisible, or rather numerable into the binary, and the ternary is able to return into that other unity, which is called the "fecund unity," beyond which one may not proceed.

And so, every operation of wonders consisting within the limits of nature descends from the unit through the binary into the ternary, but not before it arises in simplicity from the quaternary through the order of steps. For if you wish to count to four, you know it must begin with no other than one; and so you say: one, two, three, four, which when taken together make ten <note>The "Tetraktys" (1+2+3+4=10), a fundamental concept in Pythagorean and alchemical thought where the number ten represents a return to unity on a higher level.</note>. This is the perfect consummation of every number, because then a return to one is made, and beyond the denary <note>the number ten</note> there is no simple number. Those who do not know the depths of this connection are amazed, wondering what principles we use in the operation of miracles, falsely thinking that we rely either on the help of demons or on some superstition against our Christian faith. We, however, do not wonder at them judging these things of us on account of their ignorance of what we have set forth. For as the most sacred Scripture testifies concerning the internal knowledge of God, which no one understands other than he who receives it:

begins: so no one can be either imbued with these things or use them, unless they have received a singular light of understanding by divine gift <note>original: "divino munere lumen singulare"</note> from nature into nature, and there was within them, along with that light, fire; with the fire, wind; with the wind, power; and with that power, the knowledge and integrity of a sound mind. This, therefore, is the root and foundation of all deep-seated creatures. The first natural division produces the root of perfected knowledge, the annotation of which is this: There are four mothers of those things which are in the latest order, and four fathers of those who are in the beginning <note>In alchemical thought, the "four mothers" and "four fathers" usually refer to the four elements (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) acting as both passive and active principles</note>: the connection of all these, both the first connection and the final simple thing—pure, unique, and alone—colors all things. 

**Simple Earth** <note>original: "Terra simplex"</note> is a pure element and the first proceeding from the One; it is not composed, it is not changed, and it does not undergo connection, but remains that which is incorruptible; and in the One it consists as one—and yet not one; it is not a number, and it is a number; it is not numbered, and it is numbered; and between it and the One there is no number. In unity the one remains, and through complexity it produces the **ternary** <term>ternarius</term> <note>The number three, often representing the soul or the union of opposites in alchemy</note>; embracing this eight times by a marvelous nature, it leads all things back to the One: its virtue can be explained in its entirety by none of the masters. 

The thing we revere is not God himself; it is a creature, an image of the human mind, neither living nor dead, through which a wonderful effect is produced in every science. And I say to you, friend, in the highest truth of God, that whoever has been raised up by the simple knowledge of this pure simplicity shall be perfected in all natural science, and shall perform wondrous works and find astonishing effects. The Simple Good is unique, and through it flow not only similar things, but many dissimilar things as well. 

**Composite Earth** <note>original: "Terra composita"</note> is an element pure by nature, simple and unique: but because that which is composed necessarily becomes manifold, varied, and impure, it is nevertheless reducible through fire into water; from this into fire; and from that into the simple One; and it is a number, and it is numbered, and it is not a number, and it is numbered. It is not numbered because its nature is simple, yet it is composed by <term>accidents</term> <note>Philosophical properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or weight</note>. For that reason, it cannot be numbered, because there is no number before it. It is numbered as one, not absolute but included, by the unit; and it is called the one excluded, the one included, and the "one through one from the one"—namely, from the **soul of the world** <note>original: "anima mundi," the vital force that animates all nature</note>—and thus becomes the **ternary**. 

By nature, it wishes to be with the One; it is powerful through itself in the One, yet powerless in the One, and powerless in the "other"; it always revolves in a sphere; it remains as one in every fire, but it is not imagined so. If it is purified by fire and reduced to its own simplicity by an appropriate washing, it can perform all the mysteries of deep science. **Earth from the composite** is an element and is not an element, through which the **binary** <term>binarius</term> <note>The number two, representing duality or opposition</note> is reduced into the ternary, distant from the One by four steps. It contains wonders, it is varied and manifold, corruptible, and yet it does not wander outside the circle of unity: the mastery of all secrets lies in the union of this with the ternary by means of the binary. And whatever things are humanly devised, they stand firm through these wonders.

### NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
<note>original: "PHYSICA"</note>

They stand subject to its power and can be achieved through perfect operation. It observes the number, degree, and order in which every operation of nature's wonders consists. The things it is capable of doing are marvelous—even more numerous than is believed—and they bring no insult to God nor any stain upon the soul. Through it, wonderful works are performed; through it, there is full knowledge of all human inventions and effective operation in any obscure matter. This is because its virtue, proceeding from the intellect, does not allow the one who operates through the three degrees to wander into error. It discerns everything that men say. An operation begun through it can by no means be seduced into error. It knows how to perfect these things, fitted to its own principles, without any malice. This is the very **element that is not an element** <note>original: "elementum non elementum"</note>, removed from itself by number, yet simply reduced back into unity when joined to itself. Without the knowledge of this medium, end, and principle through numbers, degrees, and orders, no magus could give power to images without sin (or could even give it with wickedness); no Alchemist could imitate nature; no man could compel spirits; no prophet of nature could predict the future; nor could anyone curious about experiments understand their underlying reason. Therefore, every operation of wonders consisting within the limits of nature descends from **unity** <term>unitarium</term> through the **binary** <term>binarium</term> into the **ternary** <term>ternarium</term> <note>The numbers 1, 2, and 3, representing the progression from the Divine Source to manifest reality</note>; yet not before it rises in simplicity from the **quaternary** <term>quaternarium</term> through the order of degrees, as was said above.

Natural wisdom, therefore—which once stood firm in its pure simplicity, leaning upon the principles of nature—has been confused by so many lies, impurities, and deceptions that no one can discern one from the other or understand it, unless they are most learned in both natural and supernatural science. "How many men," he says, "wandering in natural philosophy have I alone known—otherwise most learned men—some of whom lost their time and substance by spending them on Alchemy; some lose their lives along with their possessions. Others, desiring to draw medicine from it, achieve nothing after long labors. Others, searching into the secrets of marvelous effects, could arrive at no practical experience. Others, eager to tell the future, speak falsehoods instead of truths." While these men press the windy opinions of their own heads, they take things they do not understand from the experts of old; they unskillfully produce a mix of good and true with the evil and false. Consequently, one must first note and learn these **three principles** in this natural, **spagyric** <term>spagirica</term> <note>Alchemical techniques involving the separation and recombination of the constituents of a substance</note>, and occult philosophy. Without a perfect knowledge of these, no effect follows the operator. Its virtue is purified above all things and simple—smaller than all things, yet composed upon a degree above the quaternary. Moreover, the **Pythagorean quaternary** number, supported by the ternary—if it observes the proper order and degree, purified and pure in the one—can work the wonders and secrets of nature toward the binary in the ternary. This is the quaternary in whose measure the ternary, joined to the binary in the one, performs all things that it does so miraculously. For the ternary number, reduced to unity through contemplation, contains all things in itself and can do whatever it wills.

The third principle is not a principle by itself, but between it and the binary lies the end of all science and **mystic art**, and the infallible center of the medium. Nowhere is it easier to wander into error than here, since there are very few living on earth who understand its depths. It is varied, composite, and rising through the **septenary** <note>The number seven</note> multiplied eight times into the ternary, remaining fixed. In it is the consummation of number, degree, and order; through this, all philosophers who were true seekers of nature's secrets have achieved miraculous effects. By reducing it to the simple element in the ternary, miraculous cures for infirmities and all natural sicknesses are suddenly performed, and the work follows its effect in the wisdom of the natural and the supernatural practitioner. Because the art of divine love is long, but time is short, it is always better to love the Creator in truth rather than the creature.

...ternary? <note>original: "ternarius"; the text begins mid-word from the previous page</note> What is born from unity, is it not the ternary? I am not a Trithemius of a triple mind <note>The author is making a play on his own name, "Tri-themius," suggesting "three-themed" or "triple-minded."</note>, but one rejoicing in the number three within a single mind, which truly gives birth to a marvelous offspring.

Therefore, the ternary must be entirely reduced to unity if the mind wishes to achieve a perfect understanding of these things. For the Unary is not a number, but from it every number arises. The binary, receding from unity, is the first composite number. Therefore, let the binary be cast aside, and the ternary will be convertible to the simplicity of unity. Every number consists only of units. Do not all things flow from unity by the goodness of the One, as stated above, and whatever is joined to unity cannot be diverse, but produces fruit through the simplicity and adaptation of the One? What is born from unity, is it not the ternary? The Unary, therefore, is simple, the binary composite, but the ternary is reduced to the simplicity of unity. 

For the One is a pure principle. The binary, receding from unity, is composed, because it is impossible for there to be two principles. Therefore, only the sacred and powerfully virtuous ternary, having overcome the binary, returns to its own principle—not by nature, but by participation in likeness—in which the mind understands, without contradiction, all the mysteries of the beautifully ordered secret. This is the most beautiful power of all strength, which conquers all worldly things. 

Truly, for any man wishing to work profitably in this art through natural wisdom, certain subjects are necessary. 

**First**, it is necessary that he be not only inclined toward this art by nature, but also disposed to it, or at least capable of being disposed through the instruction of a teacher, by means of a rectification from the ternary into unity through the divided binary. 

**Second**, it is necessary to have a sufficient knowledge of language, so that the common people <note>original: "vulgaris"</note> may not grasp the great majesty of the science of natural wisdom itself. It is also necessary to know the foundation of astronomical instruction, or at least to have someone else at hand who knows it. 

**Third**, a supply of books in this science is necessary—only those that are most correctly edited, of which very few are found today—either to have at hand or to have someone readily available who can truly correct their faults rather than increase them.

And after all these things, [he must know] the measure of his own soul, and the virtue and goodness of the power he is entering into. 

Seventh, he must know under the dominion of which planet, and which spirit of the hour of the day and of time any thing in the world belongs, according to its substance, its accidents <note>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, qualities that can change (like color or size) without changing the essential nature of the object</note>, and its effect, and especially the [spirits] through which they operate. For lower things are subject to higher things, and only through similarity—which consists of substance, accident, power, virtue, number, degree, and property—by the application of one to another in a manner established in the art, is a useful operation of wonders in natural wisdom produced. 

Eighth, it is necessary in this wisdom to know and for the operator to understand every property of the intelligences <term>Intelligences: spiritual or angelic beings believed to govern the movements and "influences" of the planets</term>, their degrees, places or locations, names, words, and offices or duties, how they relate to the extremes in the order, and how one must work through them in any universal intention. Or first, the science is necessary through which they are certainly perfected, just as meat is preserved with salt so that it does not rot. Ninth, in those things which he cannot complete alone, he must have companions, either worthy by nature or made worthy by education; because the unworthiness of companions hinders the effect of the operation in all workings of wisdom, both natural and supernatural.
