# TRITHEMIUS

...[dili]gent <note>original: "lentem"; likely the conclusion of "diligentem" (diligent) from the previous page</note> in natural wisdom to work with fruit, to keep all things most secretly, and to reveal to no man the progress or the failure of the operation, nor the operation itself, nor the intent, nor the art, nor the time, except to a teacher or a disciple. Because this science flees the public, and when broadcasted, it rarely produces perfect fruits. This philosophy of ours is celestial, not earthly, so that we may faithfully behold that highest principle which we call God with the gaze of the mind through faith and knowledge—beholding the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one principle, one God, and one highest good existing eternally in a trinity of persons; truly believing, purely knowing, and always worshipping with the cult of most fervent love and service, Him from whom are all things that can possibly exist anywhere. Unless the animated mind rises to this, it will understand none of those things which are beautiful, but will waste away in its own ignorance. 

This ascent is not common, nor is the imitation of those sufficient for it who are carried upward by only one wing <note>This likely refers to those who possess knowledge without faith, or reason without spirit</note>, but it is familiar to very few indeed—namely those who have reduced themselves into unity, neither rashly nor wrongly. Many indeed try, but the ternary <note>original: "ternarius"; the number three, symbolizing the Trinity and the spiritual balance of the soul</note> is not in everyone’s mind. Do we not, when about to look up at the sky, necessarily first lift our head, and bring it back down after we have looked? Although it is permitted to gaze at the sun with the eyes, the ears do not see. Therefore, so that the soul may ascend, let it not become an ear, but an eye and a heart, and let unity be made from the ternary by participation in goodness toward the principle, because there is one almighty good, not two or more. For unless unity is made, the conjunction of likeness will not occur in the mind, nor the participation in the good, and without these there is no transcending: for unless these precede, no one will be able to attain an understanding of higher things, nor the proper operation of lower things. 

Moreover, things both universal and singular are by necessity—as are the conditions of things—some manifest, some more manifest, and some most manifest. And others are hidden, others more hidden, and others most hidden, both to sense and to reason: which diversity the nature of things produces. From this it happens that some men turn out wiser than others. Moreover, he is called more wise who perceives the less perceptible. It is for the understanding of these things that we open the way. 

Accordingly, whoever pants after attained philosophy, both natural and supernatural, can prepare for himself an entrance to either through the other; yet he will proceed more safely if he reduces himself from the binary <note>original: "binario"; the number two, often representing division, conflict, or the material world</note> into the ternary <note>the number three</note> through the steps of the quaternary <note>original: "quaternij"; the number four, representing the physical elements and the structure of the cosmos</note>, before he attempts or presumes to do that very thing in natural matters. Although one can also arrive at the supernatural by means of spagyric medicine <term>Spagyric medicine: the alchemical art of "separating and recombining" the essential virtues of plants or minerals to create powerful healing agents</term>, this other way is more prone to error, and in no matter does one happen to err more than in that one: wherefore I would rather advise everyone to walk by the other path. To this gath- <note>original catchword: "congre-", likely leading to "congregatos" (those gathered)</note>

<summary>Trithemius argues that true "celestial philosophy" requires a spiritual ascent toward divine unity and the Trinity, rather than mere technical study. He explains that while alchemy (spagyric medicine) is a path to the supernatural, it is far more dangerous and prone to error than the path of numerical and spiritual meditation.</summary>

**PHYSICS**

Step forward, most excellent reader, and lift up an attentive mind just as you would prick up your ears.

### A CLEARER ELUCIDATION
->by the interpreter<-

Man is naturally one and is not counted <note>original: "non numeratur"; meaning he is a single entity in the physical world</note>, but supernaturally he is counted as two: as spirit and body, which constitute a binary <note>original: "binarius"</note> within him. Truly, because of original corruption, the latter overcomes the former, which results in the spirit being unable to produce anything wonderful. To achieve this in this life, the binary must be overcome by the ternary <note>original: "ternarius"; the number three</note>—that is, the body must be conformed to the nature of the spirit, and the spirit must be so joined to the body that it may henceforth have peace within it. Once this is done, the ternary, having arisen in a second unity, perfectly rejoices; for from the two aforementioned parts, and from the prior states, a third single thing has been made through union. 

However, this conjunction must be achieved through the steps of the quaternary <note>original: "quaternarius"; the number four</note>, which is to say, through the transmutation of the elements from which the body is composed into a single and most pure element, in this manner: First, indeed, let water be made from the earth of your body; that is: let your stony, earthy, and sluggish heart be rendered soft, and vigilant for the acquisition of the knowledge of its <term>GOD</term> and of itself, so that the images and contemplations of the spirit can be imprinted upon it, no differently than characters are pressed into the wax of a seal. Afterward, let air be made from that water; that is, lift up your contrite and humbled heart toward heaven to Him who created it, just like air always tending toward the highest heights, and by praying, knock so that your intellect may be opened to understand those things which belong to <term>GOD</term>. Finally, let fire be made from this air; that is, let every desire of your now-sublimated heart be converted into the love (to which fire is compared because of its heat) of <term>GOD</term> and of your neighbor here on earth, so that this flame may never be extinguished. 

By this very process it will happen that, through a likeness, your binary—namely spirit and body—is perfectly joined into one ternary through the three steps of the quaternary, as you have heard. Now, friend reader, you hold the key of meditative philosophy, which opens the way of ascent to the heavens, and no one can shut it against you. As for the other key of descent, which shuts so that no one can afterward open it, you shall hear of it in what follows. Since you have now ascended from the earth up into heaven, you must likewise descend from heaven back to the earth, to receive the power of things above and things below. 

Behold, with a liberal spirit I have wished to elucidate for you in my little night-studies <note>original: "lucubratiunculis"</note>, and for all students of hidden things, in how few words I have explained those things which the ancient and recent <term>spagyrists</term> <note>Spagyrists were alchemists who practiced the "spagyric art," which involved separating and then recombining the components of a substance to purify it.</note> have tried to veil in so many and such various layers of riddles. Nor, being unwearied, will I find it burdensome to open more things to you which lead greatly to this philosophy, provided you remain vigilant and attentive; it will surely be to your benefit. Listen now more broadly to the order and the steps of the numbers.

# TRITHEMII.

Number consists of order and measure. Likewise, order cannot exist without number and measure. Measure, however, consists of both number and order. Here, Unity and the <term>ternary</term> <note>original: "ternarius"; the number three, often representing the Trinity or the spiritual soul</note> do not admit number; instead, having cast off all multitude, they exist in the first order in their innate and simplest purity. This is the way to the higher powers, through which the ancient sages, proceeding through the intellect by the guidance of reason, perceived many things that are now considered by our modern "wise men" to be beyond human comprehension. Do you wish to hear of this more fully? Study generates knowledge, knowledge gives birth to love, love to likeness, likeness to communion, communion to virtue, virtue to dignity, dignity to power, and power performs a miracle. This is the unique path to the goal of attained perfections in philosophy—both divine and natural—from which every superstitious, deceptive, and diabolical thing is driven far away and confounded.

Since, therefore, the goal of meditative science (or attained science) is truth, and the goal of <term>spagyric</term> <note>the alchemical practice of separating and recombining elements to reach a purer state</note> practice is the "work" itself, we only know as much as we can grasp of the knowledge of God Almighty, who alone is truth: and we truly know only as much as we love. For true and saving science gives birth to the knowledge of God, knowledge to love, love to frequency <note>original: "frequentiam"; meaning regular presence or habitual practice</note>, frequency to familiarity, familiarity to trust, and trust to the obtaining of all that you shall ask for. Indeed, science precedes the cultivation of virtue, because no one can faithfully desire what they do not know. 

Knowledge of the true and love of the right prepare the most certain entrance to happiness. As we have said, knowledge precedes love, because no one can truly love what is unknown. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ said to the Father in the Gospel: <note>John 17:3</note> *This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.* What else is that supercelestial enjoyment of the pleasantness of the blessed spirits than the knowledge and love of the divine majesty? For the knowledge of saving science has love joined to it, nor can the intellectual mind have a partnership in eternal enjoyment if either knowledge is without love, or love is without knowledge. 

Evil demons certainly possess knowledge, but because they do not have love, they do not reach that state of enjoyment which is born from both together, and not from one alone. Some Gentiles, and many today living outside of Christianity, perhaps seem to have a love for the one supreme truth; but because they do not know the Father of the universe, the only true God, and our Lord Jesus Christ whom He sent, they have become vain in their thoughts, and by no means arrive at the enjoyment of the highest goodness. But our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, says in the Holy Gospel concerning those who do not recognize through faith that He has come into the world: <note>John 3:18</note> *He who does not believe is judged already.* For true knowledge comes from faith, and love comes from knowledge. Therefore, a man lacking faith has no knowled-

The **first step** of ascent to the heavens is the study of faith, for this disposes the heart of man toward <term>dissolution into water</term> <note>original: "solutionem in aquam"; an alchemical metaphor for softening the rigid ego or "dissolving" the base state of the soul</note>. The **second step** is the knowledge of <term>GOD</term> through faith, by which the contrite heart is prepared for ascent into the elevated <term>air</term>, and for the hope of a better life. The **third step** is love arising from the knowledge of God through faith and hope, disposing our "airy" heart toward love and charity, and toward the fiery burning of desire through the likeness of union with <term>GOD</term>. The **fourth** is frequency <note>original: "frequentia"; regular practice, presence, or constant devotion</note>, by which the conceived love is fostered through continuous cultivation—by frequent contemplations joined with prayers—into the increase of the faith, hope, and love already conceived, while the heart dwells in the heavens and is nearly united to them. The **fifth step** is familiarity, which is acquired through the frequency of such conversations with divine things. The **sixth** is confidence <note>original: "fiducia"; trust or bold assurance</note>, by which we—already frequently practiced in faith, hope, and charity—dare to offer our petitions intrepidly before God, relying on the great and undoubted certainty that we will obtain what we desire from our Father. The **seventh** is the obtaining <note>original: "impetratio"</note> of the desired petition made in the name of <term>JESUS CHRIST</term>, which we enjoy for His glory and our own salvation.

Now at last we are fit for the understanding of all secrets <note>original: "arcanorum"; hidden mysteries</note>, both natural and supernatural, and as "adept philosophers" created by God, we are filled with all wisdom. It must be noted that, just as in the first, second, and third steps, our heart ascends upward, receding from the base, filthy, and corruptible earth; likewise, through the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh steps, it descends into a **renewed earth**—incorruptible, solid, constant, and powerful enough to resist any attacks of the enemy, and no longer separable from the Unity to which it is joined. ### ON PHILOSOPHY
->Meditative.<-

Meditative philosophy is the voluntary withdrawal of a well-composed mind from the body, so that the soul may more easily engage in the pursuit of the knowledge of truth. To truly meditate, a good physical disposition is also required so that the body does not hinder the mind. This can be acquired in two ways: namely, by nature or by art. That which is natural can be assisted by art, and that which nature has denied in this regard can even be acquired—chiefly through the use of reason, through a sober diet, and through spagyric medicines; using one or all of these remedies together. The mind, therefore, is said to be well-composed whenever the spirit <note>original: "animus"; the higher, rational spirit or intellect</note> is joined to the soul <note>original: "anima"; the vital life force or sensitive soul</note> by such a bond that it is able to restrain the appetites of the body and the emotions of the heart. The "good disposition" of the body is an immunity from the vices of corruption; it is better the more its component parts have reached a balanced <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "temperaturam"; the harmonious balance of the four humors or qualities in the body</note>. In this state, the body craves its own desires less and becomes more obedient to the mind. For whatever the body craves is corrupt, but it can crave nothing except through the faculties of the soul, which is its mover. If this soul had not been corrupted from its primary nature, it would move simply, without any conception of good or evil. But because malice entered into it first, it strives to carry out that malice through the body, unless the spirit resists; for the spirit suggests nothing but the good. The soul is therefore situated between good and evil, and it has its own choice of the good—not by its own power alone, but through the good of which it had been deprived and which was restored to it—and of evil by itself and through evil. This occurs because the good allows such evil to happen due to the continuous and persistent resistance which the soul makes when dragged by the body, as opposed to the pull of the spirit, which moves only toward goodness. So that we may better derive these points from the spirit's perspective, it should be noted at this point why we assert that man consists of three parts. It is true that "soul" and "spirit" are often used interchangeably; we, however, place no other difference between them than in respect to their accidental properties. Thus, when the soul follows the pull of the Lord's spirit, and rests <note>original: "quiescit"; catchword for the next page</note>

-># PHILOSOPHY<-

<meta>catchword: all</meta>

rests there, denying itself, we call it **mind** and **spirit**, derived from the divine spirit to which it clings. Conversely, if it resists the <note>original: "Spiritui Sancto"</note> **Holy Spirit** as it impresses the testimony of salvation upon it, and instead loves itself (thereby losing itself), we call it simply the **soul**. We desire our writings to be understood in no other way, lest we be falsely accused of some impiety by others—an intention far from our heart—as we strive with all our might to draw others toward this spiritual path. 

To us, therefore, the **Mind** <note>original: "Animus"; refers here to the higher, rational, and immortal part of the human spirit</note> is the **breath of eternal life**, and the **Soul** <note>original: "anima"; the animating force that gives life to the physical body</note> is the organ of the Mind, just as the body is the organ of the soul. The soul is the life of the body through a natural union, just as the spirit is the life of the soul through a supernatural union. Furthermore, if the soul clings more to the spirit through its assent or consent than it does to the body, the **higher mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> arises, and the **inner man**—once created in the image of <term>GOD</term> through the breath of eternal life and now reborn—is elevated. On the other hand, when the soul clings more to its body by obeying it rather than the spirit, the **outer man** is left behind, becoming an abyss of outer darkness contrary to nature.

The Mind also delights in three things: namely, **reason**, **intellect**, and **memory**. 
1. **Reason** presents the image of contemplation to the intellect.
2. The **Intellect** then offers this image to be preserved in the secret memory.
3. **Reason** is the first perpetual and inviolable order of the eternal mind, of which man was made a participant by the first gift of <term>GOD</term>, along with intellect and memory—the latter of which may be called the "preserving ark" of the other two.

The soul, in turn, consists of two primary faculties: **motion** and **sense**. 
*   **Motion** is either natural or accidental. 
*   **Sense** is the perception of a thing heard, tasted, seen, smelled, or touched, through each thing's own specific organ. 

We call the members of the body through which these senses are perceived the "proper organs" of the senses. This perception of the senses brings back the knowledge of past things to the memory by representing present things; and in this, **brute animals** <note>original: "animalia bruta"; non-rational animals governed by instinct rather than reason</note> have something in common with humans. For animals recollect these things through the senses only when present objects are placed before them. There is, however, another root of memory that is far more excellent, which does not rely on any middle representation, but is cultivated by the diligent activity of a spirit that is never idle, making it flourish perpetually. This continuation of memory follows the cultivation of reason and is unique to humans alone. 

Therefore, **sense** is generally a characteristic of the animal nature, while **reason** is specifically characteristic of the intellectual nature. Indeed, brute animals do not understand anything beyond the present sense-perception; but rational animals understand through the intellect, which is moved by reason and sense—using the latter as either an end or a means. 

Again, the mind and the body in rational beings are opposite extremes and contraries which cannot be joined except through the **soul** as a mediator, which participates in both of these "enemies." But because one of these extremes is perfect and the other is imperfect, if movement occurs from the perfect one first, it must necessarily pass through the medium to reach the perfection of the imperfect, and vice versa. For this reason, God...

-># MEDITATIONS<-
->401<-

He [God] established all things under the triad <note>original: "sub tribus"</note>, so that they might come together into one. For He Himself is the author of peace, of union, and of harmony, which cannot exist without the opposition of at least two things. Therefore, two are always enemies until they come together into one through the **triad**, and through that unity become friends. Furthermore, the **spirit** <note>original: "animus"; the divine spark or highest rational part of the human</note> is equal in all people, but it is not received equally by all. Thus, the **higher mind** <note>original: "mens"; the state of the soul when it is aligned with the spirit</note> is neither the same nor equal in everyone. 

Indeed, there are very few who have their **soul** <note>original: "anima"; the animating life-force</note> joined with the spirit; there are many who participate more or less in the higher mind; but there are a great many who, cherishing the body within the soul and the soul within the body, do not recognize the spirit, nor do they perceive its warnings. For these people, there is no higher mind; instead, they have insanity in place of reason and wisdom. Therefore, the higher mind is well received whenever the spirit and soul, in agreement, are so closely received by the body that from these three, one harmonious and inseparable whole is formed.

Furthermore, this friendship can be achieved in no other way than through **division**, without which union is never fulfilled. For "One" is by its own nature solitary; if it remains alone, it would be impossible for it to be joined or united with another. If, however, it is to be united with some other, it is necessary for that other to be produced from this "One" or divided from it, since nothing exists outside of that "One." And since parts of the "One" symbolize or have sympathy with the "One," they easily come together into unity—and the more so, the less they are removed from the "One" through intervals of likeness in clarity. 

For this reason, a **detachment** <note>original: "distractio"; here meaning a mystical withdrawal or separation</note> of the higher mind from the body is necessary, so that a union between the mind and its own dwelling-place may occur. Truly, since union requires the perfection of both parts, a transition must be made from the perfect extreme (which existed before) through a middle point to the imperfect, so that the latter may be perfected. Through such a detachment of the mind from the body—which some call a **voluntary death**—the soul and spirit joined together acquire power and dominion over their body. The spirit alone did not hold this power so freely because of the resisting medium <note>the physical body and its impulses</note> through which the supernatural transition had to occur. For enemies do not come together except through a neutral separation from the side of discord, but rather through a participant that shares in the reconciliation with both.

By this very principle, **Judicial Astrology** <term>Astronomia judiciaria; the practice of predicting human fate or character based on the movement of stars and planets</term> is undermined, which teaches that the alignment of the stars exerts a compelling influence. For the stars have no power over the higher minds of men—for whose sake the stars were created—since the mind is a far more excellent and primary creature. That which is less noble cannot act upon that which is more excellent, even if it tries. 

If, however, human bodies conquer the soul and reduce it to the servitude of the corruptible body, I will not deny that then the bodies of the stars—being nobler than the bodies of men—can imprint their actions upon them through their **influence** <note>original: "influxum"; the celestial "flowing in" of energy believed to affect the material world</note>. In short, **the higher mind of the wise man shall rule the stars**, <note>original: "mens sapientis dominabitur astris"</note> but the mind of the fool is subjected not only to them, but even to lower things and to every kind of hardship. For the wise man is he who, having attained the higher mind, cultivates it; the fool, on the contrary,

-># PHILOSOPHY<-

...body, <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page regarding those who do not recognize the spirit.</note> who loves the body within the soul, or the soul within the body, while neglecting the spirit. As it says in the Word of God: *He who loves his soul* (understand this as: in the body) *will lose it, and he who hates his soul* (in the manner described above) *keeps it for eternity.* <note>original: "Qui diligit animam suam... perdet eam"; a reference to John 12:25.</note> A person is said to love his soul in the body when he follows all the depraved appetites of his physical self. Likewise, even if he does not fulfill those appetites, yet still delights in the imaginary thoughts of vanities, he is seen to love the body here in his soul. On the contrary, he "hates" his soul in the body who restrains the harmful appetites of the physical form, and he hates the body in the soul who immediately drives away and eradicates the vain imaginings of his thoughts.

This is the path toward the primary union—namely, of the soul with the spirit—and toward attaining the **higher mind** <note>original: "mens"; in this context, the state where the soul is perfectly aligned with the divine spirit</note>. Whether we call this final state "spirit" or "soul," by using one name we do not exclude the other, because of the union already achieved. However, it must be noted above all that no union is perfect unless it is inseparable. Nevertheless, the beginnings of union can be laid even if they do not immediately achieve their full effect; this does not prevent the higher mind from still being called "imperfect" to a greater or lesser degree. Truly, those who have attained a perfect higher mind are very few; those who have an incipient one are many; and those who have none are the most numerous.

Furthermore, a good physical disposition of the body is very useful for true **contemplation** <note>original: "contemplationem"; the act of deep spiritual or philosophical looking</note>, even if it is not strictly necessary. To be sure, because of its corrupt nature—by which it has become entirely diseased—the body greatly weighs down the soul and hinders it from perceiving the actions of the spirit. It happens by nature that some people are more fit than others to undergo this separation of the spiritual from the material. These are people who, in their physical formation, were not subjected to any additional "accidental" corruption beyond the natural corruption of birth. Those who are less fit are those who, in addition to their inherited corruption, hinder their own reason through their own petulance and a dissolute way of life. Examples include those agitated by worldly cares who neglect the eternal things existing outside this world, and those who use the things nature provided only for necessity more profusely than is proper.

Therefore, just as something is hindered by the addition of a corruption, it can likewise be helped by the removal of that same thing. Thus, for this purpose, certain medicines are created through the <term>spagyric art</term> <note>original: "spagiricam artem"; the alchemical practice of separating, purifying, and recombining the essential components of a substance</note>, which is more excellent than all others. These medicines are separated from their original "bodies" (their raw material state). Through the natural power of acting which they possess by nature within their own bodies—and which they retain even after their active part has been removed—they can perform that same action when applied to a different body. Indeed, they can perform it far more excellently than they were naturally able to do within their own original bodies.

Whatever is found in the nature of things that possesses both form and matter desires to be perfected as much as possible within its own kind. This innate appetite is the most powerful cause of the perfection of all things. Since nature also rejoices to be joined to a nature similar to itself and finds delight in it, the higher mind—helped by an incorruptible medicine similar to itself—triumphs in the arrangement of the body...

**of the body**, this <note>the soul/spirit union</note> is forced to descend into that same physical nature, just as previously—from the opposite direction—the soul was forced when the body was winning, strengthened by things similar to itself as corrupting forces. Lest this seem absurd to anyone, I shall add more. Every nutrient is changed into the blood of the one nourished, sharing the same temperamental nature as the nutrient itself. This is shown by the example of those who constantly feed on the flesh of fierce animals, who themselves happen to become most fierce. Nature indeed takes nothing as food except what is subtle, once the coarse and dreggy matter has been removed and ejected as waste. And again, from any surplus of nutrient, yet another waste product is ejected through the pores as sweat, or through the bladder, nostrils, or tears.

This moved **Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who revolutionized medicine by using chemistry.</note> to say that every member of the human body has its own "stomach" in which the nutrient is "cooked" <note>original: "decoquitur"; refers to the process of digestion or metabolic transformation.</note>; and within it, the separation of the superfluous from the necessary occurs. If, however, due to the weakness of some limb or organ, such surplus cannot be conveniently ejected, that surplus from poor digestion—contrary to the custom of nature—nourishes, extends, or bends the flesh or bones in that location, leading to either a tumor or an abnormal growth.

Truly, however, in **spagyric medicines** <note>original: "spagiricis medicamentis"; alchemical medicines produced by separating and then recombining the essential virtues of plants or minerals.</note>, nothing of the coarse or the superfluous remains. Therefore, every part of the body takes up this entire medicine and transforms it, without any need for separation, into a nature similar to itself. Conversely, the medicine imprints the same property it possesses—namely, being free from corruption and surplus—just as all incorrupt nature is. Furthermore, incorrupt nature is the **natural balsam** of long life, naturally implanted in any body and similar in nature to spagyric medicine. Through this balsam, the body's heat and moisture—even those that are "natural" or **radical** <note>original: "radicales"; the "radical moisture" was believed to be the fundamental fluid of life that one is born with and that slowly consumes itself over a lifetime.</note>—are preserved from corruption as much as possible. When this balsam is lacking, the whole body becomes leprous; but when it recovers through an increase from external sources, that which had been corrupted due to the scarcity of that balsam is ejected as waste.

Therefore, spagyric medicine differs from the common medicine used until now. Common medicine is passed into the stomach along with its "body" <note>its coarse, physical substance</note> and its corruptions, where it is digested and separated no differently than food, which causes the greatest distaste and nausea to nature. The spagyric medicine, however, is transformed with the highest delight, beyond all need for digestion or separation, immediately into the **radical moisture**, the natural heat, and the natural balsam. For these three most powerful parts of the physical body ought to be both nourished and restored by things similar to themselves. Hence it happens that daily food and drink are taken with their physical "bodies" because they are clearly ordained by nature for the nourishment of the **elements** <note>the physical components of the body</note> as well, and not just as medicine. **...the mind**, and its companions, we make as conformable as possible. And so the spirit of a **spagyric medicine** <note>original: "spagirici medicamenti"; alchemical medicine created through the process of separation and recombination.</note>, joined with its own soul and separated from the coarse and impure body—and afterwards united again to that body once it has been purified through the soul—nourishes and restores the mental, indeed the spiritual or vital parts, into a substance similar to itself. It also corrects the physical body, even if it has been corrupted, and protects it from all further corruption. 

We do not deny that our spagyric medicine is corporeal, but we say it is made spiritual, a state which the alchemist bestows when **the fixed becomes volatile, and the volatile becomes fixed.** <note>A core alchemical principle (Solve et Coagula) where solid matter is spiritualized and spiritual essence is stabilized into matter.</note> Truly, the physical body cannot be cured by a more excellent body than the spagyric one, nor can the human mind be better composed than by a spagyric and meditative disposition—after the gift of divine grace, however. From all these things, we conclude that **meditative philosophy** consists in the overcoming of the body through a mental union. 

But this first union does not yet produce a **sage** <term>sophum: a person who has attained true wisdom or the alchemical "Great Work."</term>; it only produces a mental disciple of wisdom. However, the second union—that of the mind with the body—presents the sage. He remains separating and awaiting that third, complete, and blessed union with the **First Unity** <note>original: "unitate prima"; referring to God or the primordial source of all being.</note>. May Almighty God grant that we all become such, and that He himself may be one in all. 

Furthermore, one must also know from where the mind is to be sought. For just as faith is truly a free gift of God, so are all the virtues. From this it does not follow that one must not labor to acquire them, because God by no means hears the idle and the sluggish; indeed, He rather rejects their prayers as blasphemies. Truly, it would be a great insanity for men to ask God for bread, yet be unwilling to plow and sow; it would be no less insane to desire a mind and wait for it while applying no diligence whatsoever to acquiring it. It is surely the greatest madness if someone were so ignorant as to think that this could be acquired by his own labor without first imploring the grace of God. He fills the diligent with His blessing while they seek what is wholesome, but God does not hear the negligent, even if they ask. A person is truly said to ask not only with the mouth, but with the heart and with deep affection when he requires something. 

Therefore, before we come to the first level of meditative philosophy, I thought that disciples should be warned about imploring divine help, and then about the most accurate diligence in disposing themselves to receive such grace. Regarding this disposition, only this much is discussed in this place; grace, however, must be sought from above from the **Giver of Lights** <note>A biblical reference to God from the Book of James.</note>, God the Best and Greatest. And because there are three most powerful parts of this prepared disposition—namely, the **spagyric**, the **moral**, and the **meditative**—it was necessary in this treatise to proceed by whatever way was needed, now by this one, now by that. For it is impossible for a man of an evil life to possess the treasure of wisdom hidden for the children [of light], and one who is of unsound mind is unfit for acquiring or inquiring after it, much less for finding it. **[huma]n body** there lies hidden a certain substance of a celestial nature known to very few, which requires no medicine at all, but is itself an incorruptible medicine. However, because it is overwhelmed and hindered by the corruptions of its own body from exercising its actions, philosophers—by a certain divine inspiration—have recognized that this power and celestial vigor can be freed from its chains. This is not done by its opposite, as the unfaithful teach, but by its like. 

Since, therefore, such a thing may be found either within man or outside him which conforms to this substance, the wise have concluded that **likes must be strengthened by likes** <note>original: "similia similibus"; a fundamental principle in alchemy and later homeopathy suggesting that substances with similar natures can reinforce one another.</note> through peace rather than war, and that contraries must be driven out by contraries. Therefore, for the skillful restoration of the body's good condition, we use a **spagyric medicine** <term>spagirico medicamento: a remedy produced by alchemically separating a substance into its components and then reuniting them in a purified state.</term>. By this remedy, we may restrain its corruption toward a natural digestion, and thus toward expulsion, while nature performs this work through a form strengthened from within. This is the preparation of our physical body made by the spagyric art, through which we more easily arrive at separation without the hindrance of corrupting influences. From this, the studious reader will gather that the safest transition is made from **meditative philosophy** first, then through the spagyric art, toward true and **attained wisdom** <note>original: "adeptam sapientiam"; the wisdom of an "Adept," one who has mastered the Great Work of alchemy.</note>. 

Now let us come to the voluntary division. Once the preparation of the body is complete, it is easily separated from the remaining parts, provided that whatever the body desires from the soul beyond physical necessity is denied to it by the persuasion of the mind. From that separation results the first **union of spirit and soul** through the continued study of **moral philosophy**. These matters had to be presented to students so they might understand by what reasoning we have mixed moral matters with spagyric, physical, and meditative ones, and how each is compared to its corresponding part—lest I be said to have blocked the entrance for readers who might otherwise remain stuck in a labyrinth. 

But our mind invites us to the first grade of **meditative philosophy**, which is occupied with study in meditation. Meditative study is the diligent search for the truth and the forgetting of worldly things, however necessary they may seem, according to the word of the Lord: *Seek first the kingdom of God, and do not be anxious about what you eat or drink, nor what you shall wear, for your Father who is in heaven knows that you have need of all these things; all that you need will be added to you, when you, intent on the word of God, obey Him alone.* <note>A translation of Matthew 6:33.</note> If, therefore, even the things necessary to us must be cast aside and driven far from the mind for the sake of true meditation, how much more must the worldly cares and superfluous thoughts of vanities—which choke the good seed—be manfully driven away whenever they arise during meditation? This should be done with the words the Lord taught us, which are most effective for this purpose: **"Get away from me immediately, Satan!** <note>original: "Abi hinc à me protinus Satana"</note> I have nothing in common with you; I desire to belong entirely to God, to whom I have dedicated myself." Truly, the contrary exists, and it ought not to be, nor does it exist except through the <term>privation</term> <note>the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note> of true essence; it is nothing else than that which truly is not. From this, some conclude that sin and death are such a "nothing," because they do not proceed from that true being, but from a deprivation of true essence. When by his own death, which he had not deserved, he took away from us the perpetual death with which we all deserved to be punished. 

See then, brothers, how great the effect of truth is, so that it is beneficial and peaceful even toward its enemies, provided they recognize it. Such a person, though strikingly cloaked in fine scarlet linen and purple, is in fact most naked. 

We inherited this vice from our first parent's original appetite: that our flesh, more than anything else, desires—rightly or wrongly—to know, to be wise, to possess, and to be honored like an idol. This is the chief pursuit of men in this age, and it is most destructive to them, as it was to Adam. Nor are there lacking among us those who turn to the worse path after Adam's fall, and no differently than he, fleeing from the face of the Lord, they seek out the hiding places of the outer darkness. This lack of faith, which for the most part tends toward despair, especially requires repentance, by which one may return to the light of truth. 

Again, truth is subject to no power or worldly strength; therefore nothing can harm it, since it is itself all true strength, overcoming the power of the whole world. And if the body of one possessing the truth were cut into a thousand pieces, his soul suffers nothing; rather, he rejoices in that martyrdom. # MEDITATIVE THOUGHTS

<column-break/>

[...justice] and piety, joined by an inseparable bond of union. Piety, moreover, is a grace fallen from heaven, which teaches everyone to truly know themselves as they are. Justice, in truth, is the retribution and restitution to each person of what is their own. Whoever truly possesses these virtues is the wealthiest of all. Piety also produces peace and mercy, about all of which more will be said later in its proper place. 

It remains for us to look at necessity. Certainly, we cannot do without food and clothing; therefore, as we said above, these are necessary. However, any person—even one who possesses them—can do without delicacies in both food and drink, as well as the luxury and display of clothing. These are not necessary, but rather superfluous. Furthermore, those who observe "philosophical necessity" <note>the minimalist lifestyle advocated by Stoic or Cynic philosophers who take only what is required for survival</note> are very few. On the other hand, is there any common man—even a simpleton—who does not unwillingly endure "common necessity" <note>the basic poverty or lack experienced by the lower classes</note>, and who desires to be without only that which he cannot obtain by any right or wrong? 

But because the common crowd judges everything superficially and according to appearance—and almost no one looks toward the center <note>the inner essence or truth of a matter</note>—truth is rendered hateful when it comes out into the open under a torn bark <note>a metaphor for truth appearing in a humble or unattractive outward form</note>. In this current age, splendid clothing, bracelets, necklaces, and jewels have more power than truth and wisdom themselves. What wonder is this, since the highest wisdom has been made "foolishness" to the world, while this worldly vanity is conversely considered "wisdom"? The Holy Scriptures testify to this. 

Truth itself—which is Christ and true wisdom—is taken away by the wise of the world because he is not of the world, yet he overcomes the world. Barabbas the thief, however, is chosen instead, because he was a man of the world, though a wicked one. Why then do we marvel if the world, having persecuted Truth itself, shrinks back from the professors of the true arts as if from poison? 

Those same "wise" followers of the world admit this when they teach that "truth breeds hatred, while compliance breeds friends" <note>original: "veritatem parere odium, & obsequium amicos"; a famous line from the Roman playwright Terence, often cited to show how people prefer flattery over honest correction</note>. These matters must be brought up here, even if they seem foreign to our meditations, because it is necessary to exclude this "diabolical leaven" <note>a biblical metaphor for a corrupting influence that spreads through a whole community</note>.

Tell me, I ask you, men of judgment: how can it be that an infidel, lacking all true light, can bring the light of truth to others? It is as if nothing were true or good except what originated from the infidels who are ignorant of the truth. For a speculative mind, aided by the light of truth, can achieve more in a single year—or even a single moment—than the persistent and wicked labor of a man who seeks light from those who lack all light, while he himself is without this guiding light. 

Furthermore, let us examine the moral doctrine of these unbelieving philosophers. They define the "highest good" <term>Latin: *summum bonum*; the ultimate goal or purpose of human life</term> as "living well," which they divide into the honorable and the useful. They consider the ambition for honors and praises to be the height of honor. Finally, they call the acquisition and preservation of wealth "useful"—whether obtained by any right or wrong, by war or by the sweat of one's brow. It is evident that they expect nothing else after death from all these things except to have left behind honors and favors for their descendants through the memory of themselves and the fame of their deeds. 

Because they partly deny and partly are ignorant of the resurrection, these wretched men have devised a thousand fables in their poems. These stories are devoid of all truth—of which they had no part—and were thought up to the ruin of mankind and their own destruction. Behold! This is why those who profess the true arts must be so greatly hated by those who carry the titles and reputation of having achieved more in various arts and faculties. Even when experience places the truth right before their eyes, it is rejected as false unless it is confirmed by the opinions of those who have never actually experienced the truth. Indeed, anyone who says they wish to profess the truth is considered a fool with the loudest of outcries. 

If someone should deservedly detest these vain authors, their disciples in the Universities soon threaten such men either with punishment or with the deepest disgrace, which they call "riding the donkey" <note>original: *equitationem asini*; an academic ritual of public shaming or hazing used to humiliate dissidents</note>. Far be it! It is more fitting for a philosopher to die than to deny the truth. In all things, truth must be observed as the highest good among Christians. Blessed are those to whom it is granted from heaven to persevere in it until the end—which, alas, happens to very few. ...the truth and power of the same thing lies hidden, to be brought into action through this art. For this to happen, their division is necessary—separating the superior from the inferior—and the purification of both parts; then finally, through spagyric means of operation, a reduction into one, or a union. Therefore, the spagyric <note>The term "spagyric" refers to alchemical processes used to separate, purify, and recombine the components of a substance, often for medicinal or spiritual purposes.</note> study, and the first step toward spagyric union, is the division or separation of the thing. 

There is, therefore, a twofold separation of elements: one is of the purer from the more impure, and this is truly spagyric; the other is of the elemental qualities, and this is common and familiar to everyone. Nature, however, works through simple mixing under only two operations, namely alteration and animation. We will deal with each in what follows; now we must speak of the separation of the pure from the impure. 

In some bodies, this happens by itself, and in others with a vehicle <term>Latin: *vehiculum*; a substance used to carry or extract another, such as a solvent</term>. Although a celestial essence—which they call the "fifth" <term>Latin: *quinta*; the "quintessence," or the purest, most refined essence of a substance</term>—exists in all bodies produced by nature, the philosophers say it is nowhere as abundant as in wine. For this reason, they preferred wine because its separation is easier. This is not because that substance is more excellent when drawn from its own body [wine] than from any other. For the virtue is universal, and is only different because of the variety of subjects (clinging to them still); yet once freed, it returns to its own unity. This is one of the secrets of nature, through which the spagyric practitioners have reached higher things. 

However, we must take care not to be misled by the name "wine," for it is twofold: "philosophical" and "common." Philosophical wine can be drawn from any body of nature. Common wine is sold by wine merchants. Therefore, when you wish, you shall separate the spirit and soul from any body. 

Let us first teach concerning philosophical wine by way of an example. Grains of wheat, barley, or rye, soaked in spring or rainwater (or any other) so that they swell, should be piled in a heap and remain until, after a few days, they heat up and sprout <note>This describes the process of "malting," where grain begins to germinate to release sugars.</note>. Once this is observed, they should be spread out, and the superfluous moisture of the water allowed to dry for a short time; afterward, they should be ground somewhat coarsely. Placed in a wooden vessel, very hot water should be poured over this flour, and the vessel covered. After this liquid has cooled and settled, it should be strained through a hair-cloth or bag so it is not at all cloudy. 

Then finally, pour more boiling water over the same flour as before, and strain: repeat this process of pouring and straining as many times as you perceive that the entire substance of the grains has been received into the waters—which you will test by tasting the last strained liquid and the flour. Finally, you should make all the strained liquids boil until, through evaporation, they are brought to the thickness of honey. In this way, you have prepared for yourself philosophical wine from grain, which you can likewise obtain from all other seeds, and even from those drier than can be separated by themselves without burning. Separation done in this manner is called "by a vehicle." Moreover, from the said philosophical wine, through...

...by distillation, you shall separate the soul, which ascends upward with the spirit, from its body. You shall sublimate such a spirit and soul as many times as necessary until it is separated and freed from all phlegm <note>In alchemy, "phlegm" refers to the tasteless, watery, and inactive byproduct of distillation.</note>. The body, having been dried in the shade or by a fire, you shall reduce into the driest ashes using a most violent fire. Pour boiling water over these ashes so that it bubbles with them for some time, so that you may have a very sharp lye <term>Latin: *lixivium*; a strong alkaline solution leached from wood ashes</term>. When this has settled, you shall separate the clear liquid from the ashes by a careful pouring, so that it is not disturbed. Pour more boiling water over the ashes as before, and prepare another lye. Add this to the first strained liquid, and do this through lye-making as many times as necessary until you perceive no more sharpness remaining in the ashes. 

Collect the lye and pass it through a linen sleeve (which they call a filter) into a most clear liquid. Evaporate this in glass vessels so that you have our tartar <term>Latin: *tartarum*; a salt-like crust that forms during fermentation or distillation, used here as a purified mineral base</term> and the salt of the nature of all things. This can be resolved into "tartarean water" upon a marble stone in a moist and cold place. 

Once you have the quintessence <term>Latin: *essentia quinta*; the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual component of a substance</term> from philosophical wine (or from common wine of any color, provided it is pure and very strong) and have rectified it perfectly as you have heard, you should reduce this juice to the highest simplicity through continuous and diligent movements of "rotation" <note>Rotation or circulation refers to a process of prolonged heating where the liquid evaporates and condenses back into itself, mimicking the cycles of the heavens.</note>. When the circle of the wheel is finished, you will see the pure separated from the impure once again, floating on top with a most serene, transparent, and lucid color like the air. Separate this from the impure by pouring it off, and save it. 

Thus far, you have seen the spagyric heaven <note>The author compares the purified alchemical liquid to the celestial heavens.</note> which you can adorn, for it is equipped with "inferior stars" in no different a way than the sky above is equipped with superior ones. Will the infidels <note>Refers to those who do not believe in the spiritual or chemical truths of alchemy.</note> now wonder at us for imitating the Natural Philosophers, handling the heaven and stars with our hands, or will they deny these things as they deny all else unknown to them? It matters little what they do. No malice or envy shall delay our purpose, by which we strive to benefit all good men and students of truth. Therefore, let us extend ourselves further, having progressed in this manner as we began. 

These "inferior stars" are any individual things produced by nature in this lower world—namely, through the conjunction of those stars and the heaven, as if the superior elements were joined with the inferior. Now I hear the voices of many growling against us, echoing these words: "Bah!" they say, "Away with them! Let such men be removed who say they can join heaven to earth." But let them shout as loudly as they wish; they shall be forced to hear things even higher and greater than these. 

The "heaven," therefore, is the celestial matter and the universal form, containing within itself all distinct forms, yet proceeding from a single universal form. This medicine will be capable of removing corruptions and diseases, whether particularly or universally and indifferently. But because these things are scarcely intelligible unless one has a full knowledge of the terms of the art, we have decided to define these in the second following step, once we have first completed our meditative knowledge. 

Meditative knowledge, therefore, is a kind of resolution of opinions conceived about any truths through certain, tested experience. Now, an "opinion" is a doubtful presumption of truth clinging in the mind. "Experience," however, is a manifest demonstration of truth. And "resolution" is the laying aside of doubt. We cannot become more certain about any doubt than by experiencing it, and nowhere better than within ourselves. 

Wherefore, let us verify what was said above about truth by making a trial starting from ourselves. We said before that piety consists in the knowledge of oneself; hence it follows that we begin to clarify meditative knowledge from that point. No one can truly know themselves unless they first see and know, through diligent meditation and inquiry into the Holy Scriptures, what they are (rather than merely "who"), on whom they depend or to whom they belong, and for what purpose they were made and created—likewise, by whom and through whom. 

When these things are known, piety itself begins to arise, which concerns two things: the Creator and the creature. For it is impossible for a creature to know itself perfectly except through its Creator. Nothing exists from itself. How then can any effect become more certain of itself before its cause? Does not every beginning precede its middle and its end, or shall anyone approach a matter from the end? God, however, is without beginning and end, existing through Himself from eternity, filled with all glory, which He did not wish to possess alone; rather, by His mere generosity, He determined to make us participants in it with Himself and to create us in His image—the first exemplar of His generosity and a mystery not to be ignored by us, nor

Just as we were created from the vilest mud, contemptible and despised by all, so too on account of the <term>prime matter: the foundational, formless substance from which all things are created</term> <note>original: *materia prima*</note> from which we consist, we are more prone toward any vile thing than toward Him who once created us out of the vile as most precious creatures, adorned with glory and honor just a little less than the angels. 

Wonder, therefore, all you wretched mortals who are with me, believing it was not done without reason that the supreme <term>Builder of things: a title for God as the divine Architect or Creator</term> <note>original: *conditor*</note> chose for Himself the vilest matter of all from which He wished to raise up the final and most perfect creature. He passed over many other things and all precious substances, such as gold, gems, and others of that kind, even though all those things were founded on account of this one creature and for its use and benefit. He did this so that, by recognizing what we are and from what we are made, we might restrain ourselves from the pride of arrogance. 

Indeed, doing entirely the opposite, there is none of us who does not hate the poor man whom God chooses, even though that poor man consists of the same mass from which we all came forth. Hence it happens that God is no respecter of persons, but a lover of poverty and humility, and an enemy of lofty pride. Furthermore, no one can know the Creator better than through His creatures, just as a <term>craftsman: or artist; the one who performs the work</term> <note>original: *artifex*</note> is known from his work. 

Let us see, therefore, who it is who was able to raise the most precious thing from the vilest; we shall find no other except Him who created both. For no one else ever could, nor ever will be able to, convert water into wine, except Him alone who had created the wine and the water. He did something even more remarkable when He transmuted earth into a living soul; indeed, what is greatest of all, He endowed it with the supreme gift of blessedness—namely, His own **image and likeness**. Through this, it is granted to all to be saved who, recognizing this gift with thanksgiving, receive it willingly. 

But what shall be given to those unwilling to receive it freely? Certainly nothing. Let those men therefore have what is their own, so that the place of justice may be preserved. Each man’s own is that which he chose from the beginning: namely, damnation. The gift of eternal salvation is free for those who receive it with thanksgiving. Since, therefore, we are at once a vile and a dear price, let each of us see which of these he ought rather to choose; the matter is clearer in itself than any explanation could make it. 

It remains for us to weigh for what purpose we were created. For Almighty God created the first man in His **image and likeness**, so that he might exist for the glory of God Himself, and be immortal, without anxiety, in need of nothing, always rejoicing in God, and not at all subject to earthly passions. But because man did not recognize so great a gift, he held it cheap. He knew, nevertheless, that he had been made perfect and wise by the Lord, but he did not remain in that knowledge. ### MEDITATIVE REFLECTIONS

...then the knowledge of the good was promised in simplicity, and yet we see how much evil the contempt for such a great gift and for the word of God has brought, since it soon rendered man mortal from his previous state of perpetual immortality. For he who dies by the <term>second death: a theological concept referring to eternal separation from God or spiritual death</term> <note>original: *secunda morte*</note> lives always in the agony of death and never ceases to die; for this reason it is called perpetual, just as life is called eternal, by which we live for God forever, since we shall never cease to live that life. 

For when our first parent <note>referring to Adam</note> made us all rebels and enemies against God along with himself, Almighty God, moved by mercy, decided to enter into peace with us hardened ones, for He is the author of peace. Who will be so stony-hearted that, when he revolves this mystery of divine goodness in his mind, he would not be reconciled with his own enemy, even if he has received the greatest injury from him? 

How does it happen, then, that among mortals neither of the enemies—whether the one who caused the offense or the one who suffered it—is willing to approach the other for the sake of reconciliation? Truly, it is for no other reason than because no one has truly known himself, nor God, nor his neighbor as an equivalent creature; thus it also happens that he who is ignorant of peace does not embrace it. For peace is the root of mercy. For he who does not possess peace will not practice mercy, nor will he even attain it until he has peace. There is no reason for us to confuse peace and mercy in this place, because peace is the cause of mercy, just as piety is the cause of peace. 

If, therefore, we wish to know whether we have peace with God, let us first examine our conscience, so that we may judge ourselves by this sign: whether we are in agreement, without envy or hatred, with our neighbor—both with an enemy and with any other person who is our equal. Should we not consider that the supreme <term>Creator of things: God as the Architect of the universe</term> <note>original: *conditor*</note> showed His mercy through the embrace of peace toward man, that little worm and slave of the devil? 

He did not wait for the one who had committed the crime against Him to approach Him to ask for mercy, as would have been fair; on the contrary, He Himself—against whom every injury of ingratitude was brought—calls gently to the author of the crime even as he was fleeing from His face and hiding himself. He does not rebuke him harshly; instead, He promises a remedy for the disease of sin: mercy and peace. 

O wretched mortals, as many of us as expect to obtain mercy from God, yet do not acknowledge our misery before Him in our deeds as we do with our mouths! From where, I ask, does mercy come? It is moved to compassion through the true confession of an offense, made through contrition of the heart toward the amendment of one's former life. Furthermore, as long as we are not ignorant of our own misery and that of our brothers, but weigh it with an equal balance, we—having become wealthier in all the goods of this world—shall not consider ourselves more abundant in eternal riches than those who are utterly destitute of worldly wealth. Who among mortals truly considers this, and will not console his needy brother through the sharing of the goods or wealth entrusted to him alone in this world? Show me one who considers what has been said, and I will soon show him...

...who understands these secrets of God. And yet, God did not wish to sufficiently explain His great love toward us through all these things alone; rather, while His own justice accused us (to which nothing can ever be diminished, no more than to His mercy), He spared us instead of His own Son, in whom **peace and justice have kissed each other**. <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10, a favorite verse for Christian philosophers to explain how God's demand for justice and His desire for mercy were reconciled through Christ.</note> Why, in turn, do we not embrace one another, having been made fathers and brothers in Christ, when the supreme Creator of all things deigns to embrace us—miserable little worms—in His Son? And why does He deign to restore us once again as more excellent creatures than before, after we were once made most wretched by our own evil? As many as recognize God in the Son, and likewise the Son in the Father through the Holy Spirit (whom they do not resist), they also recognize their brother, and no others. 

These are the true and indubitable foundations of true philosophy. However, because these things are not yet known to all, even if heard by many, a doubt might still cling to the minds of those who are not well-resolved: whether the imagination of the aforementioned things can excite the love of truth within us. It would be worth their while to set aside this ambiguity for themselves, and within themselves, by conducting an experiment in this manner: 

Let each person diligently consider within themselves those things which have already been said, casting away all worldly cares and other distracting thoughts from the mind. Once tasted, let him ruminate <note>A traditional term for deep, repetitive meditation, likened to a creature "chewing the cud" to fully digest spiritual truths.</note> upon them often with a sincere mind. Thus, little by little, he will perceive with great joy a few sparks of **divine illumination** <term>divine illumination: the spiritual insight or "inner light" granted by God to the human intellect</term> shining more and more every day through his mental eyes. Subsequently, through the perseverance of this rumination, it will grow into such a light that everything necessary for him will become known through these successes, and he will no longer hesitate in any way regarding the truth. Instead, by the exercise of piety and gradually becoming accustomed to justice through the rituals and paths mentioned before, he will feel a tranquility of soul. Attracted by this at last, he will understand that there is a greater delight in the soul than in the body, a thousand times over. 

For true knowledge does not begin until the soul, through a comparison of things eternal and things fleeting (of both life and destruction), chooses to be joined with the mind, drawn by a greater delight for the mind than for the body. Indeed, from that knowledge the mind arises, and the voluntary separation from the body is completed. This happens when the soul, looking on one side at the foulness and destruction of the body, and on the other at the excellence and perpetual happiness of the soul, desires to be connected with the latter (by divine inspiration), utterly neglecting the former. Thus, it thereafter desires only what it sees is concluded by God for His glory and its own salvation. Finally, the body is compelled to descend into the union of those two now-united parts and to obey. 

This is that wonderful **transformation** <note>original: *transmutatio*</note> of the philosophers: of the body into spirit, and of the spirit into the body, concerning which we are left with the saying from the wise: **"Make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed,"** <note>original: *fac fixum volatile, et volatile fixum*. A famous alchemical maxim referring to the process of making solid matter spiritual/gaseous, and stabilizing spiritual forces into a permanent, "fixed" state.</note> by which you may possess our **mastery** <term>mastery: or *magisterium*, the successful completion of the alchemical "Great Work," here applied to the perfection of the human soul and body</term>. Understand it in this way: make the stubborn body tractable, so that through the excellence of the mind harmonizing with the soul, it may become a most constant body for sustaining all things...

It is a wonder that anyone could desire something unknown, or seek that whose truth he does not recognize, which can promise no hope for what he seeks. The wise man seeks only what he loves, but he cannot love what he does not know; otherwise, he would be called a fool, since truth and the love of it are born from knowledge. 

All seekers of the hidden secrets of nature labor in vain when, having entered by a different path, they attempt to uncover the virtues of earthly things through the earthly. Learn, therefore, to know heaven, not through the earth, but to know the earth through the virtues of heaven. For heaven, by its own virtue and through invisible rays converging from all sides into the center of the earth, penetrates all elements and things composed of elements; it generates and nourishes them. This "offspring" of both parents—namely, of the elements and of heaven—retains their nature within itself, so that in it, both parents are findable in potential and in act. Learn, however, from yourself to recognize whatever is in heaven and on earth, especially since all this was created for your sake. Are you unaware that heaven and the elements were once one, and were divided from each other by divine craftsmanship so that they might naturally generate both you and all other things? If you know this, the rest cannot escape you. 

In every generation, therefore, a separation of this kind is necessary—the same kind I said above must be done concerning yourself—before you apply your mind's veil to the studies of true philosophy. You will never make the "one" you seek from other things, unless that "one" is first made from yourself, as you have heard and will hear more extensively in what follows. For such is the will of God: that the pious achieve the pious work they seek, and the perfect may perfect the other thing to which they have been intent. # PHILOSOPHY

### CONCERNING CHEMICAL PHILOSOPHY
### *compared to Meditative Philosophy.*

To begin, the **spagyric chaos** <term>Spagyric: Relating to alchemy, specifically the process of separating and recombining substances to create medicines. Chaos refers to the raw, unrefined starting material.</term> is the confusion <note>original: "confusio," meaning a mixed or undifferentiated state</note> of particular forms and their matters with their universal form and matter. This is indeed considered in various ways. First, as the confusion in the minds of men who do not understand this art. Second, as the confusion of the parts that constitute that final goal. Third, as the confusion in which the various intermediate substances exist alongside the extremes, moving potentially from one to the next, with everything existing in everything else <note>original: "quovis in quibusvis," a reference to the Hermetic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected</note>. Fourth, just as nature holds a middle ground between the elements and their compounds, so in this art, the artist is considered the medium between chaos, the operations, the perfect medicine, and the most perfect medicine. From these four modes, it can easily be understood that these medicines are led from their potential state into actual existence through the mediation of matter, form, heaven, and intermediate operations. For once motion is stirred by the artist, the chaos passes to the second extreme, which is the perfect medicine, and then to the most perfect, according to the order of the mediums and their arrangement toward one another. 

To understand this more sharply, our Chaos is a universal thing, containing within itself everything we work upon; from its "belly," the ingenious artist must draw out his matter, form, heaven, and elements, so that from these he may compose the medicines already mentioned. Indeed, **spagyric matter** is called the first and universal matter, or **Mercury** <term>Mercury: In alchemy, this is not just the metal, but the universal "First Matter" or life-spirit that initiates growth and transformation.</term> that moves toward growth, extracting the first matter of the particular form from the shaper, and it is considered in three ways. First, as a passive subject that undergoes motion under the artist’s stimulation through the required means; from the operations of all these, heaven arises from its own matter. Second, it is considered as any sick body that receives the form of the medicines, just as elementary things receive a vegetable form. Third, it is considered as the matter of the shaper, like the first matter subjected to the actions of heaven; for it holds the power of form in another way, as will be seen below. By this reasoning, **heaven** <term>Heaven (Cœlum): In an alchemical context, this refers to the most refined, volatile essence of a substance, which acts as an active, "celestial" force upon denser matter.</term>, which is the subject of the actions of those forms by which it turns into a white or red **tincture** <term>Tincture: A highly concentrated alchemical substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" other materials into gold or medicine.</term>, can also be said to have the nature of matter, since by its action it moves the forms of the shapers toward the perfect or most perfect medicines—which will also be heard more extensively below. From this, the best knowledge of our chaos is obtained, since one and the same substance, though by different reasonings, relates to another substance passively, and to the same substance actively, and vice versa. Very few until now have had knowledge of the spagyric matter from which the **spagyric heaven** arises. For one must have a concept of the simple...

...and of the compound reduced to simplicity through alteration, mixing, and so forth. Now, the **Form** of things is the generative power by which each thing is able to produce its like: for instance, the form of a man lies hidden within a man and not in another, the form of a tree in a tree, and likewise the form of a metal within a metal. Raw matter <note>original: "Cruda," referring to unrefined starting materials</note> must not enter the work, but should be emptied through **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: In alchemy, heating a substance until it vaporizes, then collecting the purified solid that deposits on the cool sides of the vessel.</term> to the sides of the sublimatory vessel, so that it may be free from its empty and superfluous earth. 

In this work, Form is considered in two ways: first, as the directing cause of the means of this art through the intellect. Under this governance, the perfect and most perfect medicines come forth into the light; they are led according to the manner of "intellectual means," which act like sensory instruments by which the artifice is brought to perfection. The artist of this work is said to be a "similar form." From this, it is clear that these causative means have the greatest harmony with natural things. 

Secondly, we consider **Form** as the agent that acts upon matter to form perfection, either toward the **white** <gloss>Albedo</gloss> or toward the **red** <gloss>Rubedo</gloss>. By the power of this form, these medicines transmute any other external forms of lesser ability into their own likeness. 

Neither of the two forms we have mentioned can fulfill the mastery <note>original: "magisterium," the completion of the alchemical Great Work</note> on their own; rather, they are like the male from whom the seed is cast into the belly and the **womb of our heaven**. 

Furthermore, **Heaven** is our **Mercury**, possessing a celestial color to signify that he is of a heavenly nature. For this reason, he is called "intellectual" because of his incorruptibility, being understood in the same way as heaven itself—like a man who is both sensory and intellectual. He possesses within himself the property of an incorruptible spirit, which is like a soul containing the conditions of a body, since it generates and produces seed from itself like a female. In this way, it differs from other substances <note>original: "magisterijs"</note> that enter this work. 

Because Mercury is perceived by the senses, he is called "sensory." Here, as the moving cause, he draws out the potential existing in either of the formative states into the actual state of Red or White. He carries this potential in his womb no differently than a wife carries an infant conceived by her husband. From this, it can be gathered that our "heaven" acts upon both forms; in the heaven of these forms and of all things hidden within them, it manifests the transition from potentiality to actual existence. 

For within it consists the power of both generating and nourishing, just as in the **menstrual blood** <term>Menstruum: In alchemy, this does not refer to literal blood, but to a universal solvent or "mother-liquid" that dissolves and nourishes the base matter.</term> of the male-female <note>original: "masculini feminis," likely referring to the alchemical hermaphrodite or Rebis, symbolizing the union of opposites</note>. For this reason, it is called the "menstruum" in this art, and is called "heaven" by reason of its motion. 

Indeed, just as the heaven above promotes universal form, prime matter, and the elements—as well as the species, composite elements, and individual things—our heaven also moves our forms toward the four elements, and thereafter toward the perfect and more-than-perfect medicine. Sometimes it is called **blood**, because it is nutritive; by it, the aforementioned forms are made to vegetate and grow until they reach their perfection, just as menstrual blood nourishes the embryo from a small...
