struck by any circumstance, were transmuted into true stones. Springs also gush forth in many places which, by a natural property, transform everything cast into them into the hardest stones. Having contemplated these and similar works of nature, wise men learned that similar things could likewise be done by art, provided that a similar order is maintained—the same order that nature teaches through its own instruments. We see this very thing happen in many mountains: that coals are naturally generated from stones by a certain <term>Etnean fire: a reference to volcanic heat, named after Mount Etna</term>, and these coals are very frequently used in blacksmiths' workshops. While this latter transmutation occurs through fire in the earth, the others mentioned above seem to occur through water and air. These, therefore, are the instruments of nature; they themselves act as the matter, while motion acts as the form. What then, if a natural compound of earth is made through fire, and that water through air, and this fire through fire, and that descending air is made through air, and this again through water becomes water, and finally, that water returns through fire into earth: what transmutation, I ask, do you think will come of that? If you were to experience it, you would know. The ignorant common folk do not see these things, for no other reason than that they do not consider the secrets of nature. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of these things along with the commoners and denies what nature places before everyone's eyes, is—no matter how learned or literate he may seem—unworthy of the name of philosopher or <term>physicist: in the 16th-century sense, a "physicus" was a student of "physica" or natural philosophy (the study of the physical world)</term>. From where, I ask, does Physics have its first foundation? Is it from appearance alone, or the manifest surface of natural things? Not at all; rather, it is from the most hidden operations of nature, compared to their most manifest effects. Since nature itself is imperceptible to all the senses, so too are all its operations. Who, I ask, has ever seen a tree grow, or the sun and stars move? No one. Yet everyone notices that they have grown and that the stars have moved over intervals of time. In the study of nature, therefore, there is a need for the mind above all, more than for the eyes or other senses. Although these senses serve us as indicators so that we may progress further, otherwise there would be no difference between a philosopher and a peasant.

But to return to our purpose: the **Ladder of Transmutation** has seven principal steps, which are: **Calcination, Sublimation, Solution, Putrefaction, Distillation, Coagulation,** and **Tincture**. Under **Calcination** are contained these specific branches: **Reverberation**, **Cementation**, and likewise **Incineration**. By all these operations, all things are turned into <term>lime: "calx," the powdery residue left after heating a substance</term> or into ashes. In the first step of transmutation, therefore, <term>elementated natural bodies: physical objects composed of the four elements</term> are converted into earth, using a moderate fire as the instrument. In this place, the difference between material elements and instrumental elements (which were mentioned in passing) must be noted above all. For the latter are external, while the former are internal. Once the first operation is completed—whether through calcination, reverberation, cementation, or incineration—

-># ON TRANSMUTATION<-
<meta>catchword: gillo.</meta>

[calcinatio]n; next in the order of preparations follows <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then collecting the purified solid that forms upon cooling</term>, by which the earth, already calcined, is converted either into water or into air, according to the nature and property of the thing to be converted. For the elevation of volatile parts from the fixed parts is most suitable for dry substances; therefore, sublimation is appropriate for things of that condition. If, however, a separation of moist things must be done, such as those from plants or animals, then their sublimation belongs to the fifth grade, namely, <term>distillation</term>. But because in this place we are dealing chiefly with dry things, such as metals and minerals, a similar order fitting for these must be observed. 

Furthermore, the volatile part that has been sublimated—not unlike what happens in moist substances—through <term>cohobations: the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid residue to concentrate its properties</term> (that is, the re-joining of separated parts and repeated or iterated separations), reaches such a state of <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> that they remain below with the fixed parts and no longer ascend, but instead exist in the form of an oil or a stone. For through the air, by means of <term>solution</term>, they pass into an oil, while by <term>coagulation</term> through fire, they pass into a stone. An example is any metal acted upon by <term>ammoniac salt: a mineral salt (ammonium chloride) used as a reagent</term> in sublimation; for by successive stages, it turns to stone. By this operation of sublimation, many corrosive things become sweet or mild, and vice versa—though usually with the addition of another substance. Likewise, many sharp things become sweet, and conversely, sweet things become sour; some do so by themselves, others when prepared with additional substances in this manner.

After the second stage, the third grade follows: namely, <term>solution</term>, and this is twofold—one of cold, the other of heat. Salts, corrosives, and any calcined things are coagulated by fire, but are finally resolved into liquor, water, or oil by the cold of the air, when placed in a damp place like a cellar, or in the air upon a marble stone or glass. However, fatty and sulfurous things are resolved by the heat of fire. In summary: what is dissolved by the heat of fire is eventually coagulated by the cold of the air; conversely, what is dissolved by the cold of the air is coagulated by the heat of fire. 

Note the reasoning by which we say the air is cold, which seems to conflict somewhat with the opinion of several philosophers; for they maintain that air is hot and moist. But they do not consider what air is composed of. Is it not made of fire and water? <note>The author is challenging the traditional Aristotelian view that air is an elemental "simple" body; he argues it is a composite of Fire (heat/dryness) and Water (cold/moisture).</note> For what else is air but water resolved by fire? Therefore, it sometimes borrows heat and dryness from one of its parts (namely fire), and from the other part it borrows coldness and the moisture of its water. For there are only two principal qualities; the other two are their servants. For nothing is naturally hot that is not also necessarily dry by nature; likewise, nothing is cold that is not, for that reason, moist. Whatever else happens to them, judge it to occur not by nature, but by accident. It is no different with the elements: fire and water hold the primary place, while the earth borrows its coldness from its companion, water, and the dryness it possesses from fire. By itself, however, the earth is never hot, nor moist, nor even cold or dry, but instead seems to serve its two other principles just as wax serves any [form...]

<sig>Ii 2</sig>

[se]al. Likewise, air is to be judged in the same way: for it receives heat and dryness from its father, namely from fire, and coldness and moisture from its mother, water. Thus they are generated as if from their parents, fire and water: the male air—or rather, a <term>hermaphrodite</term> <note>Alchemists often viewed air as possessing both active/male and passive/female qualities</note>—and the female earth. So much for the natural instruments and matter.

The fourth grade is **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactio"; the process of decay or breaking down a substance to its base state</note>. Because of its excellence, this stage ought by right to hold the first place, were it not that such an inversion would conflict with the true order and the **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"</note> which is hidden from many in this place and revealed to very few. Therefore, the established series must remain and not be varied, any more than the links in a chain; if a single link were to fail, the captive held by them would escape.

The property of putrefaction is such that, by consuming the old nature of things, it introduces a new one and occasionally produces the fruit of a different generation. For all living things die through corruption; once dead, they putrefy, and through the transformation of generation, they acquire life once again. Even corrosive spirits become sweet and mild through it, all colors are changed into others, and the pure is separated from the impure as the latter settles at the bottom. The parts of putrefaction are **digestion** and **circulation**.

The fifth grade is **distillation**, which is nothing other than the separation of the moist from the dry, and the thin from the thick. Its components are **ascension** <note>rising as vapor</note>, **washing**, **imbibition** <note>soaking</note>, **cohobation**, and **fixation**. **Cohobation**, which concludes the individual steps, is the repeated pouring and distilling of the distilled liquid back onto its own dregs <note>original: "faeces"</note>. Just as <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid or a sulfate mineral</note> is fixed through cohobations by its own water, it is then called **sugar alum** <note>original: "alumen saccarinum"</note>. When this is dissolved into a liquid, putrefied for a month, and then distilled, it yields a water as sweet as sugar. This is a secret medicine, excellent above many others for extinguishing the **microcosmic fire** <note>In alchemical medicine, this refers to internal fevers or inflammations within the human body, the "microcosm"</note> that afflicts metal miners, which is discussed more fully in the book on the diseases of mineral miners. In the same way, any other minerals or watery substances, such as **saltpeter** <note>original: "sal nitrum"</note>, can be fixed by cohobations.

The sixth grade is **coagulation**, which—like its opposite, solution—is twofold: of cold and of heat, which is to say, of air and of fire. Again, each type of coagulation is twofold; there are two from cold and just as many from heat. The first kind of cold coagulation occurs from common air outside of fire. The second occurs from the upper firmament by means of the **winter stone** <note>likely referring to the power of frost or freezing</note>, which congeals all waters into snow and ice. However, the first coagulation of heat is produced by industry in the art [of alchemy], following the observed gradations of fire, and this is "fixed." The other coagulations from cold are not fixed in alchemy. The second coagulation of heat is caused by the **Etnaean** <note>Volcanic or subterranean heat, named after Mount Etna</note> and mineral fire beneath the earth and under mountains, graded by the natural **Archeus** <note>The "Archeus" was considered the "internal chemist" or vital force of nature that directs the growth of minerals</note> of the earth. The fire that is excited and graded through alchemy for coagulation is not at all dissimilar to this. Whatever is coagulated by this Etnaean fire remains fixed.

...as can be seen from metals and minerals, each of which consists, from the beginning, of a certain mucilaginous matter, coagulated in the mountains into stones, metals, marcasites, salts, etc., by means of the Etnean fire <note>original: "Ætneum ignem"; referring to the geothermal or volcanic heat within the earth</note> and the **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>The 'inner craftsman' or vital force that Paracelsus believed directed the growth and formation of all natural things</note>, the natural craftsman of the earth. 

The seventh and final step of the scale of transmutation is the **Tincture** <note>original: "Tinctura"; the ultimate alchemical agent capable of transforming base metals into gold or curing all human illnesses</note>, the most noble medicine produced from all the Chemical arts. By this tincture, any metallic bodies—and human ones as well—are transformed into a substance far better, more noble, and more excellent than they were previously by nature, and are brought to the highest degree of health, color, and perfection, into a more powerful and excellent nature. There are various species of such tinctures, which are not to be recounted in this place. 

Bodies must first be removed from their metallic coagulation by fire and liquefied; otherwise they do not receive the active tincture unless they have been unlocked and opened. Furthermore, any tinctures of metals ought to be of a very **fixed** substance, and of an easily fusible and incombustible nature, so that when placed upon a glowing metal plate they flow immediately like wax and penetrate the metal without smoke more quickly than oil is seen to enter paper or water a sponge; and they should dye it into a white or red color that remains permanent in the fire and stands up to any examination. 

Therefore, in the first step of **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance until it is reduced to powder</note>, once the metals are reduced to **alcohol** <term>alcohol</term> <note>In early chemistry, this term referred to an extremely fine, impalpable powder, rather than a liquid spirit</note>, they acquire easy liquefaction—namely in the second step of **solution**. Thereafter, through **putrefaction** and **distillation**, their tinctures must be fixed, made incombustible, and unvarying in color. To recover or preserve the health of human bodies through restoration and renewal, these tinctures should be extracted from gold, pearls <note>original: "unionibus"; refers to large, fine pearls</note>, antimony, sulfur, vitriol, and similar substances. 

Various subjects of fires also have various operations in alchemy: one is the flame of wood, which they call **living fire**, by which the bodies of all metals or others are calcined and reverberated. Another is the continuous heat of a candle or lamp, by which volatile substances are **fixed**. Another is the heat of coals, by which bodies are **cemented**, colored, and purged of their dross; likewise gold and silver are brought to a higher degree of purity, **Venus** <note>original: "Venus"; the alchemical name for copper</note> is whitened, and in short, all metals are renewed. Another operation belongs to the glowing iron plate, upon which the testing of tinctures is performed; another to heat excited by fire through the medium of iron filings; another in ashes; another likewise in sand; and another in the **Bath of the Sea** or of **Mary** <term>Balneum Mariae</term> <note>a water bath or bain-marie, providing gentle, indirect heat</note> (as they call it), by which various distillations, sublimations, and coagulations are performed. There is also the **Bath of Dew**, which I have elsewhere called the "vaporous" bath, by which many solutions of physical things are made. Another is the **Horse's Belly** <term>Venter Equinus</term> <note>a heap of fermenting horse manure used to provide a gentle, steady heat for digestion processes</note>, in which the principal putrefactions and digestions take place. Finally, the **invisible fire** has an operation far different from all these; that is, the fire of the sun’s rays, which becomes evident through its operations by means of a mirror or crystal, and about which the ancients [did] not

By this fire, the **three principles** <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Sulfur (soul), Mercury (spirit), and Salt (body)</note> of every thing can be separated upon a wooden table without fear of flaming or burning, and any metals can be liquefied without visible fire, and even combustible things can be reduced to coals and ashes. ## *On the simple fire of the Chemists.*

### CHAPTER II.

After we have spoken enough to the ingenious regarding the craft of transmutations through the scale and its degrees, it will be necessary—in order to preserve the order described above—to present the instruments to the initiates before the matter itself, lest the unrefined and unskilled move their foot before their hand. Therefore, let those who lack the eye of the mind not approach here, nor those whose hands cannot serve it: for the foot and the fleshy eye, without a sound and incorrupt mind, are utterly useless. 

The most powerful and most required instrument is fire, which indeed lives by its own nature and is vivified by no other fire. From this it also follows that it has the power and strength to vivify any other fire hidden within things. Just as the **Sun** was created by God in this world to awaken the resting fire in all things, and to kindle with its own fire the spheres of the **Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn** <note>In alchemy, these planets correspond to the seven metals: Silver, Quicksilver, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead</note>, and the rest of the stars—which otherwise have no fire of their own, nor can they provide any from themselves—for they are dead in themselves, yet kindled by solar fire, they live and perform their own operations according to the property of each. 

But the Sun receives the light and life (which is fire) that it possesses from no other star; it is ruled only by God its creator, so that it may always and equally burn and shine in itself, illuminating every other natural light. Not otherwise in the <term>spagyric</term> <note>original: "spagirica"; the alchemical practice of separating and then recombining the components of substances to reach a higher state of purity</note> art is the <term>fire of the athanor</term> <note>original: "ignis athanoris"; a furnace designed to maintain a constant, uniform heat over a long period, often by means of a self-feeding fuel hopper</note> to be judged, as well as the secret furnace of the philosophers, which kindles the furnace, the sphere of the vessel, and the fire of the matter, just as the sun is seen to operate in the whole world, without which nothing at all can be generated. Likewise, in the art nothing is accomplished without this **simple fire**, since it is the most powerful part and operation of this craft, embracing all others in itself, while it is encompassed by none. It exists by itself, not needing others, but all other operations that are performed need this simple fire, from which they receive life together with the matter itself,

Elsewhere, Paracelsus speaks concerning simple fire in this manner. "This," he says, "is the most celebrated opinion of the Philosophers: Fire and **azoth** <note>original: *azot*; the universal solvent or essential "mercury" of the philosophers</note> are sufficient for you, for fire alone is the whole work and the entire art." Furthermore, as many as construct their fire simply with coals are in error, whether they keep the vessel in the fire or above it. Some have tried the fire of horse manure <note>original: *fimi equini*; manure was frequently used in alchemy to provide a gentle, steady heat through fermentation</note> in vain. By the fire of coals, they sublimated the matter directly without a medium, and yet did not dissolve it. Others excited heat with their lamps, asserting this to be the secret fire of the philosophers for fabricating their **Stone**. Some placed it in a bath, and this in heaps of ants; others in juniper ashes; some sought this fire in **quicklime** <note>calcium oxide, which generates heat when wet</note>, in **tartar**, **vitriol**, **nitre**, and similar things. Others used **burning water** <term>burning water: *aqua ardente*, usually referring to distilled alcohol or strong spirits</term>, as Thomas Aquinas falsely speaks regarding this fire, saying that God and His Angels cannot be without it, but use it daily. What blasphemy is this? Is it not a most manifest lie that God cannot be without the elementary fire of burning water—indeed, without all His creatures whenever He wishes? All heats excited by the means just mentioned are utterly useless for our work. See that you are not seduced even by **Arnaldo de Villanova**, who wrote concerning the fire of coals, for he himself will deceive you by this very thing. **Almadir** says that the invisible rays of our fire alone are sufficient. Another brings forth an example, that celestial heat by its reflections is most effective for the coagulation and perfection of **Mercury** by its continued motion. Again, the same says: "Make," he says, "a fire that is vaporous, digesting, and cooking, continuous; yet not flying or boiling, but altering and penetrating. I have now truly told you every way of exciting the heat of fire; if you are a true philosopher, you will understand well." Thus he speaks. **Salmanazar** says: "Our fire is a corrosive fire, which draws a mist and a cloud over our vessel, in which cloud the rays of this fire are hidden; if this dew of chaos and the moisture of the cloud are lacking, an error has been committed." Again, **Almadir** says, "unless the fire warms our **Sun** <note>gold or the essential male principle</note> with its moisture by the 'manure of the mountain' <note>likely a metaphor for a specific mineral or a steady heating method</note> with a tempered ascent, we shall not be participants in either the white or the red Stone." All these things demonstrate clearly enough to us the hidden fire of the wise. In summary, this is the material of our fire: namely, that it be kindled by the quiet spirit of sensible fire, which pushes upward like a heated **chaos** <note>a state of gaseous or unformed matter</note> from the opposite side and above our philosophical matter; this heat, spreading above our vessel for the movement of perfect generation, should press on constantly without intermission and indeed in a tempered way.

### On the Manifold Philosophical Fire.

## CHAPTER III.

Now that we have spoken of simple fire, it seems fitting to bring forward something concerning the manifold fire, more copiously and clearly than before; for we touched upon this latter kind briefly <note>original: *tanquam per transennam*; literally "as if through a lattice," meaning in a cursory or passing manner</note>. This fire is manifold, and it varies according to the diversity of the substance into which it flows, and through which it is later excited in other substances. Examples include the fire of ashes, of sand, of the water-bath <note>the *balneum Mariae*, or bain-marie</note>, of metal filings, and so on. These possess a mediated heat, which flows from an immediate source into the material of the instrument, and from there into the matter subjected to the art.

Indeed, in this manifold fire lies the difference of the individual <note>original: *suppositi*; the underlying individual thing or person</note>. This is the reason why nothing in the nature of things can be seen to be similar in all ways and through all things to any other, even if both belong to the same species, or are even members of the same individual. For example, one type of metallic nature produces gold, another generates silver; one brings forth lead <note>original: *saturneum*; associated with the planet Saturn</note>, another copper <note>original: *venereum*; associated with Venus</note>, another iron <note>original: *martium*; associated with Mars</note>, and so forth. Likewise, any of these varies according to the difference of the place from which it was dug and born. Not even two human beings, nor two limbs of one body, nor two leaves of the same tree are found to be identical; so it is with the rest.

This dissimilarity does not arise from the first fire of the creatures, but from the various governance of the elements through the planets, and not through the Sun alone. For at every moment, the heat in the elements is changed by this arrangement, and simultaneously the form of things decomposed is changed by the compounds, and not by the simple elements. Where the mixture of elements is not so great, **Gold** <note>represented by the Sun</note> is generated; where it is a little greater and more impure, **Silver** <note>represented by the Moon</note> is born; likewise **Copper** comes from a more imperfect mixture. Thus, according to the changes in the mixtures, the ore of each metal is unlike any other, nor do their spirits agree with one another in all respects. If they were generated from simple fire alone, without the intervention of manifold fire, no distinction of properties or forms could be made—not only in metals, but in all other creatures. As for why no more than seven in number come into use—of which six are solid and the seventh is fluid and rare <note>referring to Mercury/Quicksilver</note>—this has its own reasoning in "attained philosophy" <note>esoteric wisdom</note> and not in alchemy; therefore, these reasons are reserved for their proper place, lest we wander from our purpose. Let this suffice for what has been said concerning manifold philosophical fire, derived from physical reasoning.

### On the Visible and Local Instruments, and First Concerning the Spagyric Womb.

## CHAPTER IV.

Before we come to the matter itself, it seemed best to explain each instrument in order—both the active and the local ones—which are necessary for this art. We have said that the first active instrument is fire; the local one, truly

Indeed, the first [requirement] is the furnace, called by the alchemical name <term>Athanor</term> <note>original: *Athanor chemico nomine*; derived from the Arabic *al-tannūr*, meaning "the oven," this was a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a steady, long-lasting heat</note> by the ancients; in <term>spagyric</term> <note>the Paracelsian art of separating and recombining substances to create medicine</note> generation, this performs the role of the womb. Even if <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>the legendary "thrice-great" founder of the hermetic and alchemical tradition</note> was not the inventor of this art, he deserves to be called its restorer, no less than <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine</note> is for spagyric medicine. Hermes asserts that this spagyric work—upon which human philosophy places its final hand—took its beginning from the meditative contemplation of the "greater world" <note>the macrocosm or universe</note>, suggesting that the spagyric Athanor ought to be built in imitation of heaven and earth. 

I shall not be at all reluctant to briefly examine this comparison for the sake of exercising your wits, so that I might be of use to my readers. No physicist will deny that the Sun generates a Sun similar to itself, but not everyone will admit that this offspring exists in the center—especially those disciples of philosophers who have no knowledge of the <term>Etnean fire</term> <note>referring to Mount Etna; a metaphor for the subterranean, volcanic fire of the earth</note> other than what they have seen with the "eye of the flesh" <note>original: *oculo carneo*; meaning purely physical, non-spiritual observation</note>, like peasants. This earthly Sun, belonging to the lower or elemental machine, is ignited by the fire of the superior Sun. In no different a way is the center of our matter ignited by the center of our world (or Athanor)—which is fire—performing the role of the natural Sun in this part through a shared likeness. 

Who does not see (I ask you, brothers) that the form of the entire created world bears a resemblance to a furnace? Or, to speak more reverently, to the "matrix of the womb" containing the elements, in which the seeds of the Sun and Moon <note>symbolizing gold and silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of alchemy</note>, sent down through the various influences of the stars, are broken down, cooked, and digested into the generation of all things? But these things are clearly manifest even to children, let alone to philosophers; therefore, we shall not press the point further. 

Let us come, then, to the construction of our Athanor. First, let a furnace be built with a height of six <term>spans</term> <note>original: *spithamarum*; a span is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the pinky, roughly 9 inches or 23 cm. This furnace would be about 4.5 feet tall</note>, and an internal round width of one span. It should be slightly wider at the bottom than at the top on the inside, and polished smooth, so that the coals thrown in do not get stuck on rough patches but can easily descend while they are burned below near the <term>grate</term> <note>original: *craticulam*</note>. To balance this, there should be several holes, to which two or three side-furnaces (or "womb-furnaces") correspond—or if you wish, only one. The width of these little doors should be four fingers, and those broad ones. To each small furnace, let a copper kettle with water be fitted; let the rest be enclosed like an egg in a hen, or glass in its womb, according to the industry of the <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterij*; the professional skill or the Great Work itself</note>. 

Next, when it is time to work and everything has been prepared with the greatest diligence, let the tower be filled to the top with charcoal broken to the size of a walnut (or a little larger). Let them be lit below at the little doors. The tower must be blocked at the top, lest the coals ignited in the middle or at the top stir up a heat that destroys the entire work and burns everything down at once. When the heat seems to exceed what is right, it can be restrained by placing a small brick near the opening; conversely, if it is too weak, the coals may be stirred beneath the grate with a small iron rod. But the fire will be more aptly moderated by <term>registers</term> <note>dampers or vents used to control airflow</note>, which they call "rudders." Individual [details] are taught by...

...its use in the preparations of those things that are necessary, before that point is reached. Therefore, once the fire has been moderated to a just and equal proportion—as nature herself teaches in all things—the heat will excite the <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermentum*; in alchemy, a substance that triggers a transformation in the "base" matter, similar to how yeast makes bread rise</note>, and thereafter this heat excites the matter hidden within the <term>egg</term> <note>original: *ovo*; referring to the "Philosopher's Egg," a hermetically sealed glass vessel used for long digestions</note>. Hence, just as the sun shines in the "greater world" <note>the macrocosm or universe</note>, illuminating and giving life to all the other stars and elements, so too does the <term>spagyric fire</term> <note>alchemical fire produced through chemistry</note> illuminate its <term>athanor</term> <note>the self-feeding furnace</note> and all its instruments, warming also the <term>water-bath</term> <note>original: *maris balneum* or *bain-marie*; a vessel of hot water used to provide gentle, even heat</note>, just as a hen hatches her living egg. 

But I hear a giant <note>a metaphor for a prominent or prideful critic</note> like a roaring lion against the furnace, seeking which Paracelsus he might devour. "Behold," he says, "how he contradicts himself! Very recently he strictly forbade the building of a fire with charcoal; yet now he teaches that the use of charcoal is most vital for this art of his." You have touched upon the point, of course, but you have judged the writings of Paracelsus to be at war with themselves no better than you have judged anything else. It is your other eye that you must open, lest you appear as a one-eyed man, or one altogether blind, who has presumed to judge colors until now. Did you not see what that little phrase—"simply and without a medium"—added to the prohibition of charcoal, actually means? <note>Paracelsus likely meant that charcoal should not touch the vessel directly or be used without a regulating "medium" like sand or water to distribute the heat</note> Do you see how Paracelsus, though dead, is still able to respond to you and other slanderers through his living writings, and say: "You who judge me to be in error, you yourself err, being judged by your own words"? 

Have I not often warned you, and envious men like you, throughout almost all my writings, not to pass over a single little word without "chewing" it properly? Otherwise, it would happen to you giants, when facing my <term>pygmy homunculus</term> <note>a "little man"; here Paracelsus uses it as a self-deprecating term or a reference to his controversial theories on artificial life to mock the "giant" critic</note>, what once happened to Goliath with the boy David. Beware, I say, again and again, lest you fall by this stone of ours—this great mystery—and descend with it into the pits where you fruitlessly try to banish me. 

This is what Paracelsus seems to thunder from his tomb. Brothers, we must not speak of the dead with such unfairness; indeed, not even of those who served poorly. Let all remain in their rest, for each man's deeds await him. It is easy to find fault, but to avoid judgment today is difficult, and in the end, impossible. What are you that I am not? What am I that you are not? Again, what can happen to both of us that cannot happen to the other—namely, to err? We are all humans, to whom error happens more than to irrational beasts, which are moved by instinct alone. I confess there is error in many things; you err, and it is your place to admit it, and mine to warn, not to judge. Therefore, let it be your duty, as it is mine, not to publicly expose the failures of brothers out of envy, but first to warn them with modesty according to the discipline of true philosophy. Otherwise, neither you, nor he, nor I are worthy of the name of philosophy if we act otherwise. But this philosophical discipline is (alas!) attacked even by the most learned; the dogma of the pagan philosophers has become so celebrated among them in these times that they do not see that all of this, such as it is...

externally and internally, they pretend to seek nothing but the pure ambition for honors; this was the chief goal of their study and labors. From this, it happens that everyone tries to prepare a reputation for themselves through the undermining or blackening of another. But these wretched people do not consider that no injury can be done so great that a far greater one does not await them—provided, however, that we are all equally foolish, and no one is found who wishes to be wise in due measure. Many are wise more than enough, or most are too little so, while almost no one keeps to the middle ground. Let us see to it, therefore, lest the wisdom we claim for ourselves is transformed, by the just judgment of God, into manifest foolishness even in this age, and that by our own effort. If, therefore, any error has been made by us, and our own conscience accuses us of having provided a scandal to others that leads to deception, let us retract it without shame before God and men, both in our writings and in our deeds. As we said before, the common error of men is recognized by the wisest, but not by the dull and foolish, for whom every delirium is the true path, and vice-versa. But let us dismiss the mindless and deal more extensively with the honest and the intelligent. Having spoken of the furnace or <term>athanor</term> <note>a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant heat for long periods</note>, let us now hear something concerning the vessel.

### *Concerning the second local instrument of the spagyrics, the matrix or philosophical egg.*

### CHAPTER V.

Many philosophers, presuming too much of themselves, have wrongly understood the occult and secret <term>vessel of the philosophers</term> <note>original: *vas philosophorum*; the specialized container used for the alchemical transformation</note>. They have understood even worse what Aristotle the Alchemist (not that Greek academic) says when he speaks of the matter needing to be cooked in a triple vessel. Likewise, they very poorly understand what is said by another: that the matter in its first separation and first degree requires a metallic vessel; in the second degree of coagulation and the "whitening" of its earth, a glass vessel; and in the third degree, which is that of <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, an earthen vessel. Nevertheless, through all these descriptions, they actually mean only one single vessel used in all operations, right up to the perfection of the <term>red stone</term> <note>original: *rubei lapidis*; the final stage of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting metals into gold</note>. 

Since, therefore, our matter is our root for both the white and the red, our vessel must necessarily be of such a form that the matter within it can be governed by the <term>celestial bodies</term>. For the invisible celestial influences and the impressions of the stars are primary and necessary to the work; otherwise, it would be impossible to complete the invincible Oriental, Persian, Chaldean, and Egyptian stone by any other means. Through this vessel, <term>Anaxagoras</term> <note>a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who famously suggested that the sun was a hot stone and predicted the fall of meteorites</note> recognized the powers of the entire firmament and prophesied that a great stone would descend from heaven to the earth, which indeed happened after his death. To the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>practitioners of Kabbalah, a form of Jewish mysticism often integrated into Renaissance alchemy</note> especially, our vessel is most known, according to a truly geometric proportion and measure, and from a certain <term>squaring of the circle</term> <note>original: *circuli quadratura*; a mathematical impossibility used here as a metaphor for divine perfection and the union of opposites</note>.

must be constructed in such a way that the spirit and soul of our matter, separated from its body, can elevate themselves with it according to the height of its heaven. If the vessel should be narrower, wider, higher, or lower than is proper for what the dominant and working spirits and soul require, the heat of our secret <term>philosophical fire</term> <note>original: "ignis philosophici"; a specialized, steady heat used in alchemical digestion, often distinct from common fire</note> (which is indeed most sharp) will urge the matter, once it has been too violently excited, toward an excessive operation, so that sometimes the vessel may shatter into a thousand pieces, not without danger to the body and life of the operator. Conversely, if the vessel is more spacious than the heat is able to work upon the matter according to due proportion, the work will also be void and fruitlless. For this reason, our philosophical vessel must be fabricated with the highest diligence and industry. Truly, those alone understand what the material of our vessel consists of who, in the first <term>solution</term> <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note> of our fixed and perfect matter, have brought it back into its first essence—concerning which, enough has been said. The operator should also most diligently note what the matter sets aside and rejects from itself in the first solution. The method for describing this vessel is difficult; yet its form must be such as nature itself demands: it must be sought and investigated from one thing and another. In short, it must be such that from the height of the <term>philosophical heaven</term> <note>the upper portion of the glass vessel where vapors condense</note> elevated from the <term>philosophical earth</term> <note>the solid matter at the bottom of the vessel</note>, it can act upon the fruit of its own earthly body. Let it certainly have this form so that the separation and purification of the elements can occur when the fire drives one from the other, and so that each may occupy its own place in which it dwells. Thus, the <term>Sun</term> <note>representing Gold</note> and the other <term>planets</term> <note>representing the other metals</note> may exercise their operations around the elemental earth, and their circuits may not be hindered or agitated by a swifter motion.

In accordance with all these things that have been said, it is necessary that it has a just proportion of roundness and height. Those things which truly contribute to the first cleansing of mineral bodies are melting vessels <note>original: "vasa fusoria"; crucibles</note>, tongs, bellows, <term>cupels</term> <note>porous ceramic bowls used to separate precious metals from lead</note>, tests, cementing vessels, ash-vessels, <term>cucurbits</term> <note>the lower part of a still, shaped like a gourd</note>, bottles for <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> and <term>aqua regia</term> <note>a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, as well as those things necessary for the <term>projection</term> <note>the final stage of transmutation where the philosopher's stone is added to base metal</note> in the final work. Furthermore, concerning the vessel for this work, Paracelsus speaks in another place in this manner: For this art, it is necessary that you have a glass rightly and justly proportioned; for if it is more spacious than is right, the matter—that is, the moisture—is spread out so that nothing is born from it; if, however, it is narrower or more compressed, the germ will be suffocated, so that it can produce no fruit. This is evident from the example of that which is sown under shade or a roof, from which nothing good or fruitful is produced. Therefore, it is of great importance to turn one's mind to this glass: for an error committed through it or in it is not easily corrected; indeed, because of its hindrance, the work is not brought to its desired end. Therefore, for two ounces of matter, take two and a half ounces of glass or of the <term>philosophical egg</term> <note>the sealed glass vessel used for the "Great Work"</note>, which is to say, that which reflects this weight; however, account must be taken of the proper thickness of the glass. If these things are observed, an error is not easily committed in this part.

Thus, let what has been said concerning local instruments suffice for now.

### *Concerning the Subject or Philosophical Matter in General.*

### CHAPTER VI.

**P**reviously, we have spoken clearly enough about what the chemical instruments are; now, however, listen to what matter the **spagyrists** <note>original: "spagiri"; alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances to create medicines</note> have chosen for beginning their work: After vegetables have been **mortified** <note>original: "mortificata"; the process of decaying or "killing" a substance to release its inner essence</note>, through the meeting of two minerals—namely, sulphur and salt—they are transmuted into a mineral nature, so that from there, at last, perfect minerals result. For in the mineral caverns of the earth, certain vegetables are found which, by the long success of time and continuous heat, have cast off their vegetable nature of sulphur and put on a mineral one. This happens most especially where the proper nourishment is taken away from such vegetables, so that they are afterwards compelled to take their sustenance from the sulphurs and salts of the earth for so long until that which was previously a vegetable passes into a perfect mineral. And from this mineral condition, a certain perfect metallic essence sometimes arises, and that by progress from one degree to another. But let us return to the **philosopher's stone** <note>original: "lapidem philosophorum"</note>, the matter of which is most difficult to find and no less difficult to understand. The method of investigation for this, as for any other thing, and the most certain rule for what they contain and what they are worth, is the diligent examination of their root and seed, by which one arrives at a knowledge of the materials. To this end, the highly necessary consideration of principles contributes much: namely, by what path or by what means nature first arrived from imperfection to the end of perfection. For this consideration, it is primarily useful to hold as a proven fact that whatever things were created by nature were composed of the three first principles—namely, natural **Mercury**, **Sulphur**, and **Salt**—mixed into one, so that in some they are volatile, but in others fixed. For as often as the bodily salt is mixed into one body with the spiritual Mercury and the animated Sulphur, then at last nature begins to work in subterranean places (which it holds in place of its own vessels) through a separating fire, by which the thick and impure sulphur may be separated from the pure, and the salt of the earth may be segregated, as well as the clouds from the Mercury; those prior parts having been preserved, nature cooks them again together into one constant **geogamic** body <term>geogamic</term> <note>original: "geogamicum"; from the Greek for "earth-marriage," referring to a substance born from the union of elements within the earth</note>. This operation is indeed regarded by the Magi as a mixture and conjunction through the union of three: namely, body, soul, and spirit. Once this union is fulfilled, a pure Mercury results therefrom, which, if it should flow through subterranean passages and their veins and encounter **cahoic sulphur** <term>cahoic sulphur</term> <note>original: "cahoico sulphuri"; likely derived from "chaos," referring to the crude, unformed mineral matter found in the deep earth</note>, is by this very thing coagulated according to the condition of the sulphur. It is, however, still volatile, so that it is scarcely cooked into a metal until a hundred years later. From this source arose the common saying: namely, that Mercury and sulphur are the matter of metals, as is also evident from the reports of mineral miners. Yet, it is neither common Mercury nor common sulphur...

...are the matter of metals, but the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"; in alchemy, this refers to the principle of fluidity and transformation, not just the liquid metal</note> and **Sulphur** <note>original: "sulphur"; the principle of combustibility and "soul"</note> of the philosophers are incorporated and innate within the perfect metals and their forms, so that they may never flee from the fire, nor be corrupted by the destructive force of the elements. Certainly, through the dissolution of such a natural mixture, our Mercury is tamed, as the **spagyric** <note>original: "spagirici"; practitioners who separate and recombine substances</note> philosophers say. Under this form of words, therefore, our Mercury is to be drawn forth from the perfect bodies and the powers of the earthly planets. This is also what **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> asserts in these words: *Sol* <note>original: "Sol"; the Sun, representing Gold</note> (he says) and *Luna* <note>original: "Luna"; the Moon, representing Silver</note> are the roots of this art. The **Son of Hanuel** <note>an Arabic alchemical authority, likely Senior Zadith filius Hamuel</note> says that the philosopher's stone is water coagulated, specifically in *Sol* and *Luna*. From this, it is clearer than the sun that the matter of our stone is nothing other than *Sol* and *Luna*. This very point is also confirmed because everything naturally brings forth and generates its own likeness. And just as we know there are two stones—the white and the red—there are also two matters for the stone: *Sol* and *Luna* coupled together in their own marriage, both natural and artificial. And just as we see that a man and a woman cannot generate at all without their own seed, in the same way, our man *Sol* and his woman *Luna* cannot conceive without their own seed and sperm, nor can they attempt anything toward generation. From this, our philosophers concluded that a third thing is necessary: namely, the **animate seed** <note>original: "animatũ semen"; a "living" or "ensouled" seed</note> of both the male and female of the chemists, without which they judged their entire work to be useless and empty. This kind of sperm is Mercury, which, through the natural conjunction of both bodies of *Sol* and *Luna*, receives their nature into itself in union. Only then, and not before, is the work fit for union, entry, and generation, through the masculine and feminine strength and power. Moved by this, our philosophers said that this Mercury is composed of body, spirit, and soul, and that it has assumed the nature and property of all the elements. For this reason, with the strongest wit and intellect, they asserted that their stone is an **animal** <note>original: "animalem"; meaning it possesses "anima" or soul/life, rather than being a literal beast</note> stone, which they also called their **Adam**, who carries his invisible **Eve** hidden in his body from that moment when they were united by the power of the supreme Creator of all. For that reason, it can rightly be said that the Mercury of the philosophers is nothing other than their most hidden, composite Mercury, and not that common kind. Wisely, therefore, they said to the wise: "In Mercury is whatever the wise seek." **Almadir** <note>a medieval alchemical author</note> the philosopher says: We extract our Mercury from one perfect body and two perfect natural conditions incorporated together; this pushes its perfection outward, so that it may resist fire, and by this external perfection, whatever imperfect thing is already enclosed within it is defended from external attacks. Through this passage by the sharpest philosopher, the matter of the stone is understood to be **Adamite** <note>original: "Adamica"; referring to the "First Man" or the primordial, uncorrupted state of matter</note>, the **microcosmic limbus** <note>original: "limbus microcosmicus"; the primordial "soup" or border-state of the human-scale world</note>, and the matter of the philosophers...

...homogeneous and unique. The sayings of these philosophers, of whom we have made mention before, are truly golden and should always be held in the highest esteem, because they contain nothing superfluous and nothing invalid. In summary, therefore, the matter of the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "lapidis philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life</note> is nothing other than a fiery and perfect **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to the "living" spirit or radical moisture of metals, not common quicksilver</note> extracted through nature and art—that is, artificially prepared—and the true **hermaphrodite Adam** <note>original: "hermaphroditus Adam"; a symbol of the "Rebis" or the union of opposites (male/female, sun/moon) in a single substance</note> and the **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmus"; the "little world," implying that the Stone contains the blueprint of the entire universe</note>. Asserting this very thing, that wisest of philosophers, **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>the mythical founder of the Hermetic tradition</note>, called the stone "the orphan." Our Mercury, therefore, is that very one which contains the perfections, powers, and virtues of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"; gold</note> within itself, and which runs through the streets and houses of all the **Planets** <note>referring to the astrological properties and metallic transformations</note>, and in its regeneration has acquired the power of things above and things below. It is also to be compared to their marriage, as is evident from the whiteness and redness gathered together within it at once.

The **Magi** <note>wise men or ancient practitioners of high magic</note>, through their wisdom, affirmed that all creatures are to be brought to a unified substance. They assert that through its cleansings and purifications, this substance ascends to such a degree of subtlety, and to a divine nature and property, that it works wonders. They also considered that it would return to the earth, and through the supreme magical separation, a certain perfect substance would emerge. At last, through many industrious and very long preparations, this substance is raised from vegetable substances into mineral, and from mineral into metallic; and from a perfect metallic substance, it is lifted into a **fifth essence** <note>original: "essentiam quintam"; the Quintessence, a celestial spirit that transcends the four physical elements</note> that is divine and like unto eternity, enclosing within itself the essence of all celestial and terrestrial creatures.

The **Arabs and Greeks**, by denoting meanings through hidden characters and through the hieroglyphic descriptions of the **Persians and Egyptians**, arrived at secret and abstruse mysteries. Once these were attained—partly understood and partly not—they saw certain wonders with their own eyes through experience. But because supernatural things lay hidden more deeply than their grasp could reach, they did not call this secret "super-celestial" (according to the opinion of the Magi), but named it the "secret of the philosophers," and, following the opinion of **Pythagoras**, "their stone."

Whoever attained this stone shadowed it with various enigmatic figures, deceptive likenesses, comparisons, and fictions of words, so that its matter at least would be hidden from posterity, and no knowledge of it—or at least the very minimum—could be had. Many of the ancients revealed this matter and its preparation openly enough, yet they did so in ingenious parables and enigmatic words and figures, so that they might keep the unworthy away from such a great mystery of nature and art alike. Nevertheless, very few—even among those who are fit for this art—have sought the perpetual balsam of nature and the perfect stone, because of the massive labor entangled with difficulty which occurs everywhere during the investigation. Because of this, lazy and idle minds have ceased from the work. The greedy, however, for whom the **hunger** <note>original: "fames"; the catchword at the bottom of the page suggests the sentence continues "hunger for gold..."</note> [for gold...]

# OF METALS
<meta>catchword: hunger</meta>

Hunger and a desire for even the most base silver <note>original: "fames & argenti vilissimorum"; likely referring to the desperate greed for common wealth</note> give courage to the mind; many have persisted most diligently in this work, so much so that they neglected both life and wealth for its sake. But because such worldly happiness was not destined for them by God, they lost both their "oil and their labor" <note>original: "oleum perdiderunt ac operam"; a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort on a fruitless task</note>. Therefore, there is a need for study and the sharpest wit in this matter, so that through various comparisons and analogies, the true meaning of the authors writing on this art may be uncovered. So that the more gifted might understand to some extent, we shall bring forward a suitable analogy which prefigures the matter of the **perpetual balsam** <note>original: "balsamum perpetuum"; in Paracelsian medicine, a preservative vital force that prevents decay</note>, which acts as a similar balsam within the human body to recover and preserve total health and to repel disease, as **Paracelsus** says.

Let common and natural fire be our example: this fire is invisible to us, and therefore it must be sought and found in the air where it lies hidden. It is found by the striking of a stone against steel; however, the fire does not primarily reside in those objects, but in the air, and it is only caught by a dry object acting as tinder. For dryness immediately conceives its own heat and a nature similar to itself; and both work together in the subject until all humidity is consumed, leaving only a dry and ashen body subject to death, deprived of the fire and the fuel of life. 

In no other way must the matter be investigated by philosophers, for within it the fuel and the fire of life are most present. These must be drawn out through preparations, so that they might increase the life of a human life that is nearly failing. For just as wood that is almost entirely consumed—leaving behind only a few tiny coals or sparks—will see its flame and the life of the fire revive if wood is added as a suitable fuel, so it is in the human body: the **perpetual balsam**, added even to a residual atom of life, rouses this life back into its former flame and vigor.

But the question concerns the matter in which this rousing fire lies hidden. It is neither right nor safe, says Paracelsus, to speak of this clearly and openly to everyone equally. Does not the grace of God suffice for the **sons of light** <note>original: "lucis filiis"; those enlightened or initiated into divine and natural secrets</note>, to whom the power is given to lead light out of the darkness of shadows, figures, and riddles? The sons of darkness are tested by this reasoning, for it happens that they elicit nothing but mere shadows even from the light itself. For nature seeks a nature like itself, rejoices in it, and just as iron is drawn by a magnet, so darkness generates darkness, but light births light. 

This stone is hard; who will be able to extract the kernel from it? What is harder than a whetstone or steel, except the diamond? Yet even the diamond is worn away. But by what artifice the **Stone of the Philosophers** is to be opened, so that fire and life may be supplied to us from it, we do not yet see. The eyes of the mind must be opened, and first we must consider what medicine is made for human life above all others—being most compatible through nature and art—so that life may be preserved and maintained in health until its predestined end, remaining safe from all corruptions. No one, at least no true **physician** <note>original: "physicus"; a student of nature or natural philosopher</note>, will doubt the **metallic essences** <note>original: "metallicas essentias"; the pure, spiritualized core of metals</note>, especially those of the perfect bodies...

He warns that these secrets are reserved for the "Sons of Light" and hidden from the unworthy through riddles and metaphors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 511 regarding why metals are the ideal source for a "perpetual balsam." It transitions from the theory of vital heat to the specific errors made by alchemists when interpreting the metaphorical names of the "matter" of the Stone.</meta>

<header>ON TRANSMUTATION</header>

...of all those things which nature has produced, [they are] more durable and less corruptible. Accordingly, if life is a fire and the heat of a natural form joined to the moisture of its matter through light—as is evident from Genesis—and if light lives nowhere more brightly than in bodies less subject to corruption, what shall prevent the fire, heat, and radical moisture <note>term: 'radical moisture' (humor radicalis); the essential fluid in medieval physiology believed to be the fuel for the body's "innate heat," sustaining life and vitality</note> in metals—which are incorruptible—from being awakened from sleep into manifest life when joined to the organs of human life, thereby reviving a life that is nearly slumbering?

For those things only sleep in metallic bodies, and they rest just as a man seized by sleep lies as if dead, moved by nothing but breathing, but not by his body. In any case, if the spirit of metals is freed from the sleep of its body, it will exercise its motions and actions in any body presented to it, just as that man does when he wakes. We must judge human bodies no differently; while they are sick, the vital spirits within them fall asleep and cannot truly or freely breathe due to the drowsiness of their corrupted dwelling. Therefore, once the corruptions of darkness are removed from the body—not by an external physician, but by nature itself strengthened by the physician's aid, and by the addition of the external, incorruptible life of metals—these vital spirits freely exercise their motions in humans. 

It is no wonder, then, if marvelous cures are performed by spagyric <note>term: 'spagyric'; a branch of alchemical medicine, championed by Paracelsus, that uses chemical processes like distillation and fermentation to "separate and recombine" substances to create potent medicines</note> physicians, which would otherwise be impossible through the common medicine of the Greeks <note>note: referring to the traditional academic medicine based on the teachings of Galen and Hippocrates, which focused on balancing the four humors</note>. For this reason, those [Greek-style] physicians judged as incurable the diseases they could not expel with their own sleeping and, as it were, dead medicines. From this, spagyric medicine seems quite beautifully distinguished from the Greek: the latter sleeps with the sleeping, while the former, awake and free from all slumber, awakens the sleeping faculties of life. But to return to the investigation of the matter, this cannot be better known than through the errors committed by seekers in this regard.

->*On the various errors in the search for the matter of the perpetual balsam, or the philosopher's stone.*<-

### CHAPTER VII.

**A**rnaldus <note>note: Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist credited with writing the *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note>, observing the greatest difficulty of this art, says in his *Rosary*: "The most hidden names have been assigned to this matter of the Stone, mostly drawn from similarities." For they called it vegetable, mineral, and animal, not according to the literal sense—as those wise in divine secrets and experienced in the miracles of such a stone easily know how to devise. 

An example of this is the *lunaria* <note>note: literally 'moon-plant'; used here as a coded term rather than the botanical honesty plant</note> of Raymundus Lullius <note>note: Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic; many alchemical texts were attributed to him in the centuries after his death</note>, which produces flowers of marvelous virtues, yet very familiar to philosophers. It was not the intention of the one giving this name that it should be understood as some projection upon metals, or that a similar preparation be made from them; rather, the hidden mind of the philosophers looks elsewhere. By a similar name they called their matter *Martagon* <note>note: typically refers to the Turk's cap lily, but here functions as an alchemical code name for the 'hidden' matter</note>, to which also from here...

<summary>This page explains how the "spirit" of metals can awaken the dormant vital forces in a sick human body, contrasting this "awake" spagyric medicine with "sleeping" Greek (Galenic) medicine. It then begins a catalog of common errors alchemists make when they interpret the metaphorical names of the Stone's ingredients literally.</summary>

<header>OF METALS.</header>

They applied a hidden chemical operation to these things, though they actually denoted nothing more than a certain secret metaphor. A significant error also arose regarding vegetable juices, which many used to try and **coagulate Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"; turning liquid quicksilver into a solid form</note> and then, using "fixing waters," turn it into **silver** <note>original: "lunam" (the Moon)</note>. They believed that anyone who could solidify mercury in this way, without the help of other metals, would achieve the highest mastery of the craft. 

But although the juices of some vegetables can achieve this, it is judged to happen for no other reason than the resin, oil, or "earthy sulfur" in which they abound. These substances attract the moisture of the Mercury and mix with its substance, solidifying it in a way that is entirely useless. For it has been discovered that the thick and external sulfur found in vegetables is not fit for a perfect **projection** <note>term: "projection" (projectio); the final stage of alchemy where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transform it into gold or silver</note> in alchemy—a fact that many have learned through great financial loss. 

Even if some believed they had solidified Mercury with the white, milky juice of **spurge** <note>original: "tithymalli"</note> because of the intense and sharp heat within it, it was actually done by a hidden cold or rather a manifest opposite; for this reason, they called it **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lac virginis"</note>, yet this was a false foundation. One should think no differently of the juice of **celandine** <note>original: "chelidoniæ"</note>, even if its color deceives human eyes as if it were endowed with gold. Collecting it at a certain and determined time, they uprooted this vegetable to hunt for its "soul" or **quintessence** <note>term: "quintessence"; the purest, most concentrated essence of a substance</note>, from which they hoped to make a solidifying and transforming tincture; but from this, nothing but foolish error arose. 

Others boiled this juice to a thickness (which they call "consistency") and exposed it to the Sun so that it would harden into a solid mass. This mass was later ground into a very fine powder which they hoped would, by projection, turn Mercury into **gold** <note>original: "solem" (the Sun)</note>, but they found this to be false. Some mixed **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "sal armoniacum"; ammonium chloride</note> into this powder, others **colcothar of vitriol** <note>original: "colcotar vitrioli"; iron oxide residue from distilling sulfuric acid</note>, thinking they could finally reach their desired goal by this path. Afterwards, they turned these into yellow liquid solutions so that the salt might grant the tincture entry into the substance of the Mercury, yet nothing came of it. 

In place of the aforementioned things, some took the juices of **smartweed**, **toadflax**, **dragonwort**, willow leaves, **spurge**, **caper spurge**, **spearwort** <note>original: "persicariæ, bufonariæ, dracunculi, foliorum salicum, tithymalli, cataputiæ, flammulæ"</note>, and similar plants. They kept these sealed in a glass vessel together with Mercury itself for several days in hot ashes. It happened that the Mercury was turned into a cinder or rather a powder, but wrongly so, and with no result. For these men were deceived by the empty rumors of the common people, which spread the idea that Mercury could be solidified without metals, as we mentioned before. Many extracted salts, oils, and sulfurs from vegetables, but in vain, since no true solidification of Mercury, nor any perfect tincture or projection, can be made through these. By similarity alone—not by actual substance—the philosophers compared their matter to a golden tree with its branch—

...they compare it to the seven <note>Referring to the seven metals associated with the seven planets.</note>, understanding that it encloses the seven metals within its own seed, and lies hidden within it; for this reason they called it **vegetable**. They also called it so because, no differently than natural trees produce various flowers in their season, the matter of the Stone reveals the most beautiful colors openly during the production of its "flowers." Likewise, because a certain matter rises from the **philosophical earth** <note>A term for the purified base material used at the start of the Alchemical Work.</note>, like a shrub in the likeness of a dark sponge, they said the fruit of their tree tends toward heaven. Therefore, they claimed that the hinge of the whole art turns upon the "vegetables of nature," and not upon actual vegetable matter; and also because their Stone contains soul, body, and spirit within itself, just as living plants do.

By a not very different similarity, they said this matter is **virgin’s milk**, and the blessed blood of a rosy color, which however is suitable only for the prophets and children of God. From this, the **Sophists** <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to fraudulent or misguided alchemists who lacked true philosophical understanding.</note> gathered that the philosophical matter consists of animal or human blood—taking the opportunity from the fact that animals are nourished by vegetables. Some sought it in hair, in the salt of urine, in various things; others sought it in hen’s eggs, in the lime of those eggs, in milk, and similar things, by all of which they thought they could **fix Mercury** <note>term: "fixation"; the process of turning a volatile or liquid substance (like mercury) into a solid that can withstand fire.</note>. Some extracted salt from foul-smelling wash, nor were those lacking who believed small stones found in certain things were the matter. Others soaked egg membranes in a very sharp lye, to which they also mixed eggshells, attributing to these the secret of fixation to perfect the Mercury.

Some, comparing the white of eggs to silver and the yolk to gold, chose them as their matter; having mixed in common salt, **sal ammoniac** <note>term: "sal ammoniac"; ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy.</note>, and burnt **tartar** <note>term: "tartar"; potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking used in chemical reactions.</note>, and sealing these together in glass, they putrefied them in a **water bath** <note>original: "balneo maris"; a vessel of hot water used for gentle, even heating, also known as a bain-marie.</note>, until the white color turned into a deep red like blood. This they distilled into a foul-smelling liquid, entirely useless for the work they sought. Others putrefied the white and yolk of eggs, and from there a **basilisk** <note>original: "basiliscus"; a mythical serpent. In alchemy, this often refers to a highly toxic or potent substance produced through putrefaction.</note> was generated, which they burned into a deep red powder, thinking they could **tinge** <note>term: "tinge" (tingere); to transform the color and nature of a metal, usually into gold or silver.</note> with it. The author of this matter was **Cardinal Gilbert** in his treatise.

Most distilled the gall of oxen and other animals, mixed with common salt, into a liquid, with which they thought powders for **cementation** <note>term: "cementation" (cimentatio); a process of heating a metal with other substances to purify or color it.</note> soaked in it could transform their metals, by a certain mastery they call "**part with part**" <note>term: "part with part" (partem cum parte); a specific alchemical procedure for alloying or refining metals.</note>; but nothing was achieved from it. Some, choosing **tutia** <note>term: "tutia"; zinc oxide, often collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note> with some additions, such as **dragon’s blood** <note>term: "dragon's blood"; a bright red resin obtained from various plants, used as a pigment or medicine.</note> and other frivolous trifles of that sort, being misled, tried to change copper or **electrum** <note>term: "electrum"; a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver.</note> into gold. 

Others, following the "Art of the Venetians" (as they said), would shut twenty or so **lizards** <note>original: "stelliones"; specifically spotted lizards or geckos.</note> in a pot, and by hunger drive them to madness, so that one hungry lizard would devour another until only one survived, which they fed with filings of copper or electrum, believing that this kind of animal, through digestion alone in its stomach, would achieve the desired transformation. Finally, they burned this animal into a deep red...

...powder, which since they believed it to be gold, they were miserably deceived. Some have finally found gold in the fish known as trout, which had been cremated through smelting; this occurred for no other reason than because this species of fish, taught by nature, is accustomed to collecting and swallowing golden scales and sparks brought down by torrents and sometimes flowing down from the mountains. However, this happens only rarely. Such impostors <note>The author refers to those who use these rare natural occurrences to trick princes into funding futile alchemical experiments.</note> are mostly found in the courts of princes. Truly, the matter of the chemical philosophers is not to be sought in animals—I wish to warn everyone of this once and for all.

However, it should be known that the philosophers called their stone **animal**, because in its final operations, by the power of this most noble fiery mystery, a dark and red liquid like blood drips out from its matter and its vessel drop by drop. From this, they drew a prophecy that in the end times a most pure man would come to the earth, through whom the liberation of the world would occur; he himself would shed drops of a rosy or red and bloody color, by which the world would be redeemed from its stain <note>original: "labis." This is a clear alchemical parallel between the Philosopher's Stone and Christ, a common theme in Hermetic philosophy where the purification of matter mirrors the salvation of the soul.</note>. In a similar way, the "blood" of their stone, in its own kind, freed <term>leprous metals</term> <note>Metals considered "sick" or imperfect, such as lead or tin, which the Stone was believed to "heal" into gold.</note> as well as humans from their contagious infirmities. 

Therefore, they not without merit said their stone was **animal**. Regarding this, **Mercurius** <note>The legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note> speaks to **King Khalid** <note>Referencing "Liber de Compositione Alchimiae," an influential text presented as a dialogue between the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid and the monk Morienus.</note> in this manner: *“This mystery,”* he says, *“is permitted only to the prophets of God to know, which is why it is called the animal stone.”* For in the blood of this stone lies its soul; it is also composed of body, spirit, and soul. For a similar reason they called it their **microcosm** <note>A "little world" that contains the essence of the entire universe.</note>, because it bears the likeness of all things in the whole world; and for this reason again they say it is an animal, just as **Plato** calls the great world <note>The Macrocosm or universe.</note> an animal. 

Ignorant men came along believing the stone to be triple, and secret in a triple way—namely **vegetable, animal, and mineral**—which led them to seek it even in minerals <note>Meaning they sought it in specific, isolated mineral species rather than the "universal" matter.</note>. This view is far from the opinion of the philosophers; for they assert their stone is uniformly vegetable, animal, and mineral. It must also be noted that nature has distributed its mineral seed into various kinds, namely: *sulphurs, salts, <term>boraxes</term> <note>Various fluxing agents.</note>, <term>nitres</term> <note>Saltpeter.</note>, <term>ammoniac salts</term> <note>Sal ammoniac or ammonium chloride.</note>, alums, arsenics, <term>atramenta</term> <note>Metallic vitriols or inks.</note>, vitriols, <term>tutias</term> <note>Zinc oxides collected from chimneys.</note>, hematite, <term>orpiment</term> <note>Yellow arsenic sulfide; original: "auripigmenta."</note>, <term>realgar</term> <note>Red arsenic sulfide.</note>, magnesias, cinnabar, antimony, talc, <term>cachimias</term> <note>A term for ores that look like metals but are not yet matured.</note>, marcasites*, etc. In all of these, nature has not yet fulfilled our matter. 

Although in some of these named species nature sometimes reveals itself in a marvelous appearance regarding the transmutation of imperfect metals. For long experience and the practice of fire show a manifold transmutation in the matter of minerals, not only from one color to another, but even from one essence to another, and from imperfection to perfection. But although nature itself sometimes, by these mineral means, demonstrates such...
