->*On the fifth and very brief process of the Stone discovered by the same author.*<-

### CAP. XV.

I am not, nor do I wish to be, a teacher or follower of that Stone which is taught in diverse ways by so many others. Therefore, leaving that process behind, I have proposed to write very briefly of the one I discovered through both use and experience. This process tints <note>In alchemy, "tinting" refers to the permanent transformation of a substance's color and nature, whether in medicine or metallurgy.</note> human bodies no less than the other, though it is not prepared according to a similar method. Take Mercury—otherwise called the element of Mercury—and separate the pure from the impure. Afterward, let it be "reverberated" <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is reflected back onto the material</note> until it reaches whiteness. Sublimate this with sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> until it is dissolved. Let it be calcined and dissolved again, and then digested in a pelican <note>a specialized glass vessel designed for continuous distillation and circulation</note> for one month. Finally, let it be coagulated into a body. This body is no longer burned or consumed in any way, but remains in the same state. The bodies it penetrates become permanent in the cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; a porous ceramic bowl used to refine precious metals</note>, so that they can by no means be reduced to nothing or altered; instead, as has been frequently related, it removes all superfluous qualities from both sensible and insensible things. And although I have set down a very short way and process, it nevertheless requires long labor and is entangled in many circumstances. It requires an operator who is not easily fatigued, but one who is supremely diligent and experienced.

---

->*On a certain particular secret of the white tincture by means of arsenic.*<-

### CAP. XVI.

Some claim that arsenic is composed of mercury and sulfur; others say from earth and water; most say it is of the nature of sulfur. In whatever way it is formed, its nature is such that it transmutes red copper <note>original: "cuprum"</note> into white. It can also be brought to such perfection of preparation that it tints truly and perfectly. This is not achieved, however, by the path taught by many Sophists <note>The author uses "Sophists" as a derogatory term for alchemists whose theories he considers deceptive or impractical.</note>, such as Geber in his *Sum of Perfection*, Albertus Magnus, Aristotle the Chemist in his *Book of the Perfect Magistery*, Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"</note>, and Polydorus. For all these writers, as many as they are, err; or perhaps out of envy for the study, they write and propose various falsehoods, recipes, and their own opinions which they themselves were sometimes ignorant of. Arsenic truly contains three natural spirits: the first is combustible, corrosive, volatile, and all-penetrating. This spirit whitens Venus <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note> and after several days renders it spongy. This craftsmanship belongs properly only to those who practice the caustic <note>corrosive or burning</note> art. The second spirit is crystalline and sweet. The third

But the tinting spirit is separated from the others mentioned above. True philosophers search for these three natural properties in arsenic for the perfect <term>projection|The process of casting a small amount of an alchemical substance onto a larger quantity of molten metal to effect transmutation.</term> of the wise. Barbers, however, who practice surgery, seek the sweet and crystalline nature—separated from the tinting spirit—for use in healing wounds, and for buboes, carbuncles, anthraxes, and other defects of similar ulcers, which must be cured with a certain mild artifice. <note>In the early modern period, "Barber-surgeons" performed manual medical tasks like surgery and wound care, while University-trained physicians focused on internal medicine.</note> Furthermore, that tinting spirit, unless its pure part is separated from the impure, the fixed from the volatile, and the <term>tincture|A concentrated alchemical essence capable of transforming the color and nature of a substance.</term> secreted from the combustible, will by no means succeed in projection upon Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, Venus <note>Copper</note>, or any other imperfect metal according to one’s desire. All philosophers have hidden this most excellent secret mystery. Therefore, join the tinting spirit, separated from the other two as described above, to the spirit of the moon <note>Silver</note>, and allow them to digest together for the space of thirty-two days, until they have put on a new body. After it has been kindled to inflammation by the heat of the Sun <note>Likely referring to a specific grade of furnace heat rather than literal sunlight.</note> until the fortieth natural day, the spirit appears with a shining whiteness, endowed with the perfect secret of tinting. Finally, it is fit for projection—namely, one part of it over sixteen of an imperfect body—according to the excellence of the sharper preparation. From this results a shining and most excellent moon <note>Silver</note>, as if unearthed from the bowels of the earth. This opinion of our author seems most strongly confirmed by these very ancient Sibylline verses <note>Prophetic or riddling verses attributed to the Sibyls, often used in alchemical texts to hide secrets.</note>, which run in this manner:

> *I have nine letters, I am of four syllables; understand me.*
> *The first three have two letters each,*
> *The remaining syllables have the rest, and five are mutes [consonants];*
> *The total of the number consists of two centuries [two hundred], eight,*
> *And three times three decades [ninety], with seven. He who understands who I am*
> *Will not be unrefined or ignorant of the wisdom that is in me.*

All these things agree in this Greek word, numerically calculated in Greek: *arsenikon* <note>original: "ἀρσενικὸν"</note>, as it pertains to the white tincture. But the red tincture is not in arsenic, in whatever way it is prepared. When unprepared and crude, through melting with copper alone, it tints the metal to a supreme whiteness, but it is not <term>fixed|Stable under heat; not evaporating or changing back to its original state.</term>, because the crude tincture is similarly volatile; if it were fixed, there is no doubt that it would also provide a fixed tincture. For nothing penetrates metals in their crude state more easily than this spirit. The most important part of the work consists in its separation and fixation.

...with all [these things], the Most High Lord God adorned with wondrous gifts. They shadowed its secret in various enigmatic figures, such as this: *You shall **visit** the **interior** of the **earth**; by **rectifying**, you will **find** the **hidden stone**, the **true** medicine.* <note>original: "Visitabis interiora terræ rectificando, invenietis occultum lapidem veram medicinam." This is a famous alchemical motto; the first letters of each Latin word spell "VITRIOLUM" (Vitriol).</note> The first letters of all these words, when collected together, form the word Vitriol. By "earth" they understand vitriol, and by the "interior of the earth," its sweetness and redness. For within the secret of vitriol lies a most noble, subtle, and fragrant juice, and a pure oil; the method of its extraction should by no means be attempted through <term>calcination|The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to cause thermal decomposition or remove volatile fractions.</term> or distillation. For it must not be deprived of its greenness at all; for as soon as it is stripped of this, it necessarily lacks both its secret and its powers.

It must be noted in this place that not only minerals, but even vegetables themselves and similar things that show greenness on the outside, contain within themselves a red oil like blood, which is their secret. From this it is clear that the distillations of apothecaries are useless and vain and of no importance, because they do not know how to elicit the blood of vegetables. Most wise Nature herself teaching us, turns the waters of all vegetables into a <term>citrine|A lemon-yellow color representing a specific stage in the alchemical process.</term> color, and thereafter into a most ruby color like blood, with Art providing the assistance. That this sometimes happens too slowly is primarily caused by the excessive haste of ignorant distillers, by which the greenness is consumed. They have not learned to strengthen Nature by her own powers, by which that noble greenness must be rectified into redness by itself. Let wine be an example: though white at first, it is digested by itself into a citrine color; the green color of the grape clusters is turned into a red hiding beneath blue as time progresses. Therefore, when the greenness of vegetables and minerals is lost through the laziness of craftsmen, the essence, the spirit of the oil, and the most noble balsam of the secrets will perish. Paracelsus speaks elsewhere of this philosophical blood, where he discusses the generation of his pygmy <term>homunculus|A "little man" or artificial life form created in a flask, a concept famously associated with Paracelsus.</term> into a giant; in another place, he speaks of the blood and sperm of the nourishment of the body of mercy, etc.

Vitriol, therefore, contains many muddy and viscous imperfections within itself; wherefore its greenness must be elicited with water and rectified often, until it sheds all earthly impurities. Once all these rectifications are completed, one must be especially careful that the material is not exposed to the Sun, for this would turn its greenness to paleness, while the secret is simultaneously absorbed entirely. Let it be kept covered in a warm <term>hypocaust|A room or chamber heated from below; in alchemy, this refers to a gentle, consistent heat source used for "digesting" or maturing a substance.</term> so that it does not get dirty with dust. Afterwards, let it be digested in a closed glass for a space of several months, until various colors appear and, finally, the supreme <term>rubedo|The "Redness," the final stage of the alchemical Great Work, signifying success and the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</term>. Nor should the redness be considered sufficiently fixed by that process alone, but it must be further purged from the internal and accidental impurities of the earth, in this very manner: It must be rectified with vinegar until the earthly impurity is entirely removed and the dregs are set aside. This is [the true...] of its tincture.

Now let us apply our minds to <term>multiplication|The alchemical process of increasing the quantity or potency of the transmuting agent.</term>: mix the physical Mercury in a portion of two parts with three parts of the oil of the same weight, and let them remain together for forty days as before. By this proportion of weight and order, multiplication happens infinitely.

For this medicine sometimes colors thirty, forty, and sometimes sixty, eighty, and even a hundred parts of imperfect metal. Thus the turning point of this business depends mostly on the cleansing of the medicine and the industry of the worker, as well as the greater [susceptibility] of one imperfect [metal] over another...

to be renewed, or rather corrected, and almost deleted. For this very reason, his successors erected two stone tablets, upon which they engraved all the natural arts from their first principles, and this they did in hieroglyphic characters, so that this foreknowledge might also become known to posterity, and that a timely provision for the dangers of the future might be observed. Noah later found one of the tablets in Armenia, beneath Mount Ararat, after the flood had passed; on this tablet were designated the proportions of the upper firmament and the lower globe, as well as the courses of the planets. At length, these universal notions of this kind were pulled apart into different pieces and their powers were diminished, so that this separation produced this man as an astronomer, that one as a <term>magus|A practitioner of high magic or a wise man; in this context, someone who understands the hidden laws of nature.</term>, another as a <term>cabalist|A student of Kabbalah, a mystical Jewish tradition based on the symbolic interpretation of scripture and the universe.</term>, and a fourth as an alchemist. That "volcanic" <note>This likely refers to the "Vulcanic" or "fire-working" arts of metallurgy.</note> Abraham-Tubal-Cain <note>The author here appears to syncretize the Biblical patriarch Abraham with Tubal-Cain, described in Genesis as the first smith and forger of bronze and iron.</note>, the greatest astrologer and arithmetician, brought these traditions out of Egypt into the region of Canaan; from there, when it returned to his own people, the Egyptians rose to such a height that the wisdom of this matter passed from them even to other nations. 

Indeed, it is to be believed that the Patriarch Jacob colored the sheep with various patterns <note>A reference to Genesis 30, where Jacob uses peeled branches to influence the markings of laban's flocks.</note> by means of a branch of magic. For the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians always placed these liberal arts—as the highest philosophy—alongside Theology, to be learned by their nobles and priests. It happened no differently in the times of Moses, during which both the priests and the physicians themselves were chosen from among the magi: the former indeed in matters of judgment concerning health, especially in the diagnosis of leprosy. Moses was also instructed in the schools of the Egyptians through the care and expense of Pharaoh’s daughter. In the same way, Daniel from his earliest youth drank in the doctrine of the Chaldeans, so that he might emerge as a Cabalist: witness his divine foretellings and his interpretations of those words, *Mene Thesel phares*: <note>original: "Mene Thesel phares" — usually "Mene, Tekel, Peres" from Daniel 5. The tradition of this cabalistic art was once very familiar and much in use among Moses and the Prophets. The prophet Elijah predicted many things by his cabalistic numbers. Likewise, the ancient sages learned to know God rightly by this natural and mystical art, and they persisted and walked more firmly in His commandments through laws of this kind. 

In the same way, the Book of Samuel holds that the true <term>Berelistics|Likely a reference to "Beryllists" or crystal-gazers who used beryl stones for scrying and divine visions.</term> did not follow the fate of the devil, but were participants in true visions and apparitions by divine permission: we shall urge this point more widely in the book on celestial matters. A gift of this kind was granted by the Lord God to priests walking in divine precepts. It was the custom among the Persians to admit no one as king except a *Sophus* <note>original: "Sophum" — a wise man or philosopher.</note>, that is, one sublimated in deed and name as "Great": which is certainly evident by this very name of their kings, the *Sophi*. Such also were those Persian *Sophi* and magi who sought Christ from the East, and were called natural priests. The Egyptians likewise, from the Chaldeans

And the Persians, having attained this <term>Magic|In this context, not sorcery, but 'Magia Naturalis'—the study of the hidden powers and sympathies within the natural world.</term> and Philosophy, desired their own priests to learn the same wisdom. In this, they eventually saw such fruit that they became an object of admiration to all the surrounding regions. For this reason, Hermes was truly named <term>Trismegistus|Meaning 'Thrice-Great,' a legendary figure credited with the authorship of the Hermetic Corpus; he was traditionally considered a great king, priest, and philosopher.</term>, because he was a king, then a priest and a prophet, a master <note>original: "magus"</note> and a wise man <note>original: "sophos"</note> of natural things, just as Zoroaster also stood forth.

Afterward, when the son of Noah occupied the third part of the world after the flood, this art broke into Chaldea and Persia with a certain force, and from there into Egypt. When the superstitious and idol-worshiping Greeks caught the scent of this, some of the more clever among them betook themselves to the Chaldeans and Egyptians, so that they might carry back that same wisdom from those schools into Greece. But indeed, since the theological and biblical study of the <term>Mosaic Law|The laws and teachings attributed to Moses in the Torah/Pentateuch.</term> did not please them, and relying instead on their own innate character, they fell away from the right foundation of such natural secrets and the art of <term>Physics|Refers to 'Physice,' the study of nature and the physical world as a whole, rather than the modern narrow discipline.</term>. This is evident by example, since they perceived the doctrine of the Mosaic law so fabulously <note>That is, as if it were a collection of myths or fables.</note> and wavered in their understanding.

It was the custom of the Egyptians to propose traditions of such excellent wisdom only through enigmatic figures, hidden histories, and obscure words. All these things the Greek Homer later masked further with the fabulous artifice of his poems. Then came Pythagoras, who mixed in many things from the law of Moses and the Old Testament. Likewise Hippocrates, Thales of Miletus, Anaxagoras, Democritus, and others did not fail to apply their human intellects to these matters: although none of them was truly skilled in Astrology, Geometry, Arithmetic, nor physical Medicine. Naturally, their pride hindered them, as they were unwilling to admit disciples from other nations. And when they had perceived something from the Chaldeans and Egyptians, becoming far prouder by this accident than they were by nature before, and not fearing to sharpen the truth with more subtle fictions, they endeavored to describe a certain philosophy, which later derived from those most corrupt Greeks to the Latins and Italians. These men, at last imbued and instructed by this, also burdened the subject with their own witticisms. From all these, the art was disseminated in this masked fashion throughout all of Europe, so that it built many Academies everywhere among the nations for the propagation of such dogmas, by which youth might be instructed, or rather destroyed; and it flourishes to this very day among the Germans and other European nations.

The Chaldeans, however, the Persians, and the Egyptians held the same knowledge of the secrets of nature and of uncorrupted primal Physics, and likewise the same religion, with only the names of their wisdom changed. The Chaldeans and Persians once called their doctrine <term>Sophia|The Greek word for 'Wisdom.'</term> and Magic. But the Egyptians, on account of the sacrifice connected to it, called their wisdom the Priesthood. Both the Magic of the Persians and the Theology of the Egyptians were once taught together in the schools. Although in Arabia, Africa, and Greece many schools of the learned...

Whatever great men there once were—such as Albumazar, Abenzagel, Geber, Rhazes, and Avicenna among the Arabs; and Machaon, Podalirius, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and Rhodianus among the Greeks—nevertheless, there were various opinions and disagreements among them, and they stood at odds with the teachings of the Egyptians. Pythagoras, for that reason, did not wish to be called a "wise man" <note>original: "sophus"</note>, because in his time the priesthood of the Egyptians and their wisdom were by no means perfectly taught as was fitting, even though he nevertheless brought back many hidden mysteries from there. Anaxagoras did the same: this is evident from the disputations he held concerning the sun and its stone <note>Likely a reference to the alchemical "Stone of the Sun" or a meteoritic theory</note>, which he left behind after his death; yet in many things, he was contrary to the Egyptians. For this reason, their disciples did not wish to be called "wise men" <note>original: "sophi"</note>, nor "magi," but imitating Pythagoras in this matter, they assumed the name of "philosophers" <note>Literally "lovers of wisdom" rather than the possessors of it</note>. Yet they brought back nothing but certain sparks, like shadows, from the Magic of the Persians and Egyptians.

But in truth, Moses, Abraham, Solomon, Adam (who was the first), Elijah, and the Magi coming from the East to Christ were the true Magi and Divine Wise Men, as well as Cabalists; of whose art and wisdom the Greeks tasted little, or indeed nothing at all. Therefore, we leave behind the philosophical wisdom of those Greeks as a sophisticated speculation, degenerate and far removed from the other true arts and sciences. Many have attempted both to scrutinize the most secret magic of those wise men and to put it into practice, yet that very thing has not yet been achieved. Many in our own time exalt Trithemius, others Bacon and Agrippa, for their Magic and Cabala; yet these do not seem to agree entirely in all things. 

For <term>Magic|In this text, "Magia" refers to the study of the hidden, "occult" forces of nature rather than sorcery.</term> is the art and faculty through which one arrives at a knowledge of the elements, bodies, and their fruits, as well as their properties, powers, and hidden operations. But <term>Cabala|Derived from the Hebrew 'Kabbalah,' meaning tradition; here it refers to a mystical and spiritual path to understanding God.</term> itself, through <term>Anagogia|A method of spiritual interpretation that leads the mind upward to divine things.</term>, seems to build a path to God for men, and to teach how one must live with Him and prophesy from Him alone. For the Cabala is full of divine mysteries, just as Magic is full of natural secrets. Indeed, Magic teaches how to pronounce the foretelling of future things from the nature of the past and present; its operation consists in knowing all creatures—both celestial and earthly bodies—from the inside: what is hidden within them, what forces and virtues lie concealed, for what they were destined from the beginning, and with what properties they are endowed. These and similar things provide the bond by which celestial things are joined to earthly things, as is sometimes perceived even by the eye and the senses through their operations. Such a conjunction of celestial influences, or impression by which celestial virtues act upon inferior bodies, was once called <term>Gamaheum|A term used in older Hermetic texts to describe a talisman or the "marriage" between astral influences and physical matter.</term> by the Magi and Wise Men: the marriage of celestial powers and properties with elemental bodies. From this flowed the most excellent conjunctions and mixtures of the stars

## *On the cements and the cementation of metals.*

### CHAPTER XX.

We have previously heard about the most excellent and greatest tinctures of the philosophers; now we must bring the "lesser" ones into the light, because these are not intended for medical use for human bodies, but only for clearing away the "clouds" <note>Metaphorical term for impurities or oxidation that dull a metal's purity.</note> from metals.

1. The first cement is the "Royal Cement," described by Paracelsus not according to the common method (but from his own experience alone), and not following the practices of the ancients. Take <term>flowers of copper</term> <note>original: "florum æris"; a powdery residue or oxide of copper.</note>, antimony, crushed bricks, and common salt—half a pound of each. Grind them all very finely, mix them together, and then soak them in wine and dry them; repeat this process twenty-four times. With this powder, let <term>laminated silver</term> <note>original: "laminata luna"; "Luna" (the Moon) is the alchemical name for silver.</note> be "cemented" <note>Cementation is a process of refining a metal by heating it while it is packed in a dry powder (the cement).</note> at a medium heat for four hours, then for another four hours at a moderate heat, and finally for twelve hours at a melting heat. Then, finally, remove the <term>regulus</term> <note>The metallic lump or "heart" that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</note>, laminate it as in the first process, and cement it again with the same substances, observing the same stages of fire, repeating this four or five times. Finally, let it be refined by <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: "fulminetur per cineritium"; a refining process where metal is heated in a shallow porous bowl made of bone-ash to separate precious metals from lead and impurities.</note>, and let the slag be reduced back into silver. The instruments—namely, the vessels—must be very well sealed with clay and closed firmly. Consider that I have set down a long process here because experience has shown that short durations of fire produce nothing good. Indeed, the duration and intensity of the fire are the most powerful factors in the "fixation" <note>The process of making a substance stable in heat so that it does not evaporate or change.</note> of the Royal Cement; it would be even better if the contents were kept in such a cement for four full days. It should also be noted that the "flowers of copper" should first be extracted from copper using <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolum"; iron or copper sulfates, used as powerful acidic agents.</note>; for in that substance, a certain power of fixation is held for many reasons. Similarly, antimony must be "fixed," yet while retaining the virtues it possesses through the processes of rotting and purification; for its powers cannot be fully known. Likewise, the bricks should be taken from a good roof; for in the roof-tile itself there is a certain capacity for constricting and "fixing" the veins or pores in metals. Salt also fixes and corrects "leprous" silver by removing its "cloud." Therefore, it is necessary for these four things to meet in the composition of this cement. Furthermore, the fire must be watched, and nothing else should be added, nor any other metal; for this is sufficient on its own.

For this reason, it must undergo cementation so that it may be able to retain the volatile part of its body along with the fixed part; otherwise, this immature portion is separated from its fixed body either in the cement, or during <term>cupellation</term> <note>original: "cineritio"; a refining process where metal is heated in a porous cup called a cupel to remove impurities.</note>, and sometimes even in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid, used to separate gold from silver.</note>.

The third concern involves the weight; gold is considered of lesser value the lighter it is, for it ought to be heavier than lead and (as many maintain) heavier than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note>. This is the best cement of "the Sun" for all the aforementioned stages.

4. The fourth cementation of ores concerns those that possess perfect metal within themselves but lose it through common smelting. Let it be noted in this place that metals cannot be fixed better than while they are "raw" <note>In their unrefined, mineral state.</note>. By this path, metals are found in ores that never appear otherwise. The description of the fixation of a metal in its own ore is thus: Take one pound of the ore of Mars; to this, most finely ground, add two pounds each of antimony and <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "salis nitri"; potassium nitrate.</note>. For the spirits of metals still existing in their ores proceed in their colors and essences while raw. The description of the transmutation of ores is this: Take half a pound each of <term>saffron of Mars</term> <note>Iron oxide.</note>, <term>flowers of Venus</term> <note>Copper oxide or acetate.</note>, <term>vitriol</term> <note>Metallic sulfates, often of iron or copper.</note>, and <term>alum</term>, one pound of prepared common salt, and two pounds of ore. Let them all be melted and deprived of moisture, and let them be cemented for twelve hours. Afterward, let them be melted in Saturn and refined, which being done, the transmutation will be found in the cupel of the ash-test. A mixture of metals can also be added to this kind of transmutation, considering however the greater aptitude of one over the other, by which the transmutation may happen more easily.

Arrange it layer upon layer in a melting vessel; afterward, let it be heated slowly for the first six hours, let the fire be increased for the next six hours, and finally, let it be most violent for another twelve hours. When this is done, sublime and cement it again as before; by the fourth or fifth cementation, you will find the cinnabar "fixed" <note>Made resistant to evaporation by heat.</note>. We have completed our short book on <term>cements</term> <note>Powdered mixtures used to refine metals through high-heat chemical reactions without melting the metal.</note>, in which we have taught the methods of cementation quite fully and clearly. Although many other descriptions by various authors are held, which we exclude from our own work, we have set down only those which I have found to be most useful through practical experience. Now, let us also hear something concerning <term>gradations</term> <note>Chemical processes intended to "grade up" or improve the quality, color, and "perfection" of a metal, usually aiming for gold or silver.</note> from Paracelsus.

->*On the gradations of metals.*<-
->CHAPTER XXI.<-

It has seemed fitting to set down fourteen gradations of metals in this place; and although many more others are found, we have compiled only those which are established by certain experience and which we know to be worthy of writing. They are prepared under a triple distinction: some by <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Literally "strong water," typically nitric acid.</note>, some by oils, and the rest indeed by liquors.

1. The first gradation is made by the first *aqua fortis* in this manner: Take two pounds each of <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfate minerals.</note>, alum, and <term>saltpeter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate.</note>; one <term>verto</term> <note>original: "verto"; the text explains this as a quarter-pound.</note> (that is, a fourth part of a pound) each of <term>flowers of copper</term> <note>original: "floris æris"; likely verdigris or copper acetate.</note>, <term>saffron of Mars</term> <note>original: "croci martis"; iron oxide or rust.</note>, and hematite; half a pound of cinnabar; one and a half *vertos* of antimony, and half a *verto* of arsenic. Let all be distilled together into an *aqua fortis*, which should be purified and thinned according to the custom of similar waters. In this water, dissolve <term>Luna</term> <note>The alchemical name for silver.</note> that has been cemented, or part with part—that is, silver and <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>—and let them be held in <term>digestion</term> <note>Slow heating in a sealed vessel.</note> for one month. Afterward, let the residues be <term>fulminated</term> <note>original: "fulminentur"; a violent refining process, likely cupellation in a furnace.</note>, and the transmutation will be achieved. Whatever residue remains in the *aqua fortis* should be precipitated and fulminated as above; thus the remainder of the silver is obtained. It must be noted meanwhile that each ingredient ought to be prepared before they come into use for gradations; otherwise, every transmutation is greatly hindered by impurity.

2. The second gradation is by the second *aqua fortis*. The process of this second gradation is to be very well noted, as it is achieved with greater profit and subtlety than any others made by waters. Take, therefore, one pound each of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "salis petræ"</note> and cinnabar; let them be ground together, and from them distill a water, which you should save. You shall do this same thing also, and with the same weight, with antimony and arsenic. Mix both waters together, and let one pound each of saltpeter and alum be added. Again, let all be distilled together in the manner of *aqua fortis*. For all metals which shall have been dissolved in this water and remained in digestion, the operations, powers, and virtues of perfection are fulfilled more than can be believed; for in the ingredients of such a composition, the full faculties for a true transmutation of metals containing <term>corporeal matter</term> <note>The physical substance of the metal as opposed to its "spirit" or color.</note> within themselves lie hidden. For these three distillations, by the strength of their water, tint so vehemently that no greater or more vehement operation among *aqua fortis* can be found.

3. The third gradation is by the third *aqua fortis*. Take cinna-

Another gradation of silver with <term>oil of Mercury</term> by an appendix: Let an oil be made from sublimated mercury and <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, by <term>cohobating</term> <note>redistilling a liquid over the solid matter from which it was just distilled</note> or redistilling many times as described above, until it is converted into oil; into this, drive the spirits of aqua fortis with a most violent fire. ## *On the Vexations of Alchemists.*

### CHAPTER XXII.

**H**aving concluded the gradations and cements of metals, we have decided to come in the final place to the "vexations" <note>original: "vexationibus"; this refers to the manual operations, labors, or "troubles" involved in chemical experimentation.</note> of the alchemists, with which we shall conclude the Alchemy of Paracelsus. First, therefore, we must say what Alchemy is: it is certainly nothing other than a perceptible, yet industriously devised, true discourse, by which it is taught how the kinds of metals may be transmuted from one into another. According to this, each person can choose for themselves a better way according to the capacity of their own mind (and whoever weighs the matter more sharply thus reaches the goal), and so find the truth of this thing. In this place, one must hold the greatest account of the **stars** and **stones**, because the star is the spirit of the formation of all stones. It is also...

Of all the celestial stars, <term>Sol and Luna</term> <note>original: "Sol & Luna"; the alchemical names for Gold and Silver.</note> are but a single stone in themselves, and the earthly stone came forth from the celestial stone through the same fire, the same coals, ashes, expulsions, and the same purifications by which that celestial stone—clear and pure in its brilliance—was separated and brought back to its essence. Moreover, the whole globe of the earth is nothing other than something cast off, hardened, mixed, corrupted, crushed, and again coagulated, and partly melted into one mass of stonework, which holds its seat and rest in the very center of the sphere of the firmament.

It should further be noted that those precious stones, which are called by their proper names after the celestial stones or stars, hold the place closest to perfection, purity, beauty, clarity, virtue, incorruptibility, and constancy in fire, and they lie hidden within other earthly stones. They have the greatest affinity with the celestial stars or stones and are of their nature; for from the stars, they were derived into the stones in which they are found. The same judgment should be made concerning metals.

For Alchemy, therefore, there is no primary need for other instruments than a smelting workshop, bellows full of air, tongs, hammers, crucibles, <term>scorifiers</term> <note>original: "testis"; small shallow pots used in refining.</note>, and <term>cupels</term> <note>original: "cupellis"; porous vessels used to separate precious metals from lead.</note> constructed from beechwood ashes. Afterwards, let <term>Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Mercury, and Luna</term> <note>Lead, Tin, Iron, Gold, Copper, Quicksilver, and Silver.</note> be put in, and let them be worked through to the end of Saturn. 

If, however, metals remain buried in the earth for a very long time, they are not only consumed by rust, but are also, by perseverance, transmuted into natural stones, of which the number is infinite; but this secret is known to few. Sometimes there is found in the earth the ancient and stony coinage of the Pagans, stamped with their images and characters, which was formerly metallic, but turned into stone through a transmutation performed by nature.

Furthermore, what should be said concerning the recipes of Alchemy, its materials, vessels, and so forth, and the diversity of these things? Such as:
*   furnaces, glass vessels, and pots
*   waters, oils, <term>calces</term> <note>original: "calces"; powders produced by burning metals or minerals (oxides).</note>, sulfurs, and salts
*   saltpeter, alums, and vitriols
*   <term>chrysocolla</term> <note>originally meaning "gold-glue," used for various green minerals like malachite or borax used in soldering.</note>, atraments, and salt of glass
*   <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead</note>, red earth, and <term>tutty</term> <note>zinc oxide</note>
*   wax, <term>luting of wisdom</term> <note>original: "lutum sapientiæ"; a specialized clay sealant used to make glass vessels airtight.</note>, and crushed glass
*   verdigris, soot, and eggshells
*   <term>crocus of Mars</term> <note>iron oxide</note>, soap, crystal, and chalk
*   arsenic, antimony, and <term>minium</term> <note>red lead</note>
*   elixir, <term>lazurium</term> <note>lapis lazuli or a blue pigment</note>, and gold leaf
*   nitre salt, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and <term>calamine stone</term> <note>zinc ore</note>
*   magnesia, <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>a red medicinal earth or clay</note>, and many other things.

And what of the preparations, putrefactions, digestions, probations, solutions, cementations, filtrations, reverberations, calcinations, gradations, rectifications, amalgamations, and purifications, etc., with which the books of Alchemy are most stuffed? Or next, what of those works made from herbs, roots, seeds, wood, stones, animals, worms, bone ashes, snail shells, mussels, snails, and pitch?

These and all similar things in Alchemy are quite remote—indeed, they are the most vain burdens of labor. Even if Gold and Silver could be made through them, nonetheless they [hinder] this intention more than...

...they hinder rather than advance the work. Therefore, to speak truly, nothing is to be learned from them that pertains to the art of manufacturing <term>gold and silver</term> <note>original: "solem & lunam"; literally "the sun and the moon," the standard alchemical terms for these precious metals.</note>; for this reason, they should be entirely set aside, as they accomplish absolutely nothing with the five metals in relation to gold and silver. Nor should anyone foolishly persuade themselves that these things can be understood lightly; indeed, they are better understood through their hidden sense than their open one.

### *On the manner of seeking metals as well as their location.*

### CHAPTER XXIV.

In the earth and in stones, the hope of finding metals is most uncertain; however, because it is the primary method of acquisition, it should by no means be despised, but rather greatly praised. Such human desire and appetite should no more be allowed to perish than the lawful love of young people for marriage. For just as bees desire flowers for the sake of honey and wax—yet not for themselves—so it would be right for men, like the bees, to pant for the extraction of metal from the earth without any greed or private advantage. For he who seeks too much usually finds the least. God gifts men not only with gold or silver, but also with poverty, filth, and misery. He has also called some to a singular knowledge of metals and minerals, who have attained a shorter and easier way of manufacturing gold and silver without the need for digging or smelting. This is achieved not through common custom, nor from underground sources, but even from the five kinds of metals, through certain arts and knowledge, by means of metals already prepared by art—such as from <term>Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, and Mercury</term> <note>The alchemical names for Lead, Tin, Copper, Iron, and Quicksilver.</note>. From these, and from any of them separately, they have manufactured gold and silver, though more easily from one than from another.

Note concerning these: from Mercury, Saturn, and Jupiter it is easy, but from Mars and Venus it is difficult for gold or silver to be made. It is possible, however, with the addition of <term>ferment</term> <note>A substance added to "leaven" or trigger the transformation of the base metal.</note>. Otherwise, silver comes out of <term>magnesia</term> <note>In this context, magnesia likely refers to a specific mineral primitive matter, not modern magnesium.</note> and Saturn; from Jupiter and <term>cinnabar</term> <note>original: "cinabari"; mercury sulfide, used here as a source of the "red" or solar principle.</note> pure gold arises, as well as silver; from Jupiter, Mercury, and <term>aquarius</term> <note>Likely referring to a "watery" or liquid preparation of these metals.</note> comes pure <term>Aries-gold</term> <note>original: "aurum arietinum"; possibly referring to gold produced under the zodiac sign of Aries or gold of a particularly high, "martial" quality.</note>. An ingenious artist—such as I remember once seeing—will also be able to prepare metals with diligent attention; and so, led by true reason, he may advance the perfection of the transmutation of metals more by his own work or <term>regimen</term> <note>The controlled application of heat and timing in an alchemical operation.</note> than by the course of the twelve celestial signs or the seven planets, which some also observe in these matters...

It is superfluous to consider planetary aspects, good or bad times, the day or hour, or the prosperous or unhappy state of this or that planet; these can neither help nor harm the art of natural Alchemy, and much less can they hinder it. If you possess a process that is otherwise true or possible, work whenever you please; provided there is no defect within yourself, or in your operations and intellect, the planets and celestial stars will effect nothing against you in this work. Moreover, the perpetual place of all things—which is devoid of time, beginning, and end—operates essentially in all places. That for which there is no hope, which is reckoned impossible, and which even seems incredible and desperate, breaks forth wonderfully into truth. For God and nature do nothing in vain. It is especially to be noted that this applies to Mercury: Whatever dyes into a white color has the nature of life, and the power and property of light, which causes life to manifest. Fire, with its heat, is the origin of this life. Whatever, on the contrary, dyes into blackness or makes things black, shares a nature with death and possesses the property of darkness and the effective powers of death. The coagulation and fixation of such corruption is earth with its coldness. For the house is always dead, but the inhabitant within it lives; if you can find an example of this, you have triumphed. Burn fat herbs <note>original: "verbenas"; sacred plants often used in Roman rituals, here likely a poetic or cryptic term for specific volatile substances</note>, with Mercury united by a liquefying powder, which must be noted in this work. Take four ounces of saltpeter <note>original: "salis nitri"</note>, half as much sulfur, and one ounce of <term>aquarius</term> <note>original: "aquarij"; likely referring to a specific liquid or a substance associated with the sign of Aquarius, such as a "mineral water" or distilled substance</note>. Ground together, let them be ignited in a crucible with the mineral, and a most beautiful king <note>original: "rex"; alchemical shorthand for gold or a purified metallic "regulus"</note> will settle at the bottom.

However, a different method of treating Alchemy than before is observed here, derived from the natural foundation of the seven metals through canons. From <note>original: "miram"; the OCR begins with "ram," likely a fragment of "miram" (wonderful) or "veram" (true)</note> deep contemplation, wonderful works result which, although often contrary and far removed from the opinions of the ancient natural philosophers, are nevertheless found to be true through proof and experiment. First, nothing in this art is truer than that which is least known, and in which the least faith is placed. The sole occasion and cause of all difficulty in Alchemy—because of which many are reduced to poverty, while the rest labor in vain—is the lack of skill in the operators, and the quantity of materials being either too much or too little, or even perfectly equal; from all of these, the substances in the operations are either destroyed or reduced to nothing. But if the true process is once discovered, the matter, transforming itself day by day, approaches closer and closer to perfection. The right path is easy, but it is found by very few. Sometimes it happens that a certain speculative artist devises some technique in Alchemy through his own delusion, as if placed in a labyrinth, whether anything or nothing is achieved from it. For he must do nothing by which something is turned into nothing, or by which something arises again from nothing: this is an incredible proverb, yet not at all false. Destruction perfects the good, for the good can in no way appear because of its "hider." For the good is not at all good while it is hidden. Therefore, the hider must be removed so that the good may freely appear with clarity. The hider is the mountain and the stone, the sand of the earth, the paths of the sun, and the veins in which the metal grew. But every visible metal is a hider of the other six metals. And because any imperfect thing is corrupted, burned, and reduced to nothing by the element of fire—such as these five metals: Mercury <term>Mercury</term>, Jupiter <term>Tin</term>, Mars <term>Iron</term>, Venus <term>Copper</term>, and Saturn <term>Lead</term>—on the contrary, the perfect metals are not consumed by a similar fire, such as the Sun <term>Gold</term> and the Moon <term>Silver</term>. Thus it happens that they remain in the fire, and they take up their own body and appear to the eye from the other imperfect metals in which they were corrupted. How and by what skillful method this is done can be gathered from the seven canons set down below, as well as the nature or property of each metal, what it does with others, and what it is capable of achieving in their mixture. Truly, this must be noted above all: those seven canons cannot be understood at first sight or by a light reading by anyone, even a reader who is commonly considered very sharp. For a shallow intellect does not easily admit hidden things; therefore, each of these canons requires no small amount of discussion. There are many elite and proud spirits who rashly persuade themselves that they understand all these things contained in this little book; they believe they possess better things and are accustomed to despise these, namely the "sun between two moons" and the "sun in parentheses" <note>These refer to specific alchemical symbols or configurations used in transmutation recipes.</note>. However, so that the opinion set forth above may be proven—which states: *Every visible metal is a concealer of the other six metals* <note>original: "Vnumquodque metallorum visibilium, occultator est aliorum sex metallorum"</note>—let us see what Paracelsus teaches.

All things are hidden in all things; one out of all these is this hidden thing, the corporeal vessel, visible and mobile from the outside, in which all meltings are made manifest. No name can be found for this fluidity, or for its origin, by which it may be properly called. ### *On the nature and property of Jupiter.*
#### *The second Canon.*

What is manifest in <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Iovis"; the alchemical name for tin</note> (understand this as its physical body) contains six metals within itself, spiritually hidden, one more deep and tenacious than the other. It participates in nothing of the fifth essence, but is of the nature of the elements; for this reason, its melting is revealed when even a light fire is applied, and it is coagulated when a similar cold approaches. It has an affinity with the meltings of all other metals. For the more similar one thing is to another, the more easily it is joined to it through conjunction; the operation of things that are near to one another is also easier and more natural than those that are remote. That which is remote tends to deceive, because what seems smallest in it is actually greatest. Hence it happens that men do not yearn for the heavens, because they are so far distant from them, and they do not see their glory; likewise, they do not fear the depths of hell as much because they are remote, and no living person has known or actually experienced the misery of their state and punishment—for this reason, hell becomes as nothing to them. In the same way, more remote things are considered more base the more unrefined a place they occupy, because every thing becomes better or is changed according to the property of its location, which can be demonstrated by various examples. Accordingly, the further <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note> is from <term>Mars</term> <note>iron</note> and <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note>, and the closer it is found to the <term>Sun</term> <note>gold</note> and <term>Moon</term> <note>silver</note>, the more it seems to approach the nature of gold and silver in its body—becoming larger, stronger, more visible, more tangible, more perceptible, more lovable, more acceptable, better known, and truer than in its remote state. Again, the more remote any thing is, the more base it is considered in all the aforementioned ways, for no other reason than that the present thing is always preferred to the absent one. Therefore, the more near the manifest is, the more remote is the hidden. For this reason, Alchemists must, with the greatest diligence, consider and note the spiritual, hidden, and remote place in which the <term>Sun</term> <note>gold</note> and <term>Moon</term> <note>silver</note> exist; and whichever they desire, let them seek it in the distance, and likewise see it in the proximity. ### *On the nature and property of Mars.*
#### *The third Canon*

The six hidden metals expelled the seventh, <term>Mars</term> <note>original: "Martem"; the alchemical name for iron</note>, from themselves and rejected him, and they made him corporeal, leaving him the least value and imposing upon him the greatest hardness and the burden of labors. It is an extremely difficult and overly laborious task to make a prince or a king out of a clumsy and common man. But Mars acquires dominion with a strong and warlike hand, and occupies the place of the king. Yet there is cause for him to beware of ambushes, lest he suddenly be made a captive. There is no separation or killing of spirits, because spirits of this kind are such that they can never persist without bodies; even if the body were taken from them and killed a hundred times in a single hour, they would nonetheless always acquire another body more noble than the first. **Question:** If it is true that the Moon and any other metal take their origin and are generated from the other six, what then is the property and nature of the Moon?

**Response:** From <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead</note>, <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver</note>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note>, <term>Mars</term> <note>Iron</note>, and <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note>, nothing nor any other metal can be made but the Moon. The cause of this is that each of the other six metals has within itself two virtues, which are properly the spirits of the Moon, which (in a few words) are acquired by it in this way: For the Moon consists of six spiritual metals and their virtues, each of which has two; thus, in total, twelve virtues exist, placed in this one corporeal metal, which are compared to the seven planets and the twelve signs of the zodiac.

For the Moon has from the planet **Mercury**, and from **Aquarius** and **Gemini** (or from Aquarius and **Pisces**), its liquidity and its white splendor.

The Moon also has from **Jupiter**, **Sagittarius**, and **Taurus**, its white color and its great constancy in the fire.

The Moon has from **Mars**, **Cancer**, and **Aries**, its hardness and its good ringing sound.

The Moon has from **Venus**, **Gemini**, and **Libra**, the measure of its <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of becoming solid or semi-solid</note> and its malleability.

The Moon has from the **Sun**, **Leo**, and **Virgo**, its sincere purity and great constancy against the forces of fire.

The Moon has from **Saturn**, **Virgo**, and **Scorpio** (or **Capricorn**), a <term>homogeneous</term> body, pure cleanliness, and constancy against the violence of fire. Such is the natural knowledge of the <term>exaltation</term> <note>the refinement or elevation of a substance to its highest state</note> and the cause of the spirit and body of the Moon, with its composite nature touched upon in brief.

## *On the nature and properties of the Sun.*
<note>original: "solis"; here referring to Gold</note>

### *The seventh canon.*

The seventh of the six spiritual metals in bodily form is the **Sun** <note>Gold</note>, which in itself is nothing other than pure fire. However, the reason why it possesses a body that is externally more beautiful, yellow, more apparent, more perceptible, heavier, colder, and more uniform in sight and perception than the others is this: it contains within itself the solidifications of the other six metals, by which it has been made into a single, most compact external body. Nevertheless, its melting by means of elementary fire arises from **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, and from the zodiac signs of Pisces and the Water-Bearer <note>Aquarius</note>, which hold spiritual meltings hidden within themselves and act upon the Sun. A most clear example of this is seen when Mercury itself is very easily mixed bodily with the Sun through an embrace <note>referring to the process of amalgamation where mercury dissolves gold</note>. 

But the fact that the Sun, after melting, becomes coagulated, hard, and solid as the heat recedes and cold arrives from the outside, is caused by the remaining five metals whose natures it encompasses: namely **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>. In these five, "cold dwellings" with their own governing powers are chiefly found. From this it also happens that the Sun can hardly be melted without being set on fire, on account of the aforementioned cold. Furthermore, Mercury cannot assist with its own natural heat or fluidity, nor can it defend the Sun against the coldness of the five metals; for Mercury is not powerful enough to keep the Sun in its liquid state, because it must obey five metals rather than just one. 

Mercury's only office, by its very nature, is to flow always. Hence it also happens that it has no power to act within the solidifications of other metals, for its nature is not to make things hard or solid, but liquid. To make something fluid is the nature of heat and life, whereas coldness possesses the nature of hardness, consolidation, and immobility, which are compared to **death**. 

For example, if the six metals—Tin, Copper, Lead, Iron, Silver, and Gold—must be melted, it is necessary that this be done by the heat of fire; snow or ice, which are cold, will not accomplish this, but will rather solidify them or make them hard. As soon as a metal melted by fire is removed from it, the coldness rushing into it makes it solidified, hard, and immobile by itself. But as for Mercury flowing and always remaining "alive," tell me, I pray, whether that is caused by heat or cold? 

Whoever answers that this happens because of a cold and moist nature (as has been judged until now), and that it has its "life" from coldness, that person holds an opinion with no knowledge of nature, but has been led astray along with the common crowd. For the ignorant common folk judge nothing but falsehoods regarding natural things based on what is obvious; they firmly hold only to what they see with their "fleshy eyes." Therefore, anyone who desires to know the truth in these matters must move away from such views. Mercury indeed...

Indeed, it lives not at all from a cold nature, but from a hot and fiery one; for every living thing is fire, by this reasoning: that heat is the occasion of life, while cold is the occasion of death. The **Sun** <note>Gold</note> likewise is pure fire in itself, yet it is not a "living" organic being, but rather a hard substance, and it displays only the color of sulfur—appearing as white mixed with red in a balanced proportion.

The five cold metals—**Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>—bestow their virtues upon the Sun: their coldness upon the body itself; their fire upon the color; their dryness upon the hardness; their moisture upon the weight; and their splendor upon the "clangor" <note>the clear ringing sound of the metal when struck</note>. Furthermore, the fact that the Sun is neither consumed nor corrupted in the element of terrestrial fire is caused by the harmony of the Sun with fire; for one fire cannot burn or consume another. Rather, when fire is added to fire, it is increased and becomes more powerful in its operations. 

Certainly, the celestial fire which the Sun pours onto the earth to work among us is not the same kind of fire as exists in heaven, nor is it like our fire existing upon the earth. Instead, that celestial fire among us is a cold and congealed fire, which is the body of the Sun. Therefore, the Sun can in no way be overcome by our fire; the only thing that happens to it is that it melts, just as snow and ice are melted by the celestial Sun. Fire, therefore, does not have the power to burn fire, because the Sun is fire which exists dissolved in heaven but congealed among us. Gold, likewise, is threefold in its essence: first, celestial and dissolved; second, elemental and fluid; and third, metallic and corporeal.

->*On the heat and coagulation of Mercury.*<-

### CHAPTER XXV.

To wish to "kill" <note>solidify</note> or congeal **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>, and afterwards to turn it into the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, and to sublimate it with great labor, are vain works, since that disappearance and vanishing of the Sun and Moon existing within it are merely an illusion. For there is another path, far different and much closer, by which Mercury is transmuted into the Moon with little expense and less labor, without the need for coagulation. 

Everyone would gladly learn this art in Alchemy, being so light and easy, through which one might be able to produce a great amount of the Sun and Moon in a short time. Other writings, preparations, and words are tedious to them, declaring that it cannot be done so easily. One would gladly hear what ought to be done, and would listen to this method: "Work thus, and you shall have the Sun and Moon most abundantly, by which you will become a very wealthy man." To such a person I say: wait a little while, I pray, until this knowledge of producing the Sun and Moon from Saturn <note>Lead</note> and Mercury is declared without long words and with little labor, falling into your stomach "already chewed" <note>idiomatic: made easy to digest or understand</note>. This art is not, nor can it ever be, so common in its discovery and practice as it is easy in itself. I speak of [fabricating] the Sun and Moon...

The ease of manufacturing through **Alchemy** <term>Alchemy: The art of transmuting base metals into noble ones and seeking universal medicines</term> is more effortless than is necessary to mention in any document or writing, such as the practice usually performed with "annual snow" <note>original: *annali nive*; likely a reference to a specific white precipitate or a seasonal chemical process</note>. Certainly, all those who judge **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> to be of a cold and moist nature are deceived, proven wrong by their own manifest error. By its very nature, it is nothing if not supremely hot and moist; for this reason, it is naturally compelled to be liquid in its flow and life. For if it were moist and cold by nature, it would resemble frozen water and would exist as a permanent hard solid. Just as with "frozen" <note>solid</note> metals, fire would be required to liquefy it. Yet it needs no such thing, since it possesses liquefaction and flow from its own naturally implanted heat, which keeps it in a state of perpetual flux and renders it "living," so that it can neither die nor coagulate on its own. 

Truly, in these matters, it is most necessary to know that the seven spirits of the metals—or however many of them come into the fire mixed together—wage a battle among themselves. This is especially true of **Mercury**, so much so that each exerts its own virtues and powers upon the other out of a desire for conquering, liquefying, and transmuting. One plunders the virtue, life, and form of another, and bestows a different nature and form. For by heat, spirits of this kind are stirred up, and through their vapors, they are excited to perform a mutual transmutation upon each other from one virtue into another, until they reach perfection and purity. 

But what should finally be done with **Mercury** so that, once its moisture and heat are entirely removed and replaced with an inward, supreme coldness, it might be congealed, solidified, and altogether **mortified** <term>Mortification: The alchemical process of "killing" a substance by changing its physical state, usually making it solid or changing its color</term>? Do this as follows: Take pure **Venus** <note>Copper</note> [one ounce]. Take **Mercury**. [Use] **Venus**. [Process code: CXPCX] Take **Mercury**. Upon these, place the Mercury, very well sealed, and suspended in the middle of the place of coagulation for twenty-four hours—that is, one natural day. In this manner, the "celestial heat" is taken away from the Mercury, and through external heat and the internal coldness of **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> (both of which are of a cold nature), coldness is bestowed upon it. Thus, the Mercury is finally forced to be congealed, solidified, and hardened. 

Furthermore, it should be noted that the coldness required for the solidification and mortification of Mercury is not at all perceptible to the external senses, like the cold of snow or ice; rather, it appears as something hot on the outside. In the very same way, one must judge the heat of Mercury, by which it flows naturally: it is not a heat perceptible from the outside like our common qualities; rather, it appears as an extreme cold. For this reason, the **Sophists** <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to pseudo-alchemists who talk much but lack practical experience</note> (a tribe that speaks without experience) assert that it is of a cold and moist nature. Consequently, they strive to coagulate it with nothing but hot things. However, they wish it to be solid, but they only succeed in making it more fluid, a fact they eventually learn every day to their own loss. Otherwise, true **Alchemy**, which by a single art produces Gold <note>the Sun</note> or Silver <note>the Moon</note> from the five...

### *Concerning the plain manifestation of this art.*

### CHAPTER XXVII.

When you have caused the sky or the sphere of **Saturn** <term>Saturn: In the chemical shorthand of the time, Saturn refers to the metal Lead</term> to run with life upon the earth, impose all the planets <note>The "planets" refer to the seven metals of antiquity: Gold, Silver, Mercury, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead.</note> or whichever ones you wish, provided that the moon <note>silver</note> is not too present, but that less of it is added than the others. Allow them all to run for so long as it takes for the sky of Saturn to vanish completely. In this way, all the planets remain consistent so that, their old and corruptible bodies being dead, they have put on a new, perfect, and incorruptible body. This is the very spirit of the sky, from which the named planets become corporal and living again, as they were before. Take this new body from life and from the earth, and preserve it: this is the sun and the moon <note>Gold and Silver</note>. In this manner, you have the art entirely manifest and complete. If you do not yet understand or know it, it is well: for it ought to remain so, and not be made commonly or openly known to everyone indifferently.

# ON THE GENERATION
## of Minerals.
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' with a decorative background of swirling foliage and stems inside a square border.</image-desc>
When I had read the writings of the ancients concerning the generation of minerals with the greatest care, I discovered that they did not understand the ultimate matter <term>Ultimate matter: In alchemy, the "materia ultima" is the final, completed form of a substance, whereas "materia prima" is the raw, unformed starting material.</term> of those things, and consequently, much less did they understand the first matter. Indeed, so that the beginning of any thing may be rightly known, the end must be known first of all. Therefore, I have decided to propose to us first of all the ultimate matter of minerals, from which you will easily understand the first matter from which they take their origin. Let us first bring forward an example from medicine, where a disease must be known by its outcome, and not by its beginning (in which there is no knowledge); because that which is introduced through blindness must itself be blind. But the end is visible from the outcome, toward which the disease is perceived to tend as if toward a target set for itself. Furthermore, no thing can be better known than when it is best understood for what end it was created by God; otherwise, it will easily happen that the true use of God’s creature turns into an abuse. Whoever, therefore, undertakes any work from any material must know that very material from the roots up, so that he may complete it according to the order prescribed by God. This is to ensure that, because of an imperfect knowledge of the matter—or sometimes no knowledge at all—things do not turn out otherwise, and the work of the devil be performed instead through the abuse of matter and tools. Let this be a sufficiently rough example: of what use is an ax or a mattock, and wood or any other matter, in the hand of one who does not know how to use them? To what other end do they tend...

can be used, rather than for their destruction. However, he can and should take it into his hands who knows how to fashion a lawful and honest work from the instruments and material—one that serves the utility of his neighbor, while keeping for his own use the material as it was given by God. For God willed that every thing He created should be held and possessed by the one to whom He gave the true knowledge of its use. To this end, everyone must apply themselves who perceives in their own conscience that they are called to it, and likewise learn this, not some alien, fantastic thing suggested by the devil.

Learn, therefore, the ultimate matter <term>Ultimate matter (materia ultima): The final, perfected form of a substance after it has been processed, as opposed to the raw "first matter."</term> and the first matter of things from fire; for fire, like a key, opens the chest. It makes whatever is hidden in anything manifest. Therefore, in this place, the ultimate matter of things is that into which they are entirely resolved by fire, so that at last, among the three universal first principles <term>The Tria Prima: Paracelsus’s three primary components—Salt (the solid body), Sulfur (the soul or fuel), and Mercury (the spirit or fluid)—which make up all physical matter.</term> about which I have discussed in various places, the first and predominating one may be known. 

Take, for example, a metal dissolved by fire; it immediately reveals its first beginning to be mercurial water <note>original: "mercurialem aquam"</note>, and not sulfur, because its resolution does not burn like resins. It is also shown not to be salt, because the first sign of its resolution is not crumbling <note>original: "friatio"</note> besides melting and burning, as seems to be the case with earthy things and stones. Nonetheless, every metal contains within itself sulfur and salt, but Mercury holds the chief place in it; and so it is with the other minerals. 

Truly, it seemed good to God to create the element of water, and that every kind of mineral for the use of men should be produced from it daily, so that it might be their mother. In water, as if in their womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>, the mineral fire, and likewise salt and Mercury, are cooked into metals, stones, and every mineral substance, even though the offspring looks unlike the mother. In this way, the Most High created all things in their own nature, so that birds are in the air and fish are in the waters; and so it is with all other things, which must be committed solely to His divine will—He who makes all things as they are, and willed from eternity that they be what He makes. 

Thus, just as water is not similar to its metallic offspring, nor a son to his mother, no differently is the earth itself wood, and yet it is not the wood which nevertheless comes from it. By the same logic, stone and iron are made from water—which water is of such a kind that it does not exist as that which it becomes. Similarly, earth becomes that which it is not in itself. So also must man become that which he himself currently is not <note>This reflects a core alchemical belief: just as base metals are "born" from water to become solid iron, man must undergo a spiritual transformation to reach his "ultimate matter."</note>. 

In sum, whatever must pass into its ultimate matter must become something other than what its beginning was—each various and diverse in its own kind, even from a single mother. Thus God willed to be one in all things, and likewise that there be one first and ultimate matter of all. Such and so wonderful is the first Artisan of things, the likes of whom never was before, nor ever shall be another. But as you have heard so far concerning water as the mother of minerals, in what follows we shall teach further that the ancients wrote wrongly and incorrectly that the mother was earth—a claim they have not yet been able truly to demonstrate.

## *On the Ultimate and First Matter of Minerals.*

### CHAPTER II.

The first principle with God was the **ultimate matter** <term>Ultimate matter (materia ultima): In this context, the final, perfected form a substance takes in nature, such as a fully formed metal.</term>, which He Himself made into the **first matter**, like a fruit that might produce another fruit; that very matter contains the seed, and this seed resides in the first matter. Similarly, in the ultimate matter of minerals, the first matter was created—that is, it was made into seed. This seed is the **element of water**, which dissolves so that it becomes water. To this end, God entrusted or ordained within nature that it should produce the ultimate matter, and this matter is indeed contained within the water.

Therefore, nature takes what is in the water under its own power and separation; it segregates whatever belongs to a metal into a metal, each one by itself. It does the same for gems, stones, the magnet, and others of that kind, each separately in its own nature and according to its species. For just as God ordained for wheat its own time for harvest, and autumn for sweets <note>original: "bellariis" — referring to the pleasant fruits or delicacies of the harvest</note> and similar things in their elements, He likewise willed that the element of water should have its own proper time of harvest and autumn. He prefixed for all other things in their kind their own specific times for gathering their fruits.

Thus, the element of water is the **mother, seed, and root** of all minerals. The **Archeus** <term>Archeus: The internal "craftsman" or vital force in nature that directs the growth and transformation of matter.</term> within the water is the one who disposes each thing in a certain order, so that every single thing reaches its natural ultimate matter. This is what man finally receives as his own **artificial first matter**. That is to say: **where nature finishes, there the art of man begins**; for nature’s ultimate matter is man’s first matter. Conversely, the corruption of nature through art <note>In alchemy, "corruption" often refers to the breaking down or "killing" of a substance so it can be reborn in a higher form.</note> becomes man’s ultimate matter.

With such wondrous workmanship, God created water as the first matter of nature—a substance so soft and weak—and yet from it comes the most solid fruit: metals, stones, and so on. That from the softest should come the hardest, and that **fire should come from water** <note>original: "ex aqua ignis" — likely referring to the "igneous" or sulfurous spirit contained within metallic ores born from water</note>, is beyond the grasp of human intellect, yet it is not beyond nature. Indeed, God created marvelous offspring from that mother, just as is apparent in humans; if they are observed even within their mother, each will be found unique in talent and property—not just in body, but according to the condition of their temperament.

## *On the Field, Roots, and Trees of Minerals.*

### CHAPTER III.

The Most High created the element of water to be like a **field** in which the roots of mineral trees, sprung from their seeds, might be fixed. From there, the trunk and branches might be thrust forth into the earth, as will be described more broadly below. Therefore, He separated water from the other three elements so that it would exist not in the air, nor in the earth, nor in the heavens, but as a free body by itself, positioned in the lower sphere. Thus, it sits upon the earth and has its center within it, where it is founded. It was created in such a wondrous order that, together with the earth, it must carry man, as if on water in some ship—

...moves and maintains its position; likewise, what is more wonderful is that it is carried everywhere around the globe and does not fall outside its limits, even if the side of the **antipodes** <term>Antipodes: A term used to describe people or places on the opposite side of the earth, where "up" and "down" seem reversed.</term> seems to us to be hanging, and our side to them; nevertheless, both lie facing upward. Nor is it supported by the earth, but far more wonderfully than an egg in its shell (though it lacks one entirely), it is contained.

Therefore, the generations of all minerals are thrust out from the **element of water** into the earth, just as all fruits from the element of earth are thrust into the air, so that nothing remains in the earth except the root itself. In no different way, all metals, rock salt, stones, talc, marcasites, sulfurs, and any similar things, enter from their mother, water, into another mother—namely, the earth. In the earth, the work of their trees is perfected, just as the roots of the earth are perfected in the air. Likewise, those things which take their origin in the waters are fully completed in the earth by nature into their final, ultimate matter.

Led astray by this opinion, the ancients, because they saw metals found in the earth, did not progress further in their minds; they did not think they erred so enormously in writing about minerals. Yet, from the earth, nothing grows except wood, foliage, flowers, fruit, and herbs; what remains is born from water. One would happen to tell fables and speak foolishly if they asserted that the products of the earth took their origin from the air, simply because they are in it and are perfected there, when one sees the roots in the earth. Truly, because one has not seen the roots of minerals in the waters with fleshy eyes, he will also babble that they are fixed in the earth. Such is the **Physics of the Greeks** <note>original: "Græcorum Phyſica" — This refers to the traditional Aristotelian natural philosophy taught in universities, which Paracelsian thinkers criticized for relying on logic and "manifest" (visible) appearances rather than chemical experience.</note>, namely, derived solely from the manifest, seeing nothing of the hidden through mental experiment. It is a fiction of idle men who presume only to chatter about natural things based on what the eye sees, and do not work so that the hidden things beneath the manifest may be examined—things which are always and in all cases opposites.

### *On the fruits and harvest of minerals.*

## CHAPTER IV.

In no way differently than all the fruits of the earth have their harvest and autumn above the earth and in the air within their generation, according to a predestined limit; so the aqueous fruits, namely minerals, are gathered at their own time of maturity. Indeed, when the mineral root first germinates, they rise up into their own trunk and tree—that is, into a body from which minerals or metals are finally produced. Just as a nut or a cherry is not born immediately from the earth, but first the tree grows, from which the fruit is at last generated; nature similarly brings forth a **mineral tree** in the element of water—that is, an aqueous body. This is born in the earth; that is, it fills the pores of the earth, just as...
