From the earth, finally, fruits spring forth according to the nature and property of their species; they appear at the ends of branches, more or less abundantly, as is common in the visible trees on the surface. Therefore, one must first seek the **aqueous tree** <note>original: "arbor aquea." Paracelsus and his followers often used the metaphor of a "tree" to describe the branching veins of ore in a mine, which they believed grew from a "seed" in the water.</note> and finally its fruit, taking a lesson by example from the agriculture of the earth—not unsuitably—in this manner. Some visible trees produce their fruits covered up, such as chestnuts under a prickly husk, or walnuts under a bitter green one; beneath that is a wooden shell, under which is a bitter membrane, and finally, beneath that, the kernel. The same thing happens in minerals; their kernels—namely, the metals—must be separated from their rinds, just like those fruits. Other trees bring forth naked fruits, such as plums, **cherries** <note>The original "cera" is likely a shorthand or printer's error for "cerasa" (cherries), given the context of orchard fruits.</note>, pears, apples, clusters of grapes, and so on, from which nothing is separated. Similarly, some aqueous trees produce their gold, silver, coral, and other metals of that kind free and naked, according to the condition and nature of the water. Just as one can know from the rind what lies within or beneath it, or as a **spirit** <term>Spirit: In this context, the "spirit" refers to the essential, active property or "soul" of a substance that gives it its specific identity (e.g., being "goldness").</term> is known by its body, so in minerals the hidden spirit of the metal is known beneath its corporeal or mineral rind. Furthermore, the spirit of the aqueous element creates a body, but it is one thing in the mineral and another in the fruit. Therefore, although gold may be in a mineral body, that body is nevertheless of no importance; for that reason, it must be separated from the gold as something impure, whereas the body of the gold itself is pure. There are, then, two bodies in a mineral: one is the pure body of the fruit of gold, into which its spirit is inseparably incorporated; the other is the impure matrix. Thus, the fruits are first introduced from the element into the tree as a spirit into an impure body, and with that they are finally brought into the earth, noble and pure. The very same thing is seen in man, who happens to have two bodies: one corruptible, the other truly incorruptible—which is the **image of God** <note>The "Imago Dei." The author argues that just as a metal has a pure "spirit-body" inside a rocky shell, man has a divine, eternal essence inside a mortal frame.</note>—joined to it eternally, and it is because of this especially that he differs from all other creatures.

## On the death of the elements, and especially of water.

### CHAPTER V.

**E**lements also die because of **corruption** <term>Corruption: In the philosophical sense, this refers to the breaking down, decaying, or changing of a substance from its natural state.</term> (just as men do) within themselves. As for water, it exists as its own death, for it devours and consumes its own fruits, just as the earth does its own. For whatever is born from the earth, returning to it again, is absorbed and vanishes, like time past going through yesterday's days and nights, whose light or darkness one can never see again. Nor is the earth any heavier today than it was yesterday—not even by a **drachmula** <note>A "drachmula" is a very small unit of weight, similar to a dram.</note>—and after a thousand years it remains under the same weight; as it brings forth, it also consumes equally. Now, the death of water is in its own element, in the great boundary and center of water—namely, the sea—into which the rivers of all waters and whatever flows into it... <meta>The catchword "defluit" (flows down) indicates the continuation of the sentence on the next page.</meta>

->*On the death of the tree of minerals.*<-

### CHAPTER VI.

After nature has planted the root of the mineral tree in the center of its matrix—whether to produce a metal, stone, gem, salt, alum, vitriol, a salty spring, or one that is sweet, cold, or hot, or perhaps coral or marcasite—and has thrust its trunk into the earth, it is spread here through various branches. The substance of these branches and the trunk is a liquid, not in the fashion of water, nor oil, nor mud, nor slime; rather, it should be understood no differently than wood born from the earth, which is not earth itself, yet nevertheless has its origin from it. They extend in such a way that one branch may be separated from another by an interval of two or three climates <note>In historical geography, "climates" refers to latitudinal zones of the Earth’s surface.</note>, and as many regions: sometimes from Germany into Hungary and beyond. The branches of various trees of this kind are entwined through the entire sphere of the earth, just as veins are extended in the human body into different limbs distant from one another. The fruit, indeed, is thrust forth through the tips of the shoots from the matter of the final nature; as soon as they reach the earth, their coagulation becomes instantaneous. Then, once its entire fruit has been expelled, this tree dies and is utterly consumed by drying out in the earth, leaving its offspring <note>original: "fœtu". Refers here to the deposited mineral ore.</note> behind; shortly after, according to the condition of nature, another fresh one appears.

Thus, the first matter of minerals consists in water, and in it alone are the mineral **sulphur**, **salt**, and **mercury** <term>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury: Known as the "Tria Prima," these were the three primary principles Paracelsus believed composed all solid matter (representing soul, body, and spirit).</term>, which are the spirit and soul of that same element. They contain within themselves all minerals, metals, gems, salts, and other things of that kind, like various seeds in a sack. Once poured out into the waters, nature subsequently directs and tirelessly arranges each seed toward its own proper and final fruit according to its species and kinds. These and similar things come forth from true **Physics** <term>Physics: Used here in the classical sense of "Physica," the study of the inner workings of nature and the divine laws governing matter.</term> and the fountains of true philosophy. From these, through meditative contemplations of the wonderful works of God, there arises a genuine knowledge of the supreme Creator and His virtues. This appears in the minds and mental eyes of those who philosophize no less than the manifest light of the flesh; to them, what is hidden becomes manifest.

But that Greek Satan <note>A derogatory reference to Aristotle, whose logic-based approach Paracelsus loathed.</note> has sown false weeds and his own seed into the philosophical field of true wisdom: **Aristotle**, **Albertus**, **Avicenna**, **Rhazes**, and that sort of men, enemies of the light of God and of nature, who have perverted all physical wisdom from the time they changed the name of **Sophia** <note>original: "Sophia," the Greek word for Wisdom, often implying a divine or mystical understanding.</note> into "Philosophy" <note>The author suggests that "Philosophy" (the love of wisdom) became a mere academic exercise compared to the direct, divine insight of "Sophia."</note>.

## *On the Variation of the Primary Matter of Minerals, according to the Diversity of its Species and Individuals, and on Various Colors, etc.*

### CHAPTER VII.

We have stated previously that the <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: *materiam primam*; the fundamental, unformed substance from which all things are created</note> exists within its "mother" <note>the matrix or surrounding earth</note> as if inside a certain sac, and is composed of three things meeting as one. Yet, there are as many varieties of **Mercury**, **Salt**, and **Sulphur** as there are types and variations of "fruits" among minerals. For there is one kind of sulphur found in lead, iron, or gold, and another in sapphires, gems, and other stones, or in <term>marcasites</term> <note>a term used historically to describe various metallic ores, often iron pyrites</note> and salts. Similarly, one must judge the Salt found in metals to be distinct from that in other salts; likewise with Mercury, for one kind exists in gems and another in metals. Furthermore, due to the different compositions of these three, various individuals are found under the same species: for gold is sometimes found to be heavier or more deeply colored than other gold, and so it is with the rest.

Accordingly, there are as many diversities of sulphur, salt, and mercury for gold and other substances as there are greater and lesser degrees of quality. Nonetheless, everything that receives its specific character from a subject is always contained within the universality of one and the same Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, which are mysteriously encompassed within universal nature. In this regard, Nature could be compared to a painter who fashions infinite images from only a few colors, no two of which are entirely alike; they differ only in this: Nature produces living things, while the painter, imitating her, represents those same things to the eye, but dead.

All natural colors proceed from the **Salt** of nature, in which they reside along with the <term>balsam</term> <note>a vital, preservative essence believed to prevent decay</note> and the coagulation of things. **Sulphur** provides the substance and structure of bodies, while **Mercury** holds the virtues and <term>arcana</term> <note>secret or hidden spiritual powers</note>. God alone grants life to all things, so that from each may come that which He predestined from eternity, and in which He was pleased and willed for all things to be so.

Therefore, whoever wishes to know the bodies of natural things should learn from natural Sulphur, ensuring first that he knows it well. If he seeks to understand natural colors, let him seek their foundation in Salt. If, however, he desires to know the virtues of things, he must scrutinize the *arcana* of the Mercury of that same thing whose powers he wishes to understand. Nature herself embraces all these things together into one, separates them, distributes to each its own, takes them away, and wipes out colors. 

Consider, I pray, a tiny grain of seed, black or reddish-brown in color, from which grows a massive tree, producing such an admirable greenness in its leaves, such varied colors in its flowers, and such diverse flavors in its fruits. You will find Nature so admirable and wealthy in her mysteries regarding all other products, that you will have enough to learn for your entire life in this book of <term>physics</term> <note>original: *physices*; here meaning "the study of nature"</note> alone, leaving aside all paper books. If God, therefore, through Nature, offers Himself to be perceived by us...

### *Of the natural steward of minerals, and his subordinates.*
## CHAPTER VIII.

Just as in the craft of minerals performed by men, not just one person but several are required in succession to prepare and bring them into use, yet each of them has a specific gift of office. For what benefit are minerals dug out from the bowels of the earth without their separator, preparer, or smelter? What is the smelter without the blacksmith? Likewise, the blacksmith can do nothing without a buyer, nor the buyer without the one who knows how to adapt metals for use. Nature itself does not need all these human agents, but only its own, such as the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the "internal chemist" or vital force that directs the growth and formation of things in nature</note>, the primary steward of minerals. He has ministers under him—being himself the minister of nature—of which the first provides the bodily matter upon which the work is performed, namely mineral **Sulphur** of one condition or another. The second minister is the one who fashions and works the properties and virtues into the underlying matter, namely **Mercury**. The third is the one who, through compaction and coagulation, unites these individual parts together into one body, namely **Salt**, the confirmer of the work.

All these things, gathered together and enclosed within his <term>Athanor</term> <note>an alchemical furnace designed to maintain a steady, prolonged heat</note>, the Archeus "cooks" or digests, just as a seed is digested in the earth. And they are not only cooked within that furnace, but also mutually among themselves in this manner: Sulphur submits its body to the other two, so that they may work upon it whatever they wish and bring it to that end for which the final product is destined. Mercury joins in with the properties of its virtues, and is cooked out of the other two. When these "digestions" of all parts are completed, then finally the Salt begins to work upon its companions and upon itself—first by condensing, and then by...

## *On the Virtues and Properties of Salts in Alchemy and Medicine.*

### CHAPTER IX.

Almighty God <note>original: *O.D.M.*, likely *Optimus Deus Maximus*</note> willed through nature to bring man to such necessity that he cannot live naturally without natural salt. Therefore, this [salt] has a role in all foods. For salt is the balsam of nature, which prevents the corruption of hot <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, Sulphur represents the principle of combustion, growth, and heat</note> and moist <term>Mercury</term> <note>Mercury represents the principle of fluidity, volatility, and moisture</note>, from which natural man is composed. Since it is necessary that these first seasoning elements—and whatever is seasoned—be nourished by their like, it follows of necessity that man must use burning foods to sustain his internal Sulphur; moist foods to nourish his Mercury; and likewise salty foods to preserve the salt in its seasoning faculty. The power of its preservation is seen most clearly when it preserves dead flesh from rot for a very long time; it is easy to judge how much more it will preserve living things. To finally come to its types, there are three held to be most suitable for the use of human life. The first of these is sea salt, the second is spring salt, and the third is mineral salt. Spring salt is most conducive to health, mineral salt holds the second place, and finally sea salt. This last and the first are processed by art <note>meaning "man-made" through evaporation or boiling</note>, but the remaining one [mineral or rock salt] is cooked by nature alone. This and sea salt are not categorized under the nature of brine <note>original: *muria*</note>, but that which is boiled [spring salt] is first turned into it before it is separated from the water into coagulated salt. Therefore, we must present two descriptions of salt: one concerning brine, and the other concerning fully finished salt. First of all, however, a certain common condition for the correction <note>improvement or purification for use</note> of any salt must be considered, in this manner: Wherever salt is not added to foods, in those foods there is also no correction,

Therefore, the operations of the spirits of salt <note>original: *spirituum salis*; the volatile or essential parts of salt separated through alchemical processes</note> in the three species already mentioned must be most diligently observed through practice, which—not only in these but in all other matters—opens the eyes more than any writing or description.

## CHAPTER X.

Very recently, I mentioned two descriptions of salt: namely, brine and dry salt. Concerning brine <note>original: *muria*; a concentrated solution of salt in water</note>, the first thing to be known is that it possesses the greatest powers for drying out any superfluous moisture; indeed, it can do more in one hour than dry salt can in a month. Although the latter might also be reduced into brine, it can never provide what the natural kind does—such as curing "moist" gout <note>original: *podagra*; a painful inflammation of the joints, here described as being caused by excess fluid</note>, dropsy <note>original: *hydropisis*; a condition where excess fluid accumulates in the tissues or cavities of the body</note>, and any moist tumors of the shins and others; and, in short, to consume corrupt, unnatural fluids, provided that it has been tempered from its heat so that the patient can sit in it as in a bath without injury. The test for the perfection of brine is made by an egg thrown into it, which should float on the surface. It must be noted, however, that a bath of this kind is beneficial only to bodies that are naturally obese; for those thinned by nature into emaciation, it is not to be advised at all, because it dries too much. If perhaps after one or two bathings the humors should return to those places...

### On Dry Salt.
### CHAPTER XI.

There are various species of dry salts, such as common food salts, **salt gems** <term>sal gemmae: a pure, transparent form of rock salt</term>, stone salts, earth salts, and those congealed into the shape of cones; you should note the common power of all of these. Any of these, when mixed with **sulfur** and applied to wounds—whether in the manner of a plaster or as a wash—protects them from **worms** <note>original: *vermiculus*; in this context, referring to maggots or parasites that infest open wounds</note>, and even drives out those already born so that they may not grow further. For through the means of cleansing alone, nature heals wounds by herself with no other intervening medicine, unless some **poisonous complexion** <note>an imbalance of the body's humors or an external toxin</note> acts as an obstacle to the free operation of the **natural balsam** <term>natural balsam: an innate healing fluid or life force believed to reside in all living tissue</term>.

The cure of ulcers also depends significantly on such salts, as do all forms of **scabies** <note>a general term for itchy skin diseases or mange</note> and similar ailments, if the salts are dissolved in baths. However, the powers of **brine** <note>original: *muriæ*</note> are far more potent; these can be further increased by dissolving salts within the brine itself to treat many external defects, such as **alopecia** <note>hair loss</note> and other things of that kind, especially if these salts are corrected by addition or increased in power in the following manner.

Take dry salt and **salt of urine** <term>salt of urine: also known as microcosmic salt, obtained from evaporated human urine</term>, equal parts of whatever quantity you wish; let them be **calcined** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a friable powder</term> together for two hours, and afterward let them be dissolved in brine, or by themselves in a cold and damp place. They will yield an artificial brine only slightly less powerful than the natural kind for external surgical cares, though for other internal uses it is far weaker. The salts which have been mentioned will never be found in any other things, even if **alkali** <note>original: *alcali*; here referring to the caustic salts derived from wood ashes or specific minerals</note> is boiled out of them; this is not like the salt previously described, but is called the natural or corporeal alkali of things, which is nourished in the human body by the salts of food, or even by the preceding dry and highly nutritive salts.

For the work of **Alchemy**, however, a **water of salt** is made from such calcined salts, drawn forth into a **spirit** <note>an essence or volatile liquid obtained through distillation</note>, by which **gold** is dissolved into **oil** and separated from it, so that it remains as the best **potable gold** <term>aurum potabile: "drinkable gold," a legendary alchemical elixir believed to have universal healing powers</term> or drink. Before it reaches that final completion, it is nonetheless—as we have heard—distinguished as a noble artifice and a constant treasure for goldsmiths to gild silver and for blacksmiths to gild iron, provided they know how to prepare it through the chemical art.

It should also be noted regarding pure salt congealed by nature alone, whether into cones or into **salt gem**, that this is most suitable for the common **cementations** <term>cementation: a process where a metal is heated while packed in a powdered substance to purify it or alter its properties</term> of silver; it renders the metal **malleable** beyond the usual firings. ## *On the salt nitre.*
### CHAPTER XII.

There is also another kind of salt called **nitre** <note>original: *nitrum*; often referring to saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note>, which is naturally composed of the natural salt of animal bodies combined with the salts of nutrition within the body. From these two, a single substance is formed; the excess is processed into urine, and falling upon the earth, it is "cooked" again in its own time. The parts become more and more united until a unique and perfect salt results. Through chemical separation—using artificial boiling to remove it from the earth—it appears clearly bright and transparent in the form of cones or lumps. This occurs if it is well-separated from the superfluous salt of nutrition that was not yet digested by the animal’s internal heat when it was expelled in the urine.

The use of this salt is most frequent in **Alchemy**. It would be unnecessary to recount how much violence it can display, as first demonstrated by experience with a most ruinous outcome when composed with sulfur to create **gunpowder** <note>original: *pulvere bombardico*</note>; because of this power, it could rightly be called "earthly lightning." 

In the same way, from the salt of the earth’s liquid—which is a **universal natural balsam** <term>universal natural balsam: a theoretical life-preserving substance believed to permeate the earth</term> by which all things are preserved in their composition—this particular salt is born as it returns to the earth through the resolution of things. Afterward, straining through the pores of the earth, it coagulates into the shape of icy cones adhering to rocks, which is why its name changed from nitre to **saltpeter** <note>original: *sal petræ*, literally "salt of the rock"</note>. However, neither form is particularly suitable for internal medicine, except perhaps for bringing thinness to obese bodies. Even then, it is not a very safe remedy unless it is mixed with salt of copper through the work of extraction, so that the two or three components may come together for their intended use.

## *On the fault of nutritional salt.*
### CHAPTER XIII.

Any food salt that has not been digested by the stomach and passes into the intestines through expulsion will generate **colic or the iliac passion** <note>original: *colicam, iliacamve passionem*; severe abdominal pain often associated with bowel obstruction</note>, which is more difficult to cure than almost any other ailment. Indeed, by its corrosive nature, it has sometimes perforated the intestines, as has been seen in anatomical studies. 

If, however, it remains unexpelled in the stomach, **acidic belching and heartburn** <note>original: *orexes & arsuræ*</note>, as well as many other stomach afflictions, arise at the opening of the stomach. It also happens occasionally that undigested salt becomes blocked in the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: *venis mesaraicis*; the veins that drain blood from the intestines</note> and hardens into granules. From this arise the most serious unknown illnesses, not only in these parts but also in other parts of the entire body, and especially those around which the urine has its **excretory organ** <term>emunctorium: a biological term for an organ that carries off waste, such as the kidneys</term>. 

Let what has been said regarding the types, faults, and virtues of salts suffice for now; we must now turn to another mineral salt called **vitriol** <note>original: *vitriolum*; metallic sulfates, often associated with green or blue crystals</note>, which is the most excellent of all others in both Alchemy and Medicine.

### *On Vitriol.*
## CHAPTER XIV.

Nature produces from the depths of the earth a certain kind of salt called **vitriol** <note>original: *vitriolum*; historically referring to sulfate minerals, such as iron sulfate (green vitriol) or copper sulfate (blue vitriol)</note>, possessing such great powers and virtues that they can scarcely ever be sufficiently described by anyone. Indeed, within it lie perfect cures for **jaundice** <note>original: *ictericiæ*</note>, **gravel** <note>original: *arenæ*; small stones or sediment in the kidneys</note>, **stones**, **fevers**, **worms**, **epilepsy** <note>original: *caduci*</note>, and many other diseases of that kind which are very difficult to treat, arising from **obstructions** <note>original: *oppilationibus*; blockages of the internal organs or vessels</note>, as will be discussed more broadly below. In both branches of knowledge—namely Medicine and **Alchemy**—it performs wondrous operations and various effects according to the manner of its preparation. For from it, just as various images are carved from a single piece of wood, various excellent medicines are likewise prepared for both internal and surgical cures, such as for **scald head** <note>original: *tineam*; a fungal scalp infection</note> and leprosy. In short, whatever other medicines cannot provide due to their weakness against diseases, vitriol removes it all by uprooting the ailment from its foundation. Its virtues must be understood first: it reveals some while existing in its raw state, others when reduced to water, others when **calcined** <term>calcined: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts and reduce it to a powder</term>, and still others when turned into a green oil, or in the form of a red oil, and yet others in the form of a white oil; it takes on as many new virtues as it receives forms through preparation. It alone can substitute for a fourth part of all diseases and drugs yet devised. Therefore, there is no need for a true physician to turn his eyes here and there toward diverse things, but like a modest maiden, he should keep them fixed upon the ground. For in this earth beneath his feet, he will find far more power and wealth in this treasure of nature than India, Egypt, Barbary, or Greece could ever offer.

### *On the types of Vitriol and its testing.*
## CHAPTER XV.

The species of vitriol are as varied as the mines from which it is dug, or the springs from which it flows. Likewise, different tests are performed to determine its greater or lesser excellence. Let this be the first: if it tints an iron plate the color of **copper** <note>original: *cupri*</note> without the use of fire; the deeper the color, the better it is judged. Truly, this test is the easiest among others. The second is when the raw substance, administered by mouth, expels intestinal worms more vehemently than other remedies; the more powerfully it does so, the better it is for medicine. The third is when it transmutes iron into copper; the more perfectly and quickly it does this, the more excellent it is to be held in both faculties, for there is a great affinity between these two metals. This is not a thing to be wondered at, since through **borax water** <note>original: *aquam boracis*</note>, **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> is likewise made from lead. There are also other kinds of **cachimia** <term>cachimia: an alchemical term for mineral ores or residues that are not yet fully formed into metals</term> which convert metals, and that famous spring in **Hungary**—or rather a torrent—originating from vitriol, or rather being vitriol in its entire substance...

### *On the virtues of vitriol in medicine, raw or calcined.*

## CHAPTER XVI.

**F**or the most severe pains of the stomach, and ailments arising from the immoderate consumption of food and drink, or for its poor digestion, vitriol—raw and administered in the quantity of six scruples <note>original: *comet ʒ*; "comet" is likely an OCR error for *scrupulorum* (scruples)</note> or three drops, or even three grains—to the weak in wine or water, and to the robust in distilled wine, thoroughly purges every vice, driving it out both upward and downward. In the secret arts, vitriol is called **grillus** or **grilla** <note>original: *grillus*; literally "cricket," a coded alchemical name</note>. Neither hellebore, nor colocynth, nor diagridion <note>original: *diagridion*; a preparation of the purgative resin scammony</note> purge as vehemently or cure as perfectly as this, nor do they have the power to expel worms. There is also, during the course of treatment, no better purging for the **falling sickness** <note>original: *caducum*; epilepsy</note> than that through vitriol. Properties of this kind have fallen to it from its dual nature—namely, of acidity and saltiness—which is why it is a medicine much nobler than others. Its **colcothar**, or what they call the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>original: *caput mortuum*; literally "dead head," the useless residue left after a chemical process</note>, being red, is not to be taken internally, nor is it suitable except for surgical cares, for putrid ulcers of the first degree of malignancy; however, the oil is to be taken for those which have reached the second and third degree. Its medicinal virtues are contained in other books on medicine, such as in the *Bundle of Paracelsian Flowers*; in this place, we proposed only to treat and gather into one those things which pertain to transmutatory Alchemy, even if medicinal matters sometimes compel us to digress from our purpose. Hence, we must see what vitriol provides in chemical matters, beyond the transmutation of iron into copper as we said above, the formula of which we thought to set down first. Although it is not as difficult a work as transmuting iron into gold, God wills that the lesser things be made known first, and the greater things remain hidden for a time, until **Elias the Artist** <note>original: *Helias artis*; a legendary messianic figure in Paracelsian alchemy expected to reveal all secrets of the natural world</note> arrives; for all arts have each their own particular genius, as understood in others—

## On the triple sulphur of minerals.

### CHAPTER XVII.

**S**ulphur should properly be called the "resin of the earth," in which innumerable virtues lie hidden in both faculties <note>meaning both the medical and alchemical arts</note>; however, it is powerful in neither when raw. Its **arcanum** <term>arcanum: the secret, essential healing or transformative power of a substance</term> alone, when rescued and freed from impurities, works wonders—if it is first washed to an excellent whiteness, like that seen in snow, through the **Isopic art** <note>original: *Isopicam artem*; a reference to purification by washing, named after the hyssop plant mentioned in biblical cleansings</note>. It possesses as many diverse virtues as it has various origins. For every metal or mineral contains a different sulphur within it. As we said above concerning the likeness of chestnuts and nuts, minerals are likewise wrapped in their own husks; however, the most excellent virtue lies hidden in the kernel, which is nourished and sustained by the external parts. In this place, it should be understood regarding sulphurs that the internal one is that which excels, called **embryonated** <term>embryonated: a Paracelsian term for a substance in its early, formative, or "fetal" state within a mineral ore</term> in the spagyric sense from its specific origin, such as the sulphur of the embryo of gold, or of a stone, and so on. The external sulphur, in which the embryonated form lies, is what we call the mineral. There is also a third kind, which is extracted from the kernels of minerals or metals, which can be called nothing better than the **animated** and spagyric sulphur of the art; this is to be applied to whatever is similar to it in both faculties. Or, to be better understood: the first is universal sulphur, which is a resin...

For what we called earth, as if it were the mother or father of other sulphurs, we call **mineral** [sulphur]. The second is when this takes on a metallic or mineral appearance; then it is finally called **embryonated** <note>meaning in an early, undeveloped, or "fetal" state</note>. The third, which is purified from these, exists as **spagirically** <term>spagiric: the alchemical art of separating and recombining the constituents of a substance</term> pure and without superfluities: **animated sulphur**. 

Two conditions of embryonated sulphur are to be noted: one becomes volatile from a fixed state; the other is a pure and living fire, both invisible and visible, and both pass into a similar consumption—namely, of wood and of disease <note>implying it acts as both a fuel for fire and a potent medicine</note>. The extraction of embryonated sulphur is done either by **sublimation** or by **descent** <term>descent: *per descensum*, a distillation method where heat is applied from above and the liquid flows downward</term>. But sometimes it is found by nature not so thoroughly mixed with others that, on account of its excessive subtlety, it cannot withstand the fire in such preparations; in these cases, it must be extracted from its mineral bodies by **strong water** <term>aqua fortis: nitric acid</term> and then coagulated. 

All this, when separated according to true harmony, contains within itself a golden nature. For this reason, it is to be sought in Alchemy above all others, because it easily receives fixation; indeed, it fixes gold in **cements** <note>pastes used in the dry refining of gold</note>, and in other metals, it fixes that which is not yet mature or is volatile.

However, gold is sought from it in vain unless it is first present by nature: it contains no silver, but gold alone, some more than others, as in the embryonated sulphur of **Venus** <note>original: *Veneris*; the alchemical name for copper</note>, of red talc, and of golden or iron **marcasite** <term>marcasite: a term then used for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</term>, which rarely lack gold. Whoever wishes to apply their hand to these things should remember and note well to separate such sulphur from gold with the greatest industry, and so ingeniously that nothing of the gold is lost. 

Many could be helped at this point with further instructions, but it is true that I remain silent. And unless it fought diametrically against the will of God—that everyone should grow rich equally—it would be very easy to fulfill the wishes of many in quite a few words. Since, however, riches lead the poor entirely away from the true path, taking away humility and piety and bringing pride and elation in their place, along with petulance and lack of self-control, it is better to remain silent, leaving indigence as a bridle for the poor of this sort and those greedy for wealth.

To come to mineral sulphur, the Master of the art led his soldiers <note>a metaphor for students or practitioners of alchemy</note> there, that they might consider that nothing can be generated from a woman without her husband: they saw, therefore, that art is the father who disposes all things. He applied the **spirit of transmutation**, by which mineral sulphur was joined with linseed oil, and from there, through the **decoction of the liver or lung** <note>original: *decoctionem hepatis vel pulmonis*; likely referring to the porous, dark-red appearance of *hepar sulphuris* (liver of sulphur)</note>, a certain form resulted. From that, a **double liquor** <term>liquor duplex</term> was afterwards produced: one white like milk, dense and oily; the other like a very red oil, thick as blood. Both were together, yet neither was mixed with the other; the white liquor settled at the bottom, while the other, namely the red one, floated on top. 

Progress was made further, so that from the white a **tincture for the white** <note>a substance to transmute metals into silver</note> might be made, but it was attempted in vain. This I know: that nothing came from it, nor ever can be made, because it is a certain empty and useless matter for this art. But every crystal or beryl placed in it at its proper time, and remaining in it as...

It happens similarly with the jacinth; and also with the **sapphire**, the blue color is increased beyond its natural state, with a translucent greenness interspersed through it. There is a most excellent **tincture** <term>tincture: a substance or "dye" capable of changing the color or essential quality of a material</term> for many other gems, and likewise for **silver** <note>original: *lunæ*</note>, which turns black when placed in it and deposits a **calx of gold** <note>a fine gold powder produced through chemical action</note>, though it is not yet "fixed" <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term> until it completes the limit of its perfection. Enough has been said of this. Whoever wishes to work with this tincture should first learn to industriously master the preparations of alchemy; for this is nearly the most difficult to prepare of all chemical operations. This oil provides so much in the way of colors; however, one should not believe it performs such wonders in the "greater virtues," because the tincture of color is merely in the color itself, and not in the inner medicinal virtue. Some have even attempted to extract tinctures from metals, but they were deceived in their opinion; it is not appropriate to explain the reason in this place. 

This, however, is most certain: whoever possesses the **tincture of gold** <note>original: *solis*</note> will be able to lead the body of gold beyond its natural grade—that is, from twenty-four to thirty-six degrees, and even higher, so intensely that it can ascend no further; nevertheless, it remains constant and fixed in **antimony** <note>used here as a purifying agent in assaying</note> and in every **quartation** <term>quartation: a refining process where gold is alloyed with three parts silver and then separated with acid</term>. The sulphur of **silver** [Luna] also exalts its own body to such a degree that **copper** <note>original: *Venus*</note>, when mixed with an equal weight of this silver, passes the judgment of the **Lydian stone** <term>Lydian stone: a touchstone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave</term>. The sulphur of copper [Venus] "fixes" copper so that it withstands the trial of the lightning <note>likely referring to the intense heat of the cupellation furnace</note>, though it does not tint it; combined with the sulphur of **lead** <note>original: *Saturni*</note> it turns into the best steel; with the sulphur of **tin** <note>original: *Jovis*</note> it becomes like the best iron. 

Likewise, tin is fixed by sulphur so that it also withstands the furnace-blast, and by its own sulphur, lead is confirmed and fixed so that it no longer yields any **white lead** <note>original: *cerussam*</note> or **red lead** <note>original: *minium*</note>, nor any "spirit" from itself. But the sulphur of **mercury** [quicksilver] makes its body malleable so that it can endure the firing of copper, though not the **ash-test** <term>ash-test: cupellation, where metals are heated on a porous bowl made of bone ash to separate noble metals from base ones</term>. Likewise, the sulphur of gold [Sol] tints silver but does not fix it. Transmutations of other sulphurs injected into a body other than their own also occur, but the matter does not reach the desired result. Meanwhile, it should be noted that sulphur requires a most expert operator, and not a presumptuous or imaginary one.

...to be contained in the stone; they thought white and red **electrum** <term>electrum: historically a natural alloy of gold and silver, but in alchemy, it often refers to specific artificial alloys or "intermediate" metallic states</term> were silver and gold, until they experienced the contrary through testing; a vain labor indeed. Not content with that, they made most obstinate progress toward **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term>, and they persisted until not a house or possession remained to those wretched men—experiencing the transmutation in themselves <note>original: *transmutationem in se potius*; an ironic joke that the alchemists "transformed" into paupers rather than transforming the metal into gold</note> rather than in the metals. And what wonder is this? They attacked this work without judgment or knowledge of minerals and metals, which even today the greatest part of those working in this art still do. From the time that "electrum," a name bestowed by the ancients, fell into oblivion, the ruin of those who falsely changed this name into "gold" and "silver" soon followed; that is to say, the perdition of modern chemists. 

To define **electrum**, however: it is a metal forged by art from another, no longer similar to that from which it was made. For example: an arsenical metal, prepared according to the ritual of metallic preparation and **cemented** <term>cementation: a process where a metal is heated with powdered reagents to change its properties</term> with **Venus** <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper</term> in the usual manner, converts the copper entirely into white electrum, which is actually cheaper than the copper itself. What need is there, then, to debase metals at great expense? Would it not have been better to leave the copper in its natural state, saving money, time, and labor to be applied to a more useful work? The ancients called it electrum by its proper name; more recent men falsely call it silver. The ancients suffered no loss because they knew what electrum was; the moderns, because they have no knowledge of electrum, suffer the loss of their wealth, labor, and time. 

But since errors in **Alchemy** are always bolstered by hope, it has come to the point that people have tried to **fix** arsenic through **reverberations** <note>reverberation: heating a substance by reflecting heat from the roof of a furnace onto the material</note> of reeds for several weeks, and by other means. The result was that the arsenic turned into a red, hard, and brittle form like coral, yet it is of no use in Alchemy except for making electrum, as mentioned above. Next, through **descension** <note>descension: a method of distillation where the substance is forced downwards through heat</note> and precipitation, they achieved nothing other than their own **calcinations** <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx"</term>. Thus it happens that obstinate men are deceived in Alchemy when they do not understand the vocabulary of their own art's impositions exactly and from the foundation. 

It is true that arsenic, by its own nature, contains gold, which through the industry of the Artist can sometimes be separated in the cement, or by **projection** <term>projection: the act of casting a small amount of "Philosopher's Stone" or tincture onto a molten base metal to transform it</term>, or otherwise into silver, copper, or lead by attraction. It does not follow, however, that this was produced through their operations and tinctures; rather, that which was already inside was merely brought forth through separation, just as it usually is from its own ore. Most often gold is found in it, and only very rarely does it lack gold, like many other things. So much for arsenic as far as I know or is fitting to write; let everyone first investigate its name very well and diligently so that they understand it, otherwise a very great error easily follows in both faculties <note>likely referring to the "faculties" of medicine and alchemy</note>, which finally

### CHAP. XIX.

Having finished our discussion on salts and sulfurs, we come to **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: also known as mercury (argentum vivum), the only metal that remains liquid at room temperature</term>. This cannot rightly be called a metal, but rather a "metallic water." It is called a metal only because, through the art of alchemy, it can be brought into a solid substance and into the color of metals—sometimes **fixed** <term>fixed: made stable and resistant to evaporation by heat</term>, and sometimes not fixed. It is enough to know that it is the "prime matter" <note>original: *primam materiam*; the foundational substance from which other things are formed</note> of the alchemists, who can use it to manufacture gold, silver, copper, and so on, provided they persist in their testing. Perhaps they may even produce tin, lead, and iron; for its nature is wonderful and cannot be fully understood except through the greatest labors. In short, it reveals itself as the first matter of the alchemists in the various metallic grades, and it is the greatest **arcanum** <term>arcanum: a profound medical or chemical secret; a powerful remedy</term> in medicine. It is a water that does not wet anything it touches, and a running animal without feet <note>This is a traditional alchemical riddle describing mercury's liquid, mobile nature and its high surface tension</note>, the heaviest of all metals. Like all individual things, it consists of **sulfur, salt, and mercury** <note>These are the "Tria Prima" or Three Primes of Paracelsian chemistry: the soul, body, and spirit of all matter</note>. It reveals the first and last matter in the melting of metals—especially in those that melt from their color without catching fire, and in others through their flow.

### CHAP. XX.

There is another kind of mineral body which is neither a salt nor a metal, but is "metallic" in nature. These include **marcasites** <term>marcasites: iron sulfide minerals, often confused with pyrite or "fool's gold"</term>, white and red **chifeta** <note>chifeta: an archaic term used by Paracelsus to describe certain mineral ores, likely related to pyrites or zinc-bearing minerals</note>, perfect and imperfect **antimonials**, **arsenicals**, **orpiments** <term>orpiment: a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral (auripigmentum) used as a pigment</term>, various **talcs**, **cobalt**, **garnets**, **gems**, and so on. These are, I say, metallic because they possess the "prime matter" of metals above all else and derive their origin from the three metallic principles. Metals such as gold, silver, copper, and iron seek refuge in them and are incorporated within them. However, because a "metallic enemy" is incorporated with them at the same time, the metals cannot be separated or rescued from the tyranny of that enemy except through alchemy. There are various such enemies who commit "robbery" against the metals—much as if someone seeking refuge by a hearth were to be plundered in that very house and killed by the one whose help he implored. Some of these minerals consist mostly of sulfur, such as marcasites, chifeta, and cobalt; others consist in the body of **Mercury**, such as the arsenicals, orpiments, and antimonials; while others consist in **Salt**, such as all the talc-like minerals. Marcasites are found in two colors, white and yellow, according to the metallic...

It avoids mixture with others, being a peculiar and admirable genus among minerals. Metallic grains are also found in torrents, called **garnets** <term>garnets: "granata," here referring to metallic-rich mineral grains found in stream beds</term> because of their external shape; they melt and can sustain the hammer, yet they cannot be fashioned into any instrument. Their properties cannot be known unless they are eventually revealed through **Alchemy**. They contain many "adulterine" <note>foreign or impure</note> metals, such as silver and gold, which tend to flow toward them just as they do toward copper and lead. They consist of a certain thick sulfur. Some other types of garnets are transparent, like crystal, and within these, gold and silver are present.

### CHAP. XXI.

**Saturn** <term>Saturn: the traditional alchemical name for lead</term> has obtained the blackest and thickest body of all, with a Mercury similar to it, and a salt that is more fusible <note>easily melted</note> than the others. Through corruption <note>chemical breakdown or oxidation</note>, it is easily reduced into its spirit, into white **ceruse** <term>ceruse: white lead, often used as a pigment</term>, into yellow, into **minium** <term>minium: red lead</term>, and finally into glass, like the rest. **Tin** <note>original: *Stannum*</note> is made from white fixed sulfur and fixed salt, but from mercury that is not fixed. And because it is fixed in its body, but not in its Mercury, it easily loses its metallic fusion when the spirit flies away through fire; indeed, when that spirit is absent, it is no longer a metal, but a "vanished" body. **Iron** and **steel** consist of non-liquefiable sulfur, salt, and mercury, which are the opposites of tin and lead. It coagulates into the hardest metal of all and "marries itself"—that is, two metals are found in one: the male, which is steel, and the female, which is iron. These can be separated for their own use, each one apart. **Gold** is generated from the purest...

...with the purest **sulfur** <term>sulfur: here referring to one of the "Three Primes" (Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt), the philosophical principles thought to make up all matter</term> highly sublimated by nature, and purified from all dregs and impurities, exalted to such transparency <note>original: *diaphanitatem*</note> that no other body among the metals can ascend higher. This sulfur is one part of the **primary matter of gold** <note>the fundamental, unformed substance from which gold is created</note>, which if the Alchemists could obtain—as it is indeed found in its own tree and root—they might rightly rejoice. For this is the true **sulfur of the philosophers** from which gold is made, not that other common type from which iron, copper, and other metals are formed. This is the small portion <note>original: *scrupulus*</note> of its universal self. Its **Mercury** is also highly separated by nature from every earthly and accidental excess, transformed separately into its own Mercurial part and into an extreme clarity. This **Mercury of the philosophers** is the second part of the primary matter of gold, from which gold ought to be born just as roses are born from rose seeds; it is sequestered to the highest crystalline clarity and purified from all sharpness of salt, bitterness, acidity, and the qualities of alum or vitriol, so that absolutely nothing clings to it as it now freely rejoices in the highest luminosity and transparency. When these three <note>the Sulfur, the Mercury, and the Salt (implied as the "body" or stabilizing force)</note> come together into one, gold is "cooked" into a mass, though not always of one and the same condition or grade. For nature exhibits **thirty-two degrees of gold**, which nonetheless in the Art <term>Art: the practice of alchemy or metallurgy</term> become **twenty-four degrees** in the highest state of perfection. The cause of this is that gold is nourished in its own "tree," just as a cow is nourished in its pastures, or an Epicurean <note>a person devoted to luxury and fine food</note> in his tavern and pantry; as soon as either of these leaves their pasture, they grow thin. It happens no differently with gold: as soon as it becomes the **primary matter of man** <note>likely referring to gold's use in medicinal elixirs or the "Gold of the Physicians"</note>, it is diminished by eight degrees. Truly, sometimes such "pastures" are of poorer quality, which results in even worse or fewer degrees of gold being produced, so that nature's highest grade might descend from twenty-six to ten in the Art. The accidents, or rather the influences, of the stars or the elements sometimes hinder the generation of gold, so that nature produces something coarser or more difficult to work with. But it is especially the inequality of the weights of the first three principles that matters: an excessive portion of **salt** makes it paler; too much **mercury** makes it yellower than is right; and with a more copious amount of **sulfur**, it is rendered too red. Among nature, just as among men, errors occur through these hindrances, which can be removed by **antimony**, **cementation**, and **quartation** <term>quartation: a refining process where gold is alloyed with silver and then separated with acid</term>. Furthermore, in sulfur nothing else is to be sought but the "body"; in salt, the "confirmation" or stability; but in **mercury** resides all virtue, property, essence, and medicine, which does not exist in the others as it does in this. In the others, it is as if in a dead body lacking spirit, in which some small amount of elemental virtue still remains—just as we experience in vinegar the remnants of the "fire of wine," which still preserve consuming and corrosive powers, yet are not nourishing or strengthening as they are in wine. Natural things are judged in their manifest state to be composed of the four elements, but in their hidden state, the matter is quite different:

<page-num>598</page-num>
# ON THE GENEALOGY

For they are composed of the three aforementioned things having only a common magnet among themselves, which, in the decoction of preparation, draws the trinity of essence to itself. Ancient natural philosophers <term>physici: those who study the laws of nature and matter</term> called this a "state" because the trinity acquires a state of unity in which natural motion rests and stays its step. Truly, that magnetic virtue which attracted the medicine <note>original: *medicinam*; in alchemy, this refers to the refined essence or transmuting agent</note> into **Mercury**—in which it is also found—should rightly be called a fourth being (though not an element); however, in the final separation, **Mercury** loses a great deal of its weight. 

With all these things disposed by nature in this way, **gold** grows forth into a tree, extending first from the root through the trunk into its branches and sprays <note>original: *locustas*, referring here to the tender shoots or branch tips of the metaphorical "mineral tree"</note>, in which flowers sprout (as is seen above the ground). Even when these flowers fade, the fruit is not always found at the tips of the shoots, but sometimes a few hundred paces deeper in the tree, sometimes in the middle, or several degrees toward the surface of the earth. 

It sometimes happens that nothing sprouts except **Mercury**, when it has suppressed the others by its excess; if, however, the **salts** dominate by their corrosive nature, they eat away the tree's flowers like worms. Under the dominion of **sulfur**, everything is scorched, just as on the earth's surface by the excessive heat of the sun. 

**Copper** is made from chestnut-brown sulfur, red salt, and yellow Mercury, driven together into a metal. This contains within itself its own "male" part—that is, the dross <term>scoria: the waste matter or slag separated from metal during smelting</term>—which, if it is reduced back into its metal after being separated, returns as masculine copper which will no longer be corrupted, and the "female" part will yield no dross of itself. In hammering and melting, they differ no more than **steel** and **iron**, and in the same way they can also be separated so that two different metals are made from them. 

**Silver** is composed of white sulfur, salt, and Mercury, prepared and fixed by nature to the highest degree of purity and transparency <note>original: *diaphaneitatis*</note>; it ranks next after gold in the cupel <term>cineritio: a refining process using a dish of bone ash to separate precious metals from base metals</term>, but not in antimony, nor in royal cement, nor in quartation <note>these are various advanced metallurgical refining processes: *cimento regali* and *quartatione*</note>. The difference in "fixity" <term>fixio: the quality of a substance that remains stable and does not volatilize when exposed to fire</term> between gold and silver is understood by this: gold is the male, having the most fixed masculine powers; silver, like the female, has weaker powers. They are of one and the same primary matter, and differ in color and fixity no more than male and female. 

There are, therefore, only **seven metals** in number, even excluding Mercury itself: **Gold, Silver, Tin, Lead, Iron, Steel, and Copper**. Although this last one contains male and female within it, since both are forged together for use and are not separated by nature as steel and iron are, they are considered as one. Because they also have the same equally workable hammering properties, they are not commonly separated unless it is done chemically for the use of the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or high metallurgy</note>. It must also be noted that in metals, the male is not always found produced by nature separately without its female,

...such as gold, silver, iron, and steel, each existing on its own; but quite often both appear together, as with gold and silver in a single ore, likewise steel and iron together, or tin and lead, yet in such a way that neither obstructs the other—indeed, they cannot be separated by natural means alone. Sometimes impure <note>original: *adulterina*; here meaning naturally mixed or non-native ores rather than counterfeit</note> metals are also found, such as gold and silver naturally mixed with others because of their subtlety. This happens especially when several different "first matters" <term>materiæ primæ: the fundamental substances of alchemy, often Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt</term> converge into a single body, just as we see above the ground an infinite variety of fruits growing from the trunk of a single tree.

### CONCLUSION.

Therefore, this appropriate discussion regarding the natural generation of minerals was highly necessary; for once this is properly understood, one may more easily grasp what the "regeneration" of metals achieved through the chemical art <term>artificio chemistico: alchemical practice</term> actually is, as described in the previous section. Indeed, it is the opinion of all who philosophize in this art that a practitioner of this profession must, above all else, imitate nature in every detail with the utmost precision. Accordingly, it was necessary both to describe and to understand what Nature does in the depths of the earth while managing her mineral household <term>mineralem œconomiam: the organized system or stewardship of mineral production</term>, as well as how she operates, what matter she employs, and what instruments she uses. Whoever fails to understand by this path will by no means reach the goal toward which his mind strives by any other way. Therefore, let him who investigates such a difficult and secret <note>original: *arcanam*; hidden or hermetic</note> matter become a disciple not only of the art but of nature herself.

<margin>Knowledge of medicine is from God.</margin>
If anyone wished to consider, kind Reader, the origin of Medicine, he would not trace it back to Machaon, nor to Podalyrius, nor from Hippocrates, and even less from Galen <note>original: *Machaone, Podalyrio, Hippocrate, Galeno*. Machaon and Podalyrius were mythical healers from the Trojan War; Hippocrates and Galen were the historical foundations of Greek and Roman medicine.</note>. We must rise higher: its origin must be sought even beyond the times of Chiron, indeed, of Apollo himself <note>original: *Chironis, Apollinis*. Chiron was the centaur who taught medicine; Apollo was the Greek god of healing.</note>. Therefore, let us refer ourselves most especially to those who lived the longest lives, such as Adam, Enoch, and the others. All of these, having been taught the science of nature by God, possessed a perfect knowledge of Medicine. This knowledge began to be gradually extinguished as sins grew stronger; and it was finally led into those shadows in which we see it enveloped today. And indeed, the first parent himself <note>Adam</note>, giving names to all things by God's command and inspiration, showed himself to be most skillful in all matters. From that knowledge of things—not only of their external appearance but of their innermost depths—Medicine descends. Let us, then, trace the principle of true Medicine from the patriarchs back to the Creator of all things himself.

<margin>Medicine is part of God's great works.</margin>
Holy Scripture teaches that the Most High created Medicine from the earth, and gave science to men so that the Most High might be honored in his wonders <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1-8, a favorite passage for Christian alchemists to justify their work.</note>. For Medicine is no small part of the great and wonderful works <term>magnalia: "great things" or "mighty acts," usually referring to divine miracles or the hidden powers of nature</term> of God, which human ingenuity could by no means recognize on its own, unless God himself manifested his wonders and great works. For it is impossible to have a complete and consistent Medicine without the knowledge of God, without piety, and without illumination received from the divine.

<margin>It is easier to write a Prescription than to apply one's hand to the work.</margin>

Medicine consists not in the body but in the specific form, in which alone the virtue resides. For the body is dead and unfit for action.*

# ON PHILOSOPHICAL MINERALS AND METALS: AND
## FIRSTLY ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL MERCURY
### of the philosophers, its subtle preparation and various powers.

From Mercury or Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for liquid mercury</term>, all "sulphurousness" or all parts of sulfur, along with leaden and earthy parts, must be removed—even if this seems absurd to many philosophers and those who do not closely understand the reasoning of the philosophers.

Mercury cleanses gold <note>original: "solem," literally "the sun," the alchemical symbol for gold</note> from all other metals, and everything floats upon it except for gold.

Gold sinks as it is heavier and immediately liquefies; so too with men <note>The author implies that just as mercury purifies gold by drawing it in, the philosophical medicine acts upon the human body.</note>.

Philosophical mercury is accustomed to purge itself of its own corrupt qualities, and to powerfully direct and drive away any excess toward the channels of elimination, as follows below.

The philosophers say: Our Mercury is not at all poisonous, but it removes whatever is in excess and adds what is lacking. <margin>Its use in Epilepsy.</margin> Furthermore, it contributes greatly as a "great theriac" <term>theriaca: a universal panacea or historical antidote used for poisons and various ailments</term> for those with epilepsy, those with intestinal issues <term>cœliacus: relating to the abdominal or intestinal cavity</term>, the intoxicated, or those infected by poison. For by its subtlety, it is able to penetrate all the veins of the body in an instant; it likewise checks growths in the flesh. <margin>For Dropsy.</margin> It heals those corrupted by dropsy <term>Hydrops: an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation</term> or other infirmities, cleanses the blood, and is marvelously useful for various abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"</note>. It heals old wounds as well as fresh ones, along with rotting ulcers. It opposes dysentery and all contagious diseases; it stops bleeding and the flow of fluid from the membrane of the brain. It brings ulcers to a scar and purges filth and sores from the eyes. <margin>For Cancer.</margin> It expels cancer and cancerous fistulas in a moderate dose and quantity of portion. <margin>For Scabies.</margin> It cures scabies <note>A contagious skin infestation causing itching and sores.</note> without harm. A scented ointment <term>smegma: here used in the classical sense of a cleansing ointment or detergent</term> against scabies can also be made with Mercury. One can also use, in place of the Mercury, a certain amalgam made from six parts Mercury and one part gold <note>original: "solis," or "the sun"</note>. This Mercury resists pains of the colon and the flanks; and not only those things mentioned, but it also effects certain even greater miracles. It heals many other various conditions, as any physician will easily recognize and acknowledge according to his learning. But let 10 grains be given to a robust body, 8 to an average one, and to a weaker one (provided the digestion is not too weak), 5 at most. It heals quartan fevers <note>A type of malaria where the fever recurs every four days.</note>. It also opposes the plague, certainly by both preventing and curing it.

Therefore, many benefits come from Mercury, as is established by countless experiments. The common Mercury, or Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver"</term>, is fourfold. The first kind is gathered from springs of water, which Pliny (Book 33, Chapter 6; also Book 3) calls a certain "perpetual and eternal ulcer" <note>original: "vomica," a term Pliny used to describe liquid mercury as a plague or "boil" of the earth</note>, and it is a poison to all things; this is the form in most frequent use. Regarding the dangers of quicksilver, read Dioscorides in Book 5, Chapter 60. As a drink, it has a destructive power; for by its weight it corrodes the intestines and other organs. Likewise, see Book 6, Chapter 28. The common crowd of physicians and the ignorant—such as Jews, monks, petty priests, barbers, tooth-pullers, and old women—who understand nothing or certainly very little of the philosophers, strive with a certain insolent boldness to attribute the power of healing any dangerous conditions to quicksilver or common Mercury. By their error, many people are destroyed rather than cured, as is openly taught by Theophrastus Paracelsus and other spagyrics <term>spagyros: alchemical physicians who "separate and recombine" substances to create medicine</term>. For they are accustomed to burn quicksilver into ash, and exhibit it in potions mixed with certain other ingredients for abdominal and intestinal issues or dysentery; likewise to kill worms in infants, and similarly for the Neapolitan disease <note>The "Neapolitan disease" (morbus Neapolitanus) was a common 16th-century name for Syphilis</note>. For external conditions, indeed, when prepared with *aqua forti* <term>aqua forti: nitric acid, used here to create a mercuric precipitate</term> and precipitated, it can be effective, such as for malignant ulcers and especially the venereal plague. Likewise, for destroying boils on the neck of the bladder, it is accustomed to erode and dry out flesh even without pain. It draws out waste through the bowels and expels bad humors through the pores.

Mercury is nothing else than the bodily spirit of the world made in the belly of the earth, which receives into itself all powers—animal, vegetable, and mineral alike. Just as wax receives the impression of all forms, so Mercury receives into itself the properties of all natural things. If it has been cleansed and prepared as it ought to be, then at its most perfect and purest, it receives the impression of the purest gold and silver. Just as the Moon is the universal receptacle of all things (and especially of the Sun), so also is Mercury the universal receptacle of the virtues of all natural things (and especially of gold). Therefore, by comparison, the philosophers call it the Moon of the Earth, just as gold is called the Sun of the Earth. And just as the Moon is the first gate in the heavens, so Mercury, compared to the Moon, is the first gate to the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work" of transformation</note>. Just as when the Earth is placed between the Sun and the Moon, it hinders the Moon so that it does not receive the influence of the Sun's light, and so remains dark; similarly, the earthly impurity hidden within Mercury hinders it from receiving the perfection of the nature of the Sun. But if this "earth" were removed, then

# THE BEST PREPARATION FOR THE VENEREAL PLAGUE
## *and other diseases.*
### ADDITION.

Take 1 pound of quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," or liquid mercury</term> and dissolve it in strong water <term>aqua forti: nitric acid</term> so that a precipitate is formed. Then take distilled vinegar and dissolve that precipitate in it by boiling for four hours. Afterward, pour what has dissolved into a glass vessel and pour in more vinegar; repeat this until the vinegar has dissolved all the Mercury. Then distill all the vinegar in a Mary’s bath <term>balneum Mariae: a water bath used for gentle, even heating</term>, and a mass like salt will remain at the bottom. Over this, pour rainwater that has been distilled four times, and let it cook in a sealed glass for half a day. Afterward, let it settle; pour off the clear liquid and distill it in the water bath. You will then have a clear mass; dry it and divide the mass into two parts. Over one part, pour spirit of wine <term>spiritus vini: ethanol or highly concentrated alcohol</term> and let it sit for eight days to digest. Drive it through a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling substances at high heat</note> set in hot ashes, with a large receiver vessel attached. First the spirit of wine will come out, then the spirit of Mercury, and a very black dreg will remain at the bottom. Do not open the joints of the receiver for at least 24 hours. The crystalline spirits of Mercury stick to the sides of the vessel and do not dissolve for 12 hours. Once the receiver is opened, extract the liquors in a very gentle water bath; the spirit of wine will come out, and the essence of Mercury will remain at the bottom of the vessel in the form of an ash-colored oil. Place this liquid in a small glass vessel over very gentle heat; then, gradually dissolve the other part of the Mercury (which was reserved and ground into powder) into it. Add as much as can be absorbed into a softish mass. This done, seal the vessel and cook it in ashes, increasing the heat by degrees until it turns into a red powder. One grain of this, administered in wine or another liquid, drives out the Neapolitan disease <note>original: "morbum Neapolitanum," a historical name for syphilis</note> and performs other wonders. It is given three times a week; the patient should avoid sharp or acidic foods and drink sugared wine. It purges only through the stool and performs many other things which I omit for the sake of brevity.

## ON SULFUR AND THE UTILITY OF SULFUR,
### which is varied.

Oil of sulfur <note>original: "Sulphuris oleum"; in early modern medicine, this often referred to a spirit or acid derived from sulfur, though here it is treated as a versatile topical and internal remedy.</note> opposes both internal and external ailments as follows. Moreover, this oil has a peculiar power and capacity for drawing out [impurities]. It heals fissures of the anus, fistulas, abscesses <term>Apostemata: inflammatory swellings or tumors filled with pus</term>, itching, prolapse, piles <term>Mariscas: hemorrhoidal growths</term>, and other ailments by light contact or by smearing it on. Likewise, it cures the stomach, liver, spleen, womb, bladder, intestines, and joints—specifically those parts affected by an abundance of humors or by putrefaction. 

A very small amount of this oil is given with a distilled liquid or a decoction of a suitable herb, according to the quality of the part and the condition: a hen’s feather is dipped into the oil and then immediately pulled out, and whatever adheres to the feather is diluted in the liquid or decoction. This is given to the patient to drink for pain of the stomach and for colic caused by gas, using chamomile water. Likewise, for a lack of appetite <note>original: "orexi"; referring here to a digestive disorder</note> arising from a redundancy of phlegm, it is given with wormwood water; against worms, it is given with grass water or wormwood water. For a coldness of the liver and for dropsy <term>hydrope: an accumulation of fluid in the body, often associated with organ failure</term>, it is given with cold water. For pain of the womb, it is given with a wine decoction of Betony and Feverfew <note>original: "Matricariæ"</note>. For the suppression of urine, it is given with wine in which garlic has been boiled. 

Likewise, it is used for lice infestations <term>phthiriasin: a condition of being infested with lice</term> by dipping a certain woolen cloth into it. It assists with ear pain and ringing, ulceration, worms, and other ear defects, as well as bruised ears. It helps with arthritic diseases. For buboes <note>likely referring to the swollen lymph nodes associated with the plague</note>, a soaked woolen cloth is placed over them; it has a moderately warming power and, by reason of its mixture and composition, it binds together, wonderfully heals ulcers and wounds, and generates new flesh very quickly. By contact and smearing, it heals cancer, graying hair, ulcers of the head and affections of the brain, colic, skin blemishes, and bruised limbs along with all their symptoms. 

It draws out [fragments from] a fractured skull, thins and softens hard areas when smeared on, and heals pains and the dislocation of limbs, "creeping" skin rashes <term>Serpigines: a term for skin diseases like shingles or ringworm that seem to "creep" across the body</term>, and every kind of scabies. It cures spasms and has a power for drying out tumors and small swellings <note>original: "tubercula"</note> when a soaked woolen cloth is placed over them. It also treats ulcers of the shins, any wounds—especially those that are hollow and deep—abscesses <term>vomicas: deep-seated collections of pus</term>, varicose veins, pimples <term>varos: likely acne or facial spots</term>, and ulcers both recent and old and putrid. Finally, it treats any burn arising from any cause whatsoever. 

For ulcers and pustules of the mouth, a feather or a piece of soaked cotton is applied to the ulcerated place; by repeating this contact with the oil several times, the evil is healed. It whitens the teeth by touching them lightly. If all the teeth should ache, a warm decoction of mint mixed with one, two, or three drops of the oil should be held in the mouth. It extracts warts. It cures ailments of the spleen with tamarisk water or maidenhair fern <note>original: "capilli veneris"</note> water. It is used against swelling under the tongue of infants. Likewise, against the suffering of the colon and the twisting of the intestines <note>original: "tormina intestinorum"; severe cramping or griping pains</note>, it is given with rue water or something similar: two drops in the summer, and in the winter with "water of life" <term>aqua vitæ: high-proof distilled spirits or brandy</term> or muscatel wine.
