-># ON MEDICINES<-

It is commonly known that sulfurous waters, aluminous waters, or hot springs have the power and faculty to consolidate <note>to heal, firm up, or close wounds</note>. How much more then the "water of metals," especially that extracted from the more perfect metals? Indeed, all metals—whether perfect or imperfect—can show no power or efficacy in medicine as long as they remain in their harder substance, even though many people may boast loudly here and there about their various attributed powers. According to Aristotle and the common opinion of the philosophers, these metals must be reduced to their original or "first matter" <note>the fundamental substance from which all things were thought to be made</note>, though this must be done without the use of corrosive and poisonous waters. As David says in the Psalm, *He brought forth water from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone* <note>original: "eduxit aquam de petra, & oleum de saxo durissimo"; an allusion to Psalm 114:8 and Deuteronomy 32:13</note>. Unless a substance is turned into water, one can in no way reach perfection.

### ANNOTATION ON SATURN <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead</note>.

#### ADDITION.

Take 2 pounds <note>symbol: ℔; libra</note> of minium <term>minium: red lead (lead tetroxide)</term>. Place it in a glass vessel and pour distilled vinegar over it to a height of six fingers. Place the vessel, well-sealed, over warm ashes; stir it immediately with a stick so that the material does not stick to the bottom. On the following day, pour off the vinegar (which should now be sweet) into another vessel. Add fresh vinegar and repeat the process as described above until all the minium has been dissolved. Once all the vinegar extracts have been collected, they must be filtered through a new filter. Then, let the liquid putrefy in horse manure <note>a common alchemical method for providing a gentle, steady heat through natural decomposition</note> for 15 days.

When the time has passed, distill the vinegar to "thirds"—that is, until only one part remains out of three. Place this remaining third in a cold place, such as a cellar, and crystals will form. Then, pour off the vinegar and collect the crystals and save them. Distill the vinegar again to thirds and set it in a cold place, and more crystals will form. Repeat this until you have reduced all that material into crystals.

Take 2 ounces <note>symbol: ℥; uncia</note> of that crystalline salt and keep it until I tell you what to do next. Take all the rest of that crystalline matter and place it in a glass retort <note>a vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck</note> reinforced with the best lute <note>luto: a protective clay or paste used to seal joints and protect glass from direct fire</note>. Attach a sufficiently large receiving vessel to it, and once the joints are sealed, begin the distillation. First, a white smoke will emerge, and then a red oil. Increase the fire with dry wood until the distillation is complete. Separate the water from the oil in a <term>B.M.</term> <gloss>Balneum Mariae: a Mary’s Bath or water bath, used for gentle heating</gloss>. Save each separately. You shall purify the oil three times, and likewise clean the water separately in the water bath.

This "old man" <note>a personification of Lead/Saturn, usually depicted as an old man in alchemical imagery</note> is endowed with such prudence and wisdom that scarcely any mortal can count its benefits. Use his "sweat and blood" <note>the distilled liquids</note> in all diseases, acting both externally and internally, giving thanks to God. — B. à PORTV <note>likely referring to Giambattista della Porta or another author associated with the name "Portu"</note>.

## ON HUMAN BLOOD AND
## *Its Powers.*

From human blood, an oil and salt can be made, and after these, a red stone of wonderful efficacy and virtue. It restrains the flow of blood and expels many infirmities. Take human blood, putrefy it in warm dung <note>a common method for providing gentle, consistent heat for fermentation</note>, then distill it. A white water, like milk, will come out. Afterward, increase the fire and you will distill an oil. Finally, rectify the dregs remaining in the bottom of the vessel until they are as white as snow; when the oil is poured back on them, it will become a clear, red stone. The salt of human blood is effective against diseases of the joints, and it cures gout, hand-gout, and knee-gout <note>original: "podagræ, chiragræ ac gonagræ"; specific Latin terms for gout occurring in the feet, hands, and knees respectively</note>.

Let this now suffice regarding the more excellent and highly necessary medicines, the correct preparation of all of which is taught by the <term>Chemical</term> art. This art is condemned by the unskillful masses; for remedies are not taken or extracted only from plants—as many foolish people think and persuade the whole world—but also from metals, gems, and precious stones. These <term>Theophrastic</term> <note>referring to Theophrastus Paracelsus, the influential 16th-century physician who championed chemical medicines</note> remedies are not sharp or violent, as the ignorant and inexperienced shout, but are most sweet and very familiar to our nature. They preserve and vivify the excellence of the spirits <note>the 'vital spirits' believed to animate the body</note> and purge them of impurities, usually through sweat alone. In short, they are beneficial in their entire substance, as many learned men experience daily with happy success. It is no wonder these things seem filthy to those who are so submerged in dregs and impurities that their minds cannot emerge toward higher and more subtle things. Furthermore, by their own laziness, they flee from the labor required in the preparation of medicines. I, however, warn such men: either let them learn better things, or let them not envy better institutions; at the very least, they should not rebuke what they do not know. Otherwise, we shall not be delayed by their efforts, because the truth will obtain the palm of victory despite their vain snarling, and by finally dispelling those shadows with its brightness, it will reveal each thing as it truly is.

# PREPARATION
# OF SALTPETER.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A with foliate patterns.</image-desc>
The saltpeter <term>nitrum: saltpeter, or potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder and alchemy</term> is placed in the sun in a large dish or other leaden vessel until it turns white; then it is reduced to a white powder. Prepared in this way, it acquires more subtlety <note>In alchemy, "subtlety" refers to the refinement and penetrative power of a substance</note> and can be called purified froth of saltpeter <note>original: "aphron nitron"</note>.

Or it is calcined <term>calcined: heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile parts and reduce a substance to powder</term> by a fierce fire until it turns white; thus its gumminess is greatly diminished, and it will have greater heat and subtlety in its action.

->ADDITION.<-

Gradually melt the saltpeter in a strong crucible <note>original: "tigillum"</note>. Once melted, slowly throw in common sulfur the size of beans until it refuses to absorb any more. Pour it into a vessel full of water, filter it, coagulate it, melt it again, and throw in sulfur. Repeat this five times. Finally, dissolve, filter, and coagulate it; then it is ready.

->OIL OF SALTPETER.<-

->ADDITION.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial F with foliate patterns.</image-desc>
Melt purified lead and throw the best saltpeter upon it as you please; it will there be melted into an oil. Remove it from the fire, and it will congeal and separate from the lead. Keep it in a glass vessel. When you wish to use it, place it near a fire, and it will quickly turn into an oil, which fixes <term>fix: to make a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term> most perfectly. This oil is rectified by distilling it through a retort, for the moisture passes over and the rectified oil remains.

->FIXATION OF SALTPETER.<-

->ADDITION.<-

Take <note>The symbol ℞ stands for the Latin "Recipe," meaning "Take"</note> equal parts of saltpeter and iron filings, and 2 parts of quicklime. Grind them together and place them in a well-sealed jar, and put it in a blast furnace <note>original: "furnum venti," a furnace designed to use a draft of air to reach high temperatures</note> so that it burns for four hours. When it has cooled, pour clear water over it and let it stand overnight. Then the saltpeter will be separated from the lime; filter, evaporate, and congeal it. Once dried, melt it, and it will flow into a fixed oil.

### *For removing all skin defects and flaws: such as birthmarks, morphew <note>original: "morphæa," referring to discolored patches or blotches on the skin</note>, jaundice, mange, pustules, tumors, ringworm <note>original: "serpigenes," literally "creeping" skin eruptions</note>, and leprosy.*

Dissolve prepared saltpeter <term>nitrum: saltpeter, or potassium nitrate, here used as a topical cleansing agent</term> in warm water or a lye made from grapevines, roses, willows, rosemary, sage, hyssop, lavender, thyme, or laurel. It may also be dissolved in the distilled urine of a young boy, in distilled vinegar, in lemon juice, or macerated for three days in purified honey. Alternatively, it can be mixed with goose or swan fat, or almond oil. Apply this to the skin when going to bed; in the morning, wash the affected area with rose water, bean water, or a decoction made of barley flour, wheat bran, and mallow roots.

### *For the same purpose.*

Take: high-quality Tragacanth <note>a natural gum obtained from dried sap</note>, as much as you wish; soak it in rose water or rose vinegar until it dissolves. Add a very fine powder of Cuckoo-pint roots <note>original: "Ari," also known as Lords-and-Ladies</note>, or snakeweed which has been soaked seven times in rose water and dried in the sun; also add powder of Orris root <note>original: "Ireos"</note> and rice flour. Use an equal amount of each of these species as there is of the tragacanth. Afterward, add as much saltpeter as the weight of all the above ingredients combined. Place over a moderate fire, stirring constantly until the saltpeter melts, and continue until the mixture thickens. Then add a little camphor. When it has acquired such a consistency that it can easily be formed into pills, remove it from the fire. At the beginning, you may also dissolve a little musk, civet, or ambergris in the rose water or rose vinegar if you wish. When you are about to go to bed, moisten one pill with rose water, rose vinegar, or lemon juice and rub it on yourself; in the morning, wash with bean or rose water.

### *A lotion for ringworm.*

Take: 3 drams <note>represented by the symbol ʒ</note> of saltpeter, 1 dram of common salt, 4 ounces of dock water <note>water infused with the *Lapathum* plant</note>, and 1 ounce of squill vinegar <note>vinegar infused with sea onion, used for its skin-clearing properties</note>. Let these be dissolved and mixed. Dip a linen cloth into this warmed liquid and rub the face.

### *An ointment for removing tumors, calluses, and hardness of the skin.*

Take: saltpeter, rock salt <term>salis gemmæ: pure crystalline salt</term>, and the tops of hyssop and pennyroyal in equal parts. Let them be pounded together and incorporated into a rose cerate <term>cerato rosato: a stiff ointment made of wax, oil, and rose water</term> over a gentle fire.

### *An experiment for mange, ringworm, and itching.*

Take: 1 dram each of saltpeter, sulfur, and marjoram. Let the items to be powdered be ground, and let the marjoram be pounded; mix these with rose oil to create an ointment.

### *A wash or liniment for drawing out and curing smallpox, redness, and pustules on the body.*

Take: Saltpeter <term>nitrum: saltpeter, or potassium nitrate, here used for its cooling and cleansing properties</term> mixed with the juice of hyssop, marigold <note>original: "calthæ"</note>, and chamomile, with the addition of bitter almond oil.

### *Against leprosy.*

Saltpeter tempered with vitriol <note>likely copper or iron sulfate</note> and verdigris <note>original: "ære viridi," a green copper-based pigment used in medicine for its caustic properties</note>, when applied, removes leprosy.

### *For ripening, cleansing, and curing ulcers, carbuncles, and fistulas.*

Saltpeter mixed with turpentine <note>original: "therebinthina," the resin of the terebinth tree</note>, applied and rubbed on.

### *A potion for the disease of jaundice.*

One spoonful of saltpeter swallowed with wine on an empty stomach cures jaundice.

### *A liniment for morphew.*

Let saltpeter be dissolved in white wine, or distilled vinegar, or lemon juice; rub the skin with it when you are about to go to bed <note>morphew refers to patches of discolored or scurfy skin</note>.

### *An ointment for whitening the face and making the skin clear.*

Take: 1 ounce of psyllium seeds <note>original: "sem. psillij"</note> and 3 ounces of oil of tartar; let them soak in a lead vessel for three days. Afterward, squeeze the mucilage through a small bag; let this be mixed with rose oil, in which you then dissolve 1 drachm of saltpeter and 1 ounce of rock salt <note>original: "salis gemmæ"</note>, and let an ointment be made.

### *To make the hair golden-yellow.*

Saltpeter tempered with crushed lupin seeds and warm water makes the hair beautiful, if it is washed frequently.

### *To prevent hair from falling out.*

Let saltpeter be dissolved in Malmsey wine <note>original: "vino malvatico," a sweet, potent Mediterranean wine</note>, and let the spot be rubbed with it; afterward, apply crushed beet.

### *For removing lice, nits, and dandruff of the head.*

Let saltpeter and Samian earth <note>a white medicinal clay from the island of Samos</note> be dissolved in radish seed oil and applied.

### *Against excessive moisture of the brain and dandruff of the head.*

Let saltpeter be dissolved in white vinegar, add powdered frankincense <note>original: "olibani"</note>, and rub the affected area with it.

### *For whitening the teeth.*

Prepared saltpeter cleanses the teeth if they are rubbed with it.

### *Against toothache.*

Saltpeter boiled with wine and pepper eases toothache if it is held in the mouth.

### *For obstruction of the liver.*

Likewise, let a <term>plaster</term> be made from <term>saltpeter</term> and <term>oil of bitter almonds</term>, <term>rose oil</term>, and <term>rose vinegar</term> in which glowing <term>steel</term> was quenched; let it be applied to the region of the liver.

Likewise, let <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "clysteres"</note> be prepared from the same decoctions, with <term>oil of bitter almonds</term>, <term>chamomile</term>, <term>honey of roses</term>, and <term>saltpeter</term>.

### *Against a hardened and swollen spleen.*

Let <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>fenugreek</term>, red roses, and <term>capers</term> be dissolved in <term>oxymel</term> <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note> and <term>rose vinegar</term> in which glowing <term>steel</term> was quenched; let it be drunk on an empty stomach.

### *A plaster for the same purpose.*

Take 5 drams <note>original: "ʒ v."</note> of <term>saltpeter</term>, powder of <term>fenugreek</term> or <term>lupins</term>, <term>rose vinegar</term>, <term>omphacine</term> <note>oil or juice made from unripe grapes or olives</note>, <term>oil of bitter almonds</term>, oil of <term>chamomile</term>, <term>dill</term>, <term>elder</term>, and <term>caper roots</term>, one dram each; let a plaster be made.

### For recovering debilitated strength.

Take 3 ounces each of <term>black pitch</term>, wax, and <term>colophony</term> <note>original: "colophoniæ," a distilled pine resin</note>; let them be melted. Add 1 dram of <term>tartar</term>, 1 and a half drams of <term>saltpeter</term>, 3 drams of <term>native sulfur</term>, 2 drams of powdered pepper, 2 drams of <term>benzoin</term> <note>original: "Benioni," a fragrant tree resin</note>, half a dram of <term>euphorbium</term> <note>a caustic plant resin used as an irritant to stimulate the skin</note>, 1 dram of <term>labdanum</term> <note>original: "laudani," a sticky resin from the rockrose bush, not the later opium tincture</note>, and 1 dram each of bitter almond oil and <term>cyprus oil</term> <note>original: "olei ciprin," likely oil of henna flowers</note>. Let them be mixed to make a plaster.

### To induce sweating.

<term>Saltpeter</term> swallowed with the juice of <term>chamomile</term> and <term>marigold</term> <note>original: "calthæ"</note> in broth.

### To slow excessive sweating.

Let <term>saltpeter</term> be dissolved with powdered <term>orris root</term> <note>original: "Ireos"</note> in <term>omphacine rose oil</term> <note>oil made from unripe olives and rose petals</note>; with rose vinegar added, let the body be anointed.

### To make the parts of the body nimble.

Let the shins or other parts of the body be anointed with <term>saltpeter</term> dissolved in chamomile oil.

### To ward off the shivers of fever before an attack.

Let <term>saltpeter</term> be dissolved in olive oil, or better yet, in oil of bitter almonds, or dill, or radish seed, or nettles, or <term>castoreum</term> <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, or <term>spikenard</term> <note>original: "spicæ"</note>. Let the patient's neck, shoulder blades, and spine be anointed, as well as the tendons of the hands and feet.

### To relax the intestines.

Let <term>saltpeter</term> be drunk with powdered <term>orris root</term> in the juice of raw cabbage. Likewise, let one spoonful of powdered <term>saltpeter</term> be drunk in warm <term>whey</term>, or white wine, or a decoction of raisins.

### For burns.

<term>Saltpeter</term> roasted until it turns black and reduced to a powder is effectively applied to burns.

### Against the bites of rabid dogs and other poisonous beasts.

<term>Saltpeter</term> melted with <term>turpentine</term>, with vinegar and goose or pig fat added, cures poisonous bites when applied. Meanwhile, however, the vinegar should be strained through <term>quicklime</term> and mixed with <term>saltpeter</term>, and the wound should be washed often with it.

### For one who has eaten Henbane.

<note>original: "Hyosciamum," a highly toxic plant in the nightshade family.</note>
<term>Saltpeter</term> dissolved in warm water should be drunk; afterward, provoke vomiting with a feather or a finger.

### For one who has eaten Mandrake.

<note>original: "mandragoras," a plant known for its hallucinogenic and narcotic alkaloids.</note>
Let vomiting be induced often with <term>saltpeter</term>, hot water, and honey; then let a decoction of <term>wormwood</term> <note>original: "absynthij"</note> in <term>Malmsey wine</term> <note>original: "malvatico," a sweet, potent Greek wine</note> be drunk with <term>saltpeter</term> dissolved in it. Let the patient’s head be sprinkled with vinegar and rose oil, and use strong-smelling substances <note>to keep the patient conscious</note>. The patient should exercise vigorously and induce a sweat.

### If anyone has eaten [poisonous] mushrooms.

Let <term>lemon balm</term> <note>original: "melissa"</note> be crushed with <term>posca</term> <note>a mixture of vinegar and water</note> or vinegar, water, and salt. Dissolve <term>saltpeter</term> in this mixture, swallow it while warm, and then vomit.

### II. ANOTHER, MORE EXCELLENT [REMEDY].

Take the previously mentioned material, <term>calcined</term> <note>burnt to a powder to remove volatile impurities</note> to perfection, which you shall test upon a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "cupellam," a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying and refining precious metals</note> just like pure silver; and when it has given the sign of its purity, remove it when it has cooled. Grind it, and with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>distilled alcohol or ethanol</note> extract the tincture, and distill it gently. Again, pour on the same spirit, and repeat this four times, or until they pass through the <term>retort</term> together. You will then have a perfect essence, which you shall <term>circulate</term> <note>a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note> for the space of 14 days in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balneo," short for *balneum Mariae* or Maria's bath</note>. Two different essences will separate: one yellow, floating on top; the other red, at the bottom of the vessel. The lower is a true solvent for gold and silver, and for other stones. The upper essence, however, is a true <term>cathartic</term> <note>a purgative or cleansing agent</note> for <term>tartarous diseases</term> <note>original: "tartareorum ægritudinum," a term popularized by Paracelsus referring to ailments caused by mineral deposits or "stones" in the body, such as gout or kidney stones</note>, especially for gout. Enjoy these and be well.

### ELIXIR OF HONEY.

Take 6 pounds of the best honey and dissolve it in triple-distilled water. Filter it four times, then evaporate the water. Dissolve it again and again; this must be done until it is cleansed of all filth and dregs. This done, you shall place the honey itself in a <term>pelican</term> <note>a specialized alchemical flask with two side-arms that allow the distillate to flow back into the main body, facilitating constant circulation</note> for one month. Then, you shall separate the lighter part through an <term>alembic</term> in a water bath, but distill the other part in a heat of ashes. You shall calcine the earth remaining at the bottom and dissolve it in pure water, removing the dregs by filter; finally, by this method, once it is deprived of all moisture, let it be calcined over a slow fire for one hour. Gradually <term>imbibe</term> <note>to slowly add liquid to a dry substance so it is absorbed</note> this again with the previous water, and <term>coagulate</term> it in a water bath. Then add an equal amount of its own oil previously extracted in the heat of ashes, <term>digesting</term> and coagulating it into a thick gum. When you have added the rest of its oil, you shall digest it again as before; it will become compact and thick. It universally preserves and cleanses the human body of every imperfection, both internally and externally.

### ON THE VIRTUES OF POTABLE GOLD, AND ITS *preparation*.

There are various opinions regarding **potable gold**: some value it highly, others despise it. Therefore, it is advisable to indicate the reality of the matter. This will be done more conveniently if we first consider the virtues and properties which learned and experienced men attribute to gold in their books; and second, if we weigh whether those properties attributed to gold itself by authors can also be demonstrated by reason to be inherent in gold.

As far as the first point is concerned, namely the authorities: <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age</note>...

**Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> in his treatise on gold says that it is temperate by nature; and if it is reduced by a file, it is usefully mixed with medicines against **leprosy**, the falling out of hair, and **melancholy**. It is said to comfort the heart and prevent its tremors, and to strengthen the eye if it is reduced to a very fine powder. In this, almost all physicians who describe the virtues of <term>simple medicines</term> <note>medicines made of a single natural ingredient, rather than a compound</note> agree. It would be long and tedious to repeat the authorities and opinions of everyone. If they attributed such great powers to gold filings, what might happen if it were reduced into a **liquid and drinkable form**?

Those who have known the proper preparation for reducing it into a liquid form, and have used it in removing diseases, affirm that it has the power of purifying, purging superfluous <term>humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which were believed to determine health and temperament</note>, removing discharges from the head, and freeing the heart from malignant and foul vapors, driving away melancholy, preserving against leprosy, sharpening the <term>spirits</term> <note>the "vital spirits" believed to be the subtle substances that animated the body and mind</note>, and healing **epilepsy**.

**Arnold of Villanova** <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist famous for his work on distillation and medicinal wines.</note> in his treatise on wine or the elixir says that it treats the suppression of urine. **Archelaus** the philosopher says gold is the treasure of human life, healing the infirmities and diseases of men if some of its liquor is taken. Furthermore, he adds that if its powers were known, no more faith would be placed in the doctors who deny it—either because they fear their own profit would perish, or because they are ignorant of the method of preparation.

**Raymond** <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Ramon Lull, a name attached to many influential alchemical texts in the 14th and 15th centuries.</note> near the end of the practice of his *Testament* says that **water of gold** <note>original: "aquam auri," another term for potable gold</note> given in a drink in the proper way heals the human body of every infirmity, however old; he claims the doctor has no need to inspect the urine, nor other excrements, nor to examine the pulse, but only that he use his medicine, with a light diet or regimen of living applied.

As for these great and vast powers found in gold, Avicenna, in the treatise *On the Powers of the Heart* in the chapter on gold, says they come from its **property**. In the same treatise, in the chapter on the <term>Hyacinth</term> <note>original: "Hyacintho," a gemstone (possibly zircon or sapphire) believed to have medicinal effects</note>, he says that this property ought not to be attributed to the matter from which it is composed, but to a singular virtue resulting therefrom, just as appears in a **magnet**. Therefore, a certain philosopher says that virtue proceeds from the **entire species**—which we commonly call the **specific** [virtue] <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "specific virtue" is a power a substance has because of its essential form, rather than its elemental makeup (hot, cold, etc.).</note>. Others think that virtue is a **celestial gift** flowing into any mixture according to the greater or lesser proper proportion of the elements.

Avicenna thinks this specific power is instilled into things after the first <term>complexion</term> <note>the unique balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in an individual substance</note> of the elements. But because we are ignorant of such proportions and it is not given to us to know further, we flee to **experience**, because to experiment in such medical matters is more profitable than to argue—even if we do not deny that the inquiry into the causes of such powers can be [most highly useful...]

<meta>This page continues the technical justification for gold as a universal medicine, moving from the opinions of Avicenna and Arnold of Villanova on the previous page to the specific elemental composition of gold as defined by Rhasis and Albertus Magnus. <page-num>646</page-num>
<header>ON MEDICINES.</header>

[The work is] greatly aided by the light of nature. And if we consider the excellent composition and <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, the "complexion" was the specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—within a substance.</note> of gold, it is well known to many to be endowed with great powers. For, as **Rhasis** <note>original: "Rhasis"; refers to Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and influential medical authority.</note> says, in gold there are 10 parts hot, 10 cold, 10 moist, and 10 dry—or if you prefer, ten proportions of each. For this reason, it is almost incorruptible, because just as much as the heat warms it, the cold cools it; let the same judgment be held regarding its dryness and moisture. Since, therefore, it is tempered in its own complexion, it also has the power of tempering [others], because its matter has been purified of two superfluous moistures: namely, the flammable sulfurous moisture and the evaporating phlegmatic or watery moisture, as **Albertus** says in his *Book of Minerals*. For this reason, it has great power to purge superfluous <term>humors</term> <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which were thought to cause disease if unbalanced.</note> and to comfort its own likeness, namely the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the essential, life-sustaining fluid thought to be present in all living things from birth.</note>. Furthermore, because it enters into all metals, it is "fixed" <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat.</note> and is opposed to that which is not fixed and vanishes into smoke. 

Furthermore, it has the property of blunting vapors that rise from the lower parts [of the body]. Because it is of a <term>subtle substance</term> <note>Refined and capable of penetrating deep into the body's tissues.</note>, it has the power to thoroughly purge superfluous humors. Since it is incorruptible, it can expel corrupt humors, **leprosy**, **cancer**, and other similar diseases—I will say nothing for now of **gout**, **quartan fever**, and **dropsy**. Finally, because it is bright, it has the power to repel melancholic, dark, and gloomy humors and vapors, by which some patients are clearly afflicted; and while it does this, it grants a good intellect. In a word, the goodness of the substance found in gold demonstrates the value of its virtue, and the greatness of its virtue shows the excellence of its operation. This is clearly shown to us through its essential parts: namely, its matter and its form. For noble, pure matter deserves a noble, excellent, and divine form. And let us be permitted to estimate with **Plato** that forms are given according to the merit of the matter. **Albertus Magnus**, in the third book of his *Minerals*, proves the same. And as a certain man said, the more matter is sublimated and refined by nature, the more capable and worthy it is to receive a noble and excellent form. But the excellence of the matter of gold reveals itself in this: that fire, which consumes and devours all other things, brings no harm to it nor diminishes it. If we consider its divine form, we shall find incredible and almost divine effects. If these things are examined diligently, we may rightly compare gold to the celestial Sun; for just as the Sun animates almost the entire universe and the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>The "Great World" or the universe at large.</note> with its heat and light, so the terrestrial Sun, which we call gold, has the power of bringing life to the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," meaning the human being, viewed as a reflection of the universe.</note>, which is man.

...in sufficient quantity, which you shall place in the <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>, and extract the residue of the vinegar; and when you see the oil coming out, you shall change the receiving vessel, and provide a great fire until nothing more comes out. Take well-calcined gold, place it in a <term>matrass</term> <note>A long-necked glass flask used for boiling or digestion.</note>, pour on your vinegar, and close the neck diligently. Place it over hot ashes and dissolve; this dissolution will happen gradually—not like that which occurs in <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: "aqua regia"; "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold quickly and violently.</note>, but slowly, because it is a philosophical and masterful dissolution. When your solvent has extracted enough—which you will recognize by sight—pour it into a retort and distill off the solvent; the gold will remain like a gum or a salt. Pour your solvent back over the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after calcination.</note> to dissolve more, and proceed as before until you have a tincture, which you shall keep separately.

Take as much of our calcined <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibij"; antimony was a primary material in alchemy, thought to contain a "star-like" spirit essential for the Great Work.</note> as you wish, which you shall place in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A distilling apparatus consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap with a tube.</note> or another glass vessel. Pour on distilled vinegar—the weaker it is, the better. Let the vinegar float to a height of three or four fingers' breadth. Let it be <term>macerated</term> <note>Soaked to soften and extract components.</note> for 24 hours, and let it be moved five or six times a day with a wooden spatula. Afterward, let the vinegar be filtered, and let more be poured on so that you may have it more pure. Afterward, you shall evaporate it to half its volume; then let it cool, and part of your salt will coagulate into ice-like crystals, which you shall remove with a perforated wooden spoon. Afterward, let the remainder evaporate so that you have the whole salt, which you shall dry gradually. Proceed in this way until you have a supply of salt as you desire. 

Take that salt and, once pulverized, place it in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation.</note> filled to the halfway point. Afterward, place the retort upon ashes in an earthen vessel; attach a receiving vessel, well-sealed with <term>lute</term> <note>original: "lutatum"; a paste used to make the joints of chemical apparatus airtight.</note> and dry, so that the spirits do not escape. Let the fire be slow at the beginning, then let it be increased as the dissolution requires; the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; here referring to a potent distilled spirit or solvent.</note> will enter the receiver, now like veins, now like vapors, and toward the end, a red oil will come. Then you shall increase the fire below and above, so that the whole retort glows white-hot for four hours. Let it cool so that the spirits may rest, moving nothing for an entire day.

Then you shall place your matter in an alembic and distill it in a water bath. The water of life will ascend first with subtlety, and the oil will remain at the bottom.

Take the water of life and place it over the salt of gold, and once protected by the <term>Seal of Hermes</term> <note>original: "sigillo Hermetis"; an airtight glass seal made by melting and twisting the neck of a vessel.</note>, place it in a warm bath for 40 days. If the whole gum is not dissolved, pour off that which is dissolved—red like blood—into another retort, and pour on more water of life...

->ON THE POWERS OF THE HIDDEN SPIRIT.<-

# TO THE MOST NOBLE AND SUPREME PHILOSOPHER
### *and Mathematician, Lord Peter Winzlo of Olomouc,*
### *celebrated Physician, Bernhard G. Penotus of Port-Sainte-Marie*
### *of Aquitaine, sends many greetings.* <note>original: "S. P. D." stands for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a formal Latin greeting.</note>

Whatever is contained as actively diffused within the circumference of any circle is simultaneously contained, gathered in potential, within the center of that same circle. And when that which is gathered in potential at the center is unfolded into action, then that which was actively diffused in the circumference is hidden in potential. For example, the Light of the Heavens is dispersed in infinite and many stars, and yet it is also gathered at once and together in the single Sun. That in which it is dispersed among many is the circle of the heavenly light; that in which it is gathered into one is the center of the heavenly light. The heavenly light is twofold: masculine and feminine. The masculine is dispersed in one half of the stars, those of the summer sky. The other, the feminine, is dispersed in the other half, those of the winter sky. Furthermore, all the masculine light of the heaven is gathered into one, namely in the Sun; whereas all the feminine light of the heaven is gathered into one, namely in the Moon. Just as it is with the dispersion and gathering of the heavenly light, so it is also with the dispersion, distinction, and gathering of all other things. Thus all <term>animal virtues</term> <note>In early modern philosophy, "animal" (from "anima") refers to the life-force or soul that animates living creatures.</note> dispersed among the infinite animals of the earth are gathered into one center in a single Lion. And all animal reasons or intelligences dispersed among all the animals of the world are gathered into one in the single head of a man.

In the same way, the Earth is the womb and the receptacle of all elements, in which all the powers of hidden things are actively concealed, which can break out in potential into specific forms; whence

Rhazes <note>A reference to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Abū Bakr al-Rāzī.</note> in his *Book of Divinity* says: know that the things of nature are so bound together by a subtle artifice that in any one thing, every other thing exists potentially, even if it is not seen in actuality. Albert [the Great] in his *Book of Minerals* says that gold is found everywhere: because there is no thing composed of the four elements in which gold is not naturally found, in its ultimate refinement. And therefore he says the matter of the [Philosopher's] Stone is found everywhere. Likewise, he proves that the greatest mineral virtue exists in any human being, and especially in the head between the teeth—as in its own time gold has been found in minute, oblong grains [in the mouth]—which could not be unless that mineral virtue were in man; this is the same mineral virtue found in our Elixir.

Furthermore, a certain "virgin earth" lies hidden in the center of the earth, which must be investigated with the highest zeal. Which you (O prince of all philosophers of our age) know best: You know that one earth is better than another, and therefore more to be chosen. Let the investigators of hidden things learn to recognize it, for once known, it must be liberated from "original sin" <note>original: "peccato originali"; in alchemy, this refers to the crude impurities or "dross" that must be purged from raw matter to reveal its pure essence.</note> by fire and water. And let us celebrate the Creator of all things, who willed to reveal the riches of such a great treasure to mortals, through his only-begotten Jesus Christ. I have written these things as a monument of our devotion. May you, the glory and ornament of both this writing and its author, fare most blessedly. At Frankenthal, on the Calends of January [January 1st], 1594.

### PREPARATION OF CRYSTALS
### and of other stones.

Calcine <term>calcine: to reduce a mineral to a powder by means of intense heat.</term> the crystal and grind it into a very fine powder upon a marble slab. Repeat this until you have the crystal entirely dissolved. Filter the vinegar in which the crystal was dissolved, and evaporate it in a water bath <note>original: "balneo"; the balneum Mariae or double boiler, used for gentle heating.</note>; the "salt" of the crystal will remain at the bottom. Take it, grind it, and sprinkle it upon a marble slab: it will dissolve into a liquor. You may do the same for other precious stones.

### ON THE POWERS OF THE SPIRIT OF WHITE AMBER.

It is a most ready remedy and preventative for those who fear they are susceptible to paralysis, epilepsy, or similar diseases. Indeed, if every other day, or two or three times a week, a few drops of this spirit are taken in lavender water, lily of the valley water, or betony water, they safely protect against the aforementioned diseases. ## COLCOTAR.

<margin>Against gout and inflammations.</margin>
**C**olcotar <term>Colcotar: the brownish-red residue (iron oxide) left after the calcination of iron vitriol.</term> is vitriol calcined to redness. If the urine of a healthy man is sprinkled upon it and it is dried, and sprinkled again—and this is repeated three times—distill it as its oil is usually made. Separate the phlegm <note>original: "phlegma"; here referring to the watery part of the distillation rather than the bodily humor.</note>, by which all inflammations are cured. It is a ready defense in the pains of gout; it dissolves corals and pearls. Much more remains to be said, which we omit for the sake of brevity.

## ON MERCURY AND REGULUS.

<margin>Scrofula, Cancers, Plague.</margin>
**D**istill two parts of sublimated mercury <note>original: "Mercurij sublimati"; likely mercuric chloride, a highly toxic but common alchemical base.</note> and one part of Regulus <term>Regulus: the metallic form of a mineral, most commonly referring to Antimony in this period.</term>, according to the rules of the art. The first water heals scrofula <note>Scrofula: a form of tuberculosis causing swollen lymph nodes in the neck.</note>; the second, which flows out like milk, heals cancers, the plague, and the venereal pox <note>original: "luem veneream"; syphilis.</note>; it also treats other fevers. The dose is from 1 to 4 grains in one dram <note>original: "ʒ. j."; roughly 3.9 grams.</note> each of nightshade and plantain water. By rectifying it three times, it performs wonders, which you will prove by experience.

## DIAPHORETIC LIQUOR OF MERCURY.

<margin>Very useful for the Spanish disease and dropsy.</margin>
**I**ts greatest use is in overcoming the Spanish disease <note>Spanish disease: a common historical name for syphilis.</note>; it is also very useful for those with dropsy <note>Dropsy: an old term for edema, or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>. It moves sweats remarkably well; its dose is from 10 to 15 drops in sweet wine.

## HOW THE LIQUOR OF MERCURY IS MADE.

<margin>Thoroughly heals ulcerations of the bladder, throat, and kidneys.</margin>
**L**et the mercury be purified with dried salt and sublimated with vitriol, common salt, and saltpeter <note>original: "sale petræ"; potassium nitrate.</note>, as is the custom of the art. Afterward, let it be dissolved in distilled vinegar; let the vinegar be distilled off and the material dried. Then, let it be digested in rectified spirit of wine <note>Spirit of wine: concentrated ethanol.</note> until it turns into a mucous fatness. From this, a liquor is extracted and driven in a sand bath with a very strong fire until a liquid like milk drops out. This is poured on again, and a very white and sweet oil, free from all corrosive quality, is produced. Taken by mouth, it thoroughly heals ulcerations of the bladder, the throat, and other hidden parts, and it dispels diseases of the kidneys through sweats and urine.

## SAMECH.

<margin>Samech is salt of tartar.</margin>
**I**t is a medicine for healing wounds in a very short time. Mention of it is made by Theon in the *Archidoxis* <note>Archidoxis: a seminal work of Paracelsian alchemy; "Theon" likely refers to a commentator or a pseudonym within that tradition.</note> regarding external matters, etc.

### OIL OF PINE WOOD.

It resists poisons and greatly promotes sweating, expels fevers, and is useful for all "cold" illnesses <note>In the humoral theory of the time, "cold" diseases were thought to be caused by an excess of phlegm or black bile; warming remedies like pine oil were used to restore balance.</note>, if 5 or 7 drops are drunk in wine or some distilled water.

### BALSAM OF ST. JOHN’S WORT.

This follows the description of **Paracelsus** in his *Great Surgery* <note>original: "Magna Chirurgia"; a landmark 1536 book by Paracelsus that revolutionized wound care.</note>. It heals wounds most successfully: it disperses tumors and clotted blood resulting from a fall, etc.

### COMPOUND BALSAM OF SULFUR.

The dose is half a drachm <note>original: "ʒ ß."; an apothecaries' weight equal to approximately 1.9 grams.</note>, or as much as can be held on the tip of a knife; it is a very safe preventative against the plague.

### SIMPLE BALSAM OF SULFUR.

One scruple <note>original: "℈ j."; approximately 1.3 grams.</note> by weight is given with half a drachm of theriac <term>Theriac: a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, often used as a base for other medicines.</term> in cases of the plague and pleurisy. It cures a cough, etc.

### METHOD FOR COMPOSING BALSAM OF SULFUR.

Take 4 ounces of oil of turpentine and 2 ounces of flowers of sulfur <term>Flowers of sulfur: a fine powder produced when sulfur is heated into a vapor and then cooled back into a solid.</term>. Let the "flowers" be added gradually so they can be better dissolved; place the glass vessel over hot ashes and stir frequently. When this is finished, place it in a hot sand bath <note>A "sand bath" provided a steady, indirect heat that prevented glass vessels from cracking over an open flame.</note> for eight or ten hours until it becomes like pitch; let the fire be slow. Finally, pour the highest quality spirit of wine <term>Spirit of wine: highly concentrated ethanol or aqua vitae.</term> over this material to the height of three fingers, and leave it over a slow fire. The spirit of wine will become red; pour this into another glass. Pour fresh spirit over the dregs, and it will be tinted again; separate this slowly as well and join both spirits together. Put the tinted spirit of wine into a cucurbit <term>Cucurbit: the gourd-shaped bottom part of a distilling apparatus.</term> and, with an alembic <term>Alembic: the "head" or cap of the still used to collect and direct vapors.</term> attached, draw off a portion of that spirit. The tincture of sulfur will remain at the bottom; save this for use. It is given to those who are short of breath or troubled by a cough due to a lung condition, taken in hyssop water or syrup of licorice. This is the **simple balsam of sulfur**.

### COMPOUND BALSAM OF SULFUR.

Take 2 ounces of flowers of sulfur, three times sublimated, 1 ounce of camphor, and 4 ounces of oil of turpentine. Grind and sieve the sulfur and camphor through a silk strainer, place them in a narrow-necked cucurbit, and pour your oil over them, sealing everything well. Let the vessel be placed in sand; apply a slow fire for two hours so the sand heats up, then increase the fire until it begins to boil in the glass. In this way, the sulfur will be turned into oil.

This is an admirable balsam for healing ulcers and wounds; likewise internally for fevers, the plague, colic, against worms, and tumors.

It is extremely useful for all hardness <note>original: "duritiem"; in early modern medicine, this referred to stiff joints, hardened swellings, or tumors.</note>, for it softens them and calms pains; it provokes retained urine if three or five drops are administered with white wine and fern water <note>original: "aqua filicis"; likely a distillate of the common fern, used for its purported diuretic properties.</note>.

### OIL OF JUNIPER.

It has the same value as oil of turpentine; it preserves the body from putrefaction <note>The text suggests juniper acts as a preservative against decay, a common belief due to its strong scent and resinous nature.</note> excellently, according to the balsamic nature it possesses. It cleanses the kidneys and expels the stone through the urine, and promotes sweating. ### OIL OF TURPENTINE.

It possesses the same faculties as the oil of juniper. Then it is fit for extracting all tinctures, as much of herbs as of other things; it is highly penetrative and breaks up the kidney stone when taken with parsley water.

### OIL OF GREATER BURDOCK

The best remedy for the kidney stone. The dose is from 8 to 12 drops in white wine or maidenhair fern water <note>original: "aqua capillorum Veneris"; literally "water of the hair of Venus," referring to the Adiantum capillus-veneris fern.</note>.

### *A Secret for the Kidney Stone.*

Take two pounds <term>℔: a pound or "libra" in medicinal weight, roughly 12 ounces in the apothecary system.</term> of the bark of ash root, three pounds of juniper seeds, and two and a half pounds <term>ß: a symbol for "half" (semis).</term> of clear turpentine. Let the things to be ground be crushed and mixed with the turpentine. Put them together in twelve pounds of water in a well-sealed vessel to putrefy for three months. When the time has passed, distill it in the manner of other oils. A most excellent oil will distill out; nothing similar is found for such a condition. The dose is 8 to 12 drops; it breaks up the stone and expels it with white wine.

### OIL OF WAX.

It is recommended for bruises <note>original: "confusionibus"; likely a typo for "contusionibus" (bruises), though it could refer to internal "disorders."</note> if applied topically. If you give it in spirit of wine <term>Spirit of wine: distilled alcohol or brandy.</term> for colicky pains, it is a supreme remedy. The dose is from 8 to 12 drops. I also usually place one to one and a half drams <term>ʒ: the symbol for a dram, about 1/8th of an ounce.</term> in clysters <term>Clyster: an enema used to deliver medication or clear the bowels.</term>; it does much for ulcers of the intestines and for pains. If you rectify <note>Rectify: to purify a substance through repeated distillation.</note> it several times over washed and dry sand, it will acquire a wonderful power of penetration.

### ON COLD OILS.

Let the greater or lesser cold seeds <note>In Galenic medicine, the "Four Greater Cold Seeds" were pumpkin, cucumber, melon, and gourd; the "Lesser" were lettuce, purslane, endive, and chicory.</note> be crushed and placed in water. Let them boil a little, collect the foam, and place it in a glass vessel. Let it be digested in a bath <note>original: "balneo"; refers to a *balneum Mariae* or water bath (bain-marie) for gentle heating.</note> overnight; it will turn into a most sweet oil.

## ON JUNIPER.

Place a sufficient quantity of crushed Juniper berries into a bladder <note>original: "vesicam"; a common vessel used in early distillation, sometimes literally an animal bladder or a bladder-shaped glass vessel.</note> with water and a good amount of yeast. After a proper period of maceration <note>The process of softening or breaking down a substance by soaking it in liquid.</note>, it will yield a most copious amount of burning wine <note>original: "vinum ardens"; this refers to high-proof distilled alcohol or spirits, in this case, a precursor to gin.</note>.

### *For Extracting the Life of Vegetables.*

First, grind the herb; then distill the water using a glass alembic <term>Alembic: A classic distillation apparatus consisting of two retorts connected by a tube, used to purify liquids via heating and cooling.</term> over ashes. Next, crush more of the said herb and mix it into a body <note>A chemical "body" or base.</note> with the aforementioned water. Place it in a state of putrefaction <note>In alchemy, putrefaction was a controlled process of decomposition intended to break a substance down to its essential components.</note> for eight days with the joints of the vessel tightly sealed. Then, squeeze out all the juice and distill it again. You will have an excellent "water," and in the bottom of the vessel, you will find a powder more precious than the water itself; preserve both.

## THE PERFECT CURE FOR CATARRH <note>original: "catarrhi"; historically, this referred to any excessive buildup of mucus or inflammation of the mucous membranes, often in the respiratory tract.</note> CONSISTS IN BLACK HELLEBORE, collected in the month of October.

Perform an extraction of black hellebore <note>Black Hellebore (*Helleborus niger*), also known as the Christmas Rose, was a powerful and dangerous purgative used since antiquity to treat "melancholy" and "phlegmatic" conditions.</note> with anise water until it reaches the consistency of honey. To this, add as much breadcrumb as there is extract. Once mixed, place them in a glass retort, well-sealed, and bury it in horse dung <note>original: "fimum equinum"; horse dung was frequently used as a natural, steady source of low heat for chemical digestion.</note> for three weeks. Separate the liquid from the dregs and distill it over ashes until you detect a fatty substance. Take that substance and put it into digestion in a bath <note>original: "balneo"; a water bath or bain-marie.</note> or in dung for fourteen days. Then, remove whatever is phlegmatic <note>The watery, non-essential part of the liquid.</note> from it; what remains is the essence of hellebore, which purges the body most gently in doses of six to eight grains.

### *Another preparation.*

Let the roots be gathered in the month of October and cleaned with the best wine. Select the outer rinds; the inner parts are of no importance. Let them be macerated (or rather, sprinkled with Malmsey wine <note>original: "vino malvatico"; a sweet, high-alcohol Mediterranean wine favored in medicinal preparations.</note>) and dried in the sun or another similar heat. Repeat this process three times. Grind it into a very fine powder. Place this powder in a large glass vessel and pour over it as much juice of laxative roses <note>original: "rosarum solutivarum"; roses specially prepared for their mild purgative properties.</note> as required. Dry it again, and repeat this five times. Finally, grind it and keep it in a glass. You will have a medicine incomparable for almost all diseases, if eight to twelve grains are given with syrup of violets or another appropriate liquid.

### *Another wonderful preparation taken from a very ancient book.*

Take <note>original: "℞"; the traditional symbol for "Recipe," the command to "Take" ingredients.</note> four handfuls <note>original: "m. iiij" (manipulus); a standard medical measurement: what a hand can grasp.</note> each of Black Hellebore roots and herbs, cleaned of all impurities with wine. Let them be bruised and placed into two measures <note>original: "duas mensuras"</note> of red or Muscatel wine in a glazed vessel, well-sealed. Place this in a cauldron of boiling water for a full day and night. Afterward, take it out, squeeze the juice out strongly, and filter it. Place this filtrate over one handful of fresh, bruised Hellebore roots, five handfuls of red roses, and six drams <note>original: "ʒ. vi."</note> of previously crushed Cloves. Put them together to digest for a day...

->The use of it is as follows.<-

Let it be dissolved in four ounces <note>original: "℥ iiij"</note> of its own water (previously reserved so that it was reduced to a "fifth essence" <term>Fifth essence: Also called 'quintessence,' the purest and most concentrated form of a substance extracted through alchemy.</term>) and drunk together on an empty stomach, and this at night. It restores a decrepit man into a youth in terms of health and strength: it preserves the teeth from foul humors <note>Humors: In ancient medicine, these were bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health.</note>, the eyes from all discharge, and protects against paralysis, apoplexy, gout, and all evils of corrupt humors. A certain Dean discovered this medicine and used it, living for one hundred and eighty-six years; his epitaph is as follows:

> *Here lies a toothless, gray-haired Dean,*
> *Who grew teeth anew, turned dark-haired again, and here he rests.*
> <note>original: "Hic jacet edentulus, canus, atq; Decanus, / Rursus dentescit, nigrescit, & hic requiescit." The Latin implies a miraculous physical rejuvenation.</note>

It has as many virtues as oil of vitriol <term>Oil of vitriol: Concentrated sulfuric acid, highly corrosive and used in various alchemical processes.</term>. If the teeth are rubbed with it, it whitens them and removes rot from the gums, provided it is mixed with rose water.

# TREATISE ON VARIOUS Preparations of Tartar.

Crude Tartar <note>original: "Tartarum"; the potassium bitartrate crust that forms on the inside of wine barrels.</note> is taken, ground, placed in a retort, and distilled according to the process for oil of vitriol <note>original: "olei vitrioli"; sulfuric acid.</note>. Oil and water emerge; separate the water from the oil using a water bath <note>original: "balneum."</note>. Rectify the water over colcothar <note>original: "colcotar"; the red iron oxide residue left after distilling vitriol.</note> until the foul smell has departed. This is greatly effective against putrefactions and blockages <note>original: "oppilationibus"</note>; it resolves internal abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note> and consumes the defects of the internal organs <note>original: "præcordialium"</note>. It heals every kind of scabies <note>original: "scabiem"; a contagious skin disease causing itching and sores.</note> when drunk without any other mixture. The dose is one spoonful morning and evening by itself, or with a decoction of guaiacum wood <note>original: "ligni guayaci"; a wood from the Americas used as a primary treatment for syphilis in this period.</note>. It strongly induces sweating in the venereal plague <note>original: "lue venerea"; syphilis.</note>, and is a ready remedy for dropsy <note>original: "hydrope"; swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and long-standing obstructions.

## *ANOTHER PREPARATION OF TARTAR.*

The Tartar is calcined <note>original: "calcinatur"; burned to a white ash.</note>, ground, and spread upon a marble slab. Place it in a damp location to dissolve <note>original: "solvendum"; this process of turning to liquid by absorbing atmospheric moisture is called deliquescence.</note>, then filter and dry it; repeat this three times. Take one pound <note>original: "℔ j."</note> of this liquor and four ounces <note>original: "℥ iiij."</note> or more of the best oil of vitriol. Add it drop by drop onto the liquor of tartar. A very white coagulum <note>original: "coagulum"; a thickened or solidified mass.</note> will form. If you draw off the moisture until dry using a water bath <note>original: "B. M."; Balneum Mariae.</note>, you will then have a "fixed" tartar for dropsy, stones <note>original: "calculum"; kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and various diseases. It provokes sweating and purges through the bowels <note>original: "per inferius"</note>, provided it is mixed with honey of roses or another syrup. The dose is from half a scruple <note>original: "℈ ß."</note> to one scruple <note>original: "℈ j."</note> in white wine or parsley water.

## *ANOTHER.*

Dissolve calcined tartar upon a marble slab; keep the dissolved part and calcine the remainder. Pour its own water back over it and distill in a water bath. Again, pour its water back over it, distill, and keep it. Calcine it once more and let it be dissolved as before upon the marble. Distill and pour off; do this until it no longer solidifies but remains as an oil. With this oil, you may "fix" <note>original: "figes"; to make a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> all sublimated spirits, and you will dissolve corals and pearls. You shall heal all wounds and expel tartareous dregs <note>original: "tartareas fæces"; metabolic waste products believed to cause gout and stones.</note> from the body. The dose is from 4 to 6 drops in a suitable liquid.

## *TINCTURE OF TARTAR.*

Let spirit of wine impregnated with the tincture of Tartar be evaporated to the consistency of honey. Having put this liquor into a retort, distill it while observing the proper stages of the fire. You will have a white, acidic liquor, like oil of vitriol, which is a supreme secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> for all [diseases] of the lungs—

### *LIQUOR OF TARTAR.*

Liquor of Tartar <note>original: "Liquor tartari"</note> is calcined Tartar <note>original: "Tartarum calcinatum"; tartar burned to a white ash to extract its salts.</note> that has been dissolved <note>original: "resolutum"; allowed to liquefy by absorbing moisture from the air.</note> upon a marble slab in a cold place. If you place some of this into distilled water, over time the salt will separate itself from the water like a crystal; its effects are varied. The dose is half a scruple <note>original: "℈ ß."</note> in its own distilled water.

### *CREAM OF TARTAR.*

Take washed white wine tartar; grind it very finely; throw it into pure water and make it boil in a cauldron. Through boiling, a crust or film <note>original: "pellicula"</note> will form; remove this and save it. Take 1 dram <note>original: "ʒ j."</note> of this, and 8 grains of prepared scammony <note>original: "diagridij"; a potent plant-based purgative resin.</note>; mix them and administer it in broth. It purges gently. It is a secret remedy for conditions of the spleen <note>original: "lienis affectus"</note>.

### *A MAGISTERY OF TARTAR NOT TO BE*
### *despised.*

Dissolve Tartar that has been highly calcined in the phlegm of the spirit of wine <note>original: "aquæ vitæ phlegmate"; the watery residue left after distilling alcohol.</note>, filter it, evaporate it, and the salt will remain at the bottom. Dissolve it again in purified phlegm-water, filter as you did before, and repeat this three times until it leaves no dross <note>original: "fæces"</note> behind. Calcine it well to a perfect whiteness. Take 1 pound <note>original: "℔ j."</note> of this salt and 4 pounds <note>original: "℔ iiij"</note> of rectified spirit of wine; mix them and distill in a water bath <note>original: "B. M." or Balneum Mariae.</note>. Two parts will distill without any taste; repeat the process until the said water congeals with the said salt. For every dry thing, by its nature, drinks up its own moisture. Again, dry the salt thoroughly, mix in new spirit of wine, and distill; it will retain some part of the spirit of wine. Place this salt in a glass sublimator <note>original: "sublimatorium"; a vessel used to heat a solid until it becomes a vapor and then deposits as a solid again at the top.</note>; it will be sublimated like camphor. Take this sublimated salt and guard it as something precious; it performs wonders in the spagyric art <note>original: "spagyrica arte"; the alchemical practice of separating and recombining the essential components of a substance.</note>, for by its mediation the light of day is reduced into the first matter <note>original: "lux diei in primam materiam reducitur"; an advanced alchemical concept suggesting the preparation can capture or manifest the primal energy of light.</note>. By administering 3 grains in a suitable liquid, you shall heal sicknesses of whatever kind they may be. Fear God and give thanks to Him through Him who lives forever, Amen. God willing, we shall discuss more on this subject elsewhere; meanwhile, look upon this with favor.

## ON HYDROMEL.
<note>original: "Hydromelite"; a fermented drink made of honey and water, commonly known as mead.</note>

**I** cannot wonder enough how certain men, having cast aside all shame, claim the labors and inventions of others as their own, and sell hydromel to princes and governments as if it were some divine mystery, when it is of almost no significance. But ignorance is the mother of admiration. Pliny makes mention of it in his chapter on honey, and teaches the method of preparation. In these times, a disagreement has arisen among men and even certain women regarding the excellence and use of hydromel; they prepare it so secretly that a father or mother will not even reveal it to their son. I know many who are not ashamed to ask fifty thousand crowns for the formula of its composition. But when I had traveled to various regions and saw it sold publicly at a low price, I could not help but laugh at their impudence. For this reason, I thought I would not be doing a disservice if I described some methods of composing it in the present treatise, so that everyone may prepare it as they please and beware of such <term>apothecaries</term> <note>original: "pharmacopolis"; here used somewhat disparagingly to refer to those who sell medicines or secret formulas for profit.</note>. There are those who, in composing it, simply use no additives, but only add a bit of tincture of tartar <note>original: "tinctura tartari"; a solution derived from the sediment of wine casks, used in various chemical processes.</note> near the end, as Paracelsus teaches in his book *On the Nature of Things*; I approve of this simple preparation. Others, however, use fragrant roots and spices, which often results in the head suffering from heaviness. Still, there are those who prepare it from purgatives, and it purges no differently than the wine described by Arnaldus <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician.</note>. But it is in vain to do with many things what can be done with fewer. As I have experienced it, I will teach two ways of preparing it here. But I do not want this to be hidden from you: it is made more excellently during the Dog Days <note>original: "pendente canicula"; the hottest weeks of summer, usually from July to August, associated with the rising of the star Sirius.</note> than at any other time. Indeed, the sun impresses something more of its virtue into all things then than the heat of the elements...

### FORMULA

Take one part honey and eight parts rain or river water. Let the honey be dissolved in that water, and afterwards let them boil moderately in a kettle of sufficient capacity until a third part has been consumed, skimming off the foam. The sign of the perfect ratio is if you place a raw egg in it and it floats; then it is ready. If not, boil it down until it gives this sign. You may purify it through a clean linen cloth, then place it in a dry wooden vessel that has been previously seasoned with Malmsey wine <note>original: "vino malvatico"; a sweet, potent Mediterranean wine often used to flavor or preserve casks.</note>. Immediately put in a small bag filled with mustard seed and tied with a string, so that you may pull it out when necessary. This done, expose your vessel to the hottest sun, and your hydromel <note>mead; a fermented drink made of honey and water.</note> will boil like must <note>unfermented grape juice.</note> during the time of the vintage. When the time has passed, remove the mustard seed and place the well-sealed vessel in the cellar. This hydromel is the foundation from which you can make more at any time.

### HYDROMEL THAT TASTES LIKE WINE

Once you have prepared it, add one measure of the juice of hop flowers <note>original: "lupuli"; hops were used both for flavor and as a preservative.</note> to every thirty measures of the liquid. It will immediately begin to boil without any heat, and the vessel must be kept filled; when it has finished fermenting, you will have a hydromel so powerful that if you pour it over boiled honey-water, you will have excellent hydromel in a short space of time. And as often as you add new hop juice, you will increase its strength by that much more. The rest must be gathered by your own philosophical reasoning; I should not chew everything for you <note>A common early modern idiom meaning the author will not explain every single detail, leaving some work for the reader's intellect.</note>. Others add Clary Sage <note>original: "Ormini"; a herb historically used to enhance the intoxicating effects and flavor of ale and wine.</note> flowers after the first boiling. But I have another way: I am accustomed to impregnate the honey before I add the water. I have said enough of these things. Let us turn to others.

### ANOTHER HYDROMEL WHICH IN ITS OWN TIME
->*is turned into a very sharp vinegar, one spoonful of which*<-
->*transforms a measure of wine into the sourest vinegar.*<-

℞ <note>Take</note>: Long pepper, round pepper, nutmeg, and cinnamon, 3 ounces <note>original: "℥ iij"</note> of each. Let them be ground. Mix with 1 ½ pounds <note>original: "℔ j. ß"</note> of rye flour and temper it with hydromel. Make a ferment <note>a starter dough or leaven.</note>, from which you should take a piece the size of an egg and place it in the liquid; it will boil by itself. Leave the vessel open in a warm place, and in a short time it will be turned into a very sharp vinegar, with which I have even dissolved flints. May you finally look with favor upon and enjoy these nighttime labors of mine.

### QUESTION.
### *WHETHER MAGIC BE LAWFUL.*

Many Babylonians write that he who knows how to count knows everything. It is asked, why is man the wisest animal? The answer given is: because he knows how to count. True philosophers have not been ignorant of the fact that natural magic depends upon numbers. However, it is well established that magic is twofold: one kind belongs entirely to demons, in its operation and authority—a thing, by my faith! <note>original: "medius fidius"; a Latin idiom used to swear an oath or emphasize truth, literally "may the God of Faith help me."</note> accursed and monstrous. The other is nothing else (when it is well examined) than the absolute culmination of natural philosophy, which they call perfect and supreme wisdom. For in the Persian language, "Magus" <note>original: "Magus"; the author correctly identifies the term's origin from the Old Persian "maguš," referring to a priest or learned man.</note> signifies what we would call an interpreter and a cultivator of divine things.

There is a very great disparity and dissimilarity between these two arts, or magics. That demonic magic is condemned and execrated not only by the Christian religion, but by all laws and every well-ordered republic. Whoever practices this always conceals it, because it would bring ignominy and insult upon the author. No philosopher or man eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of this. This magic seeks out darkness and deserted places; indeed, all knowledge that avoids the public eye is suspect, just like that which draws its origin from the spirits of darkness. But the other magic is approved and embraced by all wise men and all nations devoted to heavenly and divine things. This is a higher and holier philosophy: from this, the highest clarity of letters and glory was sought in ancient times and almost always. To learn this, Pythagoras, Democritus, and Plato sailed abroad; having returned, they preached it and held it as foremost among their secrets <note>original: "arcanis"; referring to specialized or hidden knowledge.</note>.

Just as that magic of evil demons <note>original: "cacodaemonum"; from the Greek "kakodaimon," meaning an evil spirit.</note> can claim for itself the name of neither art nor science, so this true magic, full of the highest mysteries, encompasses the deepest contemplation of the most secret things, of God, and the knowledge of all nature. This magic calls forth into the light from their hiding places the virtues scattered and sown in the world by the grace of God. And just as a farmer joins elms to vines <note>original: "ulmos vitibus... maritat"; a classical agricultural metaphor where vines were "married" to trees for support; here it represents the union of different natural forces.</note>, so the mage joins the earth to the sky—that is, he connects the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher and, so to speak, marries them. This excites such admiration for the works of God, which ready charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of God's wonders, than that natural magic by which we are compelled to sing:
> The heavens are full, and all the earth is full of the majesty of your glory. <note>A paraphrase of the "Sanctus" from the Latin Mass and the Book of Isaiah 6:3.</note>
And this is enough regarding mages. ...is granted: but to whom, and when, and how much. In divine matters, silence is desired; strife is rejected; the **syllogism** <note>original: "Syllogismus"; a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. The author suggests that human logic is insufficient for divine truth.</note> is mocked: nothing precedes it [divine wisdom]. Therefore, whatever must be concluded, one must acquiesce to it. For every creature was created by God to be a witness to the word of its Creator, through which it was made; and if it fulfills this, let it be blessed; if not, let it be cursed. For every creature is naturally compelled, in its own order and place, to confess its Creator and to serve as a testimony to His word. What, I ask, moves more forcefully and persuades more than the reading of the Sacred Scriptures? They do not merely persuade, but compel, agitate, and exert force: the words of the Law may be unrefined and rustic, but they are alive, animated, fiery, sharp, penetrating to the depth of the spirit, transforming the whole man with a wondrous power. Therefore, he who separates the knowledge of created things from their Maker possesses only the shadow of all things. For this reason, for the sake of those pious and most learned men **Guillaume Le Normand of Trogny** and **Jacques Bongars** <note>Jacques Bongars (1554–1612) was a famous French scholar, diplomat, and book collector.</note>, and all those most skilled in all disciplines, I shall add other philosophical rules, of which the first is as follows.

->*The First Rule.*<-

God created nothing in truth above, without creating some likeness of it below; so that through the likeness appearing below, we may arrive at the truth of that which exists above.

->*The Second Rule.*<-

God created nothing true in the spirit invisibly, without foreshadowing the same visibly in some body, so that through the body of the visible shadow, we may arrive at the truth of the hidden spirit.

->*The Third Rule.*<-

God created nothing visibly dispersed in the infinite, without also creating the same thing invisibly gathered into a single unit, so that through that which is finite and comprehensible in one, we may arrive at that which is infinite and incomprehensible in many. Moreover, God created all infinite things because He Himself is infinite; but He created all finite things for the sake of finite man, so that all things might have their beginning from Him, from whom they come, and at the same time all things might bear witness to their end, toward which they tend.

->*An Example.*<-

All things that exist come from the heavens and participate in the nature of the heavens: for nothing is so natural as that the offspring should participate in the nature and substance of its parent. Since the heavens are the universal parent of all lower things, it is necessary that all lower things participate in the nature and substance of the heavens. And thus the heavens are hidden within all lower things, which...

## ->ON CHEMISTRY<-

...beyond all things, it is manifest on the outside. And just as it is open to view in its body across the widest surface of the world, so by its spirit it is contracted most tightly in the center of the world. Therefore, the highest of all things by its body is the heaven <note>original: "cœlum"; in this context, the author refers to the "heavens" as both the physical sky and a refined, spiritual substance.</note> set on high: and again, the deepest of all things is the heaven hidden in the lowest spiritual part. And just as it closes and rules all things by its body, so by its spirit it passes through and fills all things. For everywhere the heaven is visible in its own form, and again, the heaven is in all things by its own power. And just as nothing is more manifest through all things than the heaven, so again, nothing is more hidden in all things than the heaven.

You, however, who always see the heaven outside of all things: understand the heaven hidden within all things. And make this hidden heaven manifest: then no power of the manifest heaven will ever be hidden from you. This heaven, or the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Philosophers' Stone: A legendary alchemical substance believed to be the "key" to nature, capable of perfecting both metals and the human soul.</term>, is in all things, and passes through all the things of the whole world. And it is a certain life-giving spirit <note>original: "spiritus vivificans"</note>, substantive and essential, bestowing life, substance, and essence upon all the creatures of this world; for from it, in it, and through it they exist, live, are nourished, grow, and all things are moved. And all things are full of its power, and nothing is void of its essence and power (except that which is dead and no longer among the number of living creatures). 

This spirit is most freely diffused in the heaven by its own motion and power; but in the earth, and especially in its center, it is most tightly contracted. Therefore, in the creatures arising in the center of the earth, it is now as if condensed and incorporated into their substances: in metals it is entirely enclosed and fixed; in minerals, it is at the next level but not yet fixed. Therefore, the **philosophers** <note>In this era, "philosophers" usually refers to "natural philosophers" or alchemists who studied the secrets of nature.</note>, seeking with their greatest strength to comprehend this spirit—which exists as something infinite in the widely diffused circuit of the world—were in no way able to comprehend this entirely spiritual thing, being themselves entirely finite and corporeal. Therefore, recognizing that in the center of the world it is most tightly bound and already incorporated and limited, they chose the creatures produced in the center of the world as their subjects, and labored to extract that spirit from them, and afterward to receive it entirely within a proper subject. 

Since it was too securely sealed in metals, they took minerals <note>original: "mineralia"; the author distinguishes between the "fixed" state of metals and the more accessible state of minerals.</note> closest to metals, in whose bodies it was not yet so tightly enclosed; and from these they extracted the spirit, and with this extract, they gave life to that [the subject]. Furthermore, for that which was enclosed in metals, they assisted the nearest nature through the nearest nature, and ascending from a lower degree to a higher one through the lesser minerals, they reached the greater powers of the minerals. For thus the order of nature requires: that one ascends through the lowest to the higher things, and that through lesser things the greater things are attained, lest through the greater, the smallest things be despised. Furthermore, the lesser things are perfected by the greater. This spirit of heaven, however, lies hidden and concealed in the minerals of the earth with so many substantial virtues within, that...
