...is manifest in the firmament of heaven by the stars and lightning. Therefore, the wise philosophers called these things by the names of the stars in heaven and shaped those things with the forms of the minerals of the earth. It must be noted that this spirit can be held and preserved in no other subject than in water of its own kind and species. For by nature, a thing of a similar nature has a perpetual action and operation upon its own kind, and not in a different species, much less in a different genus. Indeed, the greater the diversity of things, the lesser is their unity. For water is the proper receptacle and dwelling place of the spirit; therefore, in the beginning of the creation of the world, this spirit was carried over the waters. Thus, if water is distilled from minerals with a strong fire, the spirit of the minerals will also be drawn out at the same time into that water, mixing with it and dwelling within it. 

Yet, that thick and corporeal spirit (or the earthly spirit of minerals) is not yet that most secret and life-giving spirit <note>original: "spiritus vivificus"</note> of heaven. Rather, this is the thick and elemental spirit which serves as the dwelling place for that subtle, celestial spirit which is called—and truly is—the soul and life of all creatures; it carries the most direct image of God. Therefore, just as God dwells in a fiery essence and is a "consuming fire," so too this spirit, which is the soul giving life to all things, dwells hidden in the fiery and most burning mineral spirit. It is also a fire that consumes all earthly things, while purifying celestial things to the highest degree. 

And so, the water distilled from minerals has three parts: the body, which is the water; that thick, elemental fiery spirit; and finally, the hidden life-giving soul, which is called the **Hidden Spiritual Sun and Moon**, the **Invisible Sulfur of Nature** <term>Sulfur of Nature: In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, masculine, or combustible principle of a substance, not merely the chemical element sulfur.</term>, and the **Living Gold of the Philosophers** <term>Gold of the Philosophers: Not common gold, but the refined spiritual essence that can "ripen" or perfect other metals.</term>. When this is incorporated into a proper subject, it powerfully dissolves corporeal, metallic gold. Then, when gold is mixed with gold in the nature of the subject, that spiritual gold gives life to the corporeal gold. This corporeal gold, in turn, makes the spiritual gold "thick" or tangible. Thus, the spirit becomes body, and the body becomes spirit, and both together become one spiritual and inseparable thing. Then, such "living gold," when incorporated, generates gold. For all generation must come from the living and the corporeal; things without bodies do not generate, and dead things do nothing. Therefore, so that they may live, it is necessary for the corporeal gold to become spiritual and the spiritual gold to become corporeal. Then, at last, the gold, being perfect and similar to itself in its own genus and species, will generate gold infinitely, if it is mixed with its proper and due matter. More on these matters can be found in the *Book of Minerals*.

## ON THE SALTS OF CERTAIN PRINCIPAL HERBS, AND their powers.

### ON THE SALT OF ST. JOHN'S WORT.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring scrolling acanthus leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Salt of St. John's Wort <term>Hipericon</term> is a most proven remedy against pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the chest lining</note>; it is given to the patient in a warm wine, in an amount that can be contained in half a hazelnut shell. The salt of St. John's Wort promotes urine and menstruation; it is suitable for tertian and quartan fevers <note>fevers that recur every three or four days, often associated with malaria</note> when drunk with wine. It relieves sciatic pain when consumed for several days, and heals burns when dissolved with vinegar: it cleanses the blood of phlegm. It cures ulcers when applied with the liquid of the salt; likewise, it heals fistulas. Furthermore, it treats putrefaction of the mouth and ulcers of the neck when mixed with honey of roses and applied with a feather in the morning, at noon, and in the evening. It is also beneficial for those with dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>. For those suffering from worms—such as those in whose stomachs "serpents" or other types of worms might grow from the putrid water they have drunk—give them 4 or 5 grains of transparent glass of antimony <note>a potent and toxic chemical preparation of the mineral stibnite</note> to eat at night with 1 scruple <note>℈ j; a unit of weight equal to about 1.3 grams</note> of rose sugar. Mix it like an electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note>, and afterward give a draught of wine in which 1 scruple of salt of St. John’s Wort has been dissolved. Let the patient sleep if they wish; once awakened by the medicine, they will copiously cast out foul humors through both the upper and lower channels <note>referring to vomiting and purging</note>. For those who cannot hold their urine, let them burn the bladders of goats and grind them into powder, to which they should add 2 drachms <note>ʒ ij; approximately 7.8 grams</note> of salt of St. John's Wort, to be taken with wine for drinking.

### ON THE SALT OF POLYPODY.

Salt of polypody <note>a type of fern</note> also cures pleurisy; likewise, it draws out black bile <note>the humor associated with melancholy</note> and phlegm from the joints. It is beneficial for quartan fevers; the dose is 1 to 2 scruples.

### ON THE SALT OF CHAMOMILE.

Salt of chamomile is beneficial for difficulty of urination if one handful is administered in warm wine: it also stimulates the menses of women when taken in water of pennyroyal <note>a medicinal herb in the mint family</note>. Its use is great in cases of colic and intestinal blockage <note>iliaca</note> caused by wind <note>gas</note> from a cold cause.

### ON THE SALT OF GENTIAN.

Salt of gentian <term>Gentiana</term> opposes all fevers, opens and purges obstructions of the internal organs, and promotes both urine and menstruation: it is also effective against snake bites when taken with salt of rue and pepper.

### ON THE SALT OF HEDGE HYSSOP OR "Grace of God."

Salt of hedge hyssop <term>Gratiola</term>, also known as *Gratia Dei*, heals dropsy, and is likewise beneficial for those suffering from melancholy who are suffused with blood and terrified <note>likely referring to manic or paranoid states</note>. It also aids those with kidney stones, the insane and demented, those with heart ailments, and those with infected blood: it also helps those who pass urine with difficulty. Furthermore, it extinguishes burns and is effective against the Hungarian disease <note>original: *Hungaricum morbum*; a term usually referring to typhus, which plagued armies in the 16th century</note> if a linen cloth is moistened in the dissolved liquid and bound around the head, repeating the process after it dries. It is also administered internally for the same disease.

### ON THE SALT OF REST-HARROW.

<margin>

diuretics.

Salt of rest-harrow <term>Ononis</term>—once the pathways and humors have been prepared and the necessary diversions and purgations have been performed, which must be diligently noted before the use of salts—crushes and expels stones in both the kidneys and the bladder when taken with its own distilled water, and it assists with difficulty of urination; likewise, when drunk in wine, it heals hemorrhoids. It also aids obstructions of the spleen, kidneys, and liver when taken with the liquid of crab's eyes, oranges, lemons, saxifrage, winter cherry <note>original: *Alkekengi*</note>, and pellitory-of-the-wall.

### ON THE SALT OF BROOM.

Salt of broom <term>Genista</term> breaks and expels stones and stimulates the flow of urine.

### ON THE SALT OF BEAN STALKS.

Salt of beans <term>Faba</term> assists with difficulty of urination, breaks and expels stones, and dissipates gas. The dose is half a drachm <note>symbol: ʒ ß; approximately 2 grams</note> in white wine.

### ON THE SALT OF MUGWORT.

Salt of mugwort <term>Artemisia</term> promotes menstruation.

### ON THE SALT OF LEMON BALM.

Salt of lemon balm <term>Melissa</term> promotes menstruation, cleanses the womb, and assists with the suffocation of the womb <note>a historical diagnosis for various respiratory or emotional distresses believed to originate in the uterus</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF CELANDINE.

Salt of celandine <term>Chelidonium majus</term> provokes the menstrual flow; its dose is one scruple <note>original: *℈ j.*</note>, which usually weighs 20 barley grains. A liquid made from this salt clarifies the eyes. This same salt, drunk in wine with salt of anise, heals the "royal disease" <note>jaundice, so called because it was thought only the most costly remedies could cure it, or because of the golden color of the skin</note>; the liquid is also effective for ulcers. It also benefits those with asthma and obstructions of the chest, cleanses the liver, and is effective against the plague, the suffering of colic, and pain and swelling of the womb. For hemorrhoids <note>original: *mariscas*</note>, it is used mixed with an equal weight of the phlegm of vitriol <note>a dilute acid distilled from iron or copper sulfates</note>. <margin>Cancerous ulcers.</margin> For "the wolf" <note>original: *lupum*; a term for corrosive or "eating" ulcers like lupus or skin cancer</note> and other poisonous, cancerous ulcers, as well as for frostbitten limbs that would otherwise have to be amputated, apply a "false water" <note>likely a prepared saline solution or a specific chemical byproduct</note> with a woolen cloth several times. Anyone who has fallen from a height or from a horse should apply this same water over the injury. <margin>Note the property of this salt.</margin> It is also effective against the bite of a rabid dog; mix this salt with honey of roses to make an ointment, which prevents ulcers from rotting. Likewise, placed upon buboes <note>swollen lymph nodes associated with the plague</note>, it draws out the poison; those suffering from the itch <term>scabies</term> should wash themselves with a solution of this salt.

### ON THE SALT OF WORMWOOD.

Salt of wormwood <term>Absinthium</term> is usefully administered for almost all diseases, especially in times of plague; it draws out water from beneath the skin <note>treating edema or dropsy</note>. It promotes urine, strengthens the stomach, and induces sweating. If used both internally and externally, it drives out the "French disease" <note>syphilis</note> and heals hemorrhoids and other internal vices; it cleanses and heals abscesses and any kind of putrid wounds by sprinkling it upon them. This salt, dissolved in water, removes warts, varicose veins, or pustules, and scars, and fills in the flesh. It is used against dropsy, putrid fevers, and both daily and four-day <note>quartan</note> fevers, following a methodical process after the body has been purged with evacuants and other suitable remedies. Combined with the waters of lemon balm, sorrel, and rue, it strengthens the liver and stomach and grants the stomach good digestion. It is also used against the pain of colic and griping of the belly; it heals ailments of the anus and rectum, and treats a prolapsed womb by irrigation and application. A liquid of this salt, applied with a feather, heals ailments of the head such as dandruff, ringworm, freckles, and impetigo. When applied with water, it drives away lice, leprosy, and other dry or parched forms of the itch. These mentioned salts heal not only these, but many other sicknesses and conditions as well.

Salt of masterwort <term>Imperatoria</term> is able to warm cold and "deadened" limbs and to dissolve thick and viscous humors <note>fluids of the body</note> that have become stuck to the sides and linings of the stomach; it can also correct other faults of the stomach, intestines, and bladder, and furthermore increase the male seed and strengthen Venus <note>libido or sexual function</note>. Salt of masterwort is effective against the plague and promotes sweating if it comes from a chill; it promotes childbirth and expels a stillbirth. ### ON THE SALT OF BEAR’S BREECH.

Salt of bear's breech <term>Branca Ursina</term> dissolved in vinegar is usefully applied upon any tumors, such as warts, varicose veins, and calluses growing upon the bones. For younger people, it may be applied at any time and according to their need. For calluses or bone growths, however, it should only be bound upon the area during a waning moon and after sunset.

### ON THE SALT OF ANGELICA.

Salt of angelica wonderfully purges the blood, and especially the brain, if twenty drops are taken in the evening during a waning moon, dissolved in oil of fennel; the treatment should be repeated often at intervals.

### ON THE SALT OF LOVAGE OR LIGUSTICUM.

Salt of lovage <term>Levisticum</term> is assigned to the bladder, kidneys, a stomach with poor digestion (especially in women), and the intestines. It dissolves small stones <note>original: *arenulas*; literally "little sands"</note> collected from a calculus of the bladder and kidneys. In the case of a bladder stone, the region of the navel should be anointed; for a kidney stone, the region of the loins above the sacred bone <term>sacrum</term> should be anointed. Finally, the salt itself should be drunk dissolved in rose vinegar. Afterward, the body should be well-covered with warm blankets to provoke sweating. Furthermore, this salt is used against jaundice, coughs, the French disease, stones, and burning fever. It drives away swelling of the neck by gargling, and it is not useless in a time of plague; it wards off poison that has been touched or drunk, draws out "fluxes" <note>excess fluid or catarrh</note> from the head, and strengthens the head.

<margin>It cures the falling of the uvula.</margin>
This salt, taken with honey of roses, cures the falling of the uvula <note>original: *casum uvae*; literally "the fall of the grape," referring to an elongated or swollen uvula</note> and consumes the flux. This salt, dissolved or taken in food and drink for some time, causes the flesh to grow <note>i.e., helps a person gain weight or recover from wasting</note>. It also cures the itch <term>scabies</term>, the suffering of colic (in both men and women), dandruff, freckles, lice infestation <term>phthiriasis</term>, creeping skin eruptions <term>serpigo</term>, and the menses of women so that they do not fall heavily ill; likewise, it cures difficulty in urinating <term>strangury</term>.

### ON THE SALT OF BURNET.
->Stone-pepper<- <note>original German: *Steinpfeffer*</note>

<margin>Burnet of the Germans, or the Rock-breaker of the Gauls <note>original: *Pimpinella Germanorum, sive saxifraga Gallorum*</note>.</margin>
The salt of Burnet <note>original: *pimpinella*</note> is very friendly and beneficial to the stomach and all the intestines. If it is properly prepared as it should be, and if one eats it in place of common salt for three days every third month (lest the stomach become so accustomed to it that it takes it as ordinary food), and if one continues this throughout their whole life, then they will undoubtedly be safe from dropsy <term>edema/fluid retention</term>, phthisis <term>tuberculosis</term>, and apoplexy <term>stroke</term>. This salt purifies the blood, opens the arteries, the liver, and the lungs, and protects against hectic fever <note>a chronic, wasting fever often associated with consumption</note>. If it is dissolved in a choice water of wild chicory <note>original: *scariola*</note> and applied as a compress <note>original: *epithematis modo*</note> around the region of the liver—especially at night when an immoderate thirst troubles women who have recently given birth—it is highly effective. The elderly and anyone of a colder temperament <note>referring to the four humors</note> should use this salt. It is useful against cold sweats and expels the plague; or, in times of plague, it induces sweat. It removes headaches coming from "coldness," the pain of colic, the "ascending cold matrix" in women <note>referring to uterine disorders or "hysterical" symptoms</note>, stones of the kidneys and bladder, vertigo, contractions of the limbs, and difficulty urinating <term>dysuria</term>.

---

### ON THE SALT OF BLACK BURNET.

<margin>Burnet of the Gauls <note>original: *Pimpinella Gallorum*</note>.</margin>
The salt of Black Burnet cleanses and heals any open or corrosive, spreading ulcers; it prevents the generation of worms and putrid flesh within them and remedies the foul odor.

---

### ON THE SALT OF CRETAN CARROT.
->Commonly called Bear-root.<- <note>original German: *Behrwurz*; likely *Meum athamanticum*</note>

If the salt of Cretan Carrot <note>original: *Daucus Creticus*</note> is consumed frequently, it effectively expels a miscarriage or a menstrual birth, such as a "mole" <note>original: *mola*; a non-viable mass or tumor in the uterus</note>.

---

### ON THE SALT OF MOUNTAIN FENNEL.

If salt of mountain fennel is sprinkled into hollow or deep ulcers, it prevents them from generating a foul odor, worms, or putrid flesh; but it should be noted that it usually tends to draw blood from the affected area in the amount of two drachms. When dissolved with alum in warm wine and given as a gargle, it strikes back at scurvy of the mouth <term>stomacace</term>, restores the natural redness to the gums, and causes the flesh to grow back.

---

### ON THE SALT OF COMMON FENNEL.

Salt of fennel reduced into an ointment with butter and applied in a similar way dries and heals ulcerous scabs of the head <term>porrigines</term> and spreading skin eruptions <term>serpigines</term> of the body. Likewise, it provokes the menses and urine, and is suitable for those suffering from jaundice <note>original: *arquato*; an old term for the "rainbow disease" or jaundice</note>.

---

### ON THE SALT OF CARAWAY.

The salt of caraway <note>original: *carvi*</note> is intended for fevers of the brain, the womb, and the seminal vessels. When drawn up through the nostrils with water, it wondrously draws out catarrhs <note>excessive mucus or "runny nose"</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF PARSLEY.

Salt of parsley <note>original: *petroselinum*</note> dissolves tumors of every kind. Therefore, if taken regularly with wine, it expels stones from the bladder as well as the kidneys. Likewise, if the mouth is rinsed with it and wine, it is an immediate remedy for scurvy <term>stomachace; an old term for mouth ulcers or bleeding gums associated with scurvy</term>. It greatly assists those suffering from gout <term>podagra</term>, hand-gout <term>chiragra</term>, and sciatica. ### ON THE SALT OF CHERVIL, OTHERWISE
### Known as Gingidium.

Salt of chervil or gingidium dissipates gas <note>flatulence</note> of every kind; it breaks and expels stones, and it does so with a gentle and mild action, yet one that is excellently penetrating. For this reason, its use in delicate bodies is not only harmless but even very healthy. Finally, if it is administered with Blessed Thistle <note>original: *cardui benedicti*</note> water, it drives out roundworms from the belly and soothes griping pains around the navel.

It should be given partly as a regular drink in noble wine, and partly applied by frequent smearing around the veins of the temples and the nostrils. Furthermore, it warms and purges a womb that has become chilled and filled with sticky humors, and it even makes childbirth easier.

### ON THE SALT OF SPEEDWELL.

Salt of speedwell <note>original: *veronica*</note> taken with theriac <term>theriaca; a complex herbal "treacle" used as a universal antidote</term> and Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, fortified wine often used as a medicinal base</note> is a remedy against the plague. If it is reduced into an oil or liquid form, use it to anoint pustules, scabies, abscesses, fistulas, and morphea <term>morphæa; a condition of hardened, discolored patches on the skin</term>. Dissolved in rose vinegar, it is effective against "French pustules" and abscesses <note>syphilis</note> if they are frequently washed with it.

### ON THE SALT OF THE STRONG HERB.

<margin>I believe this is Sideritis <note>Ironwort</note>.</margin>
Salt of the "strong herb" <note>original: *herbæ fortis*</note> drunk with wine is for the internal French disease; however, for hot and burning fevers, it should be taken in the morning with honey of roses. It is likewise effective for decay of the mouth and inflammations of the throat. It promotes menstruation in women. He who has an ulcerated neck or decayed gums should gargle with that water mixed with honey of roses. Wash pustules with the same water. The same water, mixed with essentialized antimony <term>antimonio essentificato; a purified chemical preparation of the mineral antimony</term> and drunk, is effective against the Spanish disease <note>another contemporary name for syphilis</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF PURPLE LOOSESTRIFE.

Salt of purple loosestrife <note>original: *salicaria purpurea*</note> frequently drunk on an empty stomach with wine is effective against fevers and frenzy <note>original: *phrenesin*; delirium associated with high fever</note>. It is also effective against insanity, colic, and contractions of the limbs when applied as a fomentation <note>a warm, medicinal compress</note> with water. For pestilential fevers, it is mixed with vinegar. It likewise cures jaundice when taken with betony water, as well as fistulas.

### ON THE SALT OF FUMITORY.

Let salt of fumitory <note>original: *fumariæ*</note> be dissolved in water to make a gargle; it is effective against decay of the mouth. French ulcers <note>syphilis sores</note> should be washed with the same.

### ON THE SALT OF HEMP-NETTLE OR
### Wild Balm.

Salt of hemp-nettle <note>original: *galyopsis*</note> or wild balm, taken in the morning with its own distilled water, is for asthma and heart pain. In wine, it also cures fistulas of the breasts. It promotes menstruation in women, assists in childbirth, and heals trembling of the limbs.

### ON THE SALT OF HEMP-AGRIMONY.

<margin>Of Agrimony.</margin>
Salt of hemp-agrimony <note>original: *eupatorium*</note> is used with honey of roses against inflammations of the neck; likewise, when drunk, it is used against pleurisy and other internal abscesses, internal heat, and burning fevers. It is also used against mouth ulcers <term>alcola; an old term for aphthous ulcers or thrush</term> with honey of roses. Furthermore, it is effective against intestinal worms, the plague, scabies, scurf <note>dandruff or skin flakes</note>, and lice infestations <term>phthiriasin</term>. By applying or washing with warm water containing this salt, it heals the bites of mad dogs <note>rabies</note>. It is also beneficial for blisters or ulcerated French sores. Finally, it assists burned limbs.

### ON THE SALT OF GREATER CENTAURY.

Salt of greater centaury <note>original: *sal centaurij majoris*; centaury was named after the centaur Chiron, the legendary healer</note> provides relief for those suffering from dropsy <note>original: *hydropicis*; an old term for edema or fluid retention</note> and pestilential diseases. Likewise, it is employed against poison, "melancholic blood" <note>an excess of black bile, thought to cause depression and sluggishness</note>, the falling sickness <note>original: *caducum*; epilepsy</note>, dimness of the sight and eyes, the Hungarian disease <note>original: *morbum Hungaricum*; historically identified as typhus</note>, burning fever, and jaundice <note>original: *icteritiam*</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF PELLITORY-OF-THE-WALL.

Salt of pellitory-of-the-wall <note>original: *parietariae*</note>, when reduced into a liquid form and applied as an ointment, heals St. Anthony’s Fire <note>original: *sacros ignes*; a term for skin infections like erysipelas</note>, inflamed growths <note>original: *condylomata*</note>, tumors, and swellings. It is used against the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> when combined with the liquid of "crab’s eyes" <term>oculorum cancri; stony calcium concretions found in crayfish, used as an antacid</term> and mugwort water. For colic, it is used like the salt of Roman chamomile. It works against all obstructions of the liver and spleen and against putrefaction, much like the salts of wormwood and chicory. It is also effective against gas of the stomach and intestines when taken with suitable preserves and waters.

### ON THE SALT OF CINQUEFOIL.

Salt of cinquefoil <note>original: *pentaphylli*; literally "five-leaf"</note> is powerful against diseases of the liver and lungs, as well as poisons; it also cures fistulas when sprinkled upon them.

### ON THE SALT OF BIRTHWORT.

Salt of birthwort <note>original: *aristolochiae*</note> resists poisons, hiccups, and even tremors, convulsions, and pains in the sides. Likewise, it is suitable for the spleen and for those suffering from asthma. When used as a gargle, it cleanses the gums and teeth.

### ON THE SALT OF VALERIAN.

Salt of valerian promotes menstruation, acts as a diuretic, and is beneficial for pain in the sides.

### ON THE SALT OF TORMENTIL.

Salt of tormentil suppresses the incontinence of urine and halts excessive menstrual flow.

### ON THE SALT OF PLANTAIN.

Salt of plantain is given in a drink for ulcers of the kidneys and bladder. Likewise, it assists in treating tertian fevers <note>fevers that spike every third day, typically associated with malaria</note>.

### ON THE SALT OF RIBWORT PLANTAIN.

Salt of ribwort plantain <note>original: *plantaginis minoris*</note> is used in pestilential fevers and for pains of the heart; it is also applied to ulcers of the bladder and kidneys with a good wine. Likewise, it is used against melancholic delusions, pain and swelling of the womb, and against "phrenesy" <note>original: *phrenesim*; an acute inflammation of the brain or delirium</note> and the falling sickness. It consolidates internal wounds and the abscesses resulting from the French disease <note>syphilis</note>, as well as ancient ulcers. It is effective against headaches resulting from the Hungarian disease when used frequently. Likewise, it is effective against decay of the mouth and neck, or "alcola" <note>an old term for aphthous ulcers or thrush</note>, when mixed with honey of roses for purging or gargling. Mixed with vinegar, it extinguishes the heat of burns.

### ON THE SALT OF BROADLEAF PLANTAIN.

Salt of broadleaf plantain <note>original: *plantaginis majoris*</note> cleanses "burnt blood" <note>blood that has become too thick or hot according to humoral theory</note> and benefits those of a choleric temperament. It likewise heals mouth ulcers, ulcers of the neck, or abscesses.

### ON THE SALT OF SMARTWEED.

Salt of smartweed <note>original: *persicariæ*; also known as water-pepper</note> is given to those suffering from fevers, and it corrects defects of the lungs, liver, and spleen when taken with appropriate herbal waters. Likewise, it removes the pestilence, sores of the neck <note>original: *alcolam*; a term for various skin eruptions or ulcers</note>, swelling, foul breath, cough, bladder stones, and heat of the head. It is also very useful for horses and cattle in cases of swelling, fractures, and dislocations of the legs, especially by applying it hot and soaking the area continuously until they are restored. If the head is washed with this same water, it prevents the loss of hair, stops catarrh <note>excessive mucus</note>, and keeps away scabby skin eruptions. Licorice juice dissolved in this water, or a decoction of the root mixed with honey of roses and drunk, removes swelling of the neck and helps with distress of the chest and heart, as well as asthma. It is effective against the stone and also against dysentery when used with *dianisum* <note>a medicinal compound made primarily of anise</note> and other ingredients.

### ON THE SALT OF HELLEBORO.

Salt of hellebore, dissolved in wine or some other appropriate liquid, powerfully helps to draw out the humors of epilepsy, the "comitial disease" <note>another term for epilepsy</note>, the falling sickness, apoplexy, and gout <note>original: *podagricum*</note>, as well as other corrupt and malignant humors from the womb and other places.

### ON THE SALT OF COMFREY.

Salt of comfrey <note>original: *symphyti*</note> expels the menses, the French disease, and worms; it cures heat of the liver, jaundice, and the plague; and it is beneficial for those with dysentery or those spitting blood. # ON THE SALT OF CERTAIN TREES 
### and its virtues.

## ON THE SALT OF DWARF ELDER.

Salt of dwarf elder <note>original: *ebuli*; Sambucus ebulus</note> cures dropsy <note>original: *hydropem*; swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and daily fever. Taken with its own distilled water, it cures those with dropsy in a short time.

## ON THE SALT OF ELDER.

SALT of elder <note>original: *sambuci*; the common elderberry tree</note> heals dropsy.

## ON THE SALT OF ASH.

Salt of ash <note>original: *fraxini*</note>, drunk with its own distilled water, heals those with spleen ailments <note>original: *lienosis*</note> and resists poisons; it also resists the plague, provided it is administered in blessed thistle water <note>original: *aqua cardui benedicti*</note>: the dose is one to two scruples <note>original: *℈ j. ad ij.*; a scruple was a small unit of weight in the apothecaries' system</note>.

## ON THE SALT OF THE GRAPEVINE.

Salt of the grapevine <note>original: *vitis viniferæ*</note> is effective during times of plague; it is a kind of diaphoretic <note>a substance that induces sweating to expel toxins</note>: its lye <note>original: *lixivium*; a solution produced by leaching wood ash</note> drunk by itself provokes sweat.

## SALT OF SWINE’S ANKLE-BONE.

This drink heals inflammations and long-lasting griping pains <note>original: *torminibus*; usually referring to intestinal cramps or colic</note>.

## SALT OF DEER HORN.

It benefits those with dysentery, those spitting up blood, those with abdominal disorders <note>original: *coeliacis*; here referring to general digestive distress or "belly-ache" rather than modern Celiac disease</note>, the "royal disease" <note>original: *regio morbo*; a common historical name for jaundice</note>, and pains of the bladder when taken with a medicinal powder <note>original: *traga*; an aromatic powdered medicine</note>. It helps women suffering from a flux of the womb <note>original: *fluxione vulvæ*</note> when taken with a liquid suited for this purpose. It heals ulcers of the eyes, cleanses the teeth, and when vinegar is added, it restrains eruptions of blood.

## DREGS OF VINEGAR.

By itself or with myrtle, it checks tumors; applied externally, it stops discharges of the belly and stomach. It mitigates the "female flow" <note>menstrual or vaginal discharge</note> when placed on the lower belly or genitals. It disperses glandular swellings <note>original: *panos*</note> that have not yet become ulcers. When rubbed on with vinegar, it quells bumps, stiff breasts, and those breasts which cannot bear to be touched. When burned, however, and mixed with resin, it removes nail fungus and the itch <note>original: *scabies*</note>. It dyes hair with a reddish hue. When washed, it is mixed into medicines for the eyes and clears away dimness of vision <note>original: *caligines*</note>.

## ON THE SALT OF OAK WOOD.

Salt of oak wood restrains blood and the flow from the nostrils, and is used for making a cautery <note>a tool or substance used to sear or seal tissue</note>.

## ON THE SALT OF BOXWOOD.

SALT of boxwood resists the "Spanish Disease" <note>original: *Hispanicæ lui*; a historical term for syphilis</note>; it can be taken in place of salt of guaiacum.

## ON THE SALT OF GUAIACUM.

Salt of guaiacum wood draws out venereal humors. This wood, through chemistry, is reduced into water, oil, and salt, which [by the study of] chemistry...

Scholars call these Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt <note>original: *Mercur. Sulphur & salem*; these are the *Tria Prima*, the three primary principles of Paracelsian alchemy</note>: some are cured much more quickly of the venereal plague <note>original: *venerea lue*; a common term for syphilis</note> by this preparation. Andernacus <note>Johann Winter von Andernach (1505–1574), a physician and translator</note> and other physicians have drawn from the books of Theophrastus Paracelsus, where he writes about the correction of guaiacum wood <note>a hard wood from the Americas used as a treatment for syphilis</note> and its preparation. He teaches how to make a liquor of gum and alkali from this wood, with which that venereal plague is cured better than with its decoction or broth, as is the custom among many. In the same way, boxwood <note>original: *buxus*</note> is also to be prepared for curing the venereal plague, and no symptom or other danger is to be feared from it, or from its decoction and method. In this way, pine <note>original: *pinus*</note> can also be prepared for that "Spanish disease" <note>another historical name for syphilis</note>. Likewise, ash <note>original: *fraxinus*</note> and mistletoe <note>original: *viscus*</note>; its alkali is used for the evacuation of the hepatic flux <note>a discharge or flow associated with the liver</note>, and the "French disease" <note>yet another name for syphilis</note> with its pustules. For expelling these, no strict regimen is observed—such as making the patients endure hunger—but the sick are to be nourished with good wine, food, and salt; the guaiacum liquor is his drink, and the guaiacum gum is a kind of ointment for the pustules.

### ON THE SALT OF THE STONE FOUND IN SPONGES.

The salt of the stone found in sponges, when drunk with wine, breaks the stone <note>original: *calculum*; a kidney or bladder stone</note> that is in the bladder.

### PREPARATION OF SALT GEM AGAINST *dropsy & jaundice.*

Take of salt gem <note>original: *salis gemmae*; naturally occurring rock salt</note>, and juice of Spurge <note>original: *Titymali*, that is, *esulae minoris*</note>, one ounce each. Add cherry gum to the weight of the whole. Let a bolus be made and allow it to be reverberated <note>heated in a furnace</note> in the third degree <note>a high level of heat in alchemy</note> for two hours, and extract the alkali. The dose is from 8 to 12 grains. In place of scammony <note>original: *diagridii*</note>, you may take troches of alhandal <note>original: *trociscos alhandali*; a purgative made from bitter apple or colocynth</note>. **Addition.** Take 5 scruples of this salt gem; 4 scruples each of *Reboli* <note>original: *Reboli, id est, verae mumiae liquoris*; a resinous medicinal substance, often called "mummy"</note> and centaury. Let them be mixed; the dose is from four to 12 grains taken in an egg. Its preparation is for the same diseases. Of this same salt gem, take 1 ounce; 2 ounces of juice of caper spurge <note>original: *cataputiae*</note>; and wheat flour to the weight of the whole. From this, let a well-baked bread be made, of which 1 to 2 drams <note>original: *ʒ j. ad ʒ ij.*</note> may be given.

### ON THE SALT FROM THE ANKLE-BONES OF CATTLE OR *pigs.*

This salt, when drunk, helps those with abdominal distress <note>original: *cœliacos*</note>; mixed with honey, it kills intestinal worms. Likewise, with oxymel <note>a medicinal drink of honey and vinegar</note>, it is effective against disease of the spleen.

### ON THE SALT OF DEER HORN.

Salt of deer horn benefits those with abdominal distress and dysentery.

### ON THE SALT OF DEER BLOOD.

Salt of deer blood cures joint disease <note>original: *morbum articularem*</note>, gout of the feet <note>original: *podagram*</note>, gout of the hands <note>original: *chiragram*</note>, and gout of the knees <note>original: *gonagram*</note>.

### ON THE SALT FROM GOAT HORN.

This salt is applied for those with dysentery.

<header>ON CHEMISTRY.</header>

### CONCERNING GOAT-SALT AND ITS BLOOD.

<margin>What Galen thinks about salt.</margin>
Salt derived from the blood of a goat heals diseases of the joints, specifically gout of the hands, knees, and feet <note>original: *chiragræ, gonagræ ac podagræ*; these terms specify which joints are affected by gout</note>. Let it suffice for now to have spoken of the salts prepared from herbs, wood, stones, and animals, the use of which is very ancient. For even before the year 1500 <note>This likely refers to 1,500 years prior to the author's time, referring back to classical antiquity</note>, purgative salts were used among the Greeks. Aëtius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> also mentions salt of anise. Galen, in the second book of *On the Properties of Simple Medicines*, speaking of salt, reports the following: "Burnt salt," he says, "digests more powerfully than that which has not been burnt, because the substance itself is rendered finer by the property it receives from the fire." Since he writes in the same book that substances consisting of fine parts have more efficacy—even if their inherent power is small—they penetrate better, especially for dissolving dregs and tartarous humor <note>original: *tattareum humorem*; stony or crusty deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty crystals</note>. For the salt of things is extracted by calcination <note>the process of reducing a substance to ash through high heat</note>. Moreover, salt can be dissolved by salt alone, if you understand the matter well, and thus you may know that opposites are not cured by opposites, but "likes by likes" <note>original: *similia similibus curari*; an early medical philosophy suggesting a substance that causes symptoms can also cure them</note>. And although salt can even be made from the urine of boys, from animals, and from old shoes, and can be used without danger for both external and internal medicine, I wish to omit their use because of the revulsion they cause. Note this last point: the more salts are dissolved, filtered, and purified, the more they lose their foul smell and the more strength they acquire.

### CONCLUSION OF THE WHOLE WORK

*SALTS are manifold: some are mineral and "fixed" <note>in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to fire</note>, some are vegetable-fixed, and some are animal-fixed. However, among these species of salts, both vegetable and mineral, fixed varieties are found (as will be shown below).* Fixed minerals include common salt <note>original: *sal panis*; literally "bread salt"</note>, which is extracted from the sea or from well water. Then there is Rock Salt <note>original: *sal Gemmæ*; literally "gem salt"</note>, which is the clearest of all and transparent like crystal; it is better than those mentioned above. There are two species: one is crystalline, while the other is a transparent red. It is "born" in mines and sulfurous places, appearing in various forms among large and small stones. It is found especially in Spain in a place called Cardona <note>original: *Cardons*; a town in Catalonia famous for its salt mountain</note>, and also in Hungary. There are also vegetable salts, both fixed and non-fixed, which are made from the ashes of trees and herbs. From the strongest "heads" <note>original: *capitellis*; likely referring to the first or strongest part of a distilled solution or lye</note>, once the water has evaporated from them, the salt remains at the bottom of the vessel. Depending on the nature of the ash, the salt remains fixed or non-fixed; experience will teach you. One thing I tell you: alkali salt <note>original: *sal alcali*</note> is more worthy than all other salts, especially the vegetable ones. It is a "fixed oil" which the dryness of the fire has congealed. There are some who make alkali salt from soda and say it is fixed and that it fixes other things. Therefore, set your heart upon alkali salt, for it is a most excellent secret. Since every fixed thing in a fixed state is turned into na-

## TO FAITHFUL AND PIOUS PHYSICIANS.

I recall (most learned gentlemen) having read through many books by scholarly physicians, in which I often marveled that I found no mention of the Supreme Architect of things, much less an invocation of divine help, before they administered medicines to their patients. Yet it is more certain than certainty itself that a physician's piety sometimes achieves more than the admirable scientific knowledge of many. For this reason, since physical infirmity sometimes arises from sin, it was the duty of physicians, when called to the sick, to advise and lead them above all else to call upon the "physicians of souls" <note>This refers to the practice of seeking spiritual confession or pastoral care before medical treatment, a common requirement in medieval and early modern medical ethics</note>. In this way, after the spiritual health of the sick person had been provided for, one might proceed more healthfully to the physical remedy of medicine. At least three most excellent physicians, to my knowledge, entered upon this laudable path and practiced their art with the highest praise: I mean Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>, Gordonius <note>Bernard de Gordon (c. 1270–1330), a professor of medicine at Montpellier</note>, and Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath often associated with alchemical and medical writings</note> in the operative art. These men, while visiting their patients more frequently, exhorted them to repentance, and having first implored the help of the divine power, they experienced God’s greatest blessing in their healing.

The following formula for prayer was familiar to Raymond, which I have chosen to write down here, and which ought to remind all true physicians of their duty.

## THE PRAYER OF RAYMOND LULL BEFORE the administration of medicines.

> *Lord Jesus Christ, who art the true health of all, Lord, Thou art He who created all things "very good" in Thy goodness and wisdom; without Thee, I know nothing of good in the world. Therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, I humbly adore Thy majesty, because I know and firmly believe that nothing is good without Thy goodness, nothing is great without Thy greatness, nor enduring without Thy duration, nor powerful without Thy power, nor wise without Thy wisdom, nor diligent without Thy love, nor virtuous without Thy virtue, nor true without Thy truth, nor glorious without Thy glory, nor just without Thy justice. I know also that Thou didst wonderfully create man, and more wonderfully restore him <note>original: "mirabiliter creasti, mirabilius reformasti"; a common liturgical phrase reflecting the idea that the redemption of humanity was an even greater act than its initial creation</note>; Thou who hast given medicine to repair the health of human bodies: give Thy blessing to this medicine, so that all the virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the specific healing powers or properties of the substance</note> which Thou didst place in it at the beginning may be led to their intended end: so that in the body it enters, it may merit to bring about health of mind and body, through our Lord Jesus Christ Thy son, Amen.*

# THE MOST NOBLE LORD
# BERNARD, COUNT OF THE MARCH
## Of Treviso’s Book. <note>original: "Trevisanæ Liber". Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490) was a famous Italian alchemist who allegedly spent his life and fortune seeking the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

### *Concerning the most secret Chemical work of the Philosophers, to be elaborated through nature and art.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' depicting a seated figure in a room, possibly a scholar or alchemist at work.</image-desc>In order to lead true seekers of this art away from common errors and back to the true path—so that they do not squander their resources or suffer the loss of their reputation and fame by insisting upon the false recipes of books, such as those of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy</note>, Rasis <note>Al-Razi, a Persian polymath and physician</note>, Albertus Magnus, the *Path*, the *Light*, the *Canon of Pandects*, Demophontis, the *Summa*, and other seductive men—I shall first narrate my own errors. Afterwards, I will describe how I reached the desired goal, and how I four times crafted and completed the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and healing all diseases</note> with these very hands. Thus, those who read of my process may likewise be able to achieve it through speculation and the imitation of the works of nature. 

It would be foolish to judge alongside the common crowd that this art is false because of the <term>Sophists</term> <note>In this context, "sophists" refers to fraudulent alchemists or "puffers" who used trickery to mimic chemical transformations</note> and impostors we see engaged in it daily. Nor should one think that its true authors and sages wished to deceive others in their writings because they themselves were deluded; rather, they wished to leave behind a reputation for themselves after death, not infamy or reproach. But the ignorant commoner has this idiotic trait: that as soon as he reads something he does not understand, he despises it. Therefore, whoever follows the principles of nature through steadfast imagination will profit far more than one who follows the vain and dead letter found beneath innumerable enigmatic figures and sophisticated deceits. 

However, so that I may sincerely and purely collect for you the opinions of those honorable men who have treated this subject, I wished to write this little book and divide it into four parts: 

The **first** will tell of the inventors of the art, and especially those who gained possession of it according to their desire, and through whom I myself attained it. 

In the **second**, narrating my own personal history, I will speak at length regarding everything that happened to me in my search over time, and the burdens of my labors, describing everything from beginning to end without any <term>envy</term> <note>In alchemical literature, "envy" (invidia) refers to the practice of deliberately obscuring secrets to keep them from the "unworthy" or the public</note>. 

The **third** will discourse upon the roots and principles of metals, using the most evident and philosophical demonstrations. 

The **fourth** will contain the practice itself, delivered under a parable that is not so obscure that it cannot be perfectly understood. 

Each thing is written in such a manner that, unless you understand it through this book of mine, I do not easily believe you will ever perceive it through another. Nor is it something you should think you can understand immediately at first glance; it is hardly at the tenth reading—and the more often you repeat it, the better you will be able to uncover the matter day by day. No one should grow weary of these labors or regret them, if he believes that by these means he can avoid intolerable poverty and all diseases...

He outlines a four-part structure for the book, moving from historical authorities to his personal quest, the theory of metals, and finally the practical "work" hidden in a parable.</summary>

## FIRST PART OF THE CHEMISTRY OF LORD BERNARD
### *Count of the March of Treviso: Concerning the first inventors*
### *of this art.*

The first restorer of the Chemical art, after it was forgotten following the Flood, was HERMES TRISMEGISTUS, as is read in the memorial books of the histories of ancient deeds, in the *Imperial*, and in the exposition of the *Emerald Tablet* by Clavetus. He is called HERMES or MERCURY because he was the wisest of all in his time, and *Trismegistus*—Thrice-Great or Thrice-Wise—because he mastered and taught all worldly wisdom, or the triple natural philosophy: the vegetable, the mineral, and the animal, which are all one <term>Stone</term> <note>The "three kingdoms" of nature were believed to be unified in the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Moreover, he is called the "Father" in this art because of its restoration, as is held in all the books of the *Hermetic Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>, in which mention of him is made even before Pythagoras. Furthermore, as many as have held this art shall be called the "Sons of Hermes." Regarding this man, it is read in the [histories of] the Bible that he was the first to enter the valley of Hebron, and there he found seven stone tablets. Upon these, the Seven Liberal Arts had been inscribed by the Sages before the inundation of the waters occurred, each with its own principles, so that they might not pass into oblivion. For at that time, although they were instructed enough to foresee that the world would not perish entirely but would be preserved, they nevertheless did not have such perfect wisdom as to consider that God, who had given them that knowledge at that time, could have given it to others and to another as often as He willed.

He is said to have lived before the Law and after <note>Referring to the Mosaic Law</note>, during which time many wise men lived. Aros narrates, in a certain letter to King Meffohe, that this art was revealed by God to some of the children of Israel for the purpose of decorating the Ark of the Lord with gold and completing it, as is held among the Prophets Ezekiel and Daniel, and likewise in the works of Josephus. Some reached it without manifest revelation or books, but through hidden meditations on the visible works of God in His creatures—such as Phithomea, Rebecca, Solomon, and Philip of Macedon—all of whom, however, Hermes preceded in the discovery of this art after the Flood.

From Hermes, it was passed down to many others through a small book which he titled the *Emerald Tablet*, containing these words: "It is true, certain, and most true: That which is above has the nature of that which is below, and that which ascends has the nature of that which descends. <note>original: "Verum est, certum & verissimum: Quod est superius, naturam habet inferioris, & ascendens naturam descendentis." Many have followed this art, as we read of King Calid <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince traditionally considered the first Arab alchemist.</note>, son of Bendagid of the Ternary; of Aristotle the Chemist; of Plato; and of Pythagoras, a disciple of Hermes and author of the *Codex*, a book which contains the very truth of this matter without excess or deficiency, though it is written quite obscurely. In Arabia, King Haly, the greatest astrologer, is said to have possessed knowledge of it; he taught Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note>, and he in turn taught another King of Arabia, the previously mentioned Calid. Likewise, Aros taught it to his brother Nephandin, and Saturnus to Luncabur and his sister Medera. Their number is infinite, and it would be vain to list them all. There is a massive abundance of books written about this art using metaphorical words and figures so that they cannot easily be understood by anyone except the "Sons of the Art." Reading these books often leads one into various errors rather than toward the goal. Among their number are Scotus, Arnaldus, Raymond, Jean de Meun, Hortulanus, Veridicus, and others. <note>Referring to famous medieval scholars like Michael Scot, Arnald of Villanova, and Raymond Lully, whose complex writings often confused aspiring alchemists.</note> Therefore, in order to lead students back to the right path, I wished to write this little work for them.

## SECOND PART, IN WHICH ARE DESCRIBED
### *the immense labors of the author and his great expenses, with each operation from the beginning even to the end, resulting from the truth of his persistent success.*

When I first undertook this work, there fell into my hands the book of Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and chemist.</note>, in the testing of which I wasted four years and eight hundred crowns <note>original: "coronatorum", a high-value gold coin.</note>. Likewise, I suffered a loss of more than two thousand crowns at the start regarding the books of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose works were foundational but difficult.</note>, for many impostors urged and induced me to exhaust my substance. 

Afterward, I examined the books of Archelaus for three years, in which I worked together with a certain monk; and in the books of Rupescissa <note>John of Roquetaillade, a 14th-century Franciscan who wrote on the "quintessence."</note> and Johannes de Sacrobosco, I worked with <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>literally "water of life," usually referring to concentrated alcohol or strong acids used as solvents.</note> rectified thirty times with its dregs, until it reached such a sharpness that no glass could contain it. In that labor, another three hundred crowns were lost. Having consumed twelve or fifteen years in this manner, and countless gold coins without fruit, and after many experiments with recipes for dissolving and congealing common salt, [sal] ammoniac—

...shells, pine-nuts, Saracen salts, and metallic salts, which were then calcined <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or reduce it to a powder.</note> more than a hundred times over the space of two years. Likewise, I experimented with rock alums, ice-like alums, shale, plumose alum, with marcasites, blood, hair, urine, human dung, semen, animals and vegetable herbs, copperas <note>Iron(II) sulfate</note>, vitriols, inks, and eggs. These were processed by the separation of elements in an <term>athanor</term> <note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a steady heat over long periods.</note>, by use of an <term>alembic</term> <note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</note> and a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized circulatory vessel with two side-arms that return condensed vapors back into the main body.</note>, and through circulation, cooking, reverberation, ascension, descension, fusion, ignition, elementation, rectification, evaporation, conjunction, elevation, subtilization, and by mixing.

I pursued infinite other regimes of "sophistications" <note>In alchemy, a "sophistication" is a deceptive process that produces something that looks like gold or silver but lacks its true essence.</note> in which I had already remained stuck for twelve years. Having reached the age of thirty-eight, and still persisting in the extraction of <term>Mercuries</term> <note>The essential, volatile spirit alchemists sought to isolate from various substances.</note> from herbs and animals, I had by this point uselessly squandered—partly through my own folly and partly through the deceptions of impostors—about six thousand crowns, to the point that I had almost lost heart.

But indeed, in the meantime, I never forgot to pour out my prayers to God, that He might deign to assist my endeavors. Next, I happened upon a certain Prefect <note>A high-ranking administrative official or governor.</note> of our country who was likewise investigating the art. He was attempting to construct the Stone from common salt, dissolving it in the air and congealing it in the Sun, along with many other things too long to tell. In this work, a year and a half slipped away with others in vain labor, because we were not working upon the true matter. "In vain is that sought in a thing in which that which is sought is not contained," as is read in the <term>Codex of the Assembly of Truth</term> <note>original: "Turbæ veritatis," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>. Since, therefore, common salt by no means possesses what we desire, though we repeated the process fifteen times, it never showed us any alteration of its natural properties; for this reason, we left it and attempted it no further.

Furthermore, we saw others dissolving the finest silver, copper, and other metals in <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aqua fortissima," typically referring to nitric acid.</note>; likewise <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury.</note>, each separately in its own unique vessel with the same water. Finally, after all such solutions had rested for twelve full months, they poured them together into a single vessel; they asserted that this mixture was the "marriage" of the spirit and the body. They kept this vessel over hot ashes until a third part of the water had evaporated, then exposed the remainder to the rays of the Sun, believing that crystalline stones would be produced therefrom—white, congealed, and meltable stones to make white metal from white, and red stones to make a red tincture from red metal.

From twenty-two vials half-filled with such liquor, they gave three to us. We all waited for the outcome of the generation of these small stones in the bottoms of the vessels for five years, but in vain. For indeed, as is said in the *Assembly*, nothing foreign is needed for this Stone: for it is perfected by itself within its own metallic matter. By that time, I had completed the forty-sixth year of my age, when I, together with a doctor and monk named Gotofredus Lepore, intended to seek the stone from his...

I approached the task with a deliberate intention: for we knew that any work other than the Stone <note>original: "lapidem"; the Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> was vain and fruitless. Therefore, we endeavored to fabricate it in the following manner: We bought hen's eggs to the number of two thousand, which we boiled hard and separated, calcining <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note> the shells to a supreme whiteness. The yolks and whites, however, we allowed to putrefy by themselves in horse dung <note>Alchemists used the natural heat of decomposing horse manure as a steady, low-temperature incubator for "digesting" materials.</note>, and afterward we distilled them thirty times into a "white water" and a "red oil" separately, along with many other processes which we omit for the sake of brevity. In this vain work, two and a half years were similarly lost to us without profit—indeed, at the greatest expense—whereupon we almost reached a state of despair and would have abandoned everything, had we not been sustained by a new hope. 

We began again to learn the sublimations of spirits, the distillations of "strong waters" <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; usually nitric acid or other mineral acids.</note>, the separations of elements, and the various structures of furnaces and fires, in which we were occupied for eight years. First, we distilled the sharpest vinegar eight times, in which we dissolved the said calcined vitriol and drew it off. Again, we poured it back and drew it off fifteen times every day for a space of two months. Because of its most powerful odor, I suffered from a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day; here, likely caused by inhaling toxic chemical fumes.</note> for fourteen months. We allowed this mixture to rest for an entire year, but with no fruit, for it was an "extraneous matter" <note>Meaning it lacked the essential "seed" or nature required for the Great Work.</note>.

It was later reported to us by a certain learned man that the Emperor's Confessor, whose name was Master Henry, most certainly held and possessed the mastery of the Stone. In order to gain his acquaintance, there was need for the greatest mediation of friends and an expense of more than two hundred crowns <note>A significant sum of gold currency.</note> before we could make him a familiar friend. He, however, worked in this manner: he mixed a paste of silver and Mercury with sulfur and olive oil, cooking them together over a slow fire in a "pelican" <note>A specialized circulatory vessel with two side-arms that return condensed vapors back into the main body.</note> heavily protected with lute <note>A clay or cement used to seal alchemical vessels and protect them from direct flame.</note>, incorporating them with a wooden spatula. But the matter could never be mixed into a single body, even in the space of two months. Finally, having placed this matter in another vial, similarly protected with lute and sealed, we kept it entirely buried in hot ashes and warmed it with fire all around, thinking that in the space of fifteen or twenty-one days, the Mercury would be converted into the finest silver by the power of the sulfurous body. 

When the cooking was finished, he placed lead into the vial as he saw fit and melted everything together into one mass with a most violent fire. Once this was "refined" through a cupel of ash <note>original: "capellam cineritij"; a porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</note>, we were supposed to find the silver multiplied by a third part. For my part, I had given ten marks of silver, and others thirty-two, from which we thought to receive one hundred and [thirty] <note>The catchword "ginta" at the bottom of the page suggests the word "triginta" (thirty) concludes the sentence on the next page.</note>...

...sixty marks. But it happened otherwise, for out of thirty-two marks, they obtained only twelve from the examination of my partner’s portion, while I received fourteen marks from my own ten. As a result, though I believed I held the secret of the stone <note>original: "lapidis arcanum"; the secret of the Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance that transmutes base metals into gold.</note> from the father Confessor, I was made four hundred crowns poorer once again. Grieving, I abstained for two months, utterly loathing the work, especially because all my relatives never ceased rebuking and tormenting me daily. From the sorrow, I could barely eat or drink, and I was reduced to such thinness that everyone thought I had been infected by some contagious poison. Nevertheless, shortly thereafter, I was suddenly more inflamed than before, a thousand times over, especially because I was weary of the uselessly elapsed time; for I was then in my fifty-eighth year. The sole cause of all my errors (alas!) was this: that wandering astray, I was not working with the proper material. For as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar whose Latinized works were the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note> himself says:

> Any imperfect bodies are by no means perfected by mixing with bodies that are simply perfect by nature, because they have already attained a simple form, for themselves alone, in the first degree of perfection from nature, and like dead things, they can contribute nothing of their own non-superfluous perfection to others. This is for two reasons: first, because they are rendered imperfect through the admixture of imperfection, since they have no more perfection than they need for themselves;

and second, because their principles cannot be mingled in this way through a mixing of the smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; an Aristotelian concept of the smallest possible particles of a substance.</note>, as is held in the thirteenth book of the Digests in the *Pandects* <note>While the Pandects are a collection of Roman Law, alchemists often cited them metaphorically as a "universal compendium" of rules.</note>, and in the *Book of Calib*, likewise in Geber, and in the *Natural Work* by Master Daalin, and Arnaldus de Villa Nova; in the *Mirror of Alchemy*, in the *Path of Wanderers* written by Plato <note>Likely referring to the *Liber de quartis*, an alchemical text attributed to Plato in the Middle Ages.</note>, in the *Epistle of Euvaral*, in the *Great Rosary*, and in Euclid’s *Short Treatise*, and among the rest of the non-sophists <note>The "non-sophists" were those Bernard considered true philosophers, as opposed to "sophists" who used deceptive or superficial chemical tricks.</note> in this manner:

> Common bodies, completed by nature alone in the mines, are dead, so that they cannot perfect imperfect things; but if through Art they are led to a sevenfold, tenfold, or twelvefold multiplication of their perfection, then they stain <note>original: "tingunt"; the process of "tincture," where the Stone colors and transforms base metals into gold.</note> to infinity.

For then at last they are made penetrating, entering, and staining, more than perfect and alive compared to common things. Of these it is said by Rhazes <note>A Persian physician and chemist whose works were highly influential in Europe.</note>, Aristotle the Chemist <note>The alchemical tradition attributed many texts to Aristotle that were not written by him.</note>, Aulphanus in his *Pandects*, and Daniel in the fifth chapter of his *Retractions*: "Our complete gold (they say) is more than alive." Likewise, "Our gold and our white silver, which are one and the same, are not common metals; for they are alive, while the others are dead and devoid of power," as is read in the *Golden Book of the Code* and many others. We have certainly seen countless men working in amalgamations and multiplications toward the white and the red <note>The "White Work" (albedo) and "Red Work" (rubedo) are the final stages of the Great Work, producing silver and gold respectively.</note>, in every kind of matter that can be devised, with the greatest labors and such constant perseverance that it could not be greater, but never...

I was known to no man there, and I went so that I might seek if I could somehow find anyone who might console the afflictions of my desires.

...we were able to mix, or prevent it from always floating upon the earth, even though we kept it in continuous heat for the space of seven months. This religious man possessed most excellent books on chemistry, such as the *Great Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius magnus"; a highly influential 14th-century alchemical text attributed to John Dastin or Arnold of Villanova.</note>, Arnold of Villanova, and the *Book of the Words of Mary the Prophetess* <note>Mary the Prophetess (or Maria Hebraea) was a legendary early alchemist to whom several foundational texts and laboratory apparatuses—like the bain-marie—were attributed.</note>, in which I began to study anew, abstaining from practical work for a period of eight years. It was then that I first recognized, through philosophical and evident reasoning, that whatever I had worked on before had been nothing but foolish and vain labors—especially when I considered this saying from the *Book of All Truth*:

> **Nature**, it says, **is not improved except in its own nature; nature delights in its own nature, nature overcomes nature, and nature retains nature.** <note>original: "Natura non emendatur nisi in sua propria natura, natura sua natura gaudet, natura naturam vincit, & natura naturam retinet." This is a famous alchemical axiom emphasizing that the transformation of metals must occur using substances of the same metallic nature.</note>

Having finally been taught by this book, I escaped free from all my **sophistications** <note>original: "sophisticationibus"; in an alchemical context, this refers to "fake" or "artificial" processes that mimic the appearance of gold or silver without changing the substance's essence.</note> and erroneous labors. I therefore wished to study before working again at great expense and without fruit. I spent many sleepless nights constantly arguing with myself and concluding with this sentiment:

> "What need is there," I said, "for me to seek this art from men, tormenting myself in vain by this path? If they know the art, they will never reveal it; if they do not, I spend my time with them to no purpose, and at great expense I try to capture their familiarity and friendship."

I considered instead which places in the books most agreed in the same sense; I judged that the truth lay hidden in those points of agreement, for truth cannot exist in many ways, but in only one. By this path, the truth itself came to meet me. For that which I saw most often agreed upon by all was the very thing I had so anxiously sought. Although one author may call it by one name and another by a different one, it is nonetheless one and the same substance; error is committed only in the diversity of words, and not in the points of agreement.

Therefore, my son, I wished to write this little book for your sake, so that you do not lose heart, nor be deceived as I was so miserably led astray for a long time. Indeed, the safest caution is to learn by the example of others' dangers. Truly I believe (as God may love me) that those men who write such things figuratively or in parables—mentioning hair, urine, blood, sperm, herbs, vegetables, animals, plants, or mineral stones like salts, alums, **copperas** <note>original: "cuperossas"; ferrous sulfate, used in making inks and pigments.</note>, ink-stones, **vitriols** <note>Sulfuric acid salts.</note>, boraxes, **magnesias** <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" was a broad term for various minerals used as a "transformer" or "base" for the Stone.</note>, and all manner of stones and waters—I say that they propose these to readers of this water having spent very little or nothing on it themselves, nor having endured any of the labor, or else they are moved to it by mere cruelty. For I pity all those who are entangled in this **labyrinth** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the confusing and contradictory nature of alchemical literature.</note>, or who might fall into it in the future, whenever the intolerable punishments of misery and calamity that I suffered come to mind. Therefore, whoever wishes to give me credit...

# BOOK ON ALCHEMY

...having done so to his own greatest benefit, I can only report the labor of instructing others from that experience. He who refuses to believe will eventually learn to his own loss how great a folly it is to be unmoved by the examples of others and to refuse to learn. Flee the **deceptions** <note>original: "sophisticationes"; in alchemy, this refers to fraudulent or "sophistical" chemical processes that mimic true results through trickery.</note> of wicked Alchemists, and any others who place their faith in them. For if your reading of books has taught you anything good, they will attempt to take it away with false oaths and assertions, leading you away from the right path. Having nothing with which to excuse their errors at last, they say: "I have done it many times, but now I did not have the things necessary for this work," or "if this and that were added," etc. Unless you flee these imposters and scoundrels more than the plague, you will never taste anything good in this art.

Before I had perfected this work by experiment, I had studied the art exactly from books for two years; nevertheless, when men of that sort—detestable people and the most wicked thieves—came to me, they asserted the most manifest errors as true experiments through oaths and even perjuries. I had once, in my delirium, experienced these same errors at the greatest expense. Nor could I be confirmed in my own good opinions until I deserted them entirely, intended my whole study toward that matter, and pursued it most vigilantly. 

Whoever desires to learn the true art, let him converse with the wise: that is, let him read their books and not those of imposters, even though the wise teach the art in obscure words. You will find such books described clearly and openly nowhere; therefore, possibilities must be considered from the works of **nature** by comparing the books to nature, and vice versa. 

All deceptions must be fled: likewise **sublimations**, **conjunctions**, **separations**, **congealings**, **preparations**, **disjunctions**, **connections**, and all other deceits. Let all those be silent who affirm any **tincture** <note>original: "tincturam"; the "dye" or agent of transmutation that changes base metal into gold.</note> other than ours, and any **sulfur** other than our own which is hidden in **magnesia** <note>original: "magnesia"; not the modern chemical, but a traditional alchemical term for a "mother" substance or a specific mineral like magnetite or lead ore.</note>. Likewise, those who seek to extract another **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver" or mercury.</note> except from the **red servant** <note>original: "servo rubeo"; a cryptic alchemical term often referring to a specific state of matter or a "servant" substance that assists the transformation.</note>, and another water from ours which is permanent and is joined to no thing except its own proper nature, and moistens nothing else except that which is of the unity of its own proper nature. For there is no other **vinegar** <note>original: "acetum"; often used by alchemists to refer to a corrosive or dissolving agent, not kitchen vinegar.</note> than ours, no other **regimen** <note>original: "regimen"; the specific sequence of operations or heat levels in the alchemical process.</note>, and no other colors; likewise no other sublimation, solution, congealing, or putrefaction, etc., than ours.

I advise you to leave behind all **alums**, **vitriols**, **salts**, and all **inks**, **boraxes**, **strong waters** <note>original: "aquas fortes"; mineral acids like nitric acid.</note>, animals and everything that comes from them—hair, blood, sperm, flesh, eggs—and all stones and minerals, as well as metals alone. For although our entrance and our matter are from these, as all the Philosophers assert, it must be composed from **quicksilver**, and this is found nowhere else but in metals (as appears from the works of Geber, the great Rafarius, the *Book of All Truth*, Aristotle the Chemist, Plato, Morienus, Haly, Calid, Mary, Avicenna, Constantine, Alexander, Bendegid, Esid, Serapion, Arnold of Villanova, Sarnius Lilius, Daniel,

<meta>This page continues Bernard of Trevisan’s argument regarding the true nature of the alchemical work, shifting from a warning against fraudsters to a philosophical discussion on the "First Matter" of metals, citing various authorities to support the theory that metals must be returned to their primary state before they can be transformed.</meta>

### BERNARD OF TREVISAN

...St. Thomas’s *Breviloquium*, Albert’s *The Path*, Scot’s *Abbreviation*, Seneca’s *Letter of Aros to the King of Arabia* <note>original: "Senecæ ad Aros epiſtola ad Regem Arabiæ"; this refers to an alchemical text traditionally but spuriously attributed to the Roman philosopher Seneca</note>, and Hemus, Euclid in the seventieth chapter of the *Retractions*, and the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle</note> in the third book of *Meteorology*. By all of these it is affirmed that metals are nothing other than **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term> frozen by degrees of decoctions <note>Decoction refers to the process of "cooking" or maturing substances through steady heat within the earth or a furnace.</note>. Despite all these affirmative reasons, metals themselves are not our **Stone** while they remain in their metallic form: for it is impossible for one and the same matter to possess two forms. By what reasoning could they be the Stone—which has a noble and intermediate form between metal and Mercury—unless they are first corrupted <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is a necessary stage of breakdown or decay that precedes "generation" or new life.</note>, and that metallic form is taken away? For this reason the Philosopher, and also Democritus in the 3rd book of the *Physics*, and in the 3rd chapter of *Meteorology*, say: "Let the Alchemists boast as much as they wish, they will never transmute the forms of metals except by the **reduction** of those same metals into their **first matter**." This same point is held by all books that treat the metallic form.

Truly, so that it may be understood what "reduction into the first matter" means, it must first be known that the **first matter** is the thing into which a specific form is immediately and most closely introduced; just as the first matter of a man is the seed of both the man and the woman. Many ignorant people, thinking they understand this reduction, wrongly interpret it as the **four elements**. For (as they themselves say) all things that were created consist of these elements without a doubt. But those elements are the first matter of the first matter—that is, quicksilver and sulfur consist of the four elements, and these two are ultimately the **first matter of metals**. Indeed, the four elements are just as suited to the formation of a donkey or an ox as they are to metals. For first, by nature, quicksilver and sulfur must be made; only then can they be the first matter of metals. 

For example, a man is not composed of the four elements while they still exist in their simple, elementary nature, but rather after they have been transmuted by nature into the nature of the first matter of a man. In no different a way, nature—transmuting the four elements into Mercury and sulfur—then first creates the first matter of metals. For whatever is worked upon that matter beyond that point, nothing else can result from it except the metallic form. Indeed, previously, when they were still elements and not yet quicksilver or sulfur, nature could have procreated from those same elements an ox, a plant, a man, or anything else differing from a metal. 

From the preceding, it is most clearly evident that the four elements are not the first matter of metals, but rather quicksilver and sulfur are. Otherwise, according to the opinion of those others, it would follow that men, metals, herbs, plants, and brute animals—in short, everything—would exist as nothing but one single thing without any difference; nothing more absurd than this could ever be said. Likewise, it would then follow that even men could be generated from metals, since humans, just like metals, consist of elements, and something more besides.

<summary>Trevisan argues that metals are essentially "frozen" Mercury and must be reduced to their specific "First Matter" (Mercury and Sulfur) rather than the generic four elements before transmutation can occur.</summary>
