<meta>This page continues Bernard of Trevisan’s philosophical justification for why metals must be reduced to their "first matter" before transmutation. It transitions from citing authorities to using natural analogies—specifically human and animal reproduction—to prove that nature always works toward a specific "end" and that "like produces like."</meta>

### A BOOK ON ALCHEMY. 693

If anything could be made from anything else, or if like did not produce its like, there would be no generation, nor male and female, and no difference between things, if in actuality all things were of one single substance. To return to the **first matter** <term>prima materia; the primal, formless base of all physical things</term>, we shall use this example: the seed of the man by itself, and the seed of the woman by itself, are not the first matter of a fetus, since nature—while they are thus separated—could produce something else monstrous from them, such as a worm-like substance. But from the conjunction of both into one, so that the power of one receives and embraces the power of the other within itself, then finally nature can produce nothing else from it except the form of an infant, because this is the **end** <note>original: "finis"; in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the 'final cause' or the intended goal of a process</note> of that matter and no other. Nature, therefore, cannot introduce any other form to the matter except that one toward which it is finally inclined and disposed. Therefore, the union of the seeds alone is its first matter, or the matter of those things from which the feminine parts were cut off or separated; it can receive no other form than that of its own species, for which it is prepared.

Regarding this preparation for an end, let this be a sufficiently simple example: If someone hurries on a journey, many paths occur that turn this way and that before he arrives; but once he has directed his step onto the right path and perseveres in it, he will finally arrive where he had determined to go. In this same way, individual things have their own path and matter, through which and from which they are made; not just anything is perfected from any matter, nor in just any manner. It is certainly manifest that every thing has something similar and preceding it, from which it is naturally produced, so that nothing else can be made from it. For example, in the formation of a horse, it is required that some equine nature be transmuted into a seed-like substance, united from two contrary matters (yet under the same equine species). Likewise, for a human, nature itself does not primarily take an equine substance; for every single substance has its own proper and principal seed from which it is made, and it is multiplied through itself in that seed, and not through another, nor in any other way. 

This is evident from the **Word of God**, when He created human as male and female: "Increase and multiply" from your own substance—namely, that which is like you. For He had said to His other creatures before: "Let each one produce its own fruit and seed in itself, and let it be multiplied," etc. If God had wished for everything to be generated from one single thing, He would not have made so many and such great creatures, and so diverse, nor would there have been a need for the heavens or light; instead, the four elements would have always brought forth one and the same thing, which would be most absurd. Therefore, out of all things He made diverse kinds of every genus, so that each might generate its like. Did not the Lord God say to Noah before the flood: "Take with you into the Ark of all animals united pairs, male and female, so that afterward each may be multiplied in its own species"? And do we not see it happen in no other way? It is therefore clear from the preceding points that for the generation of anything, there is a need for its own like, so that by the command of God, diverse things—

# BERNARD OF TREVISAN
### 694

...the roots of those things created by Him would be multiplied into diverse forms, each under its own proper substance. This same point is proven through the authorities of the Philosophers: for **Scotus** <note>Likely referring to Michael Scot, a 13th-century mathematician and scholar associated with alchemy</note> speaks openly, saying that the **first matter** of all metals is made from coagulated quicksilver and from sulfurous quicksilver. Likewise, in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a foundational alchemical text</note>, one named **Noscus, King of Albania**, speaks in this manner: from man, nothing but man is made; from a bird, nothing but a bird; similarly, from any brute animal, nothing but a brute beast. For nature is not corrected in anything else, but only within its own nature. The same is said by **Joannes Mechungus** <note>Jean de Meun, the French poet and author of the *Roman de la Rose*, to whom alchemical treatises were often attributed</note> in his testament: Every tree produces its own fruit, as the pear tree produces pears and the apple tree apples; likewise, metal is generated and multiplied from metal, and from nothing else. 

Also, **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in Arabic and Latin alchemy</note> wrote well on this opinion in several places in his *Summa*, although in almost all his books he is quite harsh and deceptive regarding study, saying: "We have experienced each thing most exactly by its own tests, and that with proven reasons; we could never find anything that remains in the fire except **viscous humidity** <term>viscosa humiditas; an oily, sticky moisture that does not evaporate easily, identified by alchemists as the essence of Mercury</term> alone, the root of all metals. All other humidities easily flee from the fire through evaporation, and through the separation of one element from another—like water by fire—one part goes off into smoke, another into water, and another into earth remaining at the bottom of the vessel. So it is in all things, since those things which are not well united in their generation are consumed by the smallest fire and separated from their natural composition."

But viscous humidity—namely, **Mercury**—is never consumed in it, nor separated from its earth or any other element of its own; for either they all stay together, or they depart together, so that nothing of the weight is lost at all. By these words, therefore, Geber concludes that for this precious stone, there is no need for any other thing than the substance of Mercury alone, which has been optimally cleansed by the **Art** <note>original: "per artem"; referring to the alchemical craft</note>, penetrating, tinting, standing in battle against the fire, and not permitting itself to be separated into diverse parts, but always persisting most constantly in the sole substance of its "mercuriality." Then finally (he says) it is joined to metals radically in their depths, destroying their form and introducing another according to the virtue and color of the **elixir**, or the tinting medicine. 

Likewise, **Aros**, that great and most learned King, says: "Our medicine is made from two things of one essence, namely from the mercurial union of the fixed and non-fixed nature, spiritual and corporal, cold and moist, hot and dry, and it cannot possibly be made from anything else." For the industry of Art brings in nothing new, nor does it add anything to nature in its root; but rather, nature is aided by Art (as is fitting) by loosening the bonds, and likewise Art is aided by nature by learning from its operations and in the supply of matter. Thus, both together fulfill the desire according to the wish of the diligent worker. To these things **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "Mix and project the medicine upon bodies diminished in perfection, or imperfect..."

<summary>Bernard of Trevisan cites various alchemical authorities (Scotus, Geber, Jean de Meun) to argue that Mercury is the unique "viscous humidity" and essential root of all metals. He asserts that the Alchemical Art does not create new substances but merely assists Nature in perfecting metals through the use of this refined Mercury.</summary>

# A BOOK CONCERNING ALCHEMY
### 695

...this [the Great Work] says it is nothing else except **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> exalted by art above imperfect quicksilver. From these things, they openly teach that it is nothing other than mercury. **Arnold of Villanova** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous Catalan physician and alchemist</note> adds:

> Let your whole study be directed toward digesting and cooking the **mercurial substance**; and according to its dignity, it will return worthy bodies, which exist as nothing else than decocted <note>cooked or concentrated</note> mercurial substance.

It could be proven by infinite reasons that **double Mercury** <note>Referring to the alchemical concept of "Mercury of the Philosophers," often thought to have a dual nature</note> is the only **first matter** <term>materia prima; the fundamental building block of all things</term> and the **proximate matter** <term>materia proxima; the immediate substance from which a specific thing is made</term> of all metals, and not the four elements, which are most remote. 

Someone, desiring to protect his own error, might say: "From your own words I bring a case against you: the four elements are afterward reduced by art into Mercury and sulfur, which are the first matter of metals. In this way, they are made more subtle by such a preceding separation than if they had been immediately brought into the mercurial substance and proximate matter without it." 

To refute this as erroneous and false: from that vain opinion, it would easily follow that nature is superfluous if the "seeds" <note>original: "spermata," referring to the generative principles of minerals</note> of things could be made by art. Thus, a human could be generated without a human, solely from the four elements without any intermediate nature or alteration; and in the same way, the principles of compositions would be made, which fights against all natural reason. In this art, nature has produced the matter in which it is afterward assisted by art. 

It would also follow from that falsehood that a physician, by his art or herbs, could resuscitate the dead, or heal a dying man against the saying of **Avicenna** and **Rhazes** <note>Two of the most influential Persian physicians and philosophers in the medieval world</note>. Medicine only assists nature; when nature is absent or failing, medicine can perform nothing. Just as if a laxative is cast into a dead body, it does not purge, because the action is not received by nature. **Hippocrates**, more divine than human, and like a spirit lacking a body, testifies to this in his *Aphorisms* and natural principles, saying:

> Art presupposes some thing created by nature alone, in which art provides help to nature, and nature to art.

Therefore, it is established that art requires matter which is created by nature, and not by art. For if the matter were from art, what need would there be for nature in those things where she has not worked, since nothing of her own would be present? Art alone would be able to perfect it without any other extraneous thing and beyond nature. It is clear by many irrefragable and most evident testimonies that nature procreates and prepares "spermatic" <note>generative</note> natures from itself; finally, art works within them through conjunction, tending toward the end for which nature had created them. 

Furthermore, even if it were possible for metals to be reduced into the four elements, it would be necessary for them to be separated into Mercury and sulfur first before the elements; and afterward, the elements would have to be turned back into sulfur and quicksilver to become the proximate metallic nature. What folly, I ask, would this be? Since all these things are one and the same, and the same substance, which acquires no new nature or matter from such a [process].

### 696

...reductions, but only that which had been there before remains. Why then do we need these **futile labors**, if just as much substance was held when they were in the form of the **seed of quicksilver and sulfur** <note>In alchemical theory, all metals are born from the combination of "philosophical" sulfur (the active, masculine principle) and mercury (the passive, feminine principle)</note>, as after the reduction into the four elements? They acquire nothing new—not in power, not in weight, neither in quantity nor quality. The reason for this is clear: because no other matter was joined to it which would have made it worthier, or been exalted with it. Instead, a single matter was merely led here and there without any addition. Therefore, it is just as valid in the form of its own seed as it is in the form of the elements. 

If the same objection is raised against our **Stone** <term>Lapis; the Philosophers' Stone</term>—namely, that it also acquires nothing—it is denied. For we reduce it so that in that reduction, a **conjunction** <note>The chemical "marriage" or union of substances</note> of new matter of one and same root may occur; without this reduction, the union cannot happen, and thus an addition of matter occurs. Certainly, one of the two matters assists the other, so that a far worthier matter results from it than they were by themselves separately before the conjunction. Therefore, our reduction is necessary, because through it, the matters acquire a new form and virtue because of the addition of new matter. This does not happen in those other "reductions of the elements," in which nothing else appears to happen except the movement of bare matter without form, without any innovation, exaltation, or the acquisition of any new form or matter. From this, it is clear that the reductions of those men are mere fantasies, vain and erroneous. 

In confirmation of this matter, a certain man named **William of Paris** <note>Guilhelmus Parisiensis, likely referring to William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), the Bishop of Paris, whose works on nature were often cited by alchemists</note>, a man learned in this art, speaks most openly:

> In the **creation of man** (he says), first two seeds <note>original: "spermata"</note> concur in union, differing in qualities; of which qualities, in one, it is **cold and moist**, and in the other, it is **hot and dry**. These are digested in the mother's womb by the mixing of the power of both seeds, and by the augmentation through the moisture of the **blood**, which is of the same substance as the female seed. Through the intervening action of the power of the male seed, the matter of the said mixture is nourished until it becomes a middle substance participating in the nature of both, without any diminution or excess. Furthermore, seeds are created by **Nature**, and not by **Art** <note>The alchemical "Art" refers to human technology and laboratory practice, which can only assist or mimic Nature, not create life from scratch</note>; Art could not do it in any way. Art only effects this: it joins both together in the mother's womb. Although Art can also assist in the mixing by the fostering of external heat, by rest, by the choice of the best and easily digestible foods taken with temperance and moderation—in all these things, Art does nothing else than assist those things already created by Nature.

The same author adds: To create seeds is not the task of Art; but after they have been created by Nature, then finally Art, acting through the natural power existing in the seed-matters already created by Nature, assists the existing thing by joining them, acting as the **minister of Nature**...

<summary>Bernard argues that alchemical success requires the addition of "new matter" of the same root, rather than just rearranging elements. He uses William of Paris’s analogy of human conception to show that the alchemist's role is merely to facilitate and nourish the natural union of male and female principles.</summary>

### 697

...subsisting, but not yet perfect: yet [the artist] adds nothing to its form, nor its matter, nor its power. Therefore, nature is the primary cause of generation, and art is only the secondary cause, which by itself achieves nothing without the first. For it is in vain that the earth is cultivated for a harvest unless the natural matter created by nature—namely, the grain of wheat—is present. It is certain, therefore, that each is helped by the other: nature by art, and art by nature; and in turn, both work toward the task, as much of nature as of art.

Since, therefore, **seeds** <term>spermata; the fundamental generative principles of substances</term> cannot be created by art in any way, nor can the matter of metals, it would be impossible for a man by any craft to reduce the four elements into a "spermatic" form—whether reductive, alterative, or attractive—for the purpose of receiving a form or an action that is either tending toward or disposing it. 

But if someone should argue that the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities</note> say the four elements must exist in our art: their true meaning is that in their two seeds, the four primary qualities of the elements are held. Namely, heat and dryness (Fire and Air) are held in **mature quicksilver** <note>philosophical mercury that has been "digested" or purified</note>, which is the masculine seed; and coldness and moisture are held in **raw and imperfect quicksilver** (as far as the goal is concerned), which are Earth and Water in the feminine seed. This does not mean that there are actually four elemental parts in these seeds, separated from one another as the four physical elements we see; for then they would no longer be the **First Matter** <term>Materia Prima; the original, undifferentiated substance of all things</term> of metals, nor could they be altered by any human wit or craft into the form of the two seeds of the metals' first matter. As **Calib the Philosopher** and **King of Albania** <note>likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Arabic alchemical authority</note> clearly teaches in this manner:

> Know that from the beginning of our work, we need only two matters; only two are seen, and only two are touched, and no more than two enter into the beginning, middle, and end of the mastery. However, within these two, the four qualities are present virtually. For in the greater seed, as in the worthier one, the two worthier elements are contained through their qualities: namely, fire and air. In the other seed, by its nature raw and imperfect, the remaining two qualities are held, and the other two less worthy elements: which are earth and water. 

Through Calib, it is clear enough that in this art there are only two "spermatic" matters of one and the same root, substance, and essence—namely, the mercurial. It is of a single substance and essence, a viscous and dry substance, which is joined to nothing in this world except for the **bodies** <note>The "bodies" usually refer to the solid metals, particularly gold and silver</note>. 

**Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist who reportedly taught the art to King Khalid</note> asserts the same thing clearly in his book, saying:

> Return the hard aquatic and the soft hard, so that water may be joined to it; conceal, or rather hide, the fire under or within the cold water.
> <note>original: "Durum aquaticum & molle reddito durum, ut ei conjungatur aqua, celato, vel abscondito potius ignem sub, vel in aqua frigida"</note>

This means: join the masculine seed (which is nothing other than cooked and mature Mercury, containing within itself the element of fire through digestion) with the feminine seed, which is the "living water." Likewise, **Isudrius** <note>likely Isidorus</note> speaks to the same effect in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*:

### 698

Mix water with fire; <note>original: "Aquam igni permiſceto"</note> this is the potential "spermatic union," which is closest to the noble perfection of the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> for the purpose of receiving it. Now that I have spoken sufficiently regarding the first matter of metals and have proven with the firmest arguments and worthy authorities that they are **Mercury** and **Sulfur**, I shall proceed further for the benefit and utility of my listeners. In this following third part of my book, I will explain what Mercury and Sulfur are, how metals are generated in the earth, and their differences, citing the authorities of the Philosophers from whom I learned what I know of the Stone—God granting me grace and understanding.

### THE THIRD PART OF THE BOOK OF LORD BERNARD, COUNT
### *of the March of Treviso*, in which he treats the roots
### *and principles of Metals, using the most evident reasons*
### *and authorities, as well as philosophical*
### *arguments.*

First, one must not be ignorant of this divine work of **Genesis**, by which **GOD** in the beginning created matter confused and unordered: yet by His will, it was full of many and infinite materials, from which He drew the four elements. From the mixing of these, He created living things and diverse creatures; He willed some to be intellectual, others sensitive, others vegetative, and others mineral. The intellectual creatures were created from the four elements, but fire and air dominate in them more than the other two. In sensitive creatures, however, fire is diminished, so that air dominates as much as fire—as seen in brute animals, horses, donkeys, dogs, birds, etc. Vegetative things likewise consist of the four elements; in these, air and water dominate, but the dignity of the air is diminished by the water, and the water by a certain earthy and vaporous substance. Mineral creatures, although they also consist of the four, are dominated by earth and water; yet the quality of the water is more earthy than aquatic. # BOOK ON ALCHEMY
### 699

...matter, while the others previously mentioned possess their own seed within themselves, in which lies hidden all the power of their multiplication and final composition. Metallic matter consists solely of cold and moist raw **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, in which the four elements are also present—namely, the hot, the moist, the cold, and the dry. Two of these are dominant: the cold and the moist; the hot and the dry are subject to them. The heat of celestial motion, penetrating all around the Earth and into its veins, is so gentle and tempered that it is barely perceptible, yet it is continuous: equal by night and by day alike. This heat does not originate from the **Sun** (as some fools would have it) but from the reflection of the **sphere of fire** <term>sphærę ignis; in medieval cosmology, the region of the element fire located between the atmosphere and the moon's orbit</term> surrounding the air, and also from the continuous motion of the celestial bodies, which excite a continuous and slow heat that is scarcely imaginable. 

Even if the heat of minerals were derived from the Sun (according to the opinion of **Raymond Lully** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> and **Aristotle**), the heat would nonetheless be continuous, because the Sun revolves incessantly around the Earth day and night. However, their opinion is false, because the Sun is neither hot nor cold in itself, but its motion is naturally hot. Therefore, the heat proceeding from the motion of the celestial bodies is constantly active in the veins of the earth; yet it does not "heat" the minerals (as some who speak foolishly think). For if it heated them even in the slightest, by this tiny amount of active heat, Mercury would be **decocted** <term>decoqueretur; the process of "cooking" or ripening matter through heat to reach perfection</term> into the perfection of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> in a span of time less than ten years—a process which usually takes barely a hundred. 

Furthermore, the Earth is cold and dry, and minerals are located in the center of the Earth; therefore, before they could actually perceive even a tiny bit of heat from the Sun, we who are closer to it would be utterly burned up. Indeed, the heat would have to be most intense if, after penetrating the coldest bodies of earth and water, it still retained its heat upon reaching the center without being entirely extinguished. 

Truly, however, these things ought to be understood more naturally in this way: Since Mercury itself is composed of the four elements, when these are heated by common and general forces through their own internal motion, a natural heat is excited by that very movement. Likewise, the fire and air existing within the Mercury are moved and gradually elevated, as they are more noble elements than the water and earth of the Mercury; nevertheless, moisture and coldness remain dominant. But because heat and dryness are more noble elements, they strive to overcome the other two—namely, the coldness and moisture dominating in the Mercury. For the celestial motions excite other motions of natural heat, by which the qualities of Mercury are set in motion. 

Afterward, through a long succession of time, the dryness of the Mercury overcomes one degree of its moisture, and it becomes **lead**; then it overcomes another degree in succession, and it becomes **tin**. At last, the heat of the Mercury again overcomes a little of the moisture from the coldness, and it becomes the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>. With heat dominating even more, it becomes **bronze**, or **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, and afterward **iron**...

# BERNARD TREVISAN
### 700

...and perfect gold <note>original: "sol," the Sun, used here as the alchemical term for gold</note>. In this way, the two qualities which previously yielded, overcome by cold and moisture, now conquer the others; heat and dryness dominate, which in their excitation are **sulfur**, while the coldness and moisture of Mercury are **Mercury** itself. Not that this sulfur is anything divided or separated from Mercury: rather, it is solely the heat and dryness which did not [previously] dominate the coldness and moisture of Mercury. This sulfur, once digested, holds dominion over the two other aforementioned qualities—coldness and moisture—and imprints its virtues upon them. 

Through these varieties of degrees of decoction <term>decoctio; a process of "cooking" or maturing through steady heat over time</term>, the diversities of metals are created. **Lead** continually flees and flies away from the fire for no other reason than that the coldness and moisture of its Mercury have not yet been altered by the heat and dryness of its sulfur, which in no way dominate it; otherwise, lead would not be consumed by fire, no matter how intense. On the contrary, its Mercury would rejoice in what is similar to itself <note>referring to the alchemical principle that substances are only stable when their internal elements match the external environment</note>. 

Likewise, all other metals flee from the fire except for gold, because they are still cold and moist—one more than another, according to their greater or lesser participation in said qualities. They flee (I say) from what is contrary to them and which they cannot endure. For everything naturally flees from its adversary and delights in its like; hence it follows that **gold** is nothing other than pure fire in Mercury, since it does not withdraw from fire, however intense it may be, while all others cannot endure it—one more or less than another, as they more closely approach or recede from the "complexion" <note>the specific balance of elemental qualities</note> of fire. 

For sulfur is nothing other than pure fire hidden in Mercury, which over a long succession of time is struck out in the mines and moved by the motions of the celestial bodies (as I said above). It digests the coldness and moisture in the Mercury according to the variety of degrees of decoction and alteration into different metallic forms:
1. The first is **lead** (less hot and moist)
2. The second, **tin**
3. The third, **silver**
4. The fourth, **copper**
5. The fifth, **iron**
6. The sixth, **gold**, which indeed, in the perfection of its metallic nature, is pure fire digested by the sulfur existing within the Mercury.

From these things, it is again clearly evident that sulfur is not something apart or separate from the substance of Mercury, nor is it common sulfur; otherwise, the matter of metals would not be homogeneous (which contradicts the assertions of all philosophers). They have called these dominating qualities "sulfur" by similarity, because they possess an inflammable substance, like hot and dry sulfur, in which they reside. Thus it is most clearly evident that metallic forms were created by nature solely from the pure substance of Mercury, not from anything external, as **Geber** <note>An 8th-century authority often cited as the father of Islamic and Western alchemy</note> attests. "In the depths of Mercury's nature," he says, "is sulfur, which is produced over a long succession of time in the veins of the earth's minerals." **Morienus** and **Aros** <note>Aros is a legendary figure often associated with the transmission of alchemical secrets to the Greeks or Arabs</note> speak even more clearly on this matter: Our...

# BOOK ON ALCHEMY
### 701

->...our<- **sulfur** (they say) is not the common kind, but is fixed and non-volatile, being of the nature of **Mercury**, and not from any other thing whatsoever. We imitate Nature most exactly, which in its own mines has no other material upon which it works except the pure Mercurial form, as is also apparent through the best reasoning, authorities, and experience. In this Mercury, there is a fixed and incombustible sulfur which completes our work, without any substance other than the pure Mercurial substance. **Khalid**, **Bendegid**, **Yazid**, and **Maria** <note>These are traditional alchemical authorities: Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince; "Bendegid" likely refers to an Arabic source; Yazid; and Maria the Jewess, a foundational figure in Western alchemy</note> speak no differently, but clearly in this manner: Nature procreates its metals from the heat and dryness of Mercury, which overcome its coldness and moisture by altering them; and they are perfected by no other essence, as is affirmed in all the books of the Philosophers, which would be too tedious to cite in full.

Some wrongly think that some external sulfurous matter intervenes in the procreation of metals; but on the contrary, it is clearly evident that the sulfur is included within the **Mercury** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common Latin term for quicksilver or mercury</term> when Nature works. In truth, it does not dominate within it except through warm motion, by which the said sulfur is altered, and at the same time the other two qualities of Mercury are altered. In this way, Nature—through this sulfur in the veins of the earth—generates the diverse forms of metals according to the diversity of the degrees of alteration. In this, we likewise imitate Nature, since we take nothing foreign into our material; rather, in our **mercury** <term>argentum vivum</term> there is an incombustible Mercurial sulfur. 

Nevertheless, this sulfur does not yet dominate; instead, the coldness and moisture of the volatile Mercury prevail, until—by the action of continuous heat persevering upon this our mercury—the fixed part, mixed through the whole volatile substance, comes to dominate. It overcomes the coldness and moisture of the Mercury, and finally the heat and dryness of the fixed part (which are its qualities) begin to dominate the others. According to the degrees of this alteration of Mercury through its own sulfur, various colors arise, in the same way and no differently than through Nature itself in the mines. 

Of such colors, the first is **Saturnine blackness** <note>associated with Lead</note>; the second is **Jovial whiteness** <note>associated with Tin</note>; the third is **Lunar** <note>Silver</note>; the fourth is **Venereal** <note>Copper</note>; the fifth is **Martial** <note>Iron</note>; the sixth is **Solar** <note>Gold</note>. But the seventh is brought by us one degree higher than by Nature; for we perfect it and render it more-than-perfect with a most exalted red or blood-like color. Therefore, since it is made more-than-perfect, it can to that extent perfect other things. For if it were not perfected further than its simple nature, what need would there be to spend so much time—namely nine and a half months—when we could already have such bodies created by Nature without such great labors? Indeed, it is necessary, as I said before, that the **masculine body** <note>Gold</note> be made more-than-perfect, and that through art imitating Nature, so that by its "more-than-perfection" and abundant radiation, it may be able to perfect other imperfect things in weight, color, and substance, in their mineral roots and principles. Who, therefore, is so...

# BERNARD OF TREVISO
### 702

...is anyone so presumptuous as to believe he can achieve that work, and render it such as we desire, by using some foreign substance in which no radical mixture <note>A "radical" mixture refers to a combination that reaches the very "roots" or fundamental essence of the matter.</note> is held? In the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>, a certain man named **Aristeus** <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often identified as a disciple of Pythagoras</note>—who governed the whole world for sixteen years with his wisdom and was the most excellent after **Hermes**, and of whom it is read in the *Chronicles of Solomon* that he gathered the disciples of **Pythagoras** and was the only one who never lied (wherefore he was called the "truth-teller" by the **Astrologers**) — says: "Nature is not improved except in its own nature." Therefore, our matter cannot be improved in any way other than in its own proper nature. **Parmenides** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose name was frequently invoked in alchemical texts to lend authority to the "oneness" of the matter</note> says the same thing; it was he who first drew me back from my errors and directed me onto the right path.

It is certainly clear that metallic nature is not improved except in its own metallic nature, and not in any other thing whatsoever. By this path, through our art, we may perfect in a few months what Nature herself can scarcely do in a thousand years. For in the mines there is almost no heat; if even a little were present, the work of nature would be very swift. Thus, in our art, we have a twofold heat: namely, that of sulfur and that of fire, so that the one may assist the other. Fire is not (as **Constantinus** and **Empedocles** <note>Constantinus Africanus and the Greek philosopher Empedocles</note> would have it) part of the substance of the matter, yet it increases the work; otherwise, it would follow that such heat would penetrate more and more every day, which is an error. Truly, fire alone rules the entire art, which nature uses; we can bring nothing else to it. Indeed, with a violent fire, substances are not altered by one another, nor are they moved. Let there be, therefore, a digesting fire that is continuous, not violent, subtle, enclosed, airy, surrounding, altering, and not burning. As God may love me, I have now told you the whole method of arranging the fire; therefore, consider and chew over my words piece by piece. For fire encompasses the whole art, as is clear from all parts of the *Book of Truth* <note>original: "Codicis veritatis"</note>. Consider likewise what the *Great Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius magnus," a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise often attributed to Arnald of Villanova</note> brings to this opinion:

> *Beware (it says) that you do not hasten your solution, wishing to complete it before the required time: for this haste is a sign of the deprivation of the unions. Therefore, let your fire be persevering and gentle, in the manner of nature's pace, mild to the bodies, digesting, and excluding the cold.*

**Mary the Prophetess** <note>Also known as Maria the Jewess, a foundational figure in alchemy credited with the invention of the "bain-marie" or water bath</note> also adds to this:

> *A violent fire hinders the union, and tints the white into a red the color of wild poppy flowers; this you will be able to imagine for yourself and learn from the work, just as I did. In the heat of dung I waited in vain, and in the fire of coals without a medium, my matter was sublimated <term>sublimated; turned into vapor and solidified again without melting</term>, not dissolved. But in the fire I have described—vaporous, digesting, continuous, not violent, subtle, surrounding, airy, clear, closed, non-burning, altering, penetrating, and living—it succeeded well.*

Now, if you are as a true seeker ought to be, you will easily understand through these words what sort of fire it must be. In the *Assembly*, it is held that experien-

### 703

...artificial skill will teach you what kind of fire it is. In *The Light of Aristotle the Chemist* <note>original: "In Lumine Aristotelis Chemistæ"; while the historical Aristotle was not an alchemist, many medieval texts were attributed to him to grant them authority</note>: **Mercury** (he says) must be cooked in a triple vessel to evaporate and convert the active dryness of the fire into the vaporous moisture of the air surrounding the matter. **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy</note> and **Seneca** affirm this very thing: Fire (they say) does not digest our matter, but its altering heat—which is considered dry as it moves through the air, the medium by which fire moves—is what provides the moisture. I have delayed speaking of this until now: for fire either perfects all things or destroys them. **Aros** and **Calid** <note>Calid likely refers to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince associated with alchemy</note> say: In all our work, Mercury and fire should suffice for you in the middle and at the end; but in the beginning, it is not so, since it is not our Mercury—a thing very easy to understand. Likewise, **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: Know that our **Laton** <note>original: "Latonem"; a term for the crude, impure metallic base, often compared to brass, that must be purified</note> is red; but it is useless to us until it becomes white. Know also that lukewarm water penetrates and whitens just as it is, and that a moist and vaporous fire performs all things.

Furthermore, **Bendegid**, **John of Meun** <note>original: "Jo. Mehungus"; author of the *Romance of the Rose*, to whom several alchemical treatises were attributed</note>, and **Haly**: You who spend your days and nights searching (they say), you squander your money, consume your resources and wealth, and waste your time uselessly; you twist your minds around the subtleties of books. I wish to admonish you out of charity (out of compassion), as a father moved toward his son: that you should whiten the red **Laton** through white water that is "suffocated" <note>likely referring to a sealed or contained vapor</note> and lukewarm. Moreover, break all those sophistical books, and leave behind such complex regimens and great subtleties. Believe me, so that it may be well with you: for all these works are vain except for that which I have already told you; and all things that have been written tend toward this single goal. What could ever be said better or more clearly?

The *Codex of All Truth* also says of this: Whiten the red, and afterwards make the red white; in this consists the whole art, its beginning and its end. But I say to you, unless you first make it black, you will by no means be able to whiten it; for blackness <term>Nigredo</term> <note>The first stage of the alchemical process, representing putrefaction and the "death" of the old form</note> is the beginning of whiteness, and the end of blackness is the sign of the putrefaction and mortification <note>The symbolic death of the substance</note> of the already-penetrated body. As that wise Roman philosopher **Morienus** says: Unless it putrefies and turns black, it will not be dissolved; and unless it is dissolved, it cannot be penetrated by its water, nor can it be whitened. Thus there would be no conjunction, no mixing, and consequently no union at all—which last thing cannot happen without mixing. Likewise, composition must precede alteration. In this way, through such steps, our matter is treated in imitation of the work of nature, in all things without the subtraction or addition of any foreign substance. As for weights, let no one be too anxious about what or of what kind they are which nature uses; it should be known that they are not found in the locations of minerals. For where there is only one thing, why would weights be needed, and where else but between two or more? Mercury. Indeed (as I have said before), the element of fire—which does not dominate in raw **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Mercury is often the "prima materia" or first matter, but it must be processed or "digested" to be useful</note>—is the very thing that digests the matter. For this reason, anyone who is a true Philosopher will know perfectly well how much more subtle the element of fire is than the other elements, and by what proportion it is able to overcome them. Therefore, the **weight** <note>original: "Pondus"; in alchemy, "weight" refers not just to physical mass but to the proportional strength or "virtue" of an element within a compound</note> is found in the first elemental composition of Mercury, and not in any other work. Accordingly, the composition must be made in the first place—or the conjunction—after which comes the alteration, then the mixing, and finally, at last, the union will occur. Whoever wishes to imitate nature in these things should observe only its order and weights, as the **Codex of all Truth** <note>A common way to refer to the fundamental laws of nature or a specific authoritative hermetic text</note> holds. If the preparation is made without the proper weight, the work will be delayed, which will cause you to easily lose heart. > Earthly power exerted upon that which resists it, delayed by that resistance, is the action of the agent in that matter. <note>original: "Terrena potentia super sibi resistens, pro resistentia dilata, est actio agentis in ista materia."</note>

These are truly golden words, opening to us the foundation of weights; unless you are learned, or they have been explained by someone exceptionally learned, you will not easily understand them. I would have gladly explained them to you myself, had I not made a vow to God, to equity, and to the established Philosophers that I would never explain the weight, the matter, nor the colors in plain words or common speech, but only through parables (as you will soon hear below)—true and perfect ones, without omission or excess, in imitation of the wise. 

Earlier I spoke of the inventors of this art and those who possessed it. I have also confessed that I myself possessed and perfected the **Stone** <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the "Great Work," capable of transmuting metals and prolonging life</note> from the beginning to the end. Likewise, I spoke of the deceptions I endured, and because of them, the vast expenses and unbearable labors I suffered from the eighteenth year of my age until my sixty-fourth year, before I finally attained the art. Truly, if I had possessed from the beginning all the books that I later obtained, I would undoubtedly have reached it sooner. But I read nothing but the falsest recipes and erroneous books; furthermore, it was my lot to communicate only with the most perverse thieves, worthless men, and impostors. 

But after I gained knowledge, I had familiar acquaintance with fifteen good men who likewise knew the craftsmanship of the Stone, and especially with a certain **Barbarino** <note>A fellow alchemist or scholar contemporary to the author</note>. (I had nevertheless known the art for two years before I had fully worked it out or perfected it). This man, during a dispute—when I had unexpectedly said that I had not yet tested it—tried to divert me from the true purpose, for which reason I left his company. We were disputing primarily about the method of hiding and concealing the art from unworthy men. Truly, in the structure of the fire, some writers differed from others, although they all aimed at the same goal: namely, that it should be done in such a way that the "fleeing one" <note>The volatile substance, often associated with Mercury</note> does not fly away before the "pursuer" <note>The fixing agent, or the fire's heat</note> catches it, in whatever way the fire might be prepared. I have therefore revealed the entire theory and the mineral principles, along with their reasoning, by which the true can be discerned from the false. Now, however, it seems right to attach the practice, though in obscure words, just as I myself worked it out and four times composed the said Stone. Whoever, therefore, possesses and reads this little book of mine, ought by merit to be freed from all anxiety and to know the truth without fail. For I could not have written more clearly unless I were to demonstrate the matter to the eye, which all reason advises against. You yourself, when you know it, will veil it far more cautiously than I, and you will be annoyed that I have written so openly. The will of God has forbidden it to be made manifest to everyone, for it is good that it be known to very few, as is read throughout the *Turba*.

Afterward, for the sake of refreshing my spirit, which was weary from study, I went in search of pleasant fields and meadows. I came upon a most clear **little fountain** <term>fonticulus; a common alchemical term for the solvent or "mercurial water" in which the "King" (the matter) is dissolved</term>, enclosed and fortified by a most beautiful stone. Above it was an oak trunk, and the rest was surrounded by a wall, so that no beasts might enter nor birds bathe themselves in it. Sitting above this fountain, I contemplated its beauty and saw that it was closed at the top. While I was doing this, an old man—venerable as a priest—passed by. I greeted him honorably and asked why this fountain was closed and fortified in such a manner at the top, bottom, and all sides? 

Granting me a friendly response, he said: "Know this, my friend: this fountain possesses a power more wonderful and terrible than all other fountains in the whole world. It belongs only to the **King** <note>In alchemy, the "King" represents the fixed principle, often gold or the essential "seed" of the Stone</note> of this country, whom the fountain knows very well, just as he knows the fountain. It always draws the King toward itself as he passes by, but it is not drawn by the King. He remains in that bath for **two hundred and eighty-two days** <note>An alchemical timeframe, often corresponding to the period of human gestation, representing the time needed for the matter to mature</note>, through which he is brought to such strength of youth that he cannot be conquered by anyone, no matter how robust. 

He therefore saw to it that his little fountain was enclosed with a white round stone, as you see, in which the fountain shines clearly like silver and a celestial color. To make it even stronger and prevent it from being destroyed by horses or other animals, he brought in an old oak, split through the middle, which protects it from the sun's rays by providing shade. Then, as you see, it is surrounded by a very thick wall: first it is closed with a hard, clear stone, and then finally by the hollow oak—mostly because the water is of a **terrible nature**, so much so that once ignited and provoked, it penetrates all things; likewise, if it were to evaporate, it would be the end of us." 

I asked afterward if he himself had seen the King in the said fountain. He replied that he had indeed seen him entering, but from the time he is locked inside by the guards, he appears no more until the **one hundred and thirtieth day**. Then, he emerges remarkably splendid and shining. He replied kindly and with a smile: "When the King has purposed to come here, leaving behind all his courtiers and strangers, he enters alone. No one approaches the fountain except him and his guard. A very simple man—indeed, the simplest of men—has care of it and could best fulfill his duties, since he does nothing else than heat the fountain."

I asked again whether the King was a friend to the fountain, and the fountain to him? He said: "They love each other in a marvelous way; the fountain attracts the King, and not the King the fountain, for the fountain is like a mother to him." Finally, I asked of what lineage the King was? He replied that he was born from the fountain, which had made him such as he is, without any other thing. I asked whether he had many courtiers. He said he had only six, who await the succession, so that if the King should eventually die, they might also gain possession of the kingdom as he did. For this reason they serve him, because they hope for great dominion and possession from him.

At last I asked whether he was an old man, and he replied that he was older than the fountain, and more mature than any of his subjects. "How then is it," I asked, "that they do not kill the King—from whose death they expect such a succession—especially since he is so old?" 

He said: "Although he is of a very advanced age, nonetheless none of his subjects is so enduring of cold and sweat, rain, winds, and labors as he is. Likewise, none of them by themselves, nor all together, could kill him, nor could any force." 

"How then will they possess the kingdom if he can neither die nor be killed by anyone?" 

He replied: "His six subjects are from the fountain, from which they possess everything they have, just as he does, whereby they are drawn most strongly by the fountain. The King is killed by the fountain itself just as they are, and is resurrected through it. Then, from the substance of his kingdom, which is divided into the smallest parts, each of his subjects receives a portion. And no matter how tiny a particle each has, they are made equal to the King in wealth, strength, and power, and they become equal among themselves." 

I asked again how long he would have to wait? Smiling again, he said: "Know that the King enters alone without his subjects; and although the fountain also loves them, they do not enter, because they have not yet earned this dignity. But when the King enters, he is stripped of his garment woven with leaves of pure gold and his covering, which he gives to his first **chamberlain** <term>cubicularius; a royal attendant, used here to represent a specific metal or stage in the alchemical process</term> called **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno dicto"; Saturn represents the metal Lead and the first stage of the Great Work, the blackening or "nigredo"</note>. He keeps it for forty days—sometimes two more at most—after he has first received it. Then the King strips off his black silken tunic, which he gives to his second chamberlain named **Jupiter** <note>Jupiter represents the metal Tin</note>, who guards it for twenty-two days. Then finally Jupiter, at the King's command, gives it to **the Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"; representing the metal Silver and the whitening stage or "albedo"</note>, who is the third person, beautiful and shining; she keeps it for twenty days."

Then at last the King stands in a pure white shirt <term>Latin: *camisia*; in alchemy, this represents the *albedo* or whitening stage of the matter</term> like snow, or the flower of salt. This shirt he then takes off and hands to **Mars**, who keeps it for forty days, sometimes with two others arriving. Afterward **Mars**, by God’s command, hands it to the **yellow Sun**—not yet the bright one—who keeps it for forty days. Then at last comes the most beautiful and **blood-red Sun**, who immediately seizes the shirt. I finally asked, what becomes of all these things? He said: "Next the fountain is opened, and just as he gave them the shirt, the garment, and the breastplate, in a moment he now hands over his own bloody and red flesh <note>The *rubedo* or red stage, signifying the completion of the Philosopher's Stone</note> to be eaten by all; at last they have what they desired."

I asked again whether they always waited so long, and whether they could have any reward for their services before then, unless they persevered until the very end? He replied: "As soon as they have the white shirt, four of those courtiers, if they wished, could rejoice and enjoy many riches; but they would only possess half of the kingdom. For this reason, they prefer to wait a little longer for the end and the outcome, so that they may also be crowned with the royal diadem of their lord." 

I asked whether any doctor ever approached, or anything else during that time? He replied: "None, nor anything else except a single guard who stirs up a continuous, circulating, and vaporous heat beneath, and nothing more." <note>This guard represents the alchemist maintaining the steady heat of the furnace, or *athanor*</note> I asked if this guard suffered many labors? He said: "More at the beginning than toward the end, because the fountain is set on fire." I asked whether many had seen this? He replied: "It is before the eyes of the whole world, yet no one of those who are in the world has recognized it." 

I asked more broadly what they were doing? He said: "If they wish, those six <note>The six other metals: Mercury, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Silver</note> could again purify the King in the fountain for three days, circling the place according to the capacity of the vessel, giving the breastplate on the first day, the shirt on the second, and his bloody flesh on the third." I said to this, "To what purpose are these things?" But he said: "I have answered you thus far; I am tired." 

When I perceived this, I did not want to be a nuisance, but I accompanied him some distance as he left, giving him immortal thanks, and said farewell. He was a very venerable old man and most wise, so much so that the heavens obeyed him, and all things trembled before him. Sleep also overcame me, so that returning to the fountain I intended to rest for a while, and I could not refrain from sitting upon it, so as to secretly unlock all the barriers. Meanwhile, while I was looking at my little book—the prize of our discussion—its splendor and beauty increased the sleepiness I already felt, so that with a certain yawn it slipped from my hands into the fountain. This distressed me greatly, for I wanted to keep it in memory of the honor I had achieved. And when I looked, it vanished from my eyes; thinking therefore it had fallen to the bottom of the fountain, I began to draw out the water with great diligence, so that there remained in it only a tenth part of it with...

In short, I saw toward the end everything my heart desired, without much labor; and it will not torment you so much either, provided that once you have entered the right path, you do not turn aside into errors, but imitate nature in all things.

In closing, I say to you: whoever reads this little book of mine and does not understand the Stone through it, will never understand it, no matter what he does. For in this parable of mine, the whole work is contained in its practice—in the days, colors, regimens, ways, dispositions, and continuations; I have narrated each detail as best as it could be done, moved by piety, charity, and compassion toward those desolate workers in this most precious art. Making an end, therefore, to my little book, I pray to God, the Best and Greatest <note>Latin: *Deum Optimum Maximum*; a common humanist and legal phrasing for the Almighty</note>, by whose grace it was finished, that He might open the minds of men of good will. To the ingenious, there will be little difficulty, provided they abstain from dreamed-up fantasies and the subtleties of the sophists <note>In alchemy, "sophists" refers to fraudulent practitioners who used deceptive logic and false chemicals rather than following natural laws</note>, and remain on the path of nature, which is demonstrated through my theory. Farewell in **JESU CHRISTO** all, and be mindful of the poor when you reach this inexhaustible treasure. Pray to God, who will teach you

## A LITTLE TREATISE

# ON THE NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
# OF METALS BY LORD DIONYSIUS
# ZACHARIUS, A MOST NOBLE MAN

## A French Philosopher.

->TO THE KIND READER.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter Q featuring a figure in a landscape or garden setting.</image-desc>

As many as have written in this divine art of old—learned men, wise men, and natural philosophers—they all forbade the profanation or public disclosure of its secret <term>Latin: *arcanum*; a "shut-away" or secret mystery of alchemy</term>. Nonetheless, friend Reader, when I had sufficiently considered the interpretations of the contradictions, figures, comparisons, ambiguities, and various enigmas occurring everywhere in their writings without number, I did not wish to keep hidden whatever I have resolved. This knowledge I gained through true imagination and from the books of honorable men after many useless labors and most lengthy operations concerning sophisticated recipes <note>original: "sophisticationem"; in this context, it refers to "sophistication" or "adulteration," the practice of creating fraudulent gold or silver using alloys that only look like precious metals</note>—which I would rather call entirely foolish and deceptive works. I discovered this truth through the continuous reading of the most approved authors, such as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813), a foundational figure in alchemy whose "Summa Perfectionis" was considered the ultimate textbook for medieval and Renaissance alchemists</note> in his *Summa*, and others. 

Therefore, pulling back my foot from the erroneous paths in which I had been entangled before—more than Daedalus was in his labyrinth <note>A reference to the Greek myth of the labyrinth of Crete; Zacharius uses this as a metaphor for the confusing and circular nature of false alchemical instructions</note>—I wished to set my path straight. Walking upon this path, I finally recognized the true and perfect matter, prepared for us by nature in the caverns of the earth, for the purpose of perfecting above the earth those metals which she herself generates naturally beneath it. This is just as experience (by God's mercy) has taught me, and as I shall declare in this little book more clearly than has ever been done before. In the first part of this work, I shall narrate the manner and progress by which I finally arrived at the true knowledge of this divine work. In the second, I will discuss which authors I used in seeking out the explanations of the authorities <insert>and their teachings</insert>,

->TO THE READER.<-

...explanations of terms and other difficulties. Thirdly and finally, I will declare the practice in such a way that it remains hidden from the ignorant, but for the sons of the art <term>a traditional term for "initiates" or dedicated students of alchemy</term>, it will be most manifest. For their sake, I have strived to reduce everything into the best order with the greatest diligence. In this matter, I have not imitated those men who are envious of the public good, too eager for their own profit, who refused to explain their material except under various and diverse allegories of fables—indeed, who were barely willing to show their books to others. 

I knew a certain man who had received some writings from a Venetian; he kept these hidden away, worshipping them as if they were sacred, so that he himself hardly dared to look inside, let alone show or share them with others. He perhaps thought the stone <term>the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> would emerge from that paper alone without any labor, if only the chest were kept most strictly closed, like a piece of philosophical matter under a Hermetic seal <note>original: "Hermetico sigillo"; an airtight seal, but also a metaphor for spiritual or secret concealment</note>. 

But such people do not realize that this divine science is not granted by chance to men, as the Philosophers say, while they rebuke those who work not at their own expense, but at the expense of others. No doubt I shall be most harshly judged by these people for publishing this little work, especially in the common tongue <note>The author originally wrote in French, though this text is a Latin translation. He is defending his choice to write in a "vulgar" language that anyone can read, rather than secretive code</note>, since in these times no science is more hated by the common crowd. To these people, I wish to give a brief response which they have hitherto ignored: namely, that the understanding of this divine philosophy is not within human power such that it can be understood through books alone. Rather, it rests in the will of God, who reveals it to whom He wills through His Holy Spirit, or through the mediation of some man, as is told more broadly in the second part of this book. So far am I from making it known to everyone. 

What is new if I write the art in the common tongue? For all its professors have likewise described it in no other language than their own until now: just as Hamech the Hebrew wrote in Hebrew; Thebit and Hali <note>Likely referring to Thabit ibn Qurra and Haly Abenragel, notable medieval Arabic scholars</note>, the Chaldean philosophers, in Chaldean; Homer, Democritus, and Theophrastus the Greeks in the Greek language; and by Aboholy, Geber, and Avicenna the Arabs in Arabic. Morienus, Raymond <note>Referring to the legendary hermit Morienus Romanus and the prolific (though likely pseudo-) Raymond Lull</note>, and many other Latins handed down the art in Latin, so that it might be known by...

...be recognized by their successors that this divine science was even granted at times to men of their own nation. Regarding the popular hatred of this art, it should be understood that the truth of the art itself is not despised, but rather only the false deceptions <term>sophisticationes; in an alchemical context, this refers to fraudulent methods or "sophisticated" counterfeits used to deceive the unwary</term> within it, as I shall explain more fully in the first part of this little book. 

But if they should ask why I do not write every detail clearly and openly, so that anyone might work safely from this little treatise, since by doing otherwise I offer no benefit to the readers? To answer this: who is unaware of the countless useless expenses made daily in France <note>original: "Gallia"</note> alone on account of these deceptions? If readers can be brought back to the right path by reading my book, then pious and honest readers may be kept on the path of truth through what I teach in the second part. 

The reading of the third part will not be useless to these people, as it describes the way to an altogether easy entry into the practice of the divine work. I call it "divine" for this reason: that no one can comprehend or understand it through themselves without divine inspiration, even if they are otherwise a most learned philosopher. This is as Geber <note>original: "Geber"; Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a prolific Islamic alchemist whose works formed the backbone of medieval European alchemy</note> says against all those who strive to work solely by considering natural causes and works, stating:

> In this they err greatly, thinking they can imitate nature, since such a thing is impossible for the art in all respects.

Therefore, let such slanderers abstain from reading our little work; for I have not labored for them, but for the kind and teachable "sons of doctrine" and the studious lovers of this art. I ask these friends and wish them to be warned: before they begin to work, they should compare all the doubts that arise concerning the individual operations necessary for the composition. When they encounter things that seem to contradict one another, or the ambiguities of riddles and such things, they must keep a mind so resolved and free that they may see and understand that these are nothing but pure agreements <note>original: "concordantias"</note>—not of different things, but of the same meaning expressed in various ways. This is the only way of knowing the truth, especially in this art, as Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist famous for his systematic laboratory manuals</note> says. Whoever is lazy and yawning during the reading of our books will also be unfit for preparing the materials, when—

*...indeed, one is explained by the other, and what is perhaps lacking in one is supplied in the other. Therefore, I ask all those who reach such happiness through this little work <note>original: "Opusculum"</note> of mine not to abuse it; let them not be unmindful of the poor, lest they bring condemnation upon themselves. Let them give thanks to God constantly for this and for the rest of His generous gifts, to whom alone be praise, honor, and glory forever.*

# THE FIRST PART OF THE LITTLE WORK OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS, SHOWING THE WAY THE AUTHOR ARRIVED AT TRUE KNOWLEDGE OF THIS ART AND OF THE DIVINE WORK.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring a figure amidst foliage and classical architectural motifs.</image-desc>

HERMES, the famous Thrice-Greatest <note>original: "Trismegistus"; a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note>, who was not undeservedly called the first prophet and father of all natural philosophers, author of the divine stone, and the Great Interpreter, after he had experienced the truth of this divine philosophy, left us a record. He wrote that unless he had feared the final universal judgment of God, he would never have written anything concerning this divine science, so great was the veneration he held for it. This same opinion was shared by all who imitated him in this art. Consequently, they all wrote books about it using various arguments that lead to different conclusions—as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, often cited in alchemy</note> says in his *Summa*—so that the ignorant would be forced to wander in error, while on the contrary, the "Sons of the Doctrine" <note>A traditional term for dedicated students of alchemy</note> would perceive their true meaning through the variety of such opinions. Nevertheless, it was necessary even for these students to err at the beginning, so that after they have attained the art through the greatest labors of both mind and body, they might value it more highly and keep it more secretly. 

This is certainly the greatest reason for concealment: for added to the unbearable and painful labors are enormous expenses, especially for those who learn through the reading of books alone, expecting inspiration from the Divine Spirit. This is exactly what I did for a period of ten years, as I am about to relate, while describing the means through which I came to the knowledge of this secret. When I was about twenty years old, after having been instructed at home by the care of my parents in the principles of Grammar, I was sent away to study the Arts and Philosophy. Within three years, through the diligence of my personal tutor, I made such progress that it seemed right to my guardians (for in the meantime both my parents had died) to advance me further—specifically to the study of law <note>original: "legisprudentiam"</note> under the same...

...teacher: but before I departed from the college of arts, I had entered into familiarity and friendship with many other scholars. They possessed various books of chemical recipes, which I had transcribed with the greatest diligence when they were lent to me, with the consent of my private teacher, who for a long time had also begun to labor in this art—so much so that before I left, I had collected a very voluminous book stuffed with recipes of this kind.

As soon as I had arrived with my teacher at that place where I ought to have devoted my effort to the laws <note>Zacharius was sent to study law at the University of Toulouse</note>, I began to turn over my writings. Some of these contained projections <term>Projections: The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" or powder is cast onto base metal to transmute it.</term> of one part upon ten, others upon twenty, thirty, a third part, or a half; for "red" gold of eighteen characters <note>original: "characterum"; meaning carats</note>, twenty, etc., into the gold of crowns, ducats, and of a higher color than can ever exist. One was supposed to withstand smelting, another the test of the Lydian stone <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak left on the stone</note>, and all other examinations. Similarly regarding the "white" <note>silver</note>: one was supposed to be of ten-denier fineness, another eleven, another the silver of capital coinage, returning white from the fire, another in the rubbing of the Lydian stone. In short, I thought that if I were able to perform even the smallest of these, no greater happiness could happen to me in this world. 

Especially since I read that recipes of this kind bore the signatures of great men: one of the Queen of Navarre, another of the Cardinal of Lorraine, of Tournon <note>François de Tournon, a powerful French cardinal and diplomat</note>, and of countless others, so that trust might be placed in these types of masks and titles by cautious men, by which he easily deceived me along with the rest. And so I began to have small furnaces built, and moving from the smallest to the largest, I filled a whole large room with them. I had designated one for distillation, another for sublimation, for calcination, dissolution, the "bath of Mary" <note>original: "balneum Maris"; a water bath for gentle, indirect heating, known today as a bain-marie</note>, and for fusion, so that for the first entry into my beginning, I had entirely consumed two hundred crowns—which we had received for the support of my studies for two years—partly on furnaces, partly on charcoal, infinite minerals, and glass vessels, and on gold and silver uselessly melted, mixed, and dissolved, which perished through long handling among the dross <note>original: "loppas"</note> and ashes. Thus diminished, they scarcely appeared, or only as a tiny residue, brittle and corrupted. Before the first year was even finished, I had reduced the substance of two years, or at least of the second already beginning, into smoke. 

At this time my teacher was seized by a very hot fever, caused by our heat stirred up by the coals (almost like those perceived by the casters of cannons in the Arsenal at Venice), because, already inflamed and burning inwardly, he had drunk cold liquid; I grieved most greatly over his death. Then, because my parents refused to send more money than was required for me alone, and desiring to pursue the work I had begun, I was forced to return home, so that—having been made free from guardianship and my own master <note>original: "meique juris"; a legal term for reaching the age of majority</note>—I might dispose of my paternal inheritance in whatever way I wished. This I immediately placed into a lease <note>original: "arendam"</note> (as they call it)...

<header>A SMALL WORK</header>

I labored for four years at a cost of four hundred crowns, testing a recipe I had finally received from an Italian; I supported this man with me until I could see the outcome of the matter, for he affirmed that he had seen its effect through his own experience. For this undertaking, I purchased two ounces of gold and one mark of silver; having melted them together, we dissolved them in *aqua forti* <note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid, used to dissolve silver</note>, and afterward we calcined them through evaporation. We also attempted to dissolve them with various other waters and different distillations, until three months had passed before this powder was ready for projection <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" or powder is cast onto base metal to transmute it.</term>. We performed this according to the instructions of the recipe, but in vain: for the expected gain was transmuted into a loss, so much so that out of the eight combined ounces of gold and silver, only three ounces remained. This is to say nothing of the many other expenses, by which my four hundred crowns were reduced to two hundred and thirty. Of these remaining funds, I gave twenty to my Italian so that he might go to the author of the recipe, who he claimed was in Milan, to be better instructed by him. Consequently, I waited for his return throughout the entire winter, but I might as well have waited there until the Last Judgment, for I never saw him again.

Summer finally returned, accompanied by the plague, which forced me and my other companions to leave the area for half a year. During that time, I happened upon a certain old man, commonly called a <term>Philosopher</term> <note>In this context, a "Philosopher" refers to an adept or experienced practitioner of alchemy</note>, with whom I struck up a friendship. I shared my recipes with him, asking him to note the better ones according to his judgment; he pointed out ten or twelve that seemed the most promising to him. Once the plague had ceased, I returned to my former place and began to test these shortly after my return. I worked through the entire subsequent winter until the Feast of Saint John, only to report as much profit as I had from the previous attempts: indeed, my four hundred crowns had "increased" such that I could count only seventy of them left. 

Even so, I did not lose heart. A certain Abbot had a recipe sent from a friend in Rome, from the court of Cardinal Armagnac <note>Georges d'Armagnac (1501–1585), a prominent French cardinal and diplomat known for his interest in the arts and sciences</note>. I contributed one hundred crowns to this cause, and he contributed as many, so that we might test it at our common expense. We built furnaces of different shapes than the others, because we required an excellent <term>aqua vitæ</term> <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; literally "water of life," referring to highly concentrated alcohol or spirits of wine</note> for the dissolution of a mark or a half-pound of gold. We bought a large vat of the finest wine, from which we prepared a vast quantity of this "water," rectified many times over, using a <term>pelican</term> <note>original: "pellicanum"; a specialized alchemical circulatory vessel with two side arms that return distillate to the body</note> and many glass vessels purchased for this purpose. Afterward, we took one mark of our gold—which had first been calcined for a full month—and four marks of the aforementioned "water," and placed them into two very thick glass <term>retorts</term> <note>original: "retorta"; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, one entering into the other. Once sealed and both placed in two large round furnaces, we also bought charcoal at the price of thirty crowns in a single purchase to maintain the fire beneath them continuously for a whole year, while we might also try something with other recipes in the meantime...
