# DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS

...we were testing, from which we gained no more benefit than from any other grand undertaking—which is to say, absolutely nothing at all from either. We might have kept the fires burning for infinite years before the promised coagulation <term>Coagulation: The process of turning a liquid substance into a solid or thickened state, a key stage in the alchemical "Great Work."</term> had occurred at the bottom of the vessels, since no dissolution had preceded it. We were not, however, working with the proper material, nor was that the true water of solution <note>original: "solutionis aqua vera"; the solvent required to break down the metals</note> which ought to dissolve our gold, as experience later proved. For we found the gold powder still entirely intact, or perhaps only a little finer, which we cast upon quicksilver <note>original: "vivum argentum"; mercury</note> as the recipe directed, but all in vain.

We took this misfortune poorly, especially the Abbot, who—acting like some great public secretary—had boasted before his monks that he expected nothing less than the completion of the work, and that he would eventually melt down the lead fountain in the monastery and turn it into gold. In truth, he was forced to reserve that for another time, so that he might later provide the funds for the expenses he incurred in the meantime through a passing German operator, who attempted the work fruitlessly in my absence while I was in Paris.

The Abbot, having recovered his spirit, persuaded me to gather three or four hundred crowns <term>Crown: A gold coin used across Europe, often called an 'écu' in France.</term> as my portion, to which he would add an equal amount. Taking these with me, I was to travel to Paris, where the number of those laboring at the art is infinite; I was to circulate among them until I found some perfected work to be shared between us like brothers. Once this pact was made, I again took an inventory of my possessions and brought eight hundred crowns to Paris, with the intention of not leaving until I had acquired or discovered what I desired.

I departed not without the greatest offense to all my parents and friends, who would have gladly promoted me to the rank of a senator in my homeland, believing me to be a most ready legal expert. But I, resisting them and pretending that I would use this money to purchase some official post, said my farewells. I prepared myself for the journey on the day after Christmas and arrived in Paris three days after the Feast of the Kings <note>The Feast of the Kings, or Epiphany, is January 6th.</note>.

There, for the first month, I chose to remain hidden and unknown. Soon after, however, I began to frequent the company of artists, goldsmiths, smelters, glassmakers, builders of furnaces, and others; I established such a reputation that by the end of the second month, more than a hundred operators became my familiars. Some worked on the tinting of metals through projections, others through cementation <term>Cementation: A process of purifying gold or altering its properties by heating it while surrounded by solid chemical agents.</term>, some through dissolutions, many through the joining of the essence of what is commonly called the emery stone <note>original: "lapis smirilli"; likely referring to a mineral catalyst or abrasive used in refining</note>, some through long boilings, some in the extraction of Mercury from metals, and others in the fixation of those same metals. Our congregation was so frequent—sometimes in houses, other times at the Great Temple <note>original: "summo templo"; likely referring to the Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris</note>—that even feast days and Sundays were not spared. Some said among themselves: "If only we had the means to repeat our work, we would reach perfection"; others said, "If our vessel had remained intact, things would have gone

->### A SHORT TREATISE.<-

...was proceeding well: some claimed that if we had possessed a copper vessel that was perfectly round, we would have successfully fixed Mercury with the moon <note>original: "cum luna"; "the moon" is the alchemical symbol for silver. To "fix" mercury means to turn the liquid metal into a solid that can withstand heat.</note>. In short, not one of them had performed anything that did not come with its own excuses, to which I still turned a somewhat deaf ear; for the useless expenses I had incurred through such persuasions kept rubbing my memory raw. Meanwhile, a certain Greek, considered learned by reputation, approached a treasurer known to me, promising him mountains of gold from the fixation of mercury of cinnabar <term>Cinnabar: A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the most common ore of mercury.</term>. This information gave me the opportunity, together with a friend, to pay out money for my share to execute this work. Since, therefore, there was a need for pure silver broken into filings, we bought three marks' weight of it. From this, our worker formed certain nails <note>original: "clavos"; this refers to a famous alchemical deception where silver nails were supposedly "multiplied" in weight or transformed.</note> by adding a certain artificial paste mixed with powdered cinnabar; these he cooked in a closed earthenware pot for the required time. Finally, once dried, he refined them through cupellation <term>Cupellation: A process used to separate precious metals like gold and silver from base metals by heating them in a shallow porous cup (a cupel).</term>, so much so that we found three marks—and a little more—of pure silver, which he claimed had been produced from the cinnabar: asserting that our original silver had vanished into smoke. God alone could know if there was any profit here, for we did not; I had lost, or rather spent in vain, more than thirty crowns <note>original: "coronatos"; gold coins.</note> for my share. The rumor of these "nails" spread through the entire city of Paris, so that there was no one who had not heard of them, especially among those who were accustomed to the works of sophisticated deceptions <note>original: "sophisticationum"; in alchemy, "sophistication" refers to the fraudulent imitation or adulteration of precious metals.</note>, just as the fame of "copper apples" for fixing mercury with the moon had been spread abroad before. At last, there arrived a certain nobleman remarkably skilled in these deceptions—even to the point of making a profit by selling his works to goldsmiths—with whom I entered into a friendship, not without great expense, lest he think me a pauper.

I spent an entire year in his company before he declared even the slightest thing to me; at last, he finally shared his secret with me, which, although he valued it greatly, resulted in nothing perfect. Nevertheless, I wrote to my Abbot everything that had happened, and I sent him a duplicate of this last work along with the nobleman's practical instructions. He wrote back to me that I should stay in Paris for another year and not fear the expenses, especially since I had come upon a secret which he considered no small thing for a beginning—though I had already resolved in my mind not to use any material that did not persist in the same state in which it first appeared. I proposed to myself that no one should work or labor merely to end up a rogue and an impostor, growing rich to the detriment of others. Accordingly, I stayed for another year, as he had written, making a total of two years passed there; I frequented now this man, now another, specifically those who were commonly thought to possess something good and perfect. I had consumed almost all my money when the Abbot wrote to me again, telling me that as soon as I had seen and read his letters, I should come to him without delay. This I did, for I did not wish to break the brotherly faith I had promised. As I arrived...

He presented letters from the King of Navarre <note>The King of Navarre at this time (c. 1540s-50s) was likely Henry II of Navarre, who was known for his interest in the arts and sciences.</note> (who seemed to be curious about these matters) sent to him, asking that he might arrange with me that, if I wished to do him a favor, I should go to the King immediately and teach the secret of that noble work, as well as other things he had heard from reports that I knew. He promised a reward of three or four thousand crowns <note>original: "coronatorum"; the crown (écu) was a gold coin used in France and Navarre.</note>. This sum so inflamed the Abbot that he could not have shown himself happier even if the money were already hiding in his purse, nor could he rest until I had set off for the Court. 

When I arrived there, I was unable to begin work for six weeks, as the materials had to be sought from elsewhere. When the work was finally completed, none of the reward I expected came to pass. For even if the King had intended to reward my labors (to say nothing of the favor and friendship shown to me by the locals and courtiers, though by very few in truth), nevertheless, because his people and the highest nobles—especially those who were the main reason for my arrival—dissuaded the King from his good opinion of me, I was dismissed by the King empty-handed. Only a word of thanks was given, and a promise that if there were any confiscated properties in his territories over which he had authority, I should search for them and he would grant them to me. 

Disturbed by this tedious response, I was unwilling to trust such empty promises, which were all too familiar to me from the past. I returned to the Abbot, quite dissatisfied, though not before I visited in passing a certain religious Doctor, most excellent in philosophy <note>original: "philosophia"; in this context, "philosophy" refers to natural philosophy, which included the study of chemistry and alchemy.</note>, about whose singular learning there was no small reputation. He greatly discouraged me from these sophistries <term>Sophistries: Deceptive or fraudulent alchemical practices that use clever tricks or "sophisticated" arguments instead of true natural principles.</term>. After he learned that I had devoted myself to philosophy to such an extent that I had received a Master’s degree (as they call it), as I had also told him, he said he grieved deeply that I had not possessed the best books before I had so uselessly consumed both my time and my wealth in such diabolical sophistries. 

I told him about this most recent work, and he quickly judged that it could not withstand rigorous testing. Therefore, he kindly urged me to abstain entirely from these errors henceforth and to read the books of the ancient Philosophers more attentively, so as to gain knowledge of their true matter, in which the highest perfection of this science seemed to lie. 

Accordingly, I hastened my journey back to the Abbot to render an account of the expenses I had incurred in Paris and to report on the reward I had received from the King of Navarre. When I had told him everything, he was saddened, and especially so because I did not wish to persevere in the work. For he believed me to be an industrious operator, yet all the kind words he used could not prevent me from following the Doctor’s advice, given the clear reasons he had put forward. After settling the account with the Abbot, of our shared eight hundred crowns, only ninety were found remaining. Having bid each other farewell, we parted ways; I, however...

<page-num>719</page-num>
### LITTLE WORK.

Having truly returned home so that I might get more money from my tenants <note>original: "arrendatoribus"</note>, I collected the funds and betook myself once more to Paris. I made a firm resolution that, once I arrived there, I would not leave my lodgings until I had achieved an excellent and perfect conclusion through the reading of various authors of our natural philosophy. This was to be done before I set my hand to our Great Work, leaving behind all the wicked deceptions <note>original: "sophisticationibus"; refers to the fraudulent or overly complex "short-cuts" offered by "sophist" alchemists</note> to their original authors.

I arrived in Paris, therefore, on the day after All Saints' Day [November 2nd], in the year 1546. Having purchased several books for the price of ten crowns <note>original: "coronatorum"; the gold écu</note> regarding this philosophy—some of them printed and others not, by both ancient and modern writers—such as the **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, **Trevisanus** <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist who spent his life seeking the stone</note>, **The Lamentation of Nature** <note>original: "Lamentatio naturae"; an allegorical work often attributed to Jean de Meung</note>, and many other tracts not yet in print, I rented a room in the suburb of Saint-Marceau. There I remained, along with the boy who served me, visiting no one and studying assiduously, day and night, for an entire year with the greatest diligence.

Scarcely had the first month passed when I began to propose one resolution to myself, then another—now expanding upon one, now changing it entirely. I intended to do this for as long as it took until I finally hit upon a single theory in which no variation and no contradiction of philosophical opinions could be found. In these efforts a year and a good part of the next passed by before I could draw any stable knowledge from them.

Being caught in these perplexities, it seemed expedient to visit actual operators of this divine work, leaving behind those "sophists" whom I had realized were wandering "by the whole width of the sky" (as they say) <note>a Latin idiom meaning to be as far as possible from the truth</note> and leading others astray. Truly, the ambiguity that held me back from my study now increased, even more so when I considered the various and diverse methods of operating among them. For if this man worked in gold alone, another worked in gold with Mercury; another mixed in lead, which he called <term>sounding: lead treated with mercury to alter its acoustic properties, often thought to be a stage of transmutation</term> because it had passed through a retort with quicksilver. Another likewise converted metals into quicksilver through various simple and diverse means by sublimation; another worked in <term>black vitriol: "attramento nigro," often referring to ferrous sulfate or a black mineral salt</term>, which he asserted was the true matter that **Raymundus Lullius** used in the composition of his Great Stone.

While one worked with an <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>, another, on the contrary, was found using many other diverse vessels of glass, bronze, copper, lead, silver, or even gold. Likewise, some did their decoctions <note>the process of heating a substance in a liquid</note> with a fire of large coals, others with wood, some with the fermenting skins of grapes, others with the rays of the Sun, and others in a <term>Mary’s Bath: "balneo Mariæ," a water bath used for gentle, uniform heating</term>. Indeed, the variety of such operations, together with their contradictions, almost brought me to the point of despair, until, being raised up again by the Divine Spirit, I returned once more to a serious reading of the books with more diligence and greater attention—

...sedulously re-reading the writings of *Ramon Llull* <note>original: "Raymundi Lullij"; a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note>, especially in the *Testament* and the *Codicil*. These I compared with a certain letter he wrote, when near death, to *King Robert* <note>Robert of Anjou (1277–1343), King of Naples, a frequent addressee in pseudo-Lullian literature</note>, and with a certain manuscript given to me by a Doctor—which had been useless to him—so that, in opposition to all the previous operations I had seen before, I might conclude by finally resolving upon a single path. I found one that agreed with all the books, and likewise with that resolution made by *Arnald of Villanova* <note>a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, the teacher of *Llull* in this art, near the end of his great *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarij"; the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a seminal alchemical text</note>. Persisting in this opinion, I did nothing else but assiduously read and meditate upon my resolution day and night, until the time came for my rental income <note>original: "census"</note> to arrive, so that I might return home to work. And when I was finally home, I proposed to put what I had resolved into effect, having first made provision for all things that were necessary; first I built a furnace, and on the day after Easter I began to labor. I did so not without many hindrances, of which I shall make no mention here, except for the frequent rebukes of my parents and friends, and of my neighbors.

Some would say to me: "Hey, what are you turning over in your mind? Haven't you made enough useless expenses on these trifles yet, I ask you?" Another would warn me that unless I abstained from handling such great amounts of coal, the common people would suspect me of forging counterfeit money <note>original: "monetæ falsæ"</note>, as they had already begun to murmur about this matter. Another would arrive, asserting that all the citizens—and the more prominent ones at that—wondered why I did not take up the profession of **Jurisprudence** <note>the study of law</note>, especially since I was a **Licentiate** <note>a person who holds a university degree (the Licentia) allowing them to practice a profession</note>, so that I might reach some higher office of administration **for the State**. Those who were more closely related and more familiar with me rebuked me daily without ceasing, saying: "When at last will you put an end to these follies and the squandering of your paternal inheritance? It would be better to turn such useless expenses toward the payment of your creditors and the purchase of some office." Nor did that seem to be enough, for they even threatened me that, unless I desisted, they would see to it that the officers of **Justice** rushed into the house and broke all my instruments and the rest of my equipment. "If you have no respect for us," they said, "nor for your other friends, at least have some regard for yourself; consider that although you are thirty years old, or thereabouts, you seem to be acting like a fifty-year-old. Thus your beard is tinged almost to whiteness because of excessive labors, suffered since your youth for the sake of some vain opinion."

Consider whether these words stung me most sharply: especially when I saw my work succeeding more prosperously day by day, upon which I persisted most stubbornly and constantly without weariness, even despising these and other intervening obstacles—and especially the plague <note>original: "peste"</note>, which raged through the whole summer, so that even all business dealings ceased. Every single day, certainly, I beheld the appearances of the **three colors** <note>The alchemical stages of *nigredo* (black), *albedo* (white), and *rubedo* (red)</note>, which the **Philosophers** write ought to appear before the perfection of the divine work. All these, by the grace of God, I saw...

# THE LITTLE WORK.

...successive steps one after another, and finally on the actual day of Easter the following year, I saw the perfection. This was proven through an experiment performed upon quicksilver <note>original: "vivum argentum"; mercury</note> heated in a crucible <note>original: "tigillo"; a ceramic or graphite container used for melting metals at high temperatures</note>, which was converted into pure gold before my eyes in less than an hour by using a very small amount of this divine powder <note>The "powder of projection" or the final form of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. God knows with what joy I was suffused. Yet I was not boastful or proud before the world because of it, but secretly gave immortal thanks to God, who had deigned to hear my prayers through **JESUS CHRIST** His son, our Lord. I prayed further that He might illuminate my heart and intellect with His grace, so that I might use this gift for the honor and praise of His glorious name. 

The next day I immediately prepared for a journey toward my Abbot, to fulfill the promise I had made to him; but he had died six months earlier. For this reason I was struck with the greatest grief, as well as by the death of the other Doctor, of which I was informed while traveling not far from his monastery. Consequently, I went to a certain place assigned to a close relative of mine before I had departed from my homeland, so that I might wait for him to come to me. I had left this man at my home with power of attorney to sell all my paternal goods to satisfy my creditors, and to secretly distribute the remainder to the poor and needy, so that my parents and others might share in this gift with which God wished to honor me. 

Many, and nearly all others, thought that I—like a man driven to despair and shame by such great and useless expenses—had sold everything so that I might flee to foreign regions to live in anonymity. This was reported to me by that relative of mine who arrived on the first of July. Afterwards we went to Lausanne, located in Savoy, so that from there we might travel to a certain famous marketplace in Germany with very few attendants, lest I become known even to those who might read this little work <note>original: "opusculum"</note> of mine while I am still living. Indeed, I composed this only to turn good and pious men away from sophistications <term>sophistications: fraudulent or deceptive alchemical methods that use chemical tricks to mimic the appearance of gold without achieving true transmutation</term> toward the right path of perfection in this divine work. For the conclusion of this first part, I remind everyone of what the Poet sang:

> *Happy is he whom the dangers of others make cautious.* <note>original: "Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum"; a common Latin maxim</note>

By this they may learn from my errors to flee from the useless expenses made in sophistications; on the contrary, let them patiently and constantly read and understand good authors before setting their hand to the work, always praying to God for grace and sincere understanding. For one does not arrive at this point by fate or luck, but by divine calling alone, rather than by study. To those to whom it is given, the means of veiling it from the unworthy will likewise be given, as will the means of revealing it to other honorable men, so that not everyone understands equally; and likewise the grace of using it well, in 

-> honor of the Most High, the giver of lights. <-

<meta>This page marks a transition from the author's personal narrative of success to a didactic section. DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS
# THE SECOND PART OF THE LITTLE WORK OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS
## *The section in which the author teaches the method and standard for reading the natural Philosophers according to the easiest system.*

In the first book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Physicorum libro"; Aristotle’s foundational work on the study of nature</note>, Aristotle teaches that one should not argue against those who deny fundamental principles. Rather, one should argue with those who admit the truth but are incautious through ignorance (let these men prevail as much as they can); for they do not see the "snake hiding in the grass" <note>A classical metaphor for a hidden danger or a concealed meaning</note> because of the mask placed before their eyes, which prevents them from discerning false colors from true ones. However, not wishing to dwell further on that author in this section, I shall pass to better things. He proceeds in this manner: I have wished (he says) to write this little work <term>opusculum</term> <note>A "little work" or short treatise</note> for good men and students of this art, so that they might gain no small fruit and utility from it in reading the authors, understanding obscurities and veils, and the confusion built by disordered variety.

Therefore, to meet these challenges and to assist my listeners, I will divide the narrative into an orderly sequence. First, I will state by whom this science was most especially discovered and passed down into the knowledge of successors, and which authors I have used in the composition of this little work, as well as the reason why they wrote so obscurely. 

Next, we shall prove the truth and certainty of the art through various arguments, responding likewise to the most apparent arguments brought against it. 

Thirdly, we shall teach that our art is "natural," and in what respect; likewise, why it is called "divine" because of its principal operations, while declaring therein the manifest errors of those practicing in this current time. 

Finally, we shall declare the works of nature beneath the earth which she uses in the generation of metals, in imitation of which the craftsmen <term>artifices</term> <note>In this context, the alchemists who "perfect" nature's work</note> must operate above the earth. 

Afterward, we shall indicate the matter necessary for this work. And lastly, we shall reconcile the principal terms used in this art, as well as the seemingly contradictory opinions of the ancient Philosophers, for the benefit of the "sons of the art" <note>A traditional term for initiated students of alchemy</note> and to the greatest shame, ignominy, and confusion of its detractors. I shall support each point through the authorities of the most ancient and learned Philosophers, so that no one may think their impostures are being exposed by some modern upstart.

To better declare the first inventors of our science, there is the doctrine of the blessed Apostle James, which we should call to mind, which goes as follows: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights..." <note>original: "Omnis donatio bona, & omne donum perfectum è supernis est, descendens à patre luminum"; James 1:17</note>. This sentiment is universal, and therefore it suits our intention, especially because our science is so divine and so supernatural (at least in its second operation) that it has always been, and still is, impossible for it to become known to men through any study or industry whatever, even if...

<meta>catchword: of all [omnium]</meta>

<summary>Dionysius Zacharius begins the second part of his treatise by outlining his curriculum for students of alchemy, promising to explain the art's origins, defend its validity, and reconcile the confusing contradictions found in ancient philosophical texts. He emphasizes that alchemy is a divine gift from God that cannot be mastered by human effort alone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the second part of the treatise. The previous page ended by stating the author's intent to explain who discovered the science of alchemy and why the ancient masters wrote so obscurely.</meta>

->OPUSCULUM.<-

...even the wisest of all men and most learned Philosophers, unless it is first inspired by God. For in this matter, all natural reason and experience fail us. Wherefore it has been rightly written by several that this is a secret reserved by God for those of His own who fear and honor Him, as that great prophet of ours, Hermes <note>original: "Hermes"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy</note>, says: "I have it from no one else," he says, "nor through any other, than from God through His divine inspiration." Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical author known in the Latin West as Alphidius</note> confirms this same thing in these words: "Know, my son, that God has reserved this art for the descendants of Adam, and especially for the truly poor." Geber <note>original: "Geber"; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in medieval chemistry/alchemy</note> affirms the same in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa perfectionis magisterii* (The Sum of Perfection), one of the most influential alchemical texts of the Middle Ages</note>, saying: "Our science is in the power of God, who out of His mercy gives it to whom He wills." It is not, therefore, in the power of men, nor was it devised by them. 

However, insofar as the art itself is natural, or imitates nature in its primary operations, there are various opinions in identifying the first inventor of that imitation. Some assert it was Adam; others, Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine</note>; some wish for Enoch to have had the first knowledge of it, whom they say was the same as Hermes <note>Syncresis was common in this period, identifying the biblical Enoch with the Egyptian Thoth and the Greek Hermes</note>, to whom the Greeks attributed so much honor that they called him the inventor of all occult arts.

I, for my part, would gladly agree with this last opinion, since it is most certain that he was a most excellent Philosopher, as appears from his writings. He searched out the causes of things most diligently through experiences in natural matters; once these were known, the material which nature uses in the cavities of the earth for generating metals became equally known to him. For as many as have imitated nature, all have arrived at the true knowledge of this art, such as Pythagoras, Plato, Socrates, Zeno, Haly, Senior Rasis, Geber, Morienus, Bonus, Arnaldus de Villanova, Raymond <note>referring to Raymond Lull</note>, and many others whom it would be tedious to recount. 

From all of these, as if from the foremost authorities, we have composed this present little work <term>opusculum</term> of ours, not without the greatest labor, as their own books testify. For they wrote in such a manner (since they kept the fear of God before their eyes) that it is impossible to arrive at the knowledge of this art by the reading of their books alone. As Geber says in the *Summa*: "There is no reason," he says, "for the <term>son of art</term> <note>A traditional term for a dedicated student or practitioner of alchemy</note> to lose heart in this divine work; for by assiduously meditating on the causes of natural compositions, he will finally arrive where his mind tends." On the contrary, whoever expects to find it by means of our books alone will attain the matter slowly; for the Philosophers wrote in such a way (he says in another place) that they seem to congratulate themselves alone on the true practice, mixing the method of inquiry into it. Likewise, they also placed the principal operations in various ways and in different chapters. He provides the reason: "Because if they had observed a clear order in their treatises, this divine science could have been understood by everyone on the first day, or in a single hour, so noble and admirable is it."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins and secrecy of alchemy, specifically addressing why ancient masters chose to hide their knowledge in metaphors and contradictions. This page follows the discussion of the divine origin of the art.</meta>

### DIONYSII ZACHARII <note>Dionysius Zacharias, a 16th-century French alchemist known for his autobiographical account of the "Great Work."</note>

Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical author known in the Latin West as Alphidius</note> says: We must believe that the Philosophers, our predecessors, hid their principal intention under enigmatic and equivocal speech, and through innumerable figures, lest the world suffer ruin through the manifestation of their doctrine. For all agriculture, trade, and whatever is necessary for the preservation of human life would perish; for no one would wish to labor when he saw himself filled with such great wealth, and everyone would despise necessity.

Thus it happens that Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, in the beginning of his book, says in excuse: "Little sons, it is not that you should think the Philosophers hid this secret out of envy against the learned and studious, but only so that it would not become known to the wicked and ignorant." Rosinus <note>likely referring to Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist</note> says: "By this means, the ignorant would be made equal to the wise, and a malicious, wicked man would abuse it to the detriment, ruin, and perdition of the whole people."

Geber <note>original: "Geber"; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> uses similar excuses in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa perfectionis magisterii*</note>, in the chapter on the **Administration of Solar Medicine** <note>The "Solar Medicine" refers to the preparation of the alchemical elixir or tincture used to create gold</note>, saying: "It is not that the children of doctrine deserve it, that the Philosophers wrote their books obscurely; for they did not intend it for them, but they wished this meaning to be veiled from the ignorant and unworthy under such a variety and confusion of diverse operations; while meanwhile, a path was laid out for the sons of wisdom, by which they might reach the knowledge of the art." For they did not (as it is held in another place) write the art they held only for themselves, but they gave the means by which it might be known and possessed by others.

This, therefore, is the cause of the difficulty in the books of the Philosophers. For what can be more difficult than to be explained out of so many innumerable contradictions and oppositions, not only among many authors—and indeed among nearly all of them—but even within a single author? As Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and physician</note> says: "I have demonstrated sufficiently in my books the true **ferment** <note>original: "fermentum"; a substance added to the alchemical work to initiate a transformation, similar to how yeast works in bread</note>, which indeed is needed for the multiplication of **tinctures** <note>original: "tincturarum"; the concentrated essences or "medicines" used to transform base metals into gold or silver</note> for metals; yet in another place I said it was not the true ferment, leaving the judgment of this statement and other statements to those who have a sound intellect and subtle discernment."

Likewise, if one of them says our matter is of cheap price and worth nothing, to be found everywhere in the lowest places, as Zeno says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between Greek philosophers</note>; yet against this, in the same book, Barseus says that what is sought is not of small price. Another will say the thing is most precious, not to be found without great expense. One teaches the preparation of the matter in diverse vessels and diverse operations, as Geber does in his *Summa*; soon you may find another asserting that only one vessel is needed for our divine work, such as Rhazes, Lilius, Alphidius, and others. In a book by the same Rhazes, a time of nine months is given; in another, one reads that a year is necessary to complete this work, which Rosinus and Plato <note>In alchemical literature, Plato was often cited as a master of the hidden arts</note> also assert. Finally, in their terminology such variety appears that it is impossible for the secret to be uncovered by anyone, unless by the inspiration of the Most High—either immediately from God, or through some good and wise man.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the intentional secrecy of alchemical masters. Having previously discussed why the art is hidden from the "ignorant and wicked," the author now addresses the difficulty of defining the art and asserts the underlying unity of all alchemical teachings despite their apparent contradictions.</meta>

->### TREATISE<-

...wise in this art. The most powerful cause for this [secrecy] is that no one skilled in this matter reveals themselves while living, but is only acknowledged through their writings after death. For the Philosophers would wish to keep an art acquired with such great labors hidden even from themselves, if they could—how much more so from others! Therefore, we should not marvel at this secrecy as the common people do, but rather consider with the wise by what path one may reach it.

Before we come to the second part of our division, however, we must answer an objection from detractors—those accustomed to picking apart the labors of others because they themselves lack the true light. They will say: "Was the doctrine of Aristotle not observed in the seventh book of the *Physics*, which states:
> Definition is the true form of the defined subject.
Since I had undertaken to treat the true method of this science, I should have begun with a definition." I refer these and similar critics to the ancient authors, who, when they attempted to give a definition of the divine science and found no perfect or complete one, were forced to admit that it is not possible—chiefly because it lacks "familiar principles" <note>The alchemical process often relies on principles perceived as "occult" or hidden, unlike the "familiar" or obvious laws of standard physics</note>, as Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously the teacher of King Khalid</note>, Lilius <note>Likely referring to the author of the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical text, or possibly Raymond Lull</note>, and many others say. For this reason, they were content only with various descriptions by which they could demonstrate the effects of the art.

I will, for my part, state what I believe concerning this matter. It is a certain branch of natural philosophy that teaches the way of perfecting metals above the earth <note>i.e., in the laboratory</note>, by the imitation of natural operations as closely as possible. We assert this to be true for various reasons, chiefly because there is nothing more certain among Philosophers than that truth resides where no contradiction appears, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts</note> testifies.

Moreover, as many as have written in this art in the past—whether in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or any other tongue—have agreed among themselves. Even if they used different methods of treatment through figures, ambiguous terms <note>original: "equivocationes"</note>, and riddles, they seem to have written in one and the same language and at the same time, even though some preceded others by a hundred, two hundred, or a thousand years. Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail al-Tamimi</note> says regarding this:
> Although it appears in a certain way that the Philosophers treat diverse things under various and different names, in truth they understand nothing but a single thing.
Rhasis <note>The Persian polymath Al-Razi (865–925 AD)</note> asserts the same in the *Book of Lights* <note>original: "libro Luminum"</note>, saying:
> Under different opinions, appearing to us at first glance as contrary, the Philosophers understood nothing but one and the same thing.
Testimony to this is provided by distinguished professors of other schools of thought, who, likewise writing on this divine art, affirm that this divine science revolves around one single thing.

The opinion of the Philosopher alone would suffice for us, which he states in the second book of the *Ethics*:
> Everything that is rightly performed is perfected by a single mean.
Therefore, it is the opinion of all that our divine work is completed by a single way. As Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note> testifies in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, or "The Sum of Perfection"</note>:
> Our science (he says) is not perfected through diverse things, but only through a single thing, to which we add nothing and from which we take nothing away, but only remove the superfluous...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the validity of alchemy as a science, moving from the difficulty of defining the art to the evidence of its success through experience and the authority of classical philosophy.</meta>

# THE WRITINGS OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS

...we achieve it, separating by preparation alone. Likewise, Lilius <note>likely referring to a work attributed to Raymond Lull, such as the *Lilium Alchimiae*</note> says: "Our mastery is perfected by one thing only, one regimen, and a single medium." All the Philosophers who have written on this art until now assert the same thing, even though they seem to be pulled in different directions. The greatest certainty of our science, by which we are confirmed that it is most true, is the **experience** we have gained of it, as Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabian alchemist</note> and Rhasis <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and alchemist</note> say. 

Truly, so that we may prove it to those who naturally have cause to doubt, we must admit with the other Philosophers that alchemy is contained under that part of philosophy called **operative philosophy**, and under medicine. Medicine cannot prove its own truth from any source other than experience. For instance, when it is taught that Rhubarb <note>used as a medicinal purgative since antiquity</note> purges bile, this can be perceived no better than through the eye and by experiment through the application of the said simple medicine. 

By a similar logic, we conclude in our art: if it is seen that Mercury is coagulated by the smoke of lead alone, and that a most perfect **medicine** <note>In alchemy, the "medicine" refers to the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir used to transform metals</note> can be made and composed from vitriols—one that is consistent with the nature and qualities of metals and through which other imperfect metals can be perfected simply by **projection** <note>the act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten metal to transform it into gold</note> performed upon them—especially since even compound minerals themselves can freeze Mercury and return it to its own nature. How much more will the perfect things, rightly prepared through our art, freeze it and restore it along with other imperfect metals through their immense and exuberant **decoction** <note>the process of "cooking" or heating the substance to reach maturity</note> which they possess through the administration of our art. 

To more firmly prove this intention of ours to curious men, so that they might better assent to its truth and certainty, let us bring forward the opinion of Aristotle from the fourth book of his *Meteorology*:

> Everything (he says) that performs the same operation as some compound is itself the same and similar in all respects; just as everything that has the function of an eye, is an eye. <note>original: "Omne, quod eandem cum aliquo composito operationem efficit, est idem per omnia simile, ut omne quod operationem habet oculi, est oculus."</note>

In no different a way, since our gold composed by our art is similar in all respects to the mineral gold (in which lies the whole controversy of the debate: whether the gold composed by us is true gold), we seem to have taught enough from the Philosopher's <note>referring to Aristotle</note> opinion that our art is true and most certain. This will be considered sufficiently proven to those who have seen its experience, though not to others. For those others, we shall bring forward more probable authorities of the Philosophers on this matter. In the same book of the *Meteorology*, in the fourth chapter on **Digestions**, he says this, or something similar:

> Whatever is intended for perfection, and remained in such a state [of imperfection] due to a defect of **digestion**, can be perfected by constant digestion. Such are all the imperfect metals, since they were first ordained by nature toward gold from the beginning of their composition, so that they might finally be brought to that end—namely, gold—by that same nature. They are only as they are because of imperfect digestion. <note>Aristotle's theory of metals suggested they all "strive" toward the perfection of gold within the earth, and alchemy merely accelerates this natural process</note>

Therefore, we shall hear what follows in that place where we discuss the fourth part of our division. What nature, therefore, wished to execute beneath the earth, we achieve above the earth by imitation through our art and projection,

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of alchemy against its critics, moving from the evidence of experience (as discussed on the previous page) to addressing the theoretical objections raised by classical philosophers like Aristotle and medieval authorities like Albertus Magnus.</meta>

-># A SHORT TREATISE<-

...we achieve, as will be heard more broadly below in the penultimate part of our division. Again, since the elements—which are contrary to each other in their qualities (as <term>the Philosopher</term><note>A common title for Aristotle among medieval and Renaissance scholars</note> says in the second book of *On Generation*)—can be converted into one another, how much more easily can the metals themselves be converted? For they are of one and the same substance and matter, and since they are not contrary in their qualities, they are converted from one into another most easily. For this reason, <term>Hermes</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> said that their procreation is circular—though in a somewhat improper way, as he himself admits, because they were not created by nature for the purpose of making perfect things into imperfect things, but the opposite. Therefore, their generation is not entirely circular, except in part.

Although these and similar reasons are sufficient in themselves to confirm the art, the <term>sophists</term><note>In this context, critics or those who use false logic to oppose alchemical truths</note> always bring forward arguments to the contrary that resist the truth. Unless we present those more difficult arguments—which disturb the heart and mind of students and keep them hanging between doubt and resolution—we will not be able to show how to refute others from their solutions. However, doing so for all arguments would be more long-winded than is appropriate for this little work of ours.

They argue thus from the authority of <term>the Philosopher</term> in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* (an authority likewise held by <term>Avicenna</term><note>The influential Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> and <term>Albertus Magnus</term><note>Albert the Great, a 13th-century German bishop and philosopher</note>): Alchemists labor in vain trying to perfect metals unless they reduce them into <term>prime matter</term><note>The original, formless substance from which all things are created</note>. Since they do not do this, the conclusion is reached that the works of all alchemists are deceptive, as Albert himself says in this manner: "Whosoever tints metals with various simple materials into different colors are impostors, unless they reduce them to prime matter."

Many most wise men have tried to solve this argument, as it is among the most apparent. Some of them say that although the imperfect metals are not reduced through <term>projection</term><note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" is cast upon molten base metal to transform it</note>, nevertheless a similar reduction occurs in the composition of the **medicine**—namely into **sulfur and quicksilver** <note>original: "sulphur & argentum vivum"; the two fundamental principles of metals in alchemical theory</note>, which are the true matter of metals, as will be discussed more broadly below in the fourth member of our division. Therefore, the reduction of the "agent" <note>the active substance or Stone</note> alone is sufficient, along with the supreme perfection acquired through <term>decoction</term><note>The process of heating or "cooking" the substance over a long period</note>, even if no reduction of the "passive" <note>the base metal being acted upon</note> occurs.

<term>Arnaldus de Villanova</term><note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> was of this opinion in his great *Rosary*, whom <term>Raymond Lull</term><note>A major 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> followed in his *Testament*. Yet, with all the peace and reverence due to such weighty authors, this opinion seems to contradict all the Philosophers too much. For when they concede that metals must be reduced to their prime matter—which occurs by the motion of <term>corruption</term><note>In Aristotelian physics, "corruption" is the destruction of one form so that a new one can emerge</note> according to Aristotle—they seem to believe that by the mere melting of our **divine stone** over the metals, these are corrupted in such a way as to be stripped of their first form. This is a point too unworthy for any Philosopher to concede. Many others offer different solutions, as can be seen in their books. I, however, shall put forth my own solution. If indeed we were striving to manufacture new metals, or stones from them, or anything...

He critiques the theories of earlier masters like Arnald of Villanova and Raymond Lull before beginning to offer his own resolution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of alchemy against its critics. It picks up from a discussion of Aristotle’s *Meteorology*, addressing the argument that metals must be returned to their "prime matter" (the basic building blocks of nature) before they can be changed.</meta>

<page-num>728</page-num>
->### OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIAS<-

...if the result were something else foreign to metals, they would necessarily have to be reduced to their first matter, and that by the means which have been mentioned. Since, however, our intention is only this: that we may perfect imperfect metals into gold—without any transformation into new materials that differ from their own nature—we purge and cleanse them through the <term>projection</term><note>The act of casting the "Philosopher's Stone" or medicinal powder onto molten base metal to transform it</note> of our divine work, so that they may arrive at an overflowing perfection. It is by no means necessary to reduce those metals to their first matter; for there is a great difference between perfecting the imperfect and producing or generating something entirely new from it. Otherwise, one would conclude that all half-cooked things must be reduced to their first form so that they might be completely <term>boiled</term><note>original: *decoquerentur*. In alchemy, "boiling" or "digestion" refers to the slow ripening of substances through heat, much like fruit ripening in the sun</note>—an idea indeed unworthy of any Philosopher.

I will set aside for the present other objections usually made against the chemical arts, because through the principles we have established, any other arguments can easily be solved. Regarding the authority of **Avicenna**<note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose writings were central to medieval science. He was famously skeptical of alchemists' ability to truly change the species of metals</note>, however, I remember what he wrote concerning the contradictions **Aristotle**<note>The Greek philosopher whose "four elements" theory formed the basis of alchemical physics</note> voiced against chemistry in his youth: "I recognized," he says, "the intention of those who deny our art, and of others who affirm it to be true." The former, such as Aristotle and many others, use certain arguments that appear true in name only. The latter, however, say that this science cannot or may not be proved by certain demonstrations like all others, since it proceeds by another way, contrary to all others. For it hides and veils the properties of its terms, while other sciences labor greatly to make their declarations clear.

Therefore, following the order of our division, I will take up its third part, explaining its necessary operations for the execution of our divine work. First, I will state the reason why it is called "natural" and "divine," so that the enormous errors of those working in these times may be known. **Aristotle** teaches that nature works under the earth in the procreation of metals with four qualities—or to be better understood, four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Two of these encompass the other two: earth encompasses fire, and water encompasses air. Since, therefore, our matter consists of water and of earth (as will be said more fully below in the penultimate part of our division), it is rightly called "natural," because the four elements enter into its composition: two are manifest, under which two others lie hidden, veiled from bodily eyes—namely fire and air—which must be perceived by the mind alone. 

As **Raymond Lull**<note>A 13th-century Majorcan polymath. Many alchemical texts were attributed to him in later centuries</note> says in his ***Codicillus***<note>A famous alchemical manual attributed to Lull</note>, in this manner: "Consider," he says, "the nature and property of the oil (which the <term>sophisticators</term><note>Those who use false logic or deceptive chemical methods</note> call 'air,' because they say it abounds more in its qualities); your eye will not judge its differences and properties." By these words, he sufficiently hints that the four elements in our divine work are not evident to the sight, as many have falsely thought, as will be discussed below where we shall define the terms of the art.

The science is also called "natural" because in its first operation it imitates

He refutes critics by explaining that alchemical processes mirror the hidden ways nature works underground.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that alchemy is a natural science. Having previously discussed the perfection of metals, he now moves to the specific methods—such as sublimation and dissolution—by which alchemists imitate the slow, internal processes of the Earth.</meta>

<page-num>729</page-num>
<header>SMALL TREATISE.</header>

...it imitates nature as diligently as it can; for they could not do so in all things, as **Geber**<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though "Geber" usually refers to a 13th-century European author writing under that name. His *Summa Perfectionis* was the most influential alchemical textbook in the West</note> says in his *Summa*. These things are best confirmed by the operations of the ancient natural Philosophers who preceded us. After they had learned through most diligent investigations—as **Raymond Lully** says in his letter to **King Albert**, and **Albertus Magnus**<note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop who was one of the greatest medieval scientists; he was often (though sometimes spuriously) credited with alchemical works</note> in his treatise on *Simple Animals*—that nature, for the procreation of metals, works only underground through continuous and steady <term>decoctions</term><note>In alchemy, "decoction" or "digestion" refers to the slow ripening of substances through heat, much like fruit ripening on a tree or food cooking in the stomach</note> of true matter. By these, nature separates the clean from the unclean, the pure from the impure, and the perfect from the imperfect through constant evaporations, caused partly by the heat of the mineral earth and partly by the heat of the Sun (which by itself does not complete this entire and perfect decoction).

The good **Trevisan**<note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist known for his long search for the Stone</note> declares this very well, and experience also teaches it to us: for we see in the mines a diversity of metals and materials—some coarser, and others subtler and purer, often lifted up to the heights. Therefore, our science, by imitating nature, proceeds in its first operation through <term>sublimation</term><note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then allowing it to solidify again. Alchemists used this to "spiritually" purify their materials</note>, by which it may best purify our matter. For it would be impossible for us to prepare it otherwise, as **Geber** in his *Summa* and **Rhazes** in the *Book of Lights* say: "The beginning of our work is to sublimate," which is why it is rightly called "natural." 

For this reason, those who preceded us wrote that this work of ours is not artificial. For whatever we do is nothing else than to provide to nature, through art, the matter necessary for the composition of the work—which nature herself could not join into this perfection because her actions are continuous, as **Geber** says in his *Summa*. By reason of this so wonderful joining of the elements, our science is called divine. Indeed, the Philosophers called this joining the "second operation," and some called it "dissolution," asserting it to be the secret of secrets, as **Pythagoras** says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*<note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate between ancient sages</note>: "This is a great mystery, which God willed to be veiled from men." 

Likewise, **Rhazes** in the *Book of Lights* says: "If you are ignorant of the true dissolution of our body, there is no reason for you to work; for if that is unknown, the rest will be useless." Indeed, no one can learn this from books, nor from the knowledge of natural causes; therefore it is truly called divine, as **Alexander** says. Our body (which is the hidden stone) can by no means be known, nor seen, unless God himself inspires this into us through His Holy Spirit, or teaches it through some living man, without whom our science is nothing. 

This is the stone of which **Hermes**<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" Egyptian founder of alchemy</note> speaks in his fourth treatise: "Our divine stone," he says, "is to be known, which cries out constantly: *Defend me, and I will help you; give me what is mine, and I in turn will best assist you.*"<note>original: "Defende me, & ego juvabo te, da mihi quod competit, ego tibi vicissim optime succurram." ...you: the Falcon is always crying on the mountain top: I am the white of the black, and the red of the yellow. <note>original: "Ego sum album nigri, & rubeum citrini." This is an allegorical riddle referring to the color changes of the alchemical matter: black (nigredo), white (albedo), yellow (citrinitas), and red (rubedo).</note> The reason our science is useless without this conjunction is that at the time of the birth and procreation of our divine work, the volatile part carries the fixed part away with it. For otherwise, except through this admirable and more than supernatural conjunction, we could in no way cause the work to remain fixed in the fire: so that, as all the Philosophers command, the fixed becomes volatile, and then the volatile becomes fixed. This conjunction must occur at the very hour of its birth, as **Haly** <note>Likely Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince credited with being one of the first Muslim alchemists.</note> says in the *Book of Secrets*:

> Whoever has not found our stone at the hour of its birth,
> there is no reason for him to expect another in its place.

For he who approaches our divine work without knowledge of the determined hour of its birth will never achieve anything from his work except entirely useless labors and the pains of his error. This same conjunction **Rasis** <note>The Latinized name of Al-Razi (Rhazes), a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and chemistry.</note> in the *Book of Precepts* properly calls the <term>weights of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "pondera Philosophorum." This refers not just to physical weight, but to the precise proportions and timing required for a successful reaction.</note> and the regimes, advising that we should utterly abstain from this divine work if we have not learned with the greatest exactness the weights, which the Philosophers have hidden before all other secrets, as is clear from their various writings. For where one might say that such a divine conjunction occurs on the seventh day, you will soon find another who asserts it is completed on the fortieth day; another on the hundredth; another toward the end of seven or nine months, as **Rasis** says; another at the end of a year, like **Rosinus** <note>A common Latinization of the name Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian alchemist.</note>; you will hardly be able to read two authors who agree on this matter.

Yet there is but one and the same limit, one single day, even one single and same hour, in which our conjunction must take place for its proper <term>decoction</term>. But because they vowed they would especially not reveal this secret, they intentionally wrote different time limits, although they agree among themselves when understanding the single one; once this is known, the rest is nothing else but <term>women's work and children's play</term> <note>original: "opus mulierum & puerorum ludus." This famous alchemical phrase implies that once the initial difficult preparation is achieved, the final stage requires nothing more than the simple, patient tending of a fire, much like domestic chores or simple games.</note>, as **Socrates** says. Behold, I have shown you the true arrangement of white lead (that is, the true preparation of our matter, which first appears black like lead, and afterwards becomes white through our continued cooking); if you have understood this well <unclear>x</unclear>, the rest is nothing else but women's work and children's play. He hints by these words that no work exists lighter than ours after the conjunction; which is indeed most true. Since there is no need for any labor other than the simple cooking of the two matters already joined: while they are cooking, the most desired rest is granted, as the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> says in the *Ethics*, Book 7: Rest is far more delightful than any labor. That our final cooking is done with rest <unclear>e</unclear>, and without labor or torment, **Rasis** testifies in the *Book of Three Words*, saying: All di<unclear>ss</unclear>olutions, calcinations, sublimations, whitening, reddening, and the rest of the operations which the Philosophers wrote were necessary for the divine...

...our work is to be completed, it occurs in the fire without removal. <note>original: "praeter amotionem" – meaning the vessel should not be taken off the heat until the process is finished.</note> **Pythagoras** in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," a famous early alchemical text where ancient Greek philosophers are depicted as debating alchemy.</note> asserts the same, saying:

**Barseus** says the very same in that same book:
> One must cook, dye, and calcine in this work, but truly all operations are to be perfected by decoction alone.

Lest the <term>Sophists</term> <note>Here referring to fraudulent or misguided alchemists who use false logic.</note> and detractors say that their operations are also nothing but decoctions, we shall cite other opinions of the ancient Philosophers by which their errors may be exposed. **Alphidius** says:
> In the composition of our divine work, there is nothing but one matter alone (which they properly call "water") and only one action, namely decoction, which is done in a single vessel without removal from the fire.

For now, I shall remain silent regarding the "separations of elements" (as they call them) until I treat the nature of the four elements in the section where I will speak on the terms of our art. It shall be enough for me at present to have demonstrated the manner and way of uncovering and recognizing the straying workers in this art, as well as those who persist on the right path. For, as I said before and will be said more extensively below, there is only one mode of operating: in a single vessel (which **Lullius** called the <term>Hymen</term>), <note>A reference to the "marriage" or union of the chemical substances.</note> in a single furnace (which **Trevisanus** calls a closed, moist, vaporous, continuous, and digesting fire), without removal, until the decoction is completed. Likewise, **Rasis** in his *Book of the Perfect Mastery* says that bodies and spirits are prepared by various...

...to be prepared by intermediate means, many of which he teaches. We have previously answered sufficiently that these and similar things written by the Philosophers were for no other reason than to veil and conceal the true preparation of our divine work from the unworthy. **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century figure considered the father of Arabic chemistry/alchemy.</note> attests to this in his *Summa*, in the chapter on the differences of Medicines, saying: 
> There is but one perfect way by which we are relieved from such great operations and burdens of preparations. 

Now I shall set forth nature's mode of operation in generating metals within the cavities of the earth, which art ought to imitate; and thereafter, I shall declare the true and necessary matter for their perfection above the earth. Since this is the principal point in the art (as **Geber** says at the beginning of his *Summa*, and **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational in Europe.</note>, both instructing those who do not first know the true foundations of matters and minerals to abstain from the practice of this work), I will imitate the more excellent and skilled authors in minerals by declaring those things which are especially necessary to this matter.

It is therefore the opinion of all Philosophers that everything congealed by cold abounds greatly in watery humidity in its primary matter, as **Aristotle** says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*. Since, therefore, molten metals are congealed by cold, their primary matter must necessarily abound in much aquatic humidity. However, **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century German bishop and philosopher who wrote extensively on nature and minerals.</note> (who examined minerals more exactly than others) says that this watery humidity is not like the humidity of water which we commonly see in other natural compounds. For the latter turns into smoke through the violence of fire. But molten metals are not reduced to vapor in this way; hence it must be concluded that their humidity is mixed with some matter by which they are retained in the fire and are safe from its vehemence. 

Nothing resists fire more than <term>viscous humidity</term> <note>A sticky, thick moisture that doesn't easily evaporate, thought to be the binding force in metals.</note> mixed with the subtler parts of the earth, as **Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Petrus Bonus, author of the *Precious Pearl*, a major 14th-century alchemical work.</note> says and experience teaches; wherefore it is firmly to be believed that the humidity of metals is of such a kind. Yet, since experience shows that during purification some humidities depart in smoke while the metals are nonetheless not consumed in the fire, one must admit, with the principal authors of our science, that a double viscous humidity enters into the composition of metals: extrinsic and intrinsic. 

The former is thick and not well mixed with its subtle earthly matter, which is why it is easily burnt and consumed by fire. But the latter, because it is extremely subtle and perfectly mixed with its subtle earthly part so that both parts constitute a single and simple matter, can neither be separated from the other by fire nor consumed, unless they both depart together or remain together in the fire. From humidity of this kind is procreated the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum" – literally "living silver," the liquid metal mercury, which alchemists believed was the base of all metals.</note> that we see, as is also evident by experiment. **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> testifies: 
> This (he says) makes us more certain that both previously mentioned matters are most perfectly joined in it; for either the earthly part retains the humidity with itself, or the latter carries the former away...

He introduces the concept of intrinsic and extrinsic moisture to explain why metals resist fire, identifying quicksilver as the key substance.</summary>

# LITTLE WORK #

into the air. Indeed, **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential philosopher who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note>, most diligently investigating the causes of the composition of metals, understood this best: namely, that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is in constant motion and flow because each of its parts alternately holds dominion over the other. Thus, the cause of its flux and motion is the command of humidity, while the action of terrestrial dryness upon that humidity ensures that it does not stick to what it touches, nor does it make things wet. Hence, Albert’s opinion is confirmed in his book *On Minerals*: "The primary matter," he says, "of metals is an incombustible viscous humidity, joined by a strong mixture with a subtle earthiness in the mineral cavities of the earth."

This agrees perfectly with **Geber**, who asserts in his *Summa* that the true matter of metals is quicksilver, because, he says, "nature, never idle, procreated quicksilver from the said mixed matter," and so forth. **Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemist known for his work *The New Pearl of Great Price*.</note> says that quicksilver is the proximate matter of metals, but specifically a viscous humidity mixed with its subtle earthiness. Geber also provides this definition of quicksilver in his *Summa*: "It is," he says, "a viscous humidity condensed by the aid of its terrestrial part, which enters into its composition."

Let us therefore consider diligently the progress of nature in the procreation of all things, into which she mixes a proper matter which the Philosophers called the "agent," because it does not produce itself—as **Aristotle** says: that is, it does not demonstrate its own effects. Therefore, in the procreation of metals, after nature has created the matter (that is, quicksilver), she acts with great wisdom and joins to it a proper agent: namely, a certain species of mineral earth, like its **colostrum** <note>The "first milk" produced by mammals; here used as a metaphor for a rich, nourishing substance.</note> and fatness in the mineral cavities of the earth, thickened by a long **decoction** <note>A process of heating or "cooking" within the earth over long periods of time.</note>. This we commonly call **sulfur**; in comparison to quicksilver, it is like rennet to milk, or a male to a female, or an agent to the matter subjected to it.

The Philosophers have posited two types of sulfur: one that melts very easily, and another that is only congealed and cannot be melted. Accordingly, so that nature might demonstrate the power and efficacy of the agent (that is, the sulfur) upon the matter to which it is joined, she brings about a wonderful composition so that metals are congealed by the action of *fusible* sulfur, so that they might be capable of being melted. However, she composed other simple minerals by the action of *non-fusible* sulfur, so that they would not be meltable; such are **magnesia**, **marcasites** <note>Iron pyrites or similar "fool's gold" minerals.</note>, and others of that kind.

Since, however, the agent cannot be the material part of the compound (as Aristotle says), nature, procreating metals beneath the earth, after she has mixed the said sulfur with quicksilver in an inexpressible composition, generates therefrom the most precious metal, namely **gold**. In gold, she separates her agent (the sulfur) from it through a perfect decoction. And this is the reason why it is more perfect than all other metals, and why we see that nature does not transmute it further into anything better. Likewise, for this reason, it is joined better and more easily to quicksilver, because it is nothing else...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the composition of metals, specifically the role of sulfur as a cause of imperfection and the need for its removal to achieve "perfect" gold.</meta>

than **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> decocted <note>Decoction refers to the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or ripen it.</note> by its own sulfur, and thereafter entirely separated from it by the said decoction. Just as the separation of sulfur is the perfection of gold, its remaining in other metals is the primary cause of their imperfection. From this it follows that silver is less perfect than gold, and copper less so than silver: namely, due to a lack of complete digestion, by which alone the "agent" is separated from them—that is, sulfur. In this is declared the greatest and chief secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of our whole art. Since art must imitate nature in its operations, it is necessary, before this divine work of ours is perfected, that its agent or sulfur be separated. All the **Philosophers** <note>A term for alchemists who sought the "philosophy" or hidden laws of nature.</note> have hidden this, sending us back in their books to the natural operations, which I have explained sufficiently.

To understand more perfectly, however, how our science imitates nature's operations, it will be worthwhile to declare the chief and more common way she uses in the perfection of metals. We previously said that the perfection or imperfection of metals occurs due to the removal or mixing of the agent—that is, sulfur—and we showed the first way nature is accustomed to use in the composition of the "prince of metals" and the most perfect, namely gold. Now it must be known that she also uses another progression, which although it may seem contrary to the first, is nonetheless very similar, if the end toward which the intention of nature tends is rightly considered, which is nothing other than to cleanse the metals and thoroughly purge them of their sulfur.

For that which she achieves in the first way through perfect decoction, she accomplishes in the second through continuous and long digestions, by gradually purifying the imperfect ones until they are reduced to gold. Since experience teaches us that lead is commonly found in silver mines, and in some both are mixed together, so that silver seems almost imperfect because of a lack of digestion; therefore those skilled in mining affairs <note>original: "metallicarium periti"</note> advise that, once the caverns are sealed so that the more sublime materials cannot evaporate, they be left for thirty or forty years until they are perfected.

**Albertus Magnus** records that this happened in his time in the kingdom of **Liburnia** or **Sclavonia** <note>Liburnia was a region on the Adriatic coast; Sclavonia refers to Slavonia, a historical region in modern-day Croatia.</note>; likewise, it was reported to me by an experienced mineral digger that this happens quite often. Therefore, according to this method which nature uses in perfecting metals, art imitates her in its operations to perfect the imperfect—namely by the removal of its sulfur, achieved through the **projection** <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" is cast upon molten base metal to transform it.</note> of the divine work upon them after they have been melted. By this, they are purified from their said sulfur and perfected into pure gold, by its perfect and overflowing decoction which it acquired through the administration of our art. In no other way do the various modes nature uses in the purification of metals result in different forms of gold (at least in its perfection), and likewise the modes we [use...]
