<meta>This page continues the argument that alchemical art must perfectly mirror natural processes. It transitions from the previous discussion on the separation of sulfur to the specific materials required for the "Great Work," emphasizing that alchemists must use the same "animated" quicksilver that nature uses in the earth.</meta>

### LITTLE TREATISE

### THE SMALL WORK

Although we employ various ways of perfecting this work upon the earth, our gold is not rendered different from natural or mineral gold. This is because we use the same material above the ground that nature uses beneath the earth and within its caverns. Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements and the "motive cause" underpinned medieval alchemy.</note> attests to this very fact in the ninth book of the *Metaphysics*.

"From a similar agent and matter," he says, "the operations are always similar, even though the environments <note>original: "media"</note> are different; for these and the matter are two distinct things." Truly, if the matter is one and the same in every way with the agent, all operations—which at the start appear dissimilar or even contrary—will obtain the same effect in the end. To prove that our material, which we use to perfect metals above the ground, is in all ways very similar to that which nature uses in the caverns of the earth for their procreation, we cite **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary figure in alchemy. Most Latin texts of this era attributed to him were actually written by a 13th-century European author known as Pseudo-Geber.</note> as a witness in his *Summa* <note>original: "Summa Perfectionis Magisterii," one of the most influential alchemical textbooks.</note>: "Our Art," he says, "imitates nature as closely and as possibly as it can." **Hermes**, **Pythagoras**, **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century philosopher Ibn Umayl.</note>, and many others say the same. Furthermore, if art imitates nature, it must necessarily be admitted that it uses a similar material to nature. In both cases, this can only be one thing, which we have called **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>—not merely by itself, but mixed together with its own proper agent, namely true **sulfur**. Therefore, this same material, which the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to the alchemical masters of antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> called "animated quicksilver," will be the true material of our divine science for completing our divine work. Nature uses this very thing, and no other, in the hollows of the earth for the procreation of metals as its true material, as we have already demonstrated sufficiently above.

They called it "animated quicksilver" <note>This suggests mercury that has been "quickened" or given a soul/life by being combined with the masculine principle of sulfur.</note> to show the difference between it and common quicksilver. The latter remained common because nature did not join its proper agent to it. Therefore, many have falsely believed that common quicksilver and common sulfur are the material of metals. For it has never happened at any time that those two were found mixed together in the mines; by what reasoning, then, could they be the true material of metals in the cavities of the earth, or of our art above the ground? As **Geber** speaks in his *Summa* regarding the principles of the art: "Our quicksilver," he says, "is nothing else than a viscous water, wedded by the action of its own metallic sulfur." This is our true material, which nature has prepared for our art (as **Valerandus Sylvensis** says) and reduced into a specific form known to true Philosophers, without any further transmutation of itself. **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and natural philosophy were foundational to European science.</note> similarly says: "Nature has prepared for us one single material, which our art is quite unable to compose on its own." It would be foolish, therefore, to believe that out of all the materials we might mix—even if they were metallic or any other kind—any could be the true material of our science, since nature has prepared it for us so that nothing is lacking except these two things: namely, to purify it and to perfect it.

It cites authorities like Geber and Avicenna to prove that the alchemist's role is not to create new matter, but to purify and perfect the material nature has already provided.</summary>

<page-num>736</page-num>
<header>THE WORKS OF DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS</header>

...to finish and join together through its own appropriate and congruent decoction <note>A process of "cooking" or heating a substance in its own moisture to achieve maturation.</note>. Regarding this material, **Rasis** <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD), a Persian physician and alchemist known for his systematic classification of chemical substances.</note> speaks in the *Book of Precepts*: "Our Mercury," he says, "is the true foundation of our science, from which the true tinctures of metals are extracted." **Alphidius** <note>An elusive alchemical author, likely of Arabic origin, frequently cited in medieval Latin compendiums.</note> says of the same: "Observe, my son, that the whole work of the wise Philosophers consists in quicksilver alone: wherefore **Hermes** commands us to watch this Mercury, which he calls 'coagulated' and 'hidden in gilded hiding places.'" **Geber** says of the same Mercury: "Praised be," he says, "the Most High who created this quicksilver and gave it incomparable power to perfectly accomplish the mastery of our science." In short, there was no writer among the wise who was not of the same opinion.

Modern operators will object, judging me reckless for daring to rebuke so many and such great predecessors whose theory and practice teach how to sublimate quicksilver (which they call Mercury) with vitriol <note>A term for various sulfate minerals; "oil of vitriol" is sulfuric acid. It was used as a corrosive agent to "cleanse" or transform metals.</note> and common salt, and afterwards to revivify it with hot water, so that it may finally be mixed with gold (which they called the **Sun**) and in this manner to dissolve and fix it, by which our divine work is completed. This is what **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> writes in his *Great Rosary*; likewise **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher. Many alchemical works were attributed to him posthumously.</note> in his *Testament*.

To answer them sufficiently, let it be enough to use the same authors they cite, whose writings testify that all those operations—distillations, separations of elements, reductions, and other things of that kind—were set down for no other reason than to veil the practice of our science under such masks <note>original: "larvis"</note>. We shall cite the same Arnaldus de Villanova, who after teaching those various operations in his *Rosary*, bursts forth near the end of his recapitulation in these or similar words: "We have shown," he says, "the true practice and the true way of completing our divine work, but in very brief words, which nevertheless will seem long enough to those who understand." Therefore, by so many and such diverse and long discourses on operations, he did not mean the true preparation of this divine work, nor the practice, which he said he had treated before in brief. 

Raymond says this same thing at the end of his *Codicil*, where he answers those who might perhaps ask why he described the art when he had previously said it was impossible for anyone to arrive at this art and its true knowledge by reading books. "So that," he responds, "the faithful reader may be introduced and acquire a habit by which he may arrive at a true knowledge of our divine work, the preparation of which we never sincerely set down, nor openly declared." It is clear, therefore, that the lengthy and diverse preparations of that kind which he teaches in his books are not the sole and unique practice of our divine work. Those who are a little more learned will object to me, asking why I have written that our divine work is made from one single material, namely...

<header>SMALL TREATISE</header>

...though it comes from a single and sole animated quicksilver <term>argentum vivum animatum; quicksilver that has been "awakened" or prepared for alchemical work</term>, even if **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, though the *Summa Perfectionis* cited here is likely by a 13th-century European author known as Pseudo-Geber.</note> says in the *Summa* <note>original: *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, one of the most influential alchemical textbooks of the Middle Ages.</note>, in the chapter on the coagulation of Mercury, that it is extracted from metallic bodies prepared with their arsenic. **Rosinus** <note>An Arab-Latin alchemical authority, often identified with Zosimos of Panopolis.</note>, on the other hand, says it is a true, incombustible sulfur, from which our divine work consists. **King Solomon**, the son of David, attests to this very thing, saying:

> God has preferred our true sulfur above all things existing under heaven.

**Pythagoras**, in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, an ancient Latin text where various Greek philosophers are depicted debating alchemical principles.</note>, wrote:

> Our divine work is perfected when sulfurs are joined to one another in turn, one with the other; therefore, it consists of sulfurs and not from animated quicksilver alone.

To provide an answer that might satisfy those minds wandering from the path, we must recall what we said above regarding the matter of metals: specifically, that nature, in the hollows of the earth, joins a proper active agent to quicksilver. Furthermore, because our divine work has no proper name of its own, different men have given it different titles; as **Lilius** <note>Likely referring to the author of the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical text.</note> wrote, it is called by as many names among the Philosophers as there are things created in this world—implying by these words that it is called by infinite names, even though it is always one and the same thing, consisting of a single material alone. Nevertheless, the Philosophers who came before us imposed so many and such various names upon it according to their own judgment, based on the variety of colors appearing during the decoction <term>the "cooking" or maturation of the alchemical substance through heat</term>.

Those who, like us, have called it "animated quicksilver," considered our first matter (which the ancient Philosophers called **Chaos**, taking its beginning from the very start of things) to be truly similar in every way to the nature and substance of quicksilver, from which nature composes and perfects metals in the hollows of the earth, as we demonstrated above. Likewise, those who called our divine work the **Philosophers' Stone** (which is its common name) did so out of respect for the end of the decoction of our material; for it remains "fixed" in the fire, and they are accustomed to call "stone" whatever does not flee the fire and is not sublimated <term>the process of a solid turning into vapor when heated</term> by it. Many others devised many other names according to their own reasons, which would be tedious to recount individually. As **Malvascindus** <note>Another authority cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says:

> If we say our matter is spiritual, it is true; if corporeal, we do not lie; if celestial, that is its true name; if terrestrial, we do not speak improperly.

From these words, it is clearly evident that the variety of names imposed by our ancient predecessors upon our divine work was based on different reasons, stemming from the diversity of colors and operations appearing during its decoction.

In the same way, those who called it "sulfur" (as attested by the authorities that could be brought against me) spoke thus with respect to the final decoction, in which the matter appears fixed. Thus, while in the beginning it showed the true appearance of quicksilver because it was volatile <term>likely to evaporate or change state easily</term>, in the end it is fixed; then at last the hidden and inward...

<page-num>738</page-num>
<header>DIONYSIUS ZACHARIAS</header>

...the part that exists [as a base] was unknown, namely the fixed part which we call sulfur; it is made manifest by the continued and final decoction <term>decoctio; a process of heating or "digesting" a substance in a sealed vessel until it matures</term>, in which it rules over the volatile part. For this reason, our material is no longer called "volatile" (I speak of those who consider the final decoction), but finally **fixed sulfur**, as **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist; his *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a seminal alchemical text.</note> says in his *Great Rosary* when speaking of the final decoction of our divine work:

> "It is," he says, "true red sulfur, through which quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> can be perfected into gold."

Therefore, we can truly conclude and resolve every doubt: the material from which we compose our divine work is but one single thing in all aspects, and in every way similar to that material which nature uses in the hollows of the earth for the creation of metals—notwithstanding all the authorities cited above to the contrary, or any others like them. For a diversity of names (as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose physics and logic formed the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note> says) does not make the thing itself diverse. 

To gradually bring our division to an end, it remains for us to declare the terms of our science; that is, let us compare the opinions of the best and most distinguished authors who came before us. They use four principal terms among others when discussing the composition of our divine work: the four elements, the <term>fermentum perfectum; "perfect ferment," an agent that "leavens" or transforms the base metal into gold</term>, the <term>venenum verum; "true poison," a term for the potent, transformative power of the alchemical substance</term>, and the <term>coagulum perfectum; "perfect coagulum," a substance that curdles or solidifies the liquid "mercury"</term>, which they have elsewhere called the "male" in comparison to the "female," much like rennet is compared to simple milk. 

To better explain what they mean by the "elements," one must know what the Natural Philosophers said about the "first matter," which they called <term>Chaos</term>. In this, those four elements were contained in a confused state; because of their contrary natures, they became manifest to us by demonstrating their specific actions. For this reason, **Alexander** <note>Likely referring to a pseudonymous alchemical author attributed to Alexander the Great.</note> says in his *Epistle*:

> "Whatever," he says, "was shown by the ancients to be of a hot quality, they judged to be fire; what was dry and solidified was earth; what appeared to them moist and flowing, they called water; and what was seen to be cold, subtle, and windy, they called air."

Two of these are hidden and enclosed within the other two, as **Rasis** <note>The Latinized name of the Persian polymath Al-Razi (c. 865–925).</note> says in his *Book of Precepts*:

> "Every compound," he says, "consists of the four elements, with two hidden in the other two apparent ones: namely, air in the secret part of water, and fire in the interior of the earth, as we said before."

And because the two enclosed elements cannot demonstrate their actions except through the other two, they called them "weak," while the others they called "strong." For this reason, they say compounds are perfect when the moist and the dry—that is, water and earth—are joined equally by the help of nature with the cold and the hot—which are air and fire—through the conversion of one into the other. Wherefore **Alexander** says in the *Book of Secrets*:

> "If you convert the elements one into another, you will find what you seek."

This opinion, when well and perfectly understood, demonstrates to us...

<header>A SHORT TREATISE.</header>
<sig>Aaa 2</sig>

It shows the true matter and indicates the perfect practice of our science. Therefore, so that it may be better understood, we must speak more closely of the four elements and their nature, since they are necessary in the composition of our divine work. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says: "In our earth, all other elements are created." **Alphidius** <note>An influential Arabic alchemical authority, often cited in medieval Latin texts.</note> on the other hand, puts forward that water is the chief element, from which the other elements required for the composition of our divine work were created. In these statements, as it appears, there is no contradiction. For from the beginning of the procreation of our divine work, nothing else appears than water alone, which the Philosophers have called **Mercurial water** <note>original: *Mercurialem aquam*; the "living" solvent or prime matter of the work, not common quicksilver.</note>, from which the earth was procreated when it was thickened by a supernatural conjunction and decoction <term>decoctio; the process of heating a substance in a sealed vessel until it matures</term>, other than which it is useless to us. Hence, Hermes spoke truly when he said the remaining elements were produced from the earth, since the earth alone demonstrates its qualities in the second operation, just as the water demonstrated its own in the beginning of the work. Therefore, **Alphidius** wrote to Valerandus and others that it [water] is the chief element in the composition of our divine work.

These are those two elements that the Philosophers say must be known before we undertake the work. As **Rasis** <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian physician and chemist whose works were foundational to Western alchemy.</note> says in his *Book of Lights* <note>original: *libró Luminum*</note>: "Before the work is begun," he says, "the nature and quality of **water** and **earth** must be known, because in these two the four elements are contained; otherwise, the volatile will carry the fixed away with it, and our science will be useless to us." For this reason, the conversion of the four elements is commanded, so that our divine work, properly qualified, may be fixed at the end, and so it may be able to resist every violence of fire, the corruption of air, the rust <note>original: *ærugini*; here implying elemental decay or oxidation</note> of earth, and the putrefaction of water, not otherwise than mineral gold, on account of its great perfection. This conversion of the elements (as **Raymundus Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical texts were later attributed to him.</note> says) is nothing else than making the earth (which is fixed) volatile, and making the water (which is moist and volatile) dry and fixed. This is properly achieved by our continued decoction in our vessel, without any removal or opening, lest perhaps our elements perish and fly away into the air as smoke.

The writings of **Rasis** and various other Philosophers attest to this same sentiment when they say that the true separation and conjunction of the four elements takes place in our vessel without being touched by hands or feet; because (as they say) our **stone** <term>lapis noster; the Philosopher's Stone in its developing stages</term> dissolves, coagulates, washes, purges, whitens, and reddens itself, without the addition or mixing of any external thing.

**Arnaldus de Villa Nova** is of the same opinion in his *Great Rosary* <note>original: *Rosario magno*</note>, when he says in very few words: "There is no need for any other labor than in slaying the water, that is, fixing it; for immediately..."

It emphasizes that the entire process of elemental transformation happens autonomously within a sealed vessel.</summary>

and this will be dead, for the remaining elements have been killed, that is, fixed <note>original: *fixata*; in alchemy, to "fix" a substance means to make it solid and resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates or escapes as vapor.</note>. Therefore, the deceptive separations of the elements performed by the practitioners of these times are false; they are most poorly grounded in the writings of those Philosophers who expressly forbid the destruction of simple substances in their preparations because (as they say) it is impossible for art to provide the primary forms. It is most certain that the four elements cannot be composed unless they are first destroyed. For this reason, there is no need for this deceptive and false separation of elements for the composition of the divine work. That such a separation is false is proved by what was said before: namely, that two elements are contained within the other two. As a result, we are least able to know their true separation, and much less their perfect conjunction. Experience proves that the elements which they claim to have separated have nothing in common with the nature of the true elements (as **Valerandus** <note>likely referring to a contemporary or near-contemporary alchemical author often cited alongside Zachaire</note> says). Let their "oil" be an example, which they call "air"; it moistens and wets everything it touches, which is contrary to the true nature of air.

Therefore, it shall be enough for me to have shown the nature and quality of the elements, and their conversion which is necessary in this our science, so that the ignorance of the science among modern practitioners may be made plain to the true sons of art, and so that, recognizing them, they may flee from their company. Now let us see what the Philosophers understand by this term, namely, **ferment** <note>original: *fermentum*; just as yeast or leaven transforms dough into bread, alchemical "ferment" is the substance that triggers the transformation of the "matter" into the final Philosopher's Stone.</note>. They say they have used it in two ways. In the first sense, they make a comparison of our divine work to metals: just as we see a little bread ferment transform a large amount of flour into its own nature and dough, so too our divine work converts metals into its own nature; and because it is gold, it transmutes them also into gold. Truly, because they have rarely used it in this sense (in which there is no difficulty), we shall come to the second sense, in which the greatest difficulty of our science lies.

By "ferment," therefore, in the second way, they understand the true body and the true matter which completes our divine work. This is indeed unknown to the eyes and is something perceptible only by the intellect. For from the beginning, our matter appears volatile <note>original: *volatilis*; a substance that easily evaporates or turns to gas when heated.</note> (as we have sufficiently declared before), which we must join to its own proper body, so that by this means it may retain its soul. By means of this already-made conjunction, and through the mediation of the spirit, it demonstrates its divine operations in our divine work, as is read in the <term>Turba Philosophorum</term> <note>The "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate between ancient sages.</note> in this very manner: "The Body has more strength than its two brothers, whom they call Spirit and Soul." Not that they understand this in the way that <term>Aristoteles</term> <note>Aristotle, the Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements provided the scientific foundation for medieval alchemy.</note> and other Philosophers declared (which is very worthy of note), but they called "Body" every simple substance which by its own nature can endure fire without any loss; this they otherwise call "fixed." They called "Soul" every simple substance that is by itself volatile...

volatile, having the power to carry the body away with itself and bear it up from the fire: they have called this by another name, the "volatile." They say that **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*; in alchemy, the "spirit" is the volatile substance that mediates between the fixed body and the active soul</note> is that which has the power of retaining the body and the soul, and of joining those two together so closely that they can no longer be separated, whether they be perfect or imperfect. The second reason concerns the **Mercury** (which we call the mercurial water) because this poison slaughters and fixes it <note>The "poison" kills the "living" or volatile quality of the Mercury, making it solid or "fixed."</note>. For it works the same in the body of metals as theriaca does in ours. Although even what they have written can be adapted to the joining of the perfect ferment, when the determined hour has come, because through it our divine work is perfected. Similar authorities, therefore, ought to be understood in an **allegorical sense** <note>original: *allegorico sensu*</note>, and not by the appearance of the letter, which many have falsely estimated.

Of this kind is the interpretation of the last term, which is more commonly used but less understood; for the greater part of people understand by it our divine work when it is perfected. They say it is no different than how a little **rennet** <note>original: *coaguli*; the substance used to curdle milk into cheese</note> congeals a great deal of milk; so a tiny amount of our matter projected upon **quick-silver** <note>original: *vivum argentum*; Mercury</note> congeals it and brings it to its own proper nature. But they are deceived, wandering from the truth: for by this they conclude that our matter cannot be compared to metals, because they are already congealed.

Accordingly, it must be known that when our Mercury appears simple, it is flowing; the Philosophers have called this **milk** <note>original: *lac*</note>, and they call its **rennet** that which we called above the ferment, poison, and theriaca. Because, just as rennet does not differ from milk except by a little boiling <note>original: *decoctione*; the process of heating</note>, so our rennet does not differ from our Mercury, except by the boiling which it acquired beforehand. This is the great and supernatural secret, because of which the Philosophers have said our science is **divine**: because human reasonings fail in it, as we have related above. This is the rennet which **Hermes** called the **flower of gold** <note>original: *florem auri*</note>, of which they wish to be understood when they say:

> In the congealing of the spirit, the true dissolution of the body is achieved; and conversely, in the dissolution of the body, the true congealing of the spirit is achieved.

Because by its medium the whole work is perfected, as **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemist</note> says:

> When I saw our water (that is, our Mercury) congeal by itself, I firmly believed our science to be true.

# LITTLE TREATISE

Alexander states that in our science, nothing is created except that which is made from **male and female**. He calls our **thickener** <note>original: *coagulum*; the agent that solidifies a liquid</note> the **male**, which is the principle that acts. The Philosophers have attributed action to the male and passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed.</note> to the **female**, which they say is our **Mercury**, precisely because the aforementioned thickener acts upon it, demonstrating its power. For this reason, they said the female has wings, because our Mercury is simple and volatile, yet it is held back by the aforementioned thickener. Therefore, they wrote:

> Make the female ascend over the male, and afterwards the male over the female,

meaning the same thing found in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>:

> Our King and his wife the Queen are to be honored, and the most diligent care must be taken that they are not burned,

that is, lest our **cooking** <note>original: *decoctio*; the process of heating the substance over a long period</note> be accelerated. For, as **Arnold of Villanova** says in his *Great Rosary* <note>original: *Rosario*; a famous 14th-century alchemical work</note>:

> The chief error in the practice of our divine work is an accelerated or hurried cooking.

The ancient Philosophers used similar and various terms in their writings, and because these which we have explained are the most important, we shall put an end to the interpretations of terms. Indeed, once these are properly known, the true matter cannot remain unknown, and thereafter the books of the Philosophers are made easy, as the good **Bernard of Treviso** <note>original: *Trevisanus*; a 15th-century alchemist known for his search for the Philosopher's Stone</note> says. 

It must be concluded, therefore, with all the Philosophers—whose writings I have hitherto reduced into the best order I could—that there is only **one single matter** from which our divine work is fulfilled. For it is composed solely of simple Mercury (which the Philosophers called **Mercurial water** in their own specific term, without any ambiguity) thickened by the action of its own **sulfur** (which **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> specifically called the **flower of gold**). This matter, through our long and continuous cooking, has acquired such great and excellent perfection that this work of ours is able to transmute all imperfect metallic bodies to which it is joined by **projection** <note>The act of throwing the alchemical "powder" or "elixir" onto molten base metal</note> into pure and unadulterated gold similar to that from a mine. This is done for the various reasons previously deduced and cited, by which we have sufficiently declared how it happens that imperfect metals are perfected by it.

Since, in any case, no simple things that are different or contrary in qualities can be joined or perfectly mixed together, our divine work—because it is fashioned solely from **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*</note>—can in no way suffer a union with the sulfur that remains in imperfect metals due to a defect in their "digestion," as we noted above. But in truth, since the work is most powerful and perfected by the highest digestion, it separates the said sulfur from the metals and perfects the quicksilver that remains in them into gold. It is proven by experiment: when we make a **projection** of it upon common quicksilver, we find it almost entirely converted into gold. We see it achieve the opposite when projected upon metals:

## THIRD PART OF THE LITTLE TREATISE OF DIONYSIUS
## Zacharius, on the Practice of the divine work.

The **WHOLE** earth is divided by Philosophers and **Cosmographers** <term>Cosmographers: scholars who mapped the general features of the universe and the earth</term> into three principal parts: into Asia, Africa, and Europe, situated under four quarters or regions: East, West, South, and North, and under the dominion of various Emperors, Kings, Princes, and powerful Lords. Each of these possesses various and diverse things as delights, both on account of their rarity and their singular value. This latter cause is not as pleasing as the former, as I have learned from experience while traveling through various and adverse regions. Indeed, where there was a crowd of learned men, there (to my great misfortune) I saw the very wise to be miserable and cast down, while on the contrary, the most ignorant were very rich and held in the highest esteem. 

But where there was a scarcity of learned and skilled men, even though the greatest part were utterly ignorant and unfit, in this place the wise were especially honored by all, and particularly I noticed they were pursued with the highest favor and greatest respect by the elders. No differently does the lack of wealth and minerals (from which gold and other metals are communicated to us) in those places where they are not found, create the greatest estimation of them, just as abundance brings with it a contempt for that which is held in great supply by the wealthy. Indeed, those viler things of no price, having nothing of perfection except appearance, have always blinded their eyes, so that they did not recognize the perfect and precious things. 

Wherefore the wise, being indignant when they see the ignorant preferred, betake themselves elsewhere, deliberating how to demonstrate the strength and power of their wisdom in other places. This was once done by a certain magnanimous **Governor** <note>In this allegory, the Governor likely represents the central active principle or "Seed" of the alchemical work.</note>, proposing never to cease until he had subjected the remaining part of the world, beyond his own which he possessed, to himself by the protection of his troops, and especially by the counsel of his faithful **steward** <note>original: *œconomi*; in alchemy, this often represents a catalyst or a specific salt that manages the chemical reactions</note>. Meanwhile, while he was turning these things over in his mind, he joined to himself various and diverse strangers, who, because they were not at all faithful, thought they would be more liberally received by Emperors, Kings, and other Princes. Therefore (as scouts are wont to do) they defected from him, and made public to them his...

The Emperor had brought fifty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry, and innumerable engines of war. Had they not immediately crossed the river and provided for themselves and their Prince by breaking the bridges, the greatest danger would have hung over them; yet they all escaped the hands of their enemies unharmed. 

On another day, as the enemies pursued them manfully, the Prince was forced by the advice of his followers to retreat to an impregnable place, and all the soldiery with him. It was fortified by a valley and ramparts, in the middle of which sat a most round, never-conquerable citadel upon a rock surrounded by walls. Next to it stood another most high tower, through which, by means of excavated underground tunnels, the steward was able to introduce everything necessary for both food and war without the enemies' knowledge. This was much like what once happened at **Napoli di Romania** <note>original: "Neapoli Romaniæ"; the city of Nafplio in Greece, which was a strategic Venetian and later Ottoman stronghold</note> while Suleiman, the King of the Turks, besieged it for twenty years, yet could not perceive from where the supplies of food and other things came to the city.

He remained there for the duration of the siege, for he took the highest delight in that sanctuary; it was expertly crafted, just as one may see in the **Duchy of Lorraine**. From there, through four windows, whatever machinations the enemies might make to intercept him were visible to him. Truly, they were not able to enter, because the principal door of his dwelling was closed to him in such a way that no one was able to open it except the faithful steward, who disposed and provided for everything so prudently that in a whole year of siege, nothing was lacking. ### DIONYSIUS ZACHARIUS

Because of the daily attacks launched by the Emperor’s soldiers, the Prince was forced to divide his army into five companies, so that each could take its turn standing watch. The Generals of the army persuaded the Emperor not to move his camp, saying: "If we abandon the Prince, he will rightly mock us, especially since he was once of our rank <note>In alchemical theory, gold is considered the "perfect" state of the same "rank" or essence as base metals.</note> and might say he left us because he was treated unworthily; therefore, if he escapes our hands, he will seek every opportunity for revenge." These and similar words moved the Emperor to resolve with an obstinate mind to take the Prince captive through starvation, or by whatever other means possible. 

But as winter approached, the Emperor withdrew a portion of his camp for a time, leaving the remainder to continue the siege under the leadership of a most powerful Satrap <note>A provincial governor; here likely representing a specific corrosive or resistant force in the chemical process.</note>, who launched many daily assaults against the good Prince's soldiers. The Emperor's plan was that his men should not break camp until a full year had passed. Recognizing this, the Prince, through his **steward** <term>steward: Latin "œconomus"; in alchemy, the operator or agent that manages the heat and proportions</term>, commanded his companies that each should seize one banner from the Emperor's army by force of arms and bring it to him, under penalty of his greatest displeasure if they failed. He promised a great reward to those who succeeded; furthermore, he vowed to go forth in person, accompanied by his faithful **steward**, to strike the enemy so vigorously that he would either lose his life or bring back the Emperor's primary banner, enriching all his followers—more so than all the enemies who besieged him—with the spoils.

Their courage thus restored, before the appointed time had passed, his companies brought him all the Emperor’s banners he had desired, by means of the "duplication of the circle" <note>original: "duplicationis circuli"; likely a reference to a geometric alchemical process or a specific cycle of distillation</note> which a certain Prince of France had taught his **steward**. 

The first banner belonged to the black German knights, whom they call the **Black Raiders** <note>original: "Reutherorum atrorum"; referring to the "Schwarze Reiter," German cavalry. Symbolically, this represents the *Nigredo* or the black stage of putrefaction.</note>. The second was variegated with many different colors <note>Likely the "Peacock's Tail" stage, where the matter shifts through many hues.</note>. The third was not so different from the banner of the King of France. The fourth was marked with a crescent Moon <note>Symbolizing the *Albedo* or white stage, associated with silver.</note>. The fifth was truly similar to the Emperor's greatest banner <note>Symbolizing the *Rubedo* or red stage, the final perfection of the gold.</note>. 

This success increased the Prince’s courage, so that on the following day he went forth to the walls with his **steward** and fought there with extraordinary vigor until he captured the Emperor's supreme banner. Returning at last from the fight exhausted, he was refreshed by the **steward** with the provisions remaining from the start of the siege. With his strength restored, he and his **steward** leaped manfully upon the enemy the next day. With the help of his Generals, he partly slaughtered and partly routed the Emperor's entire army, all of whom were then decorated with his own Prince’s colors. 

Thus it happened that every Power—be it the Pope, the Emperor, King, Prince, or even the Sultan <note>original: "Solimanus," referring to Suleiman the Magnificent, the contemporary Ottoman ruler.</note>—must yield the palm of victory to this one **Prince Gold** <note>original: "Auro Principi"</note> and concede the victory with the greatest applause, by the will and command of God, to whom be praise, honor, and eternal glory forever.

### *On the projection upon metals.*

Once our **King** <note>The "King" refers to the completed Alchemical Stone or the perfected Red Elixir.</note> has been multiplied in strength and nourished with food, let one ounce of it be projected upon four ounces of pure gold, melted and purified. From this will be made a brittle matter which, once pulverized, should be cooked in a **closed mountain** <note>Latin: "monte clauso"; an alchemical metaphor for a sealed furnace or a specific type of vessel like the "Athanor."</note> by the heat of a "final assault," in a very narrow vessel that is also stopped up, for a space of three days. Let one ounce of this powder be projected upon twenty-five marks of silver or copper, or upon eighteen marks of lead or tin, or upon fifteen marks of common quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note> heated in a crucible or congealed with lead. 

The matter will soon be covered with a thick foam; when the operation is complete, a crackling sound will occur, as if the crucible were breaking. Finally, let this matter be melted, and it will be found converted into gold. However, if the stated weight was not observed, the matter might not have changed to its prior color; therefore, it should be refined in a great **cupel** <term>cupel: Latin "cineritio"; a shallow porous cup used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</term> without lead, so that in the space of three hours the matter which was not transmuted may be consumed. The remainder at the bottom, which is pure, must be further purged for six hours with **royal cement** <term>royal cement: a mixture of salts and brick dust used to refine gold by removing silver and other impurities</term>. By this way, all will be held as gold, converted by the work of our great King, similar and equal in value to any mineral gold. This is the way taught by **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> in his *Codicillus* regarding projection. He teaches the second part, concerning the tincture of gems, in his *Testamentum*.

### *On the Tincture of gems and pearls.*

That great King of ours must be washed and refreshed immediately after the **white sign** <note>The "white sign" or "white stage" (Albedo) in the alchemical process, indicating a high degree of purity.</note> marked by the waxing moon is brought to him; the end of the siege is not to be awaited, but rather the time from the first meal of his refreshment. This is the Mercury which Raymond Lull called **exuberated quicksilver** <term>exuberated quicksilver: mercury that has been purified and "animated" through repeated distillations with salts or other spirits</term>. Let two or three ounces of it be placed over ashes in a small, well-closed alembic; let them be distilled first with a slow fire. When nothing more wishes to drip from this fire, the receiver should be changed and luted <note>Sealed with airtight clay or paste.</note> more strongly; finally, whatever is able to ascend should be urged on with a stronger fire. 

This second liquor should be distilled in a fresh alembic by means of a **Mary’s bath** <term>Mary's bath: "balneum Mariae" or bain-marie; a water bath used for gentle, even heating</term>, by **cohobating** <term>cohobating: the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid remains (the dregs) and re-distilling it</term> the liquor three times over the viscous dregs, and they will be dissolved by the water in a short time. On the third turn, however, let the whole be distilled through ashes, and afterwards in a fresh alembic, let it be distilled again four times through the water bath, keeping the dregs aside each time, until the distilled water is clear and shining with the white brilliance of pearls. Its use here is for **pearls** <note>Latin "uniones"; specifically referring to large, singular, high-quality pearls.</note>. Let these be placed, even if they are very small, into a small cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel.</note>, into which enough of the said water is poured so that it stands slightly above them. Let it be covered with a "blind head" <note>A still-head without a beak or spout, used for digestion rather than distillation.</note>, and after three hours they will be resolved into a white paste, and [it] will float...

### *On the use of our worthy work for the medicine*
### *of the human body.*

Let it be taken in the weight of one grain after the appearance of the **King** <note>The "King" is the completed Alchemical Stone or Red Elixir</note>, and let it be dissolved in white wine in a silver vessel. The wine will be dyed a lemon-yellow color. If this is administered to the sick shortly after midnight, they will be healed in one day if the disease is of one month's duration; if it has lasted a year, they will be healed within twelve days; or within a month, even where the disease would otherwise have been very long-lasting. To preserve health, a little of it should be taken twice every year, at the beginning of spring and autumn. By this means, one lives healthily and cheerfully until the predestined end of life, God granting—to whom be praise, honor, and glory now, always, and forever, Amen.

For the true knowledge of metals, it must not be ignored that while they still exist in their primary forms—namely in sulfur and in **quicksilver** <note>Mercury</note>—they possess two forms: one masculine, and the other feminine. ### ANNOTATIONS.

...to the other, indeed, lacking wings and much more horrible. <note>original: "alis carenti"; This refers to the "fixed" or non-volatile state of matter, often symbolized by a wingless dragon or toad, contrasted with the winged, "volatile" state.</note> If these two **seeds** <term>seeds: "spermata" in Latin; the essential principles or "souls" of the metals</term> are joined by nature in the belly of Mercury, which on account of its heat is called the fire of nature, and by some the **devouring lion** <note>original: "leo devorans"; a common alchemical symbol for an acidic solvent or Mercury's ability to "eat" or dissolve other metals</note>, and although gold and silver enter its belly, they are not consumed, because they are harder and more perfect in nature than it. Mercury is imperfect; nevertheless, common gold and silver come forth from it. Silver is the substance of the lower moon, just as gold is of the lower sun. <note>The "lower" sun and moon refer to the terrestrial metals gold and silver, as opposed to their celestial or philosophical archetypes.</note> Therefore, it is necessary for Mercury, the mother, to be slain and to die through the said seeds, and once she has been **mortified** <term>mortified: the process of "killing" the metal's outward form to release its inner essence</term> by nature, she can never again return to life. 

For even if it is frozen only a little in the terrestrial veins, there is soon present in it a **fixed grain of gold**, which produces the true sprout of Mercury from the two seeds; as can be seen from the caverns of lead, in which there is no mineral in any place that does not clearly contain a true fixed grain—that is, a grain of gold or silver. Indeed, the first freezing of Mercury is the mineral of lead, in which it has been placed by nature. 

This can truly be multiplied to its perfection without doubt or error, yet only while existing in its own Mercury and not separated from its ore. For metal existing in its ore is Mercury, from which if the grain is separated, it will be like an unripe apple taken from its tree, which is utterly destroyed. The **fixed grain** is like the apple, and **Mercury** is the tree. Therefore, the fruit must not be separated from the tree, because it cannot receive nourishment from elsewhere than from its own Mercury. It is a greater folly to put gold and silver into Mercury, no differently than trying to reattach a plucked apple to a tree. 

So that this business may be fulfilled rightly, the tree must be taken together with its fruit, so that it may be planted anew, without the removal of the fruit, into a more fertile and noble earth, which will give more nourishment in a single day than the former field would have provided in a hundred years, on account of the constant agitation of the winds. The other earth, because it is close to the sun, causes the tree to grow and flourish with continual dew and constant sun in the **philosophical garden** <term>philosophical garden: a metaphorical space representing the hermetically sealed vessel where the alchemist controls the environmental conditions</term>, morning, evening, day and night, and shining every single hour without intermission; and the tree is sprinkled and nourished by the sweetest dew, more in one year than in ten thousand in the former earth. 

Therefore, when both are placed in a furnace of continuous heat day and night, its vapor, which is the dew, prevents combustion. The heat of wood or charcoal is useless—indeed, harmful. And so the wise Philosophers did not wish to work in any other thing than in nature itself, with the moon itself, in the mother suitable for Mercury. From which at last they produced a **general Mercury**, far more powerful and stronger than that natural one. Ascend, therefore, into the mountain, so that you may see the vegetable **saturnia** <note>original: "saturniam"; relating to Saturn, the alchemical name for lead, often considered the starting point of the Work</note>, the royal and mineral herb. For let its juice be taken pure, once the dregs are cast away. For from that you will be able to complete the greatest part of your work.

->*The Fountain of Chemistry.*<-

The fountain and cavern of all metals is the mother, from whom those seven are born and proceed, according to her nature: likewise Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and the Moon. Intellectually, Lead is a **leprous gold**, etc. <note>original: "aurum leprosum"; Alchemists viewed base metals like lead as diseased or "leprous" versions of gold that needed to be cured or "perfected" through alchemy.</note> However, if the fountain of nature receives the Mercury placed within it, from that place a most excellent medicine shall be made. In the earth, Mercury is born as a leaden mass; let him who is shut in **prison** <term>prison: "carcere"; likely the sealed vessel or the physical body of the metal that binds its spirit</term> be liberated afterward, otherwise the weight and the desired measure cannot be known; yet you will be able to know the way to him. 

The Mercury of the Sun is not like the Mercury of the Moon, since the latter must always remain white so that it may procreate its own likeness; but the Mercury of the Sun must be **reddened** <note>original: "rubificandus"; referring to the *rubedo*, the final red stage of the alchemical work associated with the Sun and Gold</note>, and this is the first labor: and afterwards they can be gathered together. It must be noted that the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: "quinta essentia"; the "fifth element" or pure spiritual essence beyond the four physical elements</term> is especially necessary for us in this art, and this Mercury is found most of all in that place where the sun is in its greatest heat and produces many flowers: for after the flowers, the fruits follow. It is found similarly in the Moon when it is sought therein, in Saturn, Mars, Venus, and more safely in Mercury: "I, however," (says Flamel) "found and worked it in the Sun." 

When, therefore, these individual things come together in this philosophical work—each of which is similar to the other—then the **offspring devours the mother**, and suffocates his father in a single lake, in which flowers, milk, fruit, and blood are found together. <note>This violent imagery describes the "fixed" principle absorbing the "volatile" principle during the chemical union.</note> This metal, therefore, is to be placed alone in a single vessel, and in a single furnace. It is Mercury of which I speak, and nothing else. For the shortening of the work, there is one metal in this world in which our Mercury is found abundantly. 

Gold is hot and dry; the Moon (Silver) is indeed of a cold nature; Saturn (Lead) is heavy and soft: for which reason, being like the Sun in this itself, it is called **leprous gold**. Venus (Copper) is like the Moon in weight and malleability; Mercury is cold and moist, similar to Jupiter (Tin), who is born from it; Mars (Iron), however, is hard, heavy, and cold. 

All this business consists in two things: namely, that by fire you make your **sulphur** <term>sulphur: the active, masculine principle in alchemy, associated with heat, soul, and the power of "fixation"</term> penetrative and attractive, so that it might devour its mother, and you will have completed the work. Fix the mother into the belly of her offspring, whom she brought forth before; then finally he will be to himself a father, and a son, a perfect spirit out of two. After your sulphur has been devoured, and its Mercury **mortified** <note>original: "mortificatus"; the process of "killing" the metal's outward form to release its inner essence</note>, let it be cast into prison, in which it should remain for forty days, and you shall see what you desire, according to these verses:

This is a famous alchemical axiom referring to the processes of "solution" (turning solids into liquids/vapors) and "coagulation" or "fixation" (turning vapors/liquids into stable solids).</note>

### ### Jean de Meun on the Lamentations of Nature

What is enclosed beneath the Moon is called "heaven" in this place, because matter desires form, no differently than a woman desires a man. Matter alone is made from the four elements, from which chaos is formed, and from that chaos the King and Queen are generated. <note>The "King and Queen" are symbolic representations of the active/masculine (often gold or sulfur) and passive/feminine (often silver or mercury) principles whose union produces the Philosopher's Stone.</note> First, indeed, fire was created by God, which He placed beneath the Moon; it is free from corruption and contains within itself the purest part of the **quintessence**. <term>quintessence: "quinta essentia"; literally the "fifth essence," a celestial, incorruptible substance distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</term> Afterward, the subtle air was made, in which God likewise placed a part of the quintessence—though not as much as in the fire—with less in the water, and the least in the earth. Therefore, just as fire acts upon the air, so the air acts upon the water and the earth. The Earth is the mother and the nourisher of all things which she conceives in her womb from the fire; she fosters this very thing even into her own center without interruption. 

Since nature alone has the power of reducing the four elements back into the **first matter** <term>first matter: "prima materia"; the formless, original substance from which all things are created</term>—which is generally mixed with any elements—it would be impossible for any human operator to achieve this except through nature herself, who alone provides both the matter and the nature. For the quintessence, which is called the **golden chain**, <note>original: "cathena aurea"; a concept derived from Homer’s "Golden Chain" in the *Iliad*, interpreted by alchemists as the spiritual link connecting the divine/celestial realms to the physical world.</note> connects and harmonizes contraries in such a way that they never disagree again. Gold must be considered first, which receives its most beautiful form in heaven and its best matter on earth, as do gemstones. Heaven, therefore, informs the quintessence with form and matter contained within the element, through which the form is held; this is perfected by purification and the passage of a long time. 

Thus, gold and gemstones are composed by me, Nature, alone: for no one besides me knows the correct proportions. That which you seek is surely the highest secret of nature, descending from celestial power. Wherefore the whole of the science is owed to nature, by which the simplicity of the element is drawn forth from heaven; this is called the "primitive essence" in heaven and the "quintessence" in the element. Nature herself produces this through reductions and prolonged circulations, by converting the lower into the higher, and by preserving the cold and dry within the moist and hot. She forms stones and metals under their "radical moisture" by the celestial movements of the stars, which govern the elements and whose influences the elements obey. Thus, the purer the matter is, the more excellent the work becomes through nature. 

Celestial movement, therefore, is the "intelligence" corresponding to lower things, in which it brings all things into being through its influences. Nature, then, uses the matter in an infallible fire, because she receives all power from it. Likewise, there is a water proceeding from a dry origin, which does not moisten what it touches, and being neither receding nor volatile, it is the **incombustible oil**. <term>incombustible oil: "oleum incombustibile"; an alchemical term for a "fixed" substance that can withstand high heat without evaporating or burning—often associated with the "radical moisture" of metals.</term> No artificial fire could infuse as much heat as that which comes from heaven. Furthermore, in these matters, it must not be ignored that this entire work of ours is made from a cheap, homogeneous matter, closed in a single vessel, and contained in a single furnace,

It is no different in our art: if anyone knows how to choose such matter in which nature delights, and to enclose it, duly prepared, in its vessel and furnace, I (says Nature) and he himself shall perfect it everywhere without delay, provided he administers the required fire—natural, against nature, and not natural—and without burning heat: a fire (I say) that is hot, dry, moist, and cold. <note>This paradoxical description refers to the "Philosophical Fire," which is not a literal flame but a specific, tempered heat or a chemical property that facilitates change without destruction.</note> Consider, therefore, what sort of fire it must be: for without fire and matter, nothing happens in this science. I give you the matter (says Nature); the form is what you prepare for yourself—I do not mean substantial or accidental form, but the construction of the vessel and the furnace. Next, prepare your matter, made into powder with its own water, enclosed in a single vessel: guide it with tempered heat; this will promote action, and coldness will promote **putrefaction**. <term>putrefaction: the essential alchemical stage where the matter decomposes and turns black, signifying the death of the old form before its transformation.</term> Indeed, because of the great coldness, dryness could not hinder it, nor resist this silver, so that the quicksilver may be immediately reduced into the **prime matter** in a complete connection. <term>prime matter: "prima materia"; the original, formless substance from which all things in the universe were thought to be created.</term> Therefore, before you work (says Nature), learn to know me, who am the mother, without whom no creature can receive essence, grow, nor have a sensitive soul without the heavens and the elements. There is, in truth, a medium between Mercury and metal which must be taken for our art: it is (I say) **potable gold** and **radical moisture**, and the highest medicine which we perfect through your art and my science. <term>potable gold: "aurum potabile"; a liquid form of gold believed to be a universal cure. radical moisture: "humidum radicale"; the vital, life-sustaining fluid inherent in all things.</term> Without me, who provides the matter, you will never achieve anything; and without you, who serves, I cannot perform this work alone. It is similar to gold in substance, but dissimilar in essence: by converting its elements, you will find what you seek, by sublimating the lower things and by converting the upper and the lower. Therefore, take this quicksilver mixed with active sulfur, and enclosed also in a single vessel and a single furnace; let the vessel be buried for a third part, and let it be held over the philosophical fire; and let every species be left behind, except for the matter alone from which the mineral takes its origin.

# ANNOTATIONS

This matter remains confused and not diffused <note>original: "confusa... diffusa"; meaning mixed in a state of potential rather than spread out into specific characteristics</note> until it is specified and qualified by nature. Only then does it receive a **substantial form**, and afterward a visible **accidental form**. <note>In the philosophy of the time, "substantial form" is the essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "goldness" of gold), while "accidental form" refers to outward traits like weight or shape.</note> It transmutes the prior form so that the new form may shape the matter. For the object is subject to potential, because it sustains the substance in act, which was previously in potential. **Gold** is known to be the treasure of all minerals; however, it possesses neither the form nor the matter of such potential that it might exceed its own perfection. For it has no greater power than that of perfecting itself, no matter what the craftsman strives to do. To destroy it and attempt to bring it back into being would be a foolish task, since no more virtue or power can be obtained from it than it possesses by its own nature. No reduction occurs in those things which nature has perfected into a species or an individual, unless they are first **corrupted**. <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is a technical term for the breakdown or "death" of a substance, which is required before it can be transformed into something higher.</note> Even after corruption, the generation of a species does not occur unless there is a return to this genus. Therefore, the destruction of gold does not pave the way for its reconstruction, because nothing can be built through its own destruction: for once it is dead, its substance dies along with it, so that no more quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> or metal can be born from it. And because the element of fire is contained in earth, and air in water—the quantity, quality, and proportion of whose perfect union no one knows—the elements are not to be separated, since they cannot be restored. Therefore, only that which nature has generated and left for us should be taken for the art. In short, the effective separation of elements does not happen in quicksilver, nor in the **Sun** <note>original: "solis"; here referring to the "Philosophical Sun" or Gold</note>, who is the father of the art, imparting spirit to his son.

->*By an Unknown Author.*<-

Whatever is sought is found in **Mercury**; from it the body, spirit, and soul are drawn, and from it the purest and cleanest **tincture** <note>a potent alchemical liquid capable of transmuting metals</note> arises. It is a precious moisture that gladdens man, made of earth, water, and fire. Truly, once the body is purged and the spirit conceived, at last a clear fountain rises, at the bottom of which lies a **green lion** <note>a famous alchemical symbol, often representing raw mineral matter or a powerful acidic solvent</note> or a stretching serpent. If it is awakened, it ascends on high, and after its spirit fails, it falls back down into the bath, where it is washed for a time until it grows red. It is washed (I say) with the **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; usually a distilled alcohol or a powerful solvent</note> until it is no longer recognized. Finally, it is turned into a most worthy stone—first white, and then a lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note> beautiful to see and delightful. Therefore, be diligent concerning the true Mercury, which nature has generated, and which dwells prosperously with its father, and restores imperfect metals to a prosperous state.

placed in a bath, or in an airy heating-chamber <note>original: "aeroso hypocausto"; a hypocaust was a Roman system of underfloor heating, used here to describe a controlled alchemical furnace</note> that is moderately warm and dry, and purified from external vapor, it acquires the solidity of its parts; having been thinned of its superfluous moisture, it becomes fit for mixing. Once this is done, the <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>original: "lac virgineum"; a white, mercurial liquid produced during the early stages of the work</note> is squeezed out from its purer parts. Stripped of the variety of its heats, it rejoices with its companion, tinted with a color like snow. Then, after this, it resists the violence of fire without danger, until at last, adorned with the <term>peacock's colors</term> <note>original: "pavonis coloribus"; the *cauda pavonis* or "peacock's tail" is a stage where the matter displays a shifting iridescent spectrum, signaling that the impurities are being purged</note>, it may then emerge from its tomb with Royal and supreme power.

Although this process may seem quite brief here, it is not lacking in very lengthy circumstances and operations. Each task necessary for this work is treated concisely, yet each stage must be most carefully considered and not passed over thoughtlessly. For the truth of this divine science is more easily grasped from such a small discourse than from the most abundant and innumerable volumes, which cover the unity and simplicity of truth with a multitude and variety of words.

## CERTAIN OTHER ANNOTATIONS FROM VARIOUS AUTHORS.

### *On the solution and coagulation of the matter of Alchemy.*

Since <term>solution</term> <note>the process of turning a solid into a liquid or "water"</note> is the principal operation of this art, we must first speak of it, bringing forth the authorities of various Philosophers so that it may be more easily understood, with one interpreting the other. These, therefore, are the things we wished to collect and weave into our notebooks. Indeed, the mind of the Philosophers must be sought from their variety, if it can be reduced by comparisons to one and the same meaning. It is not to be doubted that they seem to agree most on this very thing which is sought. For the entire business of the divine philosophical work consists in these two operations, namely, in solution and <term>congelation</term> <note>also called coagulation; the process of solidifying the liquid back into a stable "Stone"</note>. Therefore, solution, according to the opinion of **Geber**, is the reduction of a dry thing into water <note>original: "rei siccæ in aquam reductio"</note>.

### THE LADDER OF PHILOSOPHERS.

The solution of the stone is its reduction into mineral water.

### VILLANOVANUS.

We dissolve (he says) when we divide bodies; we make them simple and subtle, and resolve them into their primary nature and matter.

### AVICENNA on matter.

Primary matter is twofold: proximate and remote. Proximate...

### VILLANOVA.

<note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a physician and religious reformer whose name was frequently attached to alchemical manuscripts.</note>

The true beginning of our work is the dissolution of the stone. The same author says: The first rule of the stone is to dissolve the stone, and to reduce it into its first nature.

### VILLANOVA.

You, whoever wishes to work, have need to labor first in the solution and <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of turning a solid directly into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note> of the two <term>luminaries</term> <note>original: "luminarium"; in alchemy, the "luminaries" are the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver)</note>, because the first step of the operation is that quicksilver be made from them.

### CHILDREN’S PLAY.

<note>original: "Ludus Puerorum"; a common alchemical title suggesting that once the secret is known, the Great Work is as easy as children's games.</note>

### THE SOUND.

This whole art turns on this point: that we join the moist with the dry—that is, that we dissolve and coagulate. The moist is the liquid spirit cleansed of all filth. ## THE GATHERING OF PHILOSOPHERS.
<note>original: "Congregatio Philosophorum"; a title often used for collections of authoritative alchemical sayings or a specific medieval text.</note>

Nature completes that step which it is able to complete, but which it cannot overstep. Another says: Nature contains within itself those things which it lacks: but it is not perfected unless it be moved by art and operation. Likewise: The first dispositions of the <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapidis"; referring to the Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the alchemical work</note> can be brought about by no art; nature alone can do this. Likewise: The matter of the stone is produced by nature. It [nature] can make the matter. Likewise: The matter of the stone is produced by nature. To make the matter through any artifice is impossible. For the stone is found created by nature, and it requires nothing else, except that what is superfluous in it be removed—that is, in its matter.

### AVICENNA.
<note>Avicenna is the Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational in Europe.</note>

The stone does not bear fruit until it comes to nothingness, like running water.

### THE ASSEMBLY.
<note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the earliest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>

Our entire <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the Great Work or the technical process of achieving the alchemical goal</note> is done with our water; from it, and of it, all necessary things are made. For it dissolves bodies with a true and philosophical solution, so that they are converted into the water from which they were in the beginning. Elsewhere: Unless everything is turned into water, you will in no way arrive at perfection.

### ALPHIDIUS.
<note>Alphidius was an influential, though historically obscure, alchemical author, likely of Arabic origin.</note>

Unless you thin the natures, making them into water, you can color nothing: therefore, make the bodies be water by liquefying them, which is called the <term>water of wisdom</term> <note>original: "aqua sapientiæ"</note> among the Philosophers.

### THE ROSE GARDEN.
<note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise attributed to various authors including Arnald of Villanova.</note>

<term>Permanent water</term> <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a specialized alchemical solvent that does not evaporate when heated</note>—whether it is called perennial water or "burning wine"—is called the water of the body; that is, when the body has been reduced into <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; not the common metal, but the "mercury of the wise," a purified, liquid state of matter</note>. Likewise: Permanent water cannot exist without its body, with which it was dissolved. Likewise: Without permanent water, nothing is done. It is also called the water of life. Likewise: Only with burning wine can you complete the perfect elixir.

### THE LADDER.
<note>original: "Scala"; referring to the *Scala Philosophorum* (The Ladder of the Philosophers), a text outlining the stages of the work.</note>

The Dragon is <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine principle of heat and combustion</note>, which is extracted from bodies through the mastery.

### AVICENNA.

He who sets out to make the white <term>elixir</term> <note>original: "elixir"; a substance capable of transmuting base metals or prolonging life; the "white" version specifically creates silver</note> will find white sulfur in silver, and in gold, the red. And since such sulfur is not found upon the earth except in these two bodies, the bodies must therefore be prepared subtly, so that we may have their sulfur and quicksilver from them, such as those were from which gold and silver were produced under the earth.

### THE CLANGOR.
<note>original: "Clangor"; referring to the *Clangor Buccinae* (The Clang of the Trumpet), an alchemical text known for its use of vibrant metaphors.</note>

Dissolve the perfect body into Mercury; from there you will have hidden virtue—that is, philosophical sulfur that has been digested and cooked—

### THE CHILDREN'S GAME.

### THE SOUNDING TRUMPET.

Dissolution converts the body into the nature of spirit.

### ROGER.

This is the way by which we attain the secret of making white and red sulfur, which is the soul of the body; when it is drawn from the body, it has the power of dyeing, which it commits to the spirit of the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquæ vitæ"; in alchemy, this refers to a potent solvent or "mercurial water," rather than the modern term for brandy.</note> to be preserved.

### THE LADDER.

It is proper to extract nature from the root, that is, the first essential parts, without which no transmutation of metals occurs.

### ARNALD OF VILLANOVA.

The intention of our operation is nothing other than that the purest substance be drawn and selected from the sun and moon. <note>In alchemical symbolism, "the sun" (Sol) refers to gold and "the moon" (Luna) refers to silver.</note>

### THE SOUNDING TRUMPET.

Extract the quicksilver, or the philosophical stone, as much from bodies as from living silver: since they are of one nature, you will have Mercury and sulfur from that matter above the earth, from which gold and silver were generated in the earth.

### THE COMMON OPINION.

The Mercury of the Philosophers consists of quicksilver and sulfur.

...[extra]neous addition, except for digestion, by means of which all four <note>Referring to the four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> are encompassed within the gold and are matured in equal proportion.

### A COMMON AXIOM.

The corruption of one thing is the generation of another, and this holds true as much in artificial things as in natural ones. Put another way: According to nature, nothing is generated that was not first corrupted <note>original: "corrumpatur"; in alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breakdown or "death" of a substance so it can be reborn in a higher form.</note>, and nothing rises again that has not died beforehand.

### BERNARD.
<note>Likely Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a legendary Italian alchemist who spent his life seeking the Stone.</note>

If gold is boiled or dissolved in quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note> in the proper manner and by the natural way, that quicksilver will obtain the natural properties of gold. Likewise: The dissolution which is performed by the Water of the Philosophers <note>The "Water of the Philosophers" is not common water, but a specialized alchemical solvent, often identified with a "mercurial" spirit.</note> certainly corrupts the exterior form of the dissolved bodies, but it does not corrupt the matter.

### VILLANOVA.
<note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist who served various kings and popes.</note>

That which dissolves the body is from the spirit; that which coagulates the spirit, however, is from the body. Elsewhere: The spirit dissolves, the body coagulates. Likewise: As much as the body is dissolved, so much is the spirit coagulated. For if the body were not dissolved, the spirit would not be thickened. Elsewhere: That which comes out of the dissolved body is a radiant humidity; that which dissolves the body proceeds from the spirit, and its power is germinal. Likewise elsewhere: The dissolution of the body occurs with the coagulation of the spirit, and the coagulation of the spirit with the dissolution of the body. Then the body is mixed with the spirit and becomes one with it, and they are never separated, no more than water mixed with water.

### THE SOUNDING TRUMPET.
<note>original: "Clangor Buccinae"; an influential Latin alchemical text.</note>

When the <term>seed of Mercury</term> <note>original: "sperma Mercurij"; the essential generative principle of the metal.</note> is joined with the earth of the body, the body is dissolved into the water of the seed, and they become one water without any division.

### VILLANOVA.

Understand, moreover, that the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit happen simultaneously and at the very same time.

### THE ROSARY, ACCORDING TO CALID.
<note>Referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum," citing Calid, the Latinized name of Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704), an Umayyad prince credited with being the first Arab alchemist.</note>

The dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit are two things, but they have one single operation. This is because the spirit is not coagulated except through the dissolution of the body, nor is the body dissolved except through the coagulation of the spirit. Therefore, between the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit there is no difference, nor is the work different in any way; they cannot happen one without the other. Just as we see happening when common water tries to make earth more subtle and dissolve it into its own matter: for at the same time the water becomes denser and thicker, while the earth becomes more subtle and refined.

### LULL.
<note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>

Many of the Philosophers dissolved the bodies of metals in common <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid.</note> made from vitriol and salt nitre, and by evaporation they drew off that water; then the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a metal has been burned or corroded by acid.</note> remained at the bottom of the vessel...
