->ROGER BCON<-
<note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English Franciscan friar and philosopher often associated with early experimental science and alchemy.</note>

Nothing adheres to metals, nor is joined to them, nor transmutes them, except that which is of their own kind.

->BERNARD<-
<note>Bernard of Trevisan, continuing his critique of "fools" or "false alchemists" from the previous page.</note>

Fools make corrosive waters from minerals through dissolution, into which they place the species of metals; they corrode them, but do not dissolve them with a natural solution, which requires the permanence of both—namely, the solvent and the dissolved.

->THE SAME<-

No water by natural reduction dissolves a metallic species, except that which remains with the species of metal in matter and form, and which the metals themselves are able to congeal again. This is not the case with strong waters, which do not pertain to the dissolved bodies. Indeed, bodies are corroded by strong waters, but they are not dissolved. And the more they are corroded, the more they are alienated from their metallic nature.

->VILLANOVA<-

Through dissolution, the body is mixed with the spirit and becomes one with it, so that one is never separated from the other.

->CLANGOR<-
<note>Likely referring to the "Clangor Buccinae" (The Sound of the Trumpet), an influential alchemical text.</note>

The body is dissolved into the "water of the seed," <note>original: "aquam spermatis"; the essential, generative moisture of the metal.</note> and from that, the water becomes one without division.

->THE PHILOSOPHER<-
<note>In alchemical texts, "The Philosopher" usually refers to Aristotle, though here it may refer more broadly to any master of the Hermetic art.</note>

A voluntary dissolution is better than a violent one, and a temperate one is better than a hasty one; therefore, one must be careful lest the generative power of the form be suffocated by corrosives and burning agents.

->THE ROSARY<-
<note>Referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum" (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical series of citations and illustrations.</note>

In our stone, the sun and the moon <note>Gold and Silver.</note> are alive, and they can beget other suns and moons from themselves. Other gold and other silver <note>literally "other moon."</note> are dead: for their force and power remained in the solution made by our water. Any other water would have destroyed them and rendered them sterile.

->VILLANOVA<-

Dissolution occurs only through quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; Mercury.</note>: for it alone can reduce gold and silver to their first matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the primal, undifferentiated substance from which all metals originate.</note>. The same says: The entire benefit of this art consists in Mercury, the sun, and the moon.

->ARISTOTLE<-

If we had nothing else from Mercury, except that it [dissolves] bodies...

->GEBER<-
<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a Persian polymath considered the father of early chemistry.</note>

The perfection of every dissolution is brought about with subtle waters, and especially those that are sharp, stinging, bitter, and have no dregs—such as distilled vinegar, juice of unripe grapes, pears of great acidity, distilled pomegranates, and things similar to these.

->ARNALD OF VILLANOVA<-
<note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous Catalan physician and alchemist.</note>

The nature of the dissolved body and the dissolving water is one and the same, except that the nature of the body is complete, digested, and fixed; whereas the nature of the water is incomplete, undigested, and volatile.

->REGOR<-
<note>Likely a variation of Roger Bacon or another medieval authority.</note>

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum."</note> is a fire that burns, kills, and shatters bodies.

->ROSINUS<-
<note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian alchemist.</note>

Water is so much hotter than fire, just as fire is hotter than water.

->THE ROSARY<-
<note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century alchemical text.</note>

Our water is stronger than fire, because it makes a pure spirit out of the body of gold, which fire cannot do. **The same author says:** The spirit is entirely fiery, dissolving and dividing bodies through its own fieriness.

->THE ASSEMBLY<-
<note>original: "TURBA"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between philosophers.</note>

Burn our copper <note>original: "æs"; used here in a technical alchemical sense rather than for common metal.</note> with a most powerful fire.

<note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704), an Umayyad prince credited with being one of the first Muslim alchemists.</note>

A lesser fire grinds all things: for it works less than our water, which dissolves the body, something fire is unable to do.

It can be known that the primary matter of our Stone is of the nature of living Quicksilver and sulfur; for it cannot be destroyed in fire, nor in water, nor in air.

->THE ROSARY<-

Some have said that the quicksilver of the common people <note>original: "argentum vivum vulgi"; ordinary mercury used in trade.</note> adheres to bodies, which is false. For what Geber says—"We have not found in our invention any thing more than quicksilver to be befriended by the natures of bodies"—all of this is to be understood as concerning **philosophical quicksilver**. For it alone adheres to bodies, and neither the ancient Philosophers could find any other thing, nor will the modern ones find any other thing that adheres to bodies, except philosophical quicksilver: because common quicksilver does not adhere to bodies. ### VILLANOVANUS.
<note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a celebrated physician and alchemist whose works emphasize the biological and "natural" processes of chemistry.</note>

In order for nature to change and convert nature, it needs only that which belongs to its own nature. Likewise, that which dissolves and that which is dissolved are of one and the same kind and nature. **The same author says:** A dissolution of the body is not true, nor is a coagulation of the spirit philosophical, if there is any foreign matter or external nature present in the dissolution.

### DASTINUS.
<note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386) was an English alchemist known for his correspondence with Pope John XXII regarding the legitimacy of alchemy.</note>

It is necessary that the elements of the water be of the same nature as the elements of the metal intended for transmutation; otherwise, the offspring will be degenerate. For from a diversity of parts, a diversity of the whole is born. Truly, likeness exists among those things which are of one single kind and sprout from one single root.

### THE ROSARY.
<note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century anthology of alchemical wisdom.</note>

The Philosopher’s Stone is made from three things: namely, the sun, the moon, and Mercury <note>original: "sole, luna, & Mercurio" — in alchemy, the sun represents gold, and the moon represents silver.</note>. **Likewise:** Create Mercury from the sun and moon in its own being, without using the common mercury <note>original: "Mercurio vulgi"</note>, but rather through the philosophical way.

### LULLIUS.
<note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher. Many alchemical works were attributed to him posthumously.</note>

The Stone is composed from the quicksilver <term>quicksilver: Latin *argentum vivum*, the common name for the liquid metal mercury</term> of metals, not from the quicksilver of the common people.

### THE NEW LIGHT.
<note>Refers to *Novum Lumen Chymicum*, a very influential 17th-century text written by Michael Sendivogius.</note>

Our quicksilver is not silver in its own proper nature, nor is it yet in that nature to which it was brought by the mine, but it is in that nature to which our artifice has led it.

### RICHARDUS.
<note>Likely Richard the Englishman (Richardus Anglicus), a 14th-century alchemist.</note>

Raw mercury <note>original: "Mercurius crudus"</note> prepares bodies into the first matter <term>first matter: the formless, primal substance from which all things are made</term>, but the mercury of the bodies themselves cannot do this. **The same author says:** Because through freezing <note>original: "congelationem"</note>, that raw sulfur which was in it before (that is, before freezing) is altered in its nature, and therefore it does not corrode like the first did.

### THE PHILOSOPHERS IN GENERAL.

Do not seek cleanliness from the unclean. It is foolish to seek from a thing that which was never within it. Who can give what he does not have? What is this madness, to wish to make a better thing from a worse one—that is, to make perfect things from imperfect ones?

### LULLIUS.

Heaven, the moon-plant <note>original: "lunaria"</note>, the menstruum <term>menstruum: a powerful alchemical solvent</term>, the vegetable liquor, and the water of quicksilver—rectified and sharpened with vegetables—is that with which the natural dissolution of metals is performed.

### VILLANOVANUS.

Dissolving waters made from salts, alums, and other things of that kind, which have no kinship <note>original: "cognationem"</note> with metals, do not preserve the species of the metals; on the contrary, they destroy and scatter them. Opposite to these is the water of the Philosophers, which preserves metals, renders them more subtle, then dissolves them, and by a great agreement of nature, transfers them into the first matter.

### T u r b a.
<note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various Greek sages.</note>

Take the black spirit that does not burn, and with it dissolve and divide the bodies.

### C l a n g o r.
<note>Refers to *Clangor Buccinae* (The Sound of the Trumpet), a 15th-century alchemical treatise.</note>

In the water of the Philosophers lies hidden the spirit of the fifth essence <note>original: "quintæ essentiæ" — the "quintessence" or purest, most refined element beyond the four earthly ones</note>, which alone possesses the mastery to corrupt <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the necessary decay or breakdown of a substance before it can be reborn in a higher form.</note> and transform matter into its original first state.

### R o s a r i u s.
<note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), a famous illustrated alchemical anthology.</note>

The juice of the lunaria <note>literally "moon-plant," often representing silver or a specific lunar solvent</note> is made from our wine—which is known to few of our sons—and with it our dissolution is made, and our potable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile" — a liquid gold medicine thought to grant eternal youth</note> is produced through it, and by no means without it.

### L u l l i u s.
<note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note>

The solvent <term>menstruum|A term used by alchemists to describe a powerful solvent capable of dissolving metals, named after the "menstrual" cycles of nature.</term> cannot generate the philosopher’s stone without gold and silver, nor vice versa. However, where these are joined, the solvent moves the metals toward dissolution. And in turn, the metals move the solvent to produce fire within the stones.

### C l a n g o r.

If there is one pound of twelve ounces of the imperfect body—namely, the earth—it is fixed by its own soakings for ninety days.

### L u l l i u s.

In the unique water made from the prepared red body—that is, from our prepared red earth, shaped into thin plates or reduced to a powder of filings—place two drachms (that is, a fourth part of one ounce). If you can dissolve more, add more; however, do not exceed one ounce. If any of the earth remains undissolved, leave it in the glass vessel; set aside what has been dissolved. Afterward, let the earth which remained undissolved be placed with new material to be dissolved. But of the new earth do not add two drachms, but less—namely, as much as the remaining earth weighs. Understand this, unless you perceive that the water is capable of dissolving more.

### G E B E R
<note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) is considered the father of Arabic chemistry; his works were the standard textbooks for European alchemists.</note>

The method of dissolution is twofold: namely, by warm dung and by boiling water; both have one intention and one effect. The method by dung is this: place the calcined <note>burned to a fine powder or ash</note> material in a glass flask <note>original: "ampullam vitream"</note> and pour over it twice the amount of distilled vinegar or something similar; seal its opening well so it does not breathe <note>i.e., so no vapors escape</note>, and let it be left to dissolve under warm dung <note>Dung was used in laboratories as a source of gentle, constant incubation heat.</note>. Afterward, let the dissolved part be removed through a filter. The undissolved part should be calcined again, and after calcination, dissolved in the same way, until by repeating the work, the whole is dissolved.

The method of dissolution performed by boiling water is faster: the calcined material is arranged in a flask with vinegar, with the opening sealed so it does not breathe. This flask is buried in a cauldron full of water and straw, and afterward, a fire is lit beneath it until the water boils for an hour. After

## THE PATH OF THE PATH
<note>original: "Semita Semitæ" — a title often given to practical alchemical manuals intended to guide the student step-by-step.</note>

Take one pound of the prize <note>original: "pretij" — likely referring to the metallic "subject" or material being worked upon.</note> with four pounds of water: grind and incorporate it with a little salt and vinegar until the whole becomes an amalgam. Once the prize is perfectly amalgamated, place it in a great quantity of the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note>, that is, Mercury. Place it over the ashes <note>original: "super cineres" — an ash-bath provides a steady, gentle heat.</note> and let there be a very slow fire for a natural day <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour cycle.</note>. Let the vessel cool, and strain the water through a linen cloth, so that what has been dissolved from the body may pass through. That which remains in the cloth, place back on the fire with new blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta" — a term for a purified alchemical solvent.</note> for a natural day, and strain as before. Repeat this so many times until the entire body is converted into water.

## ARNALD OF VILLANOVA
<note>Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a celebrated physician and alchemist; his name lent authority to many texts on distillation and medicine.</note>

Grind one pound of clean filings in a mortar with four pounds of Mercury. To that pound, give twelve pounds of the water of life. Place the whole in a urinal <note>original: "urinali" — a glass vessel shaped like a gourd or a modern laboratory flask, used for digestion.</note>, and over a weak and slow fire of ashes, and cook for a day. When the vessel has cooled, let the water be strained so that what has been dissolved from the body and filings may pass through with it; set that water aside. And that which is not dissolved, place back on the fire with new blessed water for a day and a night. Strain what is dissolved as before, and place this second water with the first. Do this until all the filings are converted into water, that is, into the first matter <note>original: "primam materiam" — the primordial, undifferentiated state of matter from which the Philosophers' Stone is made.</note>.

## RAYMOND LULL *in the Light of Mercuries*
<note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan polymath. Though many alchemical works are pseudonymous, his "Lullian" method focused on the use of solvents or "menstruums."</note>

Take one ounce of the purest sun <note>original: "solis" — alchemical code for gold.</note>, place that ounce in a glass vessel, and pour over it one ounce of the celestial menstruum <note>original: "cœlestis menstrui" — a powerful solvent, named after the biological cycles of life and gestation.</note>, or two at most, and immediately close the vessel so that it does not breathe; place the vessel in a fire of ashes for a natural day to boil gently. By dissolving the sun, the menstruum will be colored with a resplendent citrine <note>A golden-yellow color.</note> hue; afterwards, once the sun is dissolved, place it in a bath of Mary <note>original: "balneo Mariæ" — a water bath (bain-marie) used for gentle, even heating at the temperature of boiling water.</note> for another natural day. Afterwards, by pouring from one vessel into another, store the menstruum so colored in another vessel, and keep it aside in a sealed jar. Then, over the sun which remained undissolved at the bottom of the vessel, pour some of the new menstruum, as we said above. And finally, having closed the vessel, place it in the fire of ashes for another day. Then extract the dissolved portion by pouring it off, as above, into the other vessel with the other dissolved sun. And thus repeat the aforementioned solution with new menstruum until the menstruum is no longer colored, and at the bottom of the vessel will remain the earth of the sun without its soul <note>original: "terra solis absque anima" — the dead physical residue (caput mortuum) left after the spiritual or metallic essence has been extracted.</note>. The same author says: Take the lime <note>A metallic powder produced by heating.</note> of whatever body you wish, place it in a flask that has a long neck. Place it over the ashes, where it should boil for a natural day. Then place it in dung <note>original: "in fimo" — alchemists used the heat generated by fermenting horse manure as a steady, low-temperature incubator.</note> for two natural days, so that it may be better digested, and so that the matter may be separated by its subtle parts from its thickness. <header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

### THE SOUND OF THE TRUMPET.
<note>original: "Clangor" — referring to the *Clangor Buccinae*, an influential alchemical text</note>

To dissolve is to convert a "body" <note>solid matter</note> into the nature of a spirit. To coagulate is to make a spirit corporeal. Solution makes a fixed body volatile. Coagulation, on the contrary, makes a volatile body fixed. The same author says: The spirit—that is, the water—is not coagulated except by means of a body that has been dissolved within it. For bodies are like the "rennet" of this milk—that is, of Mercury. This rennet is either the Sun <note>gold</note> or the Moon <note>silver</note> dissolved in Mercury.

### MENABDES.

I command those who come after me to make bodies not corporeal, and incorporeal bodies: the former is done through dissolution, the latter through gentle decoction <note>slow heating or "cooking" in a liquid</note>.

### AVICENNA.
<note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to later European alchemy</note>

Salts are the roots of the work. The same author says: Salts of every kind are contrary to our art, except for the "salt of our Moon-wort," which our Moon-wort <note>original: "lunaria" — likely referring to a specific chemical solvent or treated mercury rather than the plant</note> leaves behind from dissolved bodies.

### GEBER.
<note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century father of chemistry</note>

We have need of nothing but one vessel, one furnace, and one arrangement. Understand this to apply after the preparation of the "first stone."

### THE COUNT.
<note>Likely referring to Bernard of Trevisan, the Count of the March of Treviso</note>

When you have evaporated the water with great skill and the subtle sharpness of your mind, take your salt—thus calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>—and this finest, impalpable powder, and set it aside in a clean glass vessel until it is necessary to join it to the work.

### THE ROSARY.
<note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note>

There are three stones and there are three salts from which the entire mastery consists. 

The matter of the stone is threefold: gold, silver, and philosophical water. 

There are three waters: solar <note>gold-based</note>, lunar <note>silver-based</note>, and mercurial—this last one resolves the bodies of the sun and moon into their own waters. 

The Mercury of the Philosophers is threefold: the first calcines the bodies, the second dissolves and sublimates them, and the third is joined to these two.

### THE SOUND OF THE TRUMPET.
<note>original: "Clangor Buccinae"</note>

Quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is twofold, and the names of the "First Matter" are many. The first is called the *preparer*, which dissolves the body through the Water of the Philosophers. The other is the *tingeing* <note>coloring or transforming</note> mercury, which is extracted from perfect bodies through dissolution. Such quicksilver is called "incombustible oil," "soul," "air," and the "splendor of bodies," because it grants incorruptible life to imperfect, dead metallic bodies and illuminates them.

### GEBER.

The principal natural things in the work are the "fetid spirit"—or sulfur—and living water.

<header>NICHOLAS FLAMEL’S TRUMPET-BLAST.</header>
<note>original: "Clangor" — usually referring to the "Clangor Buccinae" or "The Sound of the Trumpet," a classic alchemical title.</note>

The spirit is the **water of the Philosophers**, the place of the soul. The soul is the **tincture** <note>the coloring essence or transformative power</note> drawn from perfect bodies <note>gold and silver</note>. The water of the Philosophers is twofold, solar and lunar, from whose conjunction is made **Philosophical Mercury**, and the **virgin’s milk**, from which the white and red stone are produced.

## TREVISANUS.
<note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist known for his search for the Stone.</note>

Let everyone be silent who asserts that any tincture other than ours is of any importance, as well as those who preach a different sulfur than ours, which is hidden in **magnesia** <note>in alchemy, "magnesia" refers to the crude, dark mineral matter used as the starting point of the Work, not modern magnesium</note>. Likewise, all those who attempt to extract another quicksilver <note>mercury</note> than from the **red servant** <note>original: "servo rubeo" — a metaphorical name for a specific mineral state, often associated with iron or specialized ores</note>, and another water than ours, which is **permanent** <note>non-evaporating</note> and in no way joins itself to anything other than its own nature, and moistens nothing else except that which belongs to the union of its own proper nature. For there is no other **vinegar** <note>original: "acetum" — the acidic solvent used to break down the metals</note> than ours, no other colors, no other regimen, and no other operations.

## SCOTUS.
<note>Likely Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232), a medieval scholar and translator associated with alchemy and the court of Frederick II.</note>

Coagulated **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term> and sulfurous quicksilver are the **first matter** of metals.

## CERTAIN COLLECTIONS FROM ANCIENT WRITERS.

It is most certain that no foreign thing can perfect imperfect metals, or effect any transformation from them. For this reason, it is the opinion of foolish men that animals and vegetables can accomplish anything in this art, since minerals are found to be closely related to metals. Yet it is to be believed that the Philosophers applied this art to those things only through **analogy** <note>original: "similitudinem" — meaning they used biological terms like "milk" or "blood" as metaphors for chemical processes</note>. For from two things only—namely, **sulfur** and **quicksilver**—are any metals born, and not from others. Nothing even adheres to them, nor transforms them, except that which took its origin from them. It is clear, therefore, that only the two things mentioned are necessary for constructing the **stone**. 

However, no metal can be generated from one of them in isolation; rather, through the conjunction of both, prepared in different ways, different metals are generated. This, however, is the greatest secret of all: from which mineral substance it ought to be more closely produced. If from vegetables, it would be necessary for sulfur and quicksilver to first be made from them by art, which would be impossible; we are therefore excused from using those, because nature prepares those two for us. But if we choose quicksilver and sulfur in their own nature, just as they were created naturally, it would be necessary to join them in a **proportion** that all human wit is ignorant of. We are therefore also excused from these, especially since we have **bodies** <note>solid metals like gold and silver</note> in which they are found already proportioned by nature in the required manner: in which the whole secret lies hidden. **Gold** is a perfect masculine body, and **silver** is also perfect; if these, by melting alone or by mixing with other imperfect things, could perfect them, they would be **elixirs**,

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

...one for the white, the other for the red, but they are not of that kind, because they are simply perfected by nature. If, however, they were ten or a hundred times more than perfect, they would perfect imperfect things by that much. But because nature simply works a simple perfection in them, they remain in that state forever, unless perhaps by art they were reduced to the first nature of sulfur and quicksilver <term>quicksilver: historically known as *argentum vivum* or mercury, considered one of the two primary principles of all metals</term>. Since, therefore, perfect natural bodies <note>referring to gold and silver</note> consist of the cleanest quicksilver and a similar sulfur, why would we not choose them as our matter for the white and red elixir? The answer: Because these bodies are so compact and strongly united that we hardly find a fire capable of acting upon them, nor upon their spirits. And although we are not ignorant of fire, we could not reach their innermost purification through it because of their incredibly strong natural composition.

For this reason, we are also excused from choosing those two bodies <note>gold and silver</note>, since we can find other bodies in which clean and similar quicksilver is held, upon which nature has worked only a little. Thus, by our artificial fire, we are able to arrive at their appropriate purification, separation, and fixation through the ingenious decoction <term>decoction: a process of heating or "cooking" a substance to extract its essence or mature it, imitating the heat of the earth</term> of our work continued upon them. Therefore, a matter must be chosen in which clean, pure, clear, white quicksilver is found, not yet brought to completion, but mixed equally and proportionally, and united with such a white or red sulfur. By our natural ingenuity and our artificial fire, we may then reach their innermost purification and complete purity; once this work is finished, they will be a thousand times more perfect and stronger than those bodies in which nature has simply worked.

From these things which have been said—provided you are ingenious—you will taste this delightful nectar upon which the intention of the Philosophers is founded. Since it is necessary to make the matter manifested above more than perfect through our artificial labor, the method must not be ignored, but rather learned from nature. Nature perfects these metals through frequent and continuous operation, using only the instrument of heat which exists within the mountains of minerals, so that the thickness of the water is cooked down and thickened for so long until, in its own course of time or cycle, it passes into quicksilver. Likewise, sulfur is generated from the fatness of the earth through that same continuous decoction and heat. By this same continuous heat acting upon these two joined together, perfect or imperfect metals are generated according to their purity or impurity. What madness holds the minds of those working in this art, that they wish to proceed by a path other than nature herself: attempting to refute or overcome her, whom they can hardly imitate with any industry. God demonstrates the right way to us through her—namely, a simple and continuous decoction made by a slow fire. And although we always speak of a slow fire,

...nevertheless, in the governance of this work, it <note>the heat or the intensity of the process</note> must be gradually increased. Therefore, there is one stone, one matter, and one medicine, in which the whole mastery <term>mastery: the "magisterium" or the complete alchemical process to produce the Stone</term> consists; to this we add no foreign thing, nor do we take anything away from it, but in the preparation we remove what is superfluous. This occurs during the purification, which is completed through dissolution.

When we wish to perform our sublimation <term>sublimation: here referring to the purification of a substance by vaporizing it and letting it collect again as a solid</term> of the stone, we place it with its entire substance in our vessel, whose opening we seal firmly so it cannot breathe, and we place it in the furnace among the ashes. Finally, we stir the fire until the whole matter is dissolved into Mercurial water. Afterwards, guide it with a gentle fire, and do so until the greater part is turned into a black powder. In this manner, all the following operations are completed: namely Solution, Distillation, Descent, Washing, and Calcination <term>calcination: the reduction of a substance to a powder by heat</term>. The Philosophers wrote a specific chapter on each of these to hide the art. 

For when our stone is in our vessel and our matter feels our "sun" <note>the heat of the furnace</note>, it is soon resolved into water, which ascends to "heaven"—that is, to the top of the vessel—and afterwards descends to the "earth," or the bottom. Also, seeing such water thicken and turn into black earth—which at first stood thick upon the water—and by allowing it to thicken gradually, they saw the earth sink under the water and reside at the bottom of the vessel, black and dreggy; they said this was the operation of putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the "death" of the matter, where it decomposes and turns black before its rebirth</term>. 

Seeing also the earth become saffron-colored, then blackish and dreggy, standing under the water for a long time, and losing its black color and foul stench in our "sun," some of them called this operation Washing, or Waxing <term>waxing: also known as "ceration," the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>. Of this, *Morienus* says: <note>original: "Scitote totum hoc magisterium nihil aliud esse..."</note> "Know that this entire mastery is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the reduction of that same water back into the earth, until the earth itself rots through its own water and is purified; and after it has been purified with the help of the divinity, the whole mastery will be directed." The Philosopher says that the earth is waxed and soaked by the water, and dried by the temperate "cooking" of the sun, and the entire matter is turned into earth, if one knows how to perform the operation perfectly. 

For *Hermes* says: <note>original: "Vis ejus integra est, si versa fuerit in terram."</note> "Its power is complete if it be turned into earth." Seeing, therefore, the whole matter turned into earth and reduced into a solid substance which did not flow but stood constrained within itself, they said it was a perfect congealing. Hence *Plato* says: "Dissolve our stone, and afterwards congeal it"—that is, turn it into earth with great care—"and thus you shall have the whole mastery." This is nothing other than performing a correct dissolution and a perfect congealing, as all the Philosophers say. Therefore, for metals to be transformed, it is necessary that they be reduced to their first matter closest to the metallic kind—that is, into a flowing gum. Then at last, such a first matter, by its innate fitness, by its powers—

...and with these factors disposing it, the matter easily receives the true form of that metal which is intended philosophically: namely, through the nature of a **fixed ferment**, to which the aforementioned matter adheres inseparably in its depths. Furthermore, it flows, which crude common **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum* or mercury</term> does not do. 

However, those who—before this reduction into the **first matter** <term>first matter: *materia prima*, the primal, undifferentiated substance from which all things originate</term>—attempt to whiten or yellow the metal while the form of the previous metal remains in the matter (not vaporously joined and not inseparably mixed into a "gum" with the matter of the fixed ferment) are deceivers. They are such because they produce neither true gold nor true silver. Therefore, for any body to be changed into another form, it is necessary that it be reduced to the first matter, since transmutation is only possible by reason of the matter itself. As Aristotle says in the fourth book of *Meteorology*, in *On Generation and Corruption*, and in the *Physics*:

> Every possible body, through operations contrary to its nature, is reduced to its first matter—namely, through the corruption of its form. For every contrary operation is its corruption, and corruption is the generation of first matter. <note>original: *Omne corpus possibile, per operationes suæ naturæ contrarias reducitur ad suam materiam primam...*</note>

Demetrius, demonstrating the method of purification or "putrefaction" of both—that is, of the body and the spirit—before their perfect mixture, says:

> Never is perfection obtained from that [the spirit], until by a perfect mixture it has led its body—which is its brother—to spirituality with itself, so that both are made one, joined without separation forever. <note>original: *Nunquam autem ex illo, scilicet spiritu, habetur perfectio...*</note>

The mastery of dissolution, therefore, prepares the matter of the stone so that it can be divided by itself into the **four elements** <term>four elements: the classical building blocks of earth, air, fire, and water</term> from which it was first composed. Otherwise, the elements would persist in their own kind unless they were mixed vaporously; neither a proportioned composition nor the proper weight would be introduced as is required, nor would perfection be achieved, which is the ultimate means of "impression" and retention. 

In this manner, the perfected stone purifies and heals man of every sickness, so that he is renewed as if by a mother. For it excites motion in bodies and gives life to the elements; indeed, the elements are "enlivened" when they are stirred into their proper action. For natural life is nothing other than the action of the elements, after which the stone does not suffer dissipation or separation because of its indivisible composition. From this, it possesses the power to delay old age through the life it infuses into the human body—not unlike its effect on metals—increasing one's years through the grace of God beyond one's own native proportion; through the action naturally received, it produces life. 

Nevertheless, effects of this kind cannot be attributed to any of the elements alone, but only to the **virtue of heaven** <term>virtue of heaven: *virtus caeli*, the celestial or astrological influence believed to give the Stone its miraculous powers</term> which is within the stone itself. It is by this heavenly virtue that the stone is brought to its specific form. Although the property comes to the stone naturally from celestial impression, that which disposes the stone to receive such an impression can be the "latitude" of the mixture or the "complexion" <note>complexion: the specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance</note> which suits the species. Therefore, the whole life of the stone and the whole mastery consists in vapo- <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "re con-" suggests "vaporous" or "re-congealing."</note>

...consists in the matter, and in the refining <note>original: *subtiliatione*</note> of its water by breathing into the air. Thus the universal cause of conjunction is separation after putrefaction and the proper thinning of the body with the spirit, because once united in this way, they are properly joined. Separation after putrefaction is nothing other than the reduction of a thing from its changed nature back to the same [original nature]. This is done by that very separation which causes it to rise again from the dead; and then, because of the uniformity of their natures, they are joined together and will be glued with a strong adherence. 

And this is the specific form of our dissolution: and this is the way in which the womb of nature is revealed, by lifting her garment <note>The "lifting of the garment" is a common alchemical metaphor for removing the outer, "corrupt" layers of matter to reveal the pure essence within.</note> and manifesting what lies hidden beneath it. One must take care, however, that her garment is not lifted beyond the midpoint, so that the moisture may work upon the lesser dryness, and that which has been raised may be impressed, and the whiteness of the elevated smoke may be hidden again in the innermost caverns of things; thus the moist is joined with the restraint of the earthy dry, coagulated, and held.

And then finally, at that step, occurs the **conjunction of body and soul**, a commingling, or rather a union that is never separated.

Aristotle says that quicksilver is the element of all things that can be melted; for when they are melted, they are converted into it. It is clear, therefore, that the operation of this medicine is an operation of nature, because it is composed of nature alone. For it is most certain that everything is composed of those things into which it is resolved, just as frost or ice is resolved into water by heat, because it was previously frozen from water by cold. In the same way, our stone is resolved into quicksilver through our mastery; therefore, it was previously quicksilver. First...

[Therefore, the first] word is this: the reduction of the body into **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*, the liquid state of metals</term>, and this they have called "solution," which is the foundation of the art. Rosinus <note>Rosinus is a name frequently used in medieval Latin alchemy to refer to the 3rd-century Greek-Egyptian alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> the philosopher says: "Dissolve the bodies and the spirits, and unite them; then, from that point on, they cannot be separated by fire." Hermes <note>original: *Hermes*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "The first dissolved body, and the perennial water, congeals Mercury with a perpetual congelation," which is what all the Philosophers also say. 

He who has ears to hear, let him hear: All molten metals behave like Mercury, and if they could remain in that molten state when cold, they would be Mercury itself. It must be considered that the "moist" metals, such as **Saturn** <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for Lead</term> and **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter: the alchemical name for Tin</term>, are easily reduced into their primitive Mercury. And Mercury, when duly prepared, devours every body and reduces it into itself. For heat acting upon the "moist" produces **blackness** <term>blackness: *nigredo*, the first stage of the Great Work</term> first; acting upon the "dry" it produces **whiteness** <term>whiteness: *albedo*, the second stage</term>; and it works within the white to produce **yellowness** <term>yellowness: *citrinitas*</term> and **redness** <term>redness: *rubedo*, the final stage</term>. This can be seen in lead by **calcining** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances and reduce it to powder</term> it: first it is burned into a black ash, then into white, and finally into yellow and red. 

Therefore, the true beginning of our work is the dissolution of the stone, because dissolved bodies are reduced into the nature of the spirit—except that they are more "fixed" <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means a substance can withstand heat without evaporating, as opposed to "volatile."</note> than the spirit. Likewise: The solution of the body happens alongside the congelation of the spirit, and conversely, the congelation of the spirit happens alongside the solution of the body. Then at last the body is mixed with the spirits and becomes one with them, so that they are never separated, any more than water mixed with water, because then all things are together reduced to their own homogeneity. 

For this reason Aristotle said: "The bodies of metals cannot be transmuted unless they are first reduced into their first matter." If that happens, they easily take on another form, which is not opposed to reason. But a transition from one extreme to another does not happen except through a middle state. **Sulphur** and **quicksilver** are the extremes of all metals; therefore, metals will be the middle ground between sulphur and quicksilver. Consider, therefore, if you can digest the pure substance of quicksilver without burning it; if not, your work is in vain. 

Thus, the craftsman must use considerations, the certainty of which is handed down in other disciplines that he takes for granted. And so that his study may be directed toward the goal of experiment, he must labor and busy himself especially with two things: first, that he diligently investigate the elemental essence <note>original: *quidditate*</note> and proportion of the thing to be treated or sublimated; second, that he take account of the "curing" thing—that is, the principal agent and transmuter. # NICOLAI FLAMELLI

...the nature of the principal agent is so strong in its own essence and fortified in its own manner, that by its own natural office it is powerful enough to digest and convert the matter into gold. This nature must be disposed to that end through **refinement** <term>refinement: *subtiliationem*, the process of making a substance more subtle or pure</term> and **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of turning a solid into vapor and back again to purify it</term>. In this way, through virtues acquired by the Art, it may approach the qualities of its agent and of gold. Through these means, the principal **yellowing agent** <term>yellowing agent: *citrinans*, the substance that produces the yellow or gold color in the work</term> may, by its sharpness, convert the matter into the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone: *lapidem Philosophorum*, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term> and into gold itself. 

Therefore, let the natural craftsman examine his own intellect so that, through the condition of the aforementioned nature—which he might have previously ignored—he may find it. For we do not pass down this "disposition" to ourselves or to our children who might understand it—that is, the certain and necessary method of working—nor the method of fortifying nature and investigating its causes. Thus, the skill of this work would be impossible to discover unless the craftsman's intellect is first truly informed by nature through his own experiences. Through these experiences, nature demonstrates how she may be known, revealing the disposition by which she is perfected, and teaching the craftsman how to find the measure of her approach to perfection.

The specific work, therefore, requires its own specific disposition, since it belongs to nature itself, which informs its own **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*, or mercury</term> and works upon its contrary qualities: namely, heat combined with its tempered dryness, acting against coldness and moisture. It does this by removing what is superfluous and adding or supplying what is absent and required, so that the matter must necessarily receive the form of the completed medicine. 

Nature does not move in this way unless she is aided by Art—specifically by artificial operation and a disposition proper to her, without which nothing is accomplished. When you have found that disposition, hide it under the "cloak of philosophy," just as your predecessors did. They commanded that it be most strictly concealed, as it is the secret and mystery of this entire Art, which has not yet been revealed in writing by any philosopher. 

It must be understood that when they say, "Dissolve the bodies into water" <note>original: *Solvite corpora in aquam*</note>, they do not mean or care for waters that stick to the touch or make things wet. Instead, they mean a **permanent water**, which does not stick to the touch but runs over the surface without wetting anything—just as our quicksilver is not common quicksilver. For this matter desires nothing else to be added to it except that which comes from itself; indeed, it contains within itself everything it needs. This is said of our Stone, and not of gold or common mercury. 

Some people wrongly distill **corrosive waters** <term>corrosive waters: *aquas corrosivas*, likely strong acids like nitric or sulfuric acid</term> from lesser minerals. They place various metals into these, which corrodes them, and they believe this to be a "natural dissolution." This is false. A true **philosophical solution** <term>philosophical solution: *solutio philosophica*, a transformation that preserves the "life" of the metal rather than destroying it</term> requires the simultaneous permanence of both the solvent and the dissolved body; for new species result from the union of the **male and the female**. It is certain beyond doubt that no water can dissolve a metallic species through natural reduction, except that water which remains with them in both matter and form, and which the metals...

### ANNOTATIONS

Things that have been dissolved can freeze or solidify again; this does not happen in "strong waters" <note>original: *aquis fortibus*, typically referring to corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid</note>. Therefore, no water dissolves bodies except that which is of its own species, and through which those bodies were able to be thickened. Nor are bodies nourished by any other thing during their generation except by a similar species. Thus, the solvent differs from the thing being dissolved only by its proportion and its degree of **digestion** <term>digestion: a process of slow, consistent heating used to mature a substance</term>, but the two do not differ in their basic matter. This is because nature, through any mixture, forms one thing from another—just as nature simply produces **Gold** <note>original: *Solem*, "the Sun"</note> from **mercury** <note>original: *argento vivo*, "living silver" or quicksilver</note> in the mineral world.

Whoever has learned the art of dissolving has already reached the secret, which is to mix species and to extract from natures the effective powers that lie hidden within them. If anyone, therefore, knows how to join and unite our **sulphur** <term>sulphur: in alchemy, the active, combustible principle of a substance</term> with bodies, he has found one of the greatest secrets of nature. It is as if he said: if someone were to process a body so that it becomes a "gum" capable of being mixed with other imperfect bodies, he would have found nature’s greatest secret, etc. This is because this perfected stone is a gum and a sulphur—namely, as was said, derived from those bodies.

These are called the **sulphurous bodies of the earth**. Through the **refinement** <term>refinement: *subtiliatione*, the process of making a substance more subtle or pure</term> present in the water, the dissolution brings the stone from potential into actual reality, because it makes it entirely subtle. The joining of spirits with the body occurs when bodies are **sublimated** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then a solid again to purify it</term>, just as spirits are joined through their dissolution, grinding, and roasting with other spirits.

The Philosophers say that the "water of Mercury" is the aforementioned stone liquefied with its own proper water, which is fixed within the stone itself, and which is then flowing and white like water. Likewise, the **airy humidity** found in mercury is one and the same thing as the aforementioned earth and the other elements existing in that earth. Although this humidity is small, it is nevertheless sufficient to nourish and perfect the Stone in which it resides.

**Gold and Silver** <note>original: *sol & luna*, "the Sun and the Moon"</note> are present in this composition. And yet, it is not common gold or silver, but something better than their ordinary nature; they are present there potentially, not visibly. This stone or composite is only one single thing and of one nature (as all Philosophers say), and it is a pure and clear nature from its own minerals, which transforms the rule of fire.

Likewise, our **medicine** <note>the alchemical agent of transformation</note> is drawn from metals, which naturally transmute metals, and in no other way. For it is necessary that the **elixir** of the Philosophers be made from the Principle, the root, and the nature of metals, and that the medicine be more noble and precious than the metals themselves, etc. From this, it is clear that when Philosophers speak of mercury and other dissolving humidities, they do not mean common substances given simply by nature. Instead, they mean only the mercury separated from bodies through the artifice of **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the chemical "rotting" or breakdown of a substance to release its essence</term>. This is otherwise called **Azot** <note>a mystical name for the universal solvent or the mercury of the philosophers</note>; interpreted in Latin as "a powerful alum" capable of illuminating and clarifying every body with its own brightness. Since, therefore, such mercury—or Azot, or the **water of life** washing the **latten** <term>latten: *latonem*, a term for the impure metal or "body" that must be cleansed</term>—cannot be extracted from bodies through generation except after putrefaction...

<header>THE WORKS OF NICOLAS FLAMEL</header>

...there will be no end; therefore, its **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the stage of the Great Work where the matter turns black and "dies," allowing for its eventual purification and rebirth</term> is its generation and arrangement. The birth of mixed things and vegetables is varied and distinctive. For those things are called "simply mixed" which are born beneath the earth or near its surface beyond our sight, arising solely from the mingling of the elements with one another. The levels of such primary and simple natural mixing are multiple. The first is the bare composition of the four elements, in which no change or alteration of one element into another has occurred. The second follows the first, because once the aforementioned stones—namely, the elements—are resolved, the **minerals** about which we now speak are generated. From these, more noble subterranean species proceed, because their action and **transmutation** <term>transmutation: the transformation of one substance or metal into another, specifically into gold or silver</term> begins at this point. To join them, the Philosophers commanded that, once all external things are removed, only heat should be applied. This heat, by helping, stirs the internal natural heat of the gold to digest and actively ripen the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note>. Therefore, since seeds or "sperm" of this kind cannot be generated by art—because art does not know how to compose a mixture proportionally to produce seeds, neither in man nor in the earth where their proper place of natural generation lies—these seeds, made by nature, are joined together artificially. In this proportional action of nature and the **digestion** of the Mercury, the masculine and feminine natures remain closed up together: the feminine as earth and water, and the masculine as air and fire. The Philosophers have said that this earth and water are as Mercury, while the air and fire are as **Sulphur** <note>original: *sulphur*, the active principle</note> in our Stone. Aside from these two, nothing else enters, nor generates, nor multiplies, as is clear from what has been said. And this dissolution is called only a liquefaction of the compound, and not properly its solution, because the parts are not dissolved into things separable from one another. When the compound is dissolved in the aforementioned way, with the parts remaining inseparable (though they are separable in potential), so that the power of the digestive elements can be extracted from the things to be dissolved through the processes of dissolution—namely, the **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>—the coarse parts in such a dissolution take on the breadth of subtlety, because the body is turned into spirit, and vice versa.

For your whole ornament is skillfully declared by an overflowing number, reaching through the boundary of that number into a unity similar to divinity. If, therefore, you irrigate the dry vapor with the moist vapor, you will achieve the divine work. For let it be known that all substances and metals exist and are made as vapors; for when irrigated, vapors become moist.

The **Scythian comaris** <note>original: *Scythica comaris*; a plant or substance mentioned by the Greek alchemist Zosimos, possibly related to the arbutus or a specific dye-agent.</note> also, when mixed with new vapor, perfects all things.

# ANNOTATIONS

There is a difference between wordy alchemy, which is contained in a multitude of words, and that which is secret, hidden, or mystical. For this latter kind proceeds only by the reason of creation, so that man—looking toward God and being created by God—may learn the correct operation through theological and mystical discourses. This operation is primarily celestial, because it consists of celestial materials and forms.

The method of mystical alchemy is found in the patterns of the heavens, by whose rule these things are guided. Thus, even metallic bodies, once transmuted from their contrary nature, become level and airy.

Therefore, the seed sown in the "earth of the moon" <note>original: *terra lunæ*; in alchemy, this usually refers to purified silver or the "white" stage of the work.</note> also perfects the sun <note>original: *solem*; the traditional symbol for gold.</note>, and because of the divine operation, ash and **cadmia** <term>cadmia: An oxide of zinc or mineral ore found in smelting furnaces, used here as a transformative agent.</term> are preeminent. Likewise, the divine work and the pure **divine water** <note>original: *aqua divina*; the universal alchemical solvent.</note> with its own ash contribute toward regeneration. Listen to Mercury saying:

> If you see all things turned to ash, consider that all things have been rightly prepared.

For ash has great power and works much. Just as wood converted into ash becomes henceforth incombustible, yet is used in various wonderful works of glass and other things; so also metals, converted into ash—or rather into **calx** <term>calx: A powder produced by roasting or "calcining" a metal; the chemical "ashes" of a substance.</term>—return again into a certain virtue and operation. For their nature imitates the universal world and the elements themselves, from which they are generated anew; they possess a participation in a certain spirit, just as things which are made of material spirit. Thus our bronze—or if you prefer to understand it as the body of **magnesia** <term>magnesia: The "prime matter" or "chaos" containing the potential for the philosopher's stone.</term>—has a soul and spirit just as a man does. For these fusible bodies and metals, after they have been turned to ash, resume their spirit while existing in the fire, as the fire supplies this to them, and which they breathe in from the air that creates all these things. In the same way, humans and all living things take their vital spirit and soul from the air. 

Therefore, our burnt bronze is turned into a dry soot; being roasted further and enduring all things, it becomes a stone of an **ethereal** <note>original: *æthesius*; likely derived from the Greek for "fiery" or "burning," referring to a stone that flashes with light.</note> color, like a certain gleaming ether. After it is roasted, it is extinguished in a divine manner—which they call **divine water**—so that it receives the consistency of dissolved oil and the thickness of wine. Remaining there for forty days under gentle heat in a vessel that does not allow vapors to escape, the matter is afterward putrefied. The pure mystery of the divine water then perfects that which is sought: and this is the stone which performs these things. 

Note therefore: All things are one, through which all things exist. It begins indeed from unity or union, and terminates the fulfillment in the unity of the thing sought. For though there are many things in the nature of reality, there is said to be one most divine water—one nature overcoming all things—not in appearance, but by art, involving a rational science hidden from many. O celestial natures, creators of natures! By these words, an incorporeal nature is hinted at. ...which is completed through cloud and soot: once reasonably governed, it calls forth the powerful nature lying hidden within, which colors every body, whitens Venus <note>original: *Venerem dealbantem*; "whitening Venus" refers to the alchemical process of transmuting copper (associated with the planet Venus) into a silver-like metal.</note>, and removes the shriek from Jupiter <note>original: *Jovi stridorem auferentem*; Jupiter represents the metal tin. Sulphurous things are contained by sulphurous things—that is, the celestial and fiery elements are contained by the earthly ones, from which they can be obtained.

**The first key of the work** is that the fire of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*, or liquid mercury.</term>—namely Mercury—should be joined with the water of earthly magnesia <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" was not our modern magnesium, but a general term for various mineral ores or the "primitive matter" of the stone.</note> through its own earth. In this way, the separation of the moist from the dry occurs—that is, the souls of the air are separated from the bodies.

**The second key** is when the moon and water are joined with the fire of the aforementioned quicksilver, through the air of copper <note>original: *aerem aeris*; likely referring to the volatile "spirit" or vapor of the metal.</note> in the rising of the cloud; this is the reduction of cold things with moist ones, and the mixing of higher things with lower. The earth—that is, the dross <note>original: *scoria*</note> of copper—is joined with the solar air through fire (that is, through quicksilver).

**The third key** is when, through the roasting of putrefaction, the dross is joined with the divine water through fire. This occurs through the moon; the air of the sun is also joined with the earth (the dross) through water (the moisture).

**The fourth key** indeed occurs by the conjunction of air with earth—specifically, earth dissolved through putrefaction and the roasting of seven reductions—all forced into one water and existing in **philosophical cinnabar** <note>original: *cinabari philosophica*; a symbolic substance representing the perfect union of mercury and sulfur, often appearing as a deep red powder.</note>, which consists of the aforementioned Mercury and the sulfur of magnesia. Once these things are completed in this manner, the fire becomes hot and dry again, generating the heat of air and the dryness of earth. Similarly, when the water becomes moist and cold, it generates the moisture of air and the coldness of earth. When the earth becomes cold and dry, it generates the coldness of water and the dryness of fire. And when the air becomes hot and moist, it generates the heat of fire and the moisture of water. Since each thing has two qualities, they become an element consisting of three elements. All collected together, they become twelve, produced from three into four, according to the twelve signs and the four seasons: like the airy Spring, the fiery Summer, the watery Autumn, and the earthy Winter. This is the true composition of elements through the art. Likewise, the seven colors appearing in the work are called the bodies of the seven planets of that same composition; they are present now, but later they depart from the signs of the work, just as in the heavens they enter their signs and afterward exit. Thus, through its seven stars (which are called planets) and through its twelve fixed signs, the true mystery of the Philosophers is perfected.

The colors of the elements in the work are: from the feet up to the knees, the black earthly element; from the knees up to the navel, the shining and white watery element; from the navel to the heart, the yellow or citron-colored airy element; and from the heart to the neck, the glowing and red fiery element.

Next, when these four elements have been mixed among themselves, there is made from them the **lime and ash of the Philosophers** <note>original: *calx & cinis Philosophorum*; "lime" refers to a powder produced by heating a substance until it is friable, a process called calcination.</note>, so that they are perfectly and entirely joined through the final union, whitened, with the blackness having been cast off altogether. Therefore, this sacred and divine art and science of the Philosophers consists of and is perfected by one species, divinely and magnificently, in this way: for if you make the bodies incorporeal and the incorporeal bodies <note>This is a famous alchemical maxim: "making the fixed volatile and the volatile fixed," or turning solids into vapors and vapors back into solids.</note>, you will work miraculously and you will be the master of your wish, through the composition of the four elements; through the triple regimen; the twelve-fold mutation of the signs <note>Referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac, often corresponding to twelve stages of the alchemical process.</note>; through the aspects, species, and bodies of the seven stars; and through a certain singular, ultimate, monadic union, you will glorify the Son of God, the eternal word, in trinity and unity, who perfected this lower world from four elements, and adorned it with the four mutations of the cycles of the year, and after seven ages will introduce those who are called and chosen into eternal rest, praising the unique and unfailing light in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

There are, therefore, two things which consist of matter, since the number two signifies matter. By their conjunction, through the mediation of a third, they become the causes of all things. Inasmuch as through the number three the number two—and every number—is reduced to the simplicity of unity. Vapor, which is carried upward, is the matter of air; and smoke, or the smoky exhalation of dry things, is the matter of fire. These two do not agree with the remaining two—namely, water and earth—except through a third: that is, a bond and a fiery nature. These three things, therefore, by the said triple regimen, constitute the nine-fold, which is closest to the second unity, namely, the triple. Wherefore, in a certain **Sibylline riddle** <note>The Sibylline Oracles were ancient collections of prophecies; alchemists often hid secrets in these types of riddles.</note>, this mystery is noted in this manner:

> I have three times three letters, I am four-syllabled, consider me. Each of the first three syllables has two letters, but the remaining one has the rest; five are silent <note>original: *mutæ quinque*; referring to consonants.</note>. Of the total number, there are two hundreds, eight, and three times three decades with seven. He who understands who I am will not be unrefined or ignorant of that wisdom which is in me.

Otherwise: The hundreds of the total number are twice eight, and three times three, and four decades. Furthermore: The principles of science are sense and experience; the latter is the principle of active thought, while the former provides the thought of the appearing thing, from which follows the understanding of the soul of the world and of this prudence. For since it is exempt from all things, it completes the sensible world. Therefore, let three triples be considered from it to create the orders of immaterial substances.

Since there are also three things which pertain to the universal operation, from which a four-fold composition is afterwards made. Concerning our **Molybdocalchus** <term>Molybdocalchus: from the Greek *molybdos* (lead) and *chalkos* (copper or bronze); a specific alloy used in ancient and Hermetic chemistry.</term> (our lead), he says: Inject Mercury until it becomes incorruptible and permanent; when this happens, it will no longer be lead. All these are one, and the two tinctures differ in no color,

Venus, therefore, does not dye, but is dyed. For the earthy part of the matter, being coarse, does not dye, but that thin quality of the substance produces the tincture in the body. In this work, nothing is produced or perfected without it. Divine water <note>original: *divina aqua*; likely referring to a specialized alchemical solvent or "mercurial water"</note> is that which creates a simple, most lucid, and most pure nature, free from the shadow of bodies. It acts as if it were walling in the bodies and cleansing them; it is that which extracts the hidden nature from within the bodies. For when the form of nature is joined to it, it effects and operates a most beautiful work through nature itself. The "sharp water" is said to be raised up and called forth. For those things which hide within and are extracted are divine. Therefore, divine things are retained by divine things. Souls and spirits are extracted from divine things, and are held by those same things, penetrating the bodies by their quality. For this is the truth: **Nature delights in nature, nature embraces nature, and nature overcomes nature.** <note>This is a famous alchemical axiom often attributed to the ancient philosopher Pseudo-Democritus, expressing the internal sympathy between substances.</note> For when that which hides within is well-managed and purified by the divine water, it delights itself by penetrating, overcoming, and remaining within the body’s own nature. Thus, recognizing its own nature, it rejoices in a connected and joined change of state.

But to return to the matter: Four bodies are tinted <note>original: *tinguntur*; to be colored or chemically transformed</note>, but they do not tint other things. For whitened Magnesia <term>Magnesia: here referring to the "first matter" or a specific white stage of the process, rather than the modern element magnesium</term> does not allow the bodies to be broken, nor the "shadow of Venus" <note>Venus represents the metal copper; its "shadow" refers to its impurities or its green/dark oxidation.</note> to be introduced. But see what the Philosopher says: that four bodies are tinted and do not tint, nor does he say as before, "and when they are tinted, they tint." Understand the substance of solid bodies in this way: he says "whitened Magnesia," etc. What is this Magnesia but the whole composite substance? How then is it whitened? When it is rightly governed and roasted, and when it is purified with the divine thing, it brings back the hidden things of all solid bodies from the deep, so that the nature of the bodies may be tinted through them. For the composite, being irrigated by the divine water, does not allow the bodies to be broken; rather, the "scum of Magnesia" <note>original: *argenti spuma magnesiæ*; literally "silver froth," often referring to litharge or an oxide layer</note> mixed in takes away their shadow, whitens the body, and others of the same kind.

Look upon the beautiful and wonderful things of Magnesia—how through one thing it brings in a multitude. Some things come from unity <note>The Monad</note>; some from duality; some from the ternary <note>The number three</note>, and it even extends to more, until the whole of it is preserved. Some come from the Monad—namely, the fiery medicine <term>pharmacum: a medicinal tincture or the Elixir</term>; some from duality, as with the body of Magnesia itself; some from the ternary, namely the purification with divine water. And if it intends anything further, it brings back the roasting through others, until the entire sought-after work is kept cleansed, and the absolute work is perfected and completed.

For the material suited for making gold is Mercury itself. Mercury from cinnabar <note>original: *cinabari*; a bright red mineral (mercury sulfide)</note>, he says, comes sometimes from Venus, sometimes truly from B. <note>The letter B here likely refers to a specific chemical vessel or a shorthand for another substance, possibly Bismuth.</note> Mercury from cinnabar is Magnesia; Mercury from B. is the divine water, which is extracted from a contracted instrument <note>likely a retort or still</note>, and these are the things that change the matter. Venus, like a human, has a soul and a body. It is necessary, therefore, to strip the matter of its body, so that while the tinting spirit remains, it may be suited to the perfection of whatever is sought. What is Venus? Like a human, she is a material body. The soul is the subtle part within her, which comes forth into the light through the process of "governing" <note>regimen: the controlled application of heat</note>; that is, the spirit having the power to tint. But the body is...

...heavy and material, and its earthy part which possesses a shadow, which must be stripped away by a fiery medicine <note>original: *igneo pharmaco*; referring to a purifying agent or chemical catalyst used to "burn away" impurities</note>. To "strip away" is to humble, to corrupt, to dissolve, and to mortify <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the symbolic death or breakdown of a substance so it can be reborn in a purer state</note>. Afterwards, nothing is lacking; nothing remains except the extraction of the mist and water. 

The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, common authorities in these texts</note>, using a true figure of speech, called it the "water of vitriol" <note>original: *calcanthi*; vitriol or copper sulfate, a key mineral in the creation of acids</note>: for in that place is the generation of copper. And vitriol generates gold; the "flower of copper" <note>original: *flos aeris*; likely verdigris or the subtle essence of copper</note> (says the Philosopher) is the very thing that consumes and perfects the work; it is also the male spirit. It is explained thus: Cast forth from the substance drawn from the Most High, so that the divine power, having been perfected and converted into spirit, may perform the divine work. The divine must be sought so that matter may be stripped away and become soul alone; then the spirit, seeking the heights, may take on color, and so that it may be more combative and tenacious when faced with fire, just like the "level body" <note>an analogy to geometry: a plane has no depth and can thus "penetrate" a solid</note> of spirits and those things which penetrate: for the root of a solid is the plane.

Therefore, once converted into spirit and carried upward like fire (by the logic of this doctrine), it is in a certain way assimilated into fire, and becomes more penetrating and tenacious—principles which have been discovered from the nature of the world. For just as the four elements are transmuted into one another and become what they were not—since their substance is not contrary to substance—fire becomes earth, and earth becomes water, and water becomes air, and again water becomes earth, and earth rises even to the upper regions. Having been changed and dissolved within themselves, they perform all operations, as is written in the works of Hermes: for qualities are contrary to each other, but not substances. 

So also is the chemical composition: since it is of earth, and from water comes air, and from air comes fire. Therefore, just as from the heavens (which rest upon the earth like a vaulted chamber) all these things come from exhalations; so also from the pot, as if from the earth <insert><image-desc>small ink mark or symbol</image-desc></insert>, with the alembic <note>a cap used in a still for distillation</note> placed on top like the heavens, powerful mutations occur. And just as the putrefactions of the earth, exhaling, are transmuted, so too the "flower of copper" is transmuted as it exhales. 

You shall also observe this same thing in the human head, which is placed upon the body like a small gourd vessel <note>original: *cucurbitulae*; a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> or a helmet. As it was not said in vain, "therefore grind it," so now it is not said rashly that they are cooked gradually and raised up among themselves. For by a light boiling <note>original: *elixatione*; slow boiling or decoction</note>, the hidden tinging spirit is drawn out; that which is carried upward is the spirit devoid of body, the soul of the whole composition—that is, the body. 

Just as the soul reveals itself to bodies, fermenting all things, having three effective substances within itself—motion, sense, and ignition—so this spirit, having become fiery and a soul devoid of body, penetrates the body of the thing that tints all, if it is established therein (like a plane within a solid) by the injection of its medicine into silver thinned by fire. This joyful fiery spirit (he says) leaps in—which also hides within bodies—and seeking the heights, it retains the body itself as its own soul. Furthermore, as for what pertains to the different cause of the extracted water, let this not be a cause for fear, for it is the "flower" which is extracted, not only once, but twice or three times through the *maripetas* <note>original: *maripetas*; a technical term likely referring to a specific distillation process or a specialized vessel for separating liquids</note>. ...is according to the accident; the flower is the pure water of sulfur and serves for the purpose of fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>. For the Philosopher said: even a little bit of gum colors every body. Mary <note>original: *Maria*; Mary the Prophetess, a foundational figure in alchemy credited with inventing the *bain-marie*</note> says: The bond of all things that flee from fire is the whitest alabaster of all, the "brain-stone" <note>original: *lapis encephalus*; a symbolic term for a substance residing in the "head" or uppermost part of the vessel, often associated with the white stage of the work</note>, hidden in the mind and possessing a kind of heat. Taking this, grind it and mix it with vinegar, and placing it in a small vessel, hide it afterward under dung <note>original: *sub fimo*; horse dung was used by alchemists as a source of gentle, constant heat for digestion and fermentation</note>. For this is what is sought: that the pure water of sulfur and the rust <note>original: *rubiginem*; often referring to the red oxide or the final "red" stage of the Great Work</note> are one and the same; and here truly turns the hinge upon which the entire art depends.

In these matters, it is thereafter considered that everything happens within a single composition: that which colors and that which is colored; that which flees and that which pursues; that which is familiar and that which is contrary; male and female; bridegroom and bride; the active and the passive. For there is but one serpent, which has two compositions and the rust. The "One" is the whole, for the sake of which all things exist, and "if the whole did not contain the whole, the whole would be nothing," says the great Chimes <note>likely Zosimos of Panopolis, an early alchemist often cited under various names</note>. 

For making things fixed is not the work of sulfur alone, but also of those things which have been whitened, softened, and rarefied. When substances undergo perfection and roasting <term>assation: the process of heating a substance in its own moisture until it is dry and "roasted"</term> by white sulfur, then they themselves are made into incombustible sulfur, and they remain doing that which they have endured, giving and receiving. Then, both having become sulfur, they render the substances fixed; that is, they ensure they are not destroyed by one another.

Next, he asks: why do you seek so many species of things, when one nature overcomes all? Weighing this nature from the beginning to the end, you will see the mystery clearly: this is the "cymbals" <note>original: *cymbalia*; perhaps referring to the resonance or harmony of the chemical elements</note>. O creator-natures of the celestial natures, these, once dissolved, perform all things. What then is this "to dissolve"? Come here to the liquids and learn: Take the saffron of Cilicia <note>original: *crocum Ciliciae*; likely referring to a yellow-orange chemical precipitate</note> joined together with the flower of cinicus <note>a term for a specific mineral or botanical substance</note> and the juice of the vine, and in one series of liquids, you will find the dissolution.

Come here again to the white; and likewise, the dissolution is within it, as it teaches you itself, saying: "Leave what is below, and it will happen." He spoke truly. Some have called them "bodies," others "sulfur," and they were not deceived. And because of this, error has spread throughout the world due to the multitude of names. What is said concerning the four and five elements must be referred to these. 

They placed Saturn <note>the metal Lead</note> and, opposite it, lead at the highest peak, and after it Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, the Sun <note>Gold</note>, Venus <note>Copper</note>, Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, and in the lowest place, the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Each is distinct from the others, yet they are joined to a single circle, and one serves them and governs the same. They are loved because of one spirit, and they look upon each other with their eyes, and they move with one another, and they turn one another, and they walk within their own dwellings, just as the Most High Creator established. For they are similarly found in the earth, and they are in the air, and in the water, and in the fire; they have total peace among themselves.
